III. Alternating Fast and Slow, and Evenness-and-Clearness, and the Categories of Jin

III. Alternating Fast and Slow, and Evenness-and-Clearness, and the Categories of Jin

From the above theory one can know that any isolated slow movement or isolated fast movement does not conform to the requirement of Taiji yin and yang aiding each other. Secondly, as regards man's attention,

  • ① "Inch jin": any storing and issuing of jin within a distance of one chi is called inch jin.

· 60 · in terms of stability, from the psychological and physiological basis one can see that it is impossible to make attention engage in long-term attention of equal intensity without destroying its stability. To make attention stable and the intent not scatter, one must make the intensity of attention high and low. Now Taijiquan is an intent-and-qi movement, and it requires pouring intent into the movement; therefore, in order not to let the intent scatter, the movement must alternate fast and slow, and only thus can it suit the rising-and-falling characteristic of intent and qi, impelling attention to become stable and spirit and qi to drum-and-surge. In fact, the alternation of fast and slow in movement is also a natural instinct of mankind; it is both necessary for health and indispensable for combat. Therefore, taking a single boxing form, one requires the attainment of alternation of fast and slow (as in Figure 17). Yet taking one round of the frame, this alternation of fast and slow of each boxing form further requires an even range of variation. That is to say, from the beginning of the movement to its end, when slowness is needed it is all equally slow, and when fastness is needed it is all equally fast; in Taijiquan terminology this is to achieve "evenness-and-clarity". If one can attain this requirement, then one's breathing will certainly be regulated very "evenly and clearly", and there will be no phenomenon of gradually becoming urgent. This skill of making both movement and breathing attain "evenness-and-clarity" is a concrete manifestation of being well cultivated in Taijiquan, and is the true skill obtained from long practice. Therefore when first turning from slow to fast, one must not fear urgency of breathing and so not dare to do the speeding-up movement — that would be to give up eating for fear of choking. In short, Taijiquan should be like the waves of the great Long River, surging endlessly and yet with even clarity, rising and falling in movement.

Taijiquan is composed of the eight gates and five steps. When first learning, in order to transform away the original rigid clumsy force of the body and limbs, one may temporarily not manifest the categories of jin, and may be only round without square. The reason why it is permitted in this period not to manifest the categories of jin is that one has not practised enough, one's skill is not deep, and the habit is not yet formed; it is because if at this time one were required to manifest the categories of jin, one would easily produce the fault of straining and bulging effort, and would no longer be able to produce the elastic jin of lengthening the body and limbs.

After practising for one or two years the skill of seeking softness and destroying rigidity, and when one feels the rigid jin has been wholly removed, one may then manifest the categories of jin when walking the frame. Manifesting the categories of jin is the practising · 61 · This is indispensable to Taijiquan and is also what the eight jins require — namely that the accelerating force, on reaching the landing point, must manifest:

(1) Outward there is ward-off jin, inward there is roll-back jin, double closing there is press jin;

(2) Downward there is push jin, double separating there is pluck jin, issuing out there is rend jin;

(3) When the wrist has gone out of the square-and-circle there is elbow jin, and when the elbow and arm again go out of the square-and-circle there is shoulder jin.

Only movement like this can be called a Taijiquan composed of the eight gates and five steps. For this reason, after practising the form for a certain period, when walking the frame one should fully do well this movement of alternating fast and slow. By long practice of alternating fast and slow, one can make the eight-gate jin go from nothing to having, and from having to strong, becoming eight gates and five steps in name and reality.

Book page 65

IV. The Grasping of Alternating Fast and Slow

IV. The Grasping of Alternating Fast and Slow

(1) When first learning, strive for slowness with all one's might — when first learning, in order conveniently to check and correct every movement, one must be slow, and must progressively pass through this period of seeking slowness; one must not be impatient, lest one create difficulties for later improvement.

(2) One must seek slowness under the conditions of raised spirit and nimble conversion of intent and qi — when first learning, one cannot but be slow in order to check and correct the postures. But as said above, slowness must have a limit; that is to say, one must not be so slow as to seem to move and seem to stop, with fixed eyes and dull spirit, as if there one were thinking of something else. This kind of slowness is close to the standing skill of standing the frame, and is not what is needed for moving. Therefore slowness must be sought on the premise of raised spirit and nimble conversion of intent and qi; only thus will one not produce the faults of idiocy and scattering of spirit.

(3) One must seek fastness under the conditions of steady movement and being able to manifest the categories of jin — seeking fastness, like seeking slowness, is likewise not going toward fastness without limit; it likewise must have a limit: although fast, the movement must still be steady. Steady fastness is the fastness required by Taijiquan; unsteadiness is a morbid sign. At the same time, one must seek fastness under the condition of being able to manifest the categories of jin, because manifesting the jin limits the fastness. Such fastness is beneficial and harmless · 62 · fastness — it will not float and drift without sinking, nor be indistinct in the categories of jin, nor lose the function of square and round generating each other.

(4) Slow at the conversion, quicker when turning toward the square point — the above three points explain the measure of fast and slow one should grasp in walking one round of the frame; now let us speak further of the principle of fast and slow for each boxing form. Taijiquan lays down that at the conversions and foldings and pilings one should be slow, and after passing the conversion one uses accelerating jin to move toward fastness, and carries on thus in a cycle. At the same time, within one round of the frame, this transformation of alternating fast and slow further requires attaining "evenness-and-clarity". This is the foundation for training the eight categories of jin, making them go from nothing to having and from having to strong.

In order conveniently to grasp the eighth characteristic, its essentials are summarized as follows.

(1) When first learning one must be slow, in order to have opportunity to check and correct.

(2) Seeking slowness must take raised spirit and nimble conversion of intent and qi as its premise.

(3) As proficiency increases, one should gradually shorten the time needed to walk one round of the frame. But seeking fastness must take steady movement and being able to manifest the categories of jin as its premise.

(4) The principle of alternating fast and slow is: slow at the conversions and foldings and pilings, and after passing the conversion gradually quicken, and after passing the square point slow again. At the same time, at the conversion moving the qi must be slow, and at the landing point at the end must be fast.

(5) Within the whole round of the frame, the range of variation of alternating fast and slow is required to achieve evenness-and-clarity.

Book page 66

Conclusion

Conclusion

The eight characteristics of Taijiquan are selected and refined from the Taijiquan manuals, again and again. The precious form-practising experience left by our predecessors has long since become the principles for practising Taijiquan at present, and is also the standard that people unanimously follow in practising Taijiquan.

It should further be pointed out that although the characteristics are divided into eight, their essence is one; therefore when practising the frame or pushing hands, one must not treat these characteristics in isolation, and must in every movement gradually come to conform to these characteristics. Because every boxing form or movement must use concentrated consciousness to direct the whole course of the movement (characteristic · 63 · one), making the body and limbs elastic on the premise of raised spirit (characteristic two), and, amid nimble transformation of substantial and insubstantial (characteristic four) and forward-reverse spiral reeling silk (characteristic three), bringing about the union of inner and outer, attaining the joined-segment continuity of "when one moves, nothing does not move" (characteristic five) and the accomplishment in one breath of unbroken connection (characteristic six), manifesting the quality of firmness and softness mutually aiding (characteristic seven) and the speed of having both slow and fast (characteristic eight) — these are the special features that Taijiquan should possess.

From the above analysis one can see that these characteristics are mutually dependent, mutually constraining, mutually promoting, and mutually transforming. Therefore, if one treats them in isolation and attempts to carry out only one characteristic while abandoning the others, then one not only harms the latter but also affects the former. Hence these characteristics are not peculiar to one particular movement, and still less is it that a certain movement has only a certain one characteristic; rather, they are characteristics that every boxing form constituting the entire Taijiquan routine should possess.

In the Taijiquan popular today, whatever the style, and regardless of whether the postures are extended or compact, and regardless of whether the frame has a few more or a few fewer boxing forms, one need only observe carefully: these Taijiquan frames, though differing in outward appearance, all possess these common characteristics more or less within. The only difference is that some manifest them clearly on the outside, while others conceal them within by way of hidden jin. This also explains why Taijiquan, popular for several hundred years, has not been assimilated by other martial arts and can still stand alone as a style of its own — it is these common characteristics that have served as the mainstay. Therefore when learning Taijiquan one must not treat it lightly.

But when first learning, to wish to grasp these eight characteristics all at once is impossible. When first learning, one need only recognize these characteristics, know that they are the summary of experience left by predecessors, and understand that they are the basic elements constituting Taijiquan; then it is not difficult, following the predecessors' experience and proceeding steadily along the direction they have already pointed out, to obtain the efficacy that Taijiquan should have.

A Few Notes on the Illustrations

A Few Notes on the Illustrations

1. The action-breakdown diagrams in the illustrations of the first route were drawn from photographs of the postures of fellow student Chen Zhaokui. The action-breakdown diagrams in the illustrations of the second route (Cannon Fist) were drawn from photographs of the postures of teacher Chen Fake; in addition, according to the needs of the action breakdown, some diagrams were added, drawn according to fellow student Chen Zhaokui's build.

2. To make it convenient for readers to check the directions of the boxing forms, the directions of the postures in the photographs are agreed as follows: facing the reader equals facing south, the back to the reader equals facing north, the reader's right of the facing figure equals east, and the reader's left of the facing figure equals west. After the reader has practised proficiently, he may choose any direction according to the shape of the ground, and need not necessarily begin the preparatory form standing facing south.

3. All arrows in the diagrams, whether drawn with a solid or a broken line, indicate the direction of the action of the hand or foot, and the arrows in all the diagrams indicate the direction of action passing from this diagram to the next. Where a movement is relatively simple and can be explained by the text, its direction of action is no longer shown in the diagram, and one may refer to the text and the following diagram to understand it; moreover, for a boxing form identical with some earlier form, where the action-breakdown diagrams are abbreviated from several to one or two, one may refer to the breakdown diagrams of the same earlier boxing form, and no longer show its direction of action in the abbreviated one or two diagrams.

4. Arrows drawn with a solid line indicate the direction of action of the right hand or right foot, and arrows drawn with a broken line indicate the direction of action of the left hand or left foot.

5. Because the movement of the feet in Taijiquan is also fairly fine, in order to show the feet and the ground, shadows are drawn beside the feet to distinguish them. (See the diagram below.)

· 67 · (Continuation of point 5 of the notes on the illustrations — the method of showing the shadow of the foot on the ground)

a. A shadow joined as one body beside the foot indicates that the whole foot is on the ground.

b. Where there is no shadow beside the foot, it indicates that the whole foot is off the ground.

c. Where the shadow beside the foot is joined only at the heel, it indicates that the heel is on the ground.

d. Where the shadow beside the foot is joined only at the toe, it indicates that the toe is on the ground.

Chen-Style Taijiquan, First Route

Chen-Style Taijiquan, First Route
First Form: Preparatory Form

Stand with the body upright and centred, with the two feet a little wider apart than the shoulders, the two toes turned slightly outward, the two arms hanging naturally down, and the eyes looking level ahead. (Figure 1)

Essential points:

· 68 · The preparatory form is the preparation in consciousness and in posture before beginning the movement; it requires: solidifying the spirit within and showing ease without; hollowing the crown and holding up the top jin — that is, the head must be upright and the crown must be hollowly held up, holding the top jin as if suspended; the lips lightly closed, the teeth lightly together, the chin slightly drawn in; sinking the shoulders — that is, the two shoulders slightly rolled forward and relaxed and sunk; containing the chest and drawing up the back — that is, the chest contained without being concave inward or convex outward, and the spine and back having the intention of pulling and lengthening upward and downward; the crotch must be open and have a feeling of round emptiness; the two knees slightly bent, standing without being stiffly straight, with the knee joints keeping a margin; the whole body relaxed, the breathing natural, and the intent stored in the cinnabar field.

The above essential points must be attended to at every moment, not only when doing the preparatory form but also when doing any movement in the entire set. Moreover, as said above, although each aspect has its own requirement, they also each influence one another. For example: because the shoulders are slightly rolled forward and relaxed and sunk, it is easy to achieve containing the chest and drawing up the back, solidifying the spirit within, sinking the qi to the cinnabar field, and hollowing the crown and holding up the top jin; because the knees are slightly bent, the crotch is easily opened and rounded (the crotch is the perineal part between the two excretory openings; opening the crotch means feeling that there is qi lifted up and that the skin of this part does not sag).

Preparatory Form
Second Form: Vajra Pounds the Mortar

Action one: The body slightly squats, the two elbows slightly bent, the two palms facing down (the two hands having the intent of closing strength), and the eyes looking level ahead. (Figure 2) The body turns slightly to the left; at the same time the two hands, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, are raised toward the left front diagonal to the height of the shoulders, the two palms still facing down. (Figure 3) The body turns to the right and continues to squat, with the whole weight shifted onto the right leg, and the left foot lifted; while turning the body, the two hands still with the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward open out toward the right rear, palms facing the right rear, and the fingers stretched out and not soft. (Figure 4)

图 L1F2
Vajra Pounds the Mortar (action one): the body slightly squats, the two hands close in strength, palms facing down
图 L1F3
Vajra Pounds the Mortar (action one): the body turns slightly left, the two hands raise toward the left front diagonal
图 L1F4
Vajra Pounds the Mortar (action one): the body turns right and squats, the left foot lifts, the two hands open out toward the right rear

Action two: The left foot's toe is raised, and with the inner side of the heel touching the ground one thrusts toward the left front · 69 · out, and as the centre of gravity moves forward one gradually comes to the left foot firmly planted; at the same time the two palms still with the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, open out in reeling silk toward the right rear and sink slightly, and at the same moment as the left foot is firmly planted, the two hands follow the body weight shifting forward. (Figure 5A, Figure 5B) The centre of gravity moves forward onto the left leg, and the body turns left along with it; the right foot steps forward one step and touches the ground with the toe; at the same time the two hands, from the rear forward, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, with the left hand's palm facing down and the elbow bent, press forward, and the right hand, as the right foot steps up, sweeps forward, so that the two hands form closing strength. (Figure 6)

图 L1F5甲
Vajra Pounds the Mortar (action two): the left foot thrusts toward the left front, the centre of gravity moves forward, the two hands open out in reeling silk
图 L1F5乙
Vajra Pounds the Mortar (action two): the centre of gravity moves forward onto the left leg, the two hands close in strength
图 L1F6
Vajra Pounds the Mortar (action two): the right foot steps forward one step touching the ground with the toe, the left hand with bent elbow presses forward, the right hand sweeps forward

· 70 · Action three: The right palm changes into a fist, reeling forward from outside upward, and the left palm reels forward from inside downward; at the same time the right foot is lifted and drawn back. (Figure 7) The left palm drops to in front of the abdomen, and the right fist thereupon drops into the left palm; at the same time the right foot stamps the ground beside the left foot. (Figure 8)

图 L1F7
Vajra Pounds the Mortar (action three): the right palm changes into a fist and reels forward from outside upward, the left palm reels forward from inside downward, the right foot is lifted and drawn back
图 L1F8
Vajra Pounds the Mortar (action three): the left palm drops to in front of the abdomen, the right fist drops into the left palm, the right foot stamps

Essential points:

1. Reeling-silk jin is Taiji jin, and is the core constituting Taijiquan. It is unified from two opposed basic reelings. No movement in the entire set of Taijiquan may ever depart from reeling-silk jin. Therefore reeling-silk jin runs through the whole course of every movement. Forward and reverse reeling are universally possessed by the movements of the entire set, and each movement within a boxing form has forward and reverse reeling; therefore forward and reverse reeling are the universal basic reeling. Whereas inside-outside, up-down, left-right, front-back, and large-small — these five pairs describe the points of difference in direction and size of each movement's reeling, and therefore belong to the particular directional reeling. But it does not follow that on the universal forward-and-reverse reeling there is merely a single pair of directional reelings; rather, according to the requirements of each movement, some are single, such as left-right forward-reverse, while some have both the difference of up-down and the difference of inside-outside, as in action three (Figure 7), which is just this. Concerning reeling-silk jin one may refer to the third characteristic, and in · 71 · For reeling-silk diagrams one may refer to those in the third characteristic.

2. This form is the first posture of Taijiquan's thirteen postures; in the midst of it the application of five pairs of reeling-silk jin is passed through, and the final pound (the stamping of the foot and the right fist striking down into the left palm) indicates that this boxing form is at an end.

3. The function of stamping the foot is to make the whole body's qi sink downward, and it also benefits the blood circulation. For example, when one has stood too long and feels fatigued, and circumstances do not allow one to walk about, one may touch the ground with the toes of both feet, raise the heels, and then let them drop with a slight stamp; moving thus several times likewise produces the effect of recovering from fatigue. Moreover, the force of the foot stamp may be decided according to the practitioner's age and the strength or weakness of his body; but whether light or heavy, the sinking jin must be whole. Whether the jin is whole or not may also be judged from the sound of the stamp.

4. Every movement of Taijiquan requires "sinking the shoulders and dropping the elbows". "Sinking the shoulders" has been explained in the essential points of the preparatory form; "dropping the elbows" means that in any movement the two arms must keep the elbow joint bent to a certain degree and must not be held straight, and that the tip of the elbow has the intent of dropping down.

5. The palm in Chen-style Taijiquan requires the fingers to bend backward — that is, apart from the thumb, all the remaining four fingers curve slightly toward the back of the hand (refer to the palm shapes in the various diagrams). This can make the qi pour into the spaces between the finger pads (qi reaching the two tips), and can also guard against and eliminate the fault of the arms using clumsy force.

Third Form: Lazily Tucking the Robe
图 L1F9
The set posture in which both hands, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, close their jin in a cross before the chest, changing from the left leg solid to the right leg solid.
图 L1F10
The two hands enlarge the reeling-silk circle and separate, the right upper reeling forward and the left lower reeling reverse, forming an opening jin.

Action one: The body first turns slightly left, then turns to slightly right, and thereupon turns back to centre; at the same time the two hands, in front of the lower abdomen and following the turning of the body, circle a small circle from left outward and up and to the right and down (returning again to the posture of Figure 8). Then the body again goes from slightly left-turn to slightly right-turn; at the same time the two hands, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, cross with closing strength in front of the chest; from the left leg substantial it turns to the right leg substantial. (Figure 9) The two hands enlarge the reeling-silk circle and separate, the right reeling forward upward and the left reeling reverse downward, forming opening jin; at the opening, from the right leg substantial it changes to the left leg substantial. (Figures 10–11) The whole weight shifts onto the left leg, and the right foot is lifted and then thrust out along the ground to the right with the heel; at the same time the two hands · 72 · Continue drawing the arc, turning from the great opening into the great closing of double forward reeling (Figure 12A); the centre of gravity gradually shifts right, the right toes press down firmly, the body turns slightly left, and the right hand extends slightly to the left. (Figure 12B)

图 L1F11
The set posture of the opening jin; at the opening, the right leg solid changes to the left leg solid.
图 L1F12甲
Continuing the arc, turning from the great opening into the great closing of double forward reeling.

Movement Two: The body turns slightly right, and as the centre of gravity shifts right, the right leg gradually becomes solid; at the same time the two hands go from closing to opening again — the right hand winds its arm out to the right with a large forward reeling, while the left hand, after a small reverse reeling, turns its palm over and places it before the left waist, the left palm facing up. (Figure 13) The body turns straight, the rear kua is adjusted, the whole body relaxes and opens, and the qi sinks downward. (Figure 14)

Key points:

1. When the right foot steps out, it must be exactly the moment when the right hand sinks with a leftward forward reeling, so that there is a right · 73 · of the hand sinking to the left and pressing the right foot out to the right. When the left reverse and right forward reelings have closed again, this movement fully expresses the requirement of the fifth characteristic, "when one part moves, no part is without movement."

图 L1F12乙
The transitional posture in which, after the great closing of double forward reeling, the centre of gravity shifts gradually to the right leg, the body turns slightly left, and the right hand extends slightly to the left.

2. In Chen-style Taijiquan, at the beginning of every posture the inside must lead the outside into motion; hence in outward form there is a small circle that draws along the movement that follows. For example, when Vajra Pounds the Mortar is begun from the preparatory posture, the two hands at the sides of the kua bend at the elbow and lift slightly, that is, the palms press down lightly facing downward, forming a closing jin, and only then does the movement begin; when Lazily Tucking the Robe is begun from Vajra Pounds the Mortar, the two hands make a small circle before the abdomen (as shown by the broken lines of the two hands in Figure 8). At the completion of every posture there is an adjusting movement: the last movement of Vajra Pounds the Mortar is a pound, while the last movement of Lazily Tucking the Robe is the body turning straight and the rear kua being adjusted.

图 L1F13
The set posture: the body turns slightly right, the two hands go from closing to opening again, the right hand winds its arm out to the right with a large forward reeling, and the left hand, after a small reverse reeling, turns its palm over and places it before the left waist, the left palm facing up.
图 L1F14
The set posture of the body turning straight, the rear kua adjusted, the whole body relaxed and open, and the qi sinking downward.

3. This posture fully expresses the relation of upper and lower following one another (hands with feet). Draw a · 74 · When the circle turns to the upper ward-off, the hand is insubstantial, and the foot beneath that hand becomes substantial; the reverse is also true. This too is the key to seeking the centre-correctness of inner jin (but the case of lifting one leg and standing alone is excepted: because one foot stands, in order to keep centre-correctness and balance the centre of gravity, the single standing foot is substantial, and the hand above the substantial foot must still be substantial). This is shown most clearly in Figures 10 and 11.

4. Lazily Tucking the Robe is one of the basic postures of Chen-style Taijiquan; it is formed by the left hand's small inner reverse reeling and the right hand's large outer forward reeling. It requires that there be no hollows, no defects, and no breaks in the inner jin; the small inner reverse reeling is especially difficult, and only much attention and practice will meet the requirement. In this posture one must above all take note that within the closing (when the circle is contracted) there is opening, and within the opening (when the circle is released) there is closing jin; the secret lies in adding more of the inner-and-outer reeling within the process of closing and opening, which makes this requirement easy to attain; only when this requirement is met can one "draw along the coming and going so that the qi clings to the back."

5. The two arms' ward-off turns into a closing jin: because the qi clings to the spine and the two upper arms strike one another, the ward-off jin is not lost, and there arises the wondrous use of "opening hidden within closing"; likewise, because the two upper arms strike one another, when the two arms separate and become an opening jin, there is inwardly nonetheless a closing jin, and there arises the wondrous use of "closing hidden within opening."

图 L1F15甲
The position of the two hands before the chest and abdomen when the two arms close their jin and the qi clings to the spine.
图 L1F15乙
The position of the two hands separated front and back when the two arms open their jin and the two upper arms strike one another.
Fourth Form: Six Seals and Four Closings

· 75 · Movement One: The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity shifts left, and the left leg becomes solid; at the same time the two hands, each in its own place, first wind the arm and draw a small circle (to initiate the movement): the right hand winds its arm with a large forward reeling and wards off to before the abdomen, while the left hand with a small reverse reeling wards off to before the chest, and the two hands form a closing jin; the body turns slightly right, the centre of gravity shifts right, the left hand with the side of the thumb presses close to the right ribs and rolls inward, until the palm faces left, while the right hand reels reverse and turns the palm to face downward (Figure 15A, Figure 15B). The body turns slightly right, the centre of gravity shifts right, and the right leg becomes solid; at the same time, the right hand winds its arm with a forward reeling and the left palm makes a small reverse reeling, the two hands holding their jin together and pressing out in an arc up and to the right (Figure 16).

图 L1F16
The set posture in which the body turns slightly right, the right hand winds its arm with a forward reeling and the left palm makes a small reverse reeling, and the two hands holding their jin together press out in an arc up and to the right.
图 L1F17
The transitional posture in which the two hands support upward to the right, the left hand after its reverse reeling turns the wrist joint upward, and the right fingers hang downward.

Movement Two: The body turns slightly left again, and the centre of gravity shifts back again to the left leg, which becomes solid. At the same time, the right hand reels forward and supports upward, its jin penetrating to the palm and fingers — the fingers must not be soft; the left hand reels reverse and winds its arm, and with the back of the hand at the wrist joint arcs up and to the left in ward-off, its jin penetrating to the back of the hand, the five fingers hanging slantwise downward — the fingers must not be soft. (Figures 17–18) The body continues to turn slightly left; at the same time the two hands reel forward, turn their palms over, and place them separately beside the two ears, the palms slanting outward. (Figure 19) Immediately the two palms close their jin and press down to the right (begin to exhale deeply — when the deep breath is finished, the double press has exactly reached the bottom; exhalation is the host and the accompaniment of the movement is the guest); at the same time the body follows the two hands' rightward press and turns right, and the centre of gravity shifts accordingly onto the right leg, the left foot stepping in abreast to the right and touching with its toes beside the right foot. (Figure 20)

Key points:

· 76 · 1. Whether the two hands go from closing to opening or from opening to closing, both must be led by the waist and spine as the axis (the turning of the body); when turning left and right the upper body must still stand upright, not leaning forward or backward; when the two palms press down, the qi must cling to the spine, the armpits round and empty, with the right hand as host and the left hand as guest.

图 L1F18
The transitional posture in which the two hands go from closing to opening, led by the waist-and-spine axis, and the two palms are separated up and down.
图 L1F19
The set posture in which the body turns slightly left, the two hands reel forward, turn their palms over, and are placed separately beside the two ears, the palms slanting outward.

2. The posture Six Seals and Four Closings means six parts sealing and four parts closing. Its function resembles the "Vajra shaking force" in Hua Tuo's Five Animal Frolics. When the two hands press down, one must purse the lips and slowly breathe out one deep, long breath; this greatly helps to regulate the respiratory system.

图 L1F20
The set posture in which the two palms close their jin and press down to the right (the press exactly reaches bottom when the exhalation ends), the body turns right with the two hands, and the left foot steps in abreast.
图 L1F21
The posture in which the two palms have pressed to before the abdomen and the centre of gravity has shifted onto the right leg.
Fifth Form: Single Whip

Action one: The body turns slightly right and thereupon turns back to the left; at the same time the right hand reels forward inward, and the left · 77 · The hand reels reverse and turns over one circle outward each; thereupon the right hand changes into a hook hand and is raised to the right, and the left palm arcs across to before the abdomen; while the body turns left and right, the left foot also follows, pivoting on its toes. (Figures 21–22)

Action two: Next, the whole weight shifts onto the right leg, the left foot is lifted, the body squats, and the left foot is thrust out with the left heel along the ground, insubstantially, to the left; at this moment the kua root opens wider, and as the centre of gravity shifts left, the left toes gradually come down to the ground and the left leg becomes solid. (Figures 23–24)

图 L1F22
The transitional posture in which the right hand changes into a hook hand and is raised to the right, the left palm arcs across to before the abdomen, and the left foot pivots on its toes.
图 L1F23
Action two: the posture in which the left foot is lifted and thrust out with the left heel along the ground, insubstantially, to the left, and the kua root is opened wider.

Action three: The left palm supports upward slightly to the right from before the abdomen, thereupon arcs to the left in a forward reeling, and when it has reeled to the left side level with the shoulder, the palm root presses down slightly; when the left palm has reeled to the left side and turns to press, the right hand accompanies it with a slight forward reeling outward, forming an opening jin; at the same time the proportion of substantial and insubstantial between the two legs is increased, and once the Single Whip is formed the rear kua is loosened and the body is turned straight. (Figures 25–26)

图 L1F24
Action three: the set posture in which the left palm has reeled to the left side level with the shoulder and the palm root presses down slightly.
图 L1F25
The set posture in which the left palm has reeled to the left side, the right hand makes a slight forward reeling outward to form an opening jin, and the substantial-and-insubstantial proportion of the two legs is increased (the Single Whip is now formed).

· 78 · when [the left palm has reeled to the left side], the right hand accompanies it with a slight forward reeling outward, forming an opening jin; at the same time the proportion of substantial and insubstantial between the two legs is increased, and once the Single Whip is formed the rear kua is loosened and the body is turned straight. (Figures 25–26)

Key points:

1. In action one, when the two hands each turn over one full circle at the right of the body, one must use the waist and spine as the axis to lead them, and only then can it be done with round jin and grace; and this movement must be made to show that the jin rises from the right heel through the spine and takes form in the left fingers, and then the rear kua is loosened, and when it turns straight again it shows the jin running from the left fingers across the spine and even to where the right hand closes its ward-off and hooks up. In this movement the left heel touching the ground is taken as solid, but one must note that "insubstantial" is not being wholly without force, and "substantial" is not standing wholly dead, because while the left heel is on the ground and pivoting, the centre of gravity on the left leg also increases and decreases with the turning of the body.

图 L1F26
The set posture of the Single Whip: the two arms are extended, the right hand is a hook hand raised to the right, the left palm extends to the left, and the substantial-and-insubstantial proportion of the two legs is increased.

2. In action two, 3. Taijiquan requires that intent and qi be changed nimbly; the Single Whip is a good example: when the left hand reels to the left, the intent is fixed on the left hand, and when the body has been turned straight, the intent is again fixed on the right hand. Hence Figure 25 differs from Figure 26: the former has the intent on the left hand, the latter has already shifted it to the right hand.

4. This posture is dominated by the movement of the left hand, enlarging the amount of the left hand's movement, because in the whole · 79 · set of forms the left hand moves less than the right. Moreover, the left hand is required to wind its arm to the left and fling out like a supple whip, carrying the jin to the middle finger of the left palm (as in Figure 25). Because this posture is the counterpart of Lazily Tucking the Robe, in which the right hand's movement dominates, Lazily Tucking the Robe and the Single Whip are the second posture of Taijiquan, called the two-prime posture. Moreover, although both take practising one hand as the main thing, one must draw on it so that "when one part moves, no part is without movement," attaining joint-by-joint threading-through. This requirement is harder than practising all movements with both hands, and one must take the application of the fifth characteristic as the key point.

5. The eight characteristics of Taijiquan must be manifested in every movement; it may also be said that Taijiquan is a boxing of the eight characteristics moving in unison. However, as far as any one movement is concerned, one particular characteristic is taken as the main content and the rest as secondary — but this does not mean the remaining characteristics are no longer used. Hence one must be clear that the fifth characteristic mentioned above merely means that in this posture that characteristic is dominant.

6. Every movement of Taijiquan requires that "the jin be stored with the curve and yet have a surplus", and therefore in doing this posture one must take note to keep the right upper arm and the right knee joint slightly bent, and not straightened.

Sixth Form: Second Vajra Pounds the Mortar

Action one: The body turns slightly left and the crotch opening widens; at the same time the two arms sink, the left heavy and the right light, and the left palm at the left side reels reverse one full circle, while the right hook hand changes into a palm and reels forward outward until the palm faces outward and upward; the two arms ward off outward and close their jin together. (Figure 27)

图 L1F27
The set posture in which the body turns slightly left, the left palm at the left side reels reverse one full circle, the right hook hand changes into a palm and reels forward outward with the palm facing outward and upward, and the two arms ward off outward and close their jin together.

Action two: The two hands enlarge the reeling-silk circle and, with the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, close their jin and carry it from the left upward and around to the right; the left hand moves to before the right chest, palm facing right, and the right hand is carried to the right side level with the head; when the two hands begin to carry to the right, the centre of gravity shifts right and the right leg becomes solid. (Figure 28) What follows is the same as · 80 · the latter part of the explanation of action two of the Second Form, "Vajra Pounds the Mortar", except that the direction differs: when this posture is completed one faces due east.

Action three is the same as action three of the Second Form, "Vajra Pounds the Mortar", except that the direction differs: this posture faces due east. (Continues with Figures 7–8)

图 L1F28
The set posture in which the two hands enlarge the reeling-silk circle and, with the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, close their jin and carry it from the left upward and around to the right, the left hand reaching before the right chest, the right hand reaching the right side level with the head, and the right leg becoming solid.

Key points:

1. In action one, the two hands each reel a small circle to draw on the movement that follows, as the preparatory movement of this posture.

2. The closing jin of the two hands in Figure 27 differs from the closing jin in the closing postures above: it is a closing jin within an opening posture, and should be clearly distinguished.

3. The posture in Figure 28 is formed after the two upper arms, linked one to the other, have each reeled one circle, the left reverse and the right forward; at the same time it is the two upper arms linked and closing their jin below, completed by applying the body method with the waist and spine as the axis.

4. The rest is the same as the key points of the Second Form, "Vajra Pounds the Mortar".

Seventh Form: White Crane Spreads Its Wings

Action one is the same as action one of the Third Form, "Lazily Tucking the Robe", except that at the junction of this movement with "Vajra Pounds the Mortar" the two hands do not circle a small circle above the lower abdomen but directly make the movement of crossing before the chest. (Figures 29–31)

Action two: As the right foot steps out to the right side, the centre of gravity then shifts onto the right leg, and the left foot draws in toward the right foot, touching with its toes insubstantially beside the right foot; at the same time that the centre of gravity shifts right, the two hands both reel reverse, the right hand separating in an arc up and to the right and the left hand down and to the left. (Figure 32—) All the movements of this posture should be done facing due east; from the four plates Figures 29–32 it is · 81 · (to show their front faces)

图 L1F29
White Crane Spreads Its Wings, action one: the set posture in which the two hands cross before the chest and the two arms ward off outward.
图 L1F30
White Crane Spreads Its Wings, action two: the transitional posture in which the right hand arcs up to the right and the left hand arcs down to the left, separating.
图 L1F31
The posture in which the two hands both reel reverse, the right foot steps out to the right side, and the body squats.
图 L1F32
The set posture of White Crane Spreads Its Wings: the right hand is raised up to the right, the left palm presses down to the lower left, and the left foot draws in toward the right foot, touching with its toes insubstantially beside the right foot.

Key points:

1. This posture and the Third Form, "Lazily Tucking the Robe", both join on to "Vajra Pounds the Mortar", but the joining movements differ: this posture does not join on by circling a small circle with the two hands before the abdomen, but requires the qi to cling to the spine and the two arms first to open slightly and then to close and cross; in this way it connects with the jin of the preceding posture, and at the same time shows that intent to close must first leave off, attaining the characteristic · 82 · — the sixth, "linked and unbroken". When the closing reaches its end, one must again first close slightly and then open, which again shows that intent to open must first harbour closing. In both opening and closing one must take note of the palm root, and only then will the fault of hollows and protrusions not arise.

2. This posture is completed after two closings and two openings. The characteristic of the latter opening-and-closing is: when the two feet open, the two hands close; when the two hands open, the two feet close again; the two hands close by double forward reeling and open by double reverse reeling.

3. In doing this posture one may check whether it conforms to the requirements of "empty the collar and lift the top", "sink the shoulders and drop the elbows", "contain the chest and draw up the back", "bend the knees and round the crotch", and check whether in this posture, with the left toes touching the ground and the right foot planted firmly, it possesses the momentum of supporting the eight directions. This posture is required to manifest principally the fifth and fourth characteristics.

Eighth Form: Diagonal Brush Step

Action one: The body turns slightly left; at the same time the two hands, the right reeling forward and the left reeling reverse, each make a small circle at the left and right sides, the left hand winding its arm and raising up to before the forehead and the right hand pressing down; when the two hands have each reeled half a circle, the body turns back to the right and straight; the centre of gravity is still on the right foot, the right leg is solid, and as the body turns the left foot pivots on its toes. (Figures 33–34)

图 L1F33
Diagonal Brush Step, action one: the posture in which the left hand winds its arm and raises up to before the forehead, the right hand presses down, and the left foot pivots on its toes.
图 L1F34
The posture in which the body turns back to the right and straight, the centre of gravity is still on the right foot, and the right leg is solid.

· 83 · Action two: The body continues to turn right; the left foot is lifted and thrust out to the left front (northeast) diagonal with the heel lightly along the ground. At the same time the right hand reels reverse slightly to the right rear (southwest) diagonal and extends upward until it is level with the shoulder, the palm slanting toward the right front; the left hand reels forward and pushes out in an arc toward the front of the right shoulder (southeast), the elbow still kept bent. (Figure 35)

Action three: The body turns left, the centre of gravity shifts left, and the left leg becomes solid. At the same time the left hand continues to reel forward and downward, passes before the abdomen and sweeps across the left knee, thereupon changing into a hook and raising up to the left until level with the shoulder; the right hand goes from outward to inward reeling and turns reverse, bending the arm and reeling past the right ear, the palm facing the right ear. (Figure 36)

图 L1F35
Action two: the posture in which the left foot is thrust out to the left front diagonal with its heel along the ground, the right hand reels reverse and extends upward, the left hand reels forward and pushes out in an arc toward the front of the right shoulder, and the elbow is still kept bent.
图 L1F36
Action three: the set posture in which the left hand continues to reel forward and downward, passes before the abdomen, sweeps across the left knee, changes into a hook and raises up to the left; and the right hand bends its arm and reels past the right ear, the palm facing the right ear.

Action four: The body turns slightly right; the right hand, passing beside the right hand, continues to reel reverse from the left front to the right, separating from the left hand. (Figure 37) Loosen the right kua, turn the body slightly left, sink the two shoulders, the right hand presses down slightly, and the left hand suspends. (Figure 38 — All the movements of this posture are done facing due east; the landing place of the left foot should be the same as in Figure 39; Figures 33–38 show their front faces)

Key points:

1. In action two the right hand, the left hand, and the left foot must extend simultaneously in three directions (for the directions see the movement description).

· 84 · 2. In actions one and two, when the two hands move, it seems as though the left hand reels across the body to the right and the right hand reels across the body to the left; in fact both hands rotate at the left and right sides, completed by the body method with the waist as the axis. Therefore one must not merely swing the arms.

图 L1F37
The transitional posture in which the right hand continues to reel reverse from the left front to the right and separates from the left hand.
图 L1F38
The set posture in which the right kua is loosened, the body turns slightly left, the two shoulders sink, the right hand presses down slightly, and the left hand suspends.

3. The jin of the right palm as it reels past the right ear must have the feeling of coming from the left hand forming a hook and the left leg forming a bow. As the right palm passes beside the right ear, winds its arm and reels reverse out, the spine must be drawn taut, producing the function of the qi clinging to the spine.

4. Figures 37 and 38 appear alike, but in fact the inner jin of the former is a double opening, while the latter, through the sinking of the elbow, makes the whole body's qi sink downward and the inner jin becomes a double closing.

5. This posture is left hook and right palm, exactly opposite to the "Single Whip". This posture makes reeling silk in the left and right directions, one forward and the other reverse; they act each on its own under unified conditions, and can make the body feel light and joyful.

Ninth Form: First Herding
图 L1F39
Ninth Form, First Herding, action one: the posture in which the two toes turn slightly right with the body, the left hook hand changes into a palm and reels forward together with the right hand, closing their ward-off with the palm roots toward the front of the left chest, the left hand in front and the right hand closed beside the left elbow.

· 85 · Action one: The two toes turn slightly right with the body; at the same time the left hook hand changes into a palm and reels forward together with the right hand, closing their ward-off with the palm roots toward the front of the left chest, the left hand in front and the right hand closed beside the left elbow. (Figure 39)

Action two: The body turns slightly right and drops with a downward thrust to the right, the whole weight shifts onto the right leg, and thereupon it turns and rises, drawing the left leg back and up, the left toes hanging naturally, the right knee slightly bent, forming the right single-leg-standing posture; when the body turns right the two hands reel with the left reverse and the right forward, and as the left foot is raised the two hands change to a double reverse reeling downward, closing their jin, the two palms slanting toward the front and down. (Figures 40–41 — From Figure 39 to 45 the direction of the postures in the plates has been turned to conform to the direction in the movement descriptions)

图 L1F40
First Herding, action two: the posture in which the left leg is drawn back and up, the left toes hang naturally, the right knee is slightly bent forming the right single-leg-standing posture, the two hands reel double reverse downward and close their jin, and the two palms slant toward the front and down.
图 L1F41
The right single-leg-standing set posture: head upright and body straight, the two hands closing their jin before the left knee.

Key points:

1. In action one (Figure 39), the two palms must, with the two upper arms linked, close their jin facing one another front and back. The body turns right, and as the two hands reel half a circle to the right with the left reverse and the right forward, the two palms face downward and at the same time the right leg gradually drops; after the half circle, the two hands begin to raise, and the two palms again face one another front and back; the left foot is lifted, the body stands up, and it becomes the right single-leg-standing posture, the two palms · 86 · and again the hearts of both palms slant toward the front and down, closing their jin. In double reverse reeling one must take note of the little fingers of the two hands.

2. This posture is the meaning of drawing back the lute for the first time: it requires using the elastic jin after the right leg drops, together with the slight reeling-silk jin of the two hands (left reverse, right forward), to make the body turn and rise into the single-leg-standing posture.

3. This posture is a single-leg-standing posture of closing jin; to attain stability in it is harder than attaining stability by an opening jin. The key lies in lifting the top jin, sinking the qi to the cinnabar field, reeling the two hands reverse, and fixing the intent on the little fingers of the two hands — thus it is easy to attain stability.

Tenth Form: Forward Treading Brush Step

Action one: Next, the left foot begins to descend; at the same time the two hands fall to the right side with the left reeling forward and the right reeling reverse downward (the inner jin must not be lost; continue from the preceding posture). (Figure 42) The left foot's reeling jin descends forward (east), the toes slanting toward the left front, and the body turns left. At the same time the left hand reels forward, winds its arm to before the chest, the palm facing the right front; the right palm reels reverse to above the left forearm, the palm facing the left front; the two arms cross. The body continues to turn left. (Figures 43–44)

Action two: The centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg, and the right foot strides one step across to the right front (southeast) diagonal; at the same time the two palms reel reverse and separate, extending to left and right, the two palms both facing outward and the fingers pointing up. (Figure 45 and the front view of Figure 45)

图 L1F42
Forward Treading Brush Step, action one: the posture in which the left foot begins to descend and the two hands fall to the right with the left reeling forward and the right reeling reverse downward.

Key points:

1. From the falling of the two palms at the right side until they reel to before the chest, the inner jin must be unbroken; when the two arms cross they must tighten and close together, and then separate to left and right and extend; when extending, take note of the two · 87 · the thumbs of the palms.

图 L1F43
The posture in which the left foot descends forward (east), the toes slant toward the left front, the body turns left, and the left hand reels forward to before the chest.
图 L1F44
The posture in which the two arms cross, the right palm reels reverse to above the left forearm, and the body continues to turn left.

2. When turning to the left from the single-leg-standing posture, the step must be steady, and in the process of turning from up-and-down to left-and-right reeling silk all is closing jin, and there must be no breaks or hollows-and-protrusions.

图 L1F45
The set posture in which the right foot strides one step across to the right front (southeast) diagonal, the two palms reel reverse and separate to left and right, the two palms both facing outward and the fingers pointing up.
图 L1F45附图
The front view of Figure 45.

The movements are the same as those of the Eighth Form, "Diagonal Brush Step"; only the joining movement differs slightly, but the explanation of the Eighth Form may still be used, in conjunction with the plates. (Figures 46–48, then Figures 35–38. Figure 46 is the foot descending in the direction of the front view of Figure 45; in fact the move- · 88 · ment and the direction of the left foot's stepping are still the same as the Eighth Form's: stepping up toward the northeast diagonal)

图 L1F46
Second Diagonal Brush Step: the posture in which the body turns left, the left foot is thrust out toward the left front (northeast) diagonal with its heel along the ground, the left hand reels forward and raises, and the right hand presses down.
