Twelfth Form: Herding Again

The movements, directions, and key points are all the same as the Ninth Form, "First Herding". (Figures 39–41)

Thirteenth Form: Forward Treading Brush Step

The movements, directions, and key points are all the same as the Tenth Form, "Forward Treading Brush Step". (Figures 42–45)

Fourteenth Form: Cover-Hand Forearm Punch

Action one: The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg, and the right leg is lifted; as the body turns and the centre of gravity shifts left, the right palm changes into a fist and reels forward to before the chest; the left palm reels reverse and closes on the upper side of the right arm, crossing with the right arm, the palm facing the right shoulder. (Figure 49) The two hands reel forward and sink, and the crossing point of the two arms moves forward; at the same time the right foot stamps on the ground with a stomp as the qi sinks. (Figure 50)

Action two: The left foot steps toward the left front (northeast) diagonal, and the centre of gravity gradually shifts left; at the same time the crossing point of the two arms continues to move forward, and thereupon the two hands, the left reeling reverse and the right forward, reel to the left · 89 · up and to the right and down, separating in arcs, the right palm facing down and the left palm facing outward. (Figures 51–52)

图 L1F49
Cover-Hand Forearm Punch, action one: the posture in which the right palm changes into a fist and reels forward to before the chest, the left palm reels reverse and closes on the upper side of the right arm, crossing with the right arm, the palm facing the right shoulder.
图 L1F50
The posture in which the two hands reel forward and sink, the crossing point of the two arms moves forward, and the right foot stamps on the ground with a stomp as the qi sinks.
图 L1F51
Action two: the transitional posture in which the crossing point of the two arms continues to move forward and the two hands, the left reeling reverse and the right forward, separate in arcs up to the left and down to the right.
图 L1F52
The set posture in which the right palm faces down, the left palm faces outward, and the body turns slightly right.

Action three: The body turns slightly right, and the whole body's qi sinks downward. At the same time the right fist reels forward, goes to the right and up past before the chest, and is drawn back to the right side of the ribs; the left hand goes from reverse reeling to forward reeling and moves to before the chest. (Figure 53)

Action four: The body turns slightly left; at the same time the two hands reel forward and close before the chest, the left palm and the right fist both facing up, the right fist placed on the left palm (seemingly stopping yet not stopping, the body continuing to sink to store jin). The centre of gravity shifts rapidly left, forming a left bow stance, the right leg slightly bent and not straightened · 90 · straight. At the same time the right fist is issued swiftly toward the right front (east, slightly south), its fist-heart turning to face down; the left hand is also swiftly drawn back to the left side of the ribs. (Figure 54 — From Figure 49 onward the foot descends in the direction of the front view of Figure 45; in fact the direction of the left foot's stepping in the movement is the northeast diagonal; Figures 49–54 show their front faces)

图 L1F53
Action three: the posture in which the right fist reels forward, goes to the right and up past before the chest, and is drawn back to the right side of the ribs, and the left hand goes from reverse reeling to forward reeling and moves to before the chest.
图 L1F54
Action four: the set posture in which the centre of gravity shifts rapidly left forming a left bow stance, the right fist is issued swiftly toward the right front, its fist-heart turning to face down, and the left hand is swiftly drawn back to the left side of the ribs.

Key points:

1. This posture (Figures 51, 52) is required to manifest the covering-and-releasing jin; when covering, the crotch opening is required to sink, and only then can the jin be tightened; when releasing, one must first tighten and then separate to make the releasing jin. The covering-and-releasing jin is a drawing-along jin, and must not go beyond the circle of the hands and feet; moreover it is the basis of storing and issuing.

2. The storing jin of Taijiquan must be like drawing a bow: it must be tightened to become a store. Storing does not mean increasing the bend, but means storing to the full the elasticity before issuing and having no defects; it requires the five bows (that is, the one spine bow, the two hand bows, and the two foot bows) to ward off together. The "defect" spoken of here does not mean the jin is broken, but that the jin has not reached the back of the bow, and hence the elasticity is insufficient. Only when one has practised joint-by-joint threading-through, the whole body as one family, can one become a bow of abundant tenacity, possessing powerful elasticity.

3. In this posture, stamping the right foot and issuing the right fist must manifest the firm jin of Taijiquan. Taijiquan lays equal stress on moving jin and issuing jin. Although the Chen-style first routine takes softness and moving as its main thing, · 91 · The second routine (Cannon Fist) takes firmness and issuing as its main thing; but in the first routine too there are movements of firmness and issuing as auxiliaries (such as Cover-Hand Forearm Punch), and in the second routine too there are movements of softness and moving as auxiliaries (such as Lazily Tucking the Robe); this is in order to attain the goal of firmness and softness aiding each other and of nimble conversion used together.

4. The boxing treatise requires that "force be issued from the spine", that "issuing jin be like loosing an arrow", that "issuing jin must be calm, settled, relaxed, and quiet", and that one "concentrate on one direction". Therefore one must first "draw the bow" to store the jin, then "release the catch" from the spine and issue, the jin concentrating on the "arrowhead" side, and finally quiver like the jin of an arrow penetrating the target, to complete this movement. From the posture, at the moment of issuing jin, although one hand goes forward and the other backward (or one up and one down, one left and one right) to keep balance, the jin force still takes one side as host (substantial) and the other as guest (insubstantial), and it is not double-weighting.

Fifteenth Form: Third Vajra Pounds the Mortar

Action one: The body turns slightly right; at the same time the right fist changes into a palm and reels forward, drawing back slightly to the right rear, while the left palm still at the side of the left ribs reels reverse slightly to accompany it. (Figure 55) Then the body turns slightly left; at the same time the two hands, the right reeling forward and the left reeling reverse, arc toward the chest and cross, closing their jin, the left hand above with the palm facing down and the right palm facing up. (Figure 56)

图 L1F55
Third Vajra Pounds the Mortar, action one: the posture in which the body turns slightly right, the right fist changes into a palm and reels forward, drawing back slightly to the right rear, and the left palm still at the side of the left ribs reels reverse slightly to accompany it.
图 L1F56
The set posture in which the two hands, the right reeling forward and the left reeling reverse, arc toward the chest and cross, closing their jin, the left hand above with the palm facing down and the right palm facing up.

· 92 · Action two: The body turns right and the centre of gravity shifts right onto the right leg; at the same time the right palm reels forward to the upper right and the left palm reels reverse to the lower left, extending. (Figures 57–58 — From Figure 55 to 57 the left foot is still at the northeast diagonal, and the position of the left foot should be the same as in Figure 58; from Figure 58 to 76 the direction of the postures has been turned to conform to the direction in the movement descriptions) The whole weight shifts onto the left leg, and the right foot is drawn back and pointed forward with its toes before the left foot. At the same time the two hands reel, the left reverse and the right forward, the left hand bending its elbow with the forearm across before the chest, the palm facing down; the right hand, as the right foot comes forward, sweeps up toward the chest, and the two hands form a closing jin. (Figure 59)

图 L1F57
Action two: the posture in which the body turns right, the right palm reels forward to the upper right, and the left palm reels reverse to the lower left, extending.
图 L1F58
The posture in which the right foot is drawn back and pointed forward with its toes before the left foot, and the whole weight shifts onto the left leg.
图 L1F59
The set posture in which the two hands reel, the left reverse and the right forward, the left hand bends its elbow with the forearm across before the chest, the palm facing down, the right hand sweeps up toward the chest, and the two hands form a closing jin.

Action three is the same as action three of the Second Form, "Vajra Pounds the Mortar". (Continues with Figures 7–8)

Key points:

1. Turning from the opening jin and issuing jin of the preceding posture, Cover-Hand Forearm Punch, into the closing jin of this posture, the right hand must draw in slightly and then give a small ward-off forward in the direction of the issuing jin, to tease the broken jin back into connection, so that the inner jin is unbroken and threads through into the closing jin of the double closing that follows.

2. In this posture each half-circle movement that opens as wide as possible changes into a contracting movement that closes into an extremely small half circle; it is required to feel full throughout the body, with majestic momentum.

3. This posture differs from the first two Vajra Pounds the Mortar in that: the first time manifests the ward-off jin of the five paired directions in Taijiquan; the second is the opening jin that follows on from the Single Whip, turning · 93 · into a closing jin; the third mainly teases back into connection the broken jin after the issuing jin of the previous posture. It is the close of the fifth posture of the thirteen Taiji postures.

Sixteenth Form: Drape-Body Punch

Action one: The two hands reel reverse and extend to left and right, the five fingers hanging down and the palms facing inward. (Figure 60) The two hands continue to raise and turn to forward reeling, and when they are level with the shoulder the palms turn to face front and up. (Figure 61) The whole weight shifts onto the left leg, the right foot is lifted and thrust out with its heel along the ground to the right, and thereupon the centre of gravity shifts right, forming a horse stance; at the same time the two hands continue to raise slightly, and as the right foot steps to the right they reel forward toward the chest and cross, closing together, the left palm outside. (Figures 62–63)

图 L1F60
Drape-Body Punch, action one: the posture in which the two hands reel reverse and extend to left and right, the five fingers hang down, and the palms face inward.
图 L1F61
The posture in which the two hands continue to raise and turn to forward reeling, and when they are level with the shoulder the palms turn to face front and up.
图 L1F62
The posture in which the whole weight shifts onto the left leg and the right foot is lifted and thrust out with its heel along the ground to the right.
图 L1F63
The set posture in which the horse stance is formed and the two hands, as the right foot steps to the right, reel forward toward the chest and cross, closing together, the left palm outside.

· 94 · Action two: The two hands change into fists; the right fist, before the face, reels reverse from inward to the right and opens, thereupon turning from right to forward with a forward reeling and closing, circling one full circle, the fist-heart facing inward; the left hand reels reverse to the left and opens, thereupon turning to forward reeling and closing slightly as the right hand closes, the fist-heart facing right; when the right hand has circled half a circle to the right, the centre of gravity shifts slightly right and the body turns slightly right; when the right hand has circled one full circle, the centre of gravity shifts back and the body turns straight. (Figure 64)

图 L1F64
Drape-Body Punch, action two: the set posture in which the two hands change into fists, the right fist circles one full circle, and the left hand closes slightly as the right hand closes.

Action three: The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity shifts left, and the left leg forms a bow. At the same time the two fists reel forward, the right fist moving to before the left ear level with the head, the fist-heart facing inward; the left fist at the original place on the left side reels forward in a small circle to accompany the right fist's closing jin, the fist-heart facing the left front. (Figure 65) The centre of gravity shifts right, the right leg forms a bow, and the body turns right. As the body turns, the right fist arcs down to the right with a forward reeling to beside the right leg, the fist-heart facing up; the left fist reels forward from left to right passing before the face, level with the head, the fist-heart facing inward, closing its jin together with the right fist. (Figure 66)

图 L1F65
Action three: the posture in which the body turns slightly left, the left leg forms a bow, the right fist moves to before the left ear level with the head, and the left fist at the original place on the left side reels forward in a small circle to accompany the right fist's closing jin.
图 L1F66
The set posture in which the centre of gravity shifts right and the right leg forms a bow, the right fist arcs down to the right with a forward reeling to beside the right leg, and the left fist reels forward from left to right passing before the face, closing its jin together with the right fist.

· 95 · Key points: 1. This posture turns from the closing jin of the preceding posture, Vajra Pounds the Mortar, into a double reverse opening jin; after opening it changes to double forward reeling, the two palms turning to face outward in a closing jin of the two hands, and thereupon the two hands reel forward and cross, closing together; during these openings and closings one must take note of the substantial and insubstantial of the two hands and of the two feet, and especially of the substantial and insubstantial between hand and foot. On this point see the fourth characteristic.

2. Actions two and three (Figures 64–66) are movements after the two palms change into fists; they must be made continuous as one, and performed under the requirement that the qi cling to the spine and the waist be the axis; the key lies in specially enlarging the inner-and-outer reeling silk and in letting the earlier reeling silk lead the later reeling silk; only thus can the movements in the three figures be joined into one, and the inner jin be not lost, changing over without any hollows or protrusions. On this point see the fifth characteristic.

3. Throughout all the processes of this posture's opening-and-closing and closing-and-opening, it is rich in soft jin; it is the soft jin of the four corners, serving as an auxiliary within the four cardinal frame.

Seventeenth Form: Back-Bending Shoulder

Action one: The body turns left by 90 degrees. At the same time the right hand reels reverse and raises in an arc, the fist-heart facing left; the left hand winds its arm with a forward reeling and descends in a left arc to the side of the left waist, the fist-heart facing back. (Figure 67)

图 L1F67
Back-Bending Shoulder, action one: the posture in which the body turns left by 90 degrees, the right hand reels reverse and raises in an arc with the fist-heart facing left, and the left hand winds its arm with a forward reeling and descends in an arc to the side of the left waist with the fist-heart facing back.

Action two: The body continues to turn slightly left. At the same time the right fist winds its arm, changing from reverse reeling to forward reeling, and the right arm is bent before the top of the head; the left fist, after a very small forward-reeling circle at the left side, presses its fist face close to the left waist; thereupon the body turns slightly right and leans back to the right rear with the back near the right shoulder; at the same time the crotch opening sinks further, and the eyes look at the top of the left foot. (Figure 68)

· 96 · Key points: 1. The two upper arms must be linked one to the other with ward-off jin, so as to attain the jin of "opening hidden within closing"; as long as the waist is taken as the central axis, the right back can naturally turn over, and there is no danger of attending to one and losing the other.

2. Figure 68 shows the use of the right arm before the top of the head; a small reverse reeling must be used to turn the arm to before the top of the head; the key of this posture is to press the left fist close to the left waist, making the right back draw even tauter and manifesting the shoulder jin of the back.

图 L1F68
Back-Bending Shoulder, action two: the posture in which the right arm is bent before the top of the head, the face of the left fist presses close to the left waist, the back near the right shoulder leans to the right rear, and the crotch opening sinks further.

3. The shoulder jin issued by the posture Back-Bending Shoulder is plentiful in the second routine, Cannon Fist. This posture is one of the shoulder jins among the four-corner hand; it serves as an auxiliary within the four-cardinal frame.

Eighteenth Form: Green Dragon Emerges from Water
图 L1F69
Green Dragon Emerges from Water, action one: the posture in which the right fist winds its arm with a forward reeling and descends in an arc from above, past before the chest, to the right side of the right leg with the fist-heart facing up, and the left fist leaves the left waist with a reverse reeling and raises in a left arc with the fist-heart facing inward.
图 L1F70
The set posture in which the right fist raises in a right arc and turns again to forward reeling until the fist-heart faces left, and the left fist changes to forward reeling, bends its elbow with the forearm across, and descends past before the chest to be placed before the abdomen with the fist-heart facing up.

Action one: The centre of gravity shifts left, and the body turns slightly right. At the same time the right fist winds its arm with a forward reeling and descends in an arc from above, past before the chest, to the right side of the right leg, the fist-heart facing up; the left fist leaves the left waist with a reverse reeling and raises in a left arc, the fist-heart facing inward. (Figure 69) The right fist changes to reverse reeling and from the right arcs · 97 · in an arc upward, and turning again to forward reeling, reels until the fist-heart faces left; at the same time the left fist changes to forward reeling, bends its elbow with the forearm across, and descends past before the chest to be placed before the abdomen, the fist-heart facing up. (Figure 70)

图 L1F71
Action two: the posture in which the left fist changes into a palm and extends with a reverse reeling toward the right front with the palm facing the right rear, and the right fist reels forward, bends its elbow, and descends to be placed before the chest above the left arm with the fist-heart facing inward.

Action two: The body turns slightly left. At the same time the left fist changes into a palm and extends with a reverse reeling toward the right front, the palm facing the right rear; the right fist reels forward, bends its elbow, and descends to be placed before the chest above the left arm, the fist-heart facing inward. (Figure 71) The centre of gravity shifts slightly right. At the same time the left hand reels forward and sinks, the palm facing the right rear; the right fist reels forward and gathers in beneath the chest, closing its jin together with the left palm, drawing the spine taut. (Figure 72) The body turns slightly left, and as the kua jin sinks, the right fist winds its arm with a reverse reeling and suddenly "releases the catch" from the spine, issuing jin toward the right front with the ulnar side near the wrist; the left hand reels forward and is drawn back at the same speed as the right fist's issuing, to be placed at the side of the left waist. (Figure 73)

图 L1F72
The posture in which the left hand reels forward and sinks, the right fist reels forward and gathers in beneath the chest, closing its jin together with the left palm, and the spine is drawn taut.
图 L1F73
The set posture in which the body turns slightly left, the right fist winds its arm with a reverse reeling and "releases the catch" from the spine, issuing jin toward the right front with the ulnar side near the wrist, and the left hand reels forward and is drawn back to be placed at the side of the left waist.

Key points:

1. Chen-style Taijiquan applies reeling-silk jin not only in the two hands; in fact the two legs also simultaneously ap- · 98 · ply it. Because this posture has a long stride and a wide crotch opening, it is the clearest example of the legs manifesting reeling-silk jin. Leg reeling silk is: when the hand on one leg reels forward, that leg likewise generally reels forward with the knee turning out; conversely, the knee turns in with a reverse reeling (for the principle of leg reeling silk see the second key point of the Twenty-first Form, "Punch Beneath the Elbow"). From the posture in this figure, the two legs seem not to have moved at all, and one sees only the two arms changing movement; in fact the legs too are reeling silk.

2. Taiji jin is the inner jin that arises from the heel, is issued from the leg, is governed by the waist and spine, and takes form in the fingers; reeling silk is a fairly long path of movement through which this inner jin passes. In the whole body there are two such paths, namely from the left heel to the right fingers and from the right heel to the left fingers, and they cross each other on the spine, one after the other.

3. To thread all the joints of the whole body through like a single line, one must complete it by the spiral of reeling silk. Reeling silk is governed by the waist and spine, leads the two arms, and has its foundation in the two legs; if the legs have no reeling silk, one cannot attain the realm of the whole body as one family. On this point one should take note.

4. The reason this posture is called "emerging from water" is that this kind of issuing jin is like "a thing about to be raised being given a downward check" — that is, at the end of the downward half circle there is an upward jin, and so it is also named the shaking jin of emerging from water.

5. The issuing jin of this posture belongs to the rend jin among the four-corner hand; the reason it is not called a "strike" or a "blow" is that rend jin is a short-distance strike, and so some also call it "inch jin".

Action three: the posture in which the two hands reel forward, turn their palms over, and are placed separately beside the two ears with the palms slanting outward, the right toes pivot on the ground, and the right knee turns with the body.
图 L1F79
The set posture in which the right foot steps to the right, the centre of gravity shifts onto the right leg, the left foot steps in abreast to the right and touches with its toes beside the right foot, the body turns right, and the two palms close their jin and press down to the right as the body turns.

Key points:

1. This posture is basically the same as the movements of Six Seals and Four Closings, only the conversion in the stepping and the path of jin of the double push differ. The push jin of this posture is firmer, and when the push reaches its end the rear palm root must manifest a downward-sinking rend jin, and hence the speed of the sinking is also faster.

2. This posture joins on immediately after the issuing jin of the previous posture. Because issuing jin seeks a break in the jin, the jin cannot be unbroken, cannot go beyond the body and apply to the outside, yet it must be linked continuously without break with this posture. The former part of action one (Figure 74) plays the role of catching the issuing jin, and draws on the movements that follow. The requirement "broken yet reconnected, able to break and able to connect" is detailed in the sixth characteristic.

3. After the issuing jin of the previous posture, it turns to closing, and after closing it opens again; within this closing-and-opening · 101 · the body turns with a waist-wringing jin, turning into a double support (shuang tuo) with the left rear and right front; the double support is required, within the double forward reeling, to produce a closing jin, preparing the way for the double push.

Twentieth Form: Three Palm Changes

Action: The body turns right; at the same time the right palm draws back inward lightly past before the chest with a forward reeling, the palm facing inward; the left palm reels reverse, winds its arm, and extends forward level, turning to face the palm upward. (Figure 80) The body turns slightly left; at the same time the right palm reels forward and pushes out with ward-off jin, the palm slanting outward; the left palm, as the body turns, reels reverse and is drawn back to before the abdomen, the palm facing up. (Figure 81) The body turns right again; at the same time the right palm reels forward and is drawn back to before the abdomen, and the left palm, from before the abdomen, reels reverse upward and forward past above the right arm, pushing out with ward-off jin. (Figure 82) During the movement, as the body turns, the left toes pivot in place on the ground, and the left knee turns in the direction the body turns.

图 L1F80
Three Palm Changes: the posture in which the right palm draws back inward past before the chest with a forward reeling and the palm facing inward, and the left palm reels reverse, winds its arm, and extends forward level, turning to face the palm upward.
图 L1F81
The posture in which the right palm reels forward and pushes out with ward-off jin, the palm slanting outward, and the left palm, as the body turns, reels reverse and is drawn back to before the abdomen, the palm facing up.
图 L1F82
The posture in which the right palm reels forward and is drawn back to before the abdomen, and the left palm, from before the abdomen, reels reverse upward and forward past above the right arm, pushing out with ward-off jin.

In this posture, Three Palm Changes, when the two palms alternately extend and draw back the movement must be round and lively: when the waist and kua turn slightly right the left palm extends, and when the waist and kua turn slightly left the right palm extends; the waist and kua rotate two round trips, the left palm extends forward twice and the right palm once, hence it is called Three Palm Changes. Three Palm Changes is a method of reeling-grasp, and therefore the palms extending forward are not strikes but round-turning reeling-grasps of the opponent's jin path and joints. Although the centre of gravity is always on the right leg, because of the opening and closing during the to-and-fro of the movement, the waist and kua open and close in rotation, drawing the knee joints of the two legs also to open and close in rotation, still · 102 · still "when one part moves, no part is unmoved".

Because the movement of this posture and that of the next are joined closely without the least interruption, and because the two postures share certain essential points, the essential points of this posture are accordingly given together in the next.

Twenty-First Form: Punch Beneath the Elbow

Action: Immediately the body turns left again; at the same time the two hands, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, open out separately, the left hand down-left and the right hand up-right. (Figure 83) The body continues to turn slightly left; at the same time the two hands, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, reel slightly until level with the shoulders, both palms facing down (this is the opening stage of Punch Beneath the Elbow). (Figure 84) The body turns slightly right. At the same time the two hands, left reverse-reeling and right forward-reeling, close with jin; in the course of closing, the left arm changes from reverse reeling to forward reeling and, as it reels, the left forearm is raised upright, the palm reeling round to face right; the right palm becomes a fist, reels forward, and from the right bends its elbow forward-left with closing jin, describing a small circle beneath the left arm, and comes to rest below the left elbow, the palm facing inward. (Figure 85)

图 L1F83
The opening of Punch Beneath the Elbow: the posture in which the two hands, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, open out separately, the left hand down-left and the right hand up-right.
图 L1F84
The posture in which the two hands, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, reel slightly until level with the shoulders, both palms facing down (the opening stage of Punch Beneath the Elbow).
图 L1F85
The posture in which the two hands, left reverse-reeling and right forward-reeling, close with jin, the left arm changing from reverse to forward reeling with the left forearm raised upright and the palm reeling round to face right, and the right palm becoming a fist that reels forward and, bending its elbow forward-left with closing jin, comes to rest below the left elbow.

Essential points:

1. The distinguishing feature of the previous posture and this one is that within compact movement they attain joint-by-joint continuity and the principle that when one part moves no part is unmoved. For this reason the left knee too pivots with the left toes touching the ground, as an axle, rotating in step with the turning of the body; but note that "empty" is by no means wholly without strength, and "full" is not · 103 · wholly planted dead; on this point, see essential point 1 of the fifth form, "Single Whip".

2. To attain the requirements of Taijiquan — joint-by-joint continuity and the principle that when one part moves no part is unmoved — the key lies in employing the silk-reeling jin of the whole body; only through silk-reeling can the jin start from the heels and travel joint by joint to the fingers. Therefore the silk-reeling of the legs and that of the hands occupy equally important positions; the action descriptions do not mention the silk-reeling of the legs because the silk-reeling of the legs and that of the arms (except in lifting a leg to stand alone and in breaking free of a lock) are always consistent above and below. The principles are as follows: (1) whenever the hand reels forward, the leg (knee) below that hand also reels forward from inside to outside; (2) whenever the hand reels reverse, the leg (knee) below that hand also reels reverse from outside to inside; (3) whenever the right leg reels forward outward, the left leg reels reverse inward, and vice versa; (4) compare the reverse reeling of the hand with that of the left heel: issuing to the leg it is of course reverse; rising to the kua it naturally passes on the slant through the waist and spine, forming a spine whose left side is drawn taut and whose right side is relaxed, then passing on to the right arm, whereupon the right hand becomes forward-reeling. Thus the silk-reeling of hands and feet passes crosswise front and back through the spine, naturally forming the effect of the whole body as one family.

3. The previous posture attains joint-by-joint continuity and total movement within a compact double closing; this posture manifests the principle that when one part moves no part is unmoved in a large, expansive movement. Finally, by the closing that accompanies the turn of the body, the silk-reeling circles are reduced and the two close tightly together; although the quality of jin within differs, the drawing of coming and going and the adhesion of qi to the spine are the same. Therefore attention should be paid to the use of the spine.

4. When going straight from the previous posture to the double closing at the end of this one, one must further cause the crown jin to be raised with emptiness; after long practice, practising to this posture will make the joints and the joints of the upper thoracic vertebrae crack, and this is a phenomenon naturally produced after long practice and should not be forced, lest it give rise to abuses. Only when this realm is attained does it suffice to prove that in this posture's movement one has reached the requirements of total movement and of the joints being opened and relaxed.

Twenty-Second Form: Step Back and Roll the Arm

Action one: The centre of gravity shifts right. At the same time, the left palm passes reverse-reeling downward before the face; the right fist becomes · 104 · palm, from below the left elbow, passes before the abdomen and then upward to the right, changing from forward reeling to reverse reeling, and reels in an arc to beside the right cheek, the palm slanting toward the left front. (Figure 86) The left foot is lifted and, passing beside the right ankle, steps back in an arc to the left rear (northwest); the centre of gravity shifts back with it and the left leg becomes full. At the same time, the right palm reels reverse and pushes forward; the left palm crosses before the chest beneath the extended right forearm, that is, from the lower left, as the left foot steps back, it opens out in an arc to the left rear. (Figures 87–88; the front views of attached figures 87 and 88. The direction of the postures in figures 87 and 88 has already been turned to agree with the directions in the action description. The earlier figure 86 and the later figures 89–92 all show their front aspect, but in fact all should have the same direction as figures 87 and 88, performing the movement with the chest facing due east.)

图 L1F86
The posture in which the left palm, from below the left elbow, passes before the abdomen and then upward to the right, changing from forward to reverse reeling, and reels in an arc to beside the right cheek, the palm slanting toward the left front.
图 L1F87附图
The posture in which the left foot, passing beside the right ankle, steps back in an arc to the left rear (northwest) with the centre of gravity shifting back and the left leg becoming full, the right palm reeling reverse and pushing forward, and the left palm crossing beneath the right forearm and opening out in an arc to the left rear. The attached figure shows the rear view.
图 L1F87正面图
The front view of the same movement as the attached figure 87, with the chest facing due east.
图 L1F88附图
Continuing from the attached figure 87, the posture in which the left palm continues to open out in an arc to the left rear and the right palm pushes forward. The attached figure shows the rear view.

· 105 · Action two: The two hands and the two legs each reel forward in a small circle (by a turning jin), and then the centre of gravity shifts left. At the same time, the left palm, from the left, goes upward, changing from forward reeling to reverse reeling, and reels in an arc to beside the left cheek, the palm slanting toward the right front; the right palm, from small forward reeling to large forward reeling, reels from right to left past before the chest and downward. (Figure 89) The right foot is lifted and, passing beside the left ankle, steps back in an arc to the right rear (southwest); the centre of gravity shifts back with it and the right leg becomes full. At the same time, the left palm reels reverse and pushes forward; the right palm crosses before the chest beneath the extended left forearm, that is, from the lower right, as the right foot steps back, it opens out in an arc to the right rear. (Figure 90)

Action three is the same as action two, only left and right are reversed. (Figure 91, then follow the front view of 88)

图 L1F88正面图
The end of action one (continuing from the attached figure 88): the front view of the posture in which the left palm opens out in an arc to the left rear and the right palm pushes forward, with the chest facing due east.
图 L1F89
The beginning of action two: the posture in which the left palm, from the left, goes upward, changing from forward to reverse reeling, and reels in an arc to beside the left cheek, the palm slanting toward the right front, and the right palm reels from right to left past before the chest and downward.
图 L1F90
The posture in which the right foot, passing beside the left ankle, steps back in an arc to the right rear (southwest) with the centre of gravity shifting back and the right leg becoming full, the left palm reeling reverse and pushing forward, and the right palm crossing beneath the left forearm and opening out in an arc to the right rear.
图 L1F91
Action three, the same as action two with left and right reversed: the posture in which the right palm reels in an arc to beside the right cheek and the left palm reels past before the chest and downward, whereupon the left foot, passing beside the right ankle, steps back in an arc to the left rear, the right palm pushes forward, and the left palm opens out in an arc to the right rear.

· 106 · Essential points:

1. This posture opens and then closes, and again closes and then opens. This peculiar movement that harbours a closing within the opening and a parting within the closing is accomplished during the continuous step-back.

2. In the continuous stepping back it is not a straight, unbroken retreat. In accordance with the requirement that "advance and retreat must have conversion", amid the two backward-stepping movements there is interposed a double-opening posture and a conversion of inner jin. Only thus does it not feel like a straight unbroken retreat, but rather like the opening jin applied before and after the silk-reeling. At the same time, having conversion, it becomes a retreat that contains advance — advancing is retreating, retreating is advancing, advance and retreat at ease — making it a Taijiquan retreat method able to support all eight directions.

3. Step Back and Roll the Arm is the only form in Taijiquan that retreats continuously; it requires that amid the retreat there be a slight forward and reverse silk-reeling, and that it be done round and smoothly, so that it has no defect of gaps or bumps nor any interruption of inner jin, meeting the requirement of the sixth characteristic.

5. This posture can also be done as an outwardly manifested issuing of jin: that is, when one has stepped back and reached the landing point, the heel stamps the ground with a sound, and at the same time the forward hand issues jin outward while the rear hand holds it down with sinking jin.

Twenty-Third Form: Step Back and Press the Elbow

Action one: The body turns slightly left. At the same time, the left palm turns its arm forward-reeling and opens out to the lower left, the palm facing down; the right palm reels reverse and opens out slanting to the upper right, the palm facing outward. (Figure 92. This figure continues downward from the front view of figure 88, and therefore although figures 92–96 all show the front aspect, in fact the movement should still be performed with the chest facing east.) The body turns slightly right. At the same time, the right palm reels forward toward the front and inside, changes to reverse reeling, and circles once to the right; the left palm, as the right palm circles from the front right, shifts slightly left, that is, as the right palm circles right it reels forward and draws an arc to the right to before the right ribs. (Figure 93)

Action two: The centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg, the body turns left, the right foot lifts its heel and, with the toes touching the ground, passing inside the right ankle, steps back in a slant to the right rear (south, slightly west); on reaching the landing point the heel comes down and stamps the ground, and the centre of gravity shifts back, the body turning right at the same time. As the body · 107 · body turns left, at the same time the right palm reels forward and is drawn back in an arc, its fingers adhering to the left abdomen; the left elbow presses up past the inner side of the right palm, and the left palm reels reverse, its finger-backs adhering to the right ribs and rising; as the body turns right and the right foot stamps, at the same time the left palm pushes out on the slant toward the left front, and the right palm, its fingers adhering to the body, moves to the right abdomen. (Figures 94–95)

图 L1F92
Action one of Step Back and Press the Elbow: the posture in which the left palm turns its arm forward-reeling and opens out to the lower left with the palm facing down, and the right palm reels reverse and opens out slanting to the upper right with the palm facing outward.
图 L1F93
Continuing from figure 92: the posture in which the right palm reels forward toward the front and inside, changes to reverse reeling and circles once to the right, and the left palm, as the right palm circles right, reels forward and draws an arc to the right to before the right ribs.
图 L1F94
Action two: the posture in which the right palm reels forward and is drawn back in an arc with its fingers adhering to the left abdomen, and the left elbow presses up past the inner side of the right palm with the left palm reeling reverse and its finger-backs adhering to the right ribs and rising.
图 L1F95
Continuing from figure 94: the posture in which, as the body turns right and the right foot stamps, the left palm pushes out on the slant toward the left front and the right palm, its fingers adhering to the body, moves to the right abdomen.

Essential points:

1. In this posture, when the two arms embrace and close as a single whole circle (figure 94), it must become a tough, elastic press jin; its emphasis is that, with the qi adhering to the back, the skin of the spine is drawn taut to knead and move the spine; at the same time it is the moment of storing in readiness to issue.

· 108 · 2. Although figure 94 has already drawn the right foot back, it has not yet stamped it; the stamp must be coordinated and made one with the issuing of the left palm, so as to form the opening jin, as in the posture of figure 95.

3. Step Back and Press the Elbow is a short-range supplementary issuing of jin, requiring softness harbouring hardness; when the moving jin is well set, in the instant the dantian jin is issued with sinking jin through the left palm, it must coincide with the sound of the right heel stamping the ground, so that the whole body's jin force is complete.

Twenty-Fourth Form: Middle Plate

Action one: The body turns slightly left, then right. The left palm, as the body turns left, shifts slightly left, that is, as the body turns right, the arm reels reversely from the left up to the right to before the right ribs, the palm facing up; at the same time the right palm reels reverse and is raised to the right rear, the palm facing right. As the right palm is raised, the right foot is lifted. (Figure 96)

Action two: The body turns slightly left; the right foot comes down beside the left foot, first touching with the toes, then immediately the heel kicks out to stamp the ground, and the centre of gravity immediately shifts onto the right leg, the left heel lifting. As the right foot comes down, the right hand reels reverse (bending its elbow so the elbow tip passes above the right palm) and draws an arc from above to before the left eyebrow; the left palm reels forward and shifts down to below the left ribs, the palm facing up, and the two arms cross before the chest. (Figure 97, the front view of attached figure 97. The direction of figure 96 agrees with that of the front view 97, and therefore figure 96 too should be performed with the chest facing east.)

图 L1F96
Action one of Middle Plate: the posture in which the left palm, as the body turns right, reels reversely with the arm from the left up to the right to before the right ribs with the palm facing up, and the right palm reels reverse and is raised to the right rear with the palm facing right, the right foot being lifted as the right palm rises.
图 L1F97
Action two: the posture in which the right foot comes down beside the left foot, first touching with the toes and then stamping the ground with the heel, with the centre of gravity shifting onto the right leg and the left heel lifting, the right hand reeling reverse with its elbow bent so the elbow tip passes above the right palm and draws an arc from above to before the left eyebrow, and the left palm reeling forward and shifting down to below the left ribs with the palm facing up, the two arms crossing before the chest.
图 L1F97附图
Another view of the same movement as figure 97, showing its front aspect (chest facing east).

· 109 · Action three: The body turns slightly left; the left foot opens one step sideways to the left rear (north, slightly west) on the slant, bending the knee and squatting down; at the same time, the two hands reel forward and press outward, the palms turning outward and down, and as the left foot opens the two arms close slightly, the two palms turning inward; immediately the two hands, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, open out separately, the left hand to the upper left and the right hand to the lower right, both palms facing down. (Figures 98–99, and attached figures 98 and 99)

图 L1F98
Action three of Middle Plate: the posture in which the left foot opens one step sideways to the left rear (north, slightly west) on the slant, bending the knee and squatting down, and the two hands reel forward and press outward with the palms turning outward and down, the two arms closing slightly as the left foot opens.
图 L1F98附图
Another view of the same movement as figure 98.
图 L1F99
Continuing from figure 98: the posture in which the two hands, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, then open out separately, the left hand to the upper left and the right hand to the lower right, both palms facing down.
图 L1F99附图
Another view of the same movement as figure 99.

Essential points:

1. At the beginning of this posture, attention should be paid to the size of the forward and reverse silk-reeling. In order that the movement gain posture and gain jin, when the right palm passes below the left elbow it should tighten the diameter of its circle; this is also the time when the large and small forward and reverse reeling begins to form. Before the double opening one must inhale, and on changing to the double opening one must exhale, exhaling all the way until the two hands have opened to their fixed point; this too is what brings this movement to a state of spirits-and- · 110 · one of the methods.

2. In the double closing (figure 98), it is required that the closing harbour an opening; the key is that before the double closing the qi must adhere to the back, and when the two palms cross and close the palms must turn outward and down, for thus the closing can harbour opening jin; if one has not attained parting within the closing, the jin will be balled up and stuck on the body, losing its elasticity and becoming the defect of collapsing.

3. In this posture, when the body squats down squarely upright, the kua opening must be broad. Thus the qi of the perineum will naturally rise from the coccyx, which is very beneficial. But when squatting, the height of the kua opening must not be lower than the knee, lest a sagging crotch form; if there is a sagging crotch it will make the outer sides of the two feet float emptily, and thereby cause sluggishness in the transformation of empty and full, so at the same time one should also avoid the defect of double weighting in the legs.

Twenty-Fifth Form: White Crane Spreads Its Wings

Action one: The body turns slightly left; the right foot steps up beside the left, touching its toes beside the left toes. At the same time, the right palm turns its arm forward-reeling and draws an arc leftward past before the abdomen, the palm facing up; the left palm reels reverse, passes before the face, and bending its elbow to the right joins above the right arm. (Figure 100, the front view of attached figure 100) The right foot steps out on the slant to the right front (southeast). What follows is the same as action two of the seventh form, "White Crane Spreads Its Wings". (Continuing to figures 31–32)

See the essential points of the seventh form, "White Crane Spreads Its Wings".

Twenty-Sixth Form: Diagonal Twist Step

Twenty-Seventh Form: Flash Through the Back

Action one is the same as action one of the ninth form, "First Withdrawal". (Continuing to figure 101)

Action two: The centre of gravity shifts onto the right leg; pivoting on the right heel, the body turns to the left rear (the chest turning to face north), and the right foot follows the turning body back in an arc, coming down with its toes beside the left foot. Action five: Pivoting on the left heel, the body turns rapidly to the right rear; the right foot, its ball of the foot adhering to the ground, turns half a circle to the right rear with the turning body, and then its heel kicks out to stamp the ground. As the body turns, · 113 · The right hand reels forward and turns inward until its palm faces outward, and as the body turns it presses down in an arc to beside the right kua, the palm facing down; the left palm, bending its arm, turns upward and pushes out forward and down past beside the left ear. (Figure 106, the front view of attached figure 106)

Action four of Flash Through the Back: the posture in which the left foot steps forward one step and the centre of gravity immediately shifts forward with the left leg becoming full, the left palm passing before the chest leftward and then being placed beside the left kua with the palm facing down-right, and the right palm reeling forward and extending forward with the palm facing up.

Essential points:

1. In action four (figure 105), the left foot's stepping up and the palms' extending forward must be in accord; in action five (figure 106), the right heel's landing and stamping the ground must be in accord with the right hand's pressing down and the left hand's pushing forward.

· 114 · 2. What qigong calls "opening the three passes" requires the qi to pass through the tailbone pass, the squeeze-spine pass, and the jade-pillow pass, and it involves the whole sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system of the spine. The sitting, lying, and standing exercises of qigong use a still method to let the qi pass the three passes spontaneously, whereas this "moving exercise" of Taijiquan seeks stillness within movement: in the process of when one part moves no part is unmoved, through single-minded motion one concentrates the will, so as to obtain "stillness" within movement. The boxing theory says: "If the mind is not still, then it is not single-minded, and the movements have no fixed direction at all." In the Taijiquan moving exercise, because of the mutual assistance of a movement with a definite direction and the intention, and because at the same time in the course of the moving exercise the inner jin and the outer form must attain the tailbone-centred and spirit-through-the-crown, qi sunk to the dantian and the sea's bottom, and chest-contained and back-raised, kua opened and crotch rounded, causing the qi to pass through the crotch — thus is this great circular path from the front-below to the back-above of the whole body trained. After days, it makes the qigong "opening of the three passes" come about of itself without being sought.

3. This posture is an exercise based entirely on opening through the spine. Figure 101 is the posture in which the cervical vertebrae pass through, figure 102 is the posture in which the upper thoracic vertebrae pass through, figure 104 is the posture in which the lower thoracic vertebrae pass through, figure 105 is the posture in which the lumbar vertebrae pass through, and figure 106 is the posture in which the sacral vertebrae pass through. This is to say only that a given figure acts mainly through certain joints, not that the other joints do not move, for Taijiquan is such that when one part moves no part is unmoved.

4. In the "Compendium of Chen-Style Taijiquan" (this book was written by Chen Xin and edited and printed by Chen Jifu, in two volumes, upper and lower), the form "Needle at the Bottom of the Sea" has the two legs opened sideways, with the right palm's tiger's mouth spread open and dropped between the two legs; this is definitely helpful for the effect of opening through the back and for the qi passing from the crotch backward and rising through the tailbone up the spine.

Action one: The two hands part to left and right with opening jin. (Figure 107, the front view of attached figure 107) What follows is the same as actions one, two, three, and four of the fourteenth form, "Cover Hand and Forearm Punch", only the directions differ: when the fourteenth form is completed the left foot is in the northeast and the right foot in the southwest, whereas · 115 · when this form is completed the left foot is in the southwest and the right foot in the northwest. Twenty-Ninth Form: Six Seals and Four Closings

Action one: The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity shifts back slightly; at the same time the two hands first each turn their arms in place and draw a small circle (to set the movement going), then the right hand in a large forward reeling turns its arm and reaches to the abdo- · 116 · forward, and the left hand with a small reverse reeling circles to before the chest, the two hands forming a closing jin. (Figure 110) The body turns slightly right, the centre of gravity shifts forward, the left leg becomes full; at the same time, the right hand turns its arm forward-reeling and the left palm reels slightly reverse, and the two hands, holding jin together, squeeze out in an arc to the upper right. (Figure 111)

Action two: The body turns left, the whole centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg, and the right foot is lifted forward. At the same time, the right hand reels forward and supports upward; the left hand reels reverse, turns its arm, and with the wrist joint on the back-of-hand side makes an arc warding-off to the upper left, the five fingers hanging down. See the essential points of the fourth form, "Six Seals and Four Closings".

Thirtieth Form: Single Whip

The action and the essential points are both the same as the fifth form, "Single Whip". (Figures 21–25, then continuing to figure 113)

Thirty-First Form: Wave Hands

Action one: The body turns left, the right knee slightly extended and not straightened. At the same time, the right hooked hand becomes a palm and reels forward, moving in an arc leftward up to before the right forehead, the palm facing left; the left palm reels forward from inside to outside-left, extended slightly, the arm not straightened, the palm facing down. (Figure 114) The body turns slightly right and the left foot draws half a step toward the right, touching with its toes, the right leg becoming full. At the same time, the right palm changes from forward reeling to reverse reeling and opens out to the right, its palm changing from facing down to facing right; the left palm, from the left, goes down and reels forward rightward past before the abdomen to the right of the body, the palm slanting to the upper right. (Figure 115) The body turns slightly left, and the left foot opens half a step sideways to the left. At the same time, the right hand falls in an arc, the palm facing down; the left hand changes from forward reeling to reverse reeling, turns its arm and turns the palm to face outward, and draws an arc upward. (Figure 116)

图 L1F113
Single Whip: the action and essential points are the same as the fifth form, "Single Whip".

· 118 · Action two: The centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg; the right foot steals a step to the left (east) from behind the left foot, and the body turns slightly right. At the same time the two hands reel forward: the left palm turns its arm, passes before the face, and reels reverse to transport leftward, its palm turning to face left; the right palm turns its arm, passes before the abdomen, and reels reverse to transport leftward and upward, its palm turning over to face the upper left. (Figure 117) The body continues to turn slightly right, and the left foot opens one step sideways to the left (east). At the same time the two hands reel forward: the left palm turns its arm and, from the left, goes down and reels reverse rightward past before the abdomen to transport upward, its palm slanting to the upper right; the right palm turns its arm and, from the left, goes up and transports rightward past before the face, its palm facing right. (Figure 118) The centre of gravity gradually shifts left, and the body turns slightly left. At the same time, the right palm transports downward in an arc, the palm facing down; the left hand reels forward, turns its arm and turns the palm to face outward, and reels reverse to transport upward (see figure 116).

Actions three and four both repeat action two. (According to figures 117–118, then continuing to 116–118, then continuing to 119)

· 119 · then continuing to 119)

Essential points:

1. In this posture attention must be paid to the empty-full requirement of upper and lower following one another; check whether one has clearly manifested this requirement: that is, when a certain hand rotates to ward-off upward as empty, the centre of gravity must gradually shift onto the leg below that hand, and that leg then becomes full; as soon as the upward ward-off has passed and changed to a downward ward-off, that leg must then change to empty. In this way the empty and full of the two hands and the empty and full of the two feet are unified within the whole of upper-lower empty-full, forming everywhere always this one empty and one full (except when lifting a leg to stand alone or breaking free of a lock), attaining the requirement of nimble exchange of intention and qi, and producing the flavour of round liveliness like a pearl.

2. Because this posture steps laterally, it very readily manifests the requirement for a rounded crotch. A rounded crotch is the form that must obtain for the screw-like hidden jin of the legs to arise. A correct and standard rounded crotch is simply not to form a pointed crotch when standing high nor a sagging crotch when standing low; it requires that the movement be performed neither pointed nor sagging, so as to attain a correct rounded crotch.

3. Wave Hands is the only form in Taijiquan that trains the great silk-reeling of double-forward changing to double-reverse. This posture must fully manifest the function of waist and spine united as one, becoming a spherical axle; the key is that it is not a planar left-right silk-reeling, but has a component of inner-outer silk-reeling, which leads. Through this requirement, one can further check whether the "qi adhering to the back" adheres tightly and whether the waist, like a round axle, is roundly alive.

Thirty-Second Form: High Pat on Horse

Action one: The body turns left, the centre of gravity shifts left, and the right foot steps slanting half a step to the right front (southwest). At the same time, the left hand reels reverse and is drawn back to before the chest; the right hand reels forward, closes and gathers leftward past before the abdomen, and the two arms cross before the chest, the right arm outside. (Figure 120) The two arms first close slightly, contracting the crossed circle, and then the two hands reel reverse and open out separately to left and right, the palms slanting down; the centre of gravity shifts slightly right while the two arms close slightly, and shifts left again when the two hands open out. (Figure 121)

Action two: The body turns left, the centre of gravity shifts onto the right leg. At the same time, the right hand turns its arm re- · 120 · reels to beside the right hand, the palm slanting inward; the left hand reels slightly forward and closes rightward, the palm facing up.

图 L1F120
Action one of High Pat on Horse: the posture in which the body turns left with the centre of gravity shifting left and the right foot stepping slanting half a step to the right front (southwest), the left hand reeling reverse and being drawn back to before the chest, and the right hand reeling forward and closing and gathering leftward past before the abdomen, the two arms crossing before the chest with the right arm outside.
图 L1F121
Continuing from figure 120: the posture in which the two arms first close slightly, contracting the crossed circle, and then the two hands reel reverse and open out separately to left and right with the palms slanting down, the centre of gravity shifting slightly right while the two arms close slightly and shifting left again when the two hands open out.

(Figure 122) Pivoting on the right heel, the body continues to turn left, the whole centre of gravity shifts onto the right leg, and the left foot is drawn back, passing inside the right ankle to step back (west), touching with its toes beside the right foot, the distance between the two feet equal to shoulder width. At the same time, the left palm bends its arm and reels reverse to draw back to the left side of the waist, the palm facing up; the right palm reels forward and pushes out, the palm facing outward. (Figures 123–124, the front view of attached figure 124)

图 L1F122
Action two of High Pat on Horse: the posture in which the body turns left and the centre of gravity shifts onto the right leg, the right hand turning its arm and reeling reverse to beside the right hand with the palm slanting inward and the left hand reeling slightly forward and closing rightward with the palm facing up, the two arms extended forward.
图 L1F123
Continuing from figure 122: the posture in which, pivoting on the right heel, the body continues to turn left with the whole centre of gravity shifting onto the right leg, and the left foot is drawn back, passing inside the right ankle to step back (west), touching with its toes beside the right foot with the distance between the two feet equal to shoulder width, the left palm bending its arm and reeling reverse to draw back to the left side of the waist with the palm facing up, and the right palm reeling forward and pushing out with the palm facing outward.

Essential points:

1. In the latter part of action two, the right palm's pushing out, the left palm's drawing in, and the left foot's stepping back · 121 · must be coordinated and made one.

2. This posture follows directly upon the double opening of Wave Hands, and therefore in doing the closing-and-opening movement one must pay attention to the requirement that "when you intend to close you must first part, and when you intend to open you must first let go". That is, before closing, first sink the roots of the two palms down, then close them together; and after closing, before opening again, one must first tighten the closing circle a little, then open out doubly to left and right.

图 L1F124
The last phase of action two of High Pat on Horse: the posture (rear view) in which, pivoting on the right heel, the body turns left and the left foot is drawn back, passing inside the right ankle to step back and touching with its toes beside the right foot, the left palm bending its arm and reeling reverse to draw back to the left side of the waist while the right palm reels forward and pushes out, whereupon the two hands come together and the two arms extend forward.
图 L1F124附图
The front view of the same movement as figure 124.

3. When the right hand circles a small circle and draws back beside the right ear, one must have the qi adhering to the back and first use supporting jin. Only when the support is full and then released can one let out a kind of rotating pressing jin.

4. In this posture, when the right hand pushes forward in the high pat, it must have the force to support all eight directions. The difference between this posture and the Diagonal Twist Step is that in the Diagonal Twist Step the right hand, passing beside the right ear, uses jin that separates to left and right; whereas this posture uses jin that opens front and back while harbouring a closing, and it requires that there be no defect of gaps or bumps nor interruption of inner jin in the silk-reeling path.

Thirty-Third Form: Right Brush-Foot

Action one: The right hand reels slightly forward and turns over downward to before the abdomen, the palm facing left, the fingers pointing down; the left hand, from the side of the waist, turns its arm and reels reverse to before the chest, the palm facing up. (Figure 125, the front view of attached figure 125. The posture in figure 125 comes after the front view of figure 125, and is already at the moment of being about to kick out to the right.) The body turns slightly right, the centre of gravity still on the right leg; at the same time, · 122 · with the two hands, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, and the left hand adhering to the inner side of the right forearm, ward-off outward with the right forearm, at shoulder height. (Figure 126, the front view of attached figure 126)

Action two: The body turns slightly left. At the same time, the left hand reels reverse, goes down from the right and opens out leftward past before the abdomen, the palm facing right; the right palm reels forward and shifts slightly downward, the palm facing down, and the two arms open out (at this point the elbow tips sink downward, which is opening harbouring closing). (Figure 127, the front view of attached figure 127) The body turns slightly right, the right hand turns its arm forward-reeling and closes inward to the left of before the chest, and the left hand, from the left, goes up and draws an arc rightward to above the right arm, the two arms crossing; at the same time the left foot, passing before the right foot, steps across sideways to the right, the toes pointing forward. (Figure 128, the front view of attached figure 128)

The main action of Brush-Foot is the opening of a large inner double forward reeling changing to the closing of a large double forward reeling; when the two arms close doubly, the left leg steps across, changing from empty to full; at the same time, the right leg changes to · 124 · be empty, that is, one kicks up with the right foot, and at this moment the two arms change to a large double reverse reeling, patting and brushing to left and right; at this time attention should be paid to the little fingers of the two hands. In the course of this brush-foot with large forward and large reverse reeling, The key to making the left leg stand alone steadily lies in the flat, straight action of the right instep that kicks up.

Thirty-Fourth Form: Left Brush-Foot

Action one: The right foot is drawn back and comes down to the right (east) with its toes turned out and planted, the body turning right at the same time, the centre of gravity shifting onto the right leg, and the left heel lifting off the ground; at the same time, the two hands reel forward, going down from left and right, and gather and cross before the chest. (Figure 130, the rear view of attached figure 130) The body turns slightly right; at the same time, the two hands reel forward and go up, opening out to left and right past before the face, the palms facing outward. (Figure 131)

· 125 · Action two: The left foot, its instep stretched flat, kicks up to the left front; at the same time, the left palm reels reverse to meet and strike (brush) the left instep, and the right palm also follows, reeling reverse to pat down to the right rear. (Figure 132)

图 L1F131

图 L1F132

Essential points:

1. In the conversion of one closing and one opening, one must maintain stability; that is, when the centre of gravity moves onto the right leg, one must raise the left leg by the closing jin of the two hands. At the same time, when the centre of gravity shifts right, the body must be centred and upright.

2. One must raise the left leg when the two hands open out to left and right, and then kick the left foot upward; the direction of the kick is midway between the left side and the front, that is, it is best at 45 degrees to the boxing path.

Thirty-Fifth Form: Heel Kick

Action one: The left foot is drawn back and lifted, and, pivoting on the right heel, the body turns 135 degrees to the left rear; at the same time, the two hands cross before the chest with forward and reverse reeling; as the body turns, the two palms become fists, reeling reverse one circle and crossing with closing jin before the chest. (Figure 133, the front view of attached figure 133)

Action two: Immediately the left toes tilt up and the left heel kicks out to the left (west); at the same time the two fists are raised and, passing before the chest, are issued separately to left and right, the fists' centres facing down. (Figure · 126 · 134, the front view of attached figure 134)

图 L1F133

Essential points:

1. When the body turns, one must remain stable; in turning, the instep of the lifted left foot must be stretched as flat as possible so that the toes point down, to lighten the sagging weight of the left leg. The turn must use the momentum of the two arms' double reverse reeling to carry the body around. For this reason some call it "Hanging on the Tree and Kicking the Foot", because as the two arms reel doubly reverse above, it is as though the two hands were hung on a tree. In this posture one must also pay attention to the requirements of standing with the body centred and upright, qi sunk to the dantian, and the crown jin not lost.

Thirty-Sixth Form: Forward Wading Twist Step

Action one: The left foot is drawn back and lifted; at the same time, the two hands become palms, the left hand reeling forward and drawing an arc to before the chest, and the right hand reeling slightly reverse, both palms facing right. (Figure 135) The left foot's toes turn out and come down to the left (southwest), and the body turns left. At the same time, the left hand reels forward and turns its arm to before the chest, the palm facing right-front; the right palm reels reverse to above the left forearm, the palm facing left-front, and the two arms cross. (Figure 136)

Action two is the same as action two of the tenth form, "Forward Wading Twist Step", only the direction differs. In the tenth form the right foot steps out on the slant to the southeast, whereas in this posture the right foot steps out on the slant to the northwest. (Figure 137)

Thirty-Seventh Form: Strike the Ground with the Fist

Action two: The body turns slightly left. At the same time, the left fist reels reverse, bends its elbow and is raised to the upper left, the fist's centre facing down; the right fist reels reverse and strikes downward to the front (reeling reverse one small circle from outside to inside), the fist's centre facing inward. (Figure 140, the front view of attached figure 140)

The front view of the same movement as figure 139.

· 129 · Essential points:

1. The emphasis of this posture is that in the prone crouch one must attain the requirement that "the tailbone is centred and the spirit passes through the crown": only when the tailbone is centred will the body not topple forward; that is, because the tail vertebra presses down, the whole spine can be threaded through; so long as the spine has sufficient elasticity (with the great road of the three passes opened), one can spring up with a single bounce, and no heavy pressure can hold it down; whereas if the tailbone topples over and loses its elasticity, then one who has crouched to the ground can rise no more.

2. In the prone crouch the crown jin must not be lost; that is, because the two fists, with the jin of double forward reeling, draw a circle against the ground in opposition, this not only kneads and moves the back but also turns a small circle on the crown of the head as well. Hence it is also called "The Immortal's Single Grasp", which is that after grasping one circle it becomes a fist, and then turns another circle on the ground and strikes downward, just as, after brushing aside the dust on the ground, one plants a thing into it; therefore it is also called Planting Fist.

Action one: The body turns right, the centre of gravity is on the left foot, and the right leg is slightly extended and not straightened; at the same time, the left fist, bending its arm, shifts slightly downward as the body turns, and the right fist turns its arm, bends its elbow and bends its wrist and is raised, both fists' centres facing inward. (Figure 141, the front view of attached figure 141) Pivoting on the left heel · 130 · heel, the body continues to turn right, and the foot is drawn back half a step with the turning body, touching with its toes. At the same time, the right fist reels forward and drops to the right side of the body, the fist's centre facing up; the left fist reels reverse, comes from the left to the front, bends its elbow and is raised, the fist's centre facing inward. (Figure 142) The centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg, and the left leg squats down (strengthening the elasticity of the left leg); at the same time, the right fist turns its arm, reels reverse and is raised in an arc from behind the body, and the left fist reels reverse and drops to the left side of the body. (Figure 143)

Action two: The centre of gravity shifts forward, the right heel lands and is planted firmly, and the left foot, its instep stretched flat, kicks up forward and upward; at the same time the two fists become palms and reel reverse, the right hand forward and up, the left hand back and down · 131 · arcs, the right palm's centre facing forward and the left palm's centre facing inward-down. (Figure 144, the front view of attached figure 144) Before the left foot has landed, the right foot pushes off the ground and leaps up, kicking up forward and upward with its instep stretched flat, and the right palm immediately meets and strikes the right instep to the front, whereupon the left foot lands and the left palm, as the right palm strikes the right instep, is held level to the left. (Figures 145–146, the front view of attached figure 146)

Essential points:
