· 132 · Kick Twice is an exercise for training the leap: the two feet leave the ground one after the other and kick out, and so it is also called Kicking Twice. The Kick Twice of Chen-style Taijiquan has four methods of practice, which may be chosen according to the practitioner's bodily strength and purpose. Here they are listed in order from easy to difficult:

(1) Using a single kick in place of the double kick: that is, kicking up with the right foot alone and meeting the right instep with the right palm, without the process of both feet leaving the ground — but in practice one must still have the lifting jin of the double kick;

(2) Practising by the method given in the action description above, whose distinguishing feature is that the body's leap and the second kick are assisted by enlarging the silk-reeling circle with a great opening and expanding;

(3) Reducing the movement and shrinking the silk-reeling circle to a single reel, so that the two feet leave the ground and kick up one after the other;

(4) After Strike the Ground with the Fist, turning the body over once, whereupon the two feet leave the ground and kick up one after the other; this is the simplest kind, and also the most difficult kind.

Thirty-Ninth Form: Beast-Head Posture

(Also called Guarding-the-Heart Punch, or Tiger-Beating Posture)

Action one: The right foot falls but has not yet touched the ground when the left foot leaps up; at the same time the two hands, from the left, go up and reel forward warding-off to the upper right (the two hands must have leading jin, leading the body to rise into the air, like the shooting posture in basketball. If the practitioner is weak, he may land the right foot first and then lift the left foot, omitting the process of leaving the ground). (Figure 147. This figure continues downward from the front view of figure 146, and therefore from figure 147 to 151 one should still perform the movement with the chest facing east.) Immediately the right foot lands and the right leg squats down, and then the left foot steps out sideways to the left rear (northwest) on the slant, the left leg dropping low with the left knee slightly bent; the body turns right at the same time; and the two palms, as the body turns, drop to the right front, the palms facing down-right. (Figure 148) The body turns left, the centre of gravity shifts left, the left leg bows and the right leg is straightened with the right knee slightly bent; at the same time the two palms become fists, and turning their arms, the left reels reverse and the right reels forward: the left fist, passing before the abdomen, reels to the upper left so that its centre faces left, and the right fist reels from the right · 133 · to before the chest, its centre facing upper-left (forming the Left Tiger-Beating Posture). (Figure 149)

图 L1F147
Action one of Beast-Head Posture: the posture in which the right foot falls but has not yet touched the ground when the left foot leaps up, and the two hands, from the left, go up and reel forward warding-off to the upper right (the two hands having leading jin that leads the body to rise into the air, like the shooting posture in basketball).
图 L1F148
Continuing from figure 147: the posture in which the right foot then lands and the right leg squats down, and then the left foot steps out sideways to the left rear (northwest) on the slant with the left leg dropping low and the left knee slightly bent, the body turning right at the same time and the two palms dropping to the right front as the body turns with the palms facing down-right.
图 L1F149
Continuing from figure 148: the posture in which the body turns left with the centre of gravity shifting left and the left leg bowing while the right leg is straightened, and the two palms become fists with their arms turning, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, the left fist reeling from before the abdomen to the upper left with its centre facing left and the right fist reeling from the right to before the chest with its centre facing upper-left, forming the Left Tiger-Beating Posture.

Action two: The body turns slightly right, the right foot shifts slightly left and touches with its toes; at the same time, the left fist reels reverse, bends its arm and is drawn inward to head height, and the right fist reels forward, bends its arm and is drawn inward to before the chest. (Figure 150) The body continues to turn slightly right, the left leg squats down, and the right heel, its inner side adhering to the ground, sweeps out to the right front (south, slightly east) into a low stance; at the same time the two fists, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, sink down as the body squats. (Figure 151) The body continues to turn slightly right, the centre of gravity shifts right, and the right leg bows. At the same time the two hands turn their arms and reel reverse: the left fist shifts right with the turning body, its centre facing right-rear; the right fist, passing downward before the chest, reels to the right side of the abdomen, its centre facing inward. (Figure 152. The posture shown in this figure is the front aspect, but in fact the places where the two feet stand are still the same as in the previous figure, unmoved, and from figure 152 to 154 too the movement is still performed with the chest facing east.) The body continues to turn slightly right. At the same time, the left fist, passing before the chest, reels forward leftward to before the left waist, its centre facing inward; the right fist, from the right rear, goes up, turns its arm, bends its elbow and reels reverse to beside the right ear, its centre facing down. (Figure 153) The body turns left, the centre of gravity shifts slightly left, the left knee bends slightly, and the left fist is drawn slightly inward to before the abdomen, · 134 · The right fist turns its arm and bends its wrist inward, extending forward, both fists' centres facing inward. (Figure 154)

Essential points:

1. This posture requires a larger component of inner-outer silk-reeling, and requires that within the inner-outer movement one attain joint-by-joint continuity and the whole body as one family. Compared with the previous postures, this needs further practice. This form readily and clearly manifests the requirement that when one part moves, all move.

图 L1F150
The first phase of action two of Beast-Head Posture: the posture in which the body turns slightly right and the right foot shifts slightly left and touches with its toes, the left fist reeling reverse, bending its arm and being drawn inward to head height, and the right fist reeling forward, bending its arm and being drawn inward to before the chest.
图 L1F151
Continuing from figure 150: the posture in which the body continues to turn slightly right, the left leg squats down, and the right heel, its inner side adhering to the ground, sweeps out to the right front (south, slightly east) into a low stance, the two fists, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, sinking down as the body squats.
图 L1F152
Continuing from figure 151: the posture in which the body continues to turn slightly right with the centre of gravity shifting right and the right leg bowing, and the two hands turn their arms and reel reverse, the left fist shifting right with the turning body with its centre facing right-rear and the right fist, passing downward before the chest, reeling to the right side of the abdomen with its centre facing inward.
图 L1F153
Continuing from figure 152: the posture in which the body continues to turn slightly right, the left fist, passing before the chest, reeling forward leftward to before the left waist with its centre facing inward, and the right fist, from the right rear, going up, turning its arm, bending its elbow and reeling reverse to beside the right ear with its centre facing down.
图 L1F154
Continuing from figure 153: the posture in which the body turns left with the centre of gravity shifting slightly left and the left knee bending slightly, the left fist being drawn slightly inward to before the abdomen, and the right fist turning its arm and bending its wrist inward and extending forward, both fists' centres facing inward.

2. Because the inner-outer silk-reeling component is large, it promotes the governing function of the waist and spine acting together, and within that governance the back holds first place (as the chief · 135 · silk-reeling). Therefore this posture is one of the main forms in Taijiquan for training the inner-outer and forward-reverse silk-reeling jin.

3. When this posture is performed, the crotch opening is required to be low (but not lower than the knee); when it changes the empty and full of the legs, one especially readily feels the qi of the perineum (the middle part between the front and rear yin) rushing up to the tailbone. This is the main requirement of the rounded crotch manifested in this posture.

4. In this posture, the ward-off jin of the outer forward reeling and the ward-off jin of the inner reverse reeling require that, in turning the corners and changing the warding-off silk-reeling surface, the spiral action can reach the skin, with no defect existing within; that is to say, only a spiral on the skin can attain the pulling-and-moving effect of silk-reeling jin (whether the silk-reeling jin can reach the skin surface without defect is most readily manifested in this posture).

Fortieth Form: Whirlwind Kick
图 L1F155
The first phase of action one of Whirlwind Kick: the posture in which the body turns slightly left with the centre of gravity shifting left and the left leg bowing slightly, the left hand reeling forward and turning over downward to before the left abdomen with its centre facing up, and the right hand reeling forward and turning slightly to the right front to before the abdomen with its centre facing inward-up.
图 L1F156
Continuing from figure 155: the posture in which the body turns right with the centre of gravity shifting right and the right leg bowing while the left leg is extended but not straight, and the two fists become palms and reel reverse.
图 L1F157
Continuing from figure 156: the posture in which the centre of gravity shifts onto the right leg and the left foot is lifted with its knee bent, the two hands separating up and down before the chest.

Action one: The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity shifts left, and the left leg bows slightly. At the same time the left hand reels forward and turns over downward to before the left abdomen, its centre facing up; the right hand reels forward and turns slightly to the right front to before the abdomen, its centre facing inward-up. (Figure 155. In this figure the places where the two feet stand are still the same as in the previous figure, unmoved, and the chest still faces east; the movement of this posture begins from the chest facing east.) The body turns right, the centre of gravity shifts right, the right leg bows and the left leg is extended but not straight; at the same time the two fists become palms and reel re- · 136 · reel, and open out to the right past before the chest. (Figure 156) The two hands reel reverse, going right and down, then change to the right reeling forward and the left reeling reverse and turn upward on the ground: the left palm, passing before the abdomen, draws an arc to the upper left until level with the head, the palm facing outward; the right palm reels in an arc to before the abdomen, the palm facing left. At the same time the centre of gravity shifts left, and the right foot is lifted forward. (Figure 157)

Action two: The right toes turn out and the right foot steps forward half a step, the body weight shifts forward, and the left foot is lifted with it; as the right foot is lifted and steps up, at the same time the two hands reel forward, the right palm pushing forward and the left palm dropping in an arc rightward past before the face, the left forearm coming to rest on the right forearm, the two arms crossing with closing jin, both palms facing down. (Figure 158) The two arms reel forward and open out to left and right, both palms facing back; at the same time, the left foot, from the lower rear, wraps up in an arc with wrapping jin, meeting and striking with its inner side against the left palm. (Figure 159. At this point the chest should face south.) Pivoting on the right heel, the body turns to the right rear (180 degrees, the chest facing north); as the body turns, at the same time the two hands change from opening to closing inward, crossing before the chest with the left arm on top; and the left foot, too, sweeps around from above to the right rear with the turning body. (Figure 160) The body continues to turn slightly right, and the left foot lands; at the same time the two hands shrink the closing-jin circle, the left palm facing down and the right palm facing inward. (Figure 161, the front view of attached figure 161. The front view of figure 161 continues immediately after figure 160, and in fact the chest faces north, but from figure 161 onward it already agrees with the direction in the action description.)

图 L1F158
The first phase of action two of Whirlwind Kick: the posture in which the right toes turn out and the right foot steps forward half a step with the body weight shifting forward and the left foot being lifted with it, and as the right foot is lifted and steps up, the two hands reel forward, the right palm pushing forward and the left palm dropping in an arc rightward past before the face, the left forearm coming to rest on the right forearm, the two arms crossing with closing jin, both palms facing down.
图 L1F159
Continuing from figure 158: the posture in which the two arms reel forward and open out to left and right with both palms facing back, and at the same time the left foot, from the lower rear, wraps up in an arc with wrapping jin, meeting and striking with its inner side against the left palm (at this point the chest faces south).

· 137 · Essential points:

1. Whirlwind Kick is a sweeping-leg jin with one foot standing and one foot in the air; the first four circles manifest the opening and closing before the whirlwind sweep (figures 158–161 complete the whirlwind kick's sweeping action).

2. Figure 159 shows the whirlwind kick's sweeping lift: after the left palm strikes sideways with the left foot, the body turns; in the course of the turn, the left leg is required to turn across slightly bent and not straight, but it is not permitted to turn across with the leg bent up; this is training for leg jin and for balance on the right hand, and needs some time of practice.

3. In order to suit different practitioners, Chen-style Taijiquan divides some movements into easy and difficult methods of practice. Another method of practice for this posture is (beginning from figure 158): first step the right leg forward half a step and lift the left heel, with the two hands crossed before the chest; then the left foot kicks up forward (not a sideways sweep), and after the kick one bends the knee, draws the leg in, turns the body and drops down (not turning across with the leg straight); after the left leg is planted, the right foot is lifted and kicks out sideways with the heel. Its difference is that the sweeping jin is removed, changed into the two movements of kicking the foot and heel-kicking.

图 L1F160

· 138 · the sweeping jin is removed, changed into the two movements of kicking the foot and heel-kicking.

Forty-First Form: Heel Kick

Action one: The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity shifts slightly left; at the same time, the two palms' centres turn over to face forward, and the crossed circle contracts, whereupon the two palms reel reverse and open out to left and right past before the abdomen (the mind dwelling on the two little fingers); the body turns back to square as the two hands separate, and the crotch opening sinks further. (Figure 162) The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity shifts left, the right foot is drawn back and touches with its toes beside the left foot; at the same time, the two palms become fists and reel forward, going down from left and right to hold jin together before the abdomen, the two forearms crossing with the left arm on top, both fists' centres facing inward-down. (Figure 163, the front view of attached figure 163) The body continues to turn slightly left (the whole body's ward-off jin not lost), the two arms shrink the crossed circle (to store jin), and the right foot is lifted. (Figure 164, the front view of attached figure 146)

Action two: The two fists reel forward and issue jin to left and right; at the same time the right foot hooks up its toes and kicks out to the right side with the heel, issuing jin. (Figure 165)

Essential points:

1. The difference between this posture and the thirty-fifth form, "Heel Kick", is that the former form kicks the left foot while this one kicks the right foot. In doing this Heel Kick, one must first prepare a full storing of jin before kicking, and then issue, so as to attain the requirement of "storing and then issuing".

图 L1F162
Action one of Heel Kick: the posture in which the body turns slightly left with the centre of gravity shifting slightly left, and the two palms' centres turn over to face forward and the crossed circle contracts, whereupon the two palms reel reverse and open out to left and right past before the abdomen (the mind dwelling on the two little fingers), the body turning back to square as the two hands separate and the crotch opening sinking further.
图 L1F163
Continuing from figure 162: the posture (rear view) in which the body turns slightly left with the centre of gravity shifting left and the right foot drawn back to touch with its toes beside the left foot, and the two palms become fists and reel forward, going down from left and right to hold jin together before the abdomen, the two forearms crossing with the left arm on top and both fists' centres facing inward-down.
图 L1F163附图
The front view of the same movement as figure 163.

Forty-Second Form: Cover-Hand Forearm Punch

Action one: The right foot lifts its knee and is drawn back, the left leg standing alone; at the same time, the right fist reels forward and falls before the crotch, and the left fist reels forward and drops slightly downward. (Figure 166) With the left heel as pivot, the body turns right (east). At the same time, the right arm turns outward and reels forward inward, going up from before the crotch, and following the body's turn rolls down in an arc to the right side beside the right leg, the right arm hanging down with the fist's centre facing up; the left fist turns its arm and reels reverse from inner-low to outer-high, raising the left forearm upright with the fist's centre facing inward. (Figure 167)

图 L1F164
Continuing from figure 163: the earlier part of action two of Heel Kick, the posture (rear view) in which the body continues to turn slightly left, the two arms shrink the crossed circle to store jin, and the right foot is lifted.

The front view of the same movement as figure 164.
图 L1F165
Action two of Heel Kick: the posture in which the two fists reel forward and issue jin to left and right, while the right foot hooks up its toes and kicks out to the right side with the heel, issuing jin.

Action two: The two fists become palms and meet before the chest, both reeling forward and dropping, the right hand slightly lower than the left, the right leg still lifted. (Figure 168) The two palms rise from left and right, leading the body up (like the double leading jin of two hands shooting a basketball), the right toes lifting up. (Figures 169–170; after the body is led up in the two figures, it should still face the same direction as figure 168, and the two · 140 · figures show its front and side) the right foot presses the ground flat with the palm of the foot and extends, the body turns slightly right, the left foot steps forward-left (northeast), both legs bend at the knees and squat; at the same time, the right palm becomes a fist and reels reverse to before the left abdomen, and the left palm reels reverse and draws in to ward-off before the chest, the left palm placed crossed above the right elbow. (Figure 171)

Continuing from figure 166: the posture in which, with the left heel as pivot, the body turns right (east), the right arm turning outward and reeling forward inward, going up from before the crotch and following the body's turn rolling down in an arc to the right side beside the right leg with the right arm hanging down and the fist's centre facing up, while the left fist turns its arm and reels reverse from inner-low to outer-high, raising the left forearm upright with the fist's centre facing inward.

Continuing from above: the posture in which the right foot presses the ground flat with the palm of the foot and extends, the body turns slightly right, the left foot steps forward-left (northeast) with both legs bending at the knees and squatting, while the right palm becomes a fist and reels reverse to before the left abdomen and the left palm reels reverse and draws in to ward-off before the chest, the left palm placed crossed above the right elbow.

· 141 · Action three: The right fist turns its arm and reels forward to the lower right, and the left palm reels reverse and separates in an arc to the upper left, the right fist's centre facing down and the left palm's centre facing outward. (Continuing from figure 52; figure 51 is the changed posture of figure 171)

Action four is the same as action three of the fourteenth form, "Cover-Hand Forearm Punch". (Continuing from figures 52–54)

Essential points:

1. The right leg, after the kick, does not land. Because the two fists reel forward and are drawn back, they lead the right leg to be drawn back; in the course of drawing back, because the two fists turn over — the left forward and the right backward — the drawn-back right leg and the standing left leg are stabilised.

2. One must raise the crown (ding jin), sink the qi downward, drop the shoulders and drop the elbows, and set the left foot flat and firmly planted. Then one is naturally stable in standing alone.

3. The emphasis of this form and of the fourteenth form, "Cover-Hand Forearm Punch", lies alike in issuing jin; only the ward-off and connecting movements differ.

4. In this form, after turning the body and kicking, it turns into the two hands turning up and down to hold jin together (figure 167); after holding, the two hands separate, producing opening jin (figure 168); after separating, the two hands immediately rise and the two palms lift up, like holding a basketball and leaping up and throwing it into the basket — in this way the body can be led up.

Forty-Third Form: Small Catch and Strike

Action one: The body turns right. At the same time, the right fist becomes a palm with a large reverse reeling and a bent elbow, the palm's centre facing down and the tiger's mouth open; the left palm goes from the left flank with a small reverse reeling to below the chest. (Figure 172, the other side view of attached figure 172) The right foot's toes turn outward and step forward; at the same time, the right palm reels forward and turns over so that its centre faces up, and the left palm reels forward and lays across the right forearm. (Figure 173) Immediately after, the left foot takes a big step forward, the toes turning slightly inward, in a low stance; at the same time the two palms reel reverse and turn over, the right palm downward and the left palm forward-down separating, chopping out suddenly with the heel of the palm. (Figure 174)

· 142 · · 143 · Action two: Immediately after, the body turns slightly right. At the same time, the right palm reels forward and falls from the upper right beside the right ribs, its centre facing the ribs; the left palm reels forward and turns up from below, the forearm raised upright with its centre facing forward-up. (Figure 175) The centre of gravity shifts left, the left leg forms a bow stance, and the body turns slightly left. At the same time, the left palm reels reverse, turning its arm and dropping slightly, and the right palm reels forward from above to the left, the two palms crossing and closing inward to issue jin to the left (east). (Figure 176)

Essential points:

1. The movements of this form must be completed in one continuous run without the least pause; the aim is to give way along the demanded jin — that is, to follow the demanded direction without butting against it, and to free it through the two palms' reverse reeling and double splitting.

2. The last movement of this form must, without pausing, shift the centre of gravity left, form a bow stance with the left leg, bring the two palms together to the end point, and suddenly strike crossed to the left; at this moment one must attend to the heels of the two palms.

3. The fist form Small Catch and Strike divides into left and right parts of movement, yet it is expressed as one whole; the aim is to employ the reeling-silk spiral, complying with the demanded jin, going from the two palms' double forward reeling and double reverse-reeling opening jin, then turning into double forward closing jin and double reverse issuing jin.

Action one: The body turns slightly right. At the same time, the two palms become fists, the right fist turning its arm and reeling reverse, extending forward-down with its centre facing down; the left fist reels reverse and is drawn back from the lower left, drawing a small circle and closing to lay on the right arm, its centre facing down; the centre of gravity is still on the left, the left leg forming a bow stance. (Figure 177) The centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg; with the left heel as pivot, the body turns to the right rear, the right foot drawing in half a step, its · 144 · toes touching the ground; at the same time the two fists with a small forward reeling hold jin together before the chest, both centres facing inward-up. (Figure 178) The two fists become palms and, with a double forward reeling, tighten the crossed circle and then drop; then they turn their arms into double reverse reeling and separate to left and right, and as they are about to reach the end point they turn into double forward reeling, releasing jin with the backs of the hands, the two palms' centres facing each other; the right toes still touch the ground. (Figure 179)

Continuing from figure 178: the posture in which the two fists become palms and with a double forward reeling tighten the crossed circle and then drop, then turn their arms into double reverse reeling and separate to left and right, and as they are about to reach the end point turn into double forward reeling to release jin with the backs of the hands, the two palms' centres facing each other.

Action two of Embrace the Head and Push the Mountain: the posture in which the body turns left, the two palms shift slightly left with the body's turn and the two elbows sink, the two palms being drawn back to beside the two ears — the right reeling forward and the left reeling reverse — with their centres facing the two cheeks, and the centre of gravity shifts slightly further left with the right toes still touching the ground.
图 L1F181
Continuing from figure 180: the posture in which the right foot steps forward half a step and, as the centre of gravity moves forward, the right leg bends at the knee and becomes solid and the body turns right, the two palms dropping slightly to the right from beside the two cheeks and, with the body's turn, reeling forward and pushing out, the mind dwelling on the two little fingers with the palms' centres facing outward.

Action two: The body turns left; at the same time, the two palms shift slightly left with the body's turn, the two elbows sink, and the two palms are drawn back to beside the two ears — the right reeling forward and the left reeling reverse — with their centres facing the two cheeks; at the same time the centre of gravity shifts slightly further left, the right toes still touching the ground. (Figure 180) The right foot steps forward half a · 145 · step, and as the centre of gravity moves forward the right leg bends at the knee and becomes solid and the body turns right; at the same time, the two palms drop slightly to the right from beside the two cheeks, and then with the body's turn reel forward and push out; the mind dwells on the two little fingers, the palms' centres facing outward. (Figure 181)

Essential points:

1. The essential point of this form lies in reaching the end point by changing from double reverse opening into double forward reeling. One uses the release of the two backs of the hands and the sinking of the elbows, and by sinking the elbows turns the two palms to beside the two ears, forming the first half of the Embrace-the-Head form.

2. Among those that use the two palms joined to press jin forward, there are three kinds of jin in the first-route fist set: (1) "Six Seals and Four Closings", which is the two hands showing forward a jin of four parts closing and six parts sealing; (2) "Double Push Hands", which is the two hands pushing jin out forward with the heels of the palms; (3) "Embrace the Head and Push the Mountain", which is the two hands pressing forward, storing slightly, opening into a big step with the right knee in a bow stance, the buttocks not extending or contracting, and issuing jin from the spine.

3. These forms that press the two palms forward differ in their inner jin, as stated above. In addition, while pushing the mountain and releasing jin, one must also use exhalation (emitting a "xu" sound) to match the sinking down of the heels of the palms and let it out together, so that the push of the mountain is exactly right.

Forty-Fifth Form: Three Palm Changes

Action one: The body turns right. At the same time, the left hand reels forward and turns over, extending slightly forward so that its centre faces up; the right hand reels forward, bending its elbow and drawing in to the upper side of the left arm. At the same time one coordinates with the left knee reeling inward and the right knee reeling outward. (Figure 182) The body turns slightly left. At the same time, the right palm reels forward and turns, turning its wrist and reeling reverse, and pushes out with the palm held sideways; the left palm reels forward, bending its elbow and drawing in to before the chest with its centre facing upper-right. At the same time one coordinates with the right knee reeling outward and the left knee reeling inward (completing the first palm change). (Figure 183)

Action two: The body turns slightly right again. At the same time, the left palm, going up past before the chest, reels forward and turns into reverse reeling, pushing out with the palm held sideways; the right palm reels forward, bending its elbow and drawing in to before the chest with its centre facing upper-left. At the same time one coordinates with the right knee reeling outward and the left knee reeling inward (completing the second palm · 146 · palm). (Figure 184) The body turns slightly left, the right knee bows further forward; at the same time, the right palm, going up past before the chest, reels forward and turns into reverse reeling, pushing out with the palm held sideways; the left palm turns its arm and reels forward, dropping with its centre slanting inward-right. At the same time one coordinates with the right knee reeling outward and the left knee reeling inward (completing the third palm change). (Figure 185)

图 L1F182
Action one of Three Palm Changes: the posture in which the body turns right, the left hand reels forward and turns over, extending slightly forward so its centre faces up, and the right hand reels forward, bending its elbow and drawing in to the upper side of the left arm, with the left knee reeling inward and the right knee reeling outward.
图 L1F183
Continuing from figure 182: the posture in which the body turns slightly left, the right palm reels forward and turns, turning its wrist and reeling reverse to push out with the palm held sideways, and the left palm reels forward, bending its elbow and drawing in to before the chest with its centre facing upper-right, with the right knee reeling outward and the left knee reeling inward (completing the first palm change).
图 L1F184
Continuing from figure 183: the posture in which the body turns slightly left and the right knee bows further forward, the right palm going up past before the chest and reeling forward and turning into reverse reeling to push out with the palm held sideways, the left palm turning its arm and reeling forward and dropping with its centre slanting inward-right, with the right knee reeling outward and the left knee reeling inward.
图 L1F185
Continuing from figure 184: the set posture with the right knee bowed forward, after completing the third palm change.

Essential points:

1. This form is performed without moving the feet, and without any big opening or closing; it changes hand technique only within a very small range before the chest. Its turning of the arm to draw back is forward reeling, and when it turns to push it is reverse reeling — this is the characteristic of the palm change.

· 147 · 2. In the course of the three palm changes, one must not only attain the requirement of "when one part moves, no part is unmoved" within this small range before the chest, but also have no flaw in the ward-off jin (no concavity or convexity in the form, no interruption in the jin) during the left and right changes of the changing head; the crux lies entirely in the transformation within the chest and the waist.

3. In the three palm changes, the first is pushed out with the right palm, the second with the left palm, and the third again with the right palm; it forms three conversions without changing the leg. During the conversions, because of the alternation of waist and buttocks and the screw rotation of the legs, the substantial and insubstantial of the jin in the waist, crotch and legs also converts three times, so that it still meets the requirement that upper and lower follow one another; but one leg supports the whole body rather long, so the amount of exercise is greater. This form can not only raise the physical-training effect but also raise the transforming-jin skill for combat (this is a masterpiece of Teacher Chen Fake's later years).

Forty-Eighth Form: Front Move

Action one: The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity shifting slightly further left. At the same time, the right hook hand becomes a palm, bending its elbow and turning its arm, raising the forearm upright and reeling forward to before the face with its centre facing upper-left; the left hand reels reverse and presses to the lower left, its centre facing down. (Figure 186)

Action two: The centre of gravity shifts right; with the right heel as pivot, the body turns right and the right toes turn outward; the left foot is lifted and, with the body's turn, drawn close beside the right foot, touching with its toes beside the right foot. At the same time, the right hand turns its arm and reels reverse, spreading outward in an arc to the right with the palm held sideways, its centre facing outward; the left palm turns its arm and drops, moving right in an arc with the body's turn, its centre facing right. (Figure 187)

图 L1F186
Action one of Front Move: the posture in which the body turns slightly left with the centre of gravity shifting slightly further left, and the right hook hand becomes a palm, bending its elbow and turning its arm, raising the forearm upright and reeling forward to before the face with its centre facing upper-left, while the left hand reels reverse and presses to the lower left with its centre facing down.
图 L1F187
Action two of Front Move: the posture in which the centre of gravity shifts right, the body turns right with the right heel as pivot and the right toes turn outward, the left foot is lifted and drawn close beside the right foot touching with its toes beside it, while the right hand turns its arm and reels reverse, spreading outward in an arc to the right with the palm held sideways and its centre facing outward, and the left palm turns its arm and drops, moving right in an arc with the body's turn with its centre facing right.

· 148 · Essential points:

The movements of this form are like dancing while holding a long spear, the two arms forming a closing jin. First the left palm, like holding the spear shaft, leads up to the upper left, and the right palm, at the right and to the upper left, holds across like holding the spear pole, carrying the right leg up; at this moment the skin on the left side of the waist is tight and the right side is relaxed — this is a special movement that uses the waist to give a feeling of comfort.

Forty-Ninth Form: Rear Move

Action one: The left foot steps out sideways to the left, the centre of gravity immediately shifting left with the left leg in a bow stance. At the same time, the left hand turns its arm and reels reverse, turning over to the upper left with its centre facing outward; the right palm turns its arm and reels forward, dropping from the right with its centre facing lower-left. (Figure 188)

Action two: The body turns left, the centre of gravity continuing to shift left, and the right foot is drawn close beside the left foot, touching with its toes before the left foot;

图 L1F188
Action one of Rear Move: the posture in which the left foot steps out sideways to the left with the centre of gravity immediately shifting left into a left bow stance, the left hand turning its arm and reeling reverse and turning over to the upper left with its centre facing outward, and the right palm turning its arm and reeling forward and dropping from the right with its centre facing lower-left.

· 149 · the left hand reels reverse one circle. (Figure 189) The body turns slightly right. At the same time, the right palm turns its arm and reels reverse, turning over in an arc with its centre facing outward; the left palm turns its arm and reels forward, moving right in an arc from above downward, the two hands holding jin together above and below on the right side. (Figure 190)

Essential points:

1. The main point of Front Move is a single turn after the right palm supports; practising this turning jin raises the function of the right side of the waist, while Rear Move raises the function of the left side of the waist — hence they are called Front and Rear Move together, and may also be combined into a single fist form.

2. Front Move is placed after Single Whip; joined with Rear Move, it is also called Slanting Single Whip, meaning that after Single Whip one immediately performs a slanting-form Single Whip. It uses a small body method to knead and move the waist and spine. The emphasis is on flexible left-right alternation, giving one a sense of round-and-live interest.

· 153 ·

Essential points:

1. Wild Horse Parts Its Mane is a great spreading body method that makes the qi reach the four tips, like a wild horse galloping without restraint. The sole requirement of this form is that the skin and muscle on both sides of the chain of vertebrae from below the chin down to the spine must have the meaning of a double opening-and-separating jin, as a horse parts its mane; for in this part of the body "lengthening is easy but separating is hard", and the movement is so slight that it is difficult to separate it, so one must practise repeatedly to left and right.

2. This form most easily shows the great forward and reverse reeling-silk jin. Under the requirement of standing upright, centred, at ease, and supporting the eight directions, all its movements must relatively show the Taiji six reeling-silk jins; the two hands turn with this one up and that one down, this one down and that one up, this one inside and that one outside, this one outside and that one inside, this one forward-reeling and that one reverse-reeling, this one reverse-reeling and that one forward-reeling, opening containing closing and closing containing opening. Hence it can well serve as one example representing the Taiji six reeling-silk jins.

3. Taiji demands that all movements be governed by the waist and spine, so that the qi adheres to the back of the spine is the core of the movement. But the back of the spine (such as the seven vertebrae of the neck region) is the hardest part to separate and knead; therefore this fist form was included in the set precisely to meet this requirement.

Fifty-Third Form: Double Swinging Foot

Action one: The body turns left, the centre of gravity shifts left, the left leg forms a bow stance, and the right leg extends slightly without straightening. With the body's turn, the right hook hand becomes a palm and reels forward, reeling from the right down past before the abdomen to the left to before the left flank (note: the inner jin is not lost and not flattened), its centre facing left; the left hand reels forward and extends to the left with its centre facing down. (Figure 204) The body turns right, the centre of gravity shifts right, the right leg forms a bow stance, and the left leg extends without straightening. At the same time, the right palm turns its arm and reels reverse, going up from before the left flank past before the face and spreading out to the right with its centre facing forward; the left palm turns its arm and reels reverse, bending its elbow and lifting slightly with the body's turn, its centre facing up. (Figure 205)

图 L1F204
The earlier part of action one of Double Swinging Foot: the posture in which the body turns left with the centre of gravity shifting left into a left bow stance while the right leg extends slightly without straightening, the right hook hand becoming a palm and reeling forward, reeling from the right down past before the abdomen to the left to before the left flank (the inner jin not lost and not flattened) with its centre facing left, and the left hand reeling forward and extending to the left with its centre facing down.
图 L1F205
Continuing from figure 204: the posture in which the body turns right with the centre of gravity shifting right into a right bow stance while the left leg extends without straightening, the right palm turning its arm and reeling reverse, going up from before the left flank past before the face and spreading out to the right with its centre facing forward, and the left palm turning its arm and reeling reverse, bending its elbow and lifting slightly with the body's turn with its centre facing up.

Action two: The body continues to turn right, the left toes turn inward, the centre of gravity shifts back onto the left leg, and the right foot draws in slightly, touching the ground with its toes. At the same time, the left palm, from the left past before the face, reels reverse and drops to the upper side of the right elbow; the right palm turns its arm and reels forward, going down from the right and sweeping forward-up to before the chest. (Figure 206) The two hands reel reverse before the chest, leading the whole body up with reeling-silk jin, lifting the right leg, as the left foot pushes off the ground and leaps up. (Figures 207–208) The two feet land left first and right after (hence also called Double Landing Foot), stamping the ground and shaking the foot, the left heavy and the right light; the two palms press down as the foot stamps, their centres turning to face down. (Figure 209)

Essential points:

· 155 · 1. The inward closing of figure 207 is for storing jin, to strengthen the elasticity of the body's limbs and trunk's ward-off jin; one must, with the leading jin of the two arms slightly spread and closing and the upward springing jin of the left leg, use a single leading of the body's limbs to leap up, and then land naturally one after the other.

2. The function of the foot stamp has already been seen in essential point 3 of the second form, "Vajra Pounds the Mortar". In addition, in the old society, if someone had been injured by such techniques as "joint locking, seizing, grasping and closing" so as to fall into a swoon or become dull-witted, the usual way to restore them to normal was to lift the patient's body upright and bump it down onto the ground; the shock could restore the circulation in some part.

Fifty-Fourth Form: Jade Girl Works the Shuttles

Action one: The right foot lifts slightly, the right hand raises slightly, and the left hand coordinates before the chest to hold jin together (the posture is like figure 206). The right foot leaps forward half a step; at the same time, the right palm pushes forward level and issues jin, and leads the left foot to leap forward a big step, the body turning right accordingly, and the left palm also pushing forward accordingly (forming the process of both feet leaving the ground, as in figure 210; if one is old and weak, one may omit the airborne process, as in attached figure 210). The body, in the air, continues to turn to the right rear through 270 degrees; the left foot lands, and then the right foot also lands in a crosswise step to the right with the body's turn; at the same time, the two hands — the right reeling forward and the left reeling reverse — the right hand to the upper right and the left hand to the lower left, open out apart, forming opening jin. (Figure 211)

图 L1F210
The earlier part of action one of Jade Girl Works the Shuttles: the posture of the process in which the right foot leaps forward half a step, the right palm pushes forward level and issues jin and leads the left foot to leap forward a big step, the body turning right accordingly with both feet leaving the ground.

Continuing from figure 210: the posture in which the body in the air continues to turn to the right rear through 270 degrees, the left foot lands and then the right foot also lands in a crosswise step to the right with the body's turn, and the two hands — the right reeling forward and the left reeling reverse — the right hand to the upper right and the left hand to the lower left open out apart, forming opening jin.

· 157 · Action two: The body turns square to the left (facing south), the left knee bending slightly; the two palms close with forward reeling and separate with reverse reeling, the right up and the left down. (Figure 212)

Essential points:

1. This form joins two movements into one. Its essential point lies in linking up three successive steps — namely, the right foot leaping forward half a step, the left foot jumping forward a big step, and the right foot landing again in a crosswise step. These three steps must be completed in succession, like the shuttle on a loom passing very swiftly through two layers of thread — this is a shuttle jin worthy of the name, and it differs from the movement in the later-developed form of Jade Girl Works the Shuttles with its turnings to the four corners.

2. This form is like a special kind of triple jump, accomplished by rotating the body during the three leap-steps; in combat terms, it is suited to breaking out through an encirclement, breaking out in a posture both attacking and defending.

3. If the practice ground is small, or one is old and weak, or one wishes to reduce the amount of exercise, one may delete the airborne leaping movement and change it to a practice method of turning the body and stepping.

Fifty-Ninth Form: Swinging Foot and Falling into a Split

Action one: The body turns right, the centre of gravity shifts left, and the left knee bows out; at the same time the two palms, joined to each other, reel the right reverse and the left forward, shifting level to the right side of the body at shoulder height, both centres facing right. (Figure 213) The whole centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg, the body rises, and the right foot is lifted, going up from the left past before the chest and swinging across to the right; at the same time, the two palms — the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward — go from the right shoulder side to the left, the left palm first and the right palm after, moving across to meet and slap the outer side of the right foot's instep, striking with two successive sounds, both palms' centres facing left. (Figure 214)

图 L1F213
The earlier part of action one of Swinging Foot and Falling into a Split: the posture in which the body turns right with the centre of gravity shifting left and the left knee bowing out, and the two palms joined to each other reeling the right reverse and the left forward and shifting level to the right side of the body at shoulder height with both centres facing right.
图 L1F214
Continuing from figure 213: the posture in which the whole centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg, the body rises and the right foot is lifted, going up from the left past before the chest and swinging across to the right, while the two palms — the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward — go from the right shoulder side to the left, the left palm first and the right palm after, moving across to meet and slap the outer side of the right foot's instep with two successive sounds, both palms' centres facing left.
图 L1F215
The earlier part of action two of Swinging Foot and Falling into a Split: the posture in which the two palms become fists after slapping the foot, the left hand reeling reverse inward, going down from the left and drawing an arc to the right past before the chest while the right hand reels forward outward and falls before the abdomen, the two arms holding jin together and crossing before the chest with the left fist stacked on the right arm; and after the right foot has swung across and fallen from the right beside the left foot, stamping the ground and shaking the foot with the whole body's qi sinking down and the left heel lifting slightly.

Action two: After the two palms slap the foot's instep they become fists — the left hand reeling reverse inward, going down from the left and drawing an arc to the right past before the chest, and the right hand reeling forward outward, falling before the abdomen, the two arms holding jin together and crossing before the chest with the left fist stacked on the right arm; after the right foot has swung across and fallen from the right, it stamps the ground and shakes the foot beside the left foot, the whole body's qi sinking down, and the left heel lifts slightly. (Figure 215) The right leg bends at the knee and squats, the left toes point up, and it thrusts out to the left with its heel against the ground; the right knee turns inward, the hips loosen, the crotch closes and sinks, and the buttocks, the inner side of the right knee and the rear side of the left leg all touch the ground. At the same · 159 · time, the right fist goes up past before the face and is raised to the right in an arc with its centre slanting to the upper right; the left fist goes down along the inner side of the right arm and extends forward as the left foot thrusts out, its centre facing up. (Figure 216) The body rises forward, pushing off the right leg and bowing the left leg to form a left bow stance. At the same time, the left fist thrusts up forward with its face, its centre facing inward; the right fist turns its arm and reels forward, falling beside the right hip. (Figure 217)

图 L1F216
The later part of action two of Swinging Foot and Falling into a Split: the posture in which the right leg bends at the knee and squats while the left toes point up and the foot thrusts out to the left with its heel against the ground, the right knee turning inward with the hips loosened and the crotch closed and sinking so that the buttocks, the inner side of the right knee and the rear side of the left leg all touch the ground, and the right fist goes up past before the face and is raised to the right in an arc with its centre slanting to the upper right while the left fist goes down along the inner side of the right arm and extends forward as the left foot thrusts out with its centre facing up.
图 L1F217
The last section of action two of Swinging Foot and Falling into a Split: the posture in which the body rises forward, pushing off the right leg and bowing the left leg to form a left bow stance, with the left fist thrusting up forward with its face and its centre facing inward and the right fist turning its arm and reeling forward and falling beside the right hip.

Essential points:

1. This form divides into two stages, the swinging foot and the falling split. In the swinging-foot stage, when the foot swings it looks as though the two hands are going to slap the foot, but in fact the hands and the foot must meet each other; when the right foot swings outward and falls, the body must still be centred and upright, and when the foot stamps the sinking jin must be whole. In the falling-split stage, as far as its combat function goes, it is to guard against an inadvertent fall: one may use the buttocks to sink onto the ground and spring up — that is, push up with the rear foot and thrust up with the left fist (the two must act simultaneously and in unison) — and rise with a bound, gaining the effect of turning defeat into victory.

2. This form is rather hard to do; for those who have studied since childhood it is still easy enough. To suit different people such as the old and weak, and to suit practising on a concrete floor or in Western trousers, this form may also be changed to "Swinging Foot Low Posture" — that is, after swinging the foot, delete the fall of the later stage, changing it to the right leg bending at the knee and squatting while the left leg moves · 160 · a forward lunging low stance, and then perform the movement of figure 218 below.

Sixtieth Form: Left and Right Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg

Action one: The whole centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg, the body turns slightly left, the left leg stands up with its knee bending slightly, and the right leg is lifted with the right instep drawn flat and the toes pointing down. At the same time, the two fists reel forward — the left fist going down from the left front and the right fist going up forward from the right rear — and the two fists cross past each other before the chest; as the right leg is about to lift, the two fists become palms, the right hand reeling forward and lifting up from before the right chest while the left hand reels reverse and presses down (as in figure 222, but with left and right reversed); as the right leg lifts, the right palm reels reverse and opens out to the upper right and the left palm to the lower left, forming the left-style Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg. (Figure 218)

图 L1F218
Action one of Left and Right Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg: the posture in which the whole centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg, the body turns slightly left with the left leg standing up and its knee bending slightly, the right leg is lifted with the right instep drawn flat, and the two fists reel forward — the left fist going down from the left front and the right fist going up forward from the right rear — crossing past each other before the chest; as the right leg is about to lift the two fists become palms with the right hand reeling forward and lifting up from before the right chest while the left hand reels reverse and presses down; and as the right leg lifts the right palm reels reverse and opens out to the upper right and the left palm to the lower left, forming the left-style Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg.
图 L1F219
Action two of Left and Right Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg: the posture in which the left leg bends slightly to store jin and then springs up with both feet leaving the ground, immediately landing left first and right after and stamping the ground and shaking the foot (the left heavy and the right light; this is the Double Landing Foot) with the two knees bending slightly, and the right palm, as the right foot lands, pressing down at the same time to before the right hip while the left palm also presses down to before the left hip.

Action two: The left leg bends slightly (storing jin), then springs up with both feet leaving the ground; immediately the two feet land left first and right after, stamping the ground and shaking the foot (the left heavy and the right light; this is the Double Landing Foot), and the two knees bend slightly; the right palm, as the right foot lands, presses down at the same time to before the right hip, and the left palm also presses down to before the left hip. (Figure 219) The body turns slightly right and then turns left, and the right foot steps sideways to the right (south) in a big step, the left leg bending at the knee and squatting. The two palms, as the body turns slightly right, rise from the upper right, and then as the right foot steps out and the body turns left, they pass before the chest to the left with the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward in a great reeling · 161 · up to shoulder height, both palms' centres facing left. (Figure 220) The centre of gravity shifts right, the left foot is drawn close to the right, touching the ground with its toes beside the right foot, so that the right leg is substantial and the left leg insubstantial; at the same time the two palms reel forward, falling respectively beside the two hips. (Figure 221)

Action three: Next, the left foot is set down solidly, the centre of gravity shifts left, the left leg becoming substantial; then the centre of gravity is shifted back onto the right leg, which again becomes substantial, and the left heel is still lifted off the ground. At the same time, the left palm turns its arm and reels forward, bending its elbow and lifting up, while the right palm reels reverse and presses down in coordination on the right side. (Figure 222) Immediately after, the left leg is lifted, and as the left palm goes to the upper left and the right palm to the lower right, both reeling reverse and opening out, one forms the right-style Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg. (Figure 223)

图 L1F220
Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg: the posture in which the body turns slightly right and then turns left, the right foot steps sideways to the right (south) in a big step with the left leg bending at the knee and squatting, and the two palms, as the right foot steps out and the body turns left, pass before the chest to the left with the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward in a great reeling up to shoulder height, both centres facing left.
图 L1F221
Continuing from figure 220: the posture in which the centre of gravity shifts right and the left foot is drawn close to the right, touching the ground with its toes beside the right foot so that the right leg is substantial and the left leg insubstantial, while the two palms reel forward and fall respectively beside the two hips.
图 L1F222
Continuing from figure 221: the posture in which the left foot is set down solidly and the centre of gravity shifts left with the left leg becoming substantial, then the centre of gravity is shifted back onto the right leg which again becomes substantial with the left heel still lifted off the ground, while the left palm turns its arm and reels forward, bending its elbow and lifting up, and the right palm reels reverse and presses down in coordination on the right side.
图 L1F223
Continuing from figure 222: the posture in which the left leg is lifted and, as the left palm goes to the upper left and the right palm to the lower right, both reeling reverse and opening out, one forms the right-style Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg.

· 162 · Essential points:

1. After the previous form's falling split has sprung up (figure 218), one is ready for this form. The key to doing the stand-on-one-leg well lies in the instep of the lifted leg being drawn flat with the toes pointing down as far as possible, to lighten the weight of the leg hanging as a lever; and in the two arms spreading up and down, left and right, pulling against each other to keep balance — in this way the body can be made stable.

2. Between the first Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg and the second there are four circles, to gain stability in the course of changing position, and then one does the second Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg; in this way the second stand can, storing and then issuing, issue jin up and down together, showing the whole body's ward-off intent bursting outward.

3. Whether the previous form's falling split lands or is changed to a low posture without falling, both rise up from the lowest to reach the highest stand-on-one-leg form; it trains the elasticity of the legs and the lifting jin of the buttocks — this is the characteristic of this form. At the same time, in forming the stand, the crown jin must be suspended, the spirit must be roused, and the qi made to pervade the body, forming the image of "spirited and vigorous".

At the same time, the left palm reels reverse down past before the face; the right palm, from the right upward, turns from forward reeling into reverse reeling, reeling in an arc to beside the right cheek with its centre slanting to the left front. (Figure 224) What follows is the same as explained for figures 87–88 in action one of the twenty-second form, "Step Back and Roll the Arm". Seventy-Second Form: Cross-Shaped Swinging Lotus

Action one: Following the opening of the previous form, High Pat on Horse, the left foot is lifted back and touches the ground with its toes beside the right foot, the right leg still substantial and the left leg insubstantial; at the same time, the two palms turn their arms with the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, the left palm going from the left up to the right and the right palm from the right down to the left, drawing arcs, and the two hands cross at the wrists before the chest. (Figure 225) With the right heel as pivot, the body turns right, the left toes still touching the ground; at the same time, the two hands reel reverse, shrinking the crossed circle with the left hand inside, the two hands holding jin together. (Figure 226) The body continues to turn right, the right leg bends at the knee and squats, and the left foot is lifted and steps sideways to the left (northeast) in a big step, the centre of gravity shifting left into a left bow stance; at the same time, the two hands reel reverse, the right palm spreading to the upper right and the left palm to the lower left, both centres facing outward. (Figure 227)

图 L1F225
The earlier part of action one of Cross-Shaped Swinging Lotus: the posture in which, following the opening of High Pat on Horse, the left foot is lifted back and touches the ground with its toes beside the right foot with the right leg still substantial and the left leg insubstantial, and the two palms turn their arms with the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward, the left palm going from the left up to the right and the right palm from the right down to the left, drawing arcs, the two hands crossing at the wrists before the chest.
图 L1F226
Continuing from figure 225: the posture in which, with the right heel as pivot, the body turns right with the left toes still touching the ground, and the two hands reel reverse, shrinking the crossed circle with the left hand inside, the two hands holding jin together.
图 L1F227
Continuing from figure 226: the posture in which the body continues to turn right, the right leg bends at the knee and squats, the left foot is lifted and steps sideways to the left (northeast) in a big step with the centre of gravity shifting left into a left bow stance, and the two hands reel reverse, the right palm spreading to the upper right and the left palm to the lower left, both centres facing outward.

Action two: The body turns slightly left, the centre of gravity continuing to shift left, into a left bow stance. At the same time, the right · 165 · palm turns its arm and reels forward, going down from the right and reeling left past before the abdomen to under the left armpit, its centre facing rear-down; the left palm turns its arm and reels forward, bending its elbow so that the forearm is raised upright with its centre facing upper-right. (Figure 228) The body turns slightly right. At the same time, the left palm reels forward, going past before the neck to the right and closing onto the upper side of the right arm with its centre facing down; the right hand, under the left armpit, reels forward so that its centre turns to face down. At the same time the centre of gravity shifts further left. (Figure 229)

图 L1F228
The earlier part of action two of Cross-Shaped Swinging Lotus: the posture in which the right palm turns its arm and reels forward, going down from the right and reeling left past before the abdomen to under the left armpit with its centre facing rear-down, and the left palm turns its arm and reels forward, bending its elbow so that the forearm is raised upright with its centre facing upper-right.
图 L1F229
Continuing from figure 228: the posture in which the body turns slightly right, the left palm reels forward, going past before the neck to the right and closing onto the upper side of the right arm with its centre facing down, and the right hand under the left armpit reels forward so that its centre turns to face down, with the centre of gravity shifting further left at the same time.
图 L1F230
The earlier part of action three of Cross-Shaped Swinging Lotus: the posture in which the right foot is lifted and swings outward to the right in a half circle, going up from the left front, while the left palm reels reverse and moves to the left to meet and slap the outer side of the right foot's instep.
图 L1F231
Continuing from figure 230: the posture in which, with the left heel as pivot, the body continues to turn right and the right leg is lifted with the knee bent.

Action three: The right foot is lifted and swings outward to the right in a half circle, going up from the left front; at the same time the left palm reels reverse and moves to the left to meet and slap the outer side of the right foot's instep. (Figure 230) With the left heel as pivot, the body · 166 · the body turns right (west); at the same time the two palms become fists, the left reeling reverse and the right reeling forward; the right fist passes before the chest and goes right and down, while the left fist turns its arm, bends its elbow and, together with the other, issues energy from the left upward; the right fist is at hip height with its centre facing up, and the left fist is slightly higher than the head, with its centre facing right. (Figure 231)

Key points:

1. This posture passes from a tight closing to a great opening; at this time the momentum is required to sink. While turning left the two hips must be linked together — this is opening hidden within closing; afterwards it opens again — this is closing hidden within opening.

2. Because the left palm slaps crosswise against the outer side of the right foot's face, it is called Crosswise Lotus Swing . After the slap, the left fist lifts up and the right fist turns down, both issuing energy at the same time; the coordination of this energy-issue is what brings stability after the turn of the body.

3. In performing Crosswise Lotus Swing one often feels comfortable and the back becomes warm — this is the phenomenon of causing the chi to pervade the whole body.

Posture 73　Point-at-the-Crotch Punch
图 L1F232甲
Point-at-the-Crotch Punch action one: the posture in which the left foot springs up slightly to the left and the right foot falls to where the left foot had been, stamping the ground with a shock; the body turns right, the left foot steps diagonally forward-left (southwest) and the centre of gravity gradually shifts left; as the right foot falls and stamps, the left hand turns its arm and reels forward to the right of the chest and the right fist reels forward from the right upward and falls to the left, resting on the left forearm (front view).
图 L1F232乙
Continuing from figure 232甲: another view of the same action, the right fist reeling forward and falling onto the left forearm as the centre of gravity gradually shifts left.

Action one: The left foot springs up slightly to the left, and the right foot falls to where the left foot had been, stamping the ground with a shock; the body turns right, the left foot steps diagonally forward-left (southwest), and the centre of gravity gradually shifts left. As the right foot falls and stamps, the left hand turns its arm and reels forward to the right of the chest; the right fist reels forward from the right upward and falls to the left, resting on the left forearm; as the left foot steps out, the left fist · 167 · reeling reverse as the body turns, rises from before the chest to the right, bends its elbow and raises the forearm, thrusting the forearm slightly forward, the fist's centre facing right; the right fist reels forward and turns over to the side of the right hip, its centre facing forward.

Action two: The body turns slightly right. The left fist turns its arm and reels forward, falling before the chest; the right fist turns its arm and reels reverse from the right upward, passing beside the right ear and falling before the chest onto the inner side of the left arm, the two hands joining their strength. (Figure 233 — this figure shows a side view; in fact the two feet remain where they were, on the spots trodden by the two feet in figure 233.) The body turns left, the centre of gravity shifts left, and the left leg is bent in a bow. At the same time, the left fist turns its arm and reels forward, drawing back to circle at the left ribs, its centre facing inward; the right fist turns its arm and reels reverse, striking out toward the lower front-left and issuing energy. (Figure 234, and the side view of figure 234 in the attached figure.)

Key points:

1. In this posture one must pay special attention to storing energy. When the two fists join strength before the chest, the two hips must be greatly opened, the crotch rounded, and the chi clinging to the back. In such a posture one can most easily check the five bows — the two hand-bows, the two foot-bows, and the back-bow — to see whether they all operate together through the crotch, and whether the backs of the five bows have increased elasticity; that is to say, whether one feels a tautness on the backs of the five bows.

图 L1F233
First part of Point-at-the-Crotch Punch action two: the posture in which the body turns slightly right, the left fist turns its arm and reels forward falling before the chest, and the right fist turns its arm and reels reverse from the right upward, passing beside the right ear and falling before the chest onto the inner side of the left arm, the two hands joining strength (the figure is a side view; the two feet still remain on their original spots, unmoved).
图 L1F234
Continuing from figure 233: the posture in which the body turns left, the centre of gravity shifts left and the left leg is bent in a bow, the left fist turns its arm and reels forward, drawing back to circle at the left ribs with its centre facing inward, and the right fist turns its arm and reels reverse, striking out toward the lower front-left and issuing energy.
图 L1F234附图
The side view of figure 234, showing the side posture in which the right fist reels reverse and strikes out toward the lower front-left while the left fist is drawn back to the left ribs.

2. This posture is also a movement for practicing "hip striking" , whose source of motive power lies in · 168 · the right hip turns over, and the strength of the right fist is released, pointing at the opponent's crotch.

3. When this posture issues energy, its outward appearance is slanting to the right, as though the outer form were not upright; but the inner strength at the moment of issuing energy lies in the upward leading strength of the left hand leading backward, which is insubstantial, while the right hand that points at the crotch sinking down is substantial, and the right leg is in fact insubstantial. Because of this "upper and lower following one another", the inner strength is adjusted into balance and reaches central uprightness. This is correct central uprightness: though the outer form appears not upright, the inner strength is still central, upright and unbiased.

Posture 74　White Ape Offers Fruit
图 L1F235
First part of White Ape Offers Fruit action one: the posture in which the body turns slightly left, the right fist reels reverse and is drawn in to the left, gathering at the left side of the waist, while the left fist reels reverse before the left ribs, cooperating to circle a small round, the two hands joining strength and not collapsing.
图 L1F235附图
The side view of figure 235: a side view of the same posture, with the right fist gathered at the left side of the waist and the left fist circling before the left ribs.
图 L1F236
Continuing from figure 235: the posture in which the body turns right, the centre of gravity shifts right and then still shifts back to the left; the two hands reel reverse and move from the left forward to before the chest at chest height, and as the centre of gravity shifts back onto the left leg the two fists turn over inward and outward, joining strength.
图 L1F236附图
The side view of figure 236: showing the side posture in which the two hands reel reverse and move to before the chest while the centre of gravity returns to the left leg and the two fists turn over, joining strength.

Action one: The body turns slightly left; at the same time the right fist reels reverse and is drawn in to the left, gathering at the left side of the waist, while the left fist reels reverse before the left ribs, cooperating to circle a small round, the two hands joining strength and not collapsing. (Figure · 169 · 235, and the side view of figure 235 in the attached figure.) The body turns right, the centre of gravity shifts right and then still shifts back to the left. At the same time the two hands reel reverse, moving from the left forward to before the chest at chest height; as the centre of gravity shifts back onto the left leg, the two fists turn over inward and outward, reeling and joining strength. (Figure 236, and the side view of figure 236 in the attached figure.)

Action two: With the left heel as the pivot, the body turns left, the right leg is lifted, the top of the right foot is stretched flat and the toes point down. At the same time the right fist turns its arm and reels forward, and as the right leg is lifted it spirals and thrusts upward from the right and below, rising to eye height, its centre facing inward; the left palm turns its arm and reels reverse one circle, gathering and placing at the left side of the waist. (Figure 237)

Key points:

1. In this posture, from "the left reeling reverse inward and the right reeling forward outward" one must, without hollows or bumps, make the body spiral upward evenly; the two hands turn into upward-and-downward forward-and-reverse reeling silk, reeling the right fist to before the face and the left fist to the waist, and this must be completed without the least flaw. This is the emphasis of this posture.

2. In this posture one must master the spiral ascent after the double joining. Moreover, the left hand placed at the left side of the waist must perform a correct reverse reeling, reeling back from the outer left to the waist — this is also the key to making the left leg stand upright, central and steady.
