Form Seventy-seven: Sparrow Dragon on the Ground (Que Di Long) Action one: The body turns left, the left leg forms a forward bow. At the same time, both hands change into fists and reel reverse; the right fist goes from the right downward, passes before the belly and sweeps up to the left, the fist's centre facing up; the left fist closes to the right onto the upper side of the right arm, the fist's centre facing inward, the two hands joining their strength. (Figure 238) The centre of gravity turns right, the body turns slightly right, the right leg bends at the knee and squats down; at the same time, the two hands reel forward on the right and reverse on the left, the left fist going from the inner side of the right arm to the left and downward, the right fist going from the outer side of the left forearm to the right and upward, each opening out separately, the left fist extending to above the left knee, the left fist's centre facing upper right, the right fist's centre facing upper right. (Figure 239)

图 L1F238
Sparrow Dragon action one: the posture in which the body turns left and the left leg forms a forward bow, while both hands change into fists and reel reverse, the right fist going from the right downward, passing before the belly and sweeping up to the left with the fist's centre facing up, and the left fist closing to the right onto the upper side of the right arm with the fist's centre facing inward, the two hands joining their strength.
图 L1F239
Continuing from figure 238: the posture in which the centre of gravity turns right and the body turns slightly right with the right leg bending at the knee and squatting down, while the two hands reel forward on the right and reverse on the left, the left fist going from the inner side of the right arm to the left and downward and the right fist going from the outer side of the left forearm to the right and upward, each opening out separately, with the left fist extending to above the left knee, the left fist's centre facing upper right and the right fist's centre facing upper right.

Action two: The body turns slightly left, the left leg sinks down into a crouching leg, the right leg continues to squat down; the left fist extends forward to above the left ankle, the fist's centre facing up, the right fist sinks slightly; the eyes look level ahead. (Figure 240) The left toes turn out, the body rises forward, the right leg pushes, the left leg bows, forming a left bow step. At the same time, the left fist thrusts up and forward with the face of the fist, the fist's centre facing inward; the right fist turns its arm and reels forward, falling beside the right hip. (Figure 241)

Key points: 1. The difference between this form and the Drop-into-Split is only that one does not fall; it is that the right fist, turning its arm and going from above · 171 · When thrusting to the right, the rear right leg does not touch the ground, but one must squat down as far as possible; in all other parts the requirements are the same as those of Drop-into-Split.

图 L1F240
Sparrow Dragon action two: the posture in which the body turns slightly left, the left leg sinks down into a crouching leg and the right leg continues to squat down, with the left fist extending forward to above the left ankle, the fist's centre facing up, the right fist sinking slightly, and the eyes looking level ahead.
图 L1F241
Continuing from figure 240: the posture in which the left toes turn out, the body rises forward, the right leg pushes and the left leg bows to form a left bow step, while the left fist thrusts up and forward with the face of the fist, the fist's centre facing inward, and the right fist turns its arm and reels forward, falling beside the right hip.

2. This form, like Drop-into-Split, may, to suit different people, be changed so that the left calf does not touch the ground while one crouches as low as possible, in the manner of figure 239. 3. In this form one first makes the double-closing Ward-off energy; after warding off, one releases it (using centrifugal force), and when it has opened to the extreme and gone to the lowest, one then uses the centripetal force of the two hands closing again after the release, applying the energy to the right fist, which serves to lead the body up.

Form Seventy-eight: Step Up to the Seven Stars Action: The left toes turn out, the body turns left, the centre of gravity moves forward so that it is entirely on the left leg, and the right foot steps forward half a step, touching the ground with its toes. As the body turns left, the left fist reels forward and closes inward; the right fist reels forward, and from the right downward, as the right leg steps up, thrusts up forward past the outer side of the left wrist, the two fists crossing at the wrists, both fists' centres facing inward. As the right foot steps up and touches the ground with its toes, the two fists, using the crossing point where the wrists are pressed tightly together as an axis, describe a small circle from above inward, downward and forward, then change into palms and extend slightly forward. (Figures 242–243)

Key points: 1. Every form of Taijiquan, when practised, requires that if one part moves, no part is still;

图 L1F242
Step Up to the Seven Stars, action: the posture in which the left toes turn out, the body turns left and the centre of gravity moves entirely onto the left leg, the right foot steps forward half a step and touches the ground with its toes, the left fist reels forward and closes inward, and the right fist reels forward and, from the right downward, as the right leg steps up, thrusts up forward past the outer side of the left wrist, the two fists crossing at the wrists with both fists' centres facing inward.
图 L1F243
Continuing from figure 242: the posture in which, as the right foot steps up and touches the ground with its toes, the two fists, using the crossing point where the wrists are pressed tightly together as an axis, describe a small circle from above inward, downward and forward, then change into palms and extend slightly forward.

· 172 · and in every form there must be a main part of the movement; in this form it is the wrists, so the wrists are well trained. Of course in other forms the wrists are also active, and in this form the other parts are also active; here we speak only of which part is the main one. 2. Because Taijiquan requires that when the opponent moves quickly one responds quickly and when he moves slowly one follows slowly, and one must also adhere, connect, stick and follow, discarding the faults of butting, collapsing, losing and resisting, there are therefore more opportunities to apply joint-locks and holds on each other; this form is a kind of turning method for escaping when both hands are seized.

Form Seventy-nine: Step Back and Bestride the Tiger Action one: The two palms, before the chest, still use the crossing point where the wrists are pressed tightly together as an axis, and go from the front downward, inward and upward, still rolling the wrists back; at the same time, as the two palms turn over, and using the left heel as an axis, the body turns right (south) and the right foot steps back one step. (Figure 244) The two arms close slightly, and after contracting the crossing circle a little, give the two palms a shake, and they separate to the lower left and lower right, both palms' centres facing down. (Figure 245)

图 L1F244
Step Back and Bestride the Tiger, action one: the posture in which the two palms, before the chest, use the crossing point where the wrists are pressed tightly together as an axis and go from the front downward, inward and upward, rolling the wrists back, and then, using the left heel as an axis, the body turns right (south) and the right foot steps back one step.
图 L1F245
Continuing from figure 244: the posture in which the two arms close slightly and, after contracting the crossing circle a little, give the two palms a shake and they separate to the lower left and lower right, both palms' centres facing down.

Action two: The centre of gravity shifts right, the left foot is drawn close to the right foot, touching the ground with its toes beside the right foot; at the same time the two hands reel reverse on the right and forward on the left, the right palm going from the right upward and describing an arc before the face, the left palm going from the left upward and describing an arc before the belly, the two hands joining their strength above and below. (Figure 246) The body turns slightly · 173 · squats down; at the same time, the two palms turn their arms and reel reverse, the right palm opening out to the upper right and the left palm to the lower left, the right palm's centre facing obliquely upper right and the left palm's centre facing obliquely lower left, forming Bestride the Tiger. (Figure 247)

图 L1F246
Step Back and Bestride the Tiger, action two: the posture in which the centre of gravity shifts right and the left foot is drawn close to the right foot, touching the ground with its toes beside the right foot, while the two hands reel reverse on the right and forward on the left, the right palm going from the right upward and describing an arc before the face and the left palm going from the left upward and describing an arc before the belly, the two hands joining their strength above and below.
图 L1F247
Continuing from figure 246: the posture in which the body squats down slightly and the two palms turn their arms and reel reverse, the right palm opening out to the upper right and the left palm to the lower left, the right palm's centre facing obliquely upper right and the left palm's centre facing obliquely lower left, forming Bestride the Tiger.

Key points: 1. The only form in this set that retreats continuously is Repulse the Monkey, and the only one in which, after stepping forward, one immediately steps back one step is Step Back and Bestride the Tiger. The preceding form follows the requirement of energy and steps forward, while this form likewise follows the giving of energy and steps back. This is a method of practising one advance to one retreat.

· 174 · 2. In the preceding form the two wrists roll from below inward and forward, and there is naturally a Ward-off energy issuing; in this form, after turning back through one circle, one gives a sudden shake, an energy like slipping off a handcuff, and then the two separate and open, while at the same time the breath and the blocking energy must sink down.

Form Eighty: Turn the Body and Double Sweep the Lotus Action one: Using the right heel as an axis, the body turns 180 degrees back to the right, and the left foot is lifted and swings back to the right with the turn of the body. At the same time, the right palm, with the turning of the body, also revolves horizontally through 180 degrees, reeling reverse and lying crosswise at the upper right, the palm's centre facing right; the left palm reels forward and sweeps horizontally back to the right until it is before the right elbow, the palm's centre facing right. (Figures 248–249)

图 L1F248
Turn the Body and Double Sweep the Lotus, action one: the posture in which, using the right heel as an axis, the body turns 180 degrees back to the right and the left foot is lifted and swings back to the right with the turn, while the right palm with the turning body revolves horizontally through 180 degrees, reeling reverse and lying crosswise at the upper right with the palm's centre facing right, and the left palm reels forward and sweeps horizontally back to the right until it is before the right elbow with the palm's centre facing right.
图 L1F249
Continuing from figure 248: the same action of the body turning back to the right, with the right palm revolving horizontally and lying crosswise at the upper right and the left palm reeling forward and sweeping horizontally back to the right until before the right elbow.
图 L1F250
Turn the Body and Double Sweep the Lotus, action two: the posture in which the left foot steps down forward (northwest) on a diagonal, and as the centre of gravity shifts left with the left leg bending at the knee and squatting down while the body turns right at the same time, the two palms reel reverse on the left and forward on the right and sink slightly from the right.

Action two: The left foot steps down forward (northwest) on a diagonal, and as the centre of gravity shifts left, the left leg bends at the knee and squats down while the body turns right at the same time; at the same time the two palms reel reverse on the left and forward on the right and sink slightly from the right. (Figure 250) The centre of gravity moves entirely onto the left leg, the body stands up, the right foot is lifted and swings crosswise to the right, going from the left upward, past the chest and upward; at the same time the two palms, reeling reverse on the left and forward on the right, move from right to left, the left palm first and the right palm after, sweeping crosswise to meet and slap the outer side of the right foot's instep, striking two sounds in succession, both palms' centres facing left. (Continuing to figure 214, only the direction is slightly different; in the figure the posture's chest faces south, whereas in this form the chest should face the northeast diagonal)

Key points:

· 175 · 1. In every turning movement in which one leg stands alone and one leg is lifted, one must, in the course of the turn, show both stability and that if one part moves no part is still. The key lies in the two arms closing and then opening (closing is both reeling forward, and when it turns to opening it becomes both reeling reverse); the opening energy carries the body round, and this is because the balancing action of the reverse reeling opening in opposite directions brings the body to stability. 2. Moreover, to gain stability one must also stand with the body centred and upright. And the key to being centred depends on the top energy being suspended empty; if the top energy is not suspended emptily, but leans slightly, one immediately cannot be stable, because the head occupies the highest peak of the body, and a slight lean above greatly affects the degree of lean of the whole body below. Therefore every movement of Taijiquan must have the top energy suspended empty; thus one not only reduces the weight of the head pressing down, but also produces the effect of correcting any lean.

图 L1F251
Cannon Fired Point-Blank, action one: the posture in which the right foot, after the outer swing, steps down toward the right rear (south), while the two palms change into fists, turn their arms and reel forward, chopping down and then turning to thrust slightly forward and upward, the two fists' centres facing each other with the left fist in front and the right fist behind, and with the thrusting fists the left knee forms a forward bow.
图 L1F252
Continuing from figure 251: the posture in which the two palms change into fists, turn their arms and reel forward, chopping down, with the two fists' centres facing each other and the left fist in front and the right fist behind.
图 L1F253
Continuing from figures 251 to 252: the posture in which, after turning the arms and reeling forward to chop down, the fists thrust slightly forward and upward, and with the thrust the left knee forms a forward bow.

Form Eighty-one: Cannon Fired Point-Blank Action one: The right foot, after the outer swing, steps down toward the right rear (south); at the same time the two palms change into fists, turn their arms and reel forward, chopping down, then turn to thrust slightly forward and upward, the two fists' centres facing each other, the left fist in front and the right fist behind; with the thrusting fists the left knee forms a forward bow. (Figure 251) Action two: The centre of gravity shifts back, the right leg bends at the knee and squats down, becoming substantial, the left knee bends slightly, the body · 176 · turns right; at the same time, the two fists turn their arms and reel forward, going from the front downward, inward and upward, and are drawn back in an arc to the side of the right ribs, the left fist's centre facing inward and the right fist's centre facing left (Figure 252); the centre of gravity moves forward, the left leg bows and the right leg pushes to form a left bow step, the body turning slightly left; at the same time, the two fists turn their arms and reel forward with a shaking energy, the two elbows bending slightly, the left fist held somewhat crosswise in front, the left fist's centre facing inward and the right fist's centre facing left. (Figure 253)

Key points: 1. The whole set of Taijiquan begins with a civil image and ends with a martial image, so when one has practised to this form, Cannon Fired Point-Blank, one must, "with spirit and energy soaring", display the four energies of scattering, releasing, storing and issuing, and exert all one's ability to bring the four energies into play. ① 2. In this form one must make a last check of the dynamic aspect of Taijiquan energy, that is, whether in the course of scattering and releasing one has departed from the silk-reeling energy of Taijiquan; whether, in storing and issuing, the root is in the foot, and whether it reaches the two fists from the heel. 3. The energy issued in this form is shaking energy; shaking energy is a kind of short-range splitting energy. Shaking energy must display a startling energy like a spark landing on the skin, and must come out in a single shake.

Form Eighty-two: Diamond Pounds the Mortar Action one: The centre of gravity shifts back, the right leg bends at the knee and squats down, the right leg becomes substantial, the body turns right; at the same time, the two hands, reeling reverse on the left and forward on the right, open out toward the right rear, the palms' centres facing right rear, the fingers stretched out and not limp. (Continuing to figure 4, only the left foot is different; in the figure the left foot is off the ground, whereas in this form the left foot is set down emptily on the ground, and the direction is also different: the second form, "Diamond Pounds the Mortar", is performed with the chest facing south, whereas this form is performed with the chest facing north) Action two: The centre of gravity moves forward; at the same time the two palms, still reeling reverse on the left and forward on the right, move toward the right

  • ① "Bumping" is the contraction of a large circle into a small one, generally used for strong energy, manifested in "going"; when it has gone to the end of the silk reeling, it becomes "storing" energy. "Releasing" is the expansion of a small circle into a large one, generally used for strong energy, manifested in "sticking"; when it is released into the opponent's empty place, it becomes issuing energy.

· 177 · afterwards continues to open slightly and sink down. (Continuing to figure 5, only the north-south direction is reversed) Then the same as the explanation of action two of the second form, "Diamond Pounds the Mortar", figure 6. (Continuing to figure 6, only the north-south direction is reversed) Action three is the same as action three of the second form, "Diamond Pounds the Mortar", only the direction is different, north and south being reversed. (Figures 7–8)

Key points: The first "Diamond Pounds the Mortar" within the set of the Chen-style First Road Taijiquan shows the five pairs of forward and reverse silk reeling of Taijiquan embodied in the beginning of the movement; the second "Diamond Pounds the Mortar" shows the end of the second form; the third "Diamond Pounds the Mortar" shows the end of the fifth form; this form is the fourth "Diamond Pounds the Mortar", showing the end of the whole set. Its key points are the same as those of the second form, "Diamond Pounds the Mortar".

Form Eighty-three: Closing Action: The body stands up, the two knees bending slightly; at the same time the two hands reel reverse and hang down separately to the two sides, left and right, both palms' centres facing back, restoring the preparatory posture. (According to figure 1)

Key points: 1. In returning to the static posture, one must still check once through the key points given in the preparatory form. 2. After finishing practice, according to the degree to which one's breathing rate has increased, one can judge how well one has "moved the body with the breath" during practice, and whether the regulation of the breath has been up to standard. If panting occurs, one should check whether the coordination of movement and breath is natural. 3. The Chen-style First Road Taijiquan and the Second Road Cannon Fist both begin practice, hypothetically, facing south, and both face north when closing. If one practises the First Road or the Second Road twice in succession, or practises the First Road and the Second Road in direct succession, then at the final closing one can return to facing south.

· 180 · Chen-Style Taijiquan, Second Routine The "Second Routine" of Chen-style Taijiquan is the second set of forms, commonly called the "Second Set" and also known as "Cannon Fist" . The Second Set runs from the start all the way to the first Single Whip: that is, from the Preparatory Posture, Step-Up Buddha's Warrior Attendant Pounds the Mortar, Lazy Tying the Robe, Six Sealing and Four Closing, through to Single Whip — these five movements are exactly the same as in the First Routine. These five movements are repeated first so that the body performs several soft postures to stretch the sinews and bones, adapting it for the demands of the Second Set. Therefore, the movement descriptions of the Second Routine in this chapter begin after the first Single Whip (chest facing south). The description of the four postures before Single Whip is given in full under the First Routine and is not repeated here. For convenience of exposition, figures 1–26 and their descriptions from the First Routine diagram are not repeated in the Second Routine's diagrams; of these, figure 26 is here listed as figure 1 of this diagram section. Explanations of the diagrams are likewise given in full under the First Routine.

Form Six　Pieh-Lan Elbow (Slanting Parry Elbow) (chest facing south)

Movement: The center of gravity shifts slightly to the right; at the same time, the right hooked hand on the right side changes into a fist with a small forward reeling, with the fist-heart facing up, and the left palm changes into a fist, reeling backward from the left downward to the front of the chest. Immediately afterward the center of gravity shifts left; as it shifts left, the left fist passes across the front of the chest and strikes leftward with a horizontal blow using the fist-eye to issue power, and the right fist strikes from right to left likewise with a horizontal blow using the fist-eye to issue power — the left fist-heart facing up, the right fist-heart facing down. (Figure 2) The center of gravity shifts right; as it shifts right, both hands — the left reeling backward, the right reeling forward — strike from left to right with horizontal blows using the fist-eyes to issue power, the left fist-heart facing down, the right fist-heart facing up. (Figure 3)

图 L2F1
In a bow stance, the right hand holds the hooked hand in front of the body and the left palm extends forward; the opening posture of the Second Routine diagrams.

Key points:

This posture has two issuings of power, left and right, which must be performed in immediate succession. In the transition from Single Whip to the leftward issuance of power, the center of gravity must first shift slightly right, and then power is issued, in order to meet the requirement of "store first, then issue." When issuing power, the movement of the center of gravity and the power of the two fists must be as one, so that the power is whole.

Form Seven　Guard-the-Heart Punch (chest facing northeast)

图 L2F2
Facing forward in a bow stance, both fists strike horizontally to the left; the posture as the center of gravity then shifts right for the rightward horizontal strike.
图 L2F3
Facing forward in a bow stance, both fists strike to the right, with the right arm raised in an arc.
图 L2F4
The right leg bends and squats, the body turns left, and the left fist is lifted to guard the chest.
图 L2F5
Standing with feet apart, both hands drawing together before the chest.

Movement: The entire center of gravity shifts onto the right leg; the left foot lifts, the body turns left, the right foot pushes off the ground and springs up, then the left foot lands, and the right foot follows with a step to the left-front (southeast) diagonal. As the body turns, at the same time, the left fist reels backward and is slightly lifted inward, then follows the turning of the body toward in an arc reeling forward to the left-rear-lower, down to the left side of the waist, the fist-heart slanting toward the upper right; the right fist, first reeling backward then forward, follows the turning of the body from the right upward, passes the front side of the right forehead and goes left, and strikes downward at the same time as the right foot lands. (Figure 4) The left fist reels forward and is raised to the left to the height of the shoulder; the right fist reels forward and draws inward. (Figure 5) The left fist goes from the left forward, passes the outside of the right fist, downward and inward; the right fist goes from the inside outward; the two fists cross past each other before the chest; then both hands reel forward, the left fist draws inward, and the right fist thrusts forward with the back of the fist near the wrist; at the same time the center of gravity sinks. (Figure 6)

Key points:

In Taijiquan movements, whenever a circle is to be enlarged, it must first be made smaller; this is to strengthen the "ward-off" energy , so that under the condition of "qi clinging to the spine" the internal power is threaded through and reaches the root of the palm. When the two hands perform the inside-outside, left-right double backward reeling and open up before the chest, the combining energy arises — right in front, left behind; finally, like the character ∞, the two circles meet before the chest to guard the heart; at the same time the circles are gradually made smaller, forming stored power like a drawn bow, to strengthen the ward-off energy.

Form Eight　Slanting Twist-Step Walk (chest toward east, turning to southeast)

图 L2F6
In a bow stance with the body turned sideways, the two fists cross before the chest and the right fist thrusts forward with ward-off energy.
图 L2F7
Standing with the body turned sideways, both fists crossed and drawn in before the chest.

After the above, with the two fists guarding the chest, the two fists open into palms and perform silk-reeling — right forward, left backward — uniting before the chest. At this moment the right hand is above and the left hand below, with the right palm left, with the left palm-heart facing up. Then continue with the double division — right forward, left backward. (Figs. 7, 8, 9) Then the two hands again unite before the chest, but now the right hand has already turned downward and the left hand upward, both palm-hearts facing down. Then the right hand turns up again, the left hand turns left; at the same time the body rises, the right leg is lifted, the left leg stands alone, and the two palms hold the energy together. (Figure 10) When it next turns into issuing , the right foot is brought to the ground with a stamp and becomes full. Then the left foot takes a reeling step toward the northeast, and the right palm reels forward and sinks from front to right. At the same time the left palm reels backward, turning in an arc up to the right; when it turns to the point where the left palm opens to the left, the right palm is just then reeling forward upward to the right ear. At this moment the left leg is full — this is the rising posture. Then the right palm turns half a circle at the right ear and reels backward to release toward the right front.

图 L2F8
Standing with the body turned sideways, the two palms dividing up and down.
图 L2F9
Standing on one leg with the body turned sideways, the two palms spread up and down.
图 L2F10
Standing on the left leg with the right leg lifted, both palms joined before the chest.
图 L2F11
In a broad bow stance, the two palms divided left and right, the body upright and the posture steady.

open; at the same time, the left palm, after reeling slightly backward to the right, opens forward to the left, forming a double opening energy. At this moment the chest faces south. (Figure 11)

Key points:

In this posture, when the right foot lands, the right hand opens and the left hand closes; when the left hand turns to open to the left-outside, the right hand again turns to the right ear to close. Because of the left-close right-open and left-open right-close, the internal qi is made to spiral and sink. Finally, when completing this posture, the left and right palms simultaneously open under the double backward reeling; when they have opened to the end, they close again with a double forward reeling. In the double closing, the fingers of both hands must point upward; at the same time, the internal energy of both elbows must also combine. Then, at once, the qi sinks to the dantian, and the center of gravity simultaneously shifts to the right foot. Because of the alternation of opening and closing, together with the stamping of the foot and the rotation of looking left and right, the qi is forced to descend — this is a basic exercise for moving the energy and training the qi to sink, and also the posture in which one most easily feels the qi finally settling in the dantian.

Form Nine　Lower-the-Waist, Press-Elbow Fist (chest facing southeast)

Movement: After the two palms of the previous slanting posture have divided, the right palm on the right uses forward reeling; when it turns upward, the palm changes into a fist and is placed above the right knee. At the same time, the left palm on the left uses a small forward reeling on top and becomes a fist facing the right fist from a distance, combining energy at the upper left. The crotch sinks, forming a low round crotch; the foot changes from left-full to right-full. At this moment the chest faces south. (Figure 12)

Form Ten　Well-Barrier Straight Entry (chest facing north)

Movement: The left foot is lifted and steps out 180° to the right, turning the chest to face north. The left fist changes to a palm, and with the left foot presses down diagonally from above toward the front-lower of the chest — the energy in the root of the palm. At the same time the right fist reels forward and also changes to a palm as it sinks.

图 L2F12
In a low horse stance, the right fist placed above the right knee and the left fist combining energy above.

turn over the palm so that its heart faces up and brings it near the left of the waist. When rotating, the waist and spine serve as the central axis. At this moment the right foot is full. (Figure 13)

图 L2F13
Standing with the body turned sideways, both hands turning over at the sides of the waist, palm-hearts facing up.
图 L2F14
Standing upright with feet together, both arms spread left and right, palm-hearts facing outward.

Form Eleven　Wind Sweeps the Plum Blossoms (chest facing south)

Movement: After the left hand has completed the 180° press from above downward, the right hand then takes over the left hand's plucking-freeing energy, reeling forward from below and then upward, plucking and turning 180°; when it reaches the upper right, it again turns into a backward reeling and opens. At the same time, the left hand below reels backward and divides to the lower left, forming a double opening energy. At this moment the left foot is full and serves as the central axis of rotation; the right foot, following the body's right turn, takes a cross-step to the west of the left foot. Finally the posture of figure 13 is formed. At this moment both hands have already changed into double backward reeling.

Key points:

The function of the above three postures lies mainly in the right palm of the double opening of Form Eight: supposing it has been seized and held, one therefore, at the same time as making a small forward reeling to change the palm into a fist, follows the essential energy of the pluck, turns and presses downward, twisting the body around. This is the basis for using continuity and following to seek release. In turning the body, the downward-pressing energy of the left palm and the upward-lifting energy of the right palm are used at the same time, making the left and right hands shake up and down as one, in order to achieve the aim of release. In the course of such a large body turn, one must rotate with steady energy; the method is not to permit a flat (horizontal) rotation, but rather to make the rotation go from · 186 · above downward (in the closing), and then again from below upward (in the ward-off opening), so as to achieve, within steadiness, the freeing effect of the backward reeling. This kind of silk-reeling with a large body turn most easily produces the phenomena of "defect," "concavity/convexity," and "break/continuity." Therefore, to avoid the above shortcomings, the key point is to hold the ward-off energy with the two arms connected, and at the same time to use the waist and spine as the central axis, so that one can rotate with tension, producing a rotational momentum like that of a windmill. In the course of rotation, first press and close the energy 180° to the rear-lower, to strengthen its steadiness; at the same time, without stopping, ward-off and open the energy 180° to the rear-upper, finally completing the 360° great body turn. In the use of energy types, the upper half-circle is a closing energy rotating mainly by the left hand; the lower half-circle is an opening energy rotating mainly by the right hand. In this way the internal power continuously manifests outward and reaches the back, and no longer produces such shortcomings as defect.

Form Twelve　Buddha's Warrior Attendant Pounds the Mortar (chest facing south)

Movement: When the previous posture is completed, the double opening energy of left and right backward reeling has been used. This posture changes from the opening energy of left-right double backward reeling into the closing energy of left-right double forward reeling, making the qi pour to the little fingers. At this moment the left foot is full. (Figure 15) After closing, it again changes into a double dividing energy of upward-downward backward reeling; when it reaches the end point of right-up left-down, the right palm turns and changes into a fist, then reels forward from above downward; at the same time the left palm reels backward to the front of the lower abdomen, palm-heart facing up; finally there is a closing energy that makes the right fist fall into the left palm-heart; at the same time, when the left foot is full, the right foot is lifted and stamps the ground. (Figure 16)

图 L2F15
Standing upright with feet together, the two arms crossed before the chest, the two palms combining energy.
图 L2F16
Standing with feet together, the right fist dropped into the left palm, the right foot lifted to stamp.

Key points:

After completing the 360° great body turn, the internal qi should be like a wheel agitating in all directions, and afterward descend into the dantian and be pounded solid — this is the main function of this posture. When it changes from the mutual opening and closing of left and right into the mutual opening and closing of above and below together with the foot stamp, the qi can be more firmly pounded solid within the dantian. This foot stamp may be light or heavy; what matters is mainly the ability to use intent and qi to send it down, and not the lightness or heaviness of the stamp itself. Therefore, besides using the sound of the stamp to test whether the power is whole or not, one must also see whether one can achieve the skill of uniting movement and stillness, so as to reach "when there is one stillness, there is nothing that is not still."

图 L2F17
Sinking into a horse stance, the two hands facing each other above and below before the chest, palm-hearts facing each other.
图 L2F18
In a bow stance with the body slanting, the right arm raised above the head and the left palm pressing down.

Form Thirteen　Shelter-the-Body Punch (chest facing south)

Movement: Beginning from the closing energy after the previous posture, both hands reel backward and divide downward to left and right; at the same time as the double opening, the right leg takes a half-step sideways to the right; after opening, they close again — at this time the two hands continue reeling backward from below forward and upward, and finally the left hand is placed outside the right hand, joining before the chest, forming an open hip and round crotch, with the left foot empty. (Figure 17) This is closing then opening, and opening then closing again — a tight, small opening and small closing. Then the right palm turns to the right-rear and reels backward outward, becoming a fist; the left palm reels backward to the lower left and also becomes a fist. After the double division, the right fist reels backward from below to the upper right, then passes before the top of the head, and turns back to the left. When the left fist reeling backward arrives at the left hip, · 188 · The right fist suddenly withdraws the body and returns, issuing elbow energy to the upper right; the center of gravity shifts right, the right leg turns solid, and the whole body sinks to the right accordingly, the leg likewise lowering. (Figure 18)

Key points:

With the chest contained and the back pulled up, the circles are tightened and loosened by the double reverse-twining silk to strengthen the elastic resilience within the warding (peng) energy of both arms; this produces a kind of body-wrapping, ring-shaped energy-storage action. It mainly trains the right hand and the lumbar spine, changing from a large circle to a small circle in order to strengthen the stored energy (at the same time it also contains a rightward shoulder-leaning energy); finally, from a single small circle it advances to no circle at all, threading the energy through to the tip of the elbow. It is therefore a compact, briskly moving posture, requiring that under the joining of the double reverse-twining silk one continue turning with the double reverse-twining silk. In the course of the turn one must achieve a state in which the internal energy has neither defect nor interruption. Hence its key point lies in using the lumbar spine as the central axis; when the right hand begins with reverse twining and turns to the front and then makes one large reverse-twining circle, it must be expressed as joined link by link. When it then passes from reverse twining to forward twining and suddenly reverses once more to reverse twining, issuing elbow energy outward to the upper right, one must be able to see that the energy arises from the heel and takes form at the tip of the elbow.

Fourteenth Posture P'ieh-shen Ch'ui (Swinging-Body Punch) (chest faces south, turning southeast)

Movement: When in the preceding posture the left fist is placed at the crotch and the right elbow energy is issued, suppose that the left fist placed at the crotch is suddenly plucked; then following the essential force of the pluck, first with a small circle of right forward-twining and left reverse-twining, the torso turns slightly to the right, the right foot becomes solid, and then immediately with the left forward-twining and right reverse-twining the back of the fist is turned over to strike back out to the left side with warding energy. At the same time, the right hand, with a small reverse twining, releases energy toward the right rear in order to maintain balance (this is a double-opening issuance of energy). But the issuance of energy must concentrate on one side; in this posture the left side is the host and the right side is the guest, so the right fist belongs to the releasing of energy while the left fist belongs to the issuing of energy. At the same time, at the moment of issuing, the right leg is solid and the chest faces southeast. (Figure 19)

图 L2F19
Fourteenth Posture, P'ieh-shen Ch'ui: the body turns slightly right, the left fist turns over its back to strike out to the left side, the right fist releases energy toward the right rear, the chest facing southeast.

· 189 · Key points: When the left [fist] has turned to the left crotch and the left arm is again plucked, in order neither to lose nor to resist, one should adapt to the essential force of the pluck and, following the direction of the opponent's essential force, strike out to the left with energy. This is a direct and straightforward technique for seeking release. Therefore in this posture the left fist counter-strikes as the main action, but the root of the strike lies in the right fist, which rotates with forward twining at the upper right, and through it the internal energy is threaded and poured into the left arm.

Fifteenth Posture Chan-shou (Chopping Hand) (chest southeast, turning north)

Movement: This posture supposes that in the strike of the preceding posture "P'ieh-shen Ch'ui" no release was obtained; then once more, following the direction of the essential force, step up with the right foot; the right hand, with forward twining, turns up from the right rear and over with the body, and joins above the left hand; at the same instant that the plucked left hand is suddenly lifted, the edge of the right palm chops down like a knife, forming the double-opening forward-cleaving posture of left high and right low, accompanied by a sinking stamp of the right foot. This is stepping up with the right foot so as to place both hands within one's own square-and-round circle; it is a technique of striking free in which two hands and one foot act simultaneously. At this moment the chest has turned to the north. (Figure 20)

Key points:

图 L2F20
Fifteenth Posture, Chan-shou: stepping up with the right foot, the right hand turns up with forward twining and then the edge of the right palm chops down, the left hand simultaneously lifting, forming a double-opening forward-cleaving posture of left high and right low, the chest turning to the north.

This is the method of releasing the plucked left hand a second time. The method most commonly used in plucking energy is the downward-pressing pluck, which forces the opponent to find it hard to follow, so that the plucked person cannot but tend toward a kneeling posture; hence he cannot but adopt a hand-leading-the-body step-up, so as to hasten the method of release in which the "right chop," the "left lift," and the "foot stamp" are all three applied together. Therefore, under the requirement that the right hand's energy be unbroken, one uses a small forward-twining rotation to step up with the right foot, bringing the plucked left hand within one's own square-and-round circle; this is the basic method of using lightness to overcome heaviness. Before stepping up and after stepping up, as well as · 190 · When chopping down, the tail gate (coccyx) must in every case be centered and upright; on no account may the downward strike cause the tail gate to topple forward.

Sixteenth Posture Fan-hua Wu-hsiu (Turning the Flower, Dancing the Sleeve) (chest north turning south, then turning northeast)

Movement: Suppose the second release has still not succeeded, that is, beneath the lifting-up and chopping-down the opponent's plucking hand still cannot be chopped away; then one must, by a turning-over movement of the body, release further — that is, following the opponent's upward-resisting chop energy, suddenly leap up; the left hand, with reverse twining, lifts up and circles over the top of the head, and the body turns over. This is a great turning of the body from below upward. The inertial force of the turn is led by the left hand. At this moment the right hand also uses reverse twining from below upward to assist, and with double-opening energy the body leaps up and turns over. At the same time the left foot lifts, and brings the right foot to leap up along with it. This movement includes using the energy of both arms and the shoulder-leaning to release the plucked hand. (Fig. 21; this figure is the instant of leaping up and turning the face) Then, in the continuing top-to-bottom rotation, when the left hand on the left side passes from reverse twining to forward twining and moves downward, the left foot simultaneously lands with a foot stamp. This is an action performed by the left hand and left foot at the same time. When the left foot lands and the right foot steps forward to the right, the right palm must simultaneously pass from reverse twining at the rear-upper position to forward twining, and chop down forward with the edge of the palm (at the chop the energy is the same as the chopping energy of splitting the frame). At the same time, the left hand forms a fist and, with forward twining, strikes out to the left rear as the guest. At this moment the left foot is solid. (Fig. 22; this figure is the posture at the moment of rotating the body, landing, and giving one chop)

图 L2F21
Sixteenth Posture, Fan-hua Wu-hsiu, the leap-up and turn of the face: the body leaps up, the left hand lifts and circles over the top of the head turning over, the right hand assists, the right foot leaps up along with the left foot.
图 L2F22
Fan-hua Wu-hsiu, landing with one chop: the left foot lands with a foot stamp and becomes solid, the right foot steps forward, the edge of the right palm chops forward and down, the left fist strikes out with forward twining to the left rear.

· 191 · Key points: The characteristic of the preceding posture's chopping-hand release method is that both parties' arms are at the front, and the distances from the point of application of force to both parties are equal; whereas the body-turn of this posture "Fan-hua Wu-hsiu" employs the rotating action of the body method and the lumbar spine, causing the distances of the force's point of application suddenly to form a striking contrast (near to oneself, far from the opponent). That is to say, the release point is made far from the opponent and near to oneself. This relationship of one near and one far forms a change in the magnitude of the torque. After turning the body, of the two feet the left foot lands first with a foot stamp and the right foot lands slightly later; in this way the inertial force of the rotation of the waist axis is strengthened, and consequently the downward-chopping energy of the right hand is also strengthened — this is where the key to yet another method of seeking release lies. This kind of release uses the downward chop of the edge of the right palm to take over the rotational inertia of the right hand's forward-twining turn-over. At the same time, the downward chop must be loosened and elastic, for only thus can the next posture be prompted to leap up nimbly. This kind of release is also another example of using lightness to overcome heaviness, and is the concrete expression of one technique serving two purposes, that is to say, a dual use in which release conceals a strike and the strike conceals a release. Therefore this posture consists mainly in one hand releasing while the other hand chops down following the rotation.

Seventeenth Posture Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan (Covering-Hand Forearm Punch) (chest northeast, turning east)

Movement: This is a posture whose main purpose is the practice of storing energy and of issuing energy; within the frame of the Second Routine, it is mostly used to link things up whenever it follows a special posture. This is the first Covering-Hand Forearm Punch of the Second Routine. It borrows the elastic energy of the chop of the preceding posture: both hands, with double forward twining, leap the body up, and the front-rear positions of the left and right legs are exchanged; then the right foot lands with a foot stamp and becomes solid, and the left foot steps forward with a lifting (ch'ien/jian) movement and becomes empty. At the same time, with double reverse twining the whole body's energy is bent and stored, and the ring-circle of both arms is made smaller to strengthen the stored energy. At this moment the left hand is above and the right hand below, the right foot is empty and the left foot is solid. (Figure 23) Then, the latter half of the section is the issuance of energy. Before issuing, the right hand first makes a small reverse-twining circle and places it at the waist, the center of the fist facing upward; at the same time the left hand relatively does reverse twining, the center of the fist facing downward — this is the left storing of energy. When the right hand is at the right waist, the right hand sinks its energy, and amid that steadiness still uses reverse twining to sud- · 192 · With the momentum of the issuance, the energy is sent forward. At this moment the center of the fist faces downward. At the same time, the left hand relatively turns to reverse twining, releasing the fist backward to draw it back, and places it at the left waist. The center of the fist faces downward. When storing energy, the right foot is solid; when issuing energy, the left foot is solid. (Figure 24)

图 L2F23
Seventeenth Posture, Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan, storing energy: the right foot solid and the left foot empty, the left hand above and the right hand below, with double reverse twining bending and storing the energy.
图 L2F24
Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan, issuing energy: the right fist is sent forward, the center of the fist facing downward, the left hand releases energy backward and draws back to the left waist; at the issuance the left foot is solid.

Key points:

This posture is the one most frequently used (six times) in the second frame, and its key point lies in strengthening the practice of the energy of "storing energy like drawing a bow." It is led by containing the chest and pulling up the back, causing both arms to possess a joining energy shaped like the character 6. When practicing the issuance of energy, there must be the issuance energy of lifting a thing up and then bringing it down. Therefore the first half-section must be like drawing a bow to strengthen elasticity, and the second half-section must further have the twining energy of releasing an arrow deep into the target. This is the concrete expression of making the movement issue far and long. For this reason, before issuing energy there must be a sinking small circle, so that the drawn-out stored energy and the issued energy become one; one may not simply use a straight-line storing-and-issuing energy that has no drawing along with it.

Eighteenth Posture Fei-pu Niu-luan Chou (Flying Step, Twisted Phoenix Elbow) (chest east turning north, then turning south)

Movement: After the issuance of energy of the preceding posture "Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan," both fists make a small reverse twining in their original position, joining energy front and rear; when the right fist with reverse twining goes forward and the left fist with reverse twining goes backward to open, the right foot is accordingly lifted, and leaps forward with a flying step, landing as solid. At the same time, with · 193 · With the right foot serving as the pivot of the turning heel, the left foot sweeps an arc past the right foot and comes to the east side of the right foot, causing the body to spin in the air through 270°. (Figure 25) This supposes that in the preceding posture "Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan," after the right hand has issued its energy, it is plucked by the opponent, and it is a posture adopted when there is no time to draw it back. The opponent is applying energy along the direction of the issuance, so one cannot but follow quickly, to adapt to the person, using a flying step to comply with and transform the energy. In the course of complying with the flying step, one naturally turns the body to the left, using the back-bending-and-leaning energy to release the plucked right hand; this is similar to the various "Jade Maiden Works the Shuttle" postures of the First Routine.

图 L2F25
Eighteenth Posture, Fei-pu Niu-luan Chou, the body spin: with the right foot as the pivot of the turning heel, the left foot sweeps an arc past the right foot, the body spins in the air through 270°, the left fist with reverse twining trailing behind.
图 L2F26
After the great 270° turn, the wide horse stance: both hands draw apart to form one great ring, the body sinks into a horse stance, the left foot on the left, both fists separated front and rear.

It is likewise a leaping step, but the hand method is different. (Figure 26) After the great 270° body-turn, suppose the back-bending-and-leaning energy of the great turn still cannot release the plucked right hand; then after the turn, both hands with double reverse twining unite as one, the center of the left palm presses upon the opponent's plucking hand, causing both arms to form a transverse ring, and the right elbow energy strikes forward. This is the final application of one technique to two uses: it is release and also advance-and-attack. After the turn, the right foot is solid; at the issuance of elbow energy, the left foot is solid. The Niu-luan Chou finally formed is as in Fig. 27.

图 L2F27
Niu-luan Chou, the fixed posture: both hands with double reverse twining unite as one, the center of the left palm presses upon the opponent's plucking hand, both arms form a transverse ring, the right elbow strikes forward; after the turn the right foot is solid, and at the issuance of elbow energy the left foot is solid.

· 194 · Key points: This is the final method of using the back-bending-and-leaning energy to release the plucked right hand. Because of the rotation of the body, it can also cause the distances of the force's point of application suddenly to form a striking contrast favorable to oneself, so as to achieve overcoming heaviness with lightness; it is a posture and strike that releases without seeking to be released. At the same time, what distinguishes this posture from the preceding several is that the left palm is pressed at the right elbow, and the back and elbow are joined to strike the opponent transversely. This is a special posture that presses down the opponent's plucking forearm, fixing the opponent's plucking point so that he cannot change it, and throws the person out sideways. Therefore it is likewise one technique with two uses. Its key point lies in being able, after flying out with the step, still to land with the body established upright and centered. Most especially, one must note that after issuing, both arms must still be bent and stored with reserve, rather than extending the hands fully straight. Therefore one must use the flying step to come out in order to suit the essential energy. This is the method of final release in a whole series of release movements; that is, it is an example of the Second Frame's practice of plucking and of releasing from the pluck. Although this posture strikes forward with elbow energy, its root is still in the back-bending-and-leaning energy of the right side. For this reason, its essential requirement is that only on the basis of establishing the body upright and centered can the unity of using elbow and leaning together be obtained.

Nineteenth Posture Yün-shou (Moving Hands / Cloud Hands) (the first three, chest south)

图 L2F28
Nineteenth Posture, Yün-shou, the first segment: both hands move simultaneously to the left, the body established upright and centered, the two palms tracing arcs one front and one rear.
图 L2F29
Yün-shou, the right-turning segment: both hands move simultaneously to the right and then to the left, the two palms tracing arcs along a circular path.

Movement: Both hands move simultaneously to the left, then simultaneously to the right, and then move to the left again, forming · 195 · These make three Moving Hands, slightly different from the Moving Hands of the First Routine. After the joining energy of the preceding posture Niu-luan Chou, the center of gravity shifts entirely to the left leg, the right foot steps up alongside, with the tip of the toe touching beside the left foot; at the same time the left palm with reverse twining moves and turns to the left, and the right fist becomes a palm and, with forward twining, moves to the left. (Figure 28) Then the center of gravity shifts right, the right foot becomes solid, and the left heel first leaves the ground and lifts; at the same time both hands, the right with reverse twining and the left with forward twining, move and turn to the right, the right palm passing before the face and the left palm passing before the abdomen. (Figure 29) Then the left foot opens half a step sideways to the left, the center of gravity gradually shifts left, the left foot becomes solid and the right foot becomes empty; at the same time both hands, the left with reverse twining and the right with forward twining, move and turn to the left, the left palm passing before the face and the right palm passing before the abdomen. (Figure 30)

图 L2F30
Nineteenth Posture, Yün-shou, the third movement: the left foot opens half a step sideways to the left, the center of gravity shifts left, the left foot becomes solid and the right foot becomes empty, both hands with left reverse and right forward twining, the left palm passing before the face and the right palm before the abdomen, moving and turning to the left.

Key points:

In this posture one must, under a smooth and gentle curved movement, perform the silk-twining transformations of left forward and right reverse, and right forward and left reverse, and must lift and lower the legs under the condition of not moving the step, fully expressing the requirement of the division of solid and empty in which hands and feet follow one another above and below; this is also the basic requirement of this posture. The Second Frame, having passed through the preceding several leaping and strenuous fist postures, can here adjust its breathing movement a little. Therefore in this figure-∞ movement of the hands, the speed of movement may be slow or fast; this is the place where the Second Frame is naturally divided into sections.

Twentieth Posture Kao T'an Ma (High Pat on Horse) (chest west)

Movement: After performing the first three Moving Hands, with the left heel as the axis the body turns right, and the right heel leaves the ground; at the same time both hands, the right with reverse twining and the left with forward twining, move and turn to the right, the right palm passing before the face and the left palm passing before the abdomen; when the left palm has moved and turned to the right of the body, the center of the hand faces upward. (Figure 31) Then the right foot is lifted, and the body continues to turn right; at the same time the right palm, with forward twining, passes beneath the left palm · 196 · draws in from the side, the center of the palm facing upward, and the left hand with reverse twining pushes forward past the upper side of the right palm, the center of the palm facing outward and downward. (Figure 32)

图 L2F31
Twentieth Posture, Kao T'an Ma, the Moving Hands before it: both hands with right reverse and left forward twining move and turn to the right, and when the left palm has moved to the right of the body the center of the hand faces upward.
图 L2F32
Twentieth Posture, Kao T'an Ma, the fixed posture: the right palm draws in from the side, the center of the palm facing upward, and the left hand with reverse twining pushes forward past the upper side of the right palm, the center of the palm facing outward and downward.

Twenty-first Posture Yün-shou (Moving Hands) (the last three)

图 L2F33
Twenty-first Posture, Yün-shou (the last three), the exchange: both hands with right reverse and left forward twining, the right hand turning toward the right front and the left hand turning toward the front of the chest, the whole body with the left foot as the turning axis rotating 90°, the right foot landing with a foot stamp and becoming solid.
图 L2F34
Yün-shou (the last three), the left sideways step: the left foot opens one step sideways to the left, touching the ground first with the heel, and the center of gravity shifts to the left leg.

Movement: After performing Kao T'an Ma, then both hands, with right reverse and left forward twining, turn the right hand toward the right front, while the left hand turns toward the front of the chest. At the same time as this exchange of the two hands, the whole body, with the left foot as the turning axis, rotates 90°. At the same time, the right foot lands with a foot stamp and becomes solid, and the left foot opens one step sideways to the left, touching the ground first with the heel. (Figure 33) The center of gravity shifts to the left leg. The left foot · 197 · Steady the foot; the right foot steps half a step to the left, touching the ground first with the toe. At the same time, the two hands turn: the left hand with reverse (ni) coiling and the right hand with forward (shun) coiling; the left palm passes in front of the face and the right palm passes in front of the abdomen, moving to the left. (Figure 34) Then the right foot stamps firmly, and the left foot opens half a step sideways to the left; at the same time, the two hands turn: the right hand with reverse coiling and the left hand with forward coiling; the right palm passes in front of the face and the left palm passes in front of the abdomen, moving to the right. (Figure 35)

Key points:

In the second routine (form) there are the first three and the last three "moving hands" (yün shou); the first three face the chest south, the last three face the chest north. Their basic requirements and functions are the same, so they will not be repeated. Therefore this form's key points no longer discuss the moving-hands action itself, but only the turn from doing the high pat-on-horse (kao t'an ma) after raising the leg to the front, into the turn toward the back. This action requires turning the body around within a gentle curve, with unbroken silk-reeling and continuous inner strength; therefore one must make a good small circle of the left hand drawn back in front of the chest in reverse coiling. Through this reverse coiling one shifts the torso, and the torso and the silk-reeling can be changed over suspended in the air. In this way not only is the inner strength kept unbroken, but it can also be threaded through into the next action. Hence this form is also a rather difficult action for practising the threading-through of section after section.

In order to make the turn-around easier, after Chen Fa-ke came to Peking, and to popularize Chen-style taijiquan, he added two boxing forms — cloud hands (yün shou) and high pat-on-horse — into this turn. Thus there was no longer the requirement of threading through while turning sharply in the air, and it became easier to do.

Twenty-second Form: High Pat on Horse (chest north turning northwest)

Action: After the right turn-palm of the previous form, when the body turns left again, the two hands first both turn forward (shun) and close together, so that the two hands cross in front of the chest and pass each other; then both turn reverse (ni) and open.

图 L2F35
Hands moving with left reverse and right forward coiling, body turning and left foot opening half a step sideways

up. When closing, the left foot is full. (Figure 37) When opening, the right foot is full (Figure 38). This is a boxing form linking to the next, and its jin is the same as "white crane spreads its wings" in the first routine; only the hands are more evenly levelled in height, and the two legs straddle wider, so as to manifest a rounded crotch.

Key points:

This is a boxing form that closes from double forward (shun) coiling and then opens from double reverse (ni) coiling; it requires that in the process of turning open after closing there be no corners, ridges or hollows, so that the silk-reeling jin is carried onto the back of the bow. At the same time, it requires that in the enlarged and expanded posture one strengthen the elastic training with section-after-section threading, so as to raise the taut (beng) jin. When closing, pay attention to the two thumbs, chiefly the left-hand fingers; when opening, pay attention to the two little fingers, chiefly the right-hand fingers.

Twenty-third Form: Linked Pearl Cannon, part one (chest northwest turning west)

图 L2F36
Two hands with double forward coiling and double closing, crossed before the chest, left foot full
图 L2F37
Double reverse coiling opening up, right foot full, rounded crotch

Action: From the opening jin of the previous form to the closing jin of this form, it is a closing by double reverse coiling. At this time, the right hand reverse-coils to the right of the chest, palm facing outward left; the left hand reverse-coils to the front of the chest, palm facing outward right; the two hands close into one closing jin in front of the chest. At this time the left foot is full, the right foot empty. Then the two hands forward-coil and press out (peng) to the front; at the same time the right foot becomes full, and when the two hands press out and come down with double forward coiling, the left foot retreats one step and the centre of gravity immediately shifts left, sitting on the left leg as full. When the two hands sink down (t'a), the whole body forms a posture of storing jin. (Figure 38) Then the two hands again turn to double reverse press out (peng) forward and upward, rolling up and storing; the right foot becomes full. Then the two hands immediately come down again from the front, leftward and backward, with forward coiling. When the two hands sink down, the left foot again becomes full. This is to add one more store on the basis of the previous stored jin. Finally, with double reverse coiling, send out the pressing-out (peng) jin. At this time the right palm faces outward, the left palm faces downward. At the same moment as the jin is issued, the right foot advances half a step forward and the left foot follows with half a step, the heel grinding the ground with a sound. (Figs. 38, 39) This is the first "linked pearl cannon" action; this form has three linked-pearl-cannon actions in all.

Key points:

图 L2F38
Double reverse coiling issuing the pressing-out jin, right palm outward and left palm down, right foot advancing half a step
图 L2F39
Right foot following up half a step, the heel grinding the ground with a sound

This form is suited to the taijiquan "opening-door" hand technique for entering and moving within the opponent's circle. Its characteristic is that it takes the actively rotating two hands as the boxing form for entering the circle. Its hand technique is like pushing a water mill: the left hand rotates on the inside to defend the pit of the chest, and the right hand rotates on the outside to attack forward. The two hands, thus combined inside and outside, keep using the left hand to add "ice" (material) and the right hand to turn the millstone in motion. At the same time, the two feet follow up with the "heel-following" (gen pu) step. Although one does not seek to adhere to the opponent, yet as long as some part of the rotating, attacking right arm touches a point on the opponent, that touched place can serve as the point of adhesion, and one may thereupon stick and change in ten thousand ways. This form adopts the "advance and retreat with the body" and the flexible, transforming, centred and upright body method, so that when objectively one must meet changes and make transitions, there is always leeway, and one is sufficient to support all eight directions. Its Next: since the previous form is the double opening of spread wings, this form must first roll it up and store it. This is in order to store and then issue. At the same time, in order to issue more crisply, before issuing the jin one shrinks one more small circle, to further strengthen its elasticity, and then calmly sends the jin out. When issuing the jin, although the right foot is full, yet for the sake of the centred and upright relation of "the central earth does not leave its position," the difference between the fullness of the front foot and the emptiness of the back foot is required to be slight, so that one may quickly rotate and advance forward.

Twenty-fourth Form: Linked Pearl Cannon, part two (chest west)

Twenty-fifth Form: Linked Pearl Cannon, part three (chest west)

Action: In doing the second and third linked pearl cannons, the right hand goes from front-above with forward coiling toward the front of the chest, and the left hand goes from left-rear-below with forward coiling to close with the right hand before the chest. At this time, sitting on the left leg, the whole body again forms a stored jin. (Figure 40) Thereafter the actions from Fig. 40 to Fig. 41 are the same as the first linked pearl cannon (that is, the same as the actions from Fig. 38 to Fig. 39).

This boxing form may, according to the practitioner's need, be done several more times in succession, or taken out for special practice; its action is the same as the previous linked pearl cannons. But in order that the whole set may return to the original spot at the end, after this form has been done several extra times, the later "white snake spits out its tongue" must likewise be done several extra times, so that the number of times the two forms are done is equal. The other key points are the same as the first linked pearl cannon.

Twenty-sixth Form: Riding the Qilin Backwards (chest west turning east)

图 L2F40
Sitting on the left leg storing jin, right hand forward-coiling before the chest and closing with the left hand

Action: After the three advancing steps of the previous linked pearl cannon, the two palms close together in a double closing; first the left palm reverse-coils and turns toward the front of the chest, the fingers of the palm erect, palm facing right. At the same time, the right palm reverse-coils turning to guard outside the left forearm; the centre of gravity moves forward, the right leg is full (Figure 42). Then the right hand reverse-coils to the right-rear-above, and the left hand reverse-coils to the left-front-below; at the same time lift the left foot, the two hands separate, and with the right foot as the pivot of rotation, turn right 180° (Figure 43), turning the body to face east; when the turn reaches the east, the body is carried around by going from opening to closing. At this time the right hand is at the lower right, palm facing down; the left hand is at the upper left, the fingers of the palm erect. At this time the left foot, having been carried around with the turning body, is still lifted. (Figure 44)

Key points:

图 L2F41
Right hand reverse-coiling to guard outside the left forearm, centre of gravity moving forward, right leg full
图 L2F42
Right hand reverse-coiling to right-rear-above, left hand reverse-coiling to left-front-below, left foot lifted and hands separating
图 L2F43
Turning right 180° with the right foot as axis, the body turning to face east
图 L2F44
The body carried around from opening to closing, right hand lower right with palm down, left hand upper left with fingers erect

With the right foot as the axis, when the left foot strides over following the turning body, the upper body must still not lean forward or lean backward. Because the left foot, following the body's 180° turn to the right-rear, strides across backwards, one takes the meaning of "striding backwards (tao k'ua)" and names it "riding the qilin backwards."

Twenty-seventh Form: White Snake Spits Out Its Tongue, part one (chest east)

Action: After the left foot has strided backwards across in the previous form, immediately follow with the right hand making a small circle chiefly of forward coiling to the front, striking out with the taut (beng) jin of the fingers. At the same time, the left hand behind still, with reverse coiling, coordinates with the right hand and issues together toward the left-rear. At this time the left foot steps forward half a step and lands full, and the right foot immediately follows up, grinding the ground with a sound, completing the first "white snake spits out its tongue" pressing-out and issuing. (Figure 45) This boxing form is an "opposite-step" (ao pu) action that people do not commonly have; it takes some effort before one can be thoroughly familiar with its jin, or one may take it out for special practice.

Key points:

This form can likewise serve as an opening-door hand technique, as a way of entering the opponent's circle with the opposite step; both use the body to advance and retreat, and no leaning or tilting body method is allowed, to avoid the fault of being able to support only one side inside the circle. In order to be able to change flexibly lengthwise and crosswise, front and back, the division of full and empty within this boxing form is the same as in "linked pearl cannon"; it likewise requires "small empty, small full" (1), so that after entering the circle, on touching any part one obtains a smooth, adhering and sticking effect. The difference lies in that the previous linked pearl cannon is the forward step, while this "white snake spits out its tongue" is the opposite step (sometimes, to simplify it and make it easy, someone changes the second "white snake spits out its tongue" to (1) "Small empty, small full" refers to the ratio of weight distribution on the two feet: suppose the two legs bear a total of 100 catties, one leg 55 catties and the other 45 catties; thus with only a tiny movement one can quickly change full and empty over; therefore those of deep skill have a small difference between full and empty, and the externally visible circles are also small.

图 L2F45
After the left foot strides backwards, the right hand forward-coils and strikes out the pressing jin to the front, the left foot stepping forward half a step full and the right foot following up

"covering-hand forearm punch (yen shou kung ch'ui)," and afterwards do the third "white snake spits out its tongue"; this makes it much easier to do). When practising the forward stride of the opposite step, at first it feels a little awkward, so one must practise a great deal. At the same time, this boxing form is a short-distance storing and issuing, so one must hollow the chest and raise the back, with the spinal column leading, so as to achieve section-after-section threading and the issuing of jin from the spine. This is the representative action of the whole set for issuing jin from the spine. If the curved issuing is manifested only by the two arms, it does not meet the requirement. It would be even better if one could take it out for special practice.

Twenty-sixth Form: White Snake Spits Out Its Tongue, part two (chest east)

Twenty-seventh Form: White Snake Spits Out Its Tongue, part three (chest east)

图 L2F46
Right hand in front forward-coiling and storing to the front of the chest with palm facing left, left hand reverse-coiling to the left flank, centre of gravity shifted back with right foot full and left toe touching ground
图 L2F47
Right palm forward-coiling a small circle in front and striking out with the taut jin of the fingers

Action: The stored jin of the previous "white snake spits out its tongue" was completed by the closing posture of "riding the qilin backwards" splitting and turning and then one more closing jin. But the stored jin of this "white snake spits out its tongue" is stored after the issuing jin of the "white snake spits out its tongue." This is the point of difference between the two "white snake spits out its tongue." At the start, the right hand in front forward-coils and stores to the front of the chest, palm facing left. At the same time, the left hand, on the left, reverse-coils and turns to the left flank. When storing, the two arms hold the jin together, the centre of gravity shifts back, the right foot is full, and the left toe touches the ground as empty. (Figure 46) Then the right palm, in front, chiefly forward-coiling a small circle, strikes out with the taut (beng) jin of the fingers. At the same time, the left palm behind, with reverse coiling, coordinates with the right palm and issues together. At this time the left foot steps forward half a step and lands full, the right foot immediately follows up, grinding the ground with a sound, completing the second "white snake spits out its tongue." (Figure 47) This form also, according to the practitioner's need, may be done several extra times, the same number of times as the "linked pearl cannon."

Key points: Same as the first white snake spits out its tongue.

Thirtieth Form: Turning Over the Flower at the Bottom of the Sea (chest east turning west)

Action: This is a special boxing form. After the previous form's right hand has issued the pressing-out (peng) jin forward, it immediately closes with the left hand behind in a double forward coiling that crosses. After closing, with the double opening jin of right forward and left reverse, the body is turned right 180°. At this time the centre of gravity shifts onto the left foot, forming an independent posture. In the course of turning to the west, the left and right hands become fists; the right fist strikes with the back of the fist downward and backward, the fist-heart facing forward. The left fist strikes upward and backward, the fist-heart facing right. (Fig. 48. From Fig. 48 onward to the last figure, because formerly when photographing Teacher Chen Fa-ke all the photographs of the action were taken from the reverse side, in all the following figures, facing the reader is north, back to the reader is south, the left side as one faces the reader is east, and the right side as one faces the reader is west. This will not be repeated hereafter.)

Key points:

This boxing form chiefly exercises the elbow joint. The left fist striking backward and upward and the right fist striking backward and downward — striking up and down — is a rarely seen issuing backward, so its key point lies in requiring that the balance of the body be maintained when issuing up and down and backward.

Thirty-first Form: Covering-Hand Forearm Punch (chest west)

图 L2F48
Left and right hands form fists, right fist striking down-backward with the back of the fist and fist-heart forward, left fist striking up-backward with fist-heart right, the body turning right 180° with the centre of gravity shifted to an independent posture on the left foot

Action: In the previous form the right leg is raised, and the two fists strike backward to the sides, one above and one below backward, the right fist, after slightly lifting up with forward coiling, sinks down again with forward coiling, the back of the fist facing down, and the right foot simultaneously stamps the ground. At the same time, the left fist, coordinating with the right fist, after slightly sinking with reverse coiling, is immediately raised; the whole body's centre of gravity is all on the one stamp of the right leg. When the right fist forward-coils until the fist-heart faces up again, and after adding a sinking jin, then it changes to reverse coiling and sends the jin out. The issuing hand must still keep some leeway, and must not be fully extended. At the same time, the left fist, raised with reverse coiling, turns once into forward coiling and issues backward as the guest (secondary), so as to maintain a double issuing with host and guest.
