(Figure 49)

Key points: Same as the seventeenth form, "covering-hand forearm punch."

Thirty-second Form: Turn the Body, Six Harmonies (chest west, from north turning south)

图 L2F49
Right fist forward-coiling, lifted and sunk, back of the fist facing down, right foot stamping the ground, left fist after reverse-coiling and sinking is raised
图 L2F50
Right hand forward-coiling and gathering before the left shoulder, left hand reverse-coiling and extending before the chest, centre of gravity shifting right and the body turning right
图 L2F51
The two fists separating to left and right

Action: From the opening of the previous form "covering-hand forearm punch," the right hand which had issued in front is gathered with forward coiling before the left shoulder; at the same time, the left hand reverse-coils and extends before the chest. At the same time the centre of gravity shifts right, and the body turns right. (Figure 50) Then, next, the two fists separate to left and right. (Figure 51) Then Shift the whole weight onto the left leg; pivoting on the left heel, lift the right foot and turn the body to the right-rear; at the same time, bring both fists together and cross them in front of the abdomen, the right fist inside, both fist-hearts facing inward. (Figure 52)

Book page 195

Form 33. Left Wrap-Whip Cannon (1)

Form 33. Left Wrap-Whip Cannon (1)

Then the right foot lands with a stomp. (Figure 53) At the same time the left foot steps sideways to the left; both hands turn to double-reverse (shun), and issue power to the left and right outer sides, slightly backward. At this moment, the fist- hearts face forward and upward, and in issuing, the left hand and left foot are dominant. This is a variation within Wrap-Whip (bian). (Figure 54)

图 L2F52
Weight shifted onto the left leg, right foot lifted, body turning to the right-rear, both fists brought together and crossed before the abdomen, right fist inside
图 L2F53
Right foot landing with a stomp, the posture of the body turning right
图 L2F54
Left foot stepping sideways to the left, both hands double-reverse issuing power to the left and right outer sides, fist-hearts facing forward and up

Key points: "Hollow the chest and raise the back" means the spine is drawn taut from top to bottom. Because of the wrapping (guo) relation in this form, the back is drawn taut on all four sides—up, down, left and right. It is another special fist-form for training the emission of power from the spine, and it is also the form in the Second Routine that trains the horizontal (heng) stepping method. This is a mass-combat type of stepping. When the leg and the arm cross · 207 · This is "wrap" (guo), the storing of power in the legs. When the two legs are separated it becomes "whip" (bian), the releasing of power in the legs, which can train a person to the skill of springing sideways with a light body. The key point of this form is that before issuing, one must wrap tightly once, making the qi sink further down, and only then can power be issued crisply to left and right, displaying a firm and resilient springiness. In this way one stores and issues twice in succession. At the same time, when the two hands go from the double-reverse opening to the double-reverse closing that makes the "wrap," the whole body is tightly wrapped and the qi clings to the spine, forming a moment of fully stored power; as soon as the foot lands with a stomp, that is immediately the left-and-right issuing of power in the "whip."

Book page 196

Form 34. Left Wrap-Whip Cannon (2) (chest facing south)

Form 34. Left Wrap-Whip Cannon (2) (chest facing south)

Movement: after "turn body six harmonies" and the preceding form "Wrap-Whip Cannon" have issued to left and right, both fists turn back to double-reverse, the weight first shifts right so that the right foot becomes solid, then both fists are brought together in front of the lower abdomen and the weight shifts left; at the same time the right foot is lifted and set down to the left of the left foot, so that both fists and both feet are crossed and wrapped. This is again a "wrap." (Figure 55) At this moment the two arms are tightly wrapped, with a sinking power, and the spine must also be drawn taut. Next both fists turn to double-reverse (shun), issuing power to the left and right outer sides and slightly backward, while the left foot steps sideways to the left—this is again a "whip." (Figure 56) This form may also be repeated several times in succession as needed, the movement being the same as Left Wrap-Whip Cannon (2).

图 L2F55
Both fists brought together in front of the lower abdomen, weight shifted left, right foot lifted and set down to the left of the left foot, both fists and both feet crossed and wrapped
图 L2F56
Both fists turn double-reverse issuing power to the left and right outer sides, left foot stepping sideways to the left

· 208 · Key points: This is a mass-combat fist-form that is both "moving" (zou) and "attacking" (gong). Its key point is that when springing sideways and dropping down one must appear calm and not buoyant; at the same time, through the process of one wrap and one change, the power must not be broken, so as to meet the demand of mass combat where no gap can be found. Therefore, at the connecting point after the double-opening issuing of power of the first Wrap-Whip, one must make a fold (zhedie), so that the inner motive force connects gently along a curve into the second Wrap-Whip.

Book page 197

Form 35. Right Wrap-Whip Cannon (1) (chest turning from south to north)

Form 35. Right Wrap-Whip Cannon (1) (chest turning from south to north)

Movement: the double-reverse issuing of power of the second Wrap-Whip in the preceding form is a double-opening power; after opening, there is again a double-sinking power outward and down, and both fists change to double-reverse twisting and are stored up, brought together in front of the lower abdomen with the backs of the fists facing each other; at the same time, taking the left foot as the central pivot of rotation, lift the right foot, and using the double-closing power of both fists—the left arm making a small circle, the right arm making a large circle—carry the body turning 180° to the left, the left foot sweeping half a circle with the sole adhering to the ground as the body turns. (Figure 57) At this moment both fists also turn to double-reverse (shun) toward the left and right sides and issue firm power slightly backward. In issuing, the left hand and left foot are dominant, forming the first Wrap-Whip after the turn. (Figure 58)

图 L2F57
Taking the left foot as pivot and lifting the right foot, both fists double-reverse twisting brought together before the lower abdomen with fist-backs facing each other, body carried turning 180° to the left
图 L2F58
Both fists turning double-reverse issuing firm power to the left and right sides, left hand and left foot dominant, forming the first Wrap-Whip after the turn

Key points: It takes the left foot as the central pivot of rotation, using the stored-power "wrap" posture to turn the body · 209 · body. The left foot sweeps half a circle sideways as the body turns, and throughout this process one must still keep the body steady—this is an important condition for whether the issuing of power of the "whip" after the turn is crisp or not. The remaining key points are the same as those of the two preceding Wrap-Whips.

Form 36. Right Wrap-Whip Cannon (2) (chest facing north)

Movement: this fist-form is the same as the second Wrap-Whip before the turn, except that the chest has now turned to face north. (Figs. 59, 60, 61)

图 L2F59
Both fists brought together before the lower abdomen, right foot lifted, Right Wrap-Whip Cannon storing its power
图 L2F60
Right foot set down to the right of the left foot, both fists and both feet crossed and wrapped
图 L2F61
Both fists turning double-reverse issuing firm power to the left and right sides, chest facing north

Key points: same as Form 34.

Form 37. Beast-Head Posture (chest turning from south to northeast)

Movement: after the double-opening issuing of power of Wrap-Whip in the preceding form, the right foot arcs 90° to the right-rear, not made the same width as the left foot. Then the left foot arcs half a step to the left-rear, turning the body around. At the same time, the upper part of the body, with the right fist twisting shun, draws an arc from outside inward, turning to beneath the left elbow, the fist-heart facing inward. The left fist twists ni (reverse), rising up from outer-low to inner-high, the fist-heart facing right, forming the posture of double closing. At this moment the right foot is solid. (Figure 62) Next, the raised left arm, twisting shun, presses horizontally to the left, releasing power from right to left-rear as a feint (bin), while the left foot steps back to the left-rear, still keeping the right leg solid, so as to coordinate with the right hand turned beneath the elbow to bring the forearm forward horizontally, issuing the elbow power of the horizontal forearm with a shun twist. (Figure 63)

图 L2F62
Right fist twisting shun drawing an arc to beneath the left elbow, left fist twisting ni rising up, forming the double-closing posture, right foot solid
图 L2F63
Left arm twisting shun pressing horizontally left and releasing power, right hand turned beneath the elbow bringing the forearm forward horizontally to issue elbow power

· 210 · Key points: At the beginning of this form one raises the left arm and strikes across with the right, forming a variation that stores power, and one is required to fill the body's internal power to the full. The right foot arcing half a circle and unloading a step to the right-rear can help the power fill out. This is the function of "retreating is advancing" and "defending is attacking." For once the raised left arm has been folded across, the closing power is reinforced, and the right arm at once passes above the left arm to issue elbow power—so-called striking where it is not expected and attacking where it is unprepared, making it hard for the opponent to defend. This fist-form, which issues elbow power with the forearm held across, is, apart from the later "Seize Two Arms" (duo er gong), the only form in the Second Routine for training the issuing of elbow power; there is no other such form in the Second Routine, and so it must be practised with care. (It is said this was selected from Qi Jiguang's boxing forms.)

Book page 198

Form 38. Splitting the Frame (chest facing northeast)

Form 38. Splitting the Frame (chest facing northeast)
图 L2F64
Both palms crossed and closed together, crotch rounded and sunk, left foot stepping out into a bow stance
图 L2F65
Issuing the left-shoulder leaning power, right foot solid

Movement: after the issuing of power in "Beast-Head Posture," the right fist twists shun in a small arc downward and back up. At the same time, the left fist twists ni in a small arc upward and back down. When the relative turning brings the left fist below and the right fist above into a single vertical line, the right foot springs up; at the same time, the left foot steps forward one step. Now both fists change into palms, which close together tightly crossed, and the crotch is rounded and sunk, concealing a close-range shoulder-leaning power. At this moment the left · 211 · foot is solid. (Figure 65) The preceding movement issued the left-shoulder leaning power from within the stored power; with- out needing to store power again, one need only release the stored power of the preceding form and that is the issuing; it is issued with the left hand twisting shun upward and outward, and is the only upward-striking power in taijiquan. The target struck is the opponent's lower jaw. This form may be done either with the fist or with the palm, and it is also a rear-striking method in which the right hand twists ni downward and inward as a feint. (Figure 66)

图 L2F66
Right hand twisting ni downward and inward striking to the rear, left hand twisting shun upward and outward striking upward

Key points: This is a fist-form which, after the peng issuing of power of the preceding form, turns to storing power and embodies a releasing of power within that storing. When the two hands cross and one steps sideways half a step, the chopping power of the right hand above striking the face to the upper left and the left shoulder's outward-left shoulder-leaning power must be used simultaneously. Of the two powers only one is a leaning power—one open, one hidden; one feint, one real—and this is the special characteristic of the form. For whenever the shoulder-leaning power is issued, the head is most easily controlled by the opponent. Therefore in this form, within a close distance of seven inches, one also uses the face-striking palm in a forward-striking posture; thus it not only protects the head but also makes up for the insufficiency of the shoulder-leaning power.

· 212 · In using the leaning power while storing posture and power, one must have a steady and upright power; if the leaning power misses, then on the leaning side the elbow strike and hand ward-off (peng) are both stored and ready to issue, and at any moment can remedy what is lacking.

Fig. 66 is one of the hand methods that uses peng as the principal element. After the peng issuing power, the palm-chopping power and the shoulder-leaning power, it adds a unique upward-striking power. This is a linked-pearl (lianzhu) style of issuing power, whose aim is to strike the opponent rather than to send him out. But striking the opponent's lower jaw likewise has the possibility of making him fall. This is a special striking method among the hand methods of taijiquan. At the same time, because the preceding fist-form had already stored power to the full in both hands and both feet, the key point of this form's upward strike lies in concentrating the power to an even higher degree within one sinking of it, so that the upward-striking movement can display a firm and steady internal power.

Book page 200

Form 39. Flower-Flipping Sleeve Dance (chest turning from southeast to northeast)

Form 39. Flower-Flipping Sleeve Dance (chest turning from southeast to northeast)

Movement: this follows the upward strike of the preceding form that divided its power in two, changing into a sinking body method. Before the movement, one must add another steady elastic power, and lead the body up under the guidance of the crown-top power (ding jin). This is the requirement that "when you intend to go up, you must first lodge downward." Therefore, coordinated with the swelling of spirit that turns from rear-low to front-high, one leads the right hand from rear-low, twisting ni, forward and down. At the same time, the left hand in front makes a small circle with a shun twist, joining its power with the right hand. Next, the right hand, still twisting ni, chops downward with the edge of the palm from front-high to front-low, like chopping firewood with an axe. When chopping, the whole body must be relaxed and open, using elastic power; at the same time, the left hand strikes to the left-rear as a feint. When both hands are toward the rear-right side, lift the left foot; when both hands reach the front-high, the left foot lands and becomes solid; at the same time the right foot steps forward one step. When the right hand chops down it is solid, and the right foot is empty. (Figure 67)

图 L2F67
Right hand twisting ni chopping down with the palm edge from front-high to front-low, left hand striking to the left-rear as a feint, left foot landing solid to form a bow stance

· 213 · Key points: This form too was selected from Qi Jiguang's boxing forms, and it differs from the preceding form: the preceding form strikes upward from below, whereas this one chops downward from above. To do the downward chop well, one must first close the power at the chest, then unite the body's internal power and chop down after turning a circle. At this time, hands and feet are required to be coordinated and smooth, and under the gaining of posture and power to display one firm chop. Therefore the two hands must, after turning through one large circle, then begin the downward chop—just like holding a large hammer, turning a circle, and then striking the iron. This is the only fist-form in the Second Routine that turns a circle and chops down. When issuing the downward chop, the body must be centered and unbiased, and must have an elastic openness; this is the concrete expression of using the inertial force of the one-turn circle to strengthen the downward-chopping power. One must bring both hands and both legs into simultaneous use, so as to attain a most highly coordinated requirement.

Book page 201

Form 40. Cover-Hand Forearm Punch (chest turning from northeast to east)

Form 40. Cover-Hand Forearm Punch (chest turning from northeast to east)

Movement: this form follows "Flower-Flipping Sleeve Dance," and differs from the earlier "Cover-Hand Forearm Punch": in this form one must lead the body up under the guidance of the crown-top power, lift the right leg, and set it down parallel to the left leg with a stomp to become solid; at the same time, the left leg stretches forward a small step and is empty. This form requires that on springing up, the front and rear legs exchange places. When the body is led up, the right hand twisting shun and the left hand twisting ni close together; at the same moment that the right leg lands, the two hands separate with a double ni twist, then turn and store up again. Now the right hand changes from palm to fist, placed at the right waist, and with one sinking of its power, power is issued with the right fist as principal. At this time, the left hand releases power backward with a ni twist as a feint. (Figure 68)

Key points: In doing the downward chop within the "Flower-Flipping Sleeve Dance" form, it is a relaxed chop, giving one the momentum of spreading power in all four directions, like a bag of ash falling to the ground and the ash scattering in all directions.

图 L2F68
Right leg lifted and set down parallel to the left leg with a stomp to become solid, right hand changed from palm to fist placed at the right waist issuing power, left hand twisting ni releasing power backward

· 214 · open; because it is a relaxed chopping power, when doing the next fist-form one uses the elasticity of the downward chop to lead the body up, as if gathering the power from all four sides into a single point and lifting with it. And by the time the right foot lands with a stomp and the left foot stretches out in a step, there is again in the mind the intention of spreading the power out. This is the spirit this fist-form should have.

Book page 202

Form 41. Taming the Tiger (chest turning from east to southeast)

Form 41. Taming the Tiger (chest turning from east to southeast)

Movement: after the issuing of power of the right fist in the preceding form, the right fist is drawn back with a ni twist, while the left hand, twisting ni, becomes a fist and is released open toward the left-front. As the right fist twists ni to the rear, the right foot behind shifts a further half step to the rear-right and becomes solid; and when the right fist, twisting ni, has made one large circle to the right-outside and then a small circle, so that it reaches the left forehead corner, the fist-form of Taming the Tiger is completed. At the same time, the drawn-back left fist makes a small circle to the left-inside, and when it turns to the left waist side, it props at the left waist. Now the right foot is solid and the left foot empty. (Figure 69)

Key points: When this form rotates one large circle left and right, front and rear, up and down (a great storing of power), the body must sink ever lower as it turns, and at the same time the large circle must also turn ever smaller—this is the clearest example of forming a downward spiral of the body. What distinguishes this form from ordinary fist-forms is that it forms its stored movement in an open posture; for the lower the body turns, the greater the elasticity of the power stored in the legs. This stored power can prepare the elastic force for the light and nimble springing up of the next form. This is the lowest fist-form in the Second Routine, and also the clearest fist-form of the silk-reeling of the legs coordinated with the silk-reeling of the hands.

Form 42. Wiping the Brows Red (chest turning from southeast to north, then to south)
图 L2F69
Right fist twisting ni making a large circle to the right-outside and then a small circle to reach the left forehead corner, left fist propping at the left waist, right foot solid and left foot empty

Movement: the preceding fist-form is a great body-storing method; in doing this form, then, it is on the basis of the preceding · 215 · The enlarged body method executed when the body method has been fully stored. On the basis of the fully lengthened and elastic right side of the spine, using the gathering process of the waist-spine's elastic recovery, the right hand makes a forward-twisting downward arc and flings forward-downward (assuming the left hand of the previous posture "Crouching Tiger Wiping the Waist" has been seized), while the left fist makes a reverse-twisting full circle upward from below-behind. Borrowing the centrifugal force of the right fist's forward fling, the torso is lifted, the right foot springs forward in a big step, and the left foot follows. At this moment both feet leave the ground. (Figure 70) Leaping to the opposite side, when the right foot lands as the solid point, the torso is made to rotate 180° to the left in midair, placing the left foot to the east side of the right foot. At this time the left fist also moves from the upper reverse-twisting downward to rest at the waist. (Figure 71) During the leap-and-turn process, a "back-breaking leaning" energy is naturally manifested, in order to shed the seized left hand and draw the left hand back to rest at the waist.

Key points: This posture is primarily based on the stored energy of the previous posture. Before leaping forward, the waist and legs must sit back once to strengthen the elastic energy. Then, borrowing the elasticity of the stored energy, the body springs forward and upward — this is the key to attaining lightness and ease of turning. When turning the body, one must keep it centered and upright; this is the guarantee for safely issuing the back-breaking leaning energy, and is also how one naturally escapes without seeking to escape.

图 L2F70
Right hand flings downward with forward-twisting, left fist makes a reverse-twisting full circle upward, torso lifted with right foot springing forward and both feet off the ground
图 L2F71
Having leapt to the opposite side with the right foot landing, the torso turns 180° left in midair and the left fist lowers to the waist

basis.

Fourth-three Posture: Right Yellow Dragon Stirs the Water Three Times (chest facing south)

Movement: After this posture leaps up and turns the body, the left fist props the waist, then the right hand makes forward-twisting circles in front of the chest. When the right hand circles downward, the right foot immediately lifts as empty. (Figure 72) When the right hand circles upward, the right foot again lands as solid, completing one "stirring the water." (Figure 73) Then continue by doing two more "stirring the water" movements. (Fig. 74, 73, then again 74, 73, 74)

图 L2F72
Right hand makes a forward-twisting downward circle before the chest, right foot lifts as empty
图 L2F73
Right hand circles upward, right foot lands as solid
图 L2F74
Right hand continues circling to stir the water, left fist propping the waist, right foot shifting between empty and solid

Key points: According to the requirements of motor skill, the simpler the fist posture, the harder it is to fulfill the requirement that one movement moves everything. In this posture only the single right hand circles, with the right foot coordinating in up-and-down division of empty and solid to carry out the movement; such a movement is comparatively simple, and therefore it is a basic exercise for training the silk-reeling energy to achieve joint-by-joint continuity. To achieve "one movement moves everything," the key still lies in the leading of the waist-spine and the loosening-open of the arm's energy, circling like a whip — this is where the crux of doing this posture well lies.

This is precisely the second segment of the second routine of the form, and it may be repeated several times as needed. Because before "stirring the water," a whole series of fairly intense movements has been performed in succession, so here one may obtain a certain rest and recovery.

· 217 · Forty-fourth Posture: Left Yellow Dragon Stirs the Water Three Times (chest facing south, turning north)

图 L2F75
After turning the body, the left fist opens and meets upward to the right, the left hand circles to the left with reverse-twisting, and the right hand after a small forward-twist rests at the right waist
图 L2F76
Left hand circles to stir the water in front of the body, left foot lifts as empty
图 L2F77
Left hand circles upward, left foot lands as solid

Movement: Continuing from the previous posture, turn the body around and change to the left hand "stirring the water" and circling. Its method is basically the same as the right hand's "stirring the water" movement; the difference is that when the left and right hands alternate and the body turns, the internal energy must be kept unbroken. In the previous posture, when the right hand has circled down and turned left, the left fist propping at the left waist opens and reverse-twists upward to the right to meet it, forming a joining with the left slightly lower and the right slightly higher. At this moment the right foot lifts as empty; as soon as they cross, both hands immediately become double reverse-twisting, and led by the waist-spine and drawn by the right hand, the body turns and carries a turn of 180° to the right. At the same time, the right foot lands as solid and serves as the pivot of the rotation. Following this, the left foot also immediately arcs around with the body and is placed to the west side of the right foot, completing the process of turning the body. At the same time, the left hand circles to the left side from reverse-twisting to forward-twisting, while the right hand, after a small forward-twist, is placed at the right side of the waist. (Figure 75) This is the starting point after "Left Yellow Dragon Stirs the Water Three Times" has turned the body. Thereafter, just as with "Right Yellow Dragon Stirs the Water Three Times," when the left hand circles downward, the left foot must lift as empty. (Figure 76) When the left hand circles upward, the left foot again drops as solid. (Figure 77), completing one "stirring the water." Then do two more "stirring the water" movements. (Fig. 78, 77, then again 78, 77, 78)

Key points: The requirements of this posture itself are the same as those of "Right Yellow Dragon Stirs the Water Three Times," but special attention must be paid to the fact that at the moment of turning the body and changing hands, one must not only turn with a gentle curve, but at the same time must also keep the movement threaded through as one breath, allowing no interruption and no hollows or bumps to occur. The crux lies in that when the left hand opens and joins with the right hand, forming a mutual linkage of the two arms, one can, upon separating again for one turn, pass the energy from the right hand over to the left hand.

Although the key points and movement of this posture are the same as the previous posture, in order to give the left hand the same degree of nimbleness as the right hand, this posture may be done several or a dozen times; in this posture the position of the right foot does not change, so doing it several times in place does no harm to the structure of the entire form.

Forty-fifth Posture: Left Kick with One (Single) Leg (chest facing north)

图 L2F78
Left hand forward-twists and arcs from inside outward, left hand propping the waist opening and closing, left foot shifting between empty and solid
图 L2F79
Both hands gather and close in front of the abdomen, opposed to the body's center, both feet standing
图 L2F80
Left arm forward-twists and arcs outward, right hand opens and circles in opposition, left foot lifts — the initiating pose of the kick

Movement: After the above "stirring the water," when the left arm forward-twists and arcs from inside to outside, the right hand propping the waist opens and takes the opportunity to join in a circling that is at once opposed and at once divided; when turning after passing one circle and then turning downward, it becomes a double closing energy. At this moment palm faces palm, both hands opposed and slightly narrower than the shoulders, placed in front of the abdomen. When the right hand joins in and finally closes, the left foot goes from solid to empty. (Figure 79) With the two hands ceaselessly circling, continue to tighten into a single closing with a double forward-twist, making both palms become fists crossing before the chest. At this moment the left hand is outside and the right hand inside; at the same time, raise the left leg. (Figure 80) After reaching the end point of the crossing, issue the energy with both hands and the left foot together, each with full force to left and right. This is kicking out the left foot with energy while standing on the right foot alone. At this moment the left hand is host and the right hand is guest. (Figure 81)

Key points: The elastic energy of this posture is a double opening energy produced within the double closing, because when the two hands are in a double closing, the elbows and upper arms have a double opening energy. At the same time, when the two feet bend slightly and close doubly, the rounding of the crotch gives the legs a double opening energy as well. This shows that both arms and legs have a linked outward-bracing energy; this is the crux of being able to issue energy crisply. When the two hands and the left foot split and issue to the left and right sides together, because of the stabilizing effect of the two hands' splitting, the torso obtains a certain stability at the moment of issuing. This kind of energy issuance is a good method for training the joint ligaments and strengthening their elasticity.

Forty-sixth Posture: Right Kick with One (Single) Leg (chest facing north, turning south)

Movement: After the previous posture "Left Kick with One Leg," the two hands close to the left with reverse-twisting, drawing the torso to turn left; at the same time the left foot lands with a stamping of the foot, and the right leg is raised, forming standing on the left leg alone, with the two hands closing their energy on both sides of the right knee. (Figure 82) Then issue the energy with both hands and the right foot together, each with full force to left and right — this is kicking out the right foot with energy while standing on the left foot alone. At this moment the right hand is host and the left hand is guest. (Figure 83)

图 L2F81
After the hands have crossed to the end point, both hands and the left foot issue energy together to left and right; in the right-leg-standing posture the left foot kicks out, with the left hand as host and the right hand as guest.
图 L2F82
Standing on the left leg alone with both hands closing energy on both sides of the right knee, the right foot kicking out and issuing to left and right
图 L2F83
Standing on the left foot alone, both hands and the right foot issuing energy together to left and right

· 220 · Key points: This posture is performed by lifting the left leg and pivoting horizontally to the left; during the horizontal pivot it is not easy to attain a stable turn, therefore the key lies in the lifting of the crown energy and the two hands' reverse-twisting so as to close energy mutually, making the spine taut, with the left toe pointing down, in order to lighten the sinking weight of the left leg suspended in the air. This is the stored-energy posture one should master when turning the body before the right kick. After the left foot lands with a stamping of the foot, immediately raise the right leg, and issue the right foot and both hands to the two sides together.

Forty-seventh Posture: Sea Bottom Turns Over the Flower (chest facing west)

Movement: Same as Posture 30 "Sea Bottom Turns Over the Flower," only the extent of the body turn is smaller; all else is the same. (Figure 84)

Forty-eighth Posture: Cover-Hand Forearm Punch (chest facing west)

Movement: The right foot drops with a stamping of the foot as solid; at this time the right hand is forward-twisting and the left hand reverse-twisting. When the left hand turns toward the left front, the left foot advances one step to the left front; at the same time the right palm becomes a fist, turns to reverse-twisting and issues energy, while the left fist, after turning with reverse-twisting, issues energy to the left rear as guest. (Figure 85)

Key points: Same as Posture 17.

图 L2F84
"Sea Bottom Turns Over the Flower," turning the body with a smaller amplitude to turn over the flower
图 L2F85
"Cover-Hand Forearm Punch" issuing energy, right fist issuing forward with reverse-twisting and left fist releasing to the rear with reverse-twisting
图 L2F86
Right hand in front draws back with reverse-twisting then circles forward, left hand behind circles forward then backward with reverse-twisting
图 L2F87
Right hand draws back with reverse-twisting to before the right waist, right foot stamps, left fist raises forward-upward with reverse-twisting

· 221 · Forty-ninth Posture: Sweeping-Leg (turning the waist and smashing, chest facing east, turning north, then turning south and again turning north)

Movement: After the energy issuance of "Cover-Hand Forearm Punch," the right hand in front draws back with reverse-twisting and then makes a circle forward, while the left hand behind circles forward and then backward with reverse-twisting. (Figure 86) When the right hand again draws back with reverse-twisting from the front to before the right waist, the right foot stamps the ground with a stamping of the foot; at this moment the left fist raises forward-upward with reverse-twisting. (Figure 87) Immediately after the stamping of the foot, the right toe turns outward and steps out a small half-step to the right rear, forming a rotational momentum, carrying the body to turn toward the right rear · 222 · about 280°; the right leg squats down, and the left foot follows by extending the leg and arcing around to sweep-turn 280°, sweeping to the northwest of the right foot. (Figure 88)

Key points: This posture is for practicing the ankle-striking energy when the foot sweeps horizontally. In order to rotate the left leg stably and sweep one full circle horizontally, one must make the intent and energy manifest as though the right foot had taken root in the ground. Second, in order to strengthen the leg's horizontal sweeping energy, one must use the right foot's stepping a small half-step to the right rear with the toe turned out, to drive the rotation of the torso and form a rotational momentum. Third, one must coordinate upper and lower consistently, so that the torso can rotate nimbly yet steadily; this applies mainly to the first half-circle of the movement, where the change of posture goes from high to low, while in the latter circle of the movement the internal energy must again go from low to high and then land. This is also a comparatively difficult movement, a movement of leg-leading-body, which can lengthen and strengthen the leg muscles. In order to strengthen the leg's horizontal sweeping energy, it may be singled out for specialized free-hand practice, and one may also do two 360° sweeping-legs.

Fiftieth Posture: Cover-Hand Forearm Punch (chest facing north, turning east)

Movement: After the previous posture has turned through 280°, both hands cross and close before the chest ; then the two palms change and separately arc upward and spread out to the left and right sides; at the same time, the right foot lifts off the ground, and the left foot immediately pushes off the ground and springs up. Then the right foot lands to the southwest, and the left foot follows to land to the northeast. Both hands from above close before the chest with double reverse-twisting, then open with forward-twisting and close with reverse-twisting; then the right fist strikes out, and the left fist is drawn in beneath the left ribs. (Figure 90) What differs between this posture and the previous seventeenth posture is only the leaping-step movement; once both feet have landed, it is the same as the other "Cover-Hand Forearm Punch" postures.

图 L2F88
The left foot extends the leg and arcs around in a horizontal sweep to the northwest of the right foot, right leg squatting
图 L2F89甲
Both hands crossing and closing before the chest
图 L2F89乙
Both palms arcing open to left and right, right foot lifted off the ground and left foot pushing off to spring up

· 223 · Key points: This is a stabilizing movement at the moment when the form's spiraling ascent reaches its end point; it is a practice of spiral ascent after the great rotation of the body, and is also a good athletic training for the vestibular apparatus; to achieve this stabilizing effect, one must stand centered and upright at the conclusion of the sweeping-leg. Key points: Same as Posture 31.

Fifty-first Posture: Left Charge (chest facing east)

Movement: Because the movement begins with the left leg in front, it is named "Left Charge." After the energy issuance of the previous posture "Cover-Hand Forearm Punch," the right fist draws back with forward-twisting, and the left fist extends forward with reverse-twisting; the two fists close their energy, forming two fists opposed. (Figure 91) Then, borrowing the forward-extended left hand, both hands together sink downward and make a circle past the right rib side; when they have circled to the rear-upper, draw back the left foot and lift it as empty. (Figure 92) When the two fists again turn from above to the left waist side, the left foot lands with a stamping of the foot. When they circle to the front-lower, step out the right foot; the two fists turn to the left · 224 · Sink the energy toward the rear of the ribs (Figure 93); this is the gathering posture for the thrust punch. Then issue the shaking energy forward and upward with both forearms. When sinking after the circle, the rear left foot is full; when the two fists shake out the energy forward, the right foot is full. (Figure 94)

图 L2F91
Right bow stance, both fists thrust forward, gathering posture
图 L2F92
Knee lifted in single-leg stance, both fists raised in a circling motion
图 L2F93
Left foot full, energy sunk and gathered
图 L2F94
Right foot full, both fists shaken forward

Key points: In this form the two fists travel from the right side to the left side, describing two complete large circles, front-back and up-down. The movements must be continuous and completed in one breath; therefore the rotational momentum must be used, so that the energy can run through to the final shake. If there is a break in between, the energy-strengthening effect is lost. At the same time, this is a necessary form for practising shaking energy. For beginners, after swinging the two large circles, the shaking energy is then issued; later one may gradually— · 225 · —the swings gradually grow smaller, reducing step by step to a single circle; finally, as soon as the intention is aroused, the shaking energy can be issued in the same way. This is the deepest skill in issuing shaking energy.

Fifty-second Form — Right Thrust (chest facing east)

Movement: Because the movement begins with the right leg in front, it is called "Right Thrust". In this form the right leg is in front first, and finally changes to the left leg in front; the two fists first travel from the left rib side to the right rib side, and after describing two large circles they shake out the energy. In these two respects this form is exactly the opposite of the previous form, so its movement path is symmetrical to that form. (Figs. 95, 96, 97)

Key points: Same as "Left Thrust".

Fifty-third Form — Reverse Throw-Down (chest facing east, turning northeast)

Movement: After the previous form has issued the double shaking energy, suppose the right hand is plucked (this kind of plucking energy often makes the one plucked kneel down); in order to achieve sticking, adhering, connecting and following, so that there is no opposing resistance, the right hand follows downward with reverse twining, bringing the right hand together with the left hand. As they join, the left hand is placed beneath the plucking hand, and the right hand presses down, making a preliminary release. At this moment the right hand is full downward, the right foot steps up as empty, standing alongside the left foot with the toes touching the ground, so that the two hands are close to the upper and lower parts of one's own body; this is "release within joining", another example of overcoming weight with lightness. (Figure 98)

图 L2F95
Knee lifted with fists held, gathering and turning
图 L2F96
Bow stance advancing, both fists circling and sinking
图 L2F97
Right leg in front bow stance, both fists shaken forward

· 226 · Fifty-fourth Form — Turning the Flower at the Seabed (chest facing east)

Movement: If in the previous form the reverse insertion cannot achieve "release within joining", then sink further and suddenly turn, lengthening the body, and change into opening the hands above and below. This is done with the energy adhering to the spine, the body led up by the crown energy, as a second release; it is the method of "release within opening" after "release within joining". Simultaneously with this "opening release", the right hand twines with forward twining to the upper right and then turns to the lower right, the left hand twines with reverse twining to the lower left and then turns to the upper left; the whole body lengthens, the left foot stands alone, the right foot is lifted (as preparation for a kick); the left fist releases energy upward to the left, with the fist centre facing right; the right fist releases energy downward to the right waist side, with the fist centre facing forward. Its movement is the same as the previous "Turning the Flower at the Seabed" forms, except that this form turns the body only slightly, whereas the previous forms turned the body through a larger range. (Figure 99)

图 L2F98
Both feet together, hands joined at the side
图 L2F99
Left foot standing alone, hands opening above and below, Turning the Flower at the Seabed

Key points: Taijiquan often uses downward plucking energy, so that the opponent cannot easily use connecting and following to gain release; for this reason the right hand twines with reverse twining downward, the right foot steps forward, and the left hand is placed beneath the plucking hand. Because the right foot steps up in "Reverse Insertion", one's own two hands are brought close to one's own centre of the circle, thereby increasing the moment applied to the opponent while reducing one's own moment; one large and one small — this is again a model of overcoming weight with lightness, and can make one · 227 · —"gain the advantage". This kind of release by pressing above and padding below is the preliminary form of seeking release. If one still cannot obtain release and opposing resistance arises with the opponent, then one should follow the energy of his resistance and reverse its path, turning the left hand onto the opponent's plucking hand, and cause the left hand to chop down and the right hand to lift up, making it the same as "Chopping Hand". At the same time give the left foot a shake, so that the whole body lengthens and rises, and both hands open out their energy. This is the transformed form of release, showing that in the seabed region there are turnings and changes of double opening and double closing; it is also a technique of striking and releasing combined in one movement.

Fifty-fifth Form — Covering Hand and Forearm Punch (chest facing east)

Movement: With the right leg lifted from the previous form, continue into issuing energy; the movement is the same as the fifty-first form. (Figure 100)

Key points: Same as the thirty-first form.

Fifty-sixth Form — Seizing the Two Arms (one) (chest facing east, turning south)

图 L2F100
Bow stance, covering hand and forearm punch, right fist issuing energy forward

Movement: After the previous form "Covering Hand and Forearm Punch" has issued energy, first slightly open the two hands; thereupon the left fist twines with reverse twining and the right fist with forward twining, turning back from the right side into a joining energy. At this moment the right fist is below and outside, the left fist above and inside; at the same time the right foot follows up half a step, bringing it close to the left foot. Then the two fists change to double forward twining: the right fist is drawn upward back to the chest, the left fist sinks down to in front of the left knee; at the same time the left foot steps forward half a step (Figure 101). Next, the centre of gravity moves forward, making the left foot full; at the same time, owing to the joining energy, with the left foot as pivot the body turns 180° to the right. The rear right foot is simultaneously lifted and steps back to the left rear side (moving sideways half a step). During the turn the two fists continue to twine forward in the chest area, turning over inside and out with joined energy. When the turn brings the body to face east, the right fist is just at the inner front upper position and the left fist at the outer front lower position. As the right fist turns from the inside downward to the outside and then upward to the inside, the right foot is lifted accordingly and drawn along the ground · 228 · —back, the two arms joining their energy. At this moment the right fist is bent to the outside and the left fist bent to the inside. (Figure 102) The movement described above is storing energy; the movement that follows is the issuing of energy after storing. Beneath the encirclement of the two fists fully expanded with energy, the right fist lifts slightly upward, and after turning to the inside of the left fist immediately sinks its energy downward. At the same time the right foot gives a shake, and darts out along the ground; when it has darted to the centre of the opponent's circle, the right arm, held horizontally, issues energy from the forearm, while the left fist twines with reverse twining and releases energy to the left rear. This is a special movement in which the right hand and right foot advance together; it is also the upper and lower following one another in posture. When energy is issued, the left foot is full. (Figure 103)

图 L2F101
Both fists joined and drawn in, left foot stepping forward
图 L2F102
Right fist bent outward, left fist bent inward, energy joined and stored
图 L2F103
Right foot darting forward issuing energy, right arm thrust sideways, left fist releasing energy backward

Key points: The key point of this fist form is to turn the body round within joining energy, which differs from the preceding forms that turn the body within opening energy; this is therefore the main content practised in this form. In this form, supposing an attack comes from behind, one turns the body to dissolve that attack, and uses the turning of the body to strengthen the stored energy, so that the next fist form can be issued more crisply; this is the special function of this form. In the turn— · 229 · —ing the body, one must keep the tailbone centred and the spirit threaded to the crown; that is, the crown energy is not lost and the tailbone does not lean.

After turning the body, when the right arm is held horizontally to join energy, suppose the right wrist joint in front is plucked; then there is no need to seek another method of release — the right fist and right foot can together give a shake and dart out forward along the ground, and the right forearm issues energy outward horizontally (warding-off energy is spring energy, first of the eight energies of Taijiquan, a defensive energy. If it can be used within the issuing of warding-off energy, it amounts to two uses in one movement; this kind of strike can be issued with a single shake of the hand, so the distance is short and the effect great, making it the simplest way of issuing energy). This too is the combined action of release and strike in one movement. Its key point is that release must be obtained under "the central earth not leaving its position" and "advancing and retreating with the body"①; it is also a striking method for entering the opponent's circle, and in particular the use of warding-off in striking is the most concise method of two uses in one movement.

Fifty-seventh Form — Seizing the Two Arms (two) (chest facing south, turning west then south)

Movement: After the warding-off energy has been issued in the previous form, suppose one has still not obtained release; then one must continue to do a second "Seizing the Two Arms"; therefore there should be an upward step in the shape of the Chinese character for "person" (ren). This is a movement of stepping forward two paces following the opponent's warding-off lock; it is rarely seen within the boxing frame, so it must be practised as a single movement. This movement begins with the right fist twining forward, drawn upward and inward, while the left fist moves from below and outside upward, and the left foot follows with a step forward. (Figure 104) When the left fist has reached the outside of the right arm and presses upward, and the right arm twines downward inside the left fist, and they are brought close to one's own body with the upper and lower energies opposed, the plucked right arm has already been released. At the same time as the release, the right foot has also stepped forward; this too prepares the way for the warding-off issuing movement of the right arm—

  • ① "The central earth not leaving its position" and "advancing and retreating with the body" are Taijiquan terms, meaning that when the hands and feet advance in succession, one should move like a great banner, standing erect and not falling.
图 L2F104
Bow stance advancing, both fists twining with upper and lower energies opposed

· 230 · —preparation for storing energy. (Figure 105)

After the left step has been taken in the previous form, the second right step is taken in succession; this is the final step of the ren-shaped upward step. The two fists, like a windmill, twine over one another inside and outside in front of the chest through one large circle. In the previous movement, when the right fist twines forward, upward and inward with forward twining, the right foot is drawn back half a step with the toes touching the ground. Then the right fist sinks its energy downward in front of the chest in coordination with the left fist moving upward, so as to release the plucked right hand a second time. At the same time the right foot shakes downward in a stamp, and taking advantage of the momentum darts forward along the ground. Simultaneously the right fist, arm held horizontally, moves forward and issues energy horizontally outward. (Figure 106)

Key points: If the warding-off issuing energy of the previous form is still not enough to release the plucked right hand, then to avoid opposing resistance one must use connecting and following and, dragging along, step up in succession. Therefore the main content of practice in this form is to step forward two paces in succession without any break in energy occurring, and to have at all times the opportunity to release and to strike. To attain this requirement, the key point is that the two arms are linked together so that the two fists turn over up and down in the course of advancing, shaking the spine to shake off the plucking of the right hand.

图 L2F105
Body turned sideways, both fists twining, energy stored and ready to issue
图 L2F106
Bow stance, arm horizontal warding off forward, right fist issuing energy to the right front

Because the first "Seizing the Two Arms" still cannot obtain release, one must follow the required energy and, in the course of pushing the opponent backward, issue energy outward horizontally, releasing and striking at once. This is the unified action of pushing and releasing. Therefore, whether it steps with the left foot or the right foot, it must · 231 · —turning the spine and advancing. This is the key to whether, when warding-off energy is issued, the stored energy of the spine can be released like a bowstring slipping its catch.

Fifty-eighth Form — Linked Pearls Cannon (chest facing west)

Movement (one): After the right hand has issued warding-off energy in the previous form, the left fist stored at the left rear strikes and shakes out like a bowstring slipping its catch, while the right fist twines forward, drawn back to rest at the right rib side. When the strike is issued the left leg is full. (Figure 107)

Movement (two): Movement (one) is the shaking energy of the left fist; movement (two) is the shaking energy of the right fist. The two are basically the same; the difference is the shaking of the spine. When the left fist is drawn back with forward twining to rest in front of the chest, the right fist is sent out like linked pearls. When the right fist is sent out the right leg is empty. (Figure 108)

Movement (three): Same as movement one. (Figure 109)

Key points: "Thrust Punch" is shaking energy issued by both fists together; this form is shaking energy issued by each fist separately. Its key point lies in loosening the limbs, then suddenly shaking outward; it is a short-range hard energy. After issuing, the arm must still be bent and stored; the degree of bending and storing is determined by the ability to issue again.

图 L2F107
Left fist shaking out like a bowstring slipping its catch, right fist drawn back to the right ribs
图 L2F108
Left fist drawn back in front of the chest, right fist sent out like linked pearls
图 L2F109
Right fist shaking forward, left leg full

· 232 · The use of energy in movement (two) is like a carpenter boring a hole with a hand drill, having the effect of striking in linked succession; this is a special fist form for training the waist and spine and the elasticity of both arms.

Fifty-ninth Form — The Jade Girl Works the Shuttle (chest facing west, turning north then east)

Movement: After the previous form has issued energy, suppose the left fist is plucked; the left fist is drawn slightly inward and then immediately extended, and the left foot steps out and leaps forward with a flying step. (Figure 110) At the same time the right foot follows and advances, and the body is carried round to the right through 180°, placing the right foot to the west of the left foot, so as to release the plucking of the left fist; and with this turn of the body one strikes the opponent with back-breaking leaning energy. At the same time the two fists press down with double reverse twining in front of the chest, joining their energy. (Figure 111)

Sixtieth Form — Turning the Head to Face the Cannon (chest facing east)

From the turn of body in the previous form the left foot is full; passing through the elbow stage the right foot is full; then the fists twine with double forward twining and shake energy out forward and upward; at this moment the left foot is full. (Figure 112)

Key points: The back-breaking leaning energy of Taijiquan is always for the sake of connecting and following; it is an energy used only when unavoidable, and one does not lightly adopt body methods to strike. Because in the course of the flying body connecting and following in "The Jade Girl Works the Shuttle"— · 233 · In this, by using the lean (kao) of the turning body, one can not only free the hand that has been seized (cai), but can also promptly attack the opponent with the "turn the head and cannon at the door" (huitou dangmen pao) posture. This is the simplest method that serves both to escape and to strike, and therefore in the course of turning the body one often uses the back-bending lean (beizhe kao) to seek release. The flying-step turn of "Jade Maiden Weaves the Shuttle," striking the opponent with lean energy, is yet another example of the application of the above principle. Its key point is that before springing out one first sinks the energy in the right leg, then steps out with the left foot and springs forward. In the course of "landing" one must still take care to keep the body centered and upright—this is a necessary condition for applying lean energy. Then both fists are sent out with a shaking energy in the forward (shun) coil.

· 235 · Key points:

This is the fist-form adopted after the previous form has sent both fists shaking out to the right-front, when suddenly on the left side a possible attack is discovered. Its requirement is that as soon as one glances back, the left fist quite naturally sends out energy as a back reverse hammer. To do this strike well, the main thing is that on the basis of the crotch sinking, as though a small circle has turned in front of the lower abdomen, then led by the waist and spine, centrifugal force is used to fling out the back of the left fist.

Form 64: Twisted Phoenix Elbow (chest toward south, turns north)

Form 64: Twisted Phoenix Elbow (chest toward south, turns north)

Movement: After the left fist in the previous form has sent energy out to the left rear, supposing that after sending it the left fist is again seized, then without the least delay sink both fists' energy, turn both backward in reverse coil, and the two arms join energy. At the same time carry the body turning 180° to the left, and the right foot also follows up one large step to the east side of the left foot. The left fist opens into a palm and presses on the opponent's seizing arm (that is, it is placed on one's own right fist), making the two arms join as one arm in ring form, and using the right fist pressed within the left palm as the center of rotation, the right forearm sends elbow energy with a reverse coil toward the right of the chest. At the same time the left palm also turns upward following the rotation of the right fist, palm center facing up, and the left foot is full. (Figure 118)

After the previous form releases energy the left fist is seized; in order not to resist or oppose, one has no choice but to turn through one large step, turn the body around, press down on the opponent's point of seizure to serve as the central axis of the rotating arm, and send elbow energy forward. This is a short-range elbow energy, and also a simple method of freeing oneself from being seized. Press the palm on the opponent's seizing palm, and with this as the center, make it difficult for the opponent to change the seizing hand, then strike sideways to the right with the right elbow. This is a fierce striking method—another fist-form in which, without seeking to escape, one escapes of itself.

Form 65: Forward Phoenix Elbow (chest toward north)

Key points:

Whenever an arm goes beyond the square-round circle, it is called "going out to the corner"; whenever it enters within the square-round circle, it is called "entering the corner." Going out to the corner requires the use of seize-and-split (cai/lie); entering the corner requires the use of elbow and lean. Therefore the use of elbow and lean is like short weapons meeting in close combat—a quick battle quickly decided, with no room for delay. For this reason one must have continuous · 237 · measures used bead by bead, so as to obtain the final release. This form is the continuation of that measure. When the right hand still cannot get free, following the required energy, the right foot drills in along the ground and the right elbow strikes out to the right; at the same time the left foot kicks back along the ground behind—this forms the momentum of a bowstring slipping its catch, and forms the key point of using lightness to control heaviness and of striking with linked-bead elbows.

Form 67: Cannon in the Nest (chest toward north)

After storing the posture, the right fist immediately turns outward and strikes out toward the right front with the back of the fist; at the same time the left fist coils in reverse to the left rear to the left side of the waist and releases energy, to coordinate with the strike of the right fist. Form 63 "Withdraw the Body and Punch" is a back reverse hammer of the left hand; this form is a back reverse hammer of the right hand. In order that the energy be released more crisply, one must, under the joined energy of the two fists—right forward, left reverse—shrink the circle, to strengthen the stored energy, and then, led by the elbow and carrying the body, counter-strike out to the right and outward. This form requires that one movement moves the whole body; and this can only be done just right on the basis of the waist and spine working as one, using inertial force.

· 241 · # Chapter 4: Chen-Style Taijiquan Pushing Hands The two-person pushing-hands method of Chen-style Taijiquan was originally called "throwing hands" or "hitting hands." It is an original competitive exercise created by the Taijiquan school through inheriting and developing the martial technique methods of Ming-dynasty folk martial arts. It comprehensively inherited and developed the three methods of "seizing, throwing, and casting-and-striking," and therefore its original martial character is extremely intense. Silk-reeling sticking-following and silk-reeling spiral movement are the central content of its creative achievement. On the basis of the theory that "the Taiji has two modes, with softness and with hardness," it requires that the internal energy—flexible in change, rich in elasticity and toughness, with "hardness and softness assisting each other, lightness and heaviness both complete"—serve as the commander.

Chen Wangting said in the "General Song of the Boxing Classic": "Let go, bend, extend—no one knows; the various leans and entanglements I all rely on" ("the various leans" refers to two people leaning their arms against each other, applying the eight methods and kinds of energy: ward-off, roll-back, press, push, seize, split, elbow, lean). These two lines summarily explain the characteristics and methods of pushing hands. The original four lines of the "Song of Hitting Hands": "Ward-off, roll-back, press, push must be done in earnest; upper and lower following each other, the person is hard to invade; let anyone with giant strength come to strike me—four ounces deflect eight thousand catties"—this explains the function of "the various leans" and the principle of taking ward-off, roll-back, press, and push, the four hands, as the basic skill.

Toward the end of the eighteenth century, Wang Zongyue of Shanxi, and in the mid-to-late nineteenth century Wu Yuxiang and Li Yishe, master and disciple, of Yongnian in Hebei, all developed the theory of Taijiquan and the techniques of pushing hands, and on the basis of their own experience in practicing boxing wrote summarizing essays on Taijiquan and pushing hands. These boxing treatises, concise in words but comprehensive in meaning, were widely copied and circulated, and became in modern times · 242 · Guiding theory for practitioners of taijiquan and push-hands; Chen Zhong-shen and his son Chen Xin of the Chen family, contemporaries of Wu and Li, likewise expounded the taijiquan and push-hands theory accumulated over generations of the Chen family.

Book page 227

1. General Essentials of Push-Hands

1. General Essentials of Push-Hands

Since the Yang-style taijiquan became widespread and "xieshou" (joining hands) or "dashou" (hitting hands) came to be called "tuishou" (push-hands), the term "push-hands" has become a common name. Push-hands is a method in which two people join hands and coil around each other, using the unique training method of taijiquan movement, which is like a screw. According to the principles of "adhere, connect, stick, follow; neither lose contact nor resist; neither overshoot nor fall short; yield and extend," one uses the eight methods and kinds of jin -- peng, lu, ji, an, cai, lie, zhou, kao -- to train the sensitivity of the tactile sense of the whole body's skin and of the internal feeling, to detect the size, hardness or softness, solidity or emptiness, length, speed and direction of the opponent's jin. One selects a sticking point that accords with the lever principle as the fulcrum, uses the pulling action of elasticity and friction (the point of application of force), brings into play the skills of "draw in and let him fall into emptiness," "follow his force and borrow his power," and "overcome heaviness with lightness," grasps the strategy and tactics of "if he moves quickly, respond quickly; if he moves slowly, follow slowly" and "if he does not move, I do not move; if he moves slightly, I move first," pulls the opponent's center of gravity, and at the moment when time and point of force are most appropriate "strikes the light with the heavy, breaks the empty with the solid," issuing the jin. This kind of issuing must be "calm and steady, relaxed and quiet, concentrated on one direction," going from a curved arc straight forward at the target, steady and accurate -- just as when an arrow is shot its head sinks deep into the target -- and thereby sends the opponent out cleanly. The overall requirement is to be able both to neutralize and to issue; to neutralize with relaxed purity, to issue with crispness. This competitive sport can train strength and endurance, and can also train such physical qualities as sensitivity, skill and speed.

In order to avoid accidents of injury, the modern developed push-hands method restricts the use of such methods as grabbing, seizing, throwing, wrestling and striking; hence it has become a martial art that men, women, the old and the young can all practice.

· 243 · The practice of the taijiquan routine originally went hand in hand with "push-hands." Once the routine is practiced to mastery, fine and delicate, centered and full, with inner and outer united and with emptiness and solidity, hardness and softness all complete, one can then fully bring out the skills of push-hands. While practicing the routine, if one also practices push-hands, one can both apply the kinds of jin obtained from walking the form harmoniously within the push-hands of paired practice, and at the same time test how correct one's practice of the taijiquan routine is, making it easy to correct and enrich its postures and movements. Holding push-hands competitions can correct certain ways of practice that distort taijiquan theory and correct one-sided understandings of push-hands, so that the technique of taijiquan is restored and developed.

Book page 228

2. Chen-Style Push-Hands Methods

2. Chen-Style Push-Hands Methods

The basic footwork of Chen-style push-hands is one step forward and one step back; one may also advance continuously or retreat continuously. The hand methods are peng, lu, ji, an, called the four cardinal hands; each time four hands have pushed through one circle, there is one advance and one retreat -- the advancing one does ji and an, the retreating one does peng and lu. Once the push-hands of the four cardinal hands is familiar, one then mixes in cai, lie, zhou, kao; these are the four corner hands, also called the great lu or great kao. Once the basic footwork is familiar, one may practice "strolling" push-hands, that is, moving steps without restriction of direction, also called "randomly treading flowers."

In Chen-style push-hands, if A has the right (left) foot forward, then B has the left (right) foot forward, so that the two hands of the upper limbs push each other and the front foot of the lower limbs also sticks and neutralizes with each other, training hand and foot at the same time to be sensitive in touch. Whenever one advances, the front foot is placed on the inner side of the opponent's front foot. The two parties' front feet lean and stick to each other; this can serve as the method for later using the foot-lock, and as basic training for developing the techniques of throwing.

A. The Four Cardinal Basic Push-Hands: Peng, Lu, Ji, An

Before the two people join hands, they stand facing each other, centered, stable and comfortable, in the position of attention. Facing · 244 · The distance at which they stand is measured by both parties raising their arms forward level (fists clenched) until the faces of the fists touch. If A steps forward with the right (left) foot, then B steps forward with the left (right) foot, forming the bow stance, but the center of gravity falls between the two legs, so that when attacking one may sit solid on the front leg and when neutralizing or drawing in one may sit solid on the back leg. At the same time each pushes the right (left) hand forward in peng, no higher than the eyebrows, palm facing outward (the palm faces outward to make it easy to pluck and seize); the two shoulders relax, the elbows hang down, and the outer sides below the wrist joints stick to each other and peng. Whenever joining hands, the arms must be relaxed and soft, but the sticking point of the main attacking and defending hand must be peng'd firmly with jin led by intention, and must not be softened. Wu Yu-hsiang correctly summed it up: "in every movement, only the hand first exerts force, then immediately relaxes"; the force he refers to means the relaxed force that has elasticity and toughness, not the inflated, stiff, clumsy force. Therefore Li I-yu's "Five-Word Formula," in the entry "quiet the mind," says: "when he has force, I too have force, and my force is first; when he has no force, I too have no force (the peng jin is not lost), and my intention is still first." Chen Xin says: "one must not have force, nor must one have no force; simply strike the mean." The wrist joint faces the midline of one's own chest: when the palm faces inward, the thumb points toward the tip of the nose; when the palm faces outward, the little finger points toward the tip of the nose. At the same time the lower (right) wrist joint's ulna lightly touches the upper-arm portion above the opponent's elbow joint. (See Figure 1: Double Joining Hands.) Then one party actively attacks with the an method, the other neutralizes and draws it in with peng, and the practice of peng, lu, ji, an begins, going round and round, continuous and unbroken.

Peng jin Because the body and limbs are lengthened, a kind of elasticity is produced, just as the bowstring is stretched by the elastic force of the bow's back and produces elasticity; this forms a spring-like jin, called peng jin. Whenever intention is poured into any part of the limbs and they rotate forward and extend (following the silk-reeling), it is the action of peng jin.

In push-hands, peng is using the right (left) hand to peng the opponent's double an; the sticking point makes an axial rotation, and following the axial rotation of "the master is in the waist and spine," one takes a silk-reeling spiral arc to neutralize and dissolve, and also plucks and seizes the opponent's palm to draw him in (plucking and seizing is at present used only in Chen style). At the same time the ulna side of the left (right) hand lightly pengs the opponent's right (left) hand · 245 · the upper arm and draws him in. The plucking and the lie are combined into one, the aim being to make the opponent's stance unsteady. The body gradually sits back; at the same time the hips are drawn in, the waist turns, the foot pushes; the back foot gradually becomes solid, the front foot gradually becomes empty, forming the posture of "kicking down and swinging outward." (See Figure 2: A does an, B does peng.)

Lu jin Lu jin is also produced under the condition that the body and limbs are lengthened: when the body and limbs move inward-left or inward-right and make the reverse silk-reeling spiral, lu jin is produced. Because of the spiral, the contact surface is enlarged, and thus the friction is increased. Whenever intention is poured into any part of the limbs and it rotates backward, or left, or right, to dissolve, it is the action of lu jin.

Lu jin is the reverse side of peng jin. In push-hands, when the opponent does a double an, and after my peng neutralization he cannot get jin and so changes to ji to continue the attack, I still gradually draw an arc and peng him back, drawing him near to the left or right side of my body and dissolving him, making him fall into emptiness (drawing him in toward oneself with lu is falling into emptiness so as to lure him deep, but the hand must peng firmly, and one must take care that when lu-ing back one's own arm does not stick to one's own body -- "the elbow does not stick to the ribs" -- and the tip of the elbow must not move behind the body, lest one be pressed so that one cannot issue jin and counter). When lu-ing, sit solid on the back leg, turn the waist and drop the hips, with the crotch step kicking down and swinging outward. (See Figure 3: A does ji, B does lu. Figure 5: B does ji, A does lu.)

Ji jin The two jin of peng and lu are the principal jin of the four cardinal hands; an and ji are the auxiliary jin of peng and lu. Sometimes the elasticity of lu jin is insufficient; in order to avoid the fault of flatness, one adopts crossed hands to strengthen lu jin, joining the two arms into a ring shape -- in mechanics this is called the resultant force. In this way one can find a way out left and right, issuing jin with emptiness and solidity mutually changing; this is called ji jin. In push-hands, when my double an has been peng-neutralized and lu-drawn by the opponent and I feel I have lost the advantage, I then change the front hand (the hand that was peng'd or lu'd is the front hand) to a bent elbow, palm slanting outward and down, and push forward in a flat circle (hand and elbow level) or a vertical circle (hand below, elbow above); the rear hand sticks below the front hand's elbow joint, palm outward, to assist the front hand's force (the rear palm slants forward and up, serving as a defensive method to guard against the opponent striking the face, and also making it easy for the opponent to take over the hand and seize or lu, or to change to an, gradually forcing the opponent's stance to become unsteady, sitting forward, with the front foot solid).

图 L3F1
The two join right hands in the opening posture of double joining hands (peng).
图 L3F2
A does an, B does peng: continuing from Figure 1, one party presses out with both hands, the other pengs and draws it in to neutralize.
图 L3F3
A does ji, B does lu: A bends the elbow and pushes in with ji; B sits on the back leg, turns the waist and lu's to neutralize.
图 L3F4
The double-an posture of A doing an and B doing peng.

· 246 · An jin An takes the center of the palm as the axis; using the four sides of the palm it rotates and presses in order to seek out the opponent's emptiness, striving to go upstream, to be above the opponent's hand. In this way not only is there much use and wide range, but the field is large, and it easily turns into the other three jin of the four cardinal hands, and also easily turns into the two jin of cai and lie of the four corners. In push-hands, an is using my two palms to press the opponent's one arm and to alternate emptiness and solidity within the double an, one hand controlling the wrist joint, one hand controlling the elbow joint, so that it is not easy for the opponent to change lively or to counter; sink the shoulders, hang the elbows, sit the wrists, and enclose emptily, not using clumsy force. The long jin goes forward, lightly pressing onto the opponent's body; the hand has both lightness and heaviness. Not only do the two palms alternate emptiness and solidity, now hidden now appearing, but around a single palm too emptiness and solidity change with every breath; the palm center · 247 · rotating around above the opponent's arm -- that is, ceaselessly shifting the point of force, imagining countless forward pressings, gradually forcing the opponent's stance to become unsteady and the body to sit gradually forward, with the front foot solid. (See Figure 4: B does an, A does peng.)

In sum, the two jin of peng and lu are the hand methods of neutralizing jin: the lu jin must go down, the stepping foot must kick down and swing outward, sitting solid on the back leg; when the waist and hips shift the center of gravity, one must likewise make the shoulder and hip vertical and the two breasts and the two corners of the belly vertical, not letting the body lean forward or back or tilt, always maintaining the body centered and upright. One's own arm must be light, nimble and soft, yet must not lose the peng jin, lest one lose the momentum of "relaxing my jin and not letting it bend." Therefore the arm and elbow must never stick to one's own body; one must leave room for rotating and dissolving, and under the armpit one must always keep a gap of about a fist's width. At the same time the tip of the elbow must not move behind the body, lest one be pressed so that one cannot issue jin and counter.

The two jin of an and ji are the hand methods of attack: sit solid on the front leg; the hand should not reach out beyond the tip of the foot; the elbow joint hangs down, always bent and not straight; at any angle strive to make the shoulder and hip vertical, the two breasts and the two corners of the belly vertical, not letting the body lean forward or back or slant, and maintain "the body centered and upright" and "one line from top to bottom."

B. Four-Corner Supplementary Push-Hands: Cai, Lie, Zhou, Kao
图 L3F5
B does ji, A does lu: B bends the elbow and pushes forward with ji; A sits solid on the back leg, turns the waist, and lu's with the stepping foot kicking down and swinging outward.

Cai jin Cai jin is the opposite of ji jin: ji is a double closing, while cai is a double opening; its form is like one hand gripping a tree branch while the other hand plucks the fruit. Cai jin is the foundation of chin-na (seizing and locking). The chin-na hand developed out of cai jin. Its main function is to come out of the corner to control the corner and to pull the opponent. The boxing treatise says: "cai the sky and kao the earth, seeking each other in response." The cai method is to use the palm and fingers emptily · 248 · enclosing the opponent's arm, and, following his force and borrowing his power, suddenly plucking downward from lightness to heaviness. The speed is fast, the distance short, the point of landing accurate; a fierce pluck, not a sudden dead grip that is sluggish and heavy -- this is a method of startling and shaking, most easily pulling the opponent's heel, but it also easily jars the opponent's cranial nerves; therefore it should not be used lightly. Those of comparable skill may use it on each other to test whether the jin is applied appropriately.

Lie jin The distinguishing feature of lie jin is the use of the tip points of the fingers and palm, in the manner of a sudden attack, to shake out a kind of jin at close range; it is the foundation of the closed-cavity strikes within the former chin-na.
