Lie mainly uses shaking strikes rather than issuing jin, and is often used when the hand has reached its point and the situation for issuing has already changed, so that issuing is impossible, and one then changes to lie jin and shakes it out. If, when using lie, one feels that the opponent has been pulled, one may then follow the momentum and turn to issuing jin. This lie jin, like an jin, is a hand method of rather wide application. Besides the shaking strike that is its main function, lie jin also has an action in the opposite direction to peng jin: it is a curved-form simultaneous neutralizing and striking, only in the opposite direction. Peng is drawing and dissolving backward or to the left or right; lie is curving and slightly dissolving, then rotating and peng-ing out slantwise forward at an oblique angle, like the shape of a parabola. Peng is to make the opponent topple toward the back or left or right of me; lie is to make the opponent fall backward, spinning to his own left or right.

In sum, lie jin and cai jin are a pair of opposites. In the process of cai, when meeting obstruction, one may turn to lie; when lie meets obstruction, one may turn at once to cai. This is the unity of cai and lie, just like the two jin of peng and lu among the four cardinal hands. But cai and lie are unified within peng and lu; between them peng and lu are the host, cai and lie the guest.

Zhou jin Although zhou, kao, cai and lie are all corner hands, cai and lie are used when the wrist has gone outside the square-and-round circle, while zhou and kao are used when the hand method enters the inner circle of the square-and-round circle (see Figure 12 of Chapter 2); this likewise belongs to coming out at the corner. Therefore cai and lie are like "long weapons" engaging in battle, while zhou and kao are used as "short weapons." In the course of push-hands, if a slanting-forward out-of-circle form arises, one remedies it with cai and lie; if a leaning-back entering-the-inner-circle form arises, one uses zhou and kao as reserves.

In the use of the elbow, the other arm must come up to the forearm of the elbow that is issued forward, so that one elbow becomes two · 249 · in the use of the elbow. Forms of the second routine such as "ao luan zhou" (twisted phoenix elbow) and "shun luan zhou" (following phoenix elbow) can attack to the left and right. The use of elbow and lie is at the middle "man" position, unlike cai-the-sky and kao-the-earth; it is like the function of the advisers and ministers in Chinese chess. An elbow strike is struck by pressing the tip of the elbow or the surrounding part of the elbow tightly to a person's body; because striking a person's ribs with the elbow tip easily injures him, it is no longer permitted to apply it to the ribs. In push-hands, when using the elbow to attack the opponent's ribs, one may only press tightly against the opponent's arm and use the elbow method to release jin.

Kao jin Whoever uses some part of the body to strike a person with a shaking, vibrating, springing force is called kao jin. Kao jin is like the general or marshal in chess going personally into battle, majestic on all eight sides, overawing in momentum. There are also cases where one arm on the left or right comes out at the corner and the other arm cannot support it in time; only in such a forced situation does one use the body method to strike with the shoulder kao. Shoulder kao has the distinctions of front shoulder, side shoulder and rear shoulder. Shoulder kao must achieve that when kao-ing out the center of gravity is not biased to one side, and that one strikes out aimed at the opponent's center of gravity, lest there be the risk of falling into emptiness and losing the advantage. When doing shoulder kao, the top jin must sink; the body method is centered and upright; when the front shoulder or side shoulder kao's out, the shoulder must not go beyond the tip of the knee.

Besides shoulder kao, there is also the "seven-inch kao": when one has been peng'd or lu'd, leaning forward and losing the advantage, one then follows the momentum, advances the step, inserts into the opponent's crotch, and bends the body to lift the opponent's lower abdomen with the shoulder to meet and fell him (only one with waist-and-leg skill can do this). There is also the "back-fold kao," which is leaping up, folding and turning the body to strike with the back -- this is when one meets with being cai'd and asked for jin; in order to comply with the asked-for jin and give it, in the process of giving one turns the body with the back, which is a natural method of extricating oneself from the cai situation. At the same time one can also get an opportunity to attack: in the impact one suddenly turns and folds to issue jin -- one move with two uses; therefore it is called back-fold kao jin. In the use of the kao method, the waist, legs and body must follow the momentum and stick to the opponent's body and limbs; when the opponent moves slightly, one issues jin at once; when necessary one must also follow up slightly with the footwork, invade and occupy the opponent's position; only then can one release jin cleanly without losing one's own center of gravity.

Elbow strikes and shoulder kao are both used in push-hands by following the momentum. Some of the Chen family's senior boxers were famous for specializing in elbow strikes and shoulder kao, but generally there are also those who, when pressed and losing the advantage, then use elbow and shoulder. That is, when the wrist enters within the inner circle of the square-and-round and loses the advantage, one then uses the elbow method; when the elbow method loses the advantage, one then follows with · 250 · shoulder, the shoulder kao and the back-fold kao are all methods of striking by sticking to the body. Striking the opponent with the hip also belongs within the scope of the kao method. This method of attacking with the body -- entering the tiger's den, wading into danger with a short stretch -- is usually the manifestation of "a rogue's boldness and pure skill," of daring to press close to the opponent. It is like the marshal in chess going personally into battle: it has its definite power, but if used poorly, the crisis appears at once, and so it is not a normal method. Although taijiquan push-hands has eight methods and eight jin, its basic skill is based on the four cardinal push-hands. Therefore in the "Push-Hands Song" there is the saying "peng, lu, ji, an must be (truly) recognized; top and bottom follow each other, and it is hard for the man to enter." From this too one can see the principal-and-subordinate relation between the four cardinal push-hands and the four corner push-hands. This is precious experience summed up by earlier practitioners of the art, and is a matter worthy of our attention in practice.

Moreover, one must also recognize that: within the four cardinal push-hands, the two jin of peng and lu are the principal ones. Peng is the following silk-reeling (shun chan); lu is the reverse silk-reeling (ni chan); the reverse comes from the following, opposites completing each other. Peng and lu are mutually contradictory yet unified. The spiral following silk-reeling is centrifugal force; the spiral reverse silk-reeling is centripetal force.

Book page 234

3. Two Evolutions of Chen-Style Push-Hands

3. Two Evolutions of Chen-Style Push-Hands

Chen-style push-hands originally combined seizing, throwing, and throwing-and-striking (issuing jin), applying them together and changing lively with the momentum. The seizing method originally consisted mainly of seizing the pulse, grabbing the sinews, and bending back the bones; later, in order to avoid accidents of injury, it was no longer lightly taught or applied. When the seizing method is used in push-hands, one also stops at the appropriate point, and it developed into mainly seizing the opponent's jin path; once the seizure achieves the right opportunity and advantage, one stops. One of pure and refined skill, with a single raise of the hand or a single placement of the foot, controls the opponent's jin path roundly, softly and nimbly, and can at once make the opponent lose the opportunity and advantage, leaving him no way to change, and one can then issue jin; or one may let him change freely and then, at the point of the change, issue jin accordingly. This is the high-level technique of seizing the opponent's jin path.

In Chen-style push-hands, when one originally retreats and uses peng jin to dissolve the opponent's ji jin or kao jin, · 251 · Sink the body and sit down, yet the body method remains centered and upright, until the calf of the front leg touches the ground and the toes are raised, rising and falling with the movement (because the front foot extends far, it can serve to control the opponent's feet; when executing a falling technique this is extremely ingenious). But with such a low stance, rising and falling, coming and going, the amount of movement in the waist and legs is enormous; it is therefore not easy to achieve unless one has practiced since childhood. At present the general principle is not to sink the body and sit down, so that it is better suited to the general public.

Book page 235

4. Taijiquan Push-Hands Combines Both Yin and Yang

4. Taijiquan Push-Hands Combines Both Yin and Yang

The philosophers of ancient China held that in the world there exist two mutually inseparable yet mutually opposing forces, namely yin and yang. The two are the root of the change and development of all things; the harmony of yin and yang is the transformation and unity of the opposing sides of a contradiction. Taiji (the Supreme Ultimate) is precisely a theory of yin and yang encompassing the two forces of yin and yang. Yin and yang stand for such opposing things as movement and stillness, hardness and softness, emptiness and fullness, lightness and heaviness, slowness and speed; as for the relation between the two opposing sides, the two have a unified relation of mutual dependence, mutual restraint, and mutual use.

Taijiquan adopts the theory of yin and yang as its theoretical basis, requiring the simultaneous presence of movement and stillness, hardness and softness, emptiness and fullness, lightness and heaviness, slowness and speed, and also requiring that yang not depart from yin, nor yin from yang, with yin taking yang as principal and yang taking yin as root, so as to reach the stage of "understanding energy" (dong jin) in which hardness and softness surge together and yin and yang aid each other; and further requiring arrival at the stage of "divine illumination" (shen ming) in which yin and yang alternate without trace. Hence in practicing Taijiquan and push-hands one must not lean toward softness, nor may one lean toward hardness; yin and yang must aid each other. Whatever leans toward softness obtains only one side of Taiji and can be called only a soft fist, not Taijiquan; whatever leans toward hardness can be called only a hard fist, and is likewise not Taijiquan. Only that which can be both soft and hard, has both lightness and heaviness, achieves both emptiness and fullness, responds urgently and follows slowly, and suits both movement and stillness, is the complete Taijiquan.

The classical Taijiquan treatise says, "Extremely soft, and only then can it be extremely hard and firm," and "Transport energy like steel tempered a hundred times, nothing is too hard to break." This correctly explains that in practicing Taijiquan one must develop the soft— · 252 · —side to the extreme, and at the same time one must also develop the hard side to the extreme, so that hardness and softness surge together and interweave in manifold change; only then can one be like what the "Appended Remarks" of the Zhouyi (Book of Changes) says: "Change and movement do not abide fixed, they flow through the six voids, above and below are without constancy, hardness and softness exchange with each other, one cannot make of them a fixed rule, only change is what one adapts to." To raise the skill of Taijiquan push-hands, yang-hardness and yin-softness must both be present; only then can one finally attain the comprehensive high-level skill of being able both to neutralize and to issue, that is, "the neutralizing energy is loose and clean, the issuing energy is crisp and dry."

Book page 236

5. Essential Points of the Push-Hands Movements

5. Essential Points of the Push-Hands Movements
(1) Body Method

In push-hands one must stand with the body centered and upright, neither leaning nor inclining, with the crown suspended and the top energy placed, the qi sunk to the cinnabar field (dantian), the tailbone centered, the "striding energy" (tang jin) full, the shoulders sunk and elbows dropped, the chest held in and the back rounded, upper and lower following each other, with the baihui point at the crown of the head and the huiyin point within the crotch always maintaining a vertical line ("one line from top to bottom"); the spine must be relaxed and sunk joint by joint while also being emptily aligned, and the waist must be relaxed, sunk, and straightly vertical; there must be slight turning, and one must not be soft and collapsed, nor sway; the body method must remain centered and upright through any transformation, able to give support in eight directions; the joints of the spine and the ribs of the chest and back must be relaxed and sunk joint by joint, while the intention turns upward (the internal energy turns up from within the crotch to the spine, which is called "qi adhering to the back," "strength issued from the spine," "the ruler is in the waist"), avoiding leaning forward, or leaning left and listing right, and especially avoiding leaning backward; when hands and legs go forward, the mingmen point of the waist and spine presses backward, and the striding energy must sink — this is consistent with the requirements of practicing the form. Taking the mingmen point of the waist and spine (the rear dantian) as the axis for regulating the balance of the whole body, and as the source of the explosive power of which the waist is the ruler — we have proved in practice that it is the key to practicing push-hands technique well.

The key to the transformation of emptiness and fullness in body method lies in the drawing and exchanging of the left and right waist crevices (the two kidneys) with the mingmen point of the waist and spine as axis; when the waist crevice draws to the left, the left is full and the right empty; when the waist crevice draws to the right, the right is full and the left empty; the drawing and exchanging of the left and right kidneys with the mingmen point of the waist and spine as axis (outwardly the drawing and exchanging of the two sides of the waist) — this change of emptiness and fullness is where the total emptiness and fullness of the whole body resides, and is also where the secret lies of "the source moves in the waist and spine" and "inner movement is not known to others."

· 253 · Under the above requirements of body method, Taijiquan employs "adhere, connect, stick, follow," taking not losing and not resisting, not collapsing and not opposing as the principle: when the opponent presses, I ward off (peng); when the opponent squeezes, I roll (lu) — only these four characters, peng, lu, ji, an, cycling without end; moreover one must keep the distinction of energy clear, practice over the long term, follow the rules and regulations, and lay a solid foundation of roundness, fullness, softness, and smoothness.

Both Taijiquan and push-hands first pay attention to body method: only when the body method is upright can one control others without being controlled by them; if the body method deviates, then everywhere one gives openings to others — how could one control them? What is called "when one's person is upright, it works without giving orders; when one's person is not upright, even with orders it does not work" is precisely this principle. In Taijiquan and push-hands, emptiness and stillness are the highest attainment, and centered upright body method is the foundation: being empty, there is nothing it does not contain; being still, there is nothing to which it does not respond; when the body method is centered and upright, one can both give support in eight directions and transform in eight directions, and above and below, in four quarters, the transitions are nimble — hence the traditional theory of Taijiquan and push-hands both emphasize constant centered uprightness. The famous boxer of Chenjiagou, Chen Changxing (1771–1853), was renowned for standing centered and upright, and people of the time called him "the Great King of the Spirit Tablet." Chen-style boxers take standing centered and upright as the first essential, and the Yang and Wu style boxers who developed directly from the Chen style also strictly observe this rule; it is worth our studying where the principle lies.

(2) Hand Method

When first learning push-hands, the silk-reeling circling must be wide and large, striving for roundness, fullness, softness, and smoothness, with no place of concavity or convexity, defect, break, or resistance (see the third characteristic of Chapter One); the movements must be slow and not fast, for when fast one easily slips past everywhere; after the skill deepens, gradually make the circle smaller, being able to be both slow and fast, suiting the requirement "when the movement is urgent, respond urgently; when the movement is slow, follow slowly."

The shoulder joint must always be relaxed, soft, round, and lively, and sunk; the elbow joint must always be dropped, with the intention poured in. In attacking and neutralizing, the arms must always be relaxed and soft, using intention and not force, so that one can be nimble and without obstruction, making it hard for the opponent to perceive my movement. With the spine relaxed and sunk, the sacrum powerful, and the striding energy well sunk, one is naturally steady yet nimble. In all these, the constant value is in being strict and careful.

The secret of neutralizing and advancing to attack lies in the internal energy not being known to others, with the intention ahead of the person, and in rotating about the contact point as axis, gradually attaining "first neutralize, then advance," "half neutralize, half advance," "imme— · 254 · —diately lead and advance." As Chen Xin said, "the two hands turn like a screw thread," and "make the bones of the arm turn, and only then can one move the opponent with true energy," so that the opponent "wishing to advance, cannot find the position; wishing to retreat, does not dare — this is the wondrous state of leading and advancing." "First neutralize, then advance" is to neutralize the incoming energy so that it falls into emptiness and then advance to attack; "half neutralize, half advance" is when the part of the arm above the elbow moves back slightly while the lower dantian (lower abdomen) moves forward slightly, and from the elbow down to the wrist and palm advance accordingly, forming the posture of storing-inhaling and then issuing with exhaling; "lead and advance at once" is a small circle turning at the pass, crisp and direct, what Chen Xin called "empty encirclement and feigned enticement, all for a single turn," which is also the method of intercepting the incoming energy. Practice the form on one hand and push-hands on the other, correcting hand method, body method, step method, and eye method; in attacking and retreating, transforming and neutralizing, upper and lower follow each other, so that each accords with the essentials of Taijiquan training; know the rules and keep the rules, then leave the rules and accord with the rules; hold to principle, not taking victory or defeat to heart, not recklessly using clumsy force — only then can skill develop.

Begin from looseness and stillness, softness and lightness, the same steps as practicing the form; with time the skill deepens, and the whole body becomes one, passing from looseness and stillness, softness and lightness into steadiness; the two shoulders are relaxed, soft, and nimble, the two elbow tips sink; the front hand goes and the rear hand follows; one hand returns and the other follows, "the two hands turn like a screw thread." The two arms control the opponent's two hands, controlling their joints (the wrist joint is the tip joint, the elbow joint the middle joint, the shoulder joint the root joint), making them hard to change flexibly. Among these there are also the arts of seizing and grasping, adhering and following without disengagement, in the hand seemingly soft yet not soft, seemingly hard yet not hard, outwardly like cotton, inwardly like steel rod; able to employ the method of leading into emptiness, and only then to seek the emitting of energy; a small circle turning at the pass, crisp and direct (Chen Xin says, "empty encirclement and feigned enticement, all for a single turn"), like a flash of lightning, incomparably fast. All this is intention, not outward form; when the opponent's energy has just touched my skin, my intention has already entered his bones; with intention always ahead of the person, one will not lose or resist or clash hard, will not rely vainly on the courage of blood and qi, nor will one stiffly seek only nimbleness and lightness without seeking the fullness of internal energy (just as Chen Xin says, "seize and release the silk-reeling energy; one must understand the heavenly mechanism within this"). Thereafter, the more one practices the finer, denser, nimbler, and more skillful it becomes; responding to circumstances as they arise, the whole body nimble and light, wherever one is touched, there one moves; everywhere one can curve softly to neutralize, everywhere one can go straight to issue hardness; seek straightness within the curve, store and then issue; storing and issuing follow the heart's desire.

(3) Step Method

· 255 · The moving step must be nimble and light; the two legs must be divided into empty and full, and again within emptiness there must be fullness, and within fullness emptiness, emptiness and fullness interpenetrating, so that transformation can be nimble. In dividing the two legs into empty and full, the key lies in the drawing and exchanging of the two hip joints; the drawing and exchanging of the two hip joints accords with the drawing and exchanging of the waist crevices — that is, the step method must change along with the change of body method. When about to take a left step, the waist crevice first draws to the right and settles; the qi sinks to the right side of the abdomen; the right hip joint, following, draws in and sinks; the right foot is full; and then the left foot steps out — and the reverse is likewise so.

The step method must also echo the hand method, and must make upper and lower follow each other. What is called "above, the two arms are connected; below, the two legs follow" — and again there must be the intention of mutual attraction and connection between hand and foot. The outer three harmonies — hand with foot, elbow with knee, shoulder with hip — must be attended to, so that upper and lower are complete and not disordered. When moving, one must advance the step; when advancing, one must "cover and insert" (tao cha). Covering is when the front foot controls the outside of the opponent's front foot; inserting is when the front foot inserts between the opponent's legs and step. With cover sealing, insert pressing, the foot advancing and the shoulder following, the method of great opening and great leaning (employing the four energies of cai, lie, zhou, kao) is contained therein.

Cover-seal and insert-press are, in push-hands, methods of controlling the lower body's feet and seizing position when using the falling technique; the inward buckle and outward flare of the knee joint serve to jolt the opponent's step with springing energy, and also serve to dissolve the opponent's use of the knee joint to jolt my step. Chen Xin says, "In boxing, pushing is to be a falling method; if one does not understand the falling method, the body labors in vain." The falling method is still maintained today in Chen-style push-hands. The emptiness and fullness of the two legs must change nimbly, and one must sink the waist and drop the hips; the energy of the full leg winds and sinks as if deeply planted in the ground, so that one can be stable in the step during neutralization and transformation, and not have one's body method broken by being pressed or drawn; when adhering and neutralizing and then striking back, the hips sink first, then arc slightly upward and press forward, in accord with the spiral movement of the hand method — only then can one, when emitting energy, better use the ground's reaction force, so that the energy can rise from the heels, be poured into the waist, pass through the spine, and take form in the fingers.

In push-hands, the intention must be continuous, the form must be continuous; when about to emit energy, the step must advance secretly; victory lies in advancing the step, not being defeated lies in retreating the step; hand, body, and step must have upper and lower following each other; if the hand advances but the body does not, or the hand and body advance but the step does not, not only is the sticking and sealing not achieved, but the emitted energy will be floating and not sunk, unable to emit energy in linked succession, and moreover one will easily be pulled off balance by the opponent. When emitting energy, the body, hand, step, and eyes must · 256 · —all arrive together: the tip of the knee, the tip of the foot, the tip of the nose, the tip of the hand, and the gaze must all be aimed in the same direction, so that the point of force is concentrated.

(4) Eye Method

Among the various schools of boxing, the eye spirit is held most noble: the one who issues the order is the brain, the one who transmits the order is the eye spirit, and the subtle points depend entirely on the eye method. That my intention can enter the opponent's bones depends entirely on the eye power's being able to "know the enemy's situation beforehand," what is called "seeing through at a glance." The ancient boxers also valued "first subduing the opponent with the eye method"; in the changes of leading energy and issuing energy, the intention leads, and the gaze changes accordingly, and body, hand, and step transform with the movement of the gaze. When about to strike upward, one must first harbor a downward intention, and the gaze must first look slightly downward and then shoot forward and upward — then the direction of the issued energy is correct and the intention is far and the energy long. To control which hand is principal in the opponent's energy path, the gaze must look at that place. The gaze must never deviate from the direction of movement.

Having emitted the person out, the gaze must still be fixed forward, and only then is there the effect of "a single conquest like the first battle," "the energy breaks but the intention does not break," "the spirit and qi are not allowed to be cut off," "the emitted energy is like entering wood three parts deep." The eye spirit must also attend to the whole body up and down, so the gaze should be focused, yet the eye spirit must never stare fixedly — it must be like the eye spirit of a cat catching a mouse. Some think that the subtle points of Taijiquan lie in the sensitivity of touch and do not value the use of the eye method, and some even tilt the head and look aside to show that they are concentrating on listening to energy in the hands — this is a misunderstanding. One should know that sight, hearing, and touch are organically coordinated together, and are not to be separated.

(5) Adhere, Connect, Stick, Follow

In push-hands, not only must the two hands adhere, connect, stick, and follow, but the body method and step method must also have the intention of adhering, connecting, sticking, and following, neither first nor last, acting in coordination. This is the manifestation of achieving, in movement, upper and lower following each other, the whole body as one family. The form must be continuous, the intention must be continuous; extend and withdraw, advance and retreat, following the opponent's movement, able to not lose, not resist, not collapse, not oppose — this is called the skill of "understanding energy" (dong jin). Understanding energy comes from "yielding self and following others," being able everywhere to perceive and accord with the objective laws of change. If one can achieve upper and lower following each other in emptiness and fullness, then in attacking and retreating, transforming and neutralizing, one can yield self and follow others and · 257 · —turn round freely; while following others, the mastery still remains with me, and if I do not lose my centered uprightness without deviation, I can control others without being controlled by them. This is the function of hand method, body method, and step method having attained adhere, connect, stick, and follow.

Neutralization and transformation lie first in the waist and legs, next in the chest, and next in the hands. Therefore it is said, "The essential lies wholly in the transformation of chest and waist," and "wherever one cannot obtain the advantageous position, the body at once becomes disordered, and must end in leaning to one side; the fault must be sought in the waist and legs — and so it is with up and down, front and back, left and right." Among these, the bending and extending, coming and going of the silk-reeling spiral is the principal function of "lead in, fall into emptiness, and issue on joining." The hand, at the sticking point, does not leave the supporting surface, and makes a rotating movement about the axis, and can turn freely; from sticky neutralization one knows beforehand the opponent's emptiness and fullness. The surging energy function of the sticking point of body and hand is the marvelous use of "reeling but not reeling," and in sticky neutralization one does not lose one's own opportunity and position. When emitting energy the hand does not pass beyond the tip of the foot, the energy can sink through, and one's own body does not lose its center of gravity, so that one can maintain the stored posture of "support in eight directions," and then be able to be "ceaseless like a flowing river," with energy unbroken, and able to emit energy in linked succession.

Chen-style push-hands requires both that one not let the opponent touch one's own body while one can control the opponent's center of gravity, and also that one dare to let the opponent come close to one's own body, attaining the state of having a method the moment hands meet, and having a method when close in body. The skill of adhere, connect, stick, and follow is in the hands, and also in the body. Slightly leading at hand contact and then issuing energy is one method; at hand contact drawing the opponent to come close, receiving him and controlling him, controlling him and crushing him; using the body to receive the hands so that one or both of the opponent's hands are placed in a useless position, while my hands can still change flexibly: this is another method. Fearing neither distance nor closeness, able to be both far and near, able both to store and to issue, able both to be soft and hard — then one has exhausted the capabilities of push-hands.

When push-hands reaches the stage of understanding energy, the transport of energy must be now hidden, now appearing, seemingly present yet actually absent, seemingly absent yet actually present; when one's skill is pure, one can, following the direction of the opponent's energy movement, stick and move without the slightest error. The internal energy subtly transforms, with the intention ahead of the person; others do not know me, I alone know others; but wherever one is adhered, there one issues energy in that direction (Chen Xin says, "Strike wherever one is adhered to, form transformation without mind like a round pearl; this is the local scenery, the hardest of the hard"). Responding as one is moved, one will naturally no longer be bound by the eight methods and eight energies of peng, lu, ji, an, cai, lie, zhou, kao; this is the arrival, from adhere, connect, stick, and follow, at understanding · 258 · —energy stage, and further to attain the skill of "reaching the divine illumination," in which wherever one touches it becomes round, and one can both neutralize and issue. The general principle is: when the opponent comes with hardness, I respond with softness, and within softness harbors hardness, making it hard to guard against; at all times preserve a store of living mechanism, everywhere closely adhering to the opponent, sticking and moving giving rise to each other, with intention ahead of the person.

(6) One Body Prepared with Five Bows

Chen Zhongshen said, "Vast and surging it flows, naturally one breath. Light as willow catkins, firm as metal and stone. Fierce as the tiger's might, swift as the eagle's soar. In movement like the flow of water, at rest like the standing of a mountain. Its tidings are between the not-near and not-far; its spirit is at the moment of leading but not yet issuing." Wu Yuxiang in his "Treatise on Taijiquan" also said, "Still as a mountain peak, moving as a river." "Still as a mountain peak" expresses the stability and heaviness, the strict order and power, in a settled posture; and within stillness there is the momentum of pre-movement, which is called "seeing stillness as if moving," that is, "the spirit is at the moment of leading but not yet issuing"; "moving as a river" expresses that in movement there are waves rising and falling, ceaseless like a flowing river, forming the nimble transformation of emptiness and fullness, the unceasing arc-like yielding transformation, the unceasing straight advance and sticky press, and in the transformation the whole body still accords as one with the rules, which is called "seeing movement as if still," that is, "its tidings are between the not-near and not-far." What the anonymous "Song Formula for Practicing the Thirteen Postures" says, "Within stillness is touched movement, and in movement there is yet stillness; to change according to the enemy is the divine and marvelous," all expounds that in push-hands one must, as "still as a mountain peak, moving as a river," make the whole body one family, fulfilling the requirement "store energy like drawing a bow, issue energy like loosing an arrow." In the oral secrets of the Chen and Wu families, the mutual transformation of storing and issuing of the whole body's integrated energy requires "one body prepared with five bows." Now let us attempt to synthesize the concrete operational method of "one body prepared with five bows" of the Chen and Wu families and narrate it briefly as follows.

One body prepared with five bows means that the torso is like one bow, the two hands are two bows, and the two feet are two bows. The five bows uniting as one is the integrated energy of the whole body, "still as a mountain peak, moving as a river," able to store and to issue, ceaseless like a flowing river.

In the body bow, the waist is the bow grip; the mingmen point of the waist and spine behind the navel is always poured through with intention, centered and settled, neither leaning nor swaying; when issuing energy the mingmen point must press backward, and the "closing gate" (the seventh cervical vertebra · 259 · —section) and the tailbone serve as the bow tips, symmetrically above and below, regulating the degree of energy, strengthening the posture of storing and inhaling (in the Wu-style body bow, the great vertebra is taken as one bow tip, and the regulated degree of energy is smaller than that of the "closing gate"). When the body bow is prepared, then the waist is pliant, centered and settled, and sunk; above, the "closing gate" is emptily vertical, and the great vertebra bulges slightly with the intention of lifting up (that is, the function of pulling up the back and adhering qi to the back); below, the tailbone is sent forward while the internal energy has the intention of turning upward. The tailbone must be sent forward, then there is no fault of protruding the buttocks; the buttocks must again have the intention of floating upward, then the internal energy turns up from within the shoulders, passes through the spine to the top of the head and then descends, the qi falls to the dantian, and after a long time the ren and du channels naturally connect.

In the hand bow, the elbow is the bow grip, with the intention poured into the elbow joint, making it steady, relaxed, and still, and having a fixed direction. The wrist and the collarbone below the neck are the bow tips; the bow tips must be fixed, symmetric front and back. The hand, in being relaxed, soft, and nimble, is fixed by "sitting the wrist" (the root of the palm slightly exerting force and sinking; when the wrist joint is soft but not floppy, it is called "sitting the wrist"). The collarbone is fixed by intention, not letting it lean or sway; the collarbone governs the movement direction of the two hands, and the fixing of the collarbone is the precondition for the fixing of the two hands.

In the foot bow, the knee is the bow grip, and the hipbone and the heel are the bow tips. When the foot bow is prepared, then the knee joint is powerful and slightly thrust forward, the hipbone is relaxed and sunk and presses back, the heel sinks while the energy turns upward, and the energy of waist and legs naturally accords and follows — this is called "where there is up there must be down, where there is front there must be back, where there is left there must be right," opposites completing each other, mutually pulling in even balance; naturally the energy can rise from the heels, be ruled in the waist, pass through the spine, and take form in the fingers.

Of the five bows, the body bow is primary, and the hand bows and foot bows are auxiliary; thus the waist is the axis, above the two arms are connected, below the two legs follow, upper and lower follow each other, and the middle naturally follows. In each standing posture, the five bows are complete, forming the stored posture of support in eight directions. With the source moving in the waist and spine, and the whole body's energy integrated, one can have "the opportunity issued by oneself, the force borrowed from others," arc-like yielding transformation, straight-line issuing, mutual transformation of storing and issuing, ceaseless like a flowing river. For one whose skill is extremely deep, wherever one touches it becomes round, but wherever one is adhered, from there one issues energy.

The unification of the five bows is the concrete regulation of the integrated energy of inside and outside. In practicing the form and in push-hands alike, as soon as one moves, the five bows should be complete. When the five bows unite as one, then "still as a mountain peak, moving as a river,"

· 260 · "When the standing body is centered, upright, at ease and comfortable, it can support from all eight sides"; "power is stored through bending, and thus has surplus"; and the posture of "seeking the straight within the bent, storing and then issuing" can then appear.

(7) The lifting-gathering-storing and releasing-issuing of fa-jin In practicing push-hands, one should first become thoroughly familiar with the four hands of peng, lu, ji, and an, striving for suppleness, smoothness, and completeness, so that the whole body is one family; first learn soft neutralization, and afterward seek to issue power. In issuing power, one should strive to make the opponent's two feet leave the ground, and to throw him backward (or to the left or right) and upward through the air — that is best. In the stage of practicing fa-jin, one must study the method of combining lift and release with the breath, so that the inhale stores sufficiently and the exhale issues thoroughly. Suffering to store reveals one's skill; issuing thoroughly reveals one's excellence. Only one who can store skillfully can begin to issue excellently.

Inhaling is lifting, closing, storing; exhaling is releasing, opening, issuing. Ordinarily, one must practice the method of lift-and-release both singly and in pairs. Single practice is to take a few fist-forms and practice storing and issuing continuously on both the front and the back side; the shock and spring power of the chest, shoulders, back, hips, and buttocks all require single practice until thoroughly skilled, and one must have [point]. Paired practice is the "feeding" method for studying the correct degree of storing and issuing power. In issuing power one must be concentrated and fiercely penetrating, and especially must be deep and heavy, so that the issued power cuts in sharply and keenly. Motion values brevity; intent values distance; power values length. Concentration brings focused attention... only in this way is the power penetrating; speed takes advantage of the momentum without losing position — go when it is time to go, without falling into the fault of hesitation — then the opponent cannot easily change; heaviness controls his power and prevents him from changing nimbly; shortness of motion means that it issues at a touch, and before he can escape or neutralize, one has already sprung out. One whose skill is high and marvelous can make the opponent not see his motion while he is thrown through the air. When the intent is far and the power is long, the farther one sends the opponent. One whose skill is pure: his motion is extremely subtle, his drawing-out extremely long, his issuing extremely sudden; on the inhale he can naturally lift up the opponent's heels, profiting from his counter-force and moving his center of gravity; on the exhale he can naturally sink down and send the opponent out crisply. When inhaling and lifting, the breath sinks to the lower abdomen (the lower dantian, the Zhongji point); on exhaling, part of the breath is exhaled, part sinks to the lower abdomen, and part shifts to the chest region (the middle dantian, the Shanzhong point). On exhaling, half is spit out and half sunk — only then is there surplus that never runs out, flowing on unceasingly. The upper dantian is at the Baihui point; always keep the top of the head suspended loosely, so as to maintain the centered uprightness of the standing body during inhaling-lifting and exhaling-releasing.

Modern masters of taijiquan such as Chen Fake and Yang Chengfu, when transforming and neutralizing, are light and soft · 261 · round and alive, receiving no force at all, causing the opponent to lose balance and feel as if suspended in emptiness and weightless. In issuing power, because the speed is fast, the landing point accurate, and the internal power sufficient, one suddenly issues power at the adhering point; before the opponent can feel it or escape and neutralize it, he has already been thrown through the air — this attains the high-level skill in which storing and issuing transform into each other.

(8) Breathing, and square-and-round, hard-and-soft

The application of the coming and going of the breath is nothing other than the mutual transformation of square and round and the mutual exchange of hard and soft. Adhering, joining, close and clinging, receiving and turning softens into round; gaining the time and gaining the position, the hard power pushing forcibly becomes square. The rotation of power is round; the issuing is square. The adhering-following power, like glue and like lacquer, comes precisely from the friction produced by the centripetal and centrifugal acceleration of the spiral. The core point of the adhering-following surface is a point on the axial center of the spiral. Forward (shun) rotation is the action of centrifugal force; reverse (ni) rotation is the action of centripetal force. The intricate changes of forward and reverse rotation — the more subtle and nimble they are, "seeking the straight within the bent," "storing and then issuing" — the more the application of round-within-square and square-within-round displays its refinement. The "Song of Striking Hands": "Draw in, let it become empty, and issue as it closes; adhere, join, stick, follow, neither losing nor resisting" — this most perfectly explains the action of breathing with square-and-round, hard-and-soft. In issuing power, "seek the straight within the bent," square without and round within, bent and stored with surplus, flowing on unceasingly; on the exhale the limbs open out as square, on the inhale the limbs draw in tight as round, following the force and going along with the round in coming and going; the inhale lifts the power as soft, the exhale releases the power as hard. The highest requirement is a quick battle and a quick decision; therefore one must also cultivate the skill of victory and defeat being decided in a single inhale and exhale. Yang Banhou, who received the transmission of the Chen family, held that "a single heng and a single ha, and victory or defeat is immediately decided." Thus, because breathing affects the mutual transformation of square-and-round and hard-and-soft, one gradually trains the breath until it is extremely natural; though one uses no strength at all, one can lift and make the opponent come, so that he cannot but come; one can release and make him go, so that he cannot but go. Abandoning oneself to follow the other, and yet holding and releasing is in me; abandoning oneself to follow the other, and yet still it is from oneself; holding and releasing being in me is "from oneself," and from oneself yet still following the other. Moving in this way, one can manifest unceasingly the round within the square and the square within the round, so that its roundness responds without end. Within, the substance is hard yet soft, soft yet hard, now suddenly soft, now suddenly hard, both soft and hard; when at last hard and soft leave no trace to be sought, and square and round no form to be seen, this is to attain within push-hands the marvelous · 262 · realm of the hand.

Chen Zhongshen's quatrain "In Praise of Taijiquan" says: "Movement and stillness have no beginning, turning with the momentum; drawing in and making empty, letting whoever comes come. Were it not obtained within the taiji diagram, how could there be a divine mechanism to embrace the breast?" When one's skill reaches this stage of "ascending to the divine and luminous," the breath naturally keeps time, and hard and soft, square and round are not only all present, but also leave no trace to be sought — merged into the single round image of a taiji diagram.

(9) The role of internal power (nei jin) in push-hands

Internal power is a kind of power stored within (see Chapter One); it is a term used exclusively by the taijiquan school. It is a kind of "spring power" and "tenacious power" tempered out from the relaxed softness of "spirit at ease, body still" by the infusion of intent. Hard within soft is spring power; soft within hard is tenacious power. The saying "when there is hardness within softness, it cannot be broken; when there is no softness within hardness, it is not firm" dialectically explains the character of spring power and tenacious power and their unity of opposites. Internal power has the characteristic of "by spirit knowing what comes, by wisdom storing what has gone"; it is hidden within and does not show without, changing direction ceaselessly with the opponent's movement, neither losing nor resisting, not the slightest bit off; the internal movement is not made known to others — hence it is called "internal power." When internal power is full, elasticity and tenacity are sufficient. This is a unique power produced by the combination of the taijiquan routine and push-hands. As to the substance and operation of taijiquan's internal power, Chen Xin held that it is to move qi by intent, moving lightly, issuing from the dantian, operating within the bone joints, then from within the bone joints operating to the skin and flesh, pouring into the four extremities (the two fingers and the two toes), and returning again to the dantian, winding to and fro, light, nimble, and roundly turning, gradually producing a kind of internal power that is cotton-soft yet heavy, outwardly like cotton and inwardly like steel bars. The deeper one's skill, the higher the quality of the internal power. Wu Yuxiang, who received the transmission of the Chen family's Old Frame and New Frame, described this power as "seeming relaxed yet not relaxed, about to unfold yet not unfolded"; "moving qi like a nine-bend pearl, reaching every subtlety"; "moving power like steel tempered a hundred times, unbreakable by any hard thing."

Internal power silently and imperceptibly rotates in a spiral fashion; it flows with extreme speed, like mercury. In outward form, it is nimble without drifting into floating, steady without falling into sluggishness, rich with the interest of winding silk. Internal power comes mainly from practicing the fist-frame · 263 · tempered out; it is an extremely heavy yet extremely empty-and-spiritual kind of thick, vigorous, and lively power. In push-hands, if there is no internal power, even if one has already achieved the "whole body furnished with five bows" and grasped the organic connection of storing and issuing with the breath, it is still impossible to make the opponent "come when drawn, unable not to come; go when released, unable not to go." Chen Xin said: "But to draw without striking, following the momentum to pull him forward and shake his power with a shake; when the shake is complete his power disperses of itself, his whole body lacks strength, he wishes to advance but has no momentum, wishes to retreat but dares not — this is the marvelous realm of drawing in." This shake-power comes precisely from abundant internal power, and also explains that taijiquan's need for internal power in its winding operation is connected with the practice of push-hands.

In push-hands, if one relies only on sensitive touch while lacking a thick and nimble internal power of "extremely soft, and only then able to be extremely hard and firm," "moving power like steel tempered a hundred times, unbreakable by any hard thing," then one is as if having the passive but not the active, having light weapons but no heavy weapons; it is very difficult to draw the opponent into motion and issue power crisply — on the contrary, one is easily drawn into motion by the opponent.

The yin-soft and nimble side of taijiquan may be likened to a gentle breeze and fine rain; the yang-hard and steady side may be likened to thunder and thunderbolts. Only with both present and mutually used does one attain the completeness of "taiji's two modes, having both soft and hard." The fusion of yang-hard and yin-soft without seam is the two modes returning again to taiji. Whoever is partial to hard without soft must guard against falling and losing; whoever is partial to soft without hard finds it hard to face a strong enemy. When in every movement the light-soft and the heavy-hard are issued together, one can everywhere control the opponent's center of gravity and make him lose balance; everywhere one can pass over the opponent's defensive point and advance and retreat nimbly, making the opponent not know where my hand comes from, attaining the realm of "issuing the hand yet not seeing the hand; the hand arrives and he cannot leave." Only then is one a marvelous hand of taijiquan. Internal power contains the whole grand function of yin-yang merged into one, of soft transformation and hard issuing. Chen Xin said: "If one's skill is pure and mature, from its 'great beyond-outermost' circle one creates the realm of its 'small within-inner,' and if one does not meet an enemy that is that; but if one meets a strong enemy, the internal power bursts out suddenly, like a sudden thunder and fierce wind destroying the withered and breaking the rotten — who can withstand it?" If the adhering-joining-sticking-following of the winding power has no sufficient internal power, then on issuing the hand there is no might, and neither the neutralizing nor the issuing is done well; one wishes to draw the opponent into motion but it has no effect, and one cannot gain the opportunity and the position to control him; one wishes to neutralize the opponent's motion · 264 · when the other's power comes, one is again easily flattened and one's body-method is destroyed; thereby one falls into a passive situation of lost opportunity and lost position and is controlled by others. Chen Xin points out: "If qi is not issued from the central dantian, then qi has no root and falls into wildness, and one will surely fail. This internal power is something that must be studied and trained; if one can study and train to this point, then one's skill is divine."

Internal power is without fixed direction and yet has fixed direction: "without fixed direction" is "round"; "with fixed direction" is "square." The two transform into each other and are each other's root; it is "hard and soft both arriving and merged without trace," and is lively and ever-changing. But the method must be correct: the hard-soft and substantial-empty of taiji's two modes must both be present, and with ceaseless bitter practice can skill come upon the body and gradually reach refinement. To talk emptily of "drawing in and making empty," of "four ounces deflecting a thousand catties," while one's skill is not on the body and hard and soft are not both present — the so-called "a fist without skill is an empty show" — cannot withstand the test of push-hands competition. Chen Xin said: "Storing and transforming are formless and endless; endless skill lies in a hundred practices; not swift yet swift, attaining the true master — only thus can it be called taijiquan." In push-hands, the adhering-joining-sticking-following of silk-reeling power is the soul, but one also needs internal power, which possesses both hard and soft, as the commander. This is the training principle of the earlier generations of taijiquan masters, most dialectically carrying through the meaning of taiji. Only when the silk-reeling power has the infusion of internal power within it can it play the role of "being able to gather ten thousand methods into one and to unfold one method into ten thousand." The postures are methods; methods number thousands and tens of thousands; using one method to govern one method is like one key opening one lock. The power running through the center — this power being one kind of internal power possessing both hard and soft — one governs ten thousand, using the simple to drive the complex, which is like grasping the master key. Therefore Wang Zongyue said: "Though the transformations are ten thousandfold different, the principle is one throughout." "Transformations ten thousandfold different" are the postures; "the principle is one throughout" is the internal power of "adhere, join, stick, follow, neither losing nor resisting," with hard and soft, substantial and empty all present, that "seems relaxed yet is not relaxed," "yields and then extends." Taijiquan emphasizes internal power; gaining the one, all things are complete. Push-hands for medical or recreational purposes need not seek internal power, but push-hands as a competitive sport must seek internal power.

· 265 · Six. The guiding role of the "Taijiquan Lun" in principle for push-hands The "Taijiquan Lun" is a classic work of taijiquan theory; for push-hands too it is a very good theoretical guide. To study its content carefully and use it to guide the practice of push-hands yields twice the result with half the effort.

(1) The four basic principles of taijiquan push-hands skill

(1) The "Taijiquan Lun" says: "Taiji is born of Wuji; it is the pivot of movement and stillness, the mother of yin and yang; when moved it divides, when still it closes." What the ancients called "taiji" is the symbol of the unity of opposites, the pivot of all movement and stillness; from taiji yin and yang are born, as with forward and reverse, soft and hard, light and heavy, round and square, substantial and empty, opening and closing, and so on. In movement, centrifugal and centripetal force are fully utilized; therefore "when moved it divides, when still it closes": dividing is yang, closing is yin. Chen Xin said: "Taiji's two modes, heaven and earth, yin and yang, closing and opening, movement and stillness, the soft and the hard" — this refers to just this law. This contradiction exists throughout the whole process of push-hands, and runs through from beginning to end of every action process. Therefore the first basic principle of push-hands is that it must accord with the law of contradiction of the movement of things, namely "contradiction and opening-closing."

(2) The process of the two parties joining hands and practicing together in push-hands is also a process of ceaselessly producing contradictions and resolving them. What the "Taijiquan Lun" says — "neither overstepping nor falling short, yield with the bend and extend" — refers to the fact that the action must accord with the following four points:

  • ① One must "not overstep"; not overstepping is called "adhering power," while overstepping is called "the fault of resisting";
  • ② One must "be able to reach"; being able to reach is called "sticking power," while not reaching is called "the fault of flatness";

· 266 ·

  • ③ One must "yield with the bend"; yielding with the bend is called "connecting power," while bending without yielding is called "the fault of losing";
  • ④ One must "extend with the reach"; extending with the reach is called "following power," while extending too early is called "the fault of resisting."

All processes of push-hands require the possession of the four skills of "adhere, stick, connect, follow," and the non-occurrence of the four faults of "resisting, flatness, losing, resisting." Chen Xin said: "Adhere, connect, stick, follow — gather the spirit and concentrate the essence, move my empty spirit, and increase steadiness and weight." Therefore the second basic principle is "adhere, connect, stick, follow."

(3) The "Taijiquan Lun" says: "When the other is hard and I am soft, this is called walking; when I am forward and the other is backward, this is called sticking. When he moves urgently, respond urgently; when he moves slowly, follow slowly; though the transformations are ten thousandfold, the principle is one throughout." This is the measure for achieving the four skills and avoiding the four faults. That is to say, when the other is hard then I am soft, using "walking" to draw him in — this is the application of "rolling and closing" under a passive situation. At the same time, in order to probe his power, one uses a smooth, compliant momentum and power to force the opponent into being "backward," transforming into my being hard and the other soft, using "sticking" to press him. When sticking and walking, if the opponent moves urgently one responds urgently, if he moves slowly one follows slowly — in this way there can be the four skills and no four faults. Chen Xin said: "Front and back, left and right, above and below on all four sides, the turning and joining is nimble, the slow and urgent accompanying each other." Therefore the third basic principle is "urgent and slow sticking and walking."

(4) The "Taijiquan Lun" says: "From familiarity with the postures one gradually awakens to understanding power; from understanding power one ascends to the divine and luminous; yet without long effort, one cannot suddenly penetrate through." In push-hands, after having skillfully grasped the first three basic principles, one can apprehend the opponent's power and detect his direction of movement — this is the so-called understanding of the opponent's power. At this point, one can respond at will with the hand, attaining the automatic realm of "divine luminosity." This is the result of many years of repeated pondering, practice, and theoretical study, finally attaining sudden penetration. Therefore the fourth basic principle is "the unity of practice and theory."

· 267 · The four basic principles of push-hands skill

No.Basic principleConcrete practice
1.Contradiction and opening-closingThe movement must contain closing within opening and opening within closing, so as to attain the unity of contradictory opposites.
2.Adhere, stick, connect, followOne must attain lifting and pulling up, lingering and winding, abandoning self without separation; when he walks, respond accordingly.
3.Urgent and slow sticking and walkingMake the movement such that sticking is walking and walking is sticking, and that when he moves urgently respond urgently, when he moves slowly follow slowly.
4.Unity of practice and theoryCombine deep study of the experience of predecessors with much effort of one's own.

(2) How to arrange oneself to apply the four basic principles The "Taijiquan Lun" says: "Empty the neck and raise the top power, sink qi to the dantian; neither leaning nor inclining, now hidden now manifest; when the left is heavy then the left is empty, when the right is heavy then the right is obscure; when he looks up it is higher still, when he looks down it is deeper still; when he advances it is longer still, when he retreats it is more urgent still; a single feather cannot be added, a fly cannot alight; others do not know me, I alone know others; the hero is invincible wherever he turns — all this is attained from this." Therefore, in order to apply the four basic principles, one must, according to the above fist-treatise, do the following six points well:

(1) The top power must be raised emptily; then the spirit is naturally lifted, and at the same time qi sinks to the dantian. Because of the lifting above and sinking below, the body is even lengthened and produces elasticity, becoming peng power. Chen Xin said: "Along the way winding, moving quietly without fluster, skin and flesh and bone joints opening everywhere." If it is a stiff and rigid power, then the peng power is lost, and one can no longer seek understanding of power through adhering and sticking.

(2) The standing body must be centered, upright, at ease and comfortable, possessing the momentum of supporting from all eight sides, so that in push-hands the body does not lean to one side or depend upon the opponent's body and hands, lest one's own power be understood by him. If one leans to one side, one cannot easily and smoothly apply the skill of sticking and walking.

(3) On the premise that when spirit and qi are hidden within one is soft and when manifested without one is hard, in push-hands one must possess · 268 · a function of hard-soft transformation that is now hidden, now manifest — this is precisely the manifestation of ceaselessly probing power in the course of seeking to understand power.

(4) In push-hands one must attain the state in which the two hands have substantial and empty, the two feet have substantial and empty, and each hand and foot, above and below, must also be divided into substantial and empty, forming everywhere this one empty and one substantial. Chen Xin said: "Substantial and empty both arriving, now seen now hidden"; "within the substantial there is the empty, and man and self mutually interpenetrate; within the empty there is the substantial — who can fathom the mechanism?" Once the switching of substantial and empty is skillful, one need only attend to one hand; the other hand and the two feet, because of the mutual following of above and below, naturally also change nimbly along with it. Therefore Chen Xin also said: "A thousand ages as one day, the supreme principle cycles; above and below mutually following — this cannot be spoken of emptily." This is the foundation of probing power, neutralizing power, and the skill of understanding power.

(5) When the opponent comes up, then lead him higher, so that he has the feeling of height unattainable and loses his center of gravity; when the opponent comes down, then lead him further down, so that he feels as if on the brink of a deep abyss, tottering as if about to fall; when the opponent presses forward, then lead him ever emptier, so that he feels a length unattainable; when the opponent retreats, then stick and press so that he feels pursued and pressed. This accords with the requirements of the neutralizing power and issuing power of adhere, stick, connect, follow; in this way one can avoid the four faults of resisting, flatness, losing, resisting.

(6) In push-hands the spirit must be lifted; only thus can the whole body be nimble and spiritually threaded through, and one must be nimble enough to possess the sensitivity of "a single feather cannot be added." At the same time one must ceaselessly change in a spiraling, silk-reeling manner, and must revolve so as to form the momentum of "a fly cannot alight." If the movement shows sluggishness and heaviness without nimbleness, then it is hard to understand power; if the movement has no silk-reeling, then the neutralizing power is lost, and the silk-reeling skill of half-neutralize-half-advance, openly neutralize and secretly advance, neutralize-and-advance-at-once is also lost. Without neutralizing power, it degenerates into a contest of strength, and is no longer taiji-style push-hands. To be able to neutralize but not issue, to be able to be soft but not hard, and hard and soft unable to aid each other — these are all not the completeness of taiji's two modes.

With the above six functions, one can carry through the four basic principles of push-hands, attaining the skill of understanding others' power while others cannot understand one's own, so that in competition one can be in an invincible position.

· 269 · The Concrete Application of the Four Basic Principles

No.ItemExplanation
1Empty the collar and raise the crown, sink the qi into the cinnabar fieldThis must be realized under the conditions of the spirit being lifted, the qi descending, and the whole body being lengthened.
2Neither leaning nor incliningOne must stand with the body centered and upright, bracing the eight directions, the tailbone centered and the spirit threading to the crown.
3Now hidden, now manifestWhen hidden it is soft, when manifest it is hard; now hidden, now manifest — softness and hardness aid each other.
4When the left is heavy, then the right is empty; when the right is heavy, then the left is voidThe two hands divide into empty and full, the two feet divide into empty and full; one hand and one foot follow each other above and below, and the ground divides into empty and full.
5Raise it and it grows higher; press it and it grows deeper; advance and it grows longer; retreat and it grows more urgentThe four preceding items must be carried out accordingly, and one must never go against them; they describe the direction of adhering, connecting, sticking and following.
6A feather cannot be added, a fly cannot alightSo light and nimble that a feather cannot be added; so revolving that a fly cannot alight.
7Not known by others, yet good at knowing othersSticking is yielding, yielding is sticking; others do not know whether it is sticking or yielding; by the drawing-in of sticking and the emptying of yielding, through sticking and yielding one comes to know others.

(3) Push-hands in Taijiquan requires human force to overcome nature The "Taijiquan Lun" says: "This art has many side branches; though the postures differ, none goes beyond the strong bullying the weak and the slow yielding to the fast. The powerful striking the powerless and the slow hand yielding to the fast hand — these are all innate natural abilities, and have nothing to do with what is achieved through study. If we examine the phrase 'four ounces deflect a thousand catties', it is clearly not a victory of strength; and if we observe the form of a venerable elder able to hold off a crowd, what can speed do?" Thus it can be seen that push-hands in Taijiquan is not a contest of strength but of skill. "The strong bullying the weak, the slow yielding to the fast" is a natural instinct, not the function of skill. What is called skill is to comply with nature in order to overcome nature, attaining "the weak defeating the strong, the slow defeating the fast". The principles of the lever's fulcrum and spiral transformation in the natural world possess exactly the function of "four ounces deflecting a thousand catties". By applying this principle in push-hands, one can neutralize and dissolve all heavy force, which is called neutralizing energy (hua jin). With this neutralizing skill, one can use lightness to control heaviness. At the same time, the movement of Taijiquan employs centrifugal force, and by means of the waist · 270 · take the spine as the central axis, so that all movements travel the inner circle; travelling the inner circle, and with a slower "linear speed", one may still overcome the fast movement that travels the outer circle. This is the reason for "others arrive first, yet I arrive earlier" — and it is also the key to the slow defeating the fast.

(4) How to Prevent the "Double-Heaviness Fault"

The "Taijiquan Lun" says: "Stand as a balance-beam, move like a wheel; if one side sinks, then follow; if double-heavy, then one is stagnant. One often sees those whose years of pure practice cannot transform and neutralize — they are invariably made subject by their opponent; it is simply that they have not awakened to the fault of double-heaviness." The so-called double-heaviness fault refers to the pathological sign in which both parties in push-hands remain deadlocked and immobile. This is formed by the occurrence of head-on resistance in both the posture and the direction of energy. In order to remove this fault, in the limbs and body one must "stand as a balance-beam", and in the stepping method one must "move like a wheel". What is meant by a balance-beam is that the head is like the pointer, the waist is like the root and stem, and the two arms are linked to each other and move as two plates, so that one forms a body method like a spirit-level. Probing the opponent with such a body method, the opponent's lightness and heaviness, floating and sinking are all clearly distinguishable. If one side sinks to oneself, then yield to draw it in; if one side sinks to the opponent, then stick to follow it. This is the function of "standing as a balance-beam" in the body method. The revolving of the upper two linked arms, and the shifting and changing of the lower two following legs, are like a spirit-level mounted on a spherical wheel, which can rotate to the left and right, forward and backward, upward and downward. The step follows the body's turn, the body follows the eye's movement, the eye and body follow each other, and then revolving, advancing and retreating are all free and easy — this is the result of "moving like a wheel" in the stepping method. Therefore, when one can draw in and follow, the body method and stepping method can avoid the pathological sign of double-heaviness.

Measures for Preventing the "Double-Heaviness Sign"

No.ItemExplanation
1Stand as a balance-beamThe whole body possesses a certain peng energy; only under standing centered and upright can one attain a balance like that of a spirit-level.Probing the opponent with such a body method, its lightness and heaviness, floating and sinking are all clearly distinguishable.
2Move like a wheelWith the waist and spine as the central axis and the two arms linked to each other, the key to movement lies in the upper and lower empty and full following each other.The other function of moving like a wheel is that when the opponent is about to move, one follows and gives accordingly; when the opponent gives energy, one revolves to receive it.

· 271 · (5) The Requirement to Attain Understanding of Energy while Avoiding the "Double-Heaviness Fault"

The "Taijiquan Lun" says: "If one wishes to avoid this fault, one must know yin and yang; sticking is yielding, yielding is sticking; yin does not leave yang, yang does not leave yin; only when yin and yang aid each other is it called understanding energy." To prevent the double-heaviness fault, in terms of the direction of energy one must first understand the principle that sticking is yielding and yielding is sticking, so as to attain the unity of sticking and yielding. The unity of sticking and yielding comes from the spiral; once sticking and yielding are unified, one may mutually change at any time, and nimbly change the direction of sticking and yielding. At the instant of this change it is called "listening energy①". Listening energy is the use of touch and inner bodily sensation to probe the direction of the opponent's energy: if the opponent turns slightly back-left or back-right, one immediately adopts the sticking of forward coiling; if the opponent turns slightly left or right, one immediately adopts the yielding of reverse coiling. This is the requirement of "when the other does not move, I do not move; when the other moves slightly, I move first." Because sticking and yielding are unified, yin and yang aiding each other is then formed; because of adhering, connecting, sticking and following, the skill of understanding energy is then obtained. This is the marvellous use of attaining understanding of energy through avoiding double-heaviness.

The Skill of Attaining Understanding of Energy in the Process of Preventing the Double-Heaviness Fault

No.How to Avoid Double-HeavinessHow to Attain the Skill of Understanding Energy
1One must know yin and yangOne must know the ins and outs of the opponent's movement and the size of his energy, and must achieve the unity of sticking and yielding, such as slowness and speed, lightness and heaviness, hardness and softness, etc. — this is the basic mode of understanding energy.
2Sticking is yielding, yielding is stickingThis is the central link of push-hands; it embodies the principle that gathering is releasing and releasing is gathering. It requires that in sticking and yielding one be like a ring without beginning or end. If sticking and yielding cannot generate each other, then push-hands has no understanding of energy to speak of.
3Yin does not leave yang, yang does not leave yinSticking and yielding are the path; yin and yang are the substance. Their concrete manifestations are: fast and slow alternating, soft and hard aiding each other, round and square generating each other, light and heavy exchanging, empty and full corresponding, opening and closing connecting. All such things are contained within the concrete movements of sticking being yielding and yielding being sticking.

(6) The "Spiritual Illumination" Stage after Understanding Energy, and the Boundary of Yielding Oneself to Follow Others The "Taijiquan Lun" says: "After understanding energy, the more one practises the more refined one becomes; silently recognizing and pondering,

  • ① What is called listening energy is the use of the tactile sense of the skin and inner bodily sensation to probe the size, length and direction of the opponent's energy.

· 272 · gradually reaching the state of following the desires of the heart. This is originally yielding oneself to follow others, but many mistakenly abandon the near to seek the far. As the saying goes, 'a difference of a hair's breadth leads to an error of a thousand li' — the student cannot but distinguish this." On the foundation of proficiency, one must further undertake theoretical study; through objective feeling and subjective pondering, one brings the subjective and objective into unity. The dynamic pattern formed through practice gradually reaches the state of following the desires of the heart, attaining the automatized "spiritual illumination" stage. This is the highest skill in push-hands. At this stage, one must still clearly distinguish the boundary of yielding oneself to follow others, in order to attain correct application. Push-hands requires yielding oneself to follow others; this is the basic requirement for producing adhering, connecting, sticking and following. But in following others one must have proper measure, and must not blindly follow in every case. Its principle is: "follow the near, not the far." Going far means a lone army penetrating deep, causing oneself to go beyond the square and circle. This is to be used by others to control oneself; it is to hand others the handle. Chen Xin said: "If the enemy feigns and lures, do not pursue closely; if one exceeds the boundary, the situation is hard to turn back, and once one loses the position, though one regret it, what can be retrieved?" This is to say that in this respect, though the difference is small, it is of great importance to the final gain or loss.

· 273 · Chapter Five: The Boxing Treatises of Chen-style Taijiquan Chen Xin left behind many works on the theory of Chen-style Taijiquan; he explained in detail, posture by posture, the principles and the movements, and this became the specialized learning of the Chen family through successive generations. But the theories expounded by Chen Xin are scattered among various pieces, neither systematic enough nor concentrated enough. The author (Gu Liuxin) has always loved Taijiquan and exhaustively investigated its principles, and so he extracted Chen Xin's boxing treatises by category from several books, to serve as reference and study-material in practising the art.

The boxing treatises extracted by category below are based mainly on Chen Xin's "Illustrated Explanation of Chen-style Taijiquan" and on the Chen Xin writings contained in Chen Jifu's "Compendium of Chen-style Taijiquan". The latter's collation is careless, with many erroneous and missing characters; fortunately a manuscript copy based on the original text (originally titled "The True Classic of Taiji") was obtained from the old gentleman Li Jianhua, by which the text could be corrected, so that it is nearly free of error.

A hundred or two hundred years ago, Taijiquan was also a martial art of combat; hence many parts of the ancient boxing treatises take the movements of the Chen-style old frame as examples and expound them from the standpoint of combat. To make it convenient to study and organize Taijiquan theory, and especially to promote push-hands in Taijiquan, this book has also selected these boxing treatises as appropriate, and it is hoped that readers will accept them critically, achieving the principle of "using the ancient for the present".

· 274 · Brief Biography of Chen Xin Chen Xin, courtesy name Pinsan (1849–1929), was a man of Chenjiagou, Wen County, Henan. His grandfather Chen Youheng and his grand-uncle Chen Youben were both famous for the family-transmitted Taijiquan. Youben also created the Chen-style new frame. His father Chen Zhongsheng (1809–1871) and his uncle Chen Jisheng (1809–1865): Youheng drowned in Dongting Lake in middle age, and so Zhongsheng and Jisheng changed to study boxing under their uncle Youben.

Zhongsheng had an ape's back and a tiger's neck, and was more stalwart than ordinary children; at the age of three he already practised martial arts, and when grown he and his younger brother Jisheng both entered the military academy.
