The two-rising is purely a method of the whole body rising and lifting; the body method and the mind's strength lift upward, the whole body's spirit is roused, all leap up into the air, and only when the right foot can rise above the head-top is the form correct. The body follows the crown-strength and is urged upward; the higher the better; there are those who leap above the head-top—this cannot be done without a light body and great strength. …The upper body rises upward, and the lower body the more must use force to follow it up; the method of rising is that both feet must first stamp downward with force—the heavier the stamp, the higher the body rises."

"When the mind's strength once takes the lead, the five organs and hundred bones all rise with it."

"Both feet rise in linked succession; the whole body leaps into mid-air."

"The central breath is raised, the backbone strength is firm; the linked two-risings soar upward."

"What is meant by 'falling into the fork' (diecha): the body falls down from mid-air, the two legs split apart—this is 'falling into the fork.' In this figure the left leg extends open, the right leg is bent and held; this is the 'single falling fork.' As for the 'double falling fork,' without using the leaping method one cannot rise; it is not like the single falling fork, where one need only bring the left heel forward in a closing movement, open the right knee outward, and with force flip the right heel—then one rises and falls at once. It is somewhat easier than the other; hence used it too can overcome. And today all boxing masters do thus; for the present we follow it."

"The falling fork and the two-risings echo and answer each other: the two-risings go from below upward, flying into mid-air; this one comes from mid-air downward, the two legs touching the ground. A natural echoing, not forced to fit—such was the strictness of the ancient men's law of creating boxing."

"Strike high to alarm, take low—you must remember this; the left foot grazing the ground, the stamp benefits itself."

"It is not the shoulder and elbow that can defeat the enemy; a single foot kicks down the Phoenix Terrace."

"Were this body not made a man of iron, how would there come a sound of metal and stone when it is cast to the ground?"

"Breaking the encirclement lies in a single stamp; without great skill one cannot overcome a man with one foot."

"Stamping one heel (deng yi gen): I kick the enemy with my left foot; the enemy, with his right hand, strokes and holds my foot, wishing to twist it, to make me cry out in pain and fall to the ground, or lifting my foot, wishing to raise my whole body off the ground and then to bounce it up and strike it. I then follow the momentum, turning both hands over to press the ground, and with the right foot following the left leg, walk backward and upward, oversetting the enemy's right hand that presses my left foot—the difficulty is at once resolved. Or again, if the enemy presses my left foot, I then with my right foot stamp the enemy's right elbow-tip, or stamp his wrist-joint—both can resolve it. This is the general outline of 'stamping one heel.'

If a man comes to stamp me, I then take my left foot and step back one pace, to guard against his stamping my dove-tail (jiuwei) and below the chin-receptacle (chengjiang) down to the throat.

Yet to be cautious at the moment of the stamp is already late; better to be cautious at the moment when the previous posture is about to kick—if you see it can kick, then kick; if it cannot kick, then do not kick; do not rashly use its kick.

Even if there be a crack to seize, in kicking speed is prized, not slowness; it is prized to kick the tightly-closed acupoints, not to kick the broad thigh and thick flesh where it does not touch the painful, itching spot. This is the essential secret; the kicker must know it."

"The posture 'Wild Horse Parts its Mane': both hands grasp the ground and turn like flying, a single thread running through the middle with no leaning. Both hands brush upward along the ground, and the whole body above and below can guard itself; the central breath rises from the hundred-meetings point (baihui) above and runs down through the long-strength point (changqiang), as though threaded on one line. The two hands are like two rings, one above the other, dancing in alternation; its firmness cannot be broken, its sharpness has no equal, its turning has no interval—hence it can repel the enemy."

"The posture 'Spread-Brocade on the Ground' (pu di jin) echoes and answers the falling fork: the falling fork hangs in the air and drops straight down, the right foot stamping the ground with a sound of metal and stone, to stamp the enemy's foot; the left foot stamps the enemy's shin-bone, which can break his courage. The right hand spreads open the arm and brushes up along the ground, the left hand thrusts forward to push the enemy's chest; here, then, one sits back with the buttock and thigh to sit upon the man's knee, the right hand's fist bends with intent to strike forward, and the left leg spreads open—if one cannot win thus, both hands · 301 · …such was the strictness of the law of boxing."

"Strike high to alarm, take low—you must remember this; the left foot grazing the ground, the stamp benefits itself."

"It is not the shoulder and elbow that can defeat the enemy; a single foot kicks down the Phoenix Terrace."

"Were this body not made a man of iron, how would there come a sound of metal and stone when it is cast to the ground?"

"Breaking the encirclement lies in a single stamp; without great skill one cannot overcome a man with one foot."

"Stamping one heel (deng yi gen): I kick the enemy with my left foot; the enemy, with his right hand, strokes and holds my foot, wishing to twist it, to make me cry out in pain and fall to the ground, or lifting my foot, wishing to raise my whole body off the ground and then to bounce it up and strike it. I then follow the momentum, turning both hands over to press the ground, and with the right foot following the left leg, walk backward and upward, oversetting the enemy's right hand that presses my left foot—the difficulty is at once resolved. Or again, if the enemy presses my left foot, I then with my right foot stamp the enemy's right elbow-tip, or stamp his wrist-joint—both can resolve it. This is the general outline of 'stamping one heel.'

If a man comes to stamp me, I then take my left foot and step back one pace, to guard against his stamping my dove-tail (jiuwei) and below the chin-receptacle (chengjiang) down to the throat.

Yet to be cautious at the moment of the stamp is already late; better to be cautious at the moment when the previous posture is about to kick—if you see it can kick, then kick; if it cannot kick, then do not kick; do not rashly use its kick.

Even if there be a crack to seize, in kicking speed is prized, not slowness; it is prized to kick the tightly-closed acupoints, not to kick the broad thigh and thick flesh where it does not touch the painful, itching spot. This is the essential secret; the kicker must know it."

"The posture 'Wild Horse Parts its Mane': both hands grasp the ground and turn like flying, a single thread running through the middle with no leaning. Both hands brush upward along the ground, and the whole body above and below can guard itself; the central breath rises from the hundred-meetings point (baihui) above and runs down through the long-strength point (changqiang), as though threaded on one line. The two hands are like two rings, one above the other, dancing in alternation; its firmness cannot be broken, its sharpness has no equal, its turning has no interval—hence it can repel the enemy."

"The posture 'Spread-Brocade on the Ground' (pu di jin) echoes and answers the falling fork: the falling fork hangs in the air and drops straight down, the right foot stamping the ground with a sound of metal and stone, to stamp the enemy's foot; the left foot stamps the enemy's shin-bone, which can break his courage. The right hand spreads open the arm and brushes up along the ground, the left hand thrusts forward to push the enemy's chest; here, then, one sits back with the buttock and thigh to sit upon the man's knee, the right hand's fist bends with intent to strike forward, and the left leg spreads open—if one cannot win thus, both hands · 302 · …the right brushes toward the ground, using the sweeping-ground whip to sweep the lower shins of the crowd of enemies; then the difficulty resolves itself. Thus it echoes with things of its own kind. Again it echoes with 'Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg': the Golden Rooster raises the left leg upright, while here the left leg lies crosswise; the Golden Rooster knees a man with the right knee, and here too the right knee is bent and held; the Golden Rooster lets the left hand hang down and stretches the right arm upward, while here the right hand is bent and held and the left hand is stretched upward—hence they echo each other above and below. Again it echoes with the two-risings: the two-risings lift the body flying into mid-air, while here the body drops to the ground—hence again they make an echo above and below."

"Front and back, left and right, above and below, on all four sides—the turning and joining are nimble; slow and urgent keep pace together; strike high and take low, and each wish is gratified. …Rising to strike and dropping to strike must never be one-sided; feint to the east and strike to the west—left and right are both suitable. …Horizontal and vertical, toppled and leaning, sitting and standing tilted and upright, bowing forward and leaning back—the strange and the orthodox beget each other; whirling and leaning to the side, gathering and leaping all hit the mark (all have the central breath's release and gathering, governed within them)."

"The foot follows the hand's movement, revolving like a spirit—now up (hands and feet upward), now down (hands and feet downward); sometimes with-turning (shun) (using the with-twining method, its strength follows), sometimes against (ni) (using the reverse-turning method, its strength opposes)."

"'Tipping the Red Robe' (dao juan hong) is a retreating movement to evade left and right; 'White Goose Spreads its Wings' is a right-draw left-strike, and at the same time an upper-draw lower-strike method; 'Brush the Knee and Twist the Step' is six-sealings (above and below, front and back, left and right—all doors sealed) and four-avoidings (the four avoidings are east, west, south and north, leaving a man no crack to attack); 'Flash Through the Back' is a forward-flash (from behind flashing forward), backward-slip (when the rear cannot be pressed down, pressing hard makes one slip and fall) advancing-strike method; 'Grasp the Robe' and 'Single Whip' are both draw-one advance-one methods (this word 'advance' means advancing to strike); 'Moving Hands' is a left-right draw-one advance-one striking method; 'High Pat the Horse' is a left-arm back-bending elbow method; 'Left and Right Plant the Foot' is a lower-body forward-attacking stamping method; 'Middle Single Whip' is a left-right up-down hands-and-feet striking-together method; 'Strike the Ground Blow' is an attacking-low method, and behind the body at the same time a slipping-falling method. The secret is that the life-gate (mingmen), between the two kidneys in the middle of the two loins, is the hinge and pivot of the upper and lower body. Above and below the hinge all is reverse-turning strength; the body carries a sideways lean and holds; the right rear flank goes up, the left rear flank goes down; when the downward strength is good and the foot is planted firm, if a man is struck on the back, the body at once twists and turns—the swifter the better. If one can follow the foot method, then the man slips and falls of himself. The two-rising kick, the single kick, and the stamping of one heel are reverse-turning great body-turn methods, and with both feet · 303 · …attack methods (the hand serves as the foot, and the foot serves as the hand); 'Rolling-Hand Hammer' and 'Small Capture and Strike' are forward-attacking upper-and-lower methods; 'Embrace the Head and Push the Mountain' is a reverse-turning (referring to the body) advancing-pushing method; 'Single Whip' is a with-turning (with-turning also refers to the body method) left-and-right draw-strike method.

The above several tens of postures are for one man fighting a great battle against several tens of men; as for the method of evading the enemy, it does not go beyond above and below and the two sides—whichever side is tight, first loosen the encirclement on that side; when they come all together, as soon as the central breath moves, all are at once made to scatter. Without skill this cannot be done."

(Note: All the boxing postures mentioned above are postures of the Chen-style old frame; recorded here for reference.)

12. Firmness and Softness Both Extinguished, a Single Piece of Spirit Moving

"When the skill of movement matures, then one transforms firmness into softness, and refines softness into firmness; when firmness and softness attain the mean, then yin and yang appear. Hence this boxing cannot be named by firmness, nor named by softness; it is simply named by the nameless name of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji)."

"When it is still, what yin and yang store leaves no trace to be seen; when it moves, it seems supremely soft, yet in truth is supremely firm; it seems supremely firm, yet in truth is supremely soft. Firmness and softness alternate in operation, with no end to be found."

"The principle of Taiji circulates, handed down who knows how many years; within it there is essential meaning—movement and stillness both without bias… Opening and closing are originally without fixity (lively and flowing), bending and stretching are linked in posture (yet have a definite order). Taiji divides into yin and yang; the spirit-dragon transforms without limit; heaven and earth are father and mother; they rub and wash softness and firmness; production and production truly never cease; the strange and the orthodox are no common thing. Qian and Kun are like the bellows-pipe; Taiji is one great bellows-bag; the causes of fullness and emptiness, waxing and waning, are all stored within it. To the very end it again begins from the start; one breath moves tension and slack; the formed returns to tracelessness; things and self are both forgotten."

"Closing and opening, firmness and softness follow nature; one raising and one lowering, the principle circles."

"Ending then beginning again, beginning then ending again; only beginning and ending, circling without end."

"Taiji is nothing but the undivided chaos of yin and yang. …Faint to the point where sound and scent are both absent, yet every fine subtlety is complete—this is the work of nature (huagong). Truly, no carving is performed."

· 304 · "One coming, one going, moving a full circuit; the breath's mechanism above and below never pauses."

"The heavenly mechanism is lively; the vast breath flows; movement and stillness, slow and urgent, turn and revolve following the mind. …Extremely swift, extremely fast, winding and whirling; leaving the form yet attaining the likeness—what is not the full moon? When refinement is complete, even the smallest is a circle."

"When purely natural, then in boxing all follows the heavenly mechanism's stirring—nothing is not so of itself, lively and flowing; the original image of Taiji all pours forth from my own body."

"Every place in the human body is Taiji; every movement and every stillness is wholly undivided."

"Utterly empty, utterly numinous; every single movement is the round image of Taiji."

"Turning round and freely, vast and flowing, with no stagnation at all; each posture, when finished, still returns to the wholly undivided single Taiji manner—with no trace to seek, no thread-end to point at."

"When one has practiced boxing until thoroughly ripe, it can no longer be likened to any form or trace; like the spirit-dragon's transformations, it cannot be grasped; movement follows the intent, and of itself becomes a measure—unfathomable. When skill reaches this, it is truly of the divine rank. The principle of Taiji issues from no beginning, is completed without trace, without start or end, held out on a living platter—ah! Here one may rest in contemplation! Though boxing is a small way, what is called 'seeing the great through the small'—surely this boxing is not easy to speak of!"

"Therefore when my body's operation is sometimes high, sometimes low; sometimes reversed, sometimes upright; and now slow, now swift; now hidden, now manifest; sometimes opening wide and closing wide; now moving and now stopping—is it not all one piece of vital spirit (lingqi), displayed in visible form, truly like the kite flying and the fish leaping, the transforming mechanism lively? One who is good at observing boxing will surely not deeply admire only the drumming and dancing of ears, eyes, hands and feet amid traces and images. Therefore the student must first study its principle: when the principle is clear, then the breath of itself becomes lively and nimble—it is not that the breath can of itself be lively and nimble; in truth the principle makes it lively and nimble. Only after knowing this can one speak with him of inner strength. If one merely takes 'issuing from within outward' as inner strength, that discussion is still shallow."

"Sincere within, formed without, the thousand changes and ten thousand transformations are of themselves endless; when the fire-timing reaches pure blue, the method is dense and the principle fine; the whole body is light and numinous; left and right everything comes out, responding, responding, responding."

"The spirit reverent and deep, the appearance august, the manner wholly undivided; empty and numinous, it embodies one mind; the ten thousand images store the five · 305 · …store. Still and unmoving like a foolish man—who knows that yin and yang are joined in this body? Let him be surrounded on four sides and eight directions, hard for men to approach; even though he be braver and stronger than others and come suddenly to invade, the toppling man topples, the falling man falls, none can fathom his spirit; and moreover, to go away is hard and to advance is hard—like standing on a round stone, he cannot stand firm, truly steep and hazardous, and regret is hard to avoid. Where is there another method? Only that skill be pure; all relies on this: one opening and one closing, and one stroke sweeps across the army of a thousand men."

"Taiji's yin and yang create and transform; the kite flies and the fish leaps—let the lord watch."

"A low-grade boxing is kicking with the foot and striking with the fist; the wondrous hand—nowhere is it not wholly undivided. Let him be surrounded on all four sides by enemies; as soon as this body moves, all are toppled and laid low. Nowhere in my body is not Taiji; without mind it forms into a round pearl; whatever place is struck, that place strikes—I myself do not know the mystery of mysteries."

"One breath revolves without ever stopping; the upright breath of Qian and Kun moves through the vast chaos. When one has learned to bring the formed back to the traceless, then one knows the mystery lies in the work of heaven."

13. Cultivate the Original Root, Study Diligently and Practice Bitterly

"The heart is the master of the whole body, the kidneys are the source of nature and life; one must purify the heart and reduce desires, nurture this ground of the root, and not let it be injured. When the root is firm, then the branches and leaves flourish; all things can be done; this is of the utmost importance."

"However one may speak a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, nothing compares to purifying the heart, reducing desires, nurturing its original root, in order to nourish the original breath. When the body is originally strong, in practicing boxing one will of oneself surpass others by a head."

"In doing the work, each according to his own strength moves; as for the number of repetitions, one round is acceptable, ten rounds is also acceptable—do not be bound by the number of rounds. If you have strength, then by all means move; if without strength, then stop. There is no need to force the movement so that you exceed the rules; only follow nature and you will get it."

"Each single posture of boxing—often a thousand words cannot exhaust its wonder, yet once one has demonstrated it in person it feels quite easy. What is hard is the work; what is especially hard is long-lasting work. There is a proverb that says: 'Strike the boxing ten thousand times, and the spirit and principle will of themselves appear'—truly so."

"Play the boxing postures in the air—there is originally no fixed form. …In ordinary practice one must not fail to keep to the established rules, nor may one rigidly adhere to the established rules; this lies in the student's ability to make good use of his inner strength. As for the outward traces, when restricted by the terrain, one may consider and apply it according to the terrain."

· 306 · "From the first posture to the last, what is depicted is all boxing with form; only when one has made the formed reach to the formless, and the mind's mechanism enters the wondrous, finally returning to no-mind—only then can one speak of boxing. One sees that boxing is in my heart; in my heart the heavenly mechanism flows, and lively and flowing, wherever it touches is boxing—not to be compared with those in the world who take boxing as boxing. This is an art never exhausted in a lifetime; it is not knowing it that is hard, but doing it that is hard. The postures depicted are all the natural mechanism within Taiji. …A thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, interlacing without end—hence in a lifetime one cannot exhaust it. Let the student strive."

"When in boxing one's skill is already ripe, one is upright, reverent and solemn, respecting one's undertaking, not daring to be self-satisfied. …Not boastful, not ostentatious, with a bearing calm and unhurried—though it be called practicing martial arts, the civil is within it."

"Mencius said: 'The great craftsman teaches men, and must use compass and square.' Compass and square are the ultimate of round and square. To teach men by them is what the great craftsman can do; as for skill, the great craftsman cannot give it—it lies only with the student. If one reaches skill, then one follows the compass and square without being stuck to them, leaves the compass and square yet of oneself hits the compass and square. But the will must not be full. There is a proverb: 'Beyond heaven there is still heaven; as soon as one is full, one invites loss.'"

"Or someone says: 'This boxing cannot strike a man.' That it cannot strike a man is only that one's skill has not arrived. If the skill is thoroughly ripe, then from the circle 'great with nothing outside it' one fashions the realm 'small with nothing inside it.' If one does not meet an enemy, then so be it; but if one meets a strong enemy, then inner strength bursts out suddenly, like a swift thunder and fierce wind snapping withered branches and rotting wood—who can withstand it?"

"Students today, before doing the work, first expect the result; after a little effort, at once expect completion. What of Confucius's saying of 'first the difficulty, afterwards the obtaining'? One asks: How is the work to be done? One must, as Mencius said, 'surely have affairs, yet not be set upon them; the mind must not forget, nor must one force its growth'—only then may one succeed. If the principle is not clear, invite a clear teacher; if the road is not clear, seek a good friend. When the principle is clear and the road is clear and yet one still cannot, then add the effort of daily unremitting diligence, advancing without stopping; in time one will arrive of oneself. One asks: How long does it take? Small completion takes three years, great completion takes nine years; at the time of nine years, one can observe it. Still further, after nine years, of oneself one cannot stop though one would; daily ascending, in a lifetime there will be no place to halt. Were the divine hand to arise again, it would not alter my words. Let the impatient take heart."

· 307 · "Men say this art has a separate secret, and often will not reveal it to others. I say this art has nothing very wondrous; from youth it is hard to practice until old age. Practice until old age and one naturally awakens, suddenly threading through the wondrous spirit and principle. Looking back, one tries to think of the times of laziness—it is not that the foreknowledge did not speak of it, but that what was spoken did not enter my heart, and my heart on the contrary felt much affliction. Day after day it is spoken and day after day forgotten; if the heart is not used, when will one understand? If one can for a single day seek with effort, the waxing and waning of yin and yang will of themselves be true. Each day closely play with the Taiji diagram; one opening and one closing are in my own body. Advancing step by step, the work grows long; in time one will of oneself smell the true fragrance. Only let the work be long and without interval, and Taiji will show its round light everywhere. This is the true secret within boxing; let the lord calmly and carefully consider it."

"Every man each embodies one Taiji; only look at whether he applies effort or not. Only let the days be long and the practice without slack, and the wondrous principle circling will of itself be penetrated."

Book page 285

Four. Chen Xin's Sayings on the Thirteen Body Parts ①

Four. Chen Xin's Sayings on the Thirteen Body Parts ①
1. The Head

"The head is the chief of the six yang, the master of the whole body; the five organs and hundred bones—none but takes this as its facing and turning."

"If the crown-strength leads too much, then it hangs upward; if it cannot lead up, then it topples."

"As for the head: the ears can hear the sound of the enemy's coming, the eyes can see the color of the enemy's issuing, the head can touch front, back, left and right, and the left and right hands can again rise up to assist it."

2. The Eyes

"Where is its spirit? It is said: in the pupils. When the heart moves, the pupils transmit it—never is there any error."

"The operation is rooted in one heart, and the spirit is looked at in the eyes and pupils; the eyes are the officers that transmit the heart. Hence if the eyes do not look aside, it proves the heart is not used in two ways."

"The spirit of the eyes is especially important: it should follow the movement of the chief hand; one must not look aside—looking aside, the spirit scatters and the will is likewise not single."

  • ① Among these, the six items of crown, shoulder, elbow, chest, hip and knee have already been cited above and are not separately recorded.

· 308 · "Hand and eye are the living parts; they must not be moved rashly."

"The eye's spirit is fixed on the middle finger of the (chief) hand, without sidelong looking."

"The eye looks forward at the middle finger of the front hand, namely the middle finger, and hence must look at this—one must not look aside, letting it become scattered with nothing to rest on. The whole body's employment lies entirely in one heart, and the transmission of the spirit lies entirely in the eyes; hence one must concentrate the spirit and gaze. In the 'Grasp the Robe' (lan ca yi) posture the right hand is the chief and the left hand is the guest; the right hand initiates, the eye must look at it. The eye follows the right hand's movement; when the right hand stops, the eye must fix on the nail of the right hand's middle finger. The five fingertips must use force—this is the resting place where the front and rear hands complete their movement, hence force must be used. At this moment the moving hand seems to stop, yet its moving vital spirit in truth does not stop; once it stops, then its breath ceases, and it is cut off from the next posture. This is exactly the ceaseless revolution of heaven and earth's yin and yang—how could the two breaths alone, in my own body, rest? Only because it does not rest does the breath grow more substantial as it moves; when it moves to full satisfaction, then the next posture immediately arises. This is the meaning of 'when yang is extreme, yin is born; when yin is extreme, yang is born.'"

"The eye can shoot its light in four directions."

"The eye not looking forward, its light shoots in four directions."

"The eyes glancing left and right must be quick."

"Gather the gaze and return the hearing; concealing the light, silent."

3. The Ears

"The ears hear behind the body and to both sides."

"The ears hear behind the body, to guard against the enemy's secret plot."

"When the enemy comes, there must first be wind: if urgent, the wind is great; if slow, the wind is faint. Even without wind there must be an omen. If the enemy is in front, the eye can see him; if he is on the right, on the left, or behind the body, that is the omen… only rely on the ears to hear and the heart to guard."

"The ears hear the left and right and the back, for fear there be an unforeseen encroachment. When a man comes from behind, there must first be a sound—one can hear his sound. Sound is of itself different from no sound; hence when the heart is calm and the breath still, the ears are of themselves clear and sharp."

4. The Nose and Mouth

· 309 · "Breathing follows its own nature."

"Regulate the breath, continuous and unbroken."

"Heart and breath lean on each other."

"In practicing boxing, the nose is the middle boundary."

"Lips lightly closed, the tongue-tip lightly touching the upper palate."

5. The Neck

"The neck stands straight and must not be stiff."

"The neck must be upright and erect, like the pillar in mid-stream, neither forward nor back, neither left nor right, and must not topple—then it is right."

"The neck must be nimble; being nimble, turning left and right is of itself easy."

6. The Hand

"Use the heart to move the hand, following the momentum to turn circles."

"When the hand leads upward, the waist and the crotch all descend together; the upper body's revolution feels lively, and the lower body is likewise not dead-stiff."

"When the hand leads up and turns circles, the circles drawn by the fingers and the twining strength of the arm are one single strength—they must not be regarded as two segments."

"The hand loosely encloses." "The strength moves to the finger-tips."

"The eye looks at the middle fingernail; the middle finger corresponds with the nose-tip."

"The middle finger takes the nose-tip as its standard. Using the silk-reeling strength, twine from the shoulder to the hand; only when the central breath travels to the tip of the middle finger is the movement complete. When the middle finger's strength arrives, the other fingers' strength also arrives. Soften and hold the strength; one must not leave the slightest hard breath."

"When using the hand to move and stop things, there must be firm breath moving within it."

"The hand is like iron coming from a red furnace—men dare not touch it."

7. The Fist

"When going out, release the hand; on striking the man, it becomes a fist."

· 310 · "Fist-power is like wind and also like thunder."

"A single blow is like a thunderclap, one crash, too quick to cover the ears."

"The hammer-strike goes from behind to the front, striking like thunder from the mountain, too swift to guard against; its advance is faster than a bird's flight."

"When close to the body, bend the elbow and use stored force; how can one fail to extend the arm when going far?"

"Use the whole body's full strength to strike with the 'seizing' (na) energy, without betraying crudeness—only then does it accord with the rules. …The energy starts from the heel of the rear foot, passes over the calf, runs up along the spine to the shoulder and arm, and turning, is conveyed along the back of the arm to the back of the hand; therefore a strike made with 'held' energy is powerful. Yet although the energy starts from the heel, its use lies fundamentally in the mind; the instant the mind moves, the central qi issues from the dantian to the hand, and the whole body's full strength gathers there. As for striking a man, one judges his distance: if far, extend the arm so as to reach him; if near, the arm cannot be extended, so one strikes with a bent elbow and joined hammer-fist, which is full of restraint, showing no outward trace, and the one struck falls at once—this is the highest order. For it is easy to strike at a distance and hard to strike close in; hence one must put in much practice to be able to do so."

"The inner energy passes down from the dantian past the crotch, then runs up in reverse from the Changqiang point to Baihui, descends to the shoulders, and advances to the hammer-fist; when the whole body's spirit gathers in the hammer-fist, then there is power. The left and right feet planted on the ground, steady as a mountain on the earth, unable to be shaken—then there is power."

"In boxing, it is purely a vast vital qi circulating through the whole body, an irresistible momentum."

8. Belly

"When the waist energy pushes down, the tailbone slightly rises, and the lower belly naturally holds its energy."

"When chest and belly are broad and vast, closing together forward, the central qi running through, the whole spirit above and below, there is truly the aspect of the face covering the back. When one has practiced long and reaches this realm, one naturally knows its spirit; even upon reaching that realm, it can only be grasped by the mind, not conveyed in words."

"Regulate the breath softly and continuously, hold the inner firmly and guard it, attend to the mysterious gate; after long practice, in an instant fire issues within water, a flower blooms in snow, the two kidneys are hot as boiling broth, the bladder as if scorched by fire, and the true qi is naturally full."

9. Waist

· 311 · "The waist is the pivot and turning-gate where upper and lower body meet; it must not be soft, nor may it be hard—fold to its middle, then it is right."

"The waist is the key to the upper and lower body: above the waist the qi travels upward, below the waist the qi travels downward, seeming like a two-way contest above and below, yet in truth it is one qi running through, moving in parallel without conflict."

"The waist energy should be valued for going down, valued for being firm and solid."

"The waist energy pushing down must not be soft."

"When the waist energy goes down—the waist is where upper and lower join; if it does not go down, the upper body's qi floats and the feet are unsteady."

"The waist energy must go down, and going down must have energy; the two knees brace open, the hips close together, wanting to be round and wanting to be empty—then naturally the lower body is empty, nimble and steady, unable to be shaken."

"When the waist turns, the upper body naturally turns, matching the lower body—this is how the waist is the pivot of upper and lower body."

"The waist must be empty; once empty, both above and below are nimble."

"If the waist energy does not go down, the qi cannot return to the dantian; if the qi does not return to the dantian, then Zhongji and Huiyin lose their lightness and become buoyant, and therefore the transverse qi in the chest fills and blocks it full; even behind, at Taodao, Shenzhu, and on both sides of Lingtai, the transverse qi likewise fills and blocks abundantly, and front and back alike become stagnant and obstructed. For if one does not close forward, the flaw is a leaning back; if one closes forward, then the crotch energy becomes light and buoyant, the sole of the foot is unsteady, and the upper body is not empty and nimble either."

"The secret lies in the Mingmen between the two kidneys, in the midst of the two flanks of the waist, as the key and pivot of the upper and lower body."

10. Spine, Back

"The spine is the key to the left and right of the body."

"Turn inside and out slowly (all turns are inward or outward), the central qi running through the midst of the spine."

"If you would ask the true secret herein, you must seek it in the joints of the spine and back."

"The back is held through by the central qi."

· 312 · "The back folds and opens out; the top energy and the crotch energy are then full."

11. Crotch and Buttocks

"The two sides of the scrotum are called the 'crotch' (dang); it is valued for being round and for being empty; it must not be clamped shut."

"The crotch must be round; round, then steady."

"The two thigh-roots must open the crotch; the opening does not lie in its size—even the faintest sliver counts as open, for the moment the mind-and-intent opens, the crotch is open. One who cannot open the crotch: though his legs be split three feet wide, if it is not open, it is still not open. Herein the student must ponder with care."

"The crotch indeed must open, yet Huiyin must be empty and the lower belly must be solid."

"The crotch braced round, emptily closing together. …(when holding a posture, the left and right foot) in the method of silk-reeling energy, from the toes it winds spirally upward from inside outward to the thigh-root, and to Huiyin, …If it does not join at Huiyin, there is no crotch energy, and it cannot brace round; this silk-reeling energy must not be departed from."

"Lower the waist energy, the tailbone slightly turns up, and the crotch energy naturally closes together."

"The crotch especially must be empty; empty, then all turns are nimble."

"The turbid qi descends, the crotch energy closes together."

"The lower plate is steady, and the upper plate is likewise nimble."

"The buttock-bones turn up, the front crotch closes together, and the rear buttocks naturally turn up."

"The tailbone, the Huantiao points, and the muscles spring up; the inner thigh-roots brace open, and the crotch opens of itself; the two knees close together, and the crotch is naturally round."

"In the middle the crotch opens round; it must be empty, and must not splay like the character for "person" (a splayed shape)."

"If the hip-bones do not float up, then the front crotch cannot close and hold its energy."

"The flesh of the two buttocks must float upward; if it does not float up, the front crotch cannot close together. The soft part below the ribs is the waist; if the waist energy cannot be kneaded down, then knees and feet lack power. The tailbone, the Huantiao points, and the inner bones must join inward; if they do not join, the two thighs lose their cohesion and scatter."

"If the top energy leads too much, the upper part hangs suspended; if it cannot lead up, it topples—this is failing to lower the waist energy and the crotch energy, so that the body loses its own mastery."

· 313 · "When the crotch energy and the waist energy are both well lowered, but the buttocks do not float up, not only can the front crotch not close, but even the upper body cannot close and hold; if above and below cannot hold their energy closed, then the soles of the feet lack power, and any external thing can push me over."

12. Feet

"The thousand changes and ten thousand transformations are moved by me; the two feet of the lower body fix the foundation."

"In performing the 'hammer-fist' posture: the left and right feet planted on the ground, steady as a mountain on the earth, unable to be shaken—then there is power."

"If the feet are steady, the body cannot be shaken."

"Front, back, left, right—apply energy evenly and steadily, and one naturally stands firm."

"The emptiness or solidity of the feet follows the hands: if the hand is empty, the foot is also empty; if the hand is solid, the foot is also solid."

"A solid foot must be planted level and firm on the ground with force at both front and back of the sole, while the Yongquan point must be empty."

"Though above one relies on the hands, below one relies especially on the feet; when the feet are swift, the hands' swiftness shows all the more."

"The kidney stores the will; let the feet follow the will, and likewise follow the turning circle."

"The feet move with the hands, circling as if divine."

"After the qi of the hand has traveled fully to the feet, then the big toe joins as one with the hand; at this moment only may one plant firmly."

"Apply the art of 'drawing in and counter-striking' within the movements of hands and feet."

"As for the movement of hands and feet, it is nothing but a circle—there is never straight going or straight returning."

"The transverse qi of the diaphragm is discharged down to the soles of the feet."

"Though the energy starts from the heel, its use lies fundamentally in the mind."

"A single spirit-spark rises from the mind, going up into the blue sky and down into the earth; this qi moves within the hands and feet, neither hard nor soft, naturally at ease."

"'Cloud Hands': the two feet turn alternately, the mechanism never pausing. The left foot steps out sideways; the right foot follows, and although it also steps out sideways, the right foot, as it nears the edge of the left foot, turns back from above another five or six inches before it lands—only thus is the movement seen to have no straight step. Each time the left foot steps out, the right foot follows it, all · 314 · is so. …For instance, when the right hand turns a forward silk-reeling circle, in the first half-circle the central qi winds obliquely from within the armpit outward to the fingers; in the second half-circle it returns from outside, the energy winding obliquely from outside to beneath the armpit. The left hand is likewise. As for the feet: when the right foot turns the first half-circle, it winds from within the thigh-root outward to the toes; returning, it winds from outside inward to the thigh-root. The left foot is likewise."

"When the foot steps out, it is as if there were a deep abyss before it; when told to return, it returns at once—supremely empty, supremely nimble."

"The movement of the foot is extremely winding and never straight, and it can also move with the hand, never losing the screw energy."

"The harder the foot stomps, the higher the body rises."

"If one does not stomp, then never mind; but if one stomps, it must make the opponent fall."

"As for the feet: when [the attack] comes from the left, sway left; from the right, sway right; use kicking to guard the front, stomping to guard the rear; raising the foot is like a sudden thunderclap too quick to cover the ears. Whenever an enemy invades my lower body, the feet accomplish the most—great indeed is the use of the feet!"

"When about to kick, see whether it can be kicked, then kick; if it cannot be kicked, do not kick—one must not recklessly use the kick. Even when an opening can be seized, a kick is valued for its divine speed, not for its slowness; it is valued for kicking the closing acupoints, not for kicking broad buttocks and thick flesh where it is neither painful nor itchy. This is the essential secret; the kicker must know it."

"Kicking with the foot and striking with the fist is a low-grade boxing; where does the master not blend [all] into one?"

"The four limbs and hundred bones govern movement, but in truth it is the step that carries them out; the step is the foundation of the whole body and the pivot of movement. …The hammer-fist is judged by its posture, yet what grasps the essentials is the step; whether one is lively or not lies in the step, whether one is nimble or not also lies in the step—great indeed is the use of the step."

13. Joints (Bone-Joints)

"The joints loosen and open."

"Skin and flesh, sinews and joints—let every place open and stretch."

"Let the whole body together close and hold its energy, and moreover let each joint of the whole body correspond and join each to each, as the hand does with the foot."

"When we speak of closing, the whole body closing together is what is good; as for the body's joints—such as the left and right elbow, the left and right shoulder, above and below—where the names correspond, each and all must close together appropriately."

· 315 · "Hand and foot, elbow and knee, shoulder and hip—above and below, left and right, front and back—when revolving and when halting a posture, each also must respond and align; when one opens, all open; when one closes, all close."

"The joints must be matched; if not matched, there is no power."

"The joints sound in unison."

V. Discourse on Push-Hands (Rushou)

1. A Compilation of Discourses on Push-Hands

"Adhere, connect, stick, follow; gather spirit and concentrate essence; exercise my empty nimbleness, and make it all the more whole and weighty. …Fine and smooth, pressed close; the middle holds the balance, the rear carries the power."

"Neither approach nor depart, neither stick nor slip away; join bone to bone as a tenon to its mortise—ponder it with care."

"Qian is hard, Kun is soft; yin and yang used together; neither leaning nor tilting, neither excess nor deficiency."

"Neither first nor last, meeting and sending off in due measure; front and back, left and right, above and the four sides—turning and joining with nimbleness; the slow and the urgent are each given their due."

"By spirit one knows what comes; by wisdom one stores what has gone."

"The two hands turn like the whorls of a screw, one up one down, most even; it all depends on the true secret of Taiji—four ounces deflect eight thousand catties."

"When the central qi is full, above all avoid advancing first; taste lightly and lead; be still, awaiting movement."

"Closing and opening, movement and stillness, the soft and the hard; bending and extending, coming and going, advance and retreat, survival and ruin. One opening, one closing—there is change and there is constancy; empty and solid both attained, now appearing, now hidden. Hardness and compliance each half; drawing in and advancing, subtle and complete; now gathering, now releasing, now loosening, now stretching."

"Inwardly, discuss with a sincere mind; outwardly, with the qi of softness and compliance, lead the opponent onward—thus the hard qi lies hidden within the soft."

"When I engage the opponent, it is purely with the qi of harmonious blending that I lead him forward."

"One must not use hard qi, nor may one be too soft—fold to the middle and that is all."

"Again: half drawing in, half advancing; leading while advancing; drawing in and at once advancing; taking drawing-in as advancing—yin and yang · 316 · "are used together as one—this is what is meant by: the Way moves in parallel without conflict. Unless yin and yang unite in virtue, one cannot have the mind-mechanism move and the hand arrive at once—faster than this there is none."

"As for the method of half drawing-in and half advancing: above the elbow, draw him to advance; below the hand, send energy forward to advance. The back of the arm is yang, the inside is yin—so this is the method of yang drawing and yin advancing; unless they are mutually each other's root, it cannot be done."

"When the hand uses drawing-in energy to draw aside the opponent's hand, one must use silk-reeling energy to draw it, causing his stance to become unsteady."

"Who understands that within extension lies bending? Rare is the one who knows that within bending lies extension."

"Slowly drawing him in, men do not understand; gradually halting, the intent grows deep of itself; the right is solid, the left is empty, hiding a sudden strike; lifting above and striking below conceals release and capture."

"Drawing in first, then advancing—who recognizes it? Taiji circles round in one full revolution."

"Drawing him in and letting him fall into emptiness is foremost of all."

"When the enemy comes with his hand, I draw with my hand—drawing and striking at once; it is not striking after having first drawn. Herein is fully proven the truth that yin and yang are each other's root."

"The energy of drawing-in cannot be fully told; in one yin and one yang, watch within the hand. The true principle is: to press down, first raise up; striking a man does not lie in seizing the first whip."

"When two hands engage, I guard my own territory, neither servile nor overbearing, through nine turns of a sheep's gut; I must not yield the slightest—if I yield to another, he stands and I fall. Press the contest urgently; if you can go up, do not go down; seize one extra part, and I hold the advantage of position."

"Coming, one should listen truly; going, one values divine speed."

"Supremely swift, supremely fast—coiling and whirling round."

"Power is valued for swift issuance, the mechanism for divine speed; one delay and you lose, one swift rush and you gain the advantage."

"Advance like a fierce wind blowing a man down, like lightning flashing fiercely—the faster the better."

"Issuing the hand must be quick; if not quick, it is delayed and missed. Striking the hand must be ruthless; if not ruthless, it does not succeed."

"The momentum is like the hand pushing over a mountain, wishing to make it topple... Lead the top energy well, lower the waist energy well, brace the crotch energy round, plant the soles of the feet firmly with force, use the arm's strength up into the palm, and the whole body's strength altogether · 317 · rests upon the left and right palms; in pushing, power is valued for divine speed. Even if one cannot push him over, one can still make him retreat several paces."

"A man comes to affect me, unwilling to lightly let me go; when I affect a man, how could I be willing to lightly let him go? The momentum must reach the point of using the whole body's strength, wishing to push with the force that topples a mountain."

"This body's strength must be united as one, and one must moreover keep the mind on the region of the spine."

"Refine yourself into the Vajra, the Taiji worthy one; the whole body together applies a thousand catties of force."

"Yet it is not merely done by making the qi great; rather it is truly by the central and upright original qi revolving and pressing, so that he cannot but retreat—and moreover by applying the art of drawing-in and counter-striking within the hands and feet, so that he cannot come near my body."

"When mind, hand, eye, and foot are one qi, the enemy's being captured by me is foreordained."

"When the hard is lodged within the soft, men find it hard to guard against."

"Empty encirclement and feigned enticement—all for the sake of one turn."

"A sudden turn—men do not understand it."

"Turning to draw in, turning to strike... a single stretch of spirit-movement."

"To be hard, first be soft; to raise up, first press down; the qi of great harmony lies hidden, undifferentiated, within."

"The central qi moves within the mind; once issued, none can compare in venom; how much more when one advances like the wind—who can match such swiftness? The bodily frame is as other men's; the method of use is mine alone. It is not that there is some other secret—only that the central qi is full."

"Only rely on attaining the whole body's empty nimbleness; a single strand of central qi rises with the momentum."

"Boxing (quan) means weighing (quan). It is that by which one weighs things and knows their light and heavy. Yet its principle is truly rooted in Taiji, and its use is not confined to the two fists; moreover, in a man's single body, the whole body above and below is Taiji—that is, the whole body above and below is 'boxing'; one must not regard a single fist as 'boxing'."

"Eye-power and hand-method together with body-method—wherever it sticks, there it moves."

"When spirit and essence gather round the whole body, one is strong; turning heaven and reversing earth lies within the hand."

"After long practice one becomes nimble, and that nimbleness is beyond compare; whatever one touches, one knows; naturally there is response—neither approaching nor departing, adhering, connecting, sticking, following; like a fly fallen on glue, though it have wings it cannot fly. The subtlety herein is finer than · 318 · is subtle."

"If one's skill is mature, from the circle that is great beyond all outside, one builds up to the realm that is small beyond all within. If one does not meet an enemy, then so be it; but if one meets a strong foe, then the inner energy bursts out suddenly, like a swift thunderbolt and fierce wind snapping withered wood and rotting reeds—who can withstand it!"

"Capture at once, release at once—the silk-reeling energy; herein one must grasp the heavenly mechanism."

"Question: What use is the silk-reeling energy in practicing the boxing? Answer: One who meets hardness directly is easily dodged and easily escaped from; but if one receives with softness, then the other is easily made soft and has no fear in his heart—because he has no fear, he does not dodge. Only by receiving him with the soft silk-reeling method: if one has not yet stuck to his body, never mind; but if one has stuck to his body, then he cannot dodge. If he dodges, follow with the hand, like lacquer-glue sticking to a hard object—the object cannot dodge of itself. If he withdraws, use the winding method to wind around his arm, like a spider winding a fly with silk, or like a screw already driven in—try to pull it out by force and you cannot. Therefore, before sticking to a man's arm, never mind; but once stuck, then I use the silk-reeling method to twist and hold his flesh, and as it winds I coil it, adhere to it, connect with it, stick to it, follow it, so that he cannot advance when he would advance—if he advances he falls into the pit; and cannot retreat when he would retreat—if he retreats he fears my counter-strike, and so does not dare to break away by force. This silk-reeling energy is the most essential secret within the boxing."

"When one has reached completion, however the enemy comes, so one responds—without waiting for thought, there is naturally a method. …But wherever it sticks, there use that place (this is the scenery of one's own place—the hardest of the hard) to draw and strike him; whatever the timing, all is fitting, indescribably wonderful—truly attaining without thinking, hitting the mark without effort. Yet one who has not completed [the training] cannot do this."

"Question: When is one to be reckoned as accomplished? Answer: The levels herein are infinite, and to the end of life one does not exhaust them. But speaking in rough terms of what lies before one's eyes: great accomplishment takes nine years, small accomplishment takes seven years; as for the refinement and subtlety, it too is a study one does not exhaust in a lifetime."

"The one who closes first is struck by closing; the one who opens afterward is struck by opening. Wherever hand and foot are, there is no time that is not a time of turning circles, and thus no place that is not a place for striking a man. …How could I have the mind to strike a man! I simply practice my own boxing, doing nothing [deliberately] and that is all. When the boxing reaches this, the art is more than half [mastered]."

· 319 · "The masters of boxing created the method of silk-reeling energy, silently moving the unceasing spiral line of heaven and earth, cycling without end, divinely wondrous in all things—it reaches the very decree of life! Can it be [merely] a skill?"

2. The Sixteen Items of Push-Hands

(1) Compare (jiao)—to compare and measure superior and inferior.

(2) Contact (jie)—the two men's hands come into contact.

(3) Adhere (zhan)—hand adheres to hand, as in the line "adhere-clothes desires to dampen the apricot-blossom rain."

(4) Stick (nian)—like the sticking of glue and lacquer; once the man has stuck to my hand, he cannot leave.

(5) Follow-cause (yin)—to follow-cause is to follow the other's coming.

(6) Rely (yi)—to rely is for me to lean upon the other's body.

(7) Connect (lian)—hand connects continuously with hand.

(8) Follow (sui)—to follow the other's momentum in advancing and retreating.

(9) Draw (yin)—to entice him to come, drawing and pulling him near to me.

(10) Advance (jin)—to make the man advance, not letting him escape.

(11) Fall (luo)—as in "the completion of a building" (luocheng); eaves-water dripping down to the ground; or as a leaf falling to the ground.

(12) Empty (kong)—should be read in the departing tone; when a man comes wishing to strike my body, he falls into an empty, void place.

(13) Gain (de)—I gain the mechanism and gain the advantage.

(14) Strike (da)—when mechanism and advantage permit striking, strike at the opportunity.

(15) Swift (ji)—swift and swifter still; the least delay and one cannot strike—the mechanism is valued for its divine speed.

(16) Decisive (duan)—decisive judgment; once hesitation enters, the opportunity is lost, and past this one cannot strike.

3. The Thirty-Six Faults of Push-Hands

· 320 · (1) Drawing back (chou — chou means that one cannot gain the advantage in advancing, knowing oneself to be about to be defeated, one wishes to draw the body back)

(2) Pulling out (ba — ba means to pull out, to pull back and flee)

(3) Screening (zhe — zhe means to screen a man with the hand)

(4) Propping (jia — jia means to prop up a man's hand with the arm)

(5) Knocking-striking (keda — keda is like striking one thing with another)

(6) Fierce ramming (mengzhuang — mengzhuang means to ram forward suddenly, coming rashly, relying on brave force to ram hard forward; it does not arise from naturalness, but seeks to seize victory rashly)

(7) Dodging and evading (duoshan — duoshan means to dodge a man's hand with the body, wishing by the feint to trip him)

(8) Encroaching and oppressing (qinling — qinling means wishing to enter a man's territory and oppress him)

(9) Slashing (che — like chopping a thing with a knife)

(10) Grasping-in (lou — lou means to grasp a man's body with the hand)

(11) Striking down (dao — dao means to strike the hand downward)

(12) Rubbing (cuo — cuo is like the rubbing of two hands together; to rub the enemy with the hand and elbow)

(13) Bullying and pressing (qiya — qi is to fool a man; ya is to press down a man's hand hard with my hand)

(14) Hanging (gua — gua means to hang a man with the palm of the hand, or to hook a man with the bent foot)

(15) Separating (li — li means to leave a man's body, lest he strike me)

(16) Feinting (shanzhuan — shanzhuan means to deceive and fool a man in order to strike him)

(17) Wrenching aside (bo — bo means to wrench a man aside hard with my hand)

(18) Pushing (tui — tui means to push aside with the hand)

(19) Awkwardness (jianshe — jianshe means the hand is not ripe and skilled)

(20) Crudeness (shengying — shengying means to fight relying on breath, with roughness, seeking to win)

(21) Shoving (pai — pai means to shove aside)

(22) Blocking (dang — dang means being unable to lead and so blocking hard with the hand)

(23) Stiffening (ting — ting means hard, rigid)

(24) Domineering (ba — ba means to domineer by force afterward, as a tyrant subdues men by force)

· 321 · (25) Soaring (teng — teng means, for example, receiving a man with the right hand and then propping his hand with the left, freeing the right hand to strike the enemy)

(26) Lifting (qie — qie means, for example, lifting a man by bearing against his joints)

(27) Straightness (zhi — zhi means being too blunt and direct, without the sense of winding and turning)

(28) Solidity (shi — shi means being simple and too honest, and so being cheated by others)

(29) Hooking (gou — gou means to hook and take with the foot)

(30) Flicking up (tiao — tiao means to flick from below upward)

(31) Propping hard (shuo — shuo means propping up a man's hand with hard breath, not receiving a man's hand with central breath)

(32) Resisting (di — di means stubbornly resisting a man with strength and force)

(33) Rolling (gun — gun means fearing to be hurt oneself and rolling over to one side, and also like a round object rolling away)

(34) Root-end cudgel (gentou gunzi — in root-end cudgel I grip the small end, and am struck with the big end)

(35) Stealing a blow (touda — touda means to strike a man without clear warning, stealing a blow where the man does not guard)

(36) Scattered mind (xintan — xintan means that one's skill cannot strike a man; the mind, like food, seeks and takes; in striking a man one is certain to fail)

The above thirty-six faults: some commit all of them, some commit four or five, some commit one or two; whoever commits any of them is not a finished hand. When the hand has reached completion, no matter what the fault, none at all is committed—because it is enriched with the great harmony and original breath, which is fundamentally without perversity. Then how shall one meet a hand? It is also said: "When a man brings his hand, I lead it with my hand and make it advance, so that he cannot strike with advantage; this is called 'yielding' (zou); zou is another name for leading. Why is it both called leading and called yielding? Leading means to lure him to advance; yielding means that when the man comes I go, not meeting his force head-on—this is called yielding. Yet within the yielding there naturally carries the energy of leading-in (one whose skill is pure leads him to advance; he dare not not advance, and if he advances, then I am smooth and the other is contrary, and the seizing and releasing are in my hands). This is the subtle secret in the boxing; without long practice it cannot be done.

Zhuang's note: The sixteen items of 'grabbing the hand' and the thirty-six faults of 'grabbing the hand' are the original manuscript text of Chen Xin's Illustrated Explanation of Chen-family Taijiquan. When Tang Hao, in January 1932, together with Chen Ziming, went to Chenjiagou to investigate the history of taijiquan, he picked out these two passages and included them in Chen Ziming's Chen-family Hereditary Taijiquan. Here, with reference to what is recorded in The Collected Chen-family Taijiquan, they have been collated and supplemented. (Gu Liuxin)

· 322 · 4. Two Songs of Grabbing the Hand In grabbing, rending, squeezing and pressing you must be earnest; lead in, drop into emptiness, and let the man invade as he will. With the whole body following, the enemy cannot come near; four ounces of yielding sets eight thousand catties in motion.

Strike above at the throat, below at the groin; in the middle, the two ribs and the pit of the stomach; below, the two shins and the two knees; one palm behind the back takes the true soul.

Note: The former song is an old transmitted Chen-family formula; as seen in the Chen-family Liangyitang manuscript boxing manual it reads: "In squeezing, grabbing, rending and pressing you must be earnest; upper and lower follow one another, and a man cannot enter. Let him come striking with giant force—pull four ounces and deflect a thousand catties." The text copied by Chen Ziming from another manuscript is titled "Formula of the Grabbing Hand" and has six lines: "In grabbing, rending, squeezing and pressing you must be earnest; with the whole body following, a man cannot enter. Let a man attack with giant force—pull four ounces and deflect a thousand catties. Lead in, drop into emptiness, and issue as they join; sticking, connecting, adhering and following, one bends and extends." What the three Chen-family texts record also differs in places from the manuscript hand-copied by Li Yiyu and revised by Wang Zongyue of the salt shop of Wuyang county. Xu Zhen's Record of Verification of Taijiquan says: "For in Chenjiagou it was at first only transmitted orally by ten mouths; in time it came to differ slightly, and each, according to what he heard, wrote it down, and so it could not all agree." This too is a conjectural statement: where four lines have variant readings and are expanded to six, it may likewise be judged a blemish of later men's revision of the text.

The second song is a method of fighting to the death, seen only in Chen Xin's writings; it may be that Chen Xin collected and recorded an old formula and appended it after the four old-transmitted lines.

Book page 299

Six. A Selection of Short Essays on Boxing by Chen Xin and Others

Six. A Selection of Short Essays on Boxing by Chen Xin and Others
1. Ode to Taijiquan (in five-character folk verse)

The principle of taiji cycles round; handed down, one counts not the years. Within it there is essential meaning; in movement and stillness there is no transgression. What is drawn in is called leading; what is sent out is an arrow leaving the string (of these two lines, the first speaks of leading in and dropping into emptiness, the second of seizing the moment to strike). The tiger and leopard crouch deep in the mountains; the dragon flies in the pool's abyss (the first line speaks of stillness, the second of movement). Opening and closing are fundamentally without fixity (lively and brimming); bending and extending—the forces are linked (yet there is a certain measure). Taiji divides into yin and yang; the spirit-dragon transforms without limit. Heaven and earth are its father and mother; in their friction, the soft and the hard. Generation upon generation is fundamentally unceasing; the orthodox and the strange are not as usual. Qian and Kun are as bellows; taiji is one great bag. The causes of fullness and emptiness, waxing and waning, are all hidden within it. At the end it returns again to the beginning; one breath moves in slackening and tautening, and gives form · 323 · It returns without trace; thing and self are both forgotten (united with the Way). In the middle road of taijiquan, skill comes first; advance in order without skipping grades, and every man will of himself accord with Heaven. Idle talk is all swollen ink; actual practice is the true exposition. The kite flies up to the sky; the fish leaps down into the abyss. Above and below are both true delight; the mastery lies in fine study. If you ask what is meant within, the principle is subtle and dark; coming and going like day and night; sun and moon shine in bright roundness. If you can grasp the true secret, this is taijiquan; all things are like this, not only in [the matter of] time. After returning to simplicity and plainness, one is simply a living immortal; wherever one is, one finds the self; the great uncarved block of itself completes the spirit (returning again to taiji).

2. Poems on the Silk-Reeling Method of Taijiquan

Ancient seven-character verse: three poems

Movement begets yang, stillness begets yin; one movement and one stillness are each other's root. If truly you know the delight within the ring, turning and turning you see the heavenly truth at will.

Yin and yang have no beginning and no end; coming and going, bending and extending, hold the workings of creation. If you truly penetrate the message within this, round turning is at will, moving the primal vastness.

A while of clarity, a while of confusion; the linked closing and opening depends on lifting and tearing. Only when the threefold flavor of the principle is threaded does it shine; the spirit-realm is a single pane of glass.

Ancient five-character verse

The realm of principle is fundamentally endless; it begins from gathering like ants in sincerity. Three years not peering into the garden; single-minded and spirit-concentrated. One should follow a good teacher, and also visit lofty friends. Everywhere observe the compass and square; one thread opens the spirit's brightness. One layer deeper than another; layer upon layer, the meaning is endless; one opening linked to one closing; opening and closing hand on to one another. Sometimes one leads in to the point of fascination; the work would stop but cannot. Constantly practice with earnest effort; daily one rises, evaporating of itself; once without obstruction, suddenly one awakens to the great void.

3. On the Silk-Reeling Energy in the Beginner's Primer of Taijiquan — Chen Xin Taijiquan is a method of winding. The winding method moves like the shape of a screw upon the skin. In ordinary practice one constantly uses this energy; therefore when crossing hands with a man, this energy naturally moves upon the skin, and one does not know it—without long practice in its Way it cannot be so. Its methods are: advancing winding, retreating winding; left winding, right winding; upper winding, lower winding; inner winding, outer winding; forward (shun) winding, reverse (ni) winding; large winding, small winding.

· 324 · —but all must be done with the central breath moving within it; leading is striking, striking is leading—all is the principle that yin and yang are each other's root. Some take it for a soft hand; but how can a soft hand receive things and answer affairs? If one looks only at the outward signs, it seems not to fall short of hardness, and so it is taken for a soft hand. Its rules for the whole body: the crown-strength leads upward; the crotch-strength goes down (it must prop round, must close and hold); the two shoulders loosen downward; the two elbows sink down; the two hands close and hold; the chest closes forward; the eyes must not glance aside—take the hand in front as the target; the crown may not topple; in the chest, sink the mind and quiet the breath; the two knees close and hold strength; the waist-strength goes down; the two feet constantly use the hooking strength, and front and back must close and hold strength. As to the outward form, it is elegant as a maiden; one may not carry an arrogant air—a whole stretch of leisurely spirit; all is the model of great refinement. As for the hands, their weighing is all rooted in the mind; when things come, respond accordingly, and one naturally accords with the fitness of advance and retreat, slowness and urgency, lightness and heaviness. This is the taiji's yin and yang at rest with each other, without the least leaning, and it makes the wondrous use of opening and closing. Is its Way shallow and scant!

4. An Explanation of the Origins of Taijiquan — Chen Xin

Boxing is weighing; it is by it that one weighs things and knows their lightness and heaviness. Yet its principle is truly rooted in taiji, and its use does not leave the two fists. And in a man's one body, the whole body from top to bottom is taiji; that is, the whole body from top to bottom is boxing—one may not take a single fist as boxing.

Its pivot is in the one mind; the mind governs reverence and also governs stillness; if one can be reverent and still, one naturally preserves the empty spirit; when the heavenly lord holds sway, the hundred bones obey. Movement begets yang; stillness begets yin; one movement and one stillness are each other's root. Clear breath rises up; turbid breath descends down; the hundred-meetings point and the central pole—one body's bolt and key.

In the beginning of effort, first seek to submit and respond; the coming pulse turns at the gate, one breath begets another, hand and eye are alive, and one may not move rashly. As for its breath: it is utterly great and utterly firm; nourish it straight and it does no harm; it fills heaven and earth; matched with righteousness and the Way, it begins from gathering righteousness; vast and flowing, it is naturally one breath.

Light as willow catkins, firm as metal and stone; fierce as the tiger's might, swift as the eagle's soar. Moving, it is like the flow of water; resting, it equals the standing of a mountain. Advancing, one is beyond what a man can know; retreating, one is also beyond what a man can name for speed.

The principle is fine, the method dense; the order is analyzed thread by thread. Released, it fills the six directions; rolled up, it retreats and hides in secrecy. Its great has no outside; its small has no inside. The central harmony and original breath follow wherever the mind goes; whither the mind inclines, · 325 · Concentrate the whole spirit. In transformation like a dragon, no man can fathom it; the use lies in the mind—this is the true secret.

Neither leaning nor tilting, without excess or deficiency; inwardly to cultivate the self, outwardly to subdue the enemy. Meet the moment and suit the measure, only because one is unhurried and ample. Neither close nor apart, neither sticking nor leaving; joining bone to joint; with careful pondering, and long accumulated strength, one ascends the hall and enters the chamber.

5. The Substance and Function of Taijiquan

The Substance of Taijiquan

The Way of taijiquan is exhausted by the two words 'opening' and 'closing'; the one yin and one yang is called boxing, and its wonder lies wholly in each being the other's root.

The Function of Taijiquan

In the movement of boxing there is only the soft and the firm; when the other comes with firmness, I go with softness; when the other comes with softness, it all lies in weighing and measuring (taking my hand to weigh and hold a man's hand, as a balance weighs a thing; taking my mind to measure a man's mind, weighing whether he is up or down, fast or slow, or changes his opportunity halfway). Within firmness lodges softness, and one is not matched with the man; within softness lodges firmness, which a man finds hard to guard against. The use lies in the mind; neither vaunting nor displaying; when there is a master within, one does not give way to wildness; responding to the moment and changing accordingly, one is never alarmed.

6. A General Discussion of Taijiquan and the Boxing Classic

One. General Discussion

Pure yin without yang is a soft hand; pure yang without yin is a hard hand. One yin and nine yang is a root-end cudgel; two yin and eight yang is a scattered hand; three yin and seven yang still feels hard; four yin and six yang clearly shows a good hand; only five yin together with five yang, yin and yang without leaning, is called a wondrous hand. In the wondrous hand, each touch is one taiji; the empty emptiness of traces transforms and returns to nothingness.

Two. The Boxing Classic

Taiji is yin and yang, with softness and with firmness; within firmness lodges softness; within softness lodges firmness; firmness and softness aid each other, and transform without limit.

7. Chen Fuyuan's Discussion of Taijiquan — Chen Ziming

My late honored father, whose given name was Fuyuan and whose style was Xuchu, first studied under Gengyun Gong, and after his skill was complete studied again under Zhongshen · 326 · The duke practised the new frame, and so his issuing hand could be soft as silk and firm as steel; going and coming beyond the passes for several tens of years, he never met a rival. When Ziming was small he attended at his side and habitually heard the principles of boxing; here, from what he remembers, he writes down one or two things to make this piece. Dull and narrow as I am, I cannot express one ten-thousandth of it.

Opening and Closing, and Yin and Yang

Movement is yang, stillness is yin; one movement and one stillness—this is opening and closing. Yin changing to yang is opening; yang changing to yin is closing. This is spoken with regard to the whole body of taijiquan. With regard to movement and transformation: when the left hand leads the left half of the body to move and transform toward the left, the opening is greater-yang (taiyang), and the closing is greater-yin (taiyin). When the right hand follows it and opens, that is lesser-yang (shaoyang); closing is lesser-yin (shaoyin); the right side is likewise so. Firmness and softness are contained within this, and so taiji gives birth to the two modes, and the two modes give birth to the four images. The two modes are yin and yang, which is also opening and closing. The four images are greater-yang, greater-yin, lesser-yang and lesser-yin. Yin and yang, opening and closing, transform and beget one another; attaining their utmost, they are the undifferentiated one breath, cycling without end, changing beyond fathoming. Therefore one who does not understand yin and yang, opening and closing, does not understand how firmness and softness, movement and stillness, are each other's use; leaning to firmness or leaning to softness, unable to aid each other, he departs far from the root of taijiquan. And my teacher Master Pinsan said: "The Way of practising boxing is exhausted by the two words 'opening' and 'closing'; the one yin and one yang is called boxing, and its wonder lies only in each being the other's root." He also made two seven-character poems. The first says: "Movement begets yang, stillness begets yin; one movement and one stillness are each other's root. If truly you can know the delight within the ring, turning and turning you see the heavenly truth at will." The second says: "Yin and yang have neither beginning nor end; coming and going, bending and extending, hold the workings of creation. If you truly penetrate the message within this, taiji lies only within one ring."

Movement-Transformation and Turning the Gate

Movement-transformation is the prior mechanism of turning the gate. The gate is the joints of a man's whole body, and so turning the gate is also called turning the joints. All beginners mostly esteem clumsy force and lack the spirit-energy; therefore by movement-transformation one removes their stagnant breath, and makes the turning of the gate reach empty spirit. For if empty, one has whereby to gather; if spirit, one has whereby to respond. The empty gathers; the spirit senses. The gathering is stillness; the sensing is movement. Rising and falling, revolving and turning, opening and closing, changing—none can depart from movement-transformation and turning the gate. What is called movement-transformation and turning the gate is going from softening the sinews and enlivening the joints to fitting bone to joint-mortise (pronounced sun). If one does not know this, one is not fit to speak of the empty spirit of movement and stillness.

· 327 · Empty and Full In the instant of movement and stillness in taijiquan, there is nowhere without empty and full. Therefore in its practice method, in advancing forward, retiring back, turning left, revolving right, raising the foot is empty, and setting the foot down is full; turning left, the left is full; turning right, the right is full; advancing, the rear is empty; retiring, the front is empty. If one is careless and does not distinguish empty and full, one is sure to commit the fault of pulling the foot and dragging the leg. Seek it in refinement, and each place has its own empty and full. In practice it is so; when facing an enemy it is likewise so: when he is empty I am full; when he is full I am empty; when he is empty, fill it; when he is full, empty it. Facing the enemy and seizing the moment, by no means cling rigidly to fixed methods—this is to attain the essential meaning.

Change and Transformation

As for change and transformation: there is the change of one hand, the change of one move, the change of one posture. Yet no matter whether one hand, one move or one posture, its changing and transforming all proceeds from the simple gradually to the detailed and dense. Taking opening and closing as the change of one hand, and turning the gate as the change of one move—this is the meaning of sending up and joining down. Only the body method and the step method—revolving, turning, tightening, gathering—and changes of direction belong to the change of one posture. From expansion to tightening, by no means overstep the bounds or disorder the sequence; then of oneself one can accumulate hands into moves, join moves into postures, and link postures into sets.
