At the beginning of practice one seems to feel boundaries; after long practice, when the skill is ripe, one can of oneself suddenly penetrate through, moving and turning freely; a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, following the heart's desire.

Steps and Stages

The ancient sages said: "Things have root and branch; affairs have end and beginning. Know what is first and what is after, and one draws near the Way." If there is no distinction of shallow and deep, no order of first and after, then one loses the root; no matter how strong the teacher's ability, the student certainly cannot make his art surpass the crowd. Therefore the steps of practising taijiquan have three levels of skill: the first step—when learning, one should be slow, but slow must not become dullness; the second step—after practising, then be fast, but fast must not become disorder; the third step—after being fast, return again to slowness; this is softness, and when softness is long, firmness is of itself within it—this is firmness and softness aiding each other. The teacher must teach by this, and the student must learn by this; then one may be nearly without error.

· 328 · For one who practises taijiquan, though the slower and the softer the better, and one should not use force or carry breath, one must also know at what point one may change the energy, and at what point slowness may become swiftness and softness, and at what point it may become firmness. This concerns the responsibility of instruction; one should explain its beginning through to its end, and then put it into practice in method, so that the order of its use is easily known and it becomes the stairway for entering the gate. If one can set the progress in advance and issue it according to the person, making the learner's spirit shine and his interest arise all around, he will surely easily find the path, and advance swiftly.

The Opening and Closing of the Waist and Crotch

The practitioner of taijiquan cannot but know the key points of the two parts, waist and crotch; in each opening and closing, each movement and stillness, the waist and crotch each have their own focus, and it is prized that they be used together; therefore they should be analyzed clearly.

The key points of the waist are: wringing the waist, enlivening the waist, collapsing the waist.

The key points of the crotch are: loosening the crotch, closing the crotch, buckling the crotch.

When wringing the waist, the crotch must buckle; if it does not buckle, it scatters. When enlivening the waist, the crotch must loosen; if it does not loosen, it stagnates. When collapsing the waist, the crotch must close; if it does not close, it floats.

Generally, collapsing the waist and enlivening the crotch is storing energy; enlivening the waist and loosening the crotch is soft energy. Only when issuing energy must one buckle the crotch and wring the waist.

Here we explain by the various postures and moves: for example, among the boxing postures, Cover-Hand Punch, Drape-Body Punch, Green Dragon Emerges from Water, Peep Fist beneath the Elbow, Flash through the Back, Green Dragon Plays in Water, Two-Risings, Kick One Foot, Stamp One Heel, Small Capture, Embrace-Head Push Mountain, Forward Trick, Backward Trick, Wild Horse Parts its Mane, Jade Girl Works the Shuttle, Swing Foot Fall-Fork, Cross Foot, Point-at-Crotch Punch, Green Dragon Stirs Water, Swing Foot, Cannon-Facing-Head, and so on—all belong to buckling the crotch and wringing the waist. Buddha's Warrior Pounds the Mortar, Lazily Tuck the Robe, Single Whip, White Crane Spreads its Wings, Brush Knee and Twist Step, and the Closing Posture, Joining Posture, and so on—all belong to loosening the crotch and enlivening the waist.

Generally, when a boxing posture is completed, the crotch should close and the waist should collapse; its meaning is chiefly stillness; that is, when this move has stopped and the next move has not yet begun, the empty-spirit energy is stored within in advance, and when movement comes it must surely change and surely issue—hence its efficacy is boundless. Its time and the direction it tends cannot be fixed in advance: meeting left, it responds left; meeting right, it responds right; up and down, front and back, firm and soft, slow and urgent, light and heavy—it knows them all.

· 329 · The Circle of Taijiquan I heard from my late father that in the skill of taijiquan, having no circle is the summit of attainment; it cannot be reached in one step. One must advance in order: from the large circle contract to the small circle, from the small circle contract to no circle, and then take the inner energy as its commander, linking and threading the changes; when the use is wondrous and the skill reaches this, in form there is no longer any way to seize hold of it.

8. The Key Points of Taijiquan — Chen Ziming

On the basis of my father's and teacher's words I have made three essays on the essentials of taijiquan; and fearing that beginners may not grasp their main points, I do not shrink from repetition, and respectfully set out the key points as a reference for those who first study it.

1. Nature: As for the nature of taijiquan, though my teacher Pinsan said, "Within firmness lodges softness; within softness lodges firmness; firmness and softness aid each other, transforming without limit"—this speaks of the skill when one is a finished hand. The beginner should take natural softness and liveliness as the main thing; softness should be loose, liveliness should be led. If soft but not loose, lively but not led, then it is not natural—how can one bring about firmness and hardness in the future?

2. Method: As for the method of taijiquan, its most essential is the eight characters: "empty and full, opening and closing, rising and falling, revolving and turning." The beginner should distinguish them clearly.

3. Order: The order of practising taijiquan must be: first slow then fast; after fast, again slow; first soft then firm; only then can firmness and softness aid each other.

4. Posture: The frame at the moment when movement stops is called the posture. The key points of taijiquan posture are nothing beyond: the hand leads and the eye follows; the body is upright and the step steady; the shoulders level and the body joined; and one must especially attend to the energy of the two parts, crown and crotch, not letting there be any loss—otherwise one will surely bring about the faults of top-heavy and bottom-light, the whole body askew, and unsteady standing in profusion.

5. Movement: In the movement and stillness, the making of postures in taijiquan, one purely follows nature; the movement and transformation are nimble, cycling without end. One must know that its empty and full, opening and closing, rising and falling, revolving and turning all come from the round form. In first entering the gate, take the large circle as the method: at first softening the sinews and enlivening the joints; advancing, fitting bone to joint-mortise. If the student truly understands this, with the body acting and the mind pondering, morning and evening, seeking it in refinement, his progress will of itself be swift.

6. Breathing: Regulating the breath with breathing is enough to develop the lungs; if after the morning breathing one practises · 330 · …practise the boxing art, or if during boxing practice one has a fitting breath, regulating the breath by exhaling and inhaling along with the movement and stillness, then the muscles and the lungs will surely develop at the same time, and one will naturally have no affliction of weak lungs.

7. Spirit: The spirit of taijiquan takes empty spirit as its utmost; the beginner certainly cannot reach this realm, yet if he can hold to the key points set out, and cleave to them without letting go, in time the water will arrive and the channel be formed.

8. The whole body following: when the four limbs and hundred bones move in concert, this is called the whole body following; therefore in taijiquan, when one thing moves, nothing is unmoved; when one thing is still, nothing is unstilled.

9. Changing the move and turning the posture: In taijiquan, "changing the move" and "turning the posture" originally belong to two explanations. (One) When the previous move has stopped and the next move has not yet been made, the movement between them forms a posture and is called "changing the move"—for example, the right closing form after the pull-down of Lazily Tuck the Robe, and again the right gathering form after the pull-down of Brush Knee and Twist Step, and the two left gathering forms before Wild Horse Parts its Mane and Jade Girl Works the Shuttle—all are "changing the move." (Two) The one movement between when this move stops and the next move is to be made is called "turning the posture"—for example, the left turn after Single Whip, and again the right turn after Cover-Hand Punch, and the like—all belong to "turning the posture," and all must be distinguished clearly.

10. The body acts, the mind ponders: The proverb says, "The mouth recites, the mind ponders." If reading books is so, how much more practising the martial art? Therefore to act with the body and ponder with the mind is one of the methods that most easily makes a man progress. In the body-acting and mind-pondering of taijiquan, the most essential is this: the body should act its roundness and liveliness; the mind should ponder its empty spirit.

11. Neither greed nor rashness: In practising taijiquan the greatest taboo is greed for much, and one must especially guard against rash movement. In all application and posture one must seek correctness; then after practice is complete one will not commit faults, and refined progress will of itself be easy. One who is greedy and rash rarely achieves anything; this fault is hard for nine beginners in ten to avoid—be careful to attend to it.

(The above two essays are excerpted from Chen-family Hereditary Taijiquan by Chen Ziming, Shanghai edition, 1932.)

A classic masterwork handed down through the generations — Yang-style Taijiquan

Yang-style Taijiquan is one of the traditional schools of Taijiquan, developed and created by Yang Lukchan (1799–1872) — a native of Yongnian, Hebei — together with his son Yang Jianhou (1839–1917) and his grandson Yang Chengfu (1883–1936), building upon the Old Frame of Chen-style Taijiquan. The Yang-style form is relaxed and uncluttered, the body method centred and upright, the movements harmonious, combining lightness with steadiness. In its practice method it proceeds from looseness into suppleness, with hardness and softness mutually assisting one another, simple and plain — and so it is deeply loved by the broad public and has spread extremely widely. The Yang-style frame has high, medium and low variations, which can be adjusted in amount of exercise according to the needs of different ages and different constitutions; thus it suits both those in good physical condition seeking to build fitness, and the physically weak seeking therapy and health preservation. This book was carefully written by Fu Zhongwen — former vice-chairman of the Shanghai Wushu Association, one of China's Hundred Outstanding Wushu Figures, and a transmitter of Yang-style Taijiquan — together with his son Fu Shengyuan (National Wushu 8th Duan) and his grandson Fu Qingquan (National Wushu 6th Duan), on the foundation of many years of teaching practice. In its writing there are many new supplements to the essentials of the movements, such as the addition of the "deflecting" application in the usage notes. In the teaching method and practice method there are fairly detailed and innovative expositions — the progressive-increase method, the mnemonic formula method, the error-correction method, and so on — all of which have been tried out in teaching practice for many years with very notable results.

This book suits Taijiquan enthusiasts for study, and can also serve teachers in universities, secondary and primary schools, teachers' colleges, physical-education units and popular training classes for carrying out Taijiquan instruction.

Mr. Fu Zhongwen is a junior kinsman of Master Yang Chengfu of Yongnian, and received the master's transmission — in rules and standards he is not the slightest bit off. People call him an orthodox lineage of Taijiquan. He and Jianhua, and Yongnian, taught students at the Taiji Study Society without taking remuneration, and their achievements are very numerous. (Preface I, written by Xu Cai)

# Giving Chinese Martial Art a Worldwide Character

Book page 318

— In Praise of Three Generations of the Fu Family

— In Praise of Three Generations of the Fu Family

Grand Master Fu Shengyuan is the son of Fu Zhongwen, a master of his generation in Yang-style Taijiquan. Fu Zhongwen studied the Taiji art under Yang Chengfu, grandson of Yang Lukchan, founder of Yang-style Taijiquan, and won Master Yang's high regard; Yang had him attend at his side without ever leaving it, giving him instruction at all times. In later days Master Fu Zhongwen became a famous leading disciple of the master of his generation, Yang Chengfu.

In his youth Grand Master Fu Shengyuan absorbed the essence of Yang-style Taijiquan, and under his father's personal instruction practised assiduously; his Taiji skill reached the realm of purity and perfection, and he became the fifth-generation master and transmitter of Yang-style Taijiquan. Mr. Fu Qingquan received strict training from his grandfather and father from childhood; as a youth he took part many times as a professional athlete in domestic and overseas competitions and won championships, becoming the rising talent of this Taiji family. The two of them, father and son, have spread this art overseas, taking in a great number of students and disciples, and carried this great wealth of Chinese culture out to the countries of the world. Thanks to Master Fu's efforts, more and more people have gradually come to understand and take a liking to Taijiquan, and many people in every part of the world count it a joy to have the chance to become Master Fu's disciples and learn Taijiquan skill from him. Master Fu's spirit of dedication in spreading Chinese martial art to the world deserves to be honoured and praised.

(continued on the next page)

The world today has entered the information age. In this society filled with inexhaustible information and highly developed communications, people's outlooks are undergoing enormous change; in a sense the world has already become smaller and smaller, and time and distance no longer form an obstacle to exchange — which in turn has driven cultural exchange among people everywhere on earth, and thereby further advanced the spread of Taijiquan.

Chinese wushu has now become a common favourite of the peoples of the world. Taiji, as the martial art with the deepest cultural substance in Chinese wushu, has become one of the most valuable "gifts" offered to humanity, because of its function of strengthening the body and building health. It is especially suited to the middle-aged and elderly and to those extremely busy in their work, including a great many mental workers. It can be said with certainty that all those who practise Taijiquan may derive benefit from it.

The publication of The Authentic Lineage Yang-Style Taijiquan Coaching Method can, at a deeper level, provide Taijiquan enthusiasts with the experience and methods of teaching and practising. This book gives a detailed introduction to every movement, which is rare even among books of the Taijiquan kind. It is bound to become a good teacher and helpful friend to Taijiquan enthusiasts.

Grand Master Fu Shengyuan (Chinese Wushu 8th Duan) and his son Fu Qingquan (Chinese Wushu 6th Duan) have already effectively (Preface I, continued)

spread the art of Taijiquan, and we hope their enterprise achieves tremendous success! And may they continue to promote Taiji — this gem of Chinese culture — to the peoples of every country in the world, so that it may flourish and shine throughout the world!

Xu Cai

September 2000

Author of Preface I

Adviser, All-China Sports Federation

Honorary Chairman, Asian Wushu Federation

(Preface II, written by You Xuande)

# The Essential Meaning of Taiji Chinese kung fu has a long history, and has long enjoyed the reputation of "Wudang revered in the south, Shaolin esteemed in the north". Yet among Chinese martial arts the one that today flourishes in every part of the world and is most beloved by people is none other than the method of Taijiquan. At a time when the central government advocates fitness for all in service of society, I was delighted to hear that my martial nephew Qingquan has a work of three-generation true transmission — The Authentic Lineage Yang-Style Taijiquan Coaching Method — about to appear; at the request of my worthy elder brother Shengyuan, I write a preface for my martial nephew Qingquan's new work, to express my joy and congratulations.

The art of Taijiquan was created in the Song dynasty by the Perfected One Zhang Sanfeng of Mount Wudang in Hubei Province, and several hundred years have passed to the present day. Mount Wudang is a famous Daoist holy site and scenic resort of China. Its long cultural accumulation gave birth to the world-renowned Wudang school of martial arts, and its Taijiquan skill in particular is celebrated at home and abroad. The Wudang martial arts took disciples with extreme strictness through the ages; in the Qing dynasty Wudang martial arts passed from within the religion out to the common people, and so took shape the internal-family Taijiquan system — the Southern School represented by Zhang Songxi, the Northern School represented by Wang Zongyue. In the course of transmission the Taiji art further developed several schools, forming an exceedingly rich cultural and artistic treasure-house of Taiji art. And of those who spread the Taiji art throughout the world, none has rendered more distinguished service than the master of his generation, the elder Mr. Fu Zhongwen.

The elder Fu and I were friends despite the difference in our ages, so I have felt deeply his quality of lofty integrity, his bearing of a mind as open as a valley, his skill brought to the point of purity and perfection, and the majestic spirit that shook the martial world. In the Republican period, bouts between different schools occurred from time to time; and because the elder Fu's skill spread widely from north to south, there were many challengers too. Many boxers and famous hands, the instant they crossed hands, were thrown more than ten feet — and were left utterly mystified by the Taiji skill of looseness, sinking, roundness and liveliness; at the same time they were moved by the elder Fu's noble martial virtue, and there was no lack of those who took him as their master. After the founding of New China, the elder Fu received the State's care and commendation and won very high honours.

Qingquan is the grandson of the elder Fu by direct transmission; taught by the family's elders, he practised martial arts from childhood alongside his father (the famous martial artist and chairman of the World Yongnian Taijiquan Alliance, Mr. Fu Shengyuan), and for a long time accompanied his grandfather Fu Zhongwen to martial-arts gatherings in many places. As a youth he won the national Taijiquan championship — truly a tiger cub of a warrior house. Because Qingquan is naturally quick and bright, diligent and hard-working, he has now reached the age of thirty, and appears all the more spirited and vigorous — truly, the waves behind the Yangtze push on those before! Keeping in mind his grandfather's unfulfilled wish, Qingquan has spared no hardship in travelling at home and abroad to transmit the Taiji art, and today his students are everywhere. Many of the students he has taught have won major prizes in competitions in various regions, and China Central Television has even filmed a special instructional series with him. (Preface II, continued)

The appearance of The Authentic Lineage Yang-Style Taijiquan Coaching Method — whether one looks at the boxing theory or the boxing frame — leaves one feeling that eye and ear are made new; it does not lose the bearing of a great master, and for professional martial artists and amateur martial-arts enthusiasts alike it has high value for reference and for collecting. It is bound to become a celebrated work spanning the centuries. If the elder Mr. Fu Zhongwen has awareness in heaven, he too will surely feel deeply comforted and rest at peace in the Nine Springs. We cherish the memory of the master of his generation, Fu Zhongwen, and we hope all the more that Qingquan will compile a series of works, so that more people may learn the true skill of traditional Yang-style Taijiquan. As a transmitter of the boxing lineage within the Wudang school, and because I have long dwelt among the mountains and wilds, these few hurried words cannot exhaust the essential meaning of the book; I trust my colleagues in the martial world will discern this. This is my preface.

Author of Preface II

The Perfected One of the Grotto-Heaven, You Xuande

First month of the year 2000

(Preface, written by Fu Qingquan)

# Preface At the moment when the new century is about to arrive, our country stands in a great historical period in which politics, economy and culture are daily advancing and the people of every ethnic group live and work in peace; having largely satisfied their material needs, the broad masses urgently hope to master a scientific and simple method of fitness to preserve health of body and mind. At the same time, a nation's prosperity cannot be separated from the raising of its people's quality — including both physical quality and psychological quality. The aim of the fitness-for-all movement is to enable the greatest possible number of citizens to possess a strong physique and sound mind: and the most ideal method of popular fitness is none other than practising Taijiquan. Comrade Deng Xiaoping gave Taijiquan a high appraisal and wrote the inscription "Taijiquan is good!" — which fully embodies the long-standing attention paid by Party and State leaders to fitness for all and to traditional martial arts.

Taijiquan, as a science of movement and an art of bodily form, is a representative of our country's excellent traditional martial-arts culture, and a great contribution of the Chinese nation to the whole world. It can strengthen the body and build health, calm the spirit and nourish the brain; it can also cultivate the self and nurture the nature, and refine sentiment — and it contains, moreover, a rich cultural foundation and philosophical substance. Taijiquan has truly achieved the state of being enjoyed by both refined and popular tastes and suited to young and old alike; it has long been deeply loved by the people, and has already been spread throughout the world. In the course of its transmission Taijiquan developed and gave rise to many schools; among them the Yang style has all along been the most widely transmitted, and after Liberation it was taken by the National Sports Commission as the basis and adapted into competition routines more times than any other Taijiquan school.

My grandfather began at the age of nine to learn boxing by following the third-generation transmitter of Yang-style Taijiquan, Patriarch Yang Chengfu, and continued until his death in 1994 at the advanced age of ninety-one, devoting the energy of his whole life to the development and transmission of Yang-style Taijiquan, and winning the broad respect and affection of Taijiquan enthusiasts at home and abroad. My father likewise began at nine to learn boxing by following my grandfather, and before Liberation assisted him in promoting Yang-style Taijiquan. After the founding of New China he taught for more than thirty years as a professional martial-arts coach. After retiring he was invited to Australia, Europe and America and many other countries to spread Yang-style Taijiquan, and though he is now in his seventies he still spares no hardship in travelling the world, introducing orthodox Yang-style Taijiquan abroad, letting more foreign friends understand and take a liking to China's Taiji art, and contributing to friendly exchange between our country and others and to building our country's good international image. From the age of six I practised boxing with my grandfather and father, receiving formal martial-arts training from childhood. In the 1980s I became a professional martial-arts athlete, and represented the Shanghai team and the national team many times in domestic and international martial-arts competitions, achieving good results. Afterwards I too taught boxing at home and abroad for many years, and formed a set of teaching methods with distinctive characteristics. We, grandfather, son and grandson of three generations, are most willing to offer up without reservation the authentic Yang-style Taijiquan of our family transmission — better, more clearly and more accurately — to society, and to live up to the earnest expectations of the broad community of Taiji lovers (Preface, continued)

lovers. This wish, to a very large extent, brought about the publication of this The Authentic Lineage Yang-Style Taijiquan Coaching Method.

This book takes as its principal blueprint the earlier work by my grandfather and father, Yang-Style Taijiquan: Teaching Method and Practice Method (compiled by Fu Zhongwen and Fu Shengyuan, written up by Yao Minghua; Shanghai: Tongji University Press, 1st edition 1989), and was written by blending my grandfather's and father's decades of insight in practising boxing and experience in teaching boxing with my own personal experience of more than twenty years in practising and teaching boxing. It is a comprehensive summary of our three generations' — grandfather, son and grandson — understanding, practice and teaching of Taijiquan, and the latest crystallisation condensing three generations' wisdom and heart's blood. In the course of many years of teaching boxing, we have clearly realised that the efforts of a mere few people are far from able to satisfy the wish of the broad community of Taijiquan enthusiasts to learn authentic Taiji skill; this requires more people to take part in the process of practising and teaching Taijiquan, and to take part in the enterprise of its development and transmission. Therefore we have carefully collated and summarised three generations' methods, techniques and experience of teaching boxing, to provide genuine and effective help to all those who have set their hearts on the development and transmission of Taijiquan. In addition, in the course of teaching we have discovered that people generally overlook the martial-application function of Taijiquan, and many errors and deviations arise from this. In truth, Taijiquan was originally a martial art of technique and combat; only by understanding the correct application of each and every posture of Taijiquan can one grasp the essentials of Taijiquan at the root, accurately master the key points of every movement, and achieve the purpose of better fitness. Therefore another notable feature of this book is its emphasis on explaining the martial-application usage of Taijiquan, which can also more readily arouse the learning interest of young people.

The 21st century is a new century of swift development in science and technology. How traditional excellent culture may adapt to and keep pace with this change, and gain further development, is a serious question. The enterprise of Taijiquan's development and transmission faces this challenge likewise; on the other hand, while modern industry and civilisation bring people more convenience and richer material goods, they impose higher demands on people's physical and psychological quality. How to maintain health of body and mind amid an ever-faster social life and fierce competition for survival has already become a real problem that modern people must face seriously — and in this respect Taijiquan undoubtedly has many unique functions.

As one who practises martial arts, I feel deeply how broad and profound Taijiquan is; only by personally putting it into practice can one appreciate it. Science knows no boundaries; Taijiquan is still in constant development. Although this book has undergone the supplementing and perfecting of three generations, it still inevitably has omissions and deficiencies. At the start of the new century, I hope to study and compare notes together with the broad community of boxing friends and friends from all walks of life who engage in and care about the development and transmission of Taijiquan, and to strive together, so that Taijiquan may ascend another storey and bring more well-being to humanity.

Finally, I hope that the publication of this book may help more people benefit from Taijiquan and appreciate its inexhaustible charm. May humanity live more healthily and happily in the 21st century!

Fu Qingquan 1 August 2000 (Contents I)

(Chapter One — A Brief History of Yang-style Taijiquan, book page 1)

# Chapter One　A Brief History of Yang-style Taijiquan Yang-style Taijiquan originated in the middle of the 19th century (the Daoguang reign of the Qing dynasty). It is barely 150 years old, yet it has spread widely throughout the world and become an excellent method by which hundreds of millions of people strengthen their bodies and improve their health.

The founder of Yang-style Taijiquan was Yang Fukui (1799–1872), courtesy name Lushen, born into a peasant family at the southern gate of Yongnian county town, Guangping prefecture, Hebei. The custom of practising martial arts had a long history in Yongnian county, and Yang Lushen had studied Shaolin boxing since childhood. In the slack farming season he often took short-term work at a grain shop on the West Main Street of the county town. One day a ruffian burst into the Taihe Tang pharmacy next door to the grain shop and, bullying the pharmacist Chen Dehu because he was not a local, insisted on buying precious medicinal herbs cheaply; cursing as he did so, he was about to throw a punch. Chen Dehu merely raised his hand, and the ruffian at once went tumbling out into the street. Yang Lushen was astonished, and a few days later he asked Chen Dehu to teach him boxing. At first Chen Dehu always declined vaguely, but when he saw that Yang Lushen was honest and warm-hearted, he told him that he himself was from Chenjiagou, Wen county, Huaiqing prefecture, Henan; that many people there practised Taijiquan, also called "sticking-and-adhering boxing"; and that his own teacher was Chen Changxing of the same clan, whose boxing skill was second to none under heaven. Delighted at this news, Yang Lushen asked Chen Dehu to introduce him, went to Chenjiagou in Henan, and became Chen Changxing's disciple.

Under Chen Changxing's guidance Yang Lushen trained hard, regardless of cold or heat. Six years later he returned home with outstanding boxing skill. At that time many people in Yongnian county studied boxing, and one man of considerable reputation announced: "Lushen has come back from his studies — I shall have to ask him for a lesson." When the two did test each other, Yang Lushen was defeated. Unwilling to accept defeat, he set his mind on returning to Chenjiagou to study, and trained hard for another six years. When he came home again it happened to be the New Year, and the neighbours, taking the occasion of the New Year greetings, contended with him — and none could beat him. Everyone said that old Lu had really learned something this time. But in a certain Wu family of officials there, one man who had relatives at Chenjiagou and had also studied various boxing arts heard that Yang Lushen had come home and proposed a test; the result was a draw. Yang Lushen felt that he was still not good enough, and so he went to Chenjiagou a third time and studied under Chen Changxing for another three years. Chen Changxing was deeply moved by Yang Lushen's pursuit of the true transmission of Taijiquan and by his spirit in entering Chenjiagou three times. After secretly testing and examining Yang Lushen's determination to learn and the quality of his character, he finally passed on to him his whole body of true skill. Two years later Chen Changxing said to Yang Lushen: "You may go home now; this time no one will dare provoke you." The moment Yang Lushen got back to his home village everyone came to watch him cross hands with others — and somehow, with a single flick of his hand, he sent his opponent flying behind him. And so everyone said that Yang Lushen had truly "brought the goods back" — that is, he had learned real skill. (Chapter 1: A Brief History of Yang-Style Taijiquan, page 2)

Yang Lukchan entered the Chen family village three times to study boxing for eighteen years; having mastered Chen Changxing's true skill he was still not satisfied, and continued ceaselessly to delve into it and train hard, until at last he reached a level of the marvellous and the divine, and became a famous figure of his locality.

Before long, Yang Lukchan accepted the invitation of a distant relative, Wu Ruqing, to go to Beijing to teach boxing. Wu Ruqing was a jinshi of the Daoguang reign of the Qing and at that time served as a vice-director of the Ministry of Punishments. In the capital, Yang Lukchan first accompanied Wu Ruqing on a visit to the mansion of a certain wealthy man, Zhang. Zhang had begun with a small shop and was nicknamed "Little Shop Zhang", and afterwards made his fortune suddenly. The Zhang mansion was a place where officials, gentry and the rich sought their pleasure, and there too several martial-arts instructors were employed to teach a class of sons of wealthy families the practice of arms and boxing. At the banquet of their first meeting, Little Shop Zhang saw that Yang Lukchan was slight of build and somewhat looked down on him, seating him after a row of burly, broad-shouldered martial instructors. During the meal Little Shop Zhang asked: "Mr. Yang, can your soft boxing actually strike a man?" Yang Lukchan said: "My soft boxing cannot strike bronze men, iron men, or stone men; but anything born of father and mother with blood and flesh, it can strike." Little Shop Zhang said again: "Then could you have a contest with the gentlemen present?" Yang Lukchan said: "Very well; I shall get friendly with each of the masters" — meaning, exchange a few moves. So everyone present went out into the garden. When the contest began, one boxing master came straight at Yang Lukchan with a fierce air; and they saw Yang Lukchan merely put out a hand a little, and that boxing master at once fell several zhang away. Another boxing master, seeing this, said "He's no good — let me!" and came in at him too; and in no more than a single move he was seen to fly out. The remaining boxing masters dared not compete further. Little Shop Zhang was greatly astonished at the sight, and at once gave orders to lay the table again with silver vessels and to invite Yang Lukchan to the seat of honour. But Yang Lukchan saw that the host's attitude before and after were as different as two men, and thought little of it; so he rose angrily from the feast and strode off.

After the affair of the contest at the Zhang house got about, men came one after another attracted by his fame wanting to try conclusions with him, but all were defeated at his hands. And so, when Yang Lukchan was mentioned in the capital, everyone called him "Yang the Invincible". Afterwards Wu Ruqing introduced no small number of princes and young noblemen to study Taijiquan under Yang Lukchan, making this boxing art widely current in the capital, and at that time officials' households counted it an honour to be able to engage Yang Lukchan. In this way Yang Lukchan, with his two sons Yang Banhou (1837–1892) and Yang Jianhou (1839–1917), long resided in the Prince Duan mansion to teach boxing, and only in his later years returned to his home village.

Yang Banhou was Yang Lukchan's second son; from childhood he studied arms with his father, and trained a whole body of good skill. Though hot-tempered, his character was upright and unyielding. Once there came to Beijing a boxing master who had fought on the raised platforms of seven provinces and was known as "Ten-Thousand-Catty Strength", who declared he would test who was higher and who lower with Yang Lukchan. When the Yang father and son learned of this, Yang Lukchan thought it need not be attended to; but Yang Banhou said to his father: "Our shop has goods; if someone comes to buy, how can you not sell?" — meaning, we have true skill, so why can we not measure ourselves against another? So Yang Banhou went alone to agree with "Ten-Thousand-Catty Strength" on a contest at the Xisi Archway, and they set down a life-and-death pledge in writing. On the day, "Ten-Thousand-Catty Strength" won the crowd's cheers with his developed musculature, and at the same time people worried for the slight Yang Banhou, who was like a scholar. When the contest began, they saw "Ten-Thousand-Catty Strength" lunge in with one fist, and Yang Banhou dodged aside with a flicker; but when "Ten-Thousand-Catty Strength" attacked again, coming at Yang Banhou's face, they only heard Yang Banhou give a shout, and before anyone had seen clearly, "Ten-Thousand-Catty Strength" had been kicked several zhang away — and Yang Banhou had planted a separating kick in his crotch, killing him on the spot. And while people were still marvelling, Yang Banhou had already unhurriedly returned to the Prince Duan mansion.

(Chapter 1: A Brief History of Yang-Style Taijiquan, page 3)

Yang Lukchan's third son, Yang Jianhou, had a boxing skill in which hardness and softness assisted one another, and was especially good at using clever force; he was also extremely devoted to the study of sabre, sword and spear. His temperament was gentle, and in competition and in martial practice he slighted no one, and so he could win every contest.

The third generation of the Yang family to study the art included Yang Banhou's son Yang Lingxiao, courtesy name Zhaopeng, who studied the art under Yang Banhou's disciple Chen Xiufeng, and afterwards studied boxing with his elder cousin Yang Chengfu, and later taught boxing in Shaoxing in Zhejiang and in Guangxi and elsewhere. Yang Jianhou's eldest son Yang Zhaoxiong, style-name Shaohou, learned boxing from childhood, was at his best at free hands, moved swiftly, and had a steady frame; he kept up training all his life. And Yang Jianhou's third son Yang Zhaoqing, style-name Chengfu, was surpassingly clever, obtained his father Yang Jianhou's personal transmission in full, had refined art and high skill, and at last became a master of his generation in Yang-style Taijiquan.

Yang Chengfu (1883–1936), under his father's instruction, buried himself in study of the art in Beijing. Only after Yang Jianhou's death did he accept an invitation to go south, teaching boxing first in Wuhan, Nanjing and elsewhere. In 1928, at the invitation of Zhang Zhijiang, he taught at the Central Martial Arts Institute in Nanjing, and later, at the invitation of Zhang Jingjiang, went to Hangzhou as dean of studies at the Zhejiang Provincial Martial Arts Institute. In 1930 Yang Chengfu settled in Shanghai and published The Complete Book of Taijiquan: Substance and Application; in 1932, at the invitation of Chen Jitang and Li Zongren, he went to Guangzhou to teach boxing, and only two years later returned to Shanghai.

While Yang Chengfu was dean of studies at the Zhejiang Provincial Martial Arts Institute in Hangzhou, there was in the institute a boxing master named Gao Shouwu who practised Taiyi boxing and consistently belittled the Yang family's Taijiquan, often speaking insolently to Yang Chengfu. One day Yang Chengfu's patience ran out and he exchanged sharp words with Gao Shouwu; Gao Shouwu took up a long spear to have it out with Yang Chengfu, and Yang Chengfu, holding a long spear, gave it but a light flick — and Gao Shouwu's spear flew out of his hand and fell to the ground. At the sight Gao Shouwu was dumbstruck, and was in an instant ashamed beyond bearing.

Yang Chengfu's temperament was gentle, his boxing skill was "a needle hidden in cotton", hardness and softness assisting one another; he had the quality of being able to open out and able to gather in, expansive and generous — and so he was admired and imitated by many. Although Yang Lukchan was Chen Changxing's transmitter, he did not cling rigidly to the old rules; he further developed the art on the foundation of the Old Frame of Chen-style Taijiquan, making it more rational and more popular, and making it suitable for old and young alike so that all could practise it — and people of the time called it "Yang-style Taijiquan". Through the unceasing study and improvement of Yang Lukchan and the two generations after him, the Yang family's Taijiquan was only formally fixed in its manual in the hands of his grandson Yang Chengfu, forming a Yang-style Taijiquan whose frame is expansive and uncluttered, whose structure is strict, whose body method is centred and upright, whose movements are harmonious, and which combines lightness and agility with steadiness.

It was precisely through the efforts of three generations of the Yang family that this traditional boxing art was promoted, developed and widely transmitted — and that Taijiquan came to have its rich and varied schools: for example, Wu Yuxiang, younger brother of Wu Ruqing, who was taught by Yang Lukchan, created Wu-style Taijiquan; Wu Yuxiang taught his nephew Li Yishe, who in turn taught Hao Weizhen, who created Hao-style Taijiquan; Hao Weizhen in turn taught Sun Lutang, who created Sun-style Taijiquan; and Quan You, taught by Yang Banhou, in turn taught his son Wu Jianquan, who created Wu-style Taijiquan. Thus it may be said that Yang-style Taijiquan is the root of Wu-style, Hao-style, Sun-style and Wu-style Taijiquan. In 1956 the National Sports Commission again took the most widely transmitted Yang-style Taijiquan and created a set of Simplified Taijiquan; the boxing manual, boxing photographs and other materials adopted at that time were provided by Fu Zhongwen. The subsequent 88-Posture Taijiquan and 48-Posture Taijiquan and so on were all compiled and created by the National Sports Commission on the basis of Yang-style Taijiquan — just as the martial-arts historian Mr. Tang Hao said: "Yang-style Taijiquan and pushing hands have made the greatest contribution and have been developed most widely." (Chapter One — A Brief History of Yang-style Taijiquan, book page 4)

In the 150 years of the development of Yang-style Taijiquan, Yang Lushen taught Yang Banhou, Yang Jianhou, Wang Lanting, Wu Yuxiang and others. Yang Banhou taught Wan Chun, Ling Shan, Quan You, Hou Deshan, Chen Xiufeng, Zhang Xinyi, Li Lianfang, Zhang Yintang, Jiao Liantang, Ji Laofu and others; Yang Jianhou taught Yang Shaohou, Yang Chengfu, Xu Yusheng, Liu Shengkui, Zhang Yi and others; and Yang Shaohou taught Liu Xizhe, Xu Daishan, Tian Zhaolin, You Zhixue and others. Three generations of the Yang family devoted themselves to spreading and transmitting Taijiquan, and their students were everywhere; Yang Chengfu in particular had the greatest number of disciples. Besides his sons Yang Zhenming, Yang Zhenji, Yang Zhenduo and Yang Zhenguo, he also taught his formal disciples Chen Yuepo, Yan Zhongkui, You Zhixue, Cui Yishi, Wang Xudong, Niu Chunming, Li Chunnian, Wang Jingxing, Zhang Qinglin, Guo Zirong, Chen Weiming, Jiang Tingxuan, Liu Donghan, Zhang Qinlin, Fu Zhongwen, Wu Huichuan, Tian Zhaolin, Dong Yingjie, Chu Guiting, Zheng Manqing and others.

Three generations of the one family of Fu Zhongwen, Fu Shengyuan and Fu Qingquan have all devoted themselves to the development and spread of Taijiquan. The grandfather, Mr Fu Zhongwen (1903–1994), was a native of Yongnian county, Hebei — the famous home of Taijiquan. He began to study Yang-style Taijiquan at the age of nine, and after going to Shanghai at fourteen he studied boxing under the great Taiji master Yang Chengfu for many years. He respected his teacher and trained diligently and hard; moreover, since he married the niece of Master Yang's sister, he won Master Yang's trust and true transmission. The Taijiquan authority Mr Chen Weiming called him "the orthodox line of Taijiquan". When Yang Chengfu taught boxing in Guangzhou, Nanjing, Wuhu and elsewhere, Fu Zhongwen always demonstrated on the spot and also stepped in for Yang Chengfu in contests, winning victory after victory. In order to carry forward Taijiquan and to promote the traditional martial arts among the people so as to lift the spirit of the nation and strengthen the people and save the country, Fu Zhongwen, with the great help of gentlemen such as Huang Yanfang, Ma Gongyu and Huang Jingwan, founded the Shanghai Yongnian Taijiquan Society on 1 October 1944. After the founding of New China, Fu Zhongwen took an active part in all kinds of social activities connected with Taijiquan. In 1956 he served in Beijing as a referee at the national martial-arts competition of twelve provinces and municipalities, during which he received the kindly reception and encouragement of Comrade He Long, Vice-Premier of the State Council; in 1958 he became one of the first batch of coaches of the Shanghai municipal wushu team, contributing greatly to the training of Shanghai's wushu athletes, and he led the team to outstanding results in every national wushu competition. In 1972 Tongji University invited Fu Zhongwen and Fu Shengyuan to teach Yang-style Taijiquan, and joined with the Shanghai Institute of Sports Science, the Shanghai Institute of Hypertension, Huashan Hospital and other research units in carrying out scientific tests of the health-preserving and therapeutic functions of Yang-style Taijiquan. The research proved that Yang-style Taijiquan practice, supplemented by drug therapy, is an effective method of building health, preventing illness and treating chronic diseases such as hypertension, coronary heart disease, arthritis, stomach and intestinal complaints and neurasthenia; it also improves the functioning of the heart and lungs and increases physical strength, so that the practitioner is full of energy and his study and work efficiency rise. This research result attracted the attention of the National Sports Commission and international interest — people came from Japan, Germany, Thailand and elsewhere to learn about it. During the "Cultural Revolution" Mr Fu Zhongwen suffered persecution; in 1979 his reputation was restored and he was elected vice-chairman of the Shanghai Wushu Association. In his later years he still frequently took part in the social activities of Taijiquan. In 1984 he was named one of the "Thirteen Famous Masters of Taijiquan in China"; between 1991 and 1993 he helped to organise and led teams to the First and Second China Yongnian International Taijiquan Friendship Gatherings. In 1994, at the advanced age of 91, he was invited to visit the United States, where he was warmly received; he had also visited and taught in Singapore, Japan, Australia, Germany, Italy, Switzerland and other countries in turn, powerfully promoting the spread of Taijiquan throughout the world. On 25 September 1994, (Chapter One — A Brief History of Yang-style Taijiquan, book page 5)

Mr Fu Zhongwen unfortunately died of illness in Shanghai at the age of 91.

Mr Fu Shengyuan (1931– ) received his father's true transmission, and is a Taiji master of high prestige both in China and abroad. Mr Fu Shengyuan began studying boxing with his father at the age of nine, and before the Liberation he was already helping his father spread Yang-style Taijiquan. After the founding of New China he attended the Shanghai sports cadres' refresher course and became the first wushu coach of the Shanghai municipal sports school, and was invited to teach boxing at Tongji, Fudan and other institutions of higher learning. During the "Cultural Revolution" he was sent down to labour in a factory, after which he returned to higher education and continued to teach wushu and physical education until his retirement. In the mid-1980s, at the invitation of Australian Taijiquan enthusiasts and others concerned, he crossed the oceans and taught Yang-style Taijiquan in a number of countries in Europe, America and Australia, and afterwards settled in Australia. Though now in his seventies, he still spares no effort for the development of the Taijiquan cause. At present Mr Fu Shengyuan is based mainly in Australia, promoting Yang-style Taijiquan to the countries of Europe and America. In 1995, in view of the rapid worldwide growth of Taijiquan, the Shanghai Yongnian Taijiquan Society, then celebrating its fiftieth anniversary, had completed its historical mission, and Mr Fu Shengyuan founded the World Yongnian Taijiquan Federation on the basis of the Shanghai Yongnian Taijiquan Society and became its chairman; in 1998 he was awarded the eighth duan of Chinese wushu, and in the same year, in recognition of his contribution to the popularisation and development of Chinese wushu internationally, the Chinese Wushu Association conferred on him the "Wushu Promotion Award".

Mr Fu Qingquan (1971– ) began practising boxing with his grandfather and father at the age of six, and received formal wushu training from childhood. In the 1980s he became a professional wushu athlete; from 1985 to 1987 he won the Shanghai Yang-style Taijiquan championship for three consecutive years; in 1988 he won the taiji-sword championship and was runner-up in Yang-style Taijiquan at the national taijiquan and taiji-sword competition; in 1989 he represented the national team in the China–Japan Taijiquan competition and won the Yang-style Taijiquan championship. In the same year he moved with his father to Australia and founded the Fu Shengyuan International Taijiquan Academy, and from 1995 he served as vice-chairman of the World Yongnian Taijiquan Federation. Because of his grandfather's death, Mr Fu Qingquan from 1997 gave up his superior living conditions and high remuneration abroad and returned to China to continue the Taijiquan cause his grandfather had left unfinished. In 1998 he was awarded the sixth duan of Chinese wushu. He is now based in China, promoting Yang-style Taijiquan to Singapore, Malaysia, Japan and other Southeast Asian countries.

Mr Fu Qingquan's Taiji movements are standardised, light and nimble, natural, combining form and spirit and full of beauty; he grasps the essence of Taijiquan deeply, and enjoys the reputation of "the young marshal of Taiji". He is not only outstanding in boxing skill but also has a set of teaching methods with striking characteristics. In teaching he is especially good at combining Taijiquan theory with practice — clear in structure, vivid in imagery and full of wit — so that people can enter the gateway of Taijiquan easily and happily. He upholds the family teaching, is optimistic and open-minded, resolves doubts and dispels confusion, and is quick-witted and experienced, embodying the style of a new generation of Taiji masters. He has taught boxing for many years in China and in Australia, Japan and other countries, always with the greatest success. In 1999 China Central Television broadcast his series of teaching films on Yang-style Taijiquan, sword, sabre and pushing hands, which met with an enthusiastic response. In Mr Fu Qingquan we see the fair prospects for the vigorous development of the Taijiquan cause in the 21st century.

Looking over the history of the development of Yang-style Taijiquan, the speed and breadth of its spread are unprecedented. This shows that Yang-style Taijiquan is indeed a good method of preventing illness and improving health, a form of physical training loved by the people and full of vitality. It may be believed that, through the common efforts and constant exchanges of the great body of Taijiquan enthusiasts, (Chapter One — A Brief History of Yang-style Taijiquan, book page 6)

Yang-style Taijiquan is certain to become an international sport and to make a still greater contribution to the physical culture of the peoples of the world.

(Chapter Two — A Detailed Analysis of the Teaching and Practice Methods of Yang-style Taijiquan Movements, book page 7)

# Chapter Two　A Detailed Analysis of the Teaching and Practice Methods of Yang-style Taijiquan Movements

Book page 325

Explanation of the Illustrations in This Book

Explanation of the Illustrations in This Book

1. The movement photographs printed in the "key points of the movement" sections of Chapter Two are all of Fu Qingquan performing the form.

2. So that readers may conveniently check the direction of each posture against the illustrations, the directions of the movements shown in the figures of this book are defined as follows: facing the reader equals south; back to the reader equals north; the reader's right side of a figure facing the reader equals west; the reader's left side equals east. Once one is proficient, or when the space does not permit, one may begin in any chosen direction — one need not start by standing facing south.

3. In order to help readers understand the whole process of the movement of the hands and feet, and their coordination with the trunk, this book has added further illustrations, so that the paths of the hands and feet at every stage of a movement and their coordination are made clearer.

4. Some movement illustrations, in the interest of continuity, inevitably end up with the figure's back to or side-on to the reader; for these, this book has added front views and side views as references for practice.

5. For some rather complicated movements whose process is not easy to grasp, this book has added illustrations to help comprehension.

Repetition of movements enables the learner to understand the process of the same movement when it is joined before and after in different ways. For example, in Grasp the Bird's Tail there is the difference between the join with the left ward-off and the join without it; left Brush Knee and Twist Step connects to Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch, or to Turn Body and Throw the Fist, and the connection to Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch may have the transitional movement of shifting the weight back with the left hand sinking and the right fist extending forward, or may not have that transitional movement (Chapter Two, First Posture — Preparation, book page 8)

— and so on, so that the learner in practice can appreciate that when the same movement (posture) is joined to different movements (postures), the manner of the join is different in each case.

First Posture　Preparation (Yubei Shi)
1. Course of the Movement

Stand naturally, the feet a shoulder-width apart, the toes pointing forward (parallel); the arms hang naturally, the shoulders sunk and the elbows dropped. The head must be upright, with the intention of a suspended crown. The eyes look straight ahead (this is based on starting from a stance facing south); be relaxed, quiet and natural (see Figure 1).

2. Key Points

1. One must "suspend the crown with insubstantial energy", "contain the chest and raise the back", "keep the coccyx centred and upright", "sink the qi to the cinnabar field", and relax the whole body.

2. Both arms must relax and hang naturally, the shoulder joints relaxed, the fingers naturally slightly curved.

3. The body's centre of gravity falls evenly on both feet, so that one "stands with the body centred and at ease".

4. The mind must be quiet and the thoughts concentrated.

3. Requirements

1. The body is upright and natural; one must not arch the chest, protrude the belly, lower the head, lean forward, round the back or stick out the buttocks. From the crown of the head to the tailbone the body must be vertical; the whole body is relaxed and natural, with no place tense.

2. The Baihui point on the crown of the head is lightly lifted upward (as if a rope were suspended from above the head drawing it up), so that the head is naturally vertical, guarding against tipping forward or backward or leaning to left or right. The suspended-crown energy should be as if present and as if absent — one must not force the head stiffly upward.

3. The lips are naturally closed and the tip of the tongue lightly curled up, resting lightly against the upper palate. Breathe naturally, with the gradual aim of achieving abdominal breathing. The gaze looks straight ahead into the distance, and the mind is single-minded.

4. The lower body is steady and the upper body is light and nimble.

4. Errors Easily Made, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: raising the head, lowering the head, tilting the head, or tension in the neck muscles.

(First Posture — Preparation, book page 9)

— and so on. This is mainly because the neck is over-strained or strained improperly, and the eyes look up, down or sideways. Correction: ① relax the neck naturally. ② the eyes should look straight ahead. ③ draw the chin slightly inward.

2. Error: arching the chest. This is mainly because one is not relaxed enough, the shoulders are tensed backward, and one uses thoracic (chest) breathing; without containing the chest it is hard to neutralise an attack. From the health point of view, arching the chest stiffens the upper body and restricts the movement of the respiratory muscles. Correction: ① relax both shoulders and bring them slightly forward to close, letting both arms hang naturally. ② breathe naturally.

3. Error: hollowing (concaving) the chest. This is mainly because one pursues "containing the chest" to excess. Correction: the shoulders should not come too far forward, nor should the belly protrude.

4. Error: rounding the back. This is mainly because "raising the back" is done improperly, which hinders "rolling energy" and "releasing energy". Correction: with the first to fourth thoracic vertebrae — the highest part of the middle of the back — the intention is to bulge and lift them, drawing slightly back and upward, rather than deliberately rounding the back.

5. Error: standing with the feet splayed outward (a "V" stance). This is mainly because one uses one's ordinary relaxed way of standing. Correction: the feet parallel; the legs straight but the muscles not tightened — that is, not standing "dead": there must be substance within emptiness and emptiness within substance.

6. Error: clamping the arms tight. This is mainly because the muscles of the shoulders and arms are too tense and the shoulders are not loosened. Correction: the armpits must be loosened, leaving a space the size of a fist; this benefits the free passage of the axillary artery and vein and of the median, ulnar and radial nerves beneath the armpit, and benefits the blood supply and nervous control of the whole upper limb.

7. Error: scattered thoughts, or fixing on one point. This is mainly because a beginner's attention is not easily concentrated, or is distracted onto some one local movement. Correction: first value the form, then value the intention, and thereafter "first the intention moves, and then the form moves", until inner and outer are united; as the practice deepens with time, one can gradually reach the advanced stages of Taijiquan described as "not in the form but in the momentum, not on the outside but on the inside" and "value the intention, not the form".

5. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Repeatedly open the feet to left and right. Experience the position and direction of the feet and the relaxation and quietness of the body.

2. Check from top to bottom the correct requirements for the head, shoulders, hands, chest, abdomen, buttocks and feet. The practitioner checks each item himself, while the teacher checks from the front, (First/Second Posture, book page 10)

the side and the rear, correcting any problems found.

3. After standing relaxed, take several natural breaths, experiencing depth, length, fineness, evenness and slowness; one should gradually experience "moving the body with the qi, and making sure all is smooth and unobstructed".

4. The teacher must first establish the movement concept in the practitioner. Explain the key points and requirements of standing, so that the practitioner understands that the Preparation posture is meant to bring thought, spirit and body into the state for practising Taijiquan and to clear away distracting thoughts — that is, to put aside for the time being the things one usually thinks about too much, to devote oneself single-mindedly to the practice, and to give the cerebral cortex alternating rest. Stand well in a comfortable and reasonable position, relax the whole body, and let the qi and blood flow freely.

5. Use a heuristic method of teaching, to arouse the practitioner's enthusiasm for learning.

6. Breathing

The student should adopt the method of natural breathing.

7. Technical Analysis

The Preparation posture, as its name implies, is the stance that makes one ready before practising the form. It requires that at the beginning of practice one first stand well in a natural posture, attaining "a quiet mind", "intention", "a relaxed body" and "an upright body"; intention, body and qi are to be trained together. In practice one must be quiet and relaxed, with the qi and blood flowing freely, and must pay attention to the breathing. The breathing of Taijiquan derives from the ancient arts of daoyin (guiding and pulling) and tuna (expelling and absorbing), making the movement and the breathing naturally coordinated so as to achieve "the union of spirit and form"; it further requires that the postures of every part of the body be correct. Therefore the Preparation posture must not be regarded as a simple ordinary standing; one must deeply experience the method of training in which inner and outer are united, and it must on no account be slighted.

Book page 326

Second Posture　Beginning the Form (Qishi)

Second Posture　Beginning the Form (Qishi)
1. Application

Beginning the Form is the stance of the preparatory movement of Taijiquan. On standing, the head must be upright, the intention must contain the suspended-crown energy, the eyes look straight ahead, the chest is contained and the back raised, and one must not lean forward or backward. The shoulders must be sunk and the elbows dropped, the fingertips pointing forward, the palms facing downward; loosen the waist and hips, and, with the toes squarely to the front and the feet planted straight, the feet are parallel and apart (Second Posture — Beginning the Form, book page 11)

图 2
The arms are slowly raised in front of the body, the fingers naturally slightly spread, the palms facing downward, at shoulder distance.
图 3
When the hands have risen to about shoulder height, the shoulders sink and the elbows drop; the elbows lead the arms as the wrists are seated and pressed downward, drawing inward as they press down.
图 4
When the arms are about to straighten but are not yet straight, the wrists are seated, the elbows hang down, and the palms come to rest in front of and to the side of the hips, the heels of the palms slightly forward of the body's centre line.

apart, a shoulder-width. In particular, one must pay attention to consolidating the spirit within, sinking the qi to the cinnabar field, and letting everything be natural without forcing. Guard my own stillness in order to await the other's movement — only thus can inner and outer be united and both the exercise and its application be complete. Many people are only too apt to neglect Beginning the Form, not knowing that this is the very root of both the training method and its application. The learner is urged to put his first attention on practising this movement well.

2. Course of the Movement

1. Both hands are slowly raised from in front of the body, the fingertips pointing forward, the fingers naturally slightly spread, the palms facing downward, at shoulder distance (see Figure 2).

2. When the two hands have risen to about the height of the shoulders, first sink the shoulders; then, with the elbows leading the arms and the wrists seated, press downward, drawing inward as you press down (see Figure 3).

3. Press down until the arms are about to straighten but are not yet straight (forming an arc); seat the wrists, let the elbows hang down, the fingers still pointing forward, the palms angled slightly inward toward the sides of the hips but basically facing downward and parallel to the ground, coming to rest in front of and to the sides of the hips, with the heels of the palms slightly forward of the body's centre line (see Figure 4).

4. The eyes look straight ahead.

3. Key Points

1. Perform Beginning the Form only after the Preparation posture meets the requirements.

2. "First in the mind, then in the body": when raising the arms, first be aware of how they are to be raised, and only then raise them slowly. First put the attention on lifting the wrists; move the arms with the intention and lead the qi through to the fingers; seek stillness within movement, with the attention concentrated on the movement.

3. Consolidate the spirit within, sink the qi to the cinnabar field, let the movement be natural and do not force it.

4. All the joints of both arms must be loosened; the shoulders must be relaxed and sunk, the elbows should hang down, the wrists seated, the palms slightly extended, the fingers slightly curved, the palms naturally hollowed slightly inward and slightly curved. In this way, as days and months accumulate, the inner energy passes from the feet to the legs, to the waist, and takes form in the fingers; by this correct method of practice the inner energy arises of itself.

5. Loosen the waist and hips.

6. When pressing down, the shoulders must lead the elbows and the elbows must lead the hands.

4. Requirements

1. When pressing down, the tip of the elbow (the olecranon) must point downward throughout. (Second Posture — Beginning the Form, book page 12)

2. The path of the hands is to sink as they draw in.

3. The palms do not move purely horizontally up and down; rather, the two palms should be angled slightly inward and the backs of the hands angled slightly outward.

4. There must be room left at the armpits — they must not be clamped shut.

5. Head, chest, abdomen and feet remain natural.

6. The arms must be light, nimble and rounded, yet at the same time extremely soft and heavy; they must not float and drift.

7. Ordinary practitioners tend to neglect the simple movement "Beginning the Form", but if the form as a whole is to have a good beginning, one must practise this movement well.

5. Errors Easily Made, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: lifting the shoulders when raising the arms. The main cause is tension in the shoulders. Correction: the shoulders must be relaxed and sunk; the shoulders must lead the elbows and the elbows must lead the hands.

2. Error: when pressing down, the tips of the elbows (the olecranon) lift sideways. The main cause lies in bending the elbows outward and pressing both palms down in a completely horizontal plane. Correction: the two palms are angled slightly inward, the forearms rotate slightly outward, and the tips of the two elbows point straight down.

3. Error: the path of the hands is wrong. The main cause is that when pressing down one does not lead the hands with the elbows. It shows as: ① pressing straight down with the arms extended. ② drawing the palms in flat first, then pressing straight down. ③ going down first, then drawing in. Correction: draw in and press down at the same time.

4. Error: not seating the wrists. The main cause is that the energy is in the palms and not in the wrists. Correction: the moment the elbows go down, seat the wrists at once, and keep them so all the way down until the arms are about to straighten.

5. Error: the arms and hands are too relaxed, floating and without strength — this is called "drifting". The main cause is failure to grasp that the inner energy passes from the feet to the legs, to the waist, and takes form in the fingers, and that the intention is not consolidated within. Correction: when raising forward, do not let the wrists droop slackly; when pressing down, seat the wrists.

6. Error: when pressing down, before the hands have reached their place one goes on to the next movement — Grasp the Bird's Tail. This lies mainly in not having a complete concept of the movement. Correction: the two hands must slowly sink until the arms are about to straighten but are not yet straight, and only then take up Grasp the Bird's Tail.

6. Teaching Method and Practice Method

(Second Posture — Beginning the Form, book page 13)

1. Explain "let everything be natural" and "guard my own stillness": there must be no rigidity in any muscle or joint, the attention must be concentrated, and inner and outer must be united, with the intention leading the movement.

2. Demonstrate the width and height of the arms from the front; demonstrate the path of the hands and the action of the elbows from the side.

3. The teacher observes every detail of the movement from front and side, paying particular attention to "relaxation".

4. After practising the movement whole, do it in parts. First raise both arms forward to the horizontal, then press down (concentrating on improving the elbow and wrist action), and finally perform the movement whole.

5. If there are too many practitioners for the teacher to correct one by one, let the first row practise while the second row watches, then let the second row practise while the first row watches, alternating, so that the practitioners both help others by reporting what they have observed (the shortcomings present) and, through the help of others, come to understand their own errors and shortcomings and improve by comparison.

6. The teacher selects a fairly typical faulty movement, gives a pointed demonstration and explanation of it, and then demonstrates and explains the correct movement.

7. The practitioner must learn patiently and attend to improving details. First attend to improving the forward raise: do not lift the shoulders, the tips of the elbows (the olecranon) point downward, the palms angled inward. Then attend to the downward press: the elbows lead the wrists, the elbows sink, the wrists stand up, drawing inward and going downward at the same time. Press both hands down until the heels of the palms are at a position slightly forward of the body's centre line (to the outside of the groin).

8. Finally perform the continuous whole movement of raising up and pressing down.

7. Breathing

Natural breathing is the best; beginners in particular should attend to this, for if the breathing is not smooth and one ends up holding the breath, it is on the contrary bad for health.

8. Technical Analysis

1. Although Beginning the Form is a preparatory movement, from the very start it is required to be different from other boxing systems: one must let everything be natural and not force it, and concentrate the mind on practising the form.

2. One must attend to the union of inner and outer and to completeness of both exercise and application, so that the nervous system is regulated and coordinated, the channels and blood vessels flow freely, the muscles and joints are exercised, health is improved and disease prevented and cured. Its application is to guard (Second/Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 14)

图 5A
The right toe turns out, the weight shifts onto the right foot, the body turns right, the right leg bends at the knee and squats slightly, the left leg bends at the knee and is lifted, and both hands, palms down, swing to the right with the turn of the waist.
图 5B
The right hand rises in an arc, passes in front of the abdomen and to the right and outside, then turns back with a small circular grind toward the chest, the palm still facing down; the left hand moves in an arc to the right past the front of the abdomen, gradually turning to an upright palm slightly tilted up.

my own stillness in order to await the other's movement; after long practice one gradually attains "the other does not know me, while I alone know the other". "When the movement is urgent, respond urgently; when the movement is slow, follow slowly." Hence the relaxation of every part of the body and the consolidation of the spirit within become extremely important.

Book page 328

Third Posture　Grasp the Bird's Tail (Lan Que Wei)

Third Posture　Grasp the Bird's Tail (Lan Que Wei)

Grasp the Bird's Tail is the master movement of Taijiquan in which exercise and application are both complete. In pushing hands one is required to adhere, connect, stick and follow, going back and forth without leaving or breaking; the bird's tail is used as a metaphor for the arm, and it is taken as the general name for the movement. Its methods are four in number, called ward-off, roll-back, press and push, and they are also called the four cardinal hands.

(A) Left Ward-off

#### 1. Application From Beginning the Form: if the opponent strikes my chest from the front with his left hand, I open my right foot to the right side and settle it solid, then lift the left foot and step forward, bending the knee and settling solid, the right leg straight, forming a left bow stance with the left solid and the right empty. At the same time, bring the left hand up to the chest, palm facing inward, the elbow tip hanging slightly, and press my left wrist against the middle of the opponent's elbow-and-wrist, warding off forward and upward with a sideways energy (one must not be stiff and flat). Then the opponent's force is drawn along by me, and his position is naturally no longer stable.

#### 2. Course of the Movement 1. The right toe turns out about 45°, and at the same time the weight shifts onto the right foot; the right leg bends at the knee and squats slightly, and the body turns right about 45°; the left leg bends at the knee and is lifted, and both hands, palms down, swing to the right with the turn of the waist, the right hand rising in an arc (right hand high, left hand low), passing above the front of the abdomen and then to the right and outside, and then turning back with a small circular grind toward the chest, the palm still facing down. The left hand moves in an arc to the right past the front of the abdomen, gradually turning to an upright palm slightly tilted up with the palm facing inward, until it meets in front of the right hand; the two arms form an arc, the elbows hanging slightly lower than the wrists, and the eyes follow the body, looking level toward the diagonal front (see Figures 5A and 5B).

2. The right leg continues to squat slightly and settle solid; the left foot steps out to the left side (toward the south), the heel landing first, the toe angled inward about 45° (the toe pointing southwest, the left toe and the right heel on one line); the weight shifts left, forming a left bow stance settled solid. As the left foot steps out the upper body turns slightly (Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 15)

图 6
The left forearm wards out in an arc to the upper left with the body; the right palm gathers in an arc down to the lower right to slightly above the hip; the face is toward the west and the eyes look level ahead (west).
图 7
The whole weight shifts onto the left leg; the right foot bends at the knee and is lifted; the left elbow withdraws slightly downward and backward, and the left palm moves down to the left side of the chest; the right arm scoops in an arc to the left to the front of the abdomen, and the right arm rotates outward so that the palm turns facing inward and slightly upward.
图 8
The body turns slightly right; the right foot steps forward, the heel landing first; the right leg is bent and the left leg pushed straight to form a right bow stance; the right arm pushes forward and upward, with the point of force at the back of the wrist.

left, and after the left foot lands the upper body gradually turns right. At the same time, the left forearm, following the movement of the body, wards out first in an arc to the upper left, the left palm level with the shoulder, the wrist bent slightly inward, the point of force at the back of the wrist, the palm angled slightly upward. The right palm gathers in an arc down to the lower right to slightly above the hip, palm facing down, fingers pointing forward, wrist seated, the point of force at the outer side of the heel of the palm. At this moment the face is toward the west, the eyes look level ahead (west), but one must also be aware of both hands (see Figure 6).

(B) Right Ward-off

#### 1. Course of the Movement 1. The weight gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg; the waist leads the body in a slight turn to the left, and the right foot bends at the knee and is lifted; as the body turns, the left elbow withdraws slightly downward and backward, naturally carrying the left palm down to the left side of the chest; as it moves down the left arm rotates inward, the palm becoming upright with the palm facing forward, and the gaze attends slightly to the withdrawal of the left arm. At the same time, the right arm scoops in an arc to the left to the front of the abdomen, and with the scooping motion the right arm rotates outward so that the palm turns facing inward and slightly upward; both arms form arcs, and the gaze gradually turns toward the right arm and then looks level ahead (southwest) (see Figure 7).

2. The body turns slightly right (facing west); the right foot steps forward (west), the heel landing first, and then the weight gradually shifts onto the right foot until it is entirely settled; the right leg is bent and the left leg pushed straight to form a right bow stance. As the body turns, the right arm goes forward (west) and upward, the back of the right palm facing outward (the palm angled slightly upward), level with the shoulder, the elbow slightly lower than the palm; the left palm is placed slightly below the wrist joint, the right arm pushes forward, and the point of force is at the back of the wrist. The eyes look level ahead, and the gaze must attend to the forward ward-off of the right forearm (see Figures 8 and 9).

#### 2. Key Points 1. The two legs distinguish the substantial and the insubstantial, and rise and fall like a cat walking. When the weight shifts to the left leg, the left is substantial and the right insubstantial; when it shifts to the right leg, the right is substantial and the left insubstantial. But "insubstantial" is not "empty": the momentum of movement must not break off, and room must be left for stretching and contracting at any moment; and so-called "substantial" does not mean using excessive force. In a bow stance the bend of the leg is limited to not passing the toes; beyond that is excess force. Beginners must first seek expansiveness and afterwards seek compactness.

2. In the left ward-off the left hand must use the strength of the waist; one must not move only the hand without moving the waist and legs. "Palm, wrist, elbow and shoulder, back, waist, hip, knee and foot, above and below (Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 16)

图 9A
The right arm pushes forward (west) and upward, the back of the right palm facing outward, level with the shoulder, the elbow slightly lower than the palm; the left palm is placed slightly below the wrist joint.
图 9B
