A front view of the settled right bow stance: both arms form arcs, the right palm wards forward and the left palm is placed slightly below the right wrist joint.

nine joints of energy, and the energy issues from the waist joint by joint." The circulation of the inner energy is brought about by the waist and spine leading the four limbs; hence the boxing treatise says, "the master is in the waist."

3. When the right ward-off goes forward, the left palm acts as supporting energy.

4. The movement must form an arc — it must not go straight back and forth — but one must not be affected, nor deliberately make large circles. One must "store energy in the curve so that there is surplus".

5. One must "when one thing moves, nothing is unmoved": waist, feet and hands must move together; one must not have the feet move while the hands do not, or the hands move while the waist does not — this is what is meant by "above and below following one another".

6. The ward-off energy of Taijiquan is extremely important: the shoulder joints must be relaxed and sunk, the elbows dropped and the shoulders sunk; the arms must be extremely light, nimble and rounded, yet at the same time extremely soft and heavy; the two arms must be "as if relaxed yet not relaxed", "hardness and softness contained within", rich in elastic and tenacious ward-off energy. After long practice one comes gradually to understand the conversion of substantial and insubstantial, to grasp adhering, sticking, connecting and following, and the quality of one's ward-off energy rises step by step.

7. One must value "seating the wrist". The wrist must not be slack and weak; once the wrist slackens, the back of the hand inevitably has no ward-off energy and one is easily seized by the opponent at the wrist and controlled — but one must not use clumsy force either.

3. Requirements

1. Wherever the eyes turn, the neck turns also.

2. To go right, first go left; to go left, first go right. When starting the left ward-off the body turns right, and the two hands should not be lifted straight to the right but should circle round to the left front — though one must not deliberately trace circles.

3. The substantial and insubstantial must be clear. At the start of the left ward-off the right heel turns, and the right leg immediately squats down and becomes substantial while the left foot is lifted and becomes insubstantial. In the change one must take care that the waist, leg and hip change gradually and not abruptly; the leg must be sent out slowly and drawn back slowly. The left ward-off is a left bow stance, with the left leg substantial; when taking up the right ward-off one lifts the right leg and then slowly steps it forward, and before the right heel has landed the weight must not shift forward — at this time the left leg is still the substantial leg, and only thus is the substantial and insubstantial clearly shown.

4. One must value the waist as the master. The waist must lead the four limbs; one must not have the arms move while the waist does not — for example, when the left ward-off takes up the right ward-off, the waist must lead the withdrawal of the left hand.

5. One must "when one thing moves, nothing is unmoved". At the start of the left ward-off the right arm goes (Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 17)

forward, to the right, and in an inner arc round to the front of the abdomen, at which moment the left hand has moved from the left to the front of the abdomen, so that the two hands meet exactly — one hand must not stop there while the other is still moving.

6. In both the left ward-off and the right ward-off, when the posture is settled the hands and the feet should both have arrived: one must not have the leg already bent into the bow while the hands have not yet reached their place — above and below should follow one another.

7. One must "keep the coccyx centred and upright". In the left ward-off the upper body must not lean to the left; in the right ward-off the upper body must not lean forward too much.

8. In the right ward-off, when the right heel lands the left palm should immediately push forward along with the right arm; it must not be too late or too quick, and the knee, leg and waist of the left foot must gradually exert force, penetrating joint by joint.

9. The crotch must be opened; the two legs must not be clamped inward to form a "pointed crotch" shaped like the inverted-V of the character for "person".

10. There must be "union of shoulder and hip": above and below in accord, the two hips corresponding to the two shoulders and moving in the same direction. For example, in the settled posture of the left ward-off the shoulder faces west and the hip joint must also face west. At the start of the right ward-off the waist leads the left hand in a slight withdrawal downward and backward, and at that time the waist and hips turn toward the southwest and the shoulders must also turn toward the southwest, the right (Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 18)

When the ward-off is completed, the waist and hips turn toward the west and the shoulders must also turn toward the west.

11. The two arms must be full and rounded. At the start of the left ward-off, when the two hands come together, they must be full and rounded, not collapsed, and it is best if the two wrists are basically opposite each other; the right arm must drop its elbow (the elbow lower than the wrist).

12. In the bow stance, the knee of the front bent leg should project slightly forward of the vertical line, but must not go beyond the toes. The knee and the toes should face the same direction; the sole and heel of the rear pushing leg must be entirely on the ground, and that leg should not be straightened too much.

4. Errors Easily Made, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: when moving the arm, the upper arm is clamped tight and moves pressed against the body. The main cause is insufficient loosening of the shoulders. Correction: from the very start of swinging the arms, loosen both shoulders and leave a gap under the armpits. This benefits the free flow of the channels, qi and blood.

2. Error: at the start of the left ward-off, when the hands come together, the left arm travels fast and arrives first, waiting for the right arm's circling. The main cause is that the attention was too much concentrated on the movement of the right arm, and the too-rapid movement of the left arm was overlooked. Correction: the two arms must move evenly.

3. Error: at the start of the left ward-off, when the hands come together, the hands are either too close to the body or too far from the chest and abdomen; too close forms the two arms clamped tight and pressing on the chest, and too far makes the movement "scattered". The main cause is that the two arms do not follow one another above and below, and the shoulders do not follow the hands. Correction: the posture must be full and rounded, not slack and not shrunken; the left wrist should be below the right wrist.

4. Error: when the hands come together the hands move but the waist does not. The main cause is that the hands are not led by the waist. Correction: the hands follow the turn of the waist.

5. Error: in the left ward-off, when the left leg steps out the heel lands very heavily and the weight shifts out too early. The main cause is that the substantial and insubstantial are not clear and the right leg has not settled solid. Correction: the right leg settles solid; when the left leg extends it hangs suspended, and one must "send" the left leg to land by sitting down on the right leg, so as to step as a cat walks.

6. Error: in the left ward-off, the left bow stance is already bent forward but the two hands are still moving. The main cause is a shallow understanding of the key point "when one thing moves, nothing is unmoved". Correction: the hands and the feet must both arrive; at the same moment that the left leg bends into the bow the left arm should have warded out to its place — thus one meets the requirement. (Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 19)

7. Error: in the bow stance the two feet are awkwardly placed. The main cause is that the two feet stand on one horizontal line. Correction: for the left ward-off, when the left foot steps it should come down slightly toward the rear, so that the left toe and the arch of the right foot are roughly on one line; for the right ward-off, when the right foot steps it should come down moved slightly to the right, so that the two feet have a certain lateral distance from one another and are not on one straight line.

8. Error: in the settled posture of the left ward-off the position of the two arms is wrong — the left hand too high or too low, the right hand too close to the body. The main cause is unclear intention. Correction: the opponent is striking my chest. My wrist presses between his wrist and elbow and wards forward and upward with a sideways energy. Therefore it is enough for its height to be about level with the shoulder; any higher and one's own "doorway" is opened and it is inconvenient to defend against the opponent's renewed attack. The right hand is a separating and gathering hand; if it is too close to the body there is no supporting energy, so the right hand is best placed about 30 cm in front of the hip.

9. Error: at the start of the right ward-off the left arm does not withdraw backward and the upper body does not turn slightly left. The main cause is that the waist does not lead the hands and the wrist and waist are out of joint. Correction: before moving the hands, turn the waist first, and the turn of the waist leads the withdrawal of the left hand; the left elbow hangs down, and the left palm turns to an upright palm as it sweeps aside.

10. Error: when beginning the right ward-off the left leg is not settled solid, so that the weight shifts forward too early (the right foot landing heavily and fast). The main cause is an unclear concept of substantial and insubstantial. Correction: keeping a slight bend and squat, "send" the foot out so that the right heel lands lightly — then the movement appears light and nimble.

11. Error: the direction is skewed — the left ward-off goes either southeast or southwest, and the right ward-off does not face squarely west. The main cause is that the direction of the step is not correct. Correction: I originally stood facing south; the opponent, facing north, strikes at my chest with his left hand, so my left ward-off should of course be toward the south, and not southeast or southwest. Then the opponent, on the west side, strikes at my side ribs with his left hand; I step to the west, ward out, roll back and press, and therefore the direction of the right ward-off should be due west.

12. Error: lifting the elbow in the right ward-off. The main cause is a failure to understand the downward-dropping energy of the elbow. Correction: if the elbow is lifted away from the body and juts outward, the two ribs are too much exposed, which in combat is harmful and not beneficial. But one must also attend to "the elbow not pressing against the ribs".

(Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 20)

13. Error: in the right ward-off the upper body leans too far forward, so that the head goes beyond the knee. The main cause is inattention to the requirement of keeping the coccyx centred and upright. Correction: above and below must be basically on one line, shoulders united with hips and withdrawing together; from the crown of the head through the trunk to the tailbone one must always keep basically to one line. Leaning forward or tipping back are both faults of body method.

5. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explain the key points to establish the concept, and demonstrate the movement whole. Lay emphasis on performing the movement on a foundation of relaxation and on clearly distinguishing substantial and insubstantial.

2. To practise skill, first practise energy; to practise energy, first practise smoothness. Therefore one should first teach the course of the movement and its requirements, first seek correctness of movement, and only afterwards practise issuing energy.

3. While the practitioners try the movement, the teacher observes the correctness of their movements from every side.

4. At the crucial points the teacher should give a spoken cue: for example, when one foot has stepped out but has not yet come down, the teacher should say, "slow — light — the heel comes down." When drawing the leg back, one should also cue "slow".

5. In teaching the footwork, one requires that the leg turn first and then lead the hip and foot, after which one advances along an arc. The arced stepping must not be affected; every movement must be observed and improved; one must not go straight back and forth or straight up and down.

6. The comparative method may be used. With several tens of people practising together, all settle one leg solid and step the other leg forward; from drawing the leg in to extending it and landing, see who is slowest, with the proviso that it be without pausing; two or three people may also form a circle and compare together.

7. Use the method of division in teaching: ① both hands swing right while the body turns and grinds the right heel — attend to fixing the direction. ② the right leg squats and the left foot is lifted, preparing to step forward-left — attend to the landing position of the left foot. ③ the right hand circles in a large circle while the left hand closes in a small circle — attend to the position of the hands and their path of movement. ④ the left foot crosses and lands — attend to the direction of the left toe. ⑤ the left hand wards up and the right hand gathers down, while the left leg bends into the bow. Practise in this order one at a time, so that the practitioner can easily understand the details of the movement; but practising only in parts easily produces discontinuity, so one must use the progressive method, joining them one by one until the whole is complete.

(Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 21)

8. The progressive method: its steps are as follows: (1) first do movement ①, then movements ①②, then movements ①②③; (2) at the position of movement ③ do movement ④, then movements ④⑤; (3) finally perform the complete single movement "left ward-off".

9. Combined practice with the application: two people stand facing each other (the practitioner is A, the opponent is B). A — stands facing south; B — strikes at A's chest with his left fist (the movement should be slow and without force, to prevent injury). A — at once turns right about 45°, squats on the right leg, steps the left foot out to the left, presses the wrist of his left hand between B's elbow and wrist, wards out forward and upward with a sideways energy, and gathers down with the right hand (A's hand must stay adhering to the upper ward-off, and must not strike hard), experiencing the combative meaning of the left ward-off. In this way one can correctly understand the intention of the movement and increase the practitioner's interest.

10. Auxiliary practice: ① The right leg bends at the knee and sits solid; the left knee is lifted slowly and evenly from the left rear, then slowly stepped to the left, and the left leg bends into the bow. Then return to the original position and repeat the practice. This is to experience the substantial and insubstantial and to strengthen the legs. ② The left leg sits solid, with the same requirements, and the right leg steps forward; repeat the practice likewise.

The above practices may, as needed, serve as practice to increase the amount of exercise; the number of repetitions is to be decided by the practitioner's constitution.

11. The method of emphasis: for beginners, each practice session should have a clear emphasis according to plan — for example, if substantial-and-insubstantial is the main theme, then speak more on matters relating to substantial and insubstantial and practise more of the exercises relating to it. Other requirements may be passed over for the time being and deepened step by step. Once the movements are basically mastered, then take the commoner and more prominent problems as the emphasis for further explanation and practice; one must on no account explain everything and do everything at once — after one session the practitioners mostly do not understand and cannot do it well, which dampens their enthusiasm for learning.

12. The practitioner should repeatedly do the right turn of the body at the start of the left ward-off, the squatting of the right leg, and the outward turn of the right solid foot of about 45° (not up to 90°); hence the angle of the outward turn should also be checked.

13. Repeatedly do the right turn of the body and the squat with the two hands coming together, checking that the two hands arrive at the same time, the position of the two hands, the dropping of the elbows, and so on.

14. In the movements of the left ward-off and the right ward-off, emphasise practising the clear distinction of substantial and insubstantial. For example, in practising the left ward-off, sit solid on the right leg and extend the left leg to the left, not (Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 22)

图 10
The weight gradually shifts onto the left leg; the body turns vertically and gradually to the left; the left arm rotates inward so that the palm turns facing obliquely inward and upward; the wrist of the right arm extends slightly forward.
图 11
The right palm rolls over and rolls level to the left; the two elbows slowly drop downward, and the two palms roll level to the left.

land and then draw back, then extend again; practise repeatedly, experiencing the substantial and insubstantial (the same applies in the right ward-off). The result of such practice is inevitably to strengthen the legs and thereby promote health.

15. Repeatedly perform the left foot's heel landing and its inward turn of about 45°, checking the direction of the left foot.

16. Repeatedly practise stepping out, taking care first to draw in slightly the hip root of the side that is sitting solid, so that the abdomen of that side is full and the centre of gravity stable. Then the other leg is slowly stepped out along an arc. But the knee joint must be slightly bent, preserving stored force and flexibility.

(C) Roll-back (Lu)

#### 1. Application I am in the left ward-off position (facing west). The opponent strikes at my side ribs with his left hand. I immediately draw in my right leg and step it forward to the right (west), bend the knee and set it solid, the left foot becoming insubstantial, and the body turns to the right at the same time; the eyes follow, looking level ahead; both hands circle and move out to the right front, the right hand in front with the palm facing sideways inward, the left hand behind with the palm facing sideways inward; when the right palm has turned sideways downward and the left palm upward, quickly press the side (the ulnar side) of the space between the elbow and wrist of my right arm against the opponent's right upper arm, and with the left wrist bent sideways press and adhere the wrist and palm to the back of the opponent's wrist and up the arm, toward the outer left. The whole body sits on the left leg, with the left foot substantial and the right foot insubstantial. If the opponent attacks, I roll toward my chest and to the left side; then his root force is uprooted and his body is thrown off balance accordingly.

Variations: ① If the opponent tries to withdraw his arm, I take the opportunity to press forward. ② If the opponent attacks with a shoulder stroke, I add a left step, right foot in an insubstantial stance (toe touching the ground), contain the chest, and strike the opponent's left shoulder with my right hand, so that he falls out to the left.

#### 2. Course of the Movement 1. The body's weight gradually shifts onto the left leg, and at the same time the body turns vertically and gradually to the left; the left arm rotates inward so that the palm turns facing obliquely inward and upward; the wrist of the right arm extends slightly forward, then immediately rotates outward so that the right palm turns facing obliquely outward and downward; the two elbows slowly drop downward, and the two palms roll level to the left (see Figure 10).

2. The waist continues to turn slightly to the left, and the weight continues to shift onto the left leg, (Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 23)

the left leg sits solid, forming a right insubstantial stance; but the two arms drop their elbows slightly and continue to roll left with the turn of the body; the left palm comes to rest in front of the upper left abdomen and the right palm in front of the right chest, the right hand slightly higher and the left slightly lower. At the start of the left roll the gaze first attends to the left roll of the right arm, and as it is about to end the gaze attends slightly to the left hand, and then gradually turns to look ahead (west, slightly south) (see Figure 11).

3. Key Points

1. In the roll, the distance between the two hands must be the same as in the roll of pushing hands — that is, the right hand rests on the opponent's upper arm near the elbow, and the left hand rests on the opponent's wrist, in order to draw him in. In the rolling transformation the distance between the hands does not change, and it coordinates with the movement of the feet; this is called "the two arms being linked above".

2. In the left roll the body must always turn squarely, without leaning forward or tipping back or swaying; the key is that above and below follow one another, "neither first nor last". If one sits back too fast or too slowly, the waist and legs will come out of joint.

3. In advancing and retreating, turning left and right, one must achieve "union of shoulder and hip"; the shoulders and hips must always maintain a natural vertical relation above and below, satisfying the requirement of "basically one line above and below".

4. The two arms must roll left with the turn of the waist; the two palms must not be too far apart, but the two upper arms must not be clamped tight against the ribs either. Dropping the elbows serves to protect the ribs, and a gap about one fist wide must be left at the two armpits. The elbows not pressing the ribs leaves the arms room to circle, so that one does not trap one's own body. All subsequent movements in the form should be the same.

5. As to the direction of the roll, from its outward appearance, because the left leg is settled solid, it looks as though the two palms tend slightly downward; in fact this is due to sitting on the left leg — the correct movement should be to roll level to the left. Therefore rolling to the lower left or rolling downward are both wrong movements.

6. One must bring into play the functions of adhering, connecting, sticking and following, of not losing contact and of drawing the opponent in and making him land on nothing, and must use the wrist and palm to lead the opponent's centre of gravity.

7. One must value seating the wrist, and should generally attend to relaxed softness and flexibility. If during practice the wrist is weak and powerless, the inner energy cannot easily be poured through to the fingers, which affects the accumulation and growth of the ward-off energy of the arms, and inevitably affects the effective use of "roll", "ward-off", "press", "push" and "seize", and the effectiveness of breaking free from the opponent's "gather" and "seize" hand methods. (Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 24)

4. Requirements

1. The substantial and insubstantial must be clearly distinguished, and moreover there must be substance within insubstantiality and insubstantiality within substance. "Insubstantial" is not total emptiness, not utter absence of strength; "substantial" is not standing completely dead. One must have "yin and yang each as the root of the other" — that is, substantial and insubstantial must interpenetrate. One must know that "double-weightedness brings stagnation; a single weighting brings liveliness".

2. In the roll one must not arch the chest; contain the chest and raise the back — but one must not "cat-hunch" either (hollowing the chest).

3. Loosen the waist and hips; the waist must lead the arms; one must not move only the hands without moving the waist.

4. Above and below must follow one another: the sitting back onto the left leg and the left roll of the two arms must move together and must not come apart, one before the other.

5. In the change of hand shape when taking up the roll from the right ward-off, the palms must not turn over straight up and down; rather, the two hands must trace a small arc slightly to the right and outside and then turn back. One must be aware that after the two hands have circled, it is exactly the space between the elbow and wrist of my right arm that adheres to the opponent's left upper arm, my left wrist and palm adhering to the back of the opponent's wrist.

6. While sitting onto the left leg, the two arms begin to roll back in an arc toward the front of the body, and then gradually the waist turns and rolls level to the left and outside — one must not roll all the way back to the front of one's own body, for otherwise it is "drawing him in and letting him land solid". But neither should one send the two arms rolling to the left outside right from the start, for then one cannot get any advantage.

7. During the roll the shape of the two hands and the distance between them must not change — one must not change them up and down (left hand higher than right), front and back (shortening or widening the distance between the hands), or left and right (the left or right hand drawing close or pulling apart) — but must keep the distance between the rolling hands and the hand shape until the movement is finished.

5. Errors Easily Made, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: when beginning the change from the right ward-off to the roll, the two hands turn over straight up and down. The main cause is that one is unclear about the part of the opponent's arm to which the two hands adhere. Correction: the waist must lead the circling of the hands. The right hand goes from the back of the hand forward, turns to palm facing left, then turns to a diagonal pressing palm, and at the same time the hand extends forward-right and then turns back; the left hand turns from palm facing down to palm facing up, and at the same time the palm goes from the front to the right and then gathers back.

(Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 25)

2. Error: the two hands change shape during the roll. The main cause is a failure to understand the application of the roll. Correction: through "paired practice", experience why the position of the two hands should not change. Because what I roll is the opponent's left arm, one hand on the outer side of the elbow joint and slightly above it, the other on the outer side of the wrist joint — this determines the position of my two hands.

3. Error: the hands and feet come out of joint. Sometimes the left leg has already sat solid while the two hands are still moving; sometimes the two hands have already moved while the leg has not. The main cause is that above and below do not follow one another, each attending to itself. Correction: hands move and feet move; hands and feet arrive together.

4. Error: the body does not turn, and the face remains toward the west. The main cause is a failure to understand the application. Correction: I roll the opponent's left hand to the left with both hands. If I use only the strength of the two hands with the body unmoving, losing the cooperation of the waist, the result is that I draw him in and let him land solid, and the opponent's left fist strikes straight at my chest; but if the waist leads the hands, I can seize the opponent.

5. Error: the movements are not performed completely — rolling before the ward-off has reached its place, pressing before the roll is finished. The main cause is a failure to understand the application. Correction: when the opponent attacks, I must roll until the opponent's root is uprooted and his body is tilted, so of course I must roll to the full position; both excess and deficiency are bad.

6. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explain and demonstrate the application of the roll, so that the practitioner understands the concept of the movement.

2. Clarify the connections: do the circling well from the right ward-off, so that the preparatory movement of the roll is correct.

3. The teacher checks from the side that the left knee is squarely in the direction of the toes and the right knee slightly bent, then checks from the front the changes of the hands during the roll.

4. Repeatedly practise the circling of the two hands, becoming proficient in extending, circling and turning over the palms.

(D) Press (Ji)

#### 1. Application Following the previous posture: if the opponent draws his arm back, I immediately bend the leg and the right knee and set the right foot solid, straighten the left leg, extend the shoulder forward, and stretch and lengthen the waist, following as he retreats, the gaze also looking forward. At the same time, quickly turn over the right wrist (Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 26)

图 12
The settled right bow stance: the right arm forms an arc across the chest, and the left palm is attached to the inner side of the right forearm, pressing forward.
图 13
Side view of the press: the right arm rotates outward so that the right palm turns facing inward, and the left arm rotates inward so that the left palm turns facing outward, the fingers angled slightly upward.
图 14
Another side view of the press: the elbows sink, the right elbow slightly lower than the right wrist, and the heel of the left palm gradually comes close to the inner side of the pulse point of the right wrist as the press proceeds.

hands outward, and the heel of the left palm pressed to the inner side of the wrist joint of the right forearm; when he withdraws his arm, follow closely and press forward, the gaze directed forward.

#### 2. Course of the Movement The body turns slightly to the right, and at the same time the weight gradually shifts onto the right leg; the right knee and leg bend into the bow and the left leg pushes, forming a right bow stance (facing west). As the body turns, the right arm rotates outward so that the right palm turns facing inward, and the left arm rotates inward so that the left palm turns facing outward, the fingers angled slightly upward; the right arm forms an arc across the chest, the elbow dropped (the right elbow slightly lower than the right wrist), and the left palm, attached to the inner side of the right forearm, presses forward (west), the heel of the left palm gradually coming close to the inner side of the pulse point of the right wrist as the press proceeds. The eyes look level ahead, and the gaze must attend to the right arm (see Figures 12, 13 and 14).

#### 3. Key Points 1. In pressing forward the upper body should turn to the right, and the waist is the key to the turning of the upper body. "The master is in the waist, and it takes form in the fingers"; therefore, to move the hands one must first move the waist.

2. In pressing forward the upper body must not lean forward or tip back; the shoulders and hips must be opposite one another above and below.

3. The shoulders must not be hunched up but loosened and sunk. Whether the arms can be relaxed, soft and nimble depends on whether the shoulder joints can be loosened.

4. The elbows must not be raised, and the tips of the elbows must be slightly lower than the wrists; raising the elbows exposes the ribs and does not meet the requirements of combat.

5. The buttocks must not protrude; one must attend to drawing in the coccyx. If they protrude too much the head will inevitably lower and the back hunch, and one cannot achieve "the coccyx centred and the spirit reaching the crown". (Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 27)

6. After the press, between the left palm and the right wrist there should be an "as if touching, as if not touching; as if relaxed, as if not relaxed" — hardness and softness contained within.

4. Requirements

1. In going from the roll to the press, the right hand must not circle widely.

2. In the press the two hands must not be too close to the chest, or they collapse; and once collapsed, it is easy to "land solid", which causes passivity.

3. Hands and feet must arrive together: one must not have the leg already bent to its position while the hands are still pressing.

4. When the front leg bends into the bow, the knee must not go beyond the toes; beyond that it is easy to lose balance, and it is also called "excess force".

5. In pressing out one must leave surplus: the two arms must not be stretched fully straight, but are required to be curved and not straight, "storing energy in the curve so that there is surplus".

6. In the press the two hands must adhere and then press forward (as if adhering, as if not): they must not be far apart, nor pressed tightly together.

7. The direction of the press must be correct.

5. Errors Easily Made, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: the waist and hips are not relaxed and the movements are not nimble. The main cause is a shallow understanding of "the source of destiny and intention is in the waist crevice". Hence the movements appear sluggish and the arms float without strength. Correction: one must "at every moment keep the mind in the waist"; the waist and hips must be relaxed, sunk and held upright, and must turn slightly. If the waist and hips are not nimble, the waist and legs will find it hard to accord and follow one another.

2. Error: the hands move and the feet do not — the foot has already bent into the bow and the hands are still pressing. The main cause is a shallow understanding of "when one thing moves, nothing is unmoved": only if the energy passes from the feet to the legs, to the waist, and takes form in the fingers can there be pressing energy. In going forward there must be a support behind, otherwise the reactive force cannot be strengthened. Correction: hands move and feet move; hands and feet arrive together.

3. Error: raising the elbows. The main cause is failure to attend to sinking the shoulders and dropping the elbows and to keeping the two forearms level and exerting force. Correction: the two shoulders must sink, the elbows must be lower than the wrists, and the fingers of the left hand angled upward — only thus will the two elbows hang down naturally. Otherwise the two shoulders stiffen and the light and nimble energy is lost; and light nimbleness is not floating either — light nimbleness must be combined with steadiness, containing steadiness within.

4. Error: in the press the two hands are too high or too low. The main cause is a failure to understand the application of the "press". If too high, the pressing force goes upward, (Third Posture — Grasp the Bird's Tail, book page 28)

图 15
The two palms wipe back, wiping level back as the two elbows sink, the wrists slightly seated, both palms facing down; at the same time the weight gradually shifts back and the left leg sits solid.
图 16
As the wiping back is nearly complete, the two palms gradually become upright palms with the wrists seated, facing forward.
图 17
The two palms press forward, pressing level and straight, the width gradually narrowing; at the same time the right leg bends into the bow and the left leg pushes, forming a right bow stance.

is easily neutralised by the opponent, so that the aim of the press is not achieved, and moreover the front of the chest is empty and open to the opponent's attack; if too low it is also easily neutralised. Correction: press out from the front of the chest, level and straight forward.

5. Error: in the movement from the roll to the press the arc traced is too large. The main cause is a failure to understand the application. Two hands already adhering should not release and separate. Correction: the right wrist goes slightly down and then up, and the left hand follows upward, pressing forward. One must respond urgently to urgency and follow slowly to slowness.

6. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. The teacher demonstrates.

2. Explain the function of the press and the course of the movement.

3. As the connections are not easily grasped, repeatedly practise the turning over of the two palms, doing the preparatory movement of the press well.

4. Practise the movement whole.

5. Repeatedly practise the change of hand shape from the roll to the press. Rotate the right arm outward with the palm turning inward, and turn the left palm facing outward, close to the pulse point of the right hand, so that the connection is clear.

6. The turn of the waist, the gradual bending of the leg and the turning over of the palms must be done together, experiencing "when one thing moves, nothing is unmoved" and also bringing above and below into accord.

7. Combined practice with the application. A — performs the roll, B — with his left arm between A's two hands; B — withdraws his arm, and A bends the right knee and straightens the left leg while turning the right wrist outward, the heel of the left palm adhering between the pulse points of my right wrist, taking the opportunity to press straight forward.

(E) Push (An)

#### 1. Application Following the previous posture: if the opponent takes the opportunity to press at me, I immediately adhere to his arm with both wrists from the left side, first using sinking energy, then lifting slightly upward, so that the opponent's pressing force lands on nothing. Immediately I then make the wrists upright, sink the shoulders and drop the elbows, contain the chest, with the weight on the left leg, and quickly receive his elbow and wrist with the centres of both palms, pressing forward and squeezing; bending the right leg and sitting it solid, extending the left leg, and the waist at the same time coordinating the forward attack, the gaze following forward too.

#### 2. Course of the Movement 1. The right arm rotates slightly inward with the palm turning down; the left arm rotates slightly outward and the left palm becomes a downward-facing palm; it passes across the back of the right hand in a crossing brush, and immediately the two palms separate, （Form 3　Grasp the Bird's Tail, p. 29） The distance is slightly narrower than shoulder-width. Sink the wrists slightly, both palms facing down, and let the two elbows gradually sink, drawing both palms back with them; at the same time the center of gravity gradually shifts back, settling fully onto the left leg. The eyes look level ahead, and the gaze should take in the two palms as they draw back (see Figs. 15 and 16).

2. Both palms gradually rise to an upright palm with settled wrists, facing forward, and press forward to the front of the chest, pressing out level and straight, the width gradually narrowing; at the same time bend the right leg and straighten the left leg, forming a right bow stance. The eyes look level ahead, and the gaze should take in both palms pressing forward (see Fig. 17).

3. Key Points

1. As the center of gravity gradually shifts back, the root of the right hip draws slightly back, so that the body faces squarely to the front (it must not lean to the left side).

2. Both palms draw back together with the settling-back onto the left leg.

3. At the same time both palms must draw back level with the sinking of the two elbows; the shoulders must be relaxed and the elbows sunk — the arms must not bend at the elbow or lift the elbow.

4. As they draw back the two palms move inward toward the front of the chest (the left palm slanting slightly to the right, the right palm slanting slightly to the left); just before the press goes out, both hands form upright palms, the left palm center slanting slightly toward the right front and the right palm center slanting slightly toward the left front. As the two palms press out, their centers turn slightly forward with the press, but must not turn so far that the palms face straight ahead.

5. The two palms must press forward as the center of gravity shifts forward; when pressing out the shoulders must not lift and the force must not be overdone, otherwise balance is easily lost; the arms must be bent throughout and never straight, maintaining stored potential. The two elbows must not protrude outward.

6. In drawing back and pressing out, the two hands appear from the outside to trace an upward and downward arc; this is because of the settling back and the forward bow of the leg — in fact the two hands travel essentially level, and the arc is not large.

7. One must "gather the buttocks" — that is, relax the waist and settle the hips; this is favorable to "sinking the qi into the dantian" and to "lifting the perineum."

4. Requirements

1. The waist must be relaxed, and attention paid to keeping it straight and sunk; one must hold to the middle earth, and the middle earth must not leave its place — so first of all, relax. The upper body must not lean forward; the tailbone must be centered, the perineum lifted and the crown suspended.

2. Whether advancing or retreating, one must, as the boxing treatise says, have "baihui, zhongji and the one breath running through" — any forward lean or backward tilt fails to （Form 3　Grasp the Bird's Tail, p. 30） Requirements (continued).

3. In advancing and retreating the two hips must be upright and true, advancing and retiring together as one with the whole body. The hip joints must move in accord with the shoulders, satisfying the requirement that "hip and shoulder unite." At the same time the legs must bow in front and push back behind, with empty and full clearly distinguished.

4. One must sink the shoulders and drop the elbows. First comes relaxing the shoulders; only when the shoulders are relaxed can the elbows drop, and only when the shoulders are relaxed and sunk can the arms be relaxed, soft and nimble. Therefore, in drawing the hands back and pressing out, the shoulders must not lift and the elbows must not rise; room must be left under the armpits, and the two upper arms must not press tight against the ribs.

5. In drawing back and pressing out, the two hands must not rise and fall greatly, making the arc of their path too large — this does not meet the requirement of pressing out straight ahead. Rising and falling greatly creates disorder, and one cannot hold the opponent; the issuing force cannot be concentrated in one direction. When pressing out, the two hands should not be spread too wide laterally — about one fist apart.

5. Common Errors, Their Causes, and Corrections

1. Error: the two hands separate without first forming an overturned palm and without crossing. The main cause is insufficient understanding of how the movement travels in an arc so that the joints turn roundly and freely. Correction: in the moving posture the hand leads the elbow and the elbow leads the shoulder; therefore when the right arm rotates inward the right hand should form an overturned palm, the two hands crossing and then separating. In this way, on the contacting surface, one neither yields nor resists, and with a slight turn that avoids the solid and takes the empty one can issue force, using a lifting force to void the opponent's power.

2. Error: leaning forward when pressing out and tilting back when drawing in. The main cause is a shallow understanding of "the tailbone centered." Leaning forward loses the center of gravity; tilting back loses nimbleness and makes one easy to topple. Correction: the upper and lower must be essentially one line, and shoulder and hip must advance and retire together.

3. Error: the palm presses out flat and straight, squared to the front. The main cause is that the fingers are not relaxed and extended enough. Correction: for the beginner the fingers should be naturally extended, not pressed tight together with force nor spread apart; the palm center should slant slightly. Force should be stored in the bend and kept in reserve, otherwise one becomes stiff and cannot convey force.

4. Error: in drawing the hands back and pressing out, the arc traced by the hands is too large (in drawing back the hands sink too low). The main cause is insufficient understanding of the application. Correction: demonstrate it in paired practice. The opponent presses in from the left front; I use a lifting force to void his true strength, then both my palms adhere to his elbow and wrist, （Form 3　Grasp the Bird's Tail, p. 31） In this stage of pressing forward, large vertical arcs are not permitted; if the arms sink excessively the whole chest is exposed to the opponent. Therefore, when drawing back the heel of the palm should stay higher than the elbow, and one moves back level and straight following the opponent's pressing momentum; when pressing forward the height should correspond to the opponent's chest and ribs, so the two hands essentially keep a level to-and-fro.

5. Error: when drawing back or pressing forward the distance between the two hands is too large or too small. The main cause is a failure to understand the application. Correction: take as the standard the distance at which my two palms press the opponent's elbow and wrist (when pressing out the two thumbs are one fist apart); therefore, if too large one's own movement comes to nothing and the focus of force is not concentrated.

6. Teaching Methods and Practice Methods

1. Explain the application and the movement sequence, and demonstrate.

2. Follow-along practice. (The teacher practices the form in front, and the learners follow along behind.)

3. Incremental method: ① First practice the two hands crossing and separating. ② After the hands separate, add the settling back and drawing in. ③ After the hands separate, add the settling back and drawing in, then add the forward bow and press out.

Learn one part, add a part, and link up a part, until the whole movement is learned.

4. The teacher cues with spoken commands: ① The two hands cross, palms turning down to separate. ② When one part moves, all parts move; the hands move and the waist and legs move. ③ The center of gravity shifts back, the two hands draw back, the shoulders relax and the elbows drop. ④ The left leg settles fully; the two palms face each other, at the front of the chest and not at the abdomen. ⑤ Upper and lower are essentially one line; do not lean forward or tilt back. ⑥ The intent is on the heel of the palm pressing forward. ⑦ Repeatedly practice taking the position of the squeeze and linking it to the crossing and separating of the two hands. ⑧ Repeatedly practice drawing the two hands back. Then practice sinking the shoulders and dropping the elbows, improve the relaxed shoulder and dropped elbow, press and press out, and correct the path of the hands and the changes in the shape of the hands. ⑨ Do the complete movement, improving hand-arrives and foot-arrives, with force issuing from the legs. ⑩ Practice in pairs and correct each other. The teacher sets one requirement, everyone practices to the specified requirement, and once the basic requirement is met another is substituted.... ⑪ The teacher checks the learner's strengths and weaknesses from different angles. From the front, look at the width of the two hands; from the side, look at the path of the hands in drawing back and pressing out, watch the hands move with the waist and legs, and the hands arriving （Form 3　Grasp the Bird's Tail — Technical Analysis, p. 32） ...the foot arriving.

7. Technical Analysis

Grasp the Bird's Tail is the master hand of taijiquan, complete in both body and application. The "Song of Striking Hands" revised by my late teacher Wang Zongyue states it clearly: "Ward-off, roll-back, press and push must be done in earnest; when upper and lower follow one another the opponent finds it hard to enter. Let him come at me with tremendous force — a touch of four ounces deflects a thousand catties. Draw him in, let it come to nothing, and issue as he closes; adhere, connect, stick and follow, neither losing nor resisting." These six lines should run through the entire taijiquan set, and they are especially applicable as the basis of the technical analysis of Grasp the Bird's Tail.

In the entire Yang-style taijiquan set, Grasp the Bird's Tail appears six times. Its movement is fundamental and typical. Push-hands likewise takes ward-off, roll-back, press and push as its basic movements; therefore this movement of Grasp the Bird's Tail must be practiced well.

1. In Grasp the Bird's Tail there are many variations of bow stance, empty stance, upright palm, upward-facing palm, downward-facing palm, and of hand and foot.

2. The footwork changes a great deal — not only the empty-full changes of moving forward and back, but also empty-full changes while supported on one leg, as when the beginning posture links to left ward-off, left ward-off links to right ward-off, one leg settles fully, one leg slowly withdraws, one leg slowly extends.

3. There are requirements within the body method; in the empty-full changes the tailbone must be centered.

4. There is the application of waist strength: "at every moment keep the mind at the waist." In Grasp the Bird's Tail the beginner is very prone to leaning forward and tilting back, and to failing to do relaxed, sunk and straight properly; when the waist strength is right, one can strengthen the issuing of force.

5. There must be not only ward-off, roll-back, press and push but also adhere, connect, stick and follow; not only striking but also neutralizing; one may neither resist nor lose contact. Therefore the demands on intent are very high.

6. Points of force: ① In left ward-off, at the radial side of the left forearm near the wrist and at the outer side of the right wrist (the right hand is an opening force). ② Right ward-off is at the wrist on the radial side of the right arm. ③ Roll-back is at the right forearm near the wrist; the left hand carries ward-off force, and the force point is on the outer side of the forearm (the ulnar side). ④ Press is mainly at the heel of the left palm, with the right hand as backing. ⑤ Push is at the heel of the palm.

7. The question of empty and full in the waist and legs: whether front empty and back full, front full and back empty, left empty and right full, or left full and right empty, in emptiness there must be fullness, and in （Form 3　Grasp the Bird's Tail — Technical Analysis / Form 4　Single Whip, p. 33） ...there is emptiness within fullness. Emptiness is not total void or limp weakness, nor may fullness stand too dead. Empty and full must interpenetrate and shift imperceptibly. Only when empty and full are nimble and natural can one advance and retreat freely; therefore one demands that they appear and hide by turns. The legs must have "intent and qi that change nimbly, so that there is the delight of roundness and liveliness"; "wherever one fails to find the moment or the position, the fault must be sought in the waist and legs."

The leg bearing most of the body's weight is called full, the other empty. The shifting of empty and full in waist and legs is close to isometric exercise. One leg supports with great effort, and so those who practice taijiquan long have very strong leg muscles, walk and climb stairs lightly, and greatly improve their health. For beginners and the elderly or weak, the stance may be taken higher at first to reduce the amount of exertion, and later, as the constitution strengthens, it may gradually be lowered to increase the exertion.
