Form 4　Single Whip

Form 4　Single Whip
1. Application

If the opponent strikes at me from behind, I immediately raise the tip of my right foot slightly, turn left and settle fully, raising both hands level with the shoulders with palms facing down, and let them swing to and fro left and right with the waist; when the two hands swing to the right oblique, the five fingers of the right hand gather to form the hook hand. The body turns to the left rear, wheeling about to the back; the left foot lifts and steps out to the left; bow the left leg and bend the knee to settle fully, straighten the right leg; at the same time the left hand passes inward before the face, turning as it goes, and extends a palm out to the left, the palm center slanting outward, relaxing the waist and hips, pressing toward the opponent's chest, sinking the shoulders, dropping the elbows and settling the wrist. The gaze follows forward — the hand arrives, the eyes arrive, the foot arrives.

2. Movement Sequence

1. The weight is still on the right leg; the body turns left (about 135°) to face southeast, while the tip of the right foot lifts slightly and the body pivots on the right heel, the toes turning inward as far as possible, then settling. At the same time the two elbows sink slightly and bend a little, and the two hands, as downward-facing palms, sweep left with the body through half of a flat ellipse, both palms at shoulder height. The gaze follows the turning of the body, looking level; the hand arrives and the eyes arrive, and the gaze takes in the right hand (see Figs. 18 and 19).

2. After the body has turned to about 135° (facing southeast), the body （Form 4　Single Whip, p. 34） ...then turns right about 70° (toward the southwest), and the two palms sweep with the body, the two arms passing before the chest to the right oblique front (southwest) through another half of a flat ellipse, both palms at shoulder height. The eyes follow the turning and shift level; the gaze must take in the right palm (see Fig. 20).

3. The weight is on the right leg; the left leg lifts, and the left foot steps out along a natural arc nearer to the inside. At the same time the body continues turning slowly right, and the right arm gradually extends obliquely to the right, the tips of the five fingers drooping and gathering as it extends to form the hook hand; the left arm extends slightly forward, the left palm center facing inward, the fingers near the right wrist (see Fig. 21).

4. The body turns slowly left, the right hook hand continues to relax the shoulder and extend right, and at the same time the left foot steps out to the left (east), touching down heel-first, then settling the whole sole as the weight shifts left. Bow the left leg and push back the right leg, forming a left bow stance. At the same time the left palm passes before the face (no more than 30 cm from the face) and moves left; as the left arm rotates inward, turn the palm center to face forward and slant slightly, pushing out slowly, obliquely and levelly toward the left (east). The eyes look level at the leftward shift, following the left palm to the left; the gaze must see the left palm pushing left, and when the movement is completed the two arms should be spread about 135° apart (see Figs. 22 and 23).

图 21
The right arm gradually extends obliquely right, the tips of the five fingers drooping and gathering to form the hook hand; the left arm extends slightly forward, the left palm center facing inward, the fingers near the right wrist.
图 22A
The left palm passes before the face and moves left; the left arm rotates inward, turning the palm center forward and slanting it slightly.
图 22B
The left palm pushes out obliquely and levelly to the left, forming a left bow stance, the two arms spread about 135° apart.
3. Key Points

1. Turn the waist and hips to the left; the right foot pivots on the heel, and the toes must turn inward fully; the weight is still on the right foot, and the two hands swing left or right with the waist. The upper body must be upright, and must not lean forward or tilt back. As the left hand pushes out to the left front, the right hook hand slowly extends obliquely to the right.

2. The two palms sweep a circle to the left or right — it is a flat ellipse, （Form 4　Single Whip, p. 35） The two elbows hang down (elbows lower than the wrists); the two arms must be linked to each other, not loose and scattered; the front hand goes out and the rear hand follows, at equal distances. The hands turn with the waist, and the two arms must bend and extend roundly and livelily as the palms sweep; when the two palms sweep outward the arms must not be straight, and when they sweep inward one must slightly settle the wrists while dropping the elbows, hollow the chest and turn the waist.

3. In the settled posture the two hands and two feet must have the sense of drawing to and linking with each other above and below. The left arm and the left leg must point in the same direction and be aligned above and below; the knee must not pass beyond the toes; the wrist joint of the right hook hand must be bent, the five fingers gathered and drooping, and vertically opposed to the tip of the right foot.

4. Requirements

1. The two arms sweep the circle, and the movement must be led by the waist — the waist is the key to the turning of the upper and lower limbs.

2. In the extending and retracting of the arms through the circle one must be relaxed, soft, round and lively. To achieve this, one must first of all have the shoulder joints relaxed and sunk, and the beginner in particular should start from "relaxing." Leave room under the armpits; do not press the upper arms tight against the ribs; one should gradually reach "loosened, my force not bent," with elasticity.

3. One must "sink the shoulders and drop the elbows," not hunch the shoulders and lift the elbows; both the left arm that sweeps the circle and the right arm that forms the hook hand must have the elbow lower than the wrist.

4. When the two hands begin to sweep the circle and the waist leads the right foot to turn inward, the weight must be on the right foot, the full leg; the weight must not shift (to the left foot and then back to the right).

5. In sweeping the circle the body turns from west to southeast, then back to south slightly toward the west; the turn must not be too large, or one will "scatter."

6. After sweeping the circle, the left hand comes near the right wrist with the palm center facing inward, and as the body turns the two hands shift left; after passing due south, the left hand, as it shifts, turns the palm outward, forming a side palm, and pushes out obliquely and levelly forward (east), while the right hand moves back in translation 45°.

7. After sweeping the circle, the left foot lifts and takes a step forward-left (east); the left leg, once lifted, must step forward immediately — it must not be drawn back near the inner ankle of the right foot before stepping out.

8. In the settled posture the right hook hand should be slightly higher than the shoulder; the left knee bows forward and the right leg pushes back, but the right leg must not be straightened completely; the left hand and the left （Form 4　Single Whip, p. 36） ...the tip of the foot vertically opposed. The direction of the left toe is squarely east.

9. The right foot must turn inward fully, more than 90°.

10. During the movement the body's center of gravity must not rise and fall abruptly; in particular, when the right foot turns inward the center of gravity must not rise.

5. Common Errors, Their Causes, and Corrections

1. Error: the right foot turns inward insufficiently, making it difficult for the left foot to step toward east. The main cause is a failure to relax the waist and turn the hip. Correction: the big toe of the right foot must lead the force; the toe points and the hip loosens — so the foot leads the knee and the knee leads the thigh, and when the inward turn is complete the left leg can step smoothly.

2. Error: the body rises and the weight shifts left. The main cause is an unclear concept of empty and full. Correction: with the tip of the right foot slightly raised, pivoting on the right heel, begin from drawing in the root of the right hip and let the right knee turn left in line with the right toe. Do not push off the right leg; the right leg must bend, and the turning of the waist and hips drives the right foot to turn inward.

3. Error: the two hands do not sweep a circle but go straight back and forth, or the two hands rise and fall too greatly. The main cause is an insufficient understanding of the application. Correction: they must be raised level with the shoulders and swing to and fro to form a turning momentum; therefore the arms must be bent and not straight. If the rise and fall is too great, it is hard to gain the turning momentum; so there is some rise and fall, but it should be fairly small.

4. Error: the hand shape is poor when sweeping the circle — some hold it taut and stiff, some let it sag limply. The main cause is insufficient attention to the requirements for the palm. Correction: the empty and full of the palm must accord with the empty-full changes of the movement as a whole. The boxing treatise says, "Its root is in the foot, it issues from the leg, it is governed by the waist, and it takes form in the fingers... always it must be one complete breath of qi" — therefore, as they swing left and right, the fingers too must convey force, and so they may not be left limp; but neither may a stiff force be used.

5. Error: lifting the elbows when sweeping the circle. The main cause is a shallow understanding of the downward-sinking force of the elbow. Lifting the elbow obstructs the sinking of the shoulder and affects the breathing. Correction: relax the shoulders and drop the elbows, so that the elbow is lower than the wrist.

6. Error: in sweeping the circle, the turning of the waist and the turning of the hands and feet are not in accord; the turning of the hands and feet is divorced from the turning of the waist, and in some cases only the hands move and the waist does not. The main （Form 4　Single Whip, p. 37） ...cause is a shallow understanding of "the waist as sovereign." Correction: the waist is the key to the turning of the upper and lower body. Only when the waist strength is applied correctly can the strength of the whole body be concentrated at one point. If the hands move and the waist does not, the hands and waist are severed, and the internal force of taijiquan cannot be conveyed to the hands; there can be no turning momentum in the left-right swinging. Therefore, one must "at every moment keep the mind at the waist."

7. Error: the right hook hand is placed too far open; in the settled posture the two arms are almost 180° apart. The main cause is that the right hand moves back too far and the waist turns right too much, with the result that the chest is thrust out. Correction: the right hook hand should move slightly to the right, but still come to rest on the southwest diagonal.

8. Error: the left hand turns its palm too abruptly when pushing out. The main cause is a shallow understanding of hand technique: in taijiquan the palm, in extending forward, extends with rotation and gradually unfolds — it does not rise straight up and drop straight down, nor go straight forward and straight back; and because the force travels from the spine and back, through the shoulder and elbow, to the palm and pushes forward, if the palm is turned abruptly the force cannot be conveyed. Correction: turn the palm as it moves, keeping the fingers essentially slanting upward.

9. Error: when the left hand moves and pushes out, the palm is too far from or too close to the body. The main cause is an insufficient understanding of the application. Too far and it scatters; too close and it collapses. When the opponent strikes from behind me, my left palm presses toward his chest. If the hand is too far, one scatters before anything else; if the hand is too close, my arm is already bent and close to the body — how can I then exert my force? Correction: the left hand must be no more than 30 cm from the face.

10. Error: when the left foot steps out to the left front, the two feet stand on a single straight line. The main cause is insufficient turning of the waist, insufficient inward turn of the right foot, and insufficient opening of the hips, which makes one stand unsteadily. Correction: the right foot must turn inward fully; on the basis of the body's left turn, open the hips and extend the left leg to the left and slightly back — thus there is a proper lateral distance between the two feet. In the entire taijiquan set, whatever the direction or angle, there is never a case of the two feet standing on one straight or transverse line.

11. Error: when the left foot steps out the weight shifts left too quickly, and the left heel lands fast and heavily. The main cause is unclear empty and full and insufficient leg strength. Correction: the step must be like a cat walking. The right leg settles fully, the left leg lifts slowly and lands slowly; when the left heel touches down the weight should still be on the right foot, and only then shift slowly out.

（Form 4　Single Whip — Technical Analysis, p. 38）

6. Teaching Methods and Practice Methods

1. The teacher explains and demonstrates (with emphasis on distinguishing empty and full).

2. Breakdown method: ① Led by the waist, the tip of the right foot lifts slightly, and the right foot turns inward pivoting on the heel — foot, knee and waist must turn together. ② Sweep the circle. Where the hands move and the direction in which they settle. ③ The left hand moves and pushes out; get clear on the timing of the palm's turn. ④ Lift the left leg and step out to the left front with the turn of the body; strive to settle the right leg fully. ⑤ Check the settled posture.

3. Incremental method: ① Turn the foot in. ② Turn the foot in and add the circle sweep. ③ Turn the foot in, sweep the circle, and add the two hands settling into place. ④ As above, add lifting the left leg, turning the body, shifting the left hand, and stepping the left leg. ⑤ As above, add turning the palm and bowing the leg. ⑥ Complete practice.

4. Cue summary: ① Turn the foot in (the right foot must turn in somewhat more). ② Oblique-front hook hand (reminding of the position of the two hands). ③ Bow step, turn the waist, turn the palm (reminding of the position of the left hand).

5. As a group, practice the right-foot inward turn repeatedly, requiring the waist and knee to turn.

6. As a group, have the left hand push forward with the turning of the waist while the right hook hand gradually extends and shifts right, experiencing "when one part moves, no part is still."

7. As a group, settle the right leg fully, lift the left leg and step left with the turn of the body, landing lightly, experiencing the clear distinction of empty and full; the teacher may praise whoever distinguishes them more clearly.

8. As a group, have the left foot step out at various angles as the body turns; beginners may be asked to extend as far to the left rear as possible to compare whose turn is greater, and then the correct landing position is required.

7. Technical Analysis

1. The movement requires a change of forward direction, altering it by 180° (from west to east).

2. In the push of Grasp the Bird's Tail, the right bow stance has the right leg full and bears most of the body's weight; in linking to Single Whip, the form requires turning on the full leg. Empty and full are clearly distinguished, so the load on the leg is heavy. Because the load is heavy, repeated practice strengthens the leg muscles and thereby strengthens the constitution.

（Form 4　Single Whip — Technical Analysis / Form 5　Raise Hands and Step Up, p. 39） 3. After the right leg turns inward, the left leg lifts, forming a one-legged support on the bent right leg, with the whole body weight borne by the right leg. When, after the left leg steps and the heel lands, the weight shifts, poor control of the right leg easily causes the left heel to land quickly, so that the requirement of stepping like a cat walking cannot be met, and there is inevitably interruption and tension.

4. The "Single Whip" movement involves a change of direction and at the same time the movement of hands and feet; the beginner easily gets confused, so one must be clear about the direction of the movement and the coordination of upper and lower, so that the movement is continuous without break, upper and lower follow one another, and empty and full are clearly distinguished.

5. When the two hands begin sweeping the circle they must be laid level; attend to the shifting of empty and full — relax where it should be relaxed and tighten where it should be tightened; hard and soft must complement; it must accord with the momentum of the turn.

6. Changes in the lower limbs easily disrupt the movement of the upper body. Note that when the head turns it must be upright; when sweeping the circle do not lower the head; when lifting the left leg do not tilt the face up; when turning in any direction the head must not lean or slant left or right, but be naturally level. The facial muscles must be relaxed and natural, the lips lightly closed, the breathing natural, the ears quietly listening behind and taking in both sides. Therefore, in training the Single Whip movement one must see that every part of the body conforms to the requirements of taijiquan, and that hand, eye, body and step are coordinated.

7. Many students beginning taijiquan report knee pain after practice, lasting months or half a year at a stretch. This is because Yang-style taijiquan turns by grinding on the full foot: if, when turning, the knee and the foot are not on one line, but the knee forces an inward turn to drive the grinding of the foot, then the knee precedes and the foot follows, and over long, excessive stretching this causes chronic injury to the tendons and ligaments on the inner side of the knee, producing pain. Therefore the beginner must take care that in the full-foot grind the knee turns together with the foot.

Book page 337

Form 5　Raise Hands and Step Up

Form 5　Raise Hands and Step Up
1. Application

If the opponent strikes from the right side, I turn my body from left to right, the left foot turning inward and the body turning right; the right foot lifts and steps forward, heel landing with the toe suspended in the air, and the whole body sits on the left leg. Hollow the chest and raise the back, （Form 5　Raise Hands and Step Up, p. 40） ...relax the waist, the eyes look forward, and at the same time the two hands are raised and brought together inward — this is a closing force, the right hand in front and the left behind, the two palm centers facing each other left and right. When the two hands are raised and link up with the opponent's elbow and chest, one must store the momentum and await the opponent's change. If the opponent advances, I roll back; or one may turn the right palm center upward and close the left palm onto my right wrist to press out — there is likewise a resemblance in body method and step method to the press.

Variation: if the opponent steps up, one may also neutralize his incoming fist to the right and urgently use the right hook hand to strike upward at his chin.

2. Movement Sequence

1. The weight is still on the left foot; the tip of the left foot, pivoting on the heel, turns inward about 15°–30° and settles, the left leg settling fully; the body gradually turns right, the right hook hand becomes a palm, and the two arms drop their elbows (see Fig. 24).

图 24
The weight is still on the left foot; the tip of the left foot turns inward about 15°–30° pivoting on the heel and settles; the left leg settles fully; the body gradually turns right; the right hook hand becomes a palm; the two arms drop their elbows.

2. The right leg lifts and comes down one step in front of the left foot, landing heel-first with the toe naturally raised a little, the right knee bowing slightly to form a right empty stance. At the same time the two palms close forward, the right palm in front, fingertips at brow height, palm center facing left, an upright palm with settled wrist; the left palm behind, fingertips at chest height, palm center facing right and slanting slightly downward, squarely opposite the right elbow joint, the upper body turning slightly left. The gaze looks forward level past the right palm, forming the raise-hands posture (see Figs. 25 and 26).

图 25
The right palm is in front, fingertips at brow height, palm center facing left, an upright palm with settled wrist.
图 26
The left palm is behind, fingertips at chest height, palm center facing right and slanting slightly downward, squarely opposite the right elbow joint, with the upper body turning slightly left.
3. Key Points

1. Raise Hands and Step Up is a closing force; the movements of foot and hand must be coordinated and in accord.

2. As the right hook hand becomes a palm and the two hands close inward, when the two arms open, the two shoulders must be relaxed and the elbows dropped.

3. When the left foot turns inward the waist and hips must be relaxed, the body must stay upright, and the buttocks must not protrude.

4. The right heel touches the ground as an empty point, with the toe raised very slightly — it must not be tilted too high; the right knee must bow slightly and not be straightened — one must achieve emptiness but not total void.

5. When the two arms close, the chest must not squarely face the front; the upper body turns slightly left — only so does it meet the requirement of the application: storing the momentum and awaiting the opponent's change.

6. When the two palms begin closing inward, the right hand sinks slightly and, moving forward, （Form 5　Raise Hands and Step Up, p. 41） ...and then rises slightly. In the settled posture the left tiger's mouth faces the bend of the right elbow, the left fingers are level with the right arm, and the left hand is about one fist's width or a little more from the right arm. If the two hands are too close, roll-back is hindered.

7. The two feet must not be on a single straight line.

4. Requirements

1. Lifting the right foot and stepping forward must be light and nimble; this requires relaxing the waist and hips. In moving the foot and bringing the leg out, first draw the root of the left hip inward and settle the weight firmly on the left leg.

2. Raise Hands requires that upper and lower follow one another: the tip of the right foot squarely faces the front, the fingers of both hands must also point to the front, and the line of sight looks to the front; even the chest and abdomen must turn with the hands and feet, so that the movements of above and below, left and right, are in accord, strengthening the gathering and closing force of the whole body, so that upper and lower follow one another and one breath of qi runs through.

3. In linking from Single Whip to Raise Hands the elbows must drop and the two palms settle their wrists; they close as they move forward — the two arms must not first draw inward and close and then go forward, nor must the two arms go forward too early.

4. As the right leg lifts the knee and steps forward, the two arms close as they move forward.

5. One must hollow the chest, but must not form a hunchback.

6. The right foot must not first come near the inner ankle of the left foot and then go forward; rather, after the right leg lifts forward it steps forward in a natural arc.

5. Common Errors, Their Causes, and Corrections

1. Error: unclear empty and full. The main causes are, first, that in linking from Single Whip and turning the left foot inward, the weight easily shifts right and forms double-weighting; second, that the left leg is not settled fully when the right leg steps forward, so the weight shifts forward. Correction: "double-weighting causes stagnation." The shifting of empty and full between the two legs must be clear; the upper body must be nimble, and the lower body must be made stable. Therefore, when the right leg steps forward, only the heel may land lightly, and the weight must sit on the left leg. Therefore one should practice the full-foot turn often, sinking as one turns.

2. Error: the movements of hand and foot are separated. Commonly the right foot has already landed while the two hands are still extending forward. The main cause is that upper and lower do not follow one another. Correction: foot arrives as hand arrives — thus hand and foot are one force.

3. Error: the two elbows prop outward and lift up, protruding outward away from the body.

（Form 5　Raise Hands and Step Up, p. 42）

...The main cause is failure to attend to the requirement that the elbow not leave the knee. Correction: the elbow should unite with the knee. When linking from Single Whip the upper body begins to turn right, and one should immediately relax the shoulders and drop the elbows; if the two elbows are too exposed, this is harmful and in no way beneficial in combat.

4. Error: the position of the two hands — high or low, inner or outer — does not meet the requirement. The main cause is insufficient understanding of the application. Correction: the requirement of Raise Hands is that one's own two wrists connect with the opponent's elbow and wrist; this makes clear the reason for the requirements that the right hand is in front and the left behind, the right hand slightly higher and the left slightly lower, and the front-to-back distance between the two hands about one forearm. For this, one may use the opponent's elbow and wrist to correct the position of one's two hands.

5. Error: in the settled posture the upper body leans too far forward — this is called "cat's waist." The main cause is the loss of a centered, upright stance. Correction: Raise Hands is a storing of momentum to await the opponent's change; in order not to let the body become slack and lose its center one must hollow the chest and raise the back, and keep the tailbone centered. Thus one can roll back when retreating and press when advancing. If the two hands extend too far forward and the weight moves forward, one brings passivity upon oneself.

6. Error: in the settled posture the upper body squarely faces the front. The main cause is a shallow understanding of the application. The movement of Raise Hands is to await the opponent's change; if I squarely face him and the opponent attacks straight ahead, I have no way to draw him in, and if he is drawn straight in he easily lands on me. Correction: the body must be slightly oblique.

6. Teaching Methods and Practice Methods

1. Explanation (with emphasis on empty and full) and demonstration (with emphasis on the full-foot turn).

2. Mnemonic: turn the waist and turn in the left foot; the weight stays on the left; Raise Hands is a closing force; hand and leg go out together. Breathe naturally, store the momentum and await his movement.

3. In pairs, one attacking and one defending, experience the position of the hands; in groups of several, watch each other and correct errors.

4. Key-point cues: ① When turning the body and turning in the left foot — the weight must not change. ② When the body has turned to face south — the right hook hand becomes a palm, the elbows sink, and the two hands travel in an arc. ③ When the right leg steps forward — land lightly, hand and foot arriving together.

5. Incremental method: ① Turn the left foot inward and turn the body to the south. ② （Form 5　Raise Hands and Step Up — Technical Analysis, p. 43） Turn the left foot inward and turn the body to the south. The right hand becomes a palm and the two elbows drop. ③ Turn the left foot inward and turn the body to the south, the right hand becoming a palm and the two elbows dropping; lift the right leg forward and bring the two hands inward and forward, raised and closed.

6. To deepen the understanding of empty and full and to train the leg strength, repeatedly turn the left foot inward and settle the left leg fully, and repeatedly lift the right leg and step forward into a right empty stance.

7. In the position of the right empty stance, repeatedly practice lifting and setting down the right leg, experiencing the slightly bent knee and the light, nimble foot.

8. To deepen the understanding of the path of the hands and of their position in the settled posture, repeatedly practice the raising and closing of the two arms inward and forward, beginning from the left upright palm and right hook hand.

7. Technical Analysis

1. The whole movement is supported on the left leg, so the load on the left leg is fairly heavy.

2. The movement requires the waist to move, the hands to move and the feet to move, and the gaze to move with them; if one place does not move, there is disorder. Therefore, when turning the waist and turning the body to the right (to the south), at the same time the right hook hand must become a palm, the elbow sink slightly, the right knee lift, and the eyes look forward — upper and lower following one another.

3. In this movement, when the waist turns to the south it is easy to thrust out the chest, and when the hands close inward and extend forward it is easy to cave in the chest. If the chest is thrust out, the qi presses against the chest, the upper is heavy and the lower light, and the heels tend to float. A caved-in chest is unfavorable to breathing; a hollowed chest favors neutralizing force. The boxing treatise says, "the two arms are linked to each other," and "the whole crux lies in the transformation within the chest and waist." Therefore a hollowed chest is the "storing of momentum" of the chest; with a hollowed chest one can raise the back, and with a raised back the force can issue from the spine.

4. The right leg must step forward light and nimble; "light and nimble" means not using stiff force — once stiff force intrudes, the turning is no longer nimble. Therefore in practicing the form one must practice the union of light and sunk, and the mutual complement of hard and soft. In this movement, in the right leg's forward step one must first draw the root of the left hip inward and settle the left leg firmly; in changing from full to empty attend to nimbleness, in changing from empty to full attend to steadiness, so that the right leg's forward step involves the whole body within and without. One must attend to "both light and sunk, hard and soft contained within," storing and not issuing, with skill and force-power given equal weight.

（Form 6　White Crane Spreads Its Wings, p. 44）

Book page 339

Form 6　White Crane Spreads Its Wings

Form 6　White Crane Spreads Its Wings
1. Application

Linked to the preceding posture. If the opponent strikes with both hands from the left side of my body, I quickly withdraw the right foot, lift it and step forward across, the toe slanting slightly (toward the southeast), bending a little and settling fully as the body turns left (to the south) together with the right foot, while the left foot moves to the front (east) and touches down on the toe. At the same time the left palm center closes onto the inner side of the right arm at the elbow, sinking slightly; the right hand then rises to open up above the right forehead, the right palm center facing up and outward, and I use my right hand to lift the opponent's left hand upward. The left hand hurries downward, opening out from the left side down to beside the left hip, palm center facing down — and so the force of the opponent's two hands is dispersed and broken by me.

2. Movement Sequence

1. The weight is still on the left foot; the waist and body turn slightly left, the root of the left hip draws slightly inward, and the right foot lifts. At the same time the left elbow withdraws to the left rear, and as it withdraws the arm rotates inward so that the palm center turns downward; the right palm likewise, with the turning of the body, comes down from the front and moves in an arc to the left front beneath the left hand, and as it moves the arm rotates outward so that the palm center turns upward. The gaze attends slightly to the withdrawal of the left elbow, then turns to look level ahead (see Figs. 27 and 28).

图 27
The left elbow withdraws to the left rear, and as it withdraws the arm rotates inward so that the palm center turns downward; the right palm, with the turning of the body, comes down from the front and moves in an arc to the left front beneath the left hand.
图 28
As the right palm moves, the arm rotates outward so that the palm center turns upward; the gaze attends slightly to the withdrawal of the left elbow, then turns to look level ahead.
图 29
The right arm rises to the front of the upper abdomen, the left palm clinging to the inner side of the right forearm (facing southeast), and the gaze attends the right arm. (This figure is re-printed on the following page as a push-hands demonstration, figure 29.)

2. The right foot comes down in place, still forward of where it was, landing heel-first, and then the toe settles at about 45°. The waist gradually turns left, the weight gradually shifts entirely onto the right leg, and the right leg bends at the knee and settles fully; at the same time as the waist turns and the step is taken, the right arm rises to the front of the upper abdomen, the left palm clinging to the inner side of the right forearm (facing （Form 6　White Crane Spreads Its Wings, p. 45） ...southeast), with the eyes attending to the right arm (see Fig. 29).

3. The body turns slightly left, the left foot lifts a little and moves to the front of the body (east), touching down lightly on the toe, and the left knee bows slightly; at the same time the right palm rises, and as it rises the arm rotates inward so that the palm center turns outward (the fingers slanting upward), while the left palm likewise falls in an arc to beside the left hip, palm center facing down with settled wrist, fingertips pointing forward. The eyes attend slightly to the right palm rising, then look level forward, but the gaze must also take in the two palms. (See Figs. 30A and 30B.)

图 29
The right arm rises to the front of the upper abdomen, the left palm clinging to the inner side of the right forearm (facing southeast); the eyes attend to the right arm.
图 30A
The right palm rises, and as it rises the arm rotates inward so that the palm center turns outward (the fingers slanting upward); the left foot lifts a little and moves to the front of the body, touching down lightly on the toe, with the left knee bowing slightly.
图 30B
The left palm falls in an arc to beside the left hip, palm center facing down with settled wrist, fingertips pointing forward; the eyes then look level forward, but the gaze must also take in the two palms.
3. Key Points

1. The lifting of the right leg, the withdrawal of the left elbow, and the sinking of the right arm must all take place at the same time. The head must not be lowered, the body must not lean forward or tilt back, and the root of the left hip must draw inward — only then is upper and lower shown to be in accord.

2. There must be an upward spirit, but the right leg must still sit down and draw up the waist, so that there is the sense of upper and lower drawing apart and the limbs and body being stretched long. But note: the abdomen must not be thrust out. With the top of the head leading upward the spirit is raised, and with the qi sunk and the hips settled the lower body is steady.

3. When the posture is settled the two arms must form an arc, but the elbows must not be bent up straight; although the right palm is above and before the right forehead, the elbow must not be raised nor the shoulder hunched, （Form 6　White Crane Spreads Its Wings, p. 46） ...but relax the shoulders, drop the elbows and settle the wrists. The body must still be centered and upright; it must not lean forward or tilt back, nor thrust out the chest or protrude the buttocks.

4. Requirements

1. Empty and full must be clear. When the right foot withdraws and steps forward again, the weight is entirely on the left leg, and the left leg must settle fully. When turning left and the left leg lifts and steps forward, the weight is entirely on the right leg, and the right leg must settle fully; the shifting of the weight must not be too fast.

2. The waist is the axle, driving the rotation of the four limbs. When, with the waist's left turn, the left elbow withdraws to the left rear, the waist must lead the hands; one must not move only the hands without the waist.

3. The left leg's forward touch on the toe must be empty and must not bear the body's weight.

4. The right hand rises and the left hand presses down; there must be a sense of division, but the two hands are not unconnected — it is not shown in outer form, but intent suffices: use intent, not force.

5. When the two hands separate one must draw up the waist and stretch apart by opposition, lift the perineum and suspend the crown; it is not that the body goes upward, but there is a feeling of extension.

6. The right palm naturally slants upward; it must not be a horizontal palm — a horizontal palm requires lifting the elbow.

7. One must do the hollowing of the chest and raising of the back well; it is not a caving in of the chest with tension drawn inward, but the chest must feel broad and comfortable, the chest muscles relaxed, which favors the movement of the diaphragm. The beginner must take care not to thrust out the chest, but also must not hunch the back.

5. Common Errors, Their Causes, and Corrections

1. Error: when the right hand falls from the front, the left hand halts and does not move. The main cause is failure to withdraw the left hand. Correction: both hands must move.

2. Error: when lifting the right leg the upper body bends forward. The main cause is the wish to relieve the left leg that maintains the body's center of gravity, resulting in protruding buttocks, or a bent waist with caved chest and lowered head. Correction: the upper body must still be upright; attend to the tailbone being centered. The step must change with the body; if the body slants it loses balance. If, in the transitions of advance and retreat, empty and full are unclear and the lower body is unsteady, balance is lost and the body slants. Therefore the stance must be centered and comfortable, with upper and lower essentially on one line. （Form 6　White Crane Spreads Its Wings, p. 47） 3. Error: the right leg steps forward abruptly and lands hard. The main cause is that the weight shifts forward too early, losing lightness and nimbleness. Correction: the left leg must sink slightly, the position of the weight on the left leg must not move, and the right leg extends slowly forward — thus it can land lightly.

4. Error: in the settled posture the two legs press tight together. The main cause is that the lateral distance of the left foot is insufficient; it should move a little to the left. Correction: the root of the hip should be relaxed and held round.

5. Error: in the settled posture the head is lowered and the waist is bent like a cat's. The main cause is insufficient attention to empty-leading top-of-head energy. Correction: the baihui point on top of the head lifts gently upward, the head is naturally upright, and the body is then not apt to lean forward or tilt back; but one must not push rigidly upward, forming a stiff straightness.

6. Error: the left arm presses tight, the fingers not pointing forward. The main cause is that the shoulder is not relaxed. Correction: the shoulder must be relaxed; leave a fist's width of space under the armpit, and the left hand must settle its wrist.

6. Teaching Methods and Practice Methods

1. Explanation and demonstration (with emphasis on the movement and position of the hands), building an overall concept.

2. Group follow-along practice. Practice the two directions as two separate segments, so as not to add to the learner's difficulty of having to learn the movement and change direction at the same time.

3. The teacher observes the errors present from different positions: from south to north, watching the movement of the two hands; from east to west, watching the position of the two hands, the upward spirit, and so on.

4. Use various methods to correct, and through repeated drilling gain improvement while also strengthening the constitution.

5. Paired practice with the application: ① A — strikes with both palms from B's left side. ② B — beginning from the Raise Hands posture, withdraws the right leg and steps forward across, turns the body left, separates the two hands, the right hand rising and the left going down, separating A's two palms.

Practice repeatedly, exchanging roles, to experience the combative meaning of the movement.

6. Movement commands (for beginners): ① Withdraw the right foot and close. ② Step the right foot out in place. ③ The body turns from south to east. ④ Step the left foot out to the east. ⑤ The right hand rises and the left hand goes down; the two hands separate. ⑥ Pull up above and sit down below.

（Form 6　White Crane Spreads Its Wings — Technical Analysis, p. 48） 7. Repeatedly practice withdrawing and stepping out the right leg; note that the upper body must not lean forward or tilt back, the step must be like a cat walking, and the landing must be light. The right leg must be "sent" by the sinking of the left leg. On landing the sole slants inward about 45°. Experience this repeatedly and practice repeatedly.

8. Linking from Raise Hands into this movement: the upper body turns slightly left, the left elbow withdraws to the left rear, the right hand goes from front to down, and at the same time the right leg lifts. Practice repeatedly so that one posture links to the next without pause.

9. The beginner must repeatedly practice the right leg stepping forward with the rear heel landing first and the sole slanting inward about 45°, so as to understand this and prepare the foot well for the turn of body afterward, so that the later movements are not awkward.

10. With the right leg settled fully, practice putting the left leg out from the side to the front of the body and back from the front to the side. At that time the root of the right hip draws slightly inward and sinks, while the muscles of the left hip and leg relax, allowing the left leg to move nimbly.

11. Repeatedly compare the position of your own two hands in the settled posture, and correct each other. Do not let them be too open, too high or too low.

7. Technical Analysis

1. This movement is a separating movement, so when the practitioner separates the two hands up and down the intent must be clear; of course it should be intent, not force.

2. The settled posture is a left empty stance, but it must not be so empty as to be utterly without strength, nor so full as to stand utterly dead.

3. In taijiquan practice the elbow must at all times have a downward-sinking force. In White Crane Spreads Its Wings the right arm is raised above the shoulder, yet the internal force of the elbow is still downward-sinking. Therefore the right hand must not be a horizontal palm — a horizontal palm requires lifting the elbow.

4. In practicing this movement the stance easily rises. When practicing the whole set, the high, medium or low stance fixed at the beginning must thereafter be kept at a single height, and must not rise and fall erratically.

5. Practicing the White Crane movement easily produces disorder, and one fails to make upper and lower follow one another. Taijiquan says that one must achieve: "the body moves, the waist moves, the feet move, and the gaze also moves with them — only thus may it be called upper and lower following one another." But the beginner, in linking from Raise Hands to White Crane Spreads Its Wings, often has the right leg withdraw, the right hand withdraw, the two hands closing before the body, while the right foot is still （Form 6　White Crane Spreads Its Wings — Technical Analysis, p. 49） ...not yet stepped forward — thus a break is formed. From the point of view of application: the opponent strikes with both hands from my left side; my right hand sinks and rises with him, lifting and drawing up to open out above the right temple, while the left hand hurries downward, performing the functions of adhere, connect, stick and follow. In dividing his force it neither opposes nor breaks off, leaving him utterly without leverage, so that his force is dispersed and broken and he is controlled by me. Therefore my movements of hand and foot must make upper and lower follow one another, continuous without break; and the right hand must close and rise with him, and the body too turns east as the right foot steps out, with the gaze arriving before the hand. Thus it meets the requirement of the boxing treatise: "its root is in the foot, it issues from the leg, it is governed by the waist, and it takes form in the fingers; from foot to leg to waist, always it must be one complete breath of qi" — and so upper and lower follow one another without disorder.

6. When this posture is settled, most people cannot produce the "spirit." It is either a nodding head and caved chest, or a thrust-out chest and protruding buttocks. The difficult point is training the "intent." The movement should have an upward spirit: the spirit must be raised, one must feel a force at the top of the head pulling upward and a force in the lower abdomen sinking downward, as though the body were stretched long by two forces; in outer form the stance is extended, and in spirit it is empty, numinous and natural — then the movement meets the requirement.

7. In practicing taijiquan one must value "relaxation" — that is, loosening and being natural. The mouth and abdomen must not hold the breath; the breathing is deep, slow, soft and even. The four limbs, waist and legs must not use strong force; the whole body relaxes, and the spirit relaxes with it. Relaxation is loose and natural comfort, but it is not slackness. The beginner easily uses force; with long, repeated practice the stiff force is gradually eliminated, the movement becomes loose, relaxed and natural, and one gains "the delight of roundness and liveliness." At the same time, when training loose and relaxed and natural, the number of open capillaries in the muscles increases, making the blood vessels throughout the body free-flowing — especially as regards venous blood, for through the alternate tightening and loosening of the muscles the blood is urged back to the heart; the alternation of tension and relaxation also relaxes the blood vessels, favoring a lowering of blood pressure. Therefore, when the two hands close and the left leg settles fully, the other limbs must relax; when the right leg goes out and settles fully, then the left leg and other limbs must also relax. Thus tension and relaxation in alternation achieves loose, relaxed naturalness, coordinated breathing and free-flowing blood.

8. "The spirit is the commander, the body the servant." In practicing the form one must value the inner and outer being in accord, and value opening and closing. In opening, not only do the hands and feet open, but the mind opens with them （Form 6　White Crane Spreads Its Wings — Technical Analysis / Form 7　Brush Knee and Twist Step (Left), p. 50） ...in closing. The inner and outer must be unified into one breath of qi. There must first be inner movement, and the outer form then moves with it. Therefore one practices "training intent," "training qi" and "training the body" at the same time. The boxing treatise says, "All of this is intent, not outside" — showing that it lays particular stress on "intent." Therefore, in practicing White Crane Spreads Its Wings, the closing and separating in consciousness must be combined with the movement, the breathing, and the gathering and extending in the movement; inner and outer must be in accord, and one must value the role of "intent" — only thus can the movement be practiced well and health improved.

Book page 342

Form 7　Brush Knee and Twist Step (Left)

Form 7　Brush Knee and Twist Step (Left)
1. Application

Linked to the preceding posture. If the opponent strikes from my left side at the middle and lower levels with hand or foot, I sink my body downward, placing the force temporarily on the right leg; the left foot then lifts and steps forward, the left knee bends and settles fully, and the right leg straightens accordingly. At the same time the left hand turns up to the front of the right chest and goes outward-left and downward, brushing aside the opponent's hand or foot; the right hand at the same time, as an upward-facing palm, hangs down and turns straight back to the right rear side, rotating up to beside the ear and settling its wrist, the fingers seemingly open yet not open and seemingly closed yet not closed, palm center facing forward, sinking the shoulders and dropping the elbows, relaxing the waist and hips, pressing toward the opponent's chest. Every part of the body and hands must form a single force, and the intent too extends forward — thus one gains power.

2. Movement Sequence

1. The waist turns slightly right, the root of the right hip draws inward, and at the same time relaxing the right shoulder and sinking the right elbow naturally drives the right palm to rotate outward so that its center faces inward, falling in an arc; passing beside the hip the right arm rotates outward so that the palm center gradually turns to slant upward; at the same time the left palm, with the turning of the waist, comes from the lower left forward and upward, the base of the palm at the height of the upper abdomen, and moves in an arc to the right with the palm facing down (the two hands moving in crossing arcs, one upward and one downward). The eyes follow the turning of the waist, looking level forward, and the gaze must take in the right palm (see Figs. 31 and 32).

2. The left leg lifts, and the upper body continues to turn slightly right; with the turning, the right palm moves in an arc up to the right oblique angle, the palm slanting upward. The left palm continues in an arc to the right, falling to the front of the abdomen (nearer the right), the palm still facing down. The eyes attend slightly to the right palm, then shift to attend to the direction of the left palm (see Fig. 33).

3. The left foot comes down forward (east), touching the ground lightly with the heel, （Form 7　Brush Knee and Twist Step (Left), p. 51） ...as the weight gradually shifts onto the left leg the whole sole settles gradually, bow the left leg and push back the right leg, forming a left bow stance. At the same time the body gradually turns left, and the left palm, with the turning of the body, moves downward and forward in an arc, brushing past the left knee in an arc to beside the left hip (the left oblique front). The right palm likewise turns left with the body, moving in an arc upward, passing beside the right ear and pushing out forward (east). The eyes attend to the direction of the left palm brushing past the knee, then look level forward, and also attend to the right palm pushing forward (see Figs. 34 and 35).

图 34
The body gradually turns left, and the left palm, with the turning of the body, moves downward and forward in an arc, brushing past the left knee in an arc to beside the left hip (the left oblique front).
图 35A
The left palm brushes past the left knee; bow the left leg and push back the right leg, forming a left bow stance.
图 35B
The right palm passes beside the right ear and pushes out forward (east); the eyes attend to the direction of the left palm brushing past the knee, then look level forward.
3. Key Points

1. When the waist changes from turning right to turning left the body must not sway; otherwise the upper body will lean forward or tilt back or lean to the side, which does not meet the requirement of "the tailbone centered."

2. When stepping forward the upper body must also be upright, for the ordinary practitioner, in the course of the step, having only the crouched leg as support, will tend to push the buttocks out in order to balance the body — which does not meet the requirements of "gathering the buttocks" and "the tailbone centered."

3. Moving the right palm from below to the right upper position must be in accord with the lifting of the left foot; the body turning left and changing into the bow step must be in accord with the right palm's push out; the whole movement of Brush Knee and Twist Step must be done coordinated, round, full and soft, and must not be halting or angular.

4. When the right shoulder relaxes and sinks downward, the right shoulder must not end up lower than the left (the two shoulders must be level — and this applies throughout the whole set).

5. The arm that brushes the knee must form an arc and avoid being straight. In pushing out the right palm it must rotate slightly as it goes out, but at the settled posture the palm center must not squarely face the front but slant slightly left, nor may the left palm center squarely face the ground but must slant slightly inward; both palms must settle their wrists.

6. In the settled posture everything must arrive at the same time: one hand must not already be in place (halted) while the other is still moving, nor may the foot arrive while the hand has not. When the movement begins both hands must move; the upper hand must not move forward while the lower hand is still halted.

7. Thought and outer form must be in accord, inner and outer as one; advancing and retreating must have a certain atmosphere, with extension and compactness combined; it must not be wooden or disorderly.

4. Requirements

（Form 7　Brush Knee and Twist Step (Left) — Requirements / Common Errors, p. 52） 1. Sink the right elbow while the right arm rotates outward, the right palm turning inward; otherwise one falls into stiffness. And in thought one must sink with the elbow.

2. The right elbow sinks and the left palm arcs upward, and this must move together with the slight right turn of the waist, meeting the requirement that "when one part moves no part is still." The right palm moves up at the right oblique angle, and the left palm falls in an arc to the front of the abdomen (palm facing down); at the same time, when the left leg lifts, one hand must not move while the other does not.

3. The right arm must not shift back at too great an angle — toward the southwest, slightly west, suffices. The turn of the body must not be too much; the front of the body turning toward the southeast, slightly south, suffices.

4. The left leg comes down forward, touching lightly with the heel first; then the body slowly turns left: the left hand brushes, the right hand slowly pushes out, and the left leg bows out — all must begin together and end together in place, only thus can upper and lower follow one another.

5. When the left leg lifts and draws inward it must not come too near the inner ankle of the right foot; rather, draw it in naturally, then extend it naturally forward and step down, achieving a step like a cat walking.

6. When turning the waist the upper body must not sway; the legs must be steady and the waist relaxed.

7. In brushing one must settle the wrist, turn the waist, and let the waist lead the hands, with elbow and wrist moving together.

8. In stepping the left leg forward the upper body must not lean forward or tilt back; the right leg that bears the body's weight must settle fully. The advancing left leg must first lift the thigh, storing force in the knee, carrying up the heel with the toe hanging naturally; then, from bent to extended, it steps out slowly, the toe changing from hanging down to slightly tilted up, the heel landing lightly first, and then the sole and the toe landing, all settling firmly.

9. The two feet in the bow stance must have a somewhat wider lateral distance (slightly narrower than shoulder-width); they must not stand on one line — only thus can one stand steadily in the settled posture.

5. Common Errors, Their Causes, and Corrections

1. Error: the right elbow sinks, but the right arm does not rotate outward and the right palm does not turn inward. The main cause is a failure to understand the extending, retracting, winding and coiling function of the sinking elbow. Therefore the movement goes straight back and forth, and the elbow easily moves away from the body and protrudes outward, exposing the ribs. Correction: taiji is ward-off force; the movement

Book page 343

VII. Technical Analysis (Seventh Posture, Left Brush Knee Twist Step — continued)

VII. Technical Analysis (Seventh Posture, Left Brush Knee Twist Step — continued)

Walk the spiral: therefore the palm must rotate outward, the wrist turning and the upper arm rotating, with the elbow sinking downward.

2. Error: the right hand moves while the left hand does not. The main cause is that attention is concentrated on the right hand and the principle "when one part moves, every part moves" is neglected. Correction: the mind must be single-minded before there can be "a quiet mind directing the intention": as the right hand moves downward, the left hand must move upward at the same time, and the waist moves slightly as well.

3. Error: turning the body too far to the right — as much as 90° (the body facing south). The main cause is that the physiological and martial significance of the waist's degree of rotation is not clear. If the waist axis rotates too far, the movements of the body and limbs overshoot, so that shoulders and hips no longer match above and below. Excessive twisting of the waist takes the body off its central uprightness and easily causes breath retention. If the opponent strikes from the front while I face sideways, how can I observe his attack? So from the standpoint of martial application it is also wrong. Correction: turn about 75°, the body facing southeast-by-south, the eyes never leaving the hands, right first and then left. The method is: stop after rotating and check the degree of the turn.

4. Error: during the rotation the left hand is held against the chest, which makes the body shrink and the posture incomplete. The main cause is inattention to the requirement "relax and open so that my strength is not bent". Correction: leave room under the armpit, about the space of one fist, so the arm has room to turn and one does not trap oneself.

5. Error: the right hand, striking forward, is not drawn back to pass by the ear before going out, but is pushed sideways, far away from the shoulder. This exposes the ribs, scatters the movement, fails the martial requirement, and prevents the parts of the hand and body from combining into a single strength. The main cause is a lack of understanding of the application. Correction: the right palm moves back along an arc so that the palm passes the ear and pushes straight forward.

6. Error: when the left hand brushes the knee, the wrist is slack and the fingers hang. The main cause is insufficient attention to seating the wrist; this prevents the internal strength from reaching the fingertips and leaves the wrist powerless. Correction: lead the wrist with the elbow, seat the wrist, and brush the knee with a level palm.

7. Error: the two feet stand on a single line. The main cause is that the hip joints are not opened, so waist and legs do not look after each other. Correction: when the left leg steps forward it should shift slightly to the left, so that the lateral distance between the two feet is a little less than shoulder width; the width can be checked when the posture is settled.

than shoulder width, and the width can be checked when the posture is settled.

8. Error: in brushing the knee only the hand moves and the elbow does not. The main cause is a lack of understanding of the application. Correction: the waist should lead the elbow and the elbow lead the hand; only thus can the requirement of pouring in strength be met.

9. Error: in the left-hand brush over the knee, the arc drawn is too large or too small. The main cause is that the requirements of the application have not been deeply felt. Correction: the path of the hand should be horseshoe-shaped; it must not be too far from the knee, nor pressed against the abdomen.

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explain the course of the movement, its application and its essentials. Demonstrate from every angle in order to build up a concept of the movement.

2. Use comparison to improve the lateral distance between the feet in the bow stance: (i) with the two feet on a single line, apply a push laterally and make them move. (ii) with the two feet about shoulder-width apart, apply a push of the same magnitude laterally and compare the stability of the body. The conclusion follows: standing on a single line, the muscles of waist and legs cannot easily exert force, the support is small and the body topples easily.

3. To master "when one part moves, every part moves" well, divide the practitioners into groups of 2–3 and have them watch one another to see whether the two hands move at the same time and whether the two hands arrive at the same time.

4. Practice for distinguishing substantial and insubstantial. As a group, support on the right leg, lift the left leg, extend it slowly forward, lift it slowly again, then set it down lightly … repeat; rest and relax, then repeat again, so that the practitioners fully experience substantial and insubstantial. They may also work in groups of 2–3, watching one another's degree of substantial/insubstantial and its merits and faults.

5. When practising the joining of shoulder and hip, the turning of the waist and hip and the bowing of the leg, the hips and shoulders must advance together, matched above and below, maintaining "the tailbone centred and upright".

6. Repeatedly perform the left bow stance, the left-hand brush over the knee, and the right-hand push, experiencing the correct brushing action and the simultaneous arrival of the two hands.

VII. Technical Analysis

1. In this movement one must first do the brush-knee-and-push-palm well, especially the brush over the knee. Ordinarily the brush is done with the hand alone; but in fact, when the opponent strikes with hand or foot, if my brush lacks strength it cannot sweep aside the opponent's hand or foot.

Therefore the brush is not done with the hand alone: the strength of the elbow must be added, and further still the strength of the waist. For this reason the brushing action is one in which the waist leads the elbow and the elbow leads the hand.

2. The forward strike of the right hand is made together with the brush, so that the parts of the body do not move singly but combine into a single strength; hence hand and foot should arrive at the same time.

3. Tai chi chuan sets store by quietness, relaxation, uprightness and roundness, by evenness, ease, lightness and steadiness. Therefore, in practising the form one must first put aside distracting thoughts, concentrate the spirit, relax inside and out, so that blood and breath flow freely, the body is centred and upright and the movements are even. Hence, when one begins to practise, the teacher brings these basic requirements forward step by step, so that the practitioner masters and grasps them one stage at a time.

# Eighth Posture: Hand Strums the Lute (Shou Hui Pi Pa)

Book page 344

I. Application

I. Application
图 36
Right hand withdrawing, left hand extending forward, both hands before the chest in the lute-cradling shape (Eighth Posture, Hand Strums the Lute: the application)
图 37
Hand Strums the Lute in its settled posture: left palm extended forward, right palm drawn back to the inside of the left elbow, the body turned to face southeast-by-south

Continuing from the previous posture. Suppose the opponent uses his right hand to strike my chest; I immediately hollow the chest and bend the right knee, sitting solidly upon it. The left foot is then lifted and drawn back, then the heel touches down, gathering and storing the momentum. At the same time the right hand withdraws, closes and sinks, passing round beneath the opponent's wrist — that is, I stick my wrist to his wrist and, with the right hand, gather and close the inside of his wrist, plucking and pulling it down to the lower right. The left hand at the same time closes and draws up from the front left, sticking and adhering the palm and wrist to his elbow in the shape of one cradling a lute, carrying out a left rending and a right plucking. This method stores my own momentum in order to watch for his change; therefore is called Hand Strums the Lute.

II. Course of the Movement

The whole weight gradually shifts onto the left leg; the right foot lifts slightly and comes down essentially in its original place (slightly forward), the ball of the foot touching first; the whole weight gradually shifts onto the right leg and the body gradually turns right about 45°; the left foot lifts slightly and goes back and then forward, again coming down essentially in its original place, heel touching down with the toes slightly raised and the knee slightly bowed, forming a left empty stance. At the same time, the left palm, following the turn of the body, lifts forward along an arc, the arm rotating slightly outward as it lifts so that the palm faces right, the index finger level with the eyebrows. The right palm likewise follows the turning body slightly upward, then withdraws downward and back, the arm rotating slightly outward so that the palm faces left, coming to rest inside the left elbow, the right thumb level with the left elbow; the two palms face each other from front to back, the chest angled toward the front as though cradling a lute, the eyes looking level ahead past the left palm (see the figures on this page).

图 36
The settled lute-cradling posture, the two palms facing each other from front to back, the chest angled toward the front (Eighth Posture, Hand Strums the Lute)
图 37
Hand Strums the Lute: the left palm lifted level with the eyebrows, the right palm withdrawn to the inside of the left elbow
III. Essentials

1. In changing from Brush Knee Twist Step into Hand Strums the Lute, the right foot repositions slightly forward as it comes down; whether the weight moves forward or settles back, the upper body must be upright, never leaning forward or backward; the requirement "tailbone centred and upright" must be met — this increases the power of the downward pluck.

2. The right leg sits solid; the left hand lifting diagonally, the right hand withdrawing, and the left foot drawing back must all be carried out together with the turning of the waist.

3. When the right palm withdraws, the waist is the axis and one must relax the shoulder, drop the elbow and sink the wrist, drawing back joint by joint, letting the body lead the hand; one must not withdraw the right palm first while the waist, shoulder and elbow remain unmoving.

4. Before drawing the right hand back it should sink slightly; after drawing back it closes forward and inward, the palm held upright with a slight outward slant.

5. After the left hand has lifted diagonally upward it should draw in slightly toward the front of the body, then close forward.

6. The left foot extending forward and stepping down must be carried out together with the closing of the two hands.

IV. Requirements

1. Substantial and insubstantial must be clear. The whole weight shifts onto the left leg; the right leg lifts slowly and comes down slightly forward; the weight slowly shifts back, sitting solidly on the right leg; the left leg lifts and is set down lightly forward. All the above movements require one leg to support, sitting solid and steady, before the other leg can be nimble — only thus is there no double-weighting.

2. The crotch must be both rounded and hollow; it must not be pinched into the sharp inverted-V of the character for "person"; the hip roots must be opened and spread.

3. The elbow does not leave the ribs, and the elbow does not stick to the ribs. Therefore the elbow must not be raised, nor sunk so far that it presses against the ribs; room must be kept under the armpit.

Book page 345

V. Errors That Are Easy to Make, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

V. Errors That Are Easy to Make, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: the upper body leans forward or backward. The main cause is that when the weight moves onto the left leg and the right leg lifts, the left leg is not yet sitting solid; in order to keep the body balanced, the body is tipped forward. Again, when the weight sits on the right leg and the left leg steps forward, the right leg is not solid and the right hip root has not drawn in and rotated slightly downward; to keep balance the body falls backward. Correction: whether lifting the rear leg or stepping the front leg, the body must be straight and correct — from the crown of the head through the trunk to the perineum it must always form a single line, achieving "above and below essentially one line".

2. Error: the centre of gravity rises and falls too much. The main cause is that when the right leg lifts the left leg straightens, and when the left leg is set down the right leg sits too deep. Correction: when lifting the right leg, sit steady on the left leg, lift the thigh slowly, store strength in the knee, carrying the heel up; let the ball of the foot touch first, then the heel. When stepping the left leg, sit solid on the right leg, first lift the thigh, store strength in the knee, and let the knee go from bent to extended, extending slowly, the heel landing. The key is that the leg that is sitting solid must not perform an extending action, otherwise the body's centre of gravity will rise.

3. Error: the front and rear feet land on a single line, so that the body does not stand steadily. The main cause is an insufficient grasp of the idea of a stable lower body. Correction: after the feet are placed, check whether the lateral distance between them meets the requirement. This also widens and rounds the crotch, which helps blood and breath to flow freely and makes the change from substantial to insubstantial nimble.

4. Error: in the settled posture the upper body faces directly front. The main cause is an insufficient understanding of the application. This posture requires a left rending and a right plucking; facing directly front makes it inconvenient to issue force, does not accord with the folding strength of tai chi chuan, and easily leaves one unable to advance or retreat and inflexible in body when attacked. Correction: turn the body right about 45°, so that it faces the front obliquely; hence, when the left hand lifts diagonally and the right hand withdraws, this should be coordinated with the turning of the body.

5. Error: the path along which the hand moves does not meet the requirement. For example, some closing too near and extending too far forward, some closing with the position overshot, some with a closing but no extending action, some with the two hands too low or too high, some with the right hand between the wrist and elbow of the left arm, some with the right hand between the shoulder and elbow … The main cause is an insufficient understanding of the application. Correction: the opponent strikes my chest with his right hand; my right wrist sticks to his right wrist and my left hand sticks to his upper arm. Therefore the left hand should be a little higher than the right, and the front-to-back distance between the two hands should be about the length of one forearm.

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explain the path and position of the hands, and demonstrate (front view and side view).

2. Practise together as a group following the leader.

3. Broken-down practice: (i) from Left Brush Knee Twist Step into Hand Strums the Lute, sit solid on the left leg while the right leg lifts and steps back; the weight shifts back, and one experiences substantial and insubstantial (lifting slowly, stepping down slowly). (ii) Sit solid on the right leg, lift the left leg and step out; the left heel lands lightly, and one experiences substantial and insubstantial. (iii) One may repeat the practice both landing and not landing the foot, training the left leg and the right leg alike.

4. Mnemonic: the weight moves forward, lift the right leg, the right foot steps back a half step; the weight moves back, lift the left leg, left rend and right pluck, Hand Strums the Lute.

5. Comparison method: working in groups of 2–3, or standing in two facing rows, sit solid and support on one leg while the other leg lifts and extends forward without landing; compare how long the position is held, and compare how many times the leg can be drawn back and re-extended. In the other leg, compare lifting the leg as the weight moves forward, and stepping the right foot down as the weight moves back. This both gives a feel for substantial and insubstantial and strengthens the legs; but the number of repetitions and the time must be set according to age and constitution, with the principle of never holding the breath.

6. Progressive method: (i) the right leg lifts and steps down, the weight moving from forward to back, the two hands sinking and lifting slightly. (ii) To the above, add the left hand lifting diagonally and the right hand withdrawing. (iii) To the above, add lifting the left leg. (iv) To the above, add the two hands extending forward and closing, and the left leg stepping forward and landing. In practice the movement may be simplified — consolidate each bit as it is learned, which makes practice easier.

7. Paired application drills: A — strikes B's chest with his right fist; B — from Left Brush Knee Twist Step takes up Hand Strums the Lute, but without the rending or the plucking (when proficient, a slow, light rending and plucking may be added).

8. Practise repeatedly: the left hand lifts diagonally, the right hand withdraws, then the two hands close forward again, experiencing the path along which the hands travel.

VII. Technical Analysis

1. In this movement support on a single leg is very important; therefore the practices concerned with clearly distinguishing substantial and insubstantial should be done often.

2. In this movement my two wrists stick to the opponent's elbow and wrist, storing my momentum in order to watch for his change — "if he does not move, I do not move; if he moves but slightly, I move first." Left rending and right plucking are issued following me. Therefore, in practising the form one must have "a quiet mind directing the intention", striving to achieve "the intention moves, the form follows". Hence one must "in posture after posture keep the mind weighing the intention" and never treat the movement as simple and so do it carelessly.

3. In moving forward and back one must maintain the body's centre of gravity well; the hands and feet must be well coordinated, matching above and below, neither first nor last. As the right leg lifts slightly, the right hand relaxes the wrist and turns the palm downward; the left hand must be in front, and in this way balance is easily maintained and the centre of gravity steady.

4. The left leg or the right leg half-squats, bearing the whole body's weight — this makes considerable demands on the quadriceps at the front of the thigh. At first there will be a slight trembling and a slight swaying of the upper body; but after repeated practice the strength of waist and legs increases and this no longer occurs, and meanwhile the constitution is strengthened.

5. That no part, inside or outside, is unrelaxed is a principle. First the muscles and joints: in this movement the elbows easily press against the ribs, whereas there should be an empty space under the two armpits and the elbows should not stick to the ribs. This lets the channels flow freely and blood and breath be harmonious, and then further allows the central nervous system and the internal organs to relax at the same time. This method of training, relaxing the whole body inside and out and joining inner and outer, benefits health and disease prevention and also meets the requirements of martial application.

6. Whether advancing or retreating, leave room to spare. The right leg steps essentially down in its original place; one must not step too far, otherwise the left foot cannot be drawn back slightly and the storing and gathering of momentum is impaired.

7. Note that double-weighting makes one sluggish, while weighting to one side makes one nimble. In the settled posture the right leg is substantial and the left leg insubstantial; if the left leg lands bearing too much weight, double-weighting results and turning can no longer be nimble.

# Ninth Posture: Left and Right Brush Knee Twist Step

Book page 346

I. Application

I. Application

See the Seventh Posture, Left Brush Knee Twist Step (the Right Brush Knee Twist Step is the same with the directions reversed).

II. Course of the Movement

1. Left Brush Knee Twist Step: the waist turns slightly right, the right hip root draws in slightly, the left leg lifts and the whole weight gradually shifts completely onto the right leg. As the waist turns, the right shoulder relaxes downward and the right elbow sinks, naturally carrying the right palm down along an arc past the side of the right hip; as it descends the arm rotates outward so that the right palm gradually turns face up. At the same time the left palm, following the turning of the waist, moves forward and inward past the right chest and the front of the abdomen, descending along an arc; as it moves the left arm rotates inward so that the palm turns face down. The eyes follow the turning waist, shifting level ahead, with the gaze attending to the right palm (see the three figures at the foot of this page). The above movement is the same as the earlier Left Brush Knee Twist Step (see the corresponding figures in the Seventh Posture, pp. 51–52).

2. Right Brush Knee Twist Step: (i) The waist gradually turns left; with the left foot pivoting on the heel, the toes turn out about 45°. As the body turns, the left palm moves gradually along an arc to the left and back, the arm rotating outward so that the palm turns face up; at the same time the right palm, following the turn of the body, moves from the front inward and along an arc down to the left, the arm rotating inward so that the palm turns face down. The eyes follow the turn of the body, shifting level ahead, with the gaze attending to the left palm (see the fourth figure on this page). (ii) The whole weight gradually shifts onto the left leg, the right foot lifts and moves forward, and the body continues to turn slightly left; as the waist turns, the left palm moves along an arc up to the left diagonal, and the right palm continues to descend along an arc to the left.
