(iii) The right foot lands forward, heel first; as the weight gradually shifts onto the right leg until the whole foot is set down, the body gradually turns right at the same time, bowing the right leg and pushing back with the left, forming a right bow stance. At the same time the right palm follows the turning body downward, brushing past the front of the right knee in a horseshoe shape to beside the right hip; the left palm also continues upward along an arc as the weight moves forward and the body turns right, pushing forward past the side of the left ear. The moment the eyes see the right palm brush past the knee they look level ahead, the gaze attending to the forward strike of the left palm (see figures 43 and 44).

3. Left Brush Knee Twist Step: the movement is the same as the Right Brush Knee Twist Step, simply with left and right reversed (figures 45–48 on this page; they repeat, left-right reversed, the movements shown in figures 33, 34 and 35 of the Seventh Posture).

Book page 347

III. Essentials

III. Essentials

1. The essentials are the same as those of the earlier Left Brush Knee Twist Step.

2. In practising the Yang-style form, the front and rear feet of the bow stance must not stand on a single line, because this easily produces instability of the centre of gravity and an awkward feeling; the rear foot and the front foot must both be separated laterally (by about the width of the shoulders). Hence, whenever one steps forward or steps back (as in Step Back to Repulse the Monkey), one should take care that the landing position is somewhat opened out, so that it appears steady — "only so can one, advancing or retreating, gain the opportunity and the position."

3. In changing from left bow stance to right bow stance, the footwork requires: in advancing and retreating, in changing, substantial and insubstantial must be clearly distinguished; when the left is insubstantial the right is substantial, when the left is substantial the right is insubstantial; in advancing and retreating the body and waist must change along with it. The knee of the substantial leg must be made more stable, yet without losing its nimbleness; the standing posture must be extremely stable, the step light and nimble, striving to "step as a cat steps", never double-weighted and sluggish; the foot must land light, nimble and steady, never swaying.

4. The turning of the waist must lead the hands. When the two hands are about to finish moving to the left (or right) diagonal rear, one should turn the waist to lead one hand in brushing and the other in striking forward, embodying "the ruler is in the waist" and "power issues from the spine".

5. In going from the Left Brush Knee to the Right Brush Knee, as the right hand moves the left hand must turn at the same time, achieving "when one part moves, every part moves".

6. In brushing, the waist leads the elbow, the elbow leads the wrist, and the wrist must seat downward.

7. The front foot faces squarely in the direction of advance (east); the rear foot is at a slant. In taking up the next brush knee, first turn the waist and turn the toes outward; then the position of the leg is in order.

IV. Requirements

1. The change of the bow stance requires substantial and insubstantial to be clearly distinguished. Taking the change from Left Brush Knee Twist Step to Right Brush Knee Twist Step as the example: the right foot lifts lightly, moves forward, and extends slowly forward; before the right heel lands, the left leg must bear the whole weight of the body — only thus can the substantial and insubstantial of the legs be distinguished.

2. The palm that strikes forward must rotate: that is, in the course from back to front the wrist must turn, advancing in a spiral.

3. In the turning of the upper body the substantial and insubstantial lie in the waist, and secondarily in the chest; the alternation of drawing in the left and right waist creases is used to distinguish substantial and insubstantial. If the turn is insufficient, the two arms that of the movement is restricted; if the turn is too much, "scattering" results.

4. In the linking of "left–right–left" brush knee, there must be no pause: the moment one settled posture is reached, one blends fluidly into the next brush knee; yet one must not go into the next brush knee before the hand has arrived and the knee has bowed fully.

V. Errors That Are Easy to Make, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: turning the body too much. The main cause is that shoulder and hip do not form a vertical line; in turning left and right, shoulder and hip should stay aligned vertically above and below. If the body turns too much the shoulders turn too much, which destroys the correctness of the body and produces an awkward feeling. Correction: the direction in which the line joining the two shoulders points is also required to be the direction of the two hips.

2. Error: in going from Left Brush Knee into Right Brush Knee Twist Step, the left hand has not turned over but merely moves as an upturned palm slanting back and up. The main cause is that in initiating movement one does not lead the elbow with the hand and the shoulder with the elbow. Correction: "the upper arm follows the wrist, the wrist follows the palm", forming a circle at every point. Therefore, when the right hand moves the left hand should turn palm upward, moving along an arc up to the left diagonal.

3. Error: in going from Left Brush Knee into Right Brush Knee, the right hand moves while the left hand halts and does not move. The main cause is a shallow feel for "when one part moves, every part moves". Correction: as the waist turns and the right hand moves inward, along an arc down to the left, the left arm must rotate outward so that the palm turns face up and moves to the left and back.

4. Error: one leg has not yet sat solid when the other leg steps out, and the weight moves forward too quickly, producing double-weighting, and the movement is also not even. The main cause is weakness in the supporting leg, and the hip root on the supporting side not drawing in slightly, so that the leg has not sat steady. Correction: only after the supporting leg has sat steady may the forward-stepping leg extend slowly, and before it lands the weight must not shift forward.

5. Error: the three brush-knee twist steps have no settled posture that is "as if stopped yet not stopped"; instead the two arms go on drawing arcs forward without pause. The main cause is a shallow understanding of continuity and roundness-and-liveliness. Every posture has a beginning, a continuation, a turn and a close; once a posture is complete, it must close at every point. Correction: every settled posture must have a moment of "as if stopped yet not stopped", so that the spirit gathers and concentrates; only thus can the conditions for the next posture be created. Therefore, in link- ing, both falling short of and overshooting in roundness-and-liveliness are incorrect.

6. Error: the two eyes always stare fixedly straight ahead. The main cause is a shallow understanding of "the eyes follow the hands as they turn, and the light glances in all four directions". That is to say, hand arrives and eye arrives, and to look ahead is right; but one must not stare blankly ahead. Correction: the eyes must turn with the principal hand or foot, achieving "eye arrives where hand arrives".

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explain (laying stress on the lateral distance between the feet and on "when one part moves, every part moves") and demonstrate.

2. At each settled posture, stop and check the lateral distance between the feet. Have groups of 2–3 check and correct one another; one may also practise as a group and stop to check oneself.

3. Paired application drills: in pairs. A — strikes B's middle and lower body from the front with fist or foot; B — sinks the body down, sits solid on one leg, steps the other leg one step forward, one hand parries A's hand or foot aside and the other presses toward his chest. Left-right-left, three times in succession.

4. Progressive method — from Left Brush Knee Twist Step into Right Brush Knee Twist Step: (i) repeatedly turn the left toes outward. (ii) While the left toes turn outward the left palm turns up, the right hand draws back along an arc to the left, the weight moves forward and the right leg lifts. (iii) As above, the two hands continue moving, the right leg extends slowly forward and the heel lands lightly, while the left hand moves diagonally back and up and the right hand moves down. (iv) As above, bow the right knee into a right bow stance, while the right hand brushes the knee and the left hand pushes and presses forward.

Improve one section, add one section, like going up a staircase — one more step up from where you already are, until the whole movement is learned and mastered.

5. Supplementary practice: with the two hands hanging naturally, do the bow stance forward step repeatedly, to improve the ability to command substantial and insubstantial, strengthen the legs, and thereby improve health.

6. In practice one should repeatedly perform the linking of left and right brush-knee twist steps.

VII. Technical Analysis

1. The three brush-knee twist steps cover both left and right directions, which benefits the balanced development of the body and its all-round activity.

2. Beginners, faced with movements that are identical but reversed in direction, very easily get muddled, so the right brush-knee twist step should be practised more.

3. The three brush-knee twist steps should embody what the Treatise on Tai Chi Chuan says: "The long form is like the great Yangtze and the ocean, ever flowing without cease." Each must follow on from the last, round, lively and continuous, with no pause (and so it should be with every movement in the whole set).

4. In the three steps forward, the rear leg goes from lifting to extending forward to landing lightly, all carried out evenly and slowly; this not only exercises the muscles of the straight supporting leg but, through the bending and extending of the forward-stepping leg, also exercises the muscles of thigh and calf and the muscles of waist and hip.

# Tenth Posture: Hand Strums the Lute The explanation of the movement is the same as for the Eighth Posture; see figures 49 and 50 in the left-hand column (the same as figures 36 and 37 of the Eighth Posture).

Hand Strums the Lute: the right hand withdrawn and the left hand extended forward in the lute-cradling posture (the movement is the same as 图 36)

Left Brush Knee Twist Step: the right hand pushing forward past the side of the ear, the left hand brushing past the left knee
图 52
Left Brush Knee Twist Step: the settled posture, the left palm pushing forward and the right palm beside the right hip

Left Brush Knee Twist Step: the movement of 图 33–图 35

# Twelfth Posture: Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch

Book page 348

I. Application

I. Application

Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent strikes with his right hand, I immediately opens the left foot slightly to the left side and the waist accordingly turns left; the left hand then turns over backward to beside the left chest, the palm slanting downward. The right hand, wrist turned down, follows the turning body to the front of the left ribs and closes into a fist; turning the wrist, the waist turns right and the right fist follows the rotation to below the right ribs — this is called the "ban" (deflecting). At the same time the right foot lifts and is set down solidly to the right side; the waist and hips relax and sink, and my left hand brushes the opponent's right arm across to my left, whereupon the left hand strikes forward flat and straight with the side of the palm — this is called the "lan" (parrying). The left foot at the same time lifts and steps out one pace into a left bow stance, and the right fist, in unison with the action of waist and legs, punches forward — this is called the "chui" (the punch). The whole subtlety of this punch lies in neutralizing the opponent's right punch: first using my right wrist to stick to his right wrist and deflect it from above the left ribs to below the right ribs. At this point, fearing that the opponent may withdraw his arm and change step, I immediately send my left hand straight forward, following the step, containing an opening strength. When parrying his right hand, I at once drive my right fist at the opponent's chest, so that he has no time to evade and must be struck by me. Hence the whole subtlety of this punch lies in the correct method of the "deflect" and the "parry".

The slanting variation: if the opponent's right palm strikes with especially great force, I take advantage of his momentum and, listening to his strength (high, low, left, right), follow it at random — my right arm deflects to the right, my left hand parries his right forearm to the left, and I then strike him hard with my right fist.

Book page 349

II. Course of the Movement

II. Course of the Movement

1. The body gradually turns left, the left toes turn out 45°; the weight then gradually moves forward onto the left leg, the right heel leaves the ground and the step begins. As the waist turns, the right palm moves naturally along an arc down to the left, as low as the ribs, changing into a fist as it moves, and the right arm rotates inward so that the fist faces down; the left palm also moves slightly back as the waist turns. The gaze attends to the right hand moving down, but one must not bow the head (see the first figure in the left-hand column).

2. The whole weight gradually shifts onto the left leg, the right leg lifts and moves forward; at the same time the right fist goes along an arc to the left past the front of the left ribs and up to the front, and the left palm draws an arc upward (no higher than the chest), the arm rotating slightly inward into an upright palm as it arcs, so that the palm slants to the right. The gaze attends briefly to the right fist, then turns level ahead (see the second figure in the left-hand column).

图 54
Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch: the body turning left, the right palm moving along an arc down to the left at rib height and changing into a fist as it moves
图 55
Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch: the right fist arcing up to the left and forward past the front of the left ribs, the left palm arcing upward into an upright palm
图 56A
Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch: the right foot stepping out one pace to the right front, heel touching down first with the toes turned out
图 56B
Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch: the right fist deflecting out forward and to the right past the chest, the arm rotating outward as it deflects so that the fist eye faces up
图 57
Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch: the right hand closing toward the left, the heel of the left palm against the inner side of the right wrist; as it deflects out the two hands are about level with the shoulders
图 58
Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch: the weight on the right leg, the left leg lifted; the right fist withdrawing along an arc to the right, the fist centre gradually turning up, and the left palm parrying forward past the right inner side
图 59
Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch: the left bow stance, the right fist punching forward with the fist eye facing up and the left palm drawn back close to the wrist on the inner side of the right forearm

3. The body gradually turns right (to face east); the right foot steps out one pace to the right front (slightly toward the southeast), heel touching down first with the toes turned out, At the same time the right fist deflects out forward and to the right past the chest, the arm rotating outward as it deflects so that the fist centre gradually turns over and the fist eye faces up. The left palm closes in toward the right hand, its heel resting against the inner side of the right wrist; as it deflects out the two hands are about level with the shoulders. Immediately the ball of the right foot is set down solidly, the whole weight gradually shifts onto the right leg, the left leg lifts and moves forward, and the waist gradually turns right at the same time. As the waist turns the right fist gradually draws back along an arc to the right, the right arm rotating outward so that the fist centre gradually turns up; the left palm likewise follows the turning waist and parries forward past the right inner side (see the first and second figures in the left-hand column).

4. The left foot steps one pace forward, heel touching down first; at the same time the body continues to turn right, and as it turns the left palm continues to strike forward flat and straight (with the side (This page also carries an unnumbered wide photograph: Fu Zhongwen in a light practice suit demonstrating the deflect-and-parry posture from the front, with the left hand pressing the right wrist. It bears no printed figure number, so it receives no figure note.)

of the palm upright), the right fist drawing back along an arc to beside the waist with the fist centre facing up (the two hands drawing apart, one forward and one back) (see the first figure on this page).

5. The weight then gradually shifts onto the left leg until the whole foot is set down; the left leg bows and the right leg pushes back, forming a left bow stance. At the same time the body gradually turns left, and as the waist turns the right fist punches forward, the fist eye gradually turning to face up; the left palm draws back slightly toward the chest, seating the wrist, the fingertips slanting upward and the palm facing right, moving to a point on the middle of the right forearm nearer the wrist, as if touching yet not touching (see the second figure on this page).

III. Essentials

1. In the successive steps forward, one must "step as a cat steps", and the speed must be even, matching above and below. The body must be straight and correct, never slanted, never leaning forward or back.

2. The right foot steps to the right front; this step is required to be rather wider than an ordinary step, but one must avoid the upper body tipping to the right as the right foot steps.

3. The movements of the four limbs must turn with the waist. The right palm arcing to the left and down is precisely the turning of the body to the left. The right fist arcing and deflecting forward is precisely the turning of the upper body to the right; the right fist punching forward is precisely the moment when the upper body turns left and the left leg bows while the right leg pushes back.

4. When the right fist deflects out it must not be too far from the body, and care must be taken not to raise the elbow.

5. In punching out one must "let the fist issue from the heart" — that is, not extend it at random but strike with deliberation, so that inner and outer are as one.

6. In parrying, hand and foot must arrive together, matching above and below.

7. The fist must be closed naturally and firmly, not clenched with force (and so with the whole set), but it must not be a hollow fist either.

IV. Requirements

1. At the point where the punch lands (the settled posture) the back of the fist must form a straight line with the forearm; it must not be bent inward or turned outward, otherwise the wrist is easily injured when a resisting force strikes it.

2. Substantial and insubstantial must be clearly distinguished. The left foot must turn out and sit solid before the right leg is gradually lifted and brought forward; at the moment the right heel lands the weight is still on the left foot, and the weight must then be moved forward slowly — in this way the step will not drag weight with it.

3. The head must be straight and upright and must have the lifting strength — that is, the spirit runs through to the crown; but the head and neck are not exerted strongly, it is not a hard pushing upward, and forcing the neck makes blood and breath not flow freely; hence one must naturally "let the nape lift the crown".

4. In the parry the left hand is in front and the right fist behind, in opposite directions but answering each other; one must achieve "drawing apart and lengthening, seeking the straight within the curved".

5. The deflect is a circling movement along an arc — "one marvellous hand makes one tai chi". Within this circle there must be both yielding and firm, both insubstantial and substantial, firmness and yielding aiding each other, substantial and insubstantial interpenetrating — it is not a circle suddenly drawn in the middle.

Book page 350

V. Errors That Are Easy to Make, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

V. Errors That Are Easy to Make, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: when deflecting, the right fist circles down in too big a loop. The main cause is an insufficient grasp of the martial requirement of the "deflect". Correction: the action should use my right wrist to deflect the opponent's right wrist from the left ribs across to the right ribs; so the right elbow should be the pivot and the fist should go down to the left, passing from between the left ribs, turning the wrist as the waist turns right, over to below the right ribs.

2. Error: the fist and the waist fall out of step — in the "deflect" only the hand moves and the waist does not, and in punching out the waist is not used to drive it either. The main cause is insufficient attention to "at every moment keep the mind at the waist". Correction: one must carefully experience "palm, wrist, elbow and shoulder, back, waist, hip, knee and leg — nine joints above and below, and every joint issues from the waist". Hence raising a hand or stepping a leg must all be driven by the waist; the movement of the hand alone cannot neutralize an incoming punch.

3. Error: in the "deflect" the right fist goes from the lower left forward, and before the movement is finished the right arm is drawn back. The main cause is an insufficient understanding of the application. With the opponent's right fist striking straight forward, if my deflecting movement goes from the lower left forward, then the opponent's right fist is still in front of my body and I am still under attack. If I then deflect to the right, the opponent's right fist is beside my body, and because the straight-striking fist has been carried left and then right by me, its strength is neutralized by me, creating the conditions for my own forward attack. Correction: the deflecting movement should go from between the left ribs to below the right ribs.

4. Error: the deflecting movement is too low. The main cause is a failure to understand the application. Because the opponent's punch comes at the chest and ribs, if I circle in front of the abdomen I do not accord with the actual situation of the neutralization. Correction: the right fist and left hand should be about level with the chest.

5. Error: hand and leg fall out of step — in the "deflect", the "parry" and the "punch" there is no support from the legs. The main cause is inattention to the actions of the lower body here. Correction: within advancing there must be a supporting-back. The feet must be as if rooted in the ground, the base steady; only then is the fist powerful and can the lower body gain the opportunity and the position.

6. Error: the fist or palm is carried too far from the body when striking. The main cause is insufficient attention to storing the momentum. Correction: if fist or palm passes too far beyond the knee, the stability of the centre of gravity is easily lost and the strength becomes rigid and interrupted. Therefore one must note that "strength is stored in the bent so that there is a surplus"; in punching or pushing out the palm one must not straighten the arm and extend it far.

7. Error: the centre of gravity rises and falls too much. The main cause is poor command of the substantial and insubstantial of the two legs. Correction: stepping a leg out or drawing a leg back must both be done while one leg is sitting solid; in this way substantial and insubstantial become clear and the rise and fall small.

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explain, and demonstrate. After demonstrating the movement as a whole, break it down into deflect, parry and punch so that the concept of the whole movement is clear.

2. Mnemonic for the movement: turn out the foot and close the fist, raise the right foot; turn the body and join the hands in an arcing deflect; sit solid on the right leg and draw apart in the parry; left leg bows and right fist punches, arriving together.

3. Practise the whole movement as a group.

4. Take the three actions — deflect, parry and punch — separately, and learn them one by one.

5. Progressive method: (i) turn the left toes outward, the left hand goes back and the right hand down to the left. (ii) As above, lift the right foot and sit solid on the left leg. (iii) As above, bring the right leg forward, the right fist arcing forward and up and deflecting to the right, the left hand moving up to the right to near the right wrist, the right leg stepping out forward with the right heel landing. (iv) As above, continue turning the body right, the left hand parries out, the right fist draws back to the waist, the left leg steps out and the heel lands. (v) As above, bow the left leg, the body turns slightly left, the left hand draws back slightly, the right fist punches forward, and the left hand rests at the right elbow and wrist.

Once a part of the preceding movement has been basically mastered, then add the following part — practise the two parts together, and so on; finally, practise the movement in its entirety.

6. Paired application drills: (i) A — stands upright and strikes forward with his right fist; B — from the position of Left Brush Knee, steps out with the right foot and uses the deflecting method to carry A's right fist from the left across to the right. (ii) A — steps back; B — steps out with the left foot and strikes straight forward with the left palm. (iii) A — steps back; B — bows the left leg and punches straight out with the right fist. This makes the actions of deflect, parry and punch vivid and concrete.

7. Observe from different angles to find and correct errors: (i) from the front, watch the turning out of the foot and the closing of the fist. (ii) From the left side, watch the height and distance of the deflect and the position of the left hand. (iii) From the front, watch the lateral distance of the right foot. (iv) From the right side, watch the height of the drawing-apart palms in the parry, and that the right fist withdraws without exposing the elbow. (v) From the side, watch that bowing the leg and punching out arrive together.

8. Students help one another.

9. Practise more: sitting solid on the left leg, slowly lifting the right leg and stepping out to the right front (east, slightly toward the south), a little wider than an ordinary step.

Book page 351

VII. Technical Analysis

VII. Technical Analysis

1. This movement requires two steps forward, while the hands are in unceasing motion; hence it makes high demands on clearly distinguishing substantial and insubstantial and on a stable lower body. For this reason one must take care that one leg sits solid while the other moves lightly and nimbly.

2. The actions of deflect, parry and punch must be closely coordinated with the turning of waist and hips; use intention, not force — but the intention must be brought to bear.

3. The movement must be continuous. Let there be no defect, no hollow or protruding place, no interruption: the three actions are finished in a single breath.

# Thirteenth Posture: Apparent Close-Up (Ru Feng Si Bi)

I. Application
图 60
Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch: the left leg bowed and the right fist punching straight out (demonstration for the technical analysis)
图 61A
Apparent Close-Up: the left hand raised and passed beneath the right elbow, the palm stuck to the elbow to guard the arm and parrying away toward the opponent's left wrist
图 61B
Apparent Close-Up: the right fist opened and drawn and folded inward to the breast, the two palms crossing at a slant face inward to form a slanted cross sealing bar

Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent grasps my right fist with his left hand, I immediately raise my left hand and pass it under my right elbow, sticking the palm to the elbow to guard the arm, and parry away toward the opponent's left wrist. If the opponent changes hands to press in, I then open out my right fist, drawing and folding it inward toward my breast until the two palms face inward and cross at a slant, forming a slanted cross like a sealing bar, so that the opponent cannot enter — as though closing a door. This is called "as if sealing" (ru feng). At the same time, hollowing the chest and sitting the hips, the two hands then separate, changing so that the two palms are about to press and hold his elbow and wrist, so that he can neither escape nor neutralize, as though his door were shut and could not be opened — this is called "as if closing" (si bi). Then, swiftly using a long strength, pressing outward with the press posture, the eyes looking ahead, the strength of the waist also joining in the attack, The left leg bends and sits solid, the right leg straightens with the hip; they combine into a single strength and strike at the opponent — this too is a closing method. Variation: if my right fist is grasped, the right hand sinks down and I then step in with a shoulder-lean.

II. Course of the Movement

1. The right leg bends and the weight gradually shifts back onto the right leg; at the same time the left palm extends forward past the right elbow, along under the forearm, the arm rotating outward as it extends so that the palm faces up, then rotating inward so that the palm turns inward. The right fist becomes a palm, the elbow sinking, and draws back inward; as it draws back the arm rotates outward so that the palm also turns inward. The two arms cross, the right arm inside, the fingertips slanting up, the two palms and fingers level with the shoulders, forming a slanted cross shape. The gaze attends to both palms (see the figures 60 and 61 at the top of the right-hand column).

2. The weight continues to shift back; sit solid on the right leg (the left leg must not straighten completely). The two palms separate to left and right, a little wider than the shoulders, and as they separate the two arms rotate inward, gradually turning the two palms over until they face each other (see the first figure in the left-hand column).

3. The weight gradually moves forward; the left leg bows and the right pushes back, forming a left bow stance. At the same time the two palms press out forward, and as they press the two arms continue rotating inward so that the palms turn to face obliquely forward, the wrists slightly below shoulder height. The gaze must attend to the forward press of the two palms (see the second figure in the left-hand column).

III. Essentials

1. The two arms should draw back and close as the body sits back. When the two arms cross, one must avoid the shoulders hunching or lifting; the shoulders must sink and the elbows hang, and room must be kept under the armpit, about enough to hold a fist. But the elbows must not protrude or lift outward, nor may they be withdrawn behind the body, so that one does not trap oneself.

2. In sitting the weight back, relax waist and hips and sit solid on the right leg; one must not fail to shift the weight back while merely drawing the arms in and tilting the body back, nor bend forward while pressing out. Whether sitting back or bowing forward, the upper body must stay straight and correct with the tailbone centred and upright. When the weight moves forward and back, note that chest and abdomen advance and retreat together, neither first nor last; then the body method stays centred and upright and the upper body will not tip forward or lean back.

3. The drawing back and the pressing out of the two hands are essentially horizontal, backward and forward; the elbow has a sinking action, but the hand does not sink down.

IV. Requirements

1. One must be able to keep the arms relaxed, soft and rounded while extending, contracting and turning the circle.

图 62A
Apparent Close-Up: the two palms separating to left and right a little wider than the shoulders, the two arms rotating inward so that the palms gradually face each other
图 62B
Apparent Close-Up: the two palms separated, the palms gradually facing each other
图 63
Apparent Close-Up: in the left bow stance the two palms press out forward, the palms facing obliquely forward and the wrists slightly below shoulder height

The key lies in whether the shoulder joint can be loosened; hence the requirement "sink the shoulders and hang the elbows" must be approached from the notion of "relaxation".

2. Sink the shoulders and hang the elbows, but also note that "the elbow does not stick to the ribs", so that the arm has room to turn; note that one must "relax and open so that my strength is not bent".

3. In advancing and retreating, shoulder and hip must stay aligned above and below, advancing and retreating together; then one will not behave like a rowing boat, with the seat unmoving while only the body tips forward and leans back.

4. The movement must be completed: do not separate the two hands before the slanted cross has formed.

5. As the hands move, the feet must at the same time sit slowly back. When the hand presses home, the foot is also required to bow home.

V. Errors That Are Easy to Make, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: the legs move while the hands do not, or the hands move while the legs do not. For example, at the start, as the left hand passes to below the right ribs and the right fist becomes a palm, the foot does not move at all. The main cause is insufficient attention to "when one part moves, every part moves". Correction: the moment the two hands above begin to move, the weight below must shift.

2. Error: the two hands cross for too long, held close against the chest, producing "inviting in and letting it land". The main cause is a shallow understanding of the application. The cross was originally formed to prevent the opponent's hand from entering, holding the intention of sealing; but if I myself bring the two hands close against my chest, then of course his pressing hand also lands on my body. Correction: the two hands must keep a certain distance from the chest, so that even when the opponent presses in I still have room to turn.

3. Error: when the two hands draw back the chest is hollowed and the shoulders tense and draw in. The main cause is failing to distinguish a hollowed chest from a contained chest. Containing the chest means the chest feels broad and at ease, which aids breathing, and the two shoulders close slightly forward. Hollowing the chest is a tense drawing in, which is bad for the neutralizing strength of the two hands. Correction: the shoulder joints must relax, the two shoulders close slightly forward, the chest broad — but one must not puff out the chest either.

4. Error: in moving the two hands forward and back, the rise and fall is great. The main cause is pursuing an outward "roundness and liveliness" while neglecting the requirements of the application. Correction: the two hands should move essentially level and straight. Because of the step type changes, the two hands seem to move up and down; only thus is it favourable for sealing the opponent's elbow and wrist so that he cannot escape or neutralize, and favourable for my own pressing out.

5. Error: on the forward press the fingers become stiff, or else collapse limply. The main cause is insufficient attention to the requirements of an upright wrist and relaxed, extended fingers. Correction: both pushing out and drawing back the palm should be chiefly natural and extended; one must not clench the fingers tight or spread them with force. The wrist joint must be round and lively, and on the forward push the heel of the palm should apply a slight force.

6. Error: in the forward bow the left knee goes beyond the toes — this is called "overshooting the strength". The main cause is a subjective belief that this makes the movement fuller, whereas in fact it makes the change-over sluggish. Correction: the knee joint may go slightly forward of the vertical line of the lower leg, but it must not pass beyond the toes.

7. Error: the left leg bows first while the two palms are still slowly pressing forward, so that hand and foot do not arrive together. The main cause is a shallow understanding of the application. "Issuing strength requires above and below to match, and then one goes forward invincibly." If the foot arrives but the hand does not, above and below do not match; such a press has only the strength of the hand and cannot make the strength rise from the heel. Correction: hand must arrive with foot; the pressing hand requires the coordination of a forward bow and a backward push. Hence, within advancing, there must be a supporting-back.

Book page 352

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explain, and demonstrate.

2. Practise together as a group, following the leader.

3. From the front, check the distance between the separated hands; from the left side, look at the point where the left hand passes the right elbow; from the right side, look at the amount the two hands rise and fall as they move forward and back.

4. Mnemonics for the movement: (i) thread through, cross, turn over, press; (ii) parry, seal, close, press.

5. The successive positions of the two hands as they move should be practised section by section, so that the student has a clear understanding of the requirements of the movement.

6. Paired application drills: A — takes up the settled posture of Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch; B — stands upright and grasps A's right hand with his left. A — parries forward with his left hand from below the right elbow; B — steps up with the left foot and, changing hands, presses forward with both palms. A — the two hands cross at a slant, then separate, holding down B's elbow and wrist and pressing out with a long strength.

VII. Technical Analysis

1. Although this movement has no stepping, sitting back and bowing forward make high demands on the beginner's tailbone being centred and upright. Therefore one must earnestly practise shoulders and hips advancing and retreating together.

2. The sealing and closing movement travels a short distance and changes fast; a moment's inattention and the movement is easily performed perfunctorily. Hence the requirements on relaxing the shoulders, containing the chest and holding the wrist upright are high.

3. Practising tai chi chuan requires quiet: one must set aside distracting thoughts and be calm and even in temper. At first one thinks only of the method of the movement, the direction, the angle and so on, and easily loses one thing while attending to another; after long practice the movements become skilful and the mind gradually quiets of itself. This exerts a very good regulating effect on the cerebral cortex and is of good use in preventing and treating various chronic diseases and strengthening the constitution.

# Fourteenth Posture: Cross Hands (Shi Zi Shou)

I. Application
图 64
Cross Hands: the two hands separating from above and joining from below, forming the cross shape in front of the forehead

Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent comes at me from my right side, from above downwards, I immediately open out my right arm upward and wide to the right, and the body turns right at the same time, while the left foot turns in to the right. The two hands separate from above and then join from below, forming a cross shape. The whole body sits on the left leg; the right foot is immediately lifted and drawn back half a step to the left, the two feet planted flat as in the Opening Posture. This is an opening energy and a closing energy. When I use opening energy to separate the opponent's hands, I guard against the opponent seizing the opening to strike at my chest, and so I at once make the two hands into a closing energy. At this moment the palms face inward, pinning the opponent's arm. If the opponent presses in with both hands, I use both hands to separate his arms from the inside out to left and right, palms up or palms down, either will do. But when the cross hands are formed, the knees and waist must at the same time relax somewhat and sink down a little, and then the force coming from the opponent is of itself scattered and broken.

II. Course of the Movement

1. The body turns right, and at the same time the left toes turn in (facing south), sitting firmly on the left leg. As the waist turns and the elbows bend, the two hands move to the right (south) until they reach in front of the forehead (see the first figure on this page). They stop about two of the practitioner's fists from the forehead. As they move the two arms rotate slightly inward so that the palms face forward and the arms form a ring. Following the turning of the waist, the gaze passes between the two palms and looks level ahead.

2. The centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely to the left leg; the right heel leaves the ground first and the whole foot lifts, drawing in to the left, touching down toes-first toward the south (shoulder-width), then the whole foot gradually presses flat; at once the centre of gravity shifts right, the two legs gradually straighten, and at the same time the left toes lift slightly and the two knees bend slightly, forming a feet-apart stance. At the same time the two palms separate, each descending from left and right, passing in front of the abdomen; the right palm on the outside joins and crosses and arcs upward to in front of the collarbone, the left wrist about three fists' distance from the chest. As the two palms move down to below shoulder height, the two arms rotate outward as they move so that the palms gradually turn to face inward. The eyes first follow the arcing of the two palms, and when the two arms are about to cross they look level ahead (see the second and third figures on this page).

III. Key Points

1. As the left toes turn in and gradually press flat, the two hands move with the turning of the body (toward the south), arcing upward as they move.

2. The right foot gradually lifts off the ground and steps down; the centre of gravity gradually shifts to the right leg. It should be like a see-saw, one end rising as the other falls; the two feet must not share the body's weight equally (double weighting).

3. As the two hands move up, the mind must attend to the point of energy — the ulnar side of the two wrists.

图 65
Cross Hands: the body turns right, the two hands move in front of the forehead, the two arms forming a ring
图 66
Cross Hands: the right foot draws in to the left and presses flat, the two palms descending from left and right past the front of the abdomen
图 67
Cross Hands: the two palms cross and arc upward to enfold in front of the collarbone, the gaze level ahead

4. As the two hands move down, the left leg must sink, and at the same time "send down" the right leg.

5. When the two hands cross in front of the chest they must go slightly upward and outward, until the heels of the two palms are level with the shoulders, so that the movement is rounded and possesses ward-off energy.

6. The whole Cross Hands movement must have upper and lower accompanying each other: the hands' and feet's movements should begin at the same time and end at the same time, and must be coordinated.

7. When the two legs rise, the body must be upright and every part must relax.

Book page 353

IV. Requirements

IV. Requirements

1. When the left toes turn in and you sit solidly on the left leg, the waist and the crotch must be relaxed and mobile and the hip joints loosened; then waist and legs can follow each other.

2. Sit solidly on the left leg, draw the hip root slightly inward, rotate and sink; the right leg slowly lifts. When the right leg approaches the left leg, relax the left waist and knee somewhat and let the body sink down a little; the left leg must not sit so solidly as to be completely rigid.

3. As the two hands move up, the fingers are about level with the head.

4. As the two hands move down, the two elbows must not hang from above but form a full arc; the heels of the two palms must not drop below the waist.

5. When the cross hands are formed, the two arms must make a ring; relax the shoulders and sink the elbows; do not shrug the shoulders or lift the elbows.

V. Errors Easily Committed, Their Causes, and Their Correction

1. Error: the two palms rise too high. The main cause is an unclear grasp of the application of "separating". When I use opening energy to separate the opponent's hands, if the two hands are too high my own chest is left empty. Correction: the height of the two hands should not exceed the head by much.

2. Error: the right foot steps down, but not by bending the left leg to "send" it down. The main cause is tension in the hip root. Correction: after the right leg lifts, loosen the left hip root. First squat down on the left leg, while the right leg slowly descends. This is a strenuous way of practising; long practice can develop the muscles of waist and legs and make the step light and quick.

3. Error: hand and foot fall out of step — only the hands move while the feet do not, and the movement is broken. The main cause is failure to meet the requirement that upper and lower accompany each other. Correction: hands up, right foot lifts; hands down, right foot steps down; the two feet rise and the two hands go up.

4. Error: double weighting of the two feet at the settled Cross Hands. The cause The main cause is that most people take the section as finished — this is a resting movement. Correction: like a see-saw, when the right foot is solid the left foot must become empty; one foot does the work, not two feet sharing the weight — only then is there no double weighting. Otherwise the two feet stand dead, which is unfavourable for flexibly taking up the next movement.

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

1. Explain (with emphasis on double weighting) and demonstrate.

2. The group practises along, with emphasis on the coordination of hand and foot movements.

3. Students observe and correct one another, e.g. the height of the hands and the "sending" down of the right leg.

4. Each person senses the solidity and emptiness of the two feet, and compares and experiences double weighting.

5. Paired practice using the application: A — takes up the settled posture of Sealing and Closing; B — strikes down from above on A's right side. A — at once turns the left toes in and arcs the two hands upward to separate; B — presses with the right hand on A's chest from the front. A — moves the two hands down to join and form the cross and move it up, pinning the opponent's arm. The two then exchange roles.

6. Practise the linkages: ① as the press of Sealing and Closing is ending, in the moment between seeming to stop and not stopping, at once connect the right turn of the body, the turning in of the left toes and the moving of the two arms to the right. ② as Cross Hands ends, in the moment when the two hands seem to stop and yet do not, at once connect the turning in of the left toes, without allowing a pause, so that the link is round and lively.

图 68
Cross Hands linking into Embrace the Tiger and Return to the Mountain: the two hands arc upward and separate, the left toes turn in, the body turns right
图 69
Cross Hands linking into Embrace the Tiger and Return to the Mountain: the two hands come down, join and form the cross and move upward

# Fifteenth Posture: Embrace the Tiger and Return to the Mountain (Bao Hu Gui Shan)

I. Application

Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent closes in and strikes at my right side or from behind me, and there is no time to tell whether he is using hand or foot, I hastily turn my waist to the right, separate the two hands, step out with the right foot, bend the knee and sit solidly, the left leg straightening; the right hand, following the turning of the waist, intercepts toward the opponent's waist and then embraces back, while the left hand hastily follows forward to press. So the right hand first intercepts with the waist and then withdraws as an upward-facing palm, as in making the Embrace-the-Tiger posture. If the opponent's hand and foot are very fast and I fail to embrace him, but only deflect or press him out, and he then changes to strike with the left hand, I ward him back with the "unfold" energy; hence the unfold, squeeze and press movements of Grasp the Bird's Tail are appended below.

II. Course of the Movement
(1) Embracing the Tiger

1. The left toes turn in about 90° and press flat; the left leg gradually bends at the knee and squats down, and as the centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg the right foot gradually lifts (heel leaving the ground first); at the same time the body turns right about 135°. As the waist turns, the left palm withdraws downward from in front of the chest, the arm rotating inward to arc to the left, and is raised level with the left shoulder with the palm facing south-west; the right elbow sinks and naturally carries the right palm down, rotating inward as it moves so that the palm turns to face down. The eyes first attend to the raising of the left palm to the left, then turn right to look level ahead (see the first two figures on this page).

2. The right foot steps out diagonally to the right front (north-west), touching down heel first; as the centre of gravity gradually shifts onto the right leg the whole foot comes flat, the right leg bows and the left leg pushes, forming a right bow stance; the body continues to turn right. As the waist turns, the right palm continues downward, passes in front of the waist and gathers to the right side of the body, while the left palm goes from left upward past the left ear and strikes forward with the turning of the waist. The eyes attend slightly to the right palm embracing to the right, then look level ahead, and then attend to the left palm's forward strike (see the third, fourth and fifth figures on this page).

图 70
Embrace the Tiger and Return to the Mountain: the right foot steps out diagonally to the right front, the right hand gathering in past the front of the waist
图 71A
Embrace the Tiger and Return to the Mountain: the right leg bowing and the left leg pushing to form a right bow stance, the left palm striking forward
图 71B
Embrace the Tiger and Return to the Mountain: the settled posture with the left palm striking forward
(2) The Unfold Movement

1. The centre of gravity gradually shifts to the left leg and the waist gradually turns left; at the same time the left elbow sinks and the left arm rotates outward so that the palm faces inward and slantingly upward; the right palm arcs forward from the right side of the body and, passing inside the left hand, is raised in front of the left palm, the palm slanting downward.

2. The movement is the same as the unfold of Grasp the Bird's Tail, only the direction differs, This movement goes from the north-west diagonal toward the south-east, whereas the earlier Grasp the Bird's Tail unfolds from west toward east (see the first two figures on this page).

3. The squeeze movement (see the third and fourth figures on this page).

4. The press movement (see the fifth and sixth figures on this page).

Book page 354

III. Key Points

III. Key Points

1. The Embrace-the-Tiger movement turns from the Cross Hands, which face south, to face north-west behind and to the right; therefore the left toes must turn in fully, the waist turn and the stepping out of the right leg must be complete, and it must reach the true diagonal.

2. The right leg travels a direction of about 135°; therefore the left leg must sit solid and the waist and hips must be fully loosened so that the right leg moves fully with the turning of the waist.

3. The right hand embraces to the right rear, so its height is higher than in Brush the Knee — about level with the waist.

4. In linking Cross Hands into Embrace the Tiger and Return to the Mountain the two feet must not double-weight. The right heel steps down, the left toes lift slightly and turn in first, and at the same time the sole of the left foot presses flat and the right heel at once lifts.

5. After the right leg has stepped out and pressed flat, if you feel the turn is insufficient or awkward, you may let the sole of the left foot stay on the ground and rotate the heel outward.

IV. Requirements

1. As the left toes turn in, this must be coordinated with the squatting, the turning of the waist and the movement of the two arms; upper and lower move together, otherwise it does not accord with the principle "one part moves, no part is still".

2. After the waist turns right, the diagonal position in which the right leg steps out must be accurate, so that the left palm's strike goes in the north-west direction.

3. The toes must turn in properly. For the outward splaying and inward turning of the toes bear on the accuracy of the whole movement. In Embrace the Tiger and Return to the Mountain, if the left toes turn in insufficiently the strike direction comes out too far west, or if the right foot is forced to step out too far north, the hips are opened too wide and the two feet end up in an awkward, unstable stance. So the movement of the toes and the movement of the whole body are mutually related and mutually constraining; a moment's inattention makes the whole movement incorrect.

4. Solid and empty must be clear. After the waist turns right, the right leg must, in stepping out, be required to touch down slowly and lightly.

5. In the unfold of Embrace the Tiger, the right hand's forward extension and the left hand's withdrawal of the welcoming palm must happen at the same time as the centre of gravity slowly shifts back; otherwise the foot moves while the hand does not, or the hand moves while the foot does not — not "one part moves, no part is still".

V. Errors Easily Committed, Their Causes, and Their Correction

1. Error: double weighting at the very start of the movement, as the left toes turn in and the body turns. The main cause is an unclear conception of the movement. Correction: when the left toes turn in, most of the centre of gravity must be on the left foot; the left toes turn in and press flat, and the right heel lifts off the ground at once. In this way it is both light and free of double weighting.

2. Error: the turning of the waist and the movement of the two hands fall out of step — a commonly committed — the error of moving the hands without turning the waist. The main cause is a shallow grasp of the principle "the lord is in the waist, expressed in the fingers … it must always be one complete breath of energy". Correction: one must understand that the waist is the key to the turning of the upper and lower body, and therefore moving the hands requires turning the waist — that is, the waist must lead the hands. So in Embrace the Tiger the body does not first turn to face north-west and only then move the hands; rather the hands move as the waist turns, and the hands must arrive where the waist arrives.

3. Error: the direction in which the right foot lands when stepping out to the right rear is wrong; usually the angle of travel is insufficient. Then the direction of the hands' press comes out too far west. The main causes are that the left toes do not turn in enough and the hips do not open enough. Correction: the left toes must turn in as fully as possible. But often, because the two feet are placed too close together in Cross Hands, the left foot cannot turn in fully. Therefore correct the two feet of Cross Hands: the lateral distance should be about shoulder-width.

4. Error: during the unfold, hand and foot are poorly coordinated. One way is that the foot does not move and only the hands move — the right hand forward, the left hand back, the two hands moving while the feet do not. The other is that the centre of gravity shifts back quickly and sits entirely on the left leg, so that in the unfold there is only hand movement and no foot movement. The main cause is a shallow understanding of the application of the unfold. Correction: as the right hand goes forward and the left hand withdraws, the two legs must move slightly together and the centre of gravity gradually shift back.

Book page 355

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

1. Explain the course of the movement, its key points and its application.

2. Demonstrate: ① the movement as a whole. ② broken down, with emphasis on Embrace the Tiger and the preparation for the unfold.

3. Use contrast: compare the differing heights of the hands in Embrace the Tiger and in Brush the Knee and Twist the Step.

4. Study the passage from Embrace the Tiger into the unfold as a focus: first demonstrate and compare the movement of hands-without-feet and of feet-without-hands, let the students observe the results of the two errors, and then demonstrate and study the correct movement.

5. After the Embrace-the-Tiger posture the right hand extends forward, and this varies from person to person; the teacher should break it down for practice — in extending the right hand forward one must "hold the palm upright", that is, slightly — has a slanting palm spiralling forward.

# Sixteenth Posture: Fist Beneath the Elbow (Zhou Di Kan Chui)

I. Application

Continuing from the previous posture. On discovering the opponent striking from behind, the movement is like the Single Whip body-turn studied earlier and may be applied by reference. As the body is about to turn back to the front, the left foot plants flat straight to the front (east); the right foot then steps out half a step diagonally to the right front. When the right foot sits solid, the left foot lifts and lands on the heel with the toes raised. The two hands are level with the shoulders, and the body turns left along with them; at this moment I use my left wrist to meet the opponent's right wrist flat on the outside and push it aside to the left. When he loses his centred balance I drop the fingers of the left hand, approach his wrist and wind a small circle inward; the right hand at the same time goes left to meet his left hand and stick and join from above, so that both his hands are in an unfavourable position and he has lost the direction in which he wants to exert force. I then take my left wrist and press down his right wrist, and the right hand hastily forms a fist and turns to beneath the left elbow, tiger's mouth upward, storing strength in order to issue it wherever an opportunity offers.

A side variation: if, at my fist-beneath-the-elbow, the opponent uses his right hand to press slantingly on my left hand from my right, I take the opportunity to loose the right step and use the right hand to pluck the opponent's right wrist.

II. Course of the Movement

1. The waist turns left; at the same time the right toes turn in as far as possible and press flat, the left foot is empty, the two elbows sink slightly and bend a little, the two palms dip slightly, level with the shoulders, and with the turning of the waist wipe round half a flat ellipse to the left (the body turning from north toward south-west), the gaze following the turn of the body and looking level ahead, reaching the left slightly before the left palm arrives there, but the gaze must also attend to the right hand (see the first figure on this page).

图 78
Fist Beneath the Elbow: the right toes turning in and pressing flat, the two palms wiping round half a flat ellipse to the left with the turning of the waist

2. The body slowly turns right and the two palms, slightly outward, wipe round with the turning of the body inward past the front of the chest, arcing right through another half flat ellipse (body and arms turning from south-east toward south-west), the gaze shifting level with the turn of the body and also attending to the two palms (see the second figure on this page).

图 79
Fist Beneath the Elbow: the two palms wiping inward past the front of the chest, arcing right through another half flat ellipse
图 80
Elbow-Under-Fist: the left arm rotates outward and translates left along an arc, the right hand forms an upright palm with the palm turning to face left; both elbows sink slightly and bend a little, the two hands facing each other across a distance. (This figure is re-printed on the following page, before figure 81.)

3. The centre of gravity is still entirely on the right leg; the body slowly turns left and the left leg lifts and steps out toward the left rear (due east). With the turning of the body the left arm rotating outward so that the palm turns to face inward, translates in an arc to the left, and the right palm follows closely, also translating in an arc to the left, so that the right hand holds its palm upright and the palm turns to face left. The two elbows sink slightly and bend a little so that the two hands face each other at a distance. The gaze attends to the left palm moving left (see the first two figures on this page).

图 81
Fist Beneath the Elbow: the two hands facing each other at a distance, the gaze attending to the left palm moving left
图 82
Fist Beneath the Elbow: the left foot coming down to the left (east), touching down heel first and pressing flat
图 83
Fist Beneath the Elbow: the two palms translating in an arc to the left, the palms turning to face down
图 84
Fist Beneath the Elbow: the right leg lifting, shifting slightly forward and coming down, the centre of gravity moving onto the right leg
图 85
Fist Beneath the Elbow: with the turning of the body the left palm moves to slightly left of the front of the body and arcs down to the left
图 86
Fist Beneath the Elbow: the settled posture with the left palm moved by the turning of the body to slightly left of the front of the body

4. The left foot comes down to the left (east), touching down heel first, and the centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg. With the turning of the body the two palms translate in an arc to the left, and the left arm rotates inward as it moves so that the two palms turn to face down. The right leg lifts, shifts slightly forward and comes down, and the centre of gravity at once moves onto the right leg. When, with the turning of the body, the left palm has moved to slightly left of the front of the body it arcs down to the left. The gaze first attends to the left palm moving left, and when the right palm is about to arrive in front of the chest, to the right palm (see the third, fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh figures on this page).

图 87
Fist Beneath the Elbow: the left palm going from the left downward and inward, passing inside the right forearm and piercing forward and up, the right palm covering and grasping outside the left palm to form a fist placed beneath the left elbow

5. The centre of gravity shifts entirely to the right leg; the left foot lifts a little, moves slightly forward and comes down, touching down on the heel with the toes slightly raised; the body continues to turn slightly left. The left palm goes from the left downward and inward, passes inside the right forearm, and turns and pierces forward and up, palm facing right, the index finger level with the eyebrows and aligned with the tip of the nose; the right palm passes to the left outside the left palm, covering and grasping to form a fist, which is placed beneath the left elbow, the eye of the fist upward, and the upper body turns slightly right. The eyes attend a little to the left palm circling down to the left; when the left palm is about to pierce out past the inside of the right arm they look level ahead, but the gaze must still attend to the piercing out of the left palm (see the eighth figure on this page).

Book page 356

III. Key Points

III. Key Points

1. Solid and empty must be clear. The right toes turn in fully and the right leg bears the whole body's weight; only then can the left leg lift light and nimble.

2. The arms turn with the waist. It is through rotating the waist and turning the spine that movement is transmitted from the turning of the wrist and the turning of the upper arm to the tips of the hands. Therefore the movement of the arms must be as the boxing theory says, "the lord is in the waist" — one must not move only the arms without moving the waist.

3. It must proceed according to "when one part moves, no part is still; when one part is still, no part moves" and to the requirement of unbroken continuity — without corners, without pauses, rounded and coordinated. In the two movements of lifting the right foot and slightly lifting and setting down the left foot, the hands move as the feet move. Just as the settled posture of the hidden fist beneath the elbow is completed, the opportunity for the left-right opposing brace arises at this moment of seeming to stop and not stopping, and not as something joined and again broken; for the old force is spent and the new force not yet born, and this is the moment when one is most easily taken by an opponent seizing the opening.

4. The two feet must not double-weight; they must rise and fall in turn like a see-saw. When lifting the right foot or lifting the left foot, one leg must bear the body's weight.

5. When the two palms translate to the left, the right palm must not lie flat or swing down but must sit the wrist and stand upright; and the left hand must go forward while the right hand follows, at an equal distance.

6. In the settled posture the left knee must naturally bend slightly and the two shoulders must not shrug. The two arms form an arc and must not be held straight. The waist and hips must be relaxed, and the chest must not face the front squarely but turn slightly toward the right-front diagonal, while the two arms still face straight to the front (east), and the left palm must sit the wrist.

7. When the two hands translate eastward, the back of the left hand faces outward and the right palm faces left and outward; when the body turns to face the front (east) the left hand goes down first and the right hand goes forward afterwards — not both downward at the same time, because at this moment I use my left wrist to meet the opponent's right wrist flat on the outside and push it aside to the left, while the right hand goes to the left hand to meet his left hand; each has its own purpose.

IV. Requirements

1. Particular attention must be paid to the stepping: advance and retreat, and the transitions of solid and empty must be distinct. When the two arms begin to translate to the left, the right leg is solid and the left leg must be empty. When the body turns to the front, the left leg is solid and the right leg lifts easily; when the centre of gravity moves onto the right leg the left leg is empty and the landing step must be steady — the change of solid and empty is gradual, not sudden.

2. One must "let the hands follow the movement of the feet, and the feet follow the movement of the hands", with "upper and lower accompanying each other".

3. One must take the waist as the axis; the strength of the waist must be used appropriately, and only then does it aid the body's balance. The waist must not sway away from centre; therefore the body must not lean forward or backward.

4. When the right toes turn in, the right is solid and the left is empty; the centre of gravity should not shift left.

5. The movements of the hands must be clear. When the two hands swing level the distance between them is about 20 centimetres; too large or too small is incorrect.

6. The fingers should be slightly curved but must not be stiff. If the fingers are too curved, it is hard to carry the intent through to the fingertips; if they are too straight, that is stiffness. The intent must reach the fingertips, with the pads of the fingers exerting a very slight force; with long practice this makes the qi and blood flourish in the fingers.

Book page 357

V. Common Errors, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

V. Common Errors, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: the right foot is not turned in sufficiently, so the waist and hip cannot turn to the left fully. Main cause: the hip-root is not adducted enough and the knee is twisted too much, with too little foot-turning. Correction: lift the ball of the right foot slightly; the foot follows the knee and the knee follows the waist, so that the right sole turns in no less than 90°.

2. Error: when turning the foot in and turning the waist, the centre of gravity shifts left, producing double-weighting. Main cause: there is no right-fullness, and so no left-emptiness. The movement then cannot rotate freely, cannot gain power, and cannot keep a stable centre. Correction: the body's weight must settle fully on the right leg; during the turn the centre of gravity does not move — turn on the full right leg. The waist must be straight and the central axis must not sway, so that the upper body does not lean to one side. The waist-gap governs the two legs: on the solid side of the waist-gap, the leg below is also solid. Hence the left waist-gap must be empty.

3. Error: as the waist turns left and the left foot lifts and steps back to the left, the centre of gravity shifts left too quickly, destroying the principle of "uniform tempo in every movement." Main cause: the right foot is not fully turned in and the hip-root is not opened; added to that, at the moment the right foot turns in the centre of gravity is wrongly shifted left, so the right leg cannot exert its normal supporting power. The left leg is therefore forced to land quickly to gain support. Correction: turn the right foot in fully; the right knee stays under the centre of gravity without shifting; open the hip-root, and let the left leg step slowly.

4. Error: the two hands move left too high or too low. Main cause: insufficient attention to the application. The left hand meets the opponent's left hand flat, and the right hand connects with his left hand; if my hand is too high or too low it does not meet the requirement of "connecting." Correction: the proper height is with both hands level with the shoulders.

5. Error: after the body turns square (to the east), both hands press down at the same time. Main cause: insufficient attention to the application. The left hand should first push out to the left and then circle down in a small arc; the right hand then goes left-and-back, forming a fist that is carried lightly beneath the left elbow. Correction: the left hand goes down first while the right hand is still moving forward; the two hands must not press down simultaneously.

6. Error: moving the hands without moving the waist, so that upper and lower are disconnected. Main cause: there is no whole-body consideration governed by the waist — it is a tree without roots. Correction: when the hands go forward they must have a sinking, root-driven quality; the soles of the feet take the force, and as the waist and legs move forward the two hands move in the same direction.

7. Error: at the set position the upper body faces squarely to the front. Main cause: a shallow understanding of storing power. Correction: the body should be turned to the side. If the body faces squarely forward, the right fist that has turned in beneath the left elbow loses the stored impulse to strike at the ready, and the chest is also compressed, which obstructs the free flow of qi and blood.

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explanation (with emphasis on turning the foot in and on the movement of the two hands).

2. Demonstration of the whole movement.

3. Progressive-addition method:

  • ① Begin from the set position of Grasp the Sparrow's Tail / Embrace the Tiger and Return to Mountain, making a good link; immediately turn in the right foot while the two arms shift level to the left and to the right, arriving at the forward-right diagonal.
  • ② As above, then continue: the back of the left hand turns outward, the right hand forms a vertical palm; the left leg lifts, the upper body turns left, and the left leg steps forward with the heel landing first; the two arms follow the waist and transfer to the front of the body. Once ② is grasped at a basic level, join it to ①.
  • ③ Shift the centre of gravity forward; the two hands move forward with the waist; the centre of gravity gradually moves onto the left foot; the right leg lifts slightly; the left hand turns to a downward palm. Once grasped at a basic level, join ①②.
  • ④ Shift the centre of gravity back; the right foot shifts slightly to the right and comes down, seating the right leg; the left hand circles in a small arc inside the right arm and threads out; the right hand forms a fist and is placed beneath the left elbow; the left foot lifts and comes down slightly forward-left, heel landing first. Once grasped at a basic level, join ①②③.
  • ⑤ The complete movement. Note: in the progressive-addition practice, take particular care that the movement is unbroken and continuous, with no place where it halts.

4. Paired practice combining the application:

  • ① A — takes the set position of Embrace the Tiger and Return to Mountain (facing northwest); B — comes out from behind A (the east); A — turns the body left, seats the right leg, and shifts the two hands level to the left and right; turning the body left, A steps the left foot out to the front (east), meets B's right wrist level with his own left wrist, pushes out toward B's right, then drops and, clinging to B's wrist, circles inward in a small arc; the right hand meets B's left hand and adheres to it from above. ② A's left wrist rolls B's right wrist, while A's right hand turns

…the fist turns to beneath the left elbow, waiting there at the ready, or immediately strikes forward.

5. Mnemonic: turning left, turn in the right foot; both hands shift level as the body turns; left hand horizontal, right hand vertical palm; turning left, step out the left foot; the rear foot is reset; the front foot lifts and comes down again; the left arm circles in a small arc; the right fist hides beneath the elbow.

6. The student should first concentrate on training emptiness and fullness: the right foot turned in fully, the right leg seated solidly, the centre of gravity not shifting left. Lift the left foot toward the rear-left (east); the right leg must be steady, the hip must be open; as the body turns square, the right knee must follow the direction of the toes and must not twist inward. The body turns about 45° + 180°; so if the right foot is not turned in fully and the lower body is not stable, turning the body square is difficult. Hence emptiness and fullness must be practised repeatedly.

7. Turning the waist, shifting the centre of gravity, and the movement of the hands — these three are "upper and lower following one another," and may be practised separately (practising only the waist turn, only the weight shift, only the hand movement). This lets the beginner learn the movement rather quickly; but take care: separating is for the sake of joining, and in the end the upper and lower must follow one another. Fortunately, in the later stage of this movement the body turns slightly right, the left foot lifts slightly and comes down again, and at the same time the left palm threads out and the right palm becomes a fist — so that upper and lower do follow one another, rather than each going its own way.

Book page 358

VII. Technical Analysis

VII. Technical Analysis

1. In this movement one must first be clear about the change of direction. From the set position of Embrace the Tiger and Return to Mountain, where the body faces northwest, the two arms shift level first toward the southeast and then toward the southwest, and finally move to the east — and to this are added the changes of step of the two feet and the differing actions of the two hands… The movement is thus fairly complex. One must therefore concentrate on the progressive-addition method of learning: be clear about the direction, be clear about the movement, and climb as if going up stairs, one step at a time — firmly fix each part as you learn it, and only then add the next.

2. In this movement the body's weight is alternately supported on one leg. It looks like an alternation; but because the movement is slow, with one leg supporting and the other lifted clear for a long time, the actual time under static load is considerable. The demands this makes on the strength of the muscles of the waist, hips and legs are high. And precisely because of this, the muscles concerned are very well trained.

3. After the right foot is turned in and the right leg seated solidly, the left leg is empty and the left hip is relaxed. The leftward turn of the waist carries the two arms in a level shift to the left; at this moment the two shoulder-joints are required to line up level with the two shoulders, striving to achieve "shoulder and hip joined together." Therefore …the demands on the opening and relaxing of the hip-joint are very high; otherwise, with so large an angle of rotation, how could the movement be completed smoothly?

4. The burden carried by the full right leg is very great. It is like the movement of the trunk and branches of a great tree: because the root and limbs are as firm as a great root and a deep root, it stands steady and unmoving — and so this is a very demanding form of training.

# Seventeenth Posture: Step Back and Repulse the Monkey, Left and Right (Zuo You Dao Nian Hou)

I. Application

Continuing from the preceding posture: if the opponent uses his right hand to grip my left wrist or forearm tightly, and with his left hand supports the fist beneath my elbow, then I am first constrained by him and cannot execute my movement. At this moment I turn my left fist over upward, and with a sinking energy relax the waist and hip, withdrawing it back-left, while the left foot also steps back one pace, bending the knee and seating it solidly, and the right foot becomes empty. The opponent's grip is then lost at once. At the same time, the right hand separates to the rear, and at the instant he loses his grip I press forward swiftly. Although this posture takes one step backward, it can still repulse the opponent's energy — hence it is called "Repulse the Monkey." In this movement, take care to relax the shoulders and sink the elbows.

II. Movement Sequence
(A) Left Repulse the Monkey

1. The right hip-root draws in slightly; sit firmly on the right leg; the left leg lifts slightly with the toes hanging naturally; the body turns slightly right. At the same time the left palm drops slightly and extends slightly forward; the right fist becomes a palm, drawing from beneath the left elbow past the front of the abdomen, curving down-and-across to the side of the right hip; as it draws, the right arm rotates outward so that the palm gradually turns upward. The gaze follows the forward extension of the left palm (see the figures on this page).

2. The centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely onto the right leg, and the body continues to turn slightly right; the left foot slowly lifts and draws in past the inside of the right ankle. At the same time the right palm continues to arc up to the rear and slightly right until it is level with the shoulder, the palm facing slanting upward.
