# Twenty-eighth Posture: Wave Hands Like Clouds (Yun Shou)

Book page 371

I. Application

I. Application

Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent attacks my chest or ribs with his right hand from the right of my front, I immediately lower my right hand with the palm facing inward, and join the upper side of my wrist (the radial side) to the lower side of the opponent's wrist (the ulnar side), warding from the left upward and rotating to the right; then I turn it downward and move it across to the left, drawing one great circle, like white clouds drifting in the sky, without a break. The left hand at the same time lowers, palm facing down, with the same intent as the right hand. The body also turns with the right wrist, and the gaze follows the wrist, attending as it turns.

the hand and chest turning, the gaze following the wrist as it turns, attending as it turns.

The right foot moves half a step to the left from the right rear side and settles firmly, and the left foot at once steps out one step to the left, the weight shifting left into a horse-riding stance (for an instant). At this moment the two hands have arrived exactly opposite the chest and navel, and then the right foot again becomes empty and moves half a step further in to the left, and the second movement continues. But when changing from empty to full and back in the interwoven turning, there must never be any intent of concavity, convexity, interruption or discontinuity. The subtle use of this posture lies entirely in turning the waist and hips: because the turning can draw along the opponent's root strength, one turns the hand out in response. The learner should savour and grasp this carefully.

The slanting application: when the opponent thrusts straight in with his right palm or right fist, I ward with my right hand, and at the same time immediately hollow the chest and sink onto the back leg, turning the waist and sinking downward to neutralize the force of his incoming energy; then I may use Shoulder or Elbow, or attack out with Press.

II. The Course of the Movement

1. Turn the waist slightly to the right without changing the weight; turn the left toes inward and set them down firmly, toes pointing forward. At the same time the left palm, following the turning of the body, bends the arm slightly and sinks the elbow, palm facing down, and moves naturally and very slightly to the right. The right hook hand changes into a palm and arcs down from the right, moving across horizontally at the bottom of the arc to the front of the right abdomen. The gaze attends to the right palm as it moves down (see the first figure at the right-hand side of this page, the second figure at the right-hand side of this page).

2. The weight gradually shifts entirely to the left leg; the right foot lifts and draws in towards the left (the heel leaving the ground first), the body turns slightly left, and the left palm follows the waist's turning. At the same time it transports out to the left (with a slight arc), and as the arm turns inward the wrist is held upright so that the palm slopes downward and gradually turns to face down. The right palm, following the turning of the body, travels in an arc from the lower right across the front of the abdomen to the left, and as it travels the arm turns outward so that the palm faces inward, and it gradually travels up to the left to near the left wrist. The gaze shifts as the body turns, looking level ahead, and it must attend to the right palm travelling left (see the third figure at the right-hand side of this page).

图 149
Wave Hands Like Clouds: the right hand changing from the hook hand into a palm and arcing down from the right to the front of the right abdomen
图 150
Wave Hands Like Clouds: the left palm bending the arm and sinking the elbow as the body turns, palm facing down and shifting slightly right
图 151
Wave Hands Like Clouds: the right palm travelling in an arc across the front of the abdomen to the left, arriving near the left wrist

3. The left leg continues to squat down and "sends" the right leg down (the right foot half a step towards the left), the toes touching the ground first, and as the weight gradually shifts right the whole foot is set down firmly; the two feet are about a shoulder's width apart, parallel and facing forward, and the left foot at once becomes empty. At the same time the body turns slightly right. The right palm, following the waist's turning, travels in an arc from the left upward and to the right (the fingers level with the shoulder), the palm still facing inward. This is joining the upper side of my right wrist to the lower side of the opponent's wrist, rotating from the left downward and then upward again, using the strength of the turning waist and hips to turn out to the right, so as to draw along the opponent's root strength. The left palm at the same time arcs down from the left and towards the right, and as it travels the arm turns slightly outward so that the palm gradually turns to face inward (slanting slightly upward). The two hands have travelled up and down to exactly opposite the chest and navel, the right hand above and the left hand below. The gaze accompanies the turning of the body, attending to the right palm travelling right (see the first figure at the left-hand side of this page).

4. The weight gradually shifts entirely to the right leg; the left foot lifts (the heel leaving the ground first) and the body continues to turn slightly right, and at the same time the right palm, following the turning of the body, arcs to the right and downward, and as it travels the arm turns inward so that the palm gradually turns to face down. The left palm, crossing the front of the abdomen, continues to travel to the upper right, drawing near to the right wrist to the right. The gaze attends to the right palm travelling right (see the second figure at the left-hand side of this page).

5. Repeat from the start of movement two. The left foot strides half a step across to the left, the toes touching the ground first, and as the weight gradually shifts left the whole foot is set down firmly, toes pointing forward; at the same time the body gradually turns left, and the left palm, following the turning of the body, continues from the right upward past the face (the fingers level with the eyebrows), travelling to the left. This is joining the upper side of my left wrist to the lower side of the opponent's wrist, rotating from the left downward and then upward again, using the strength of the turning waist and hips to turn out to the left, so as to draw along the opponent's root strength (the application is the same as for the right hand). The right palm continues to travel in an arc from the right downward and to the left, and as it travels the arm turns slightly outward so that the palm gradually turns to face inward (slanting slightly upward) and travels to the front of the abdomen. The two hands have travelled up and down to exactly opposite the chest and navel, the left hand above and the right hand below. The gaze shifts as the body turns, looking level, and must attend to the left palm travelling left (see the third figure at the left-hand side of this page, the fourth figure at the left-hand side of this page).

6. The weight gradually shifts entirely to the left leg; the right foot lifts to the right and towards towards the left (the heel leaving the ground first), while the body continues to turn left and the left palm continues to travel in an arc from above, downward to the left. As it travels the arm turns inward so that the palm gradually turns to face down. The right palm, following the turning of the body, continues across the front of the abdomen to the left, and travels in an arc from below upward to near the left wrist. 7. Repeat the movement: the three plates at the foot of the next page repeat, in order, the third, first and second plates at the sides of this page.

In order to increase the amount of exercise, "Wave Hands Like Clouds" may also be done as three, five, or seven movements.

But the number must be odd, and "Step Back and Repulse the Monkey" must likewise be done three, five, or seven times accordingly. Otherwise, when one comes to the closing and gathering up, one will not be able to return to the original place.

Book page 372

III. Essential Points

III. Essential Points

1. "Wave Hands Like Clouds" requires unbroken continuity, with intent and without force. One "Wave Hands Like Clouds" must follow another, endlessly continuous, going round and round without end. What the boxing treatises say — "like the long Yangtze and the great sea, rolling on and on without cease, threaded through as one breath" — means exactly that there must be no place of pause in the middle of the movement.

2. The two feet must not be double-weighted — that is, the two feet must not bear the body's weight on the ground at the same time. As soon as the heel of the descending foot has set down firmly, the other foot's heel must immediately leave the ground, rising and falling in turn like a see-saw, so that the two feet alternate without ever pausing.

3. The circling of the hands must take the turning of the waist and hips as its foundation: the waist is like an axle, the four limbs like wheels. The waist is the key to the turning of the upper and lower body, and it plays the principal role in the changes of the whole body's movement, in adjusting and steadying the centre of gravity, and in driving the jin power out to every part of the limbs. Therefore the turning must take the waist and spine as its axis and turn slowly; one must not swing about at random, the upper body must not lean or slant, must not stoop forward or lean back, and one must maintain "the tailbone centred and upright."

图 161

4. The two arms must travel with the waist: turning left, the left hand's upward scooping leads; turning right, the right hand's upward scooping leads. When the left hand leads, the right hand follows; when the right hand leads, the left hand follows — one up, one down, one left, one right, closely coordinated better still.

# Twenty-ninth Posture: Single Whip (Continuing from the twenty-seventh posture, Single Whip; both the application and the course of the movement are identical.) (See the figures on the following pages.)

circling without scattering or stagnating; when the turn reaches the top the elbow must not lift, and the forearm must ward loosely and keep circling. The two arms must maintain their arcs.

5. There must be "evenness from form to form". When the left leg steps out the movement must be slow and set down lightly; when the right leg lifts it must rise slowly and draw in towards the left, to a shoulder's width, and must not be sometimes fast and sometimes slow.

6. Every movement of Yang-style Taijiquan is constituted by a circle — hence the saying, "a marvellous hand is one movement, and one movement is a taiji." Within this circle are contained the two forces of yin and yang: there must be softness and there must be firmness, emptiness and fullness, firmness and softness assisting each other, emptiness and fullness interpenetrating. The carrying out of its movements always has the appearance of drawing circles and travelling along arcs; it never goes straight out and straight back — this too is a characteristic of Taijiquan. "Wave Hands Like Clouds" is a typical movement of this kind, and it plays an important part in raising the standard of the techniques of "continuous adhering and following" and "drawing in to make the opponent fall into emptiness."

Book page 373

IV. Requirements

IV. Requirements

1. The circling of the hands must be led by the waist, and the waist and hands must not come apart. When the opponent uses his right hand to strike my chest or ribs from the right of my front, my right wrist receives his wrist, turning up and over from below, to the left and then to the right; this must be coordinated with the turning of the waist and hips for the power to be obtained.

2. The two feet stand parallel, about a shoulder's width apart, neither too wide nor too narrow, and the two feet must not turn into the inward splay or the outward splay. The feet are the foundation of the stance forms and the stepping methods; if the foundation is unsteady, then at the least deviation the stance forms and stepping methods are certain to go awry.

(This page carries one unnumbered push-hands photograph at the foot; it has no figure number and no caption.)

3. There must be no double-weighting, for double-weighting makes one sluggish. The left foot supports while the right foot lifts and draws in towards the left; when the right foot squats down and the right heel drops, the left heel must lift at the same moment, otherwise it is double-weighting.

4. When the two arms circle they must not be straightened but must form an arc, and the distance from the body must be appropriate. If the arms are too far from the body they will be strained straight; if too close they will "deflate".

5. The two hands must have ward-off jin; they must not go slack, but neither may they use stiff force.

6. The movements must be continuous — this is the requirement of "Wave Hands Like Clouds" that stands out most. The circling of the hands must be like white clouds moving across the sky, without a break.

7. The shoulders must be relaxed, but not relaxed to excess such that they become "empty" or "loose".

8. The hand circling below must embody the action requirement of "scooping".

V. Common Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Fault: "double-weighting", that is, the two feet bearing the weight at the same time. The principal cause is an insufficient grasp of the clear division of empty and full. "When one side is heavy it follows; when double-weighted it is sluggish. One constantly sees those with several years of pure practice who cannot transform, and in every case they end up being controlled by others: the fault of double-weighting has not been understood." Therefore one foot must be on the ground bearing the whole body's weight, so that the empty foot can be light, nimble and lively. Correction: as the right heel sets down, the left heel must leave the ground at the same moment.

2. Fault: the foot moves sideways while the two hands move up and down, and the beginner's body tends to keep facing straight forward (south) without the waist and hips turning. The principal cause is that the movements of the limbs do not take the waist as their guiding principle and as their hub. If the waist is used properly it helps both to maintain the balance of the whole body and to keep the circulation of internal jin full and concentrated. Otherwise, the movement that moves the hands without moving the waist is a tree without roots, and internal jin cannot travel from the waist and spine out to the limbs — whereas the whole subtle use of "Wave Hands Like Clouds" lies in turning the waist and hips. Otherwise, when my wrist joins the opponent's wrist and turns up and over, it will appear powerless. But the waist must not turn too far either: some turn the waist and hips so much that they reach 90°, almost turning to due east or due west, and thus the body and limbs are thus overdone, which on the contrary gives the opponent a chance to attack. Correction: as the two hands and waist and hips turn the body, it is best to take an oblique angle a little to the east, or towards the south-west.

3. Fault: the two feet turning into the inward or outward splay. The principal cause of the inward splay of the two feet is that when the left foot steps out sideways the heel is pressed out too far; the outward splay comes from the left foot stepping out to the left without the heel pressing slightly outward, while the right foot, drawing in to the left, is not properly set straight. The direction the toes point governs how far the hip joints open and how great the amount of exercise is; therefore the outward turning and inward drawing of the toes, and the leftward and rightward turning of the heels, must all be clear and orderly in their empty and full, principal and subordinate. Correction: in "Wave Hands Like Clouds" the toes of both feet should point straight forward. Take special care that when the left foot steps out to the left, after the ball of the foot has landed you must let the left heel gradually press out towards the left, pressing and setting down as you go until the whole sole is firmly planted; in this way the toes will point straight forward and the requirement of the two feet being parallel will be met.

4. Fault: the movement is uneven, sometimes fast and sometimes slow, which is especially obvious when the left foot is about to land after stepping out to the left and when the right foot has just lifted. The principal cause is that when the strength of the legs and of the waist and hips is insufficient the speed suddenly increases, and thus the whole movement becomes uneven in pace. The movement must, within its continuous and threaded arc, be complete and rounded, neither hurried nor sluggish, neither concave nor convex, with no defects and no sharp corners. The changes must be light, nimble and lively, so that emptiness and fullness can interchange and turn. Correction: practise more to strengthen the leg power step by step, and take care that when the left leg steps out the right leg is set solid, and when the right leg lifts the left leg is set solid; only when empty and full are clearly divided can the movement be light and nimble.

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explain the essential points. 2. Demonstrate the movement; demonstrate the application. 3. First practise it broken down; then immediately follow with whole-movement practice, alternating fast practice and slow practice. 4. The two hands hang loosely. The two feet stand a shoulder's width apart, in a half squat. The left foot lifts and steps out to the left, and the weight gradually shifts onto the left foot. The right leg lifts and draws in to the left, setting down at a shoulder's width; the weight gradually shifts onto the right foot, the left foot lifts and steps out to the left … practise in this continuous way to master the leg movements well — empty and full, the two feet parallel and pointing forward, the centre of gravity not rising and falling, and so on.

5. The two feet stand a shoulder's width apart, in a slight squat, the right hand above and the left hand below. The left hand moves in an arc from below to the right, upward and to the left, while the right hand turns its palm outward and moves from the right downward, turning the palm inward and travelling across the front of the abdomen to the left (palm facing inward). Immediately afterwards the left palm turns outward, and from the left it turns downward and inward and travels across the front of the abdomen to the right, while the right hand goes upward and to the right. At this moment the two hands are again one above and one below in front of the body, returning to the starting position — that is, one movement of "Wave Hands Like Clouds" is completed. Practise continuously in this way to master the hand movements well — the path of the hands, the direction the palms face, the height of the hands, when to turn the palm, and so on.

6. Whole-movement practice must follow on closely, otherwise a split will form; one should follow the teacher's movements at a slower pace, one movement at a time, and so learn.

7. The improvement of empty and full may be undertaken once whole-movement practice is basically mastered. The left leg is set solid and the right leg lifts; when the right leg, having drawn in to the left, is about to land, the left leg must "send" the right leg down. When the left leg steps out to the left, the right leg must be firmly set solid, and the weight must not be moved before the left heel has landed.

Book page 374

VII. Technical Analysis

VII. Technical Analysis

1. "Wave Hands Like Clouds" should be performed as 3–5 continuous movements. Its distinguishing feature is "unbroken connection", threaded through movement after movement, so that at the moment of seeming to stop and not stopping, the opportunity for the next movement arises of itself. Therefore there must be no place of pause; the inside and outside, above and below, left and right, front and back must be coordinated as one, so that above and below follow each other and "one breath runs through". For this reason the movement of "Wave Hands Like Clouds" must be continuous, rounded and lively.

2. "Wave Hands Like Clouds" makes high demands on the two hands: it requires that "the whole movement depend on the two hands turning without leaving the centre line." The left hand governs the left half of the body and the right hand the right half, with the nose and navel as the centre line between them, so that even in the circular turning the movement does not leave the centre line. The arms must be relaxed, soft, rounded and lively, with firmness and softness assisting each other; they must rotate along arcs — across and straight, with and against, rising and falling, extending and withdrawing must all travel along curved lines — and they must turn with the waist and hips, and the two hands must not be allowed to go slack.

3. This movement should be done 3–5 times, and throughout those 3–5 movements the frame must not be sometimes high and sometimes low — that is, the centre of gravity must not rise and fall. The stepping out of the feet and the lifting of the right leg must both be light and nimble, and this requires that throughout the whole movement the centre of gravity stay always on one level, without rising or falling. If the centre of gravity rises and falls, it will lead to uneven pace in the movement.

attend to the gradual change when empty and full interchange.

4. The gaze in "Wave Hands Like Clouds": the beginner tends to watch the palm as it turns, which is of course wrong. But some simply look straight ahead, which is also wrong: the method of the eyes is to follow the movement of the principal hand while looking level ahead. The gaze must first look ahead in the direction one is intending to go, and then the body method, hand method and step method follow.

# Twenty-ninth Posture: Single Whip

I. Application

The same as the fourth posture, Single Whip.

II. The Course of the Movement

The body continues to turn slightly right, and the weight gradually shifts entirely onto the right leg; the left leg lifts. At the same time the right palm, following the turning of the body, extends slightly to the right oblique, and as it extends the arm turns inward so that the palm gradually turns to face down, and the five fingers droop and gather together to form the hook hand; the left palm continues to travel to the upper right, drawing near the right wrist. The gaze attends to the right palm travelling right, and attends to the left palm travelling left (see the figure at the right-hand side of this page).

The movements that follow are the same as movement four of the fourth posture, "Single Whip"; see the three figures in the bottom row of this page (the same as the plates of the fourth posture).

The essential points and so on are all the same as those of the fourth posture.

# Thirtieth Posture: High Pat on Horse (Gao Tan Ma)

Book page 375

I. Application

I. Application

Continuing from the previous posture, Single Whip. If the opponent's left hand passes over my left wrist, I at once loosen the left wrist slightly, palm facing up, and fold his wrist down and gather it back towards my breast. At the same time the left foot is drawn back, the toes touching the ground, the waist relaxed and the chest hollowed, the right knee slightly bent and set solid; then the right hand is turned round from the rear, upward and forward, and the palm probes towards the opponent's face. The eyes look forward, the spine is slightly raised, with the intent of probing and extending forward.

II. The Course of the Movement

1. The weight gradually shifts to the right leg; the left toes lift naturally as the weight moves back, the chest is hollowed and the back raised, and at the same time the right hook hand changes into a palm, the right elbow bends, and it moves in an arc to the front of the right shoulder; the left arm rotates outward so that the palm gradually turns to slant upward. The gaze attends to the turning over of the left palm (see the first figure in the left-hand column of this page).

2. The weight shifts entirely onto the right leg; the left foot is drawn back and set down half a step inward, the toes touching the ground, and the right leg at the same time gradually straightens up (the knee still slightly bent), forming a high left empty stance; the body gradually turns slightly left (facing east), and as the body turns the right palm arcs forward, passing slightly to the left over the upper side of the left wrist. The fingers point obliquely to the left front, the palm facing down, at eyebrow height; the left palm arcs down under the lower side of the right wrist and withdraws to the front of the upper left abdomen, the fingers pointing obliquely to the right front, the palm facing up. The eyes look level ahead, and the gaze must attend to the right palm probing forward (see the second and third figures in the left-hand column of this page).

III. Essential Points

1. The weight gradually shifts to the right leg, which must be set solid, and the left hip joint gradually draws inward to lead the left leg up. At this moment the upper body must not stoop forward or lean back.

2. As soon as the left foot has left the ground and is drawn back, the right leg gradually straightens up; at this moment the spine is relaxed and sunk, upright; the breath sinks to the lower abdomen and the crotch jin sinks down; the power at the sole of the foot seems to take root in the ground; and the point at the crown of the head must naturally be lifted, with the sense of rising to the heavens. This is the practice of "empty the collar, lift the crown, sink the breath to the elixir field" and "lift the crotch and carry the crown".

3. The knee joint of the right leg is bent and not straight; the sole of the foot is set flat and solidly on the ground, its power seeming to take root in the ground, while the power rises from the heel and the intent turns upward.

图 170
High Pat on Horse: the right hook hand changes into a palm and moves, with the elbow bent, in an arc to the front of the right shoulder, while the left arm rotates outward and the palm turns over
图 171
High Pat on Horse: the right palm arcs slightly left and probes forward over the upper side of the left wrist, while the left palm withdraws downward under the lower side of the right wrist
图 172
High Pat on Horse: the left palm withdrawn to the front of the upper left abdomen, the right palm probing forward at eyebrow height, forming a high left empty stance

4. The right arm extends forward, the intent far-reaching and the jin long, the elbow joint bent and not straight — this is used to strengthen the arm's sinking jin. The foot jin presses down and the hand jin issues forward: this has the meaning of the two hands and two feet lengthening against each other, seeking straightness within the curve.

5. When the right arm probes forward the shoulder must not be shrugged; the shoulder must be relaxed and sunk. In this way the arm's extending and withdrawing, winding and coiling can follow one's intention.

6. When the right hand probes forward the fingers must not point forward, otherwise the meaning of "seating the wrist" is lost.

7. The waist must be lifted, but not lifted stiffly upward, otherwise the flexibility of the waist's rotation will be affected; nor may the chest be thrust out or the back arched.

IV. Requirements

1. When the left foot is drawn back the right leg must be set solid; the sole of the left foot must not scrape the ground as it is drawn back.

2. After the left foot has been drawn back it must not be fully straightened, nor may the right knee be fully straightened. The knee must be slightly bent and the right leg set solid.

3. When the right hand probes forward, the chest must be hollowed and the back raised, with the intent of advancing — but this is not shrugging the shoulders.

4. "The source moves in the waist and spine, the jin penetrates to the four extremities." Both the upper and lower limbs must carry jin. The left hand gathers back towards the breast and the right hand seats the wrist and probes forward, lengthening against each other; both must strive to issue from the spine and reach the fingers. The shoulders relax downward and the elbows drop; the elbow joint is bent and not straight.

V. Common Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Fault: the left foot is not drawn back but scraped and dragged back along the ground. The principal cause is that the body's weight does not shift back far enough — that is, the right leg is not set solid and the weight is between the two feet. Correction: shift the weight fully back, bend the right leg slightly and set it solid, first lift the thigh and store the jin in the knee, and then slowly draw the left leg back; in this way it will not scrape the ground.

2. Fault: the left hand is too high or too low. The principal cause is that in probing forward with the right hand to attack the opponent — which is easy for people to understand — one pays little attention to the fact that the left hand, palm facing up, is drawn back beside the upper abdomen; and so the hand's height, and its position front and back, have nothing to go by and it is placed at random. One should first know that it is gathering back towards the breast, and that "towards the breast" is neither beside the hip nor in front of the chest; then the position of the left hand will be understood without being said.

3. Fault: the movement pauses. When Single Whip is followed by High Pat on Horse, the right hook hand has already changed into a palm, the left palm already faces up, and the weight has already moved back; and here, in preparing to exert force to lift the left leg, one often pauses. The principal cause is that when the jin breaks the intent breaks too, and the strength of the waist, hips and legs is insufficient. Correction: the intention must from the first command the movement without a break; in this way there will be no pause, and "when yin reaches its extreme it gives rise to yang, and when yang reaches its extreme it gives rise to yin", and "yin and yang are each the root of the other." In addition the right leg must be set solid, and one must attend to lifting the leg rather than dragging the foot.

4. Fault: when the right hand probes forward the upper body stoops forward too much. The principal cause is that one fixes too much attention on the forward-probing action of the right hand and forgets that there is also the gathering action of the left hand: if the upper body stoops forward too far, the right hand may go out, but the gathering of the left hand has its effect reduced — and this does not accord with the application. Therefore one must "keep the tailbone centred and upright." As the boxing proverb says, how can the body form and the lifting of the crown be dispensed with? Correction: probe forward, but without stooping forward or protruding the buttocks.

5. Fault: the right palm issues slack and without power. The principal cause is an insufficient grasp of the palm methods of Taijiquan. Correction: the distinguishing feature of the palm methods of Yang-style Taijiquan is that the fingers are relaxed and extended, the thumb slightly bent and separated from the index finger, the other four fingers neither tense nor slack, each joint slightly curved, and the wrist seated. "In moving the breath and conveying the jin there must be no point however small that is not reached" — the jin must penetrate to the five fingers. But of course, using too much force and tensing the palm and fingers into stiff jin is also wrong.

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. A mnemonic: sit back and lift the leg, the front foot empty; gather with the left and probe with the right, the eyes looking before them.

2. The difficulty of this movement lies in the large bow stance of Single Whip.

(This page carries one unnumbered push-hands photograph at the foot; it has no figure number and no caption.)

To make the weight shift from the left leg to the right leg, and the left foot become empty and be drawn lightly and slowly back, is very far from easy; therefore in practising this movement the emphasis must be placed on the key point of changing from the bow stance to the empty stance.

3. The height to which the right arm probes out must be taught according to the application. The right palm probes towards the opponent's face, and therefore the palm's height should be a little above the shoulder — level with the shoulder or below the shoulder would not meet the requirements of the application.

4. In teaching the body method there should be a slight raising of the spine, with the intent of probing and extending forward, but this must not be overdone: overdone, it produces a forward stooping of the upper body and loses the upright centring of the body. In teaching, one must follow the characteristics of the body method of Taijiquan and value centredness, ease and comfort, lightness, nimbleness and roundness, and calm steadiness — while of course also guarding against thrusting the chest out.

5. In teaching, one must attend to the upper and lower following each other: if the foot moves first and the hand afterwards, then the opponent's attacking left hand will either attack forward or escape backward; if the hand moves first and the foot afterwards, not only is the distance moved small, but the waist power will also be misapplied and the force hard to concentrate — and then the effect of gathering will not be produced. Therefore in teaching one must emphasise the upper and lower following each other, and make the left hand, the right hand and the drawing back of the left foot move together.

6. Compare correct and incorrect movements, so that through this vivid teaching the student can deeply grasp the application and understand the meaning of the movement.

7. Paired practice based on the application: A — takes up the settled posture of Single Whip. B — passes his left hand under A's left wrist and flicks it from the inside towards the right. A — at once loosens the left wrist slightly, palm facing up, folds the wrist down and gathers it back towards the breast, while the right knee bends slightly and is set solid, the left foot is drawn back, and the right hand probes forward. Practise repeatedly, then A and B exchange places and practise, savouring the application of the movement.

Book page 376

VII. Technical Analysis

VII. Technical Analysis

1. In this movement the distance the weight travels is comparatively large, and the left foot is far from the support of the right foot; to lift the left foot with the support of one foot (the right) requires very great strength in the muscles at the front of the foot and elsewhere. Practised repeatedly in this way, it both trains the strength of the right leg to bear the body's weight and to control and balance the centre of gravity, and trains the strength of the muscles concerned in lifting the left leg.

2. In performing the Single Whip movement that precedes High Pat on Horse, if the centre of gravity is low and the step large, then performing High Pat on Horse makes the leg power work still harder and the amount of exercise still greater, which imposes too heavy a burden on the elderly and the weak; and so some practitioners find they cannot lift the left leg and it turns into a dragging back. Therefore the elderly and the weak may take a higher frame when practising.

3. In the settled posture the right leg must not be straightened: straightened it becomes a dead stance, and a dead stance loses the opportunity.

# Thirty-first Posture: Part the Wild Horse's Mane to Left and Right (Zuo You Fen Jiao)

I. Application

Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent uses his left hand to receive my right wrist as it probes out, I at once use my right wrist to press down on the opponent's left elbow, dropping the elbow and sinking the shoulder, and at once ward the opponent's left arm back towards the left; at the same time my left hand sticks to the opponent's left wrist, palm facing down, covertly using the gathering jin. The left foot at the same time steps out half a step forward and to the left and is set solid, the waist leans obliquely to the left, and then the right foot is lifted and, with my toes and the instep of the foot, kicks straight and level at the opponent's left ribs; at the same time the two palms stand on edge and separate level with the shoulders to left and right, so as to match the action of parting the foot. The eyes follow the right hand, the chest is hollowed and the back raised, and the settling power is of itself sufficient; then the opponent's posture can no longer be directed by himself.

The left part-the-foot movement has the same application, in the opposite direction.

II. The Course of the Movement
(A) Part the Foot to the Right

1. The weight gradually shifts entirely onto the right leg, the right leg gradually squats down, the centre of gravity descends and the left foot lifts, and the body turns slightly left with it (facing north-east). At the same time the right palm, following the turning of the body, turns inward in an arc to the right, and the left palm wipes forward in an arc to the left; the gaze attends to the right palm wiping to the right (see the first two figures in the left-hand column of this page).

2. The left foot steps forward (to the north-east), the heel touching the ground first, and then the weight gradually shifts onto the left foot, the left leg bending and the right leg pushing straight to form a left bow stance. As the body turns right (to the south-east), the left palm wipes a circle inward from the left, forward and to the right, passing under the lower side of the right arm, and the left arm comes to a rounded, crosswise bend. The left (The left-hand column of this page holds three plates, stacked top to bottom, showing the course of this posture.)

The palm is held crosswise in front of the chest (beside the right elbow), the palm slanting inward and upward; the right palm wipes a flat circle from the right inward to the left over the upper side of the left arm, that is, probing out to the right front, standing the palm, the palm slanting to the left front, the fingertips slanting upward. The gaze attends to the right palm wiping, turning and probing out (see the first figure in the right-hand column of this page).

3. The weight gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg; the body turns left with it (facing north-east) and the right leg is lifted forward; at the same time the left palm moves in an arc forward and upward, palm facing inward, and the right palm scoops in an arc from the right downward to the outside of the left palm, and as it scoops the arm turns outward so that the palm turns to face inward. The two hands cross, the left palm inside. The gaze attends to the crossing of the two palms (see the second and third figures in the right-hand column of this page).

4. The left leg gradually straightens up (the knee still slightly bent); the body turns right (facing south-east) and the right foot parts out to the right oblique front (south-east), the instep naturally drawn level, at hip height; at the same time the two palms separate to the left, both palms slanting outward, the fingertips upward, the two palms at about shoulder height. The gaze attends to the right palm as it parts out, and looks level to the right past the right palm (see the first figure in the left-hand column of the next page).

(B) Part the Foot to the Left

1. The left foot gradually squats down and the right foot comes down (the weight still entirely on the left foot), and the body turns slightly right; at the same time the left palm, with the elbow bent, draws near the chest and wipes from the inside towards the right, and as it wipes the arm turns inward so that the palm gradually turns to face down; the right palm wipes from the right front towards the left, and as it wipes the arm turns outward so that the palm gradually turns to face up (see the second figure in the right-hand column of the next page).

2. The body turns left (to the north-east); at the same time the right palm wipes and turns from the right, forward and to the left, passing under the lower side of the left arm, nearly a full circle, and the right arm comes to a rounded, crosswise bend with the right palm held crosswise in front of the left chest (beside the left elbow), the palm slanting inward and upward; the left palm wipes a flat circle from the left inward to the right over the upper side of the right arm, that is, probing out to the left front, standing the palm, the palm slanting to the left front, the fingertips slanting upward. 3. The weight gradually shifts entirely onto the right leg; the body turns right with it (facing south-east) and the left leg is lifted forward; at the same time the right palm moves in an arc forward and upward, palm facing inward, and the left palm scoops in an arc from the left downward to the outside of the right palm, and as it scoops the arm turns outward so that the palm turns to face inward. The two hands cross, the right hand inside. The gaze attends to the crossing of the two palms (see the third figure in the left-hand column of this page and the first figure in the right-hand column of the next page).

4. The right leg gradually straightens up (the knee still slightly bent); the body turns left (facing north-east) and the left foot parts out to the left oblique front (north-east), the instep naturally drawn level, at hip height. At the same time the two palms separate to the left, both palms slanting outward, the fingertips upward, the two palms at about shoulder height. The gaze attends to the left palm as it parts out, and looks level to the left (see the second figure in the right-hand column of the next page).

Book page 377

III. Essential Points

III. Essential Points

1. In the first part-the-foot the body must turn to four directions, the face must also turn to four directions, and the eyes must likewise follow the turning of the body to look in four directions.

(This page carries two unnumbered photographs at the foot; they have no figure numbers and no captions.)

图 177
Part the Foot to Left and Right: the right leg lifted forward, the left palm moving in an arc forward and upward, palm facing inward
图 178A
Part the Foot to Left and Right: the right palm scooping in an arc from the right downward to the outside of the left palm, the two hands crossing with the left palm inside
图 178B
Part the Foot to Left and Right: the left leg straightening up, the right foot parting out to the right oblique front, the two palms separating to the left

2. In the second part-the-foot, the right foot parts to the south-east and the left foot parts to the north-east.

3. When the two hands grind and turn, the front hand must carry jin through wrist and elbow: the hand circles and the elbow circles too; the arm must form an arc, the elbow slightly sunk, and the circle must be even. When the right arm probes out after wiping and turning it too must not be straightened, and the turning of the waist must lead the hands to move.

4. The left foot steps up, facing north-east, and the waist turns to the north-east; only then does one straighten up.

5. In parting the foot one must lift the knee before extending the leg.

6. When the two hands separate the arms must form arcs, the elbows slightly sunk (the elbow lower than the wrist) and the palms higher than the shoulders (but the shoulders must not be shrugged).

7. When the two palms enfold, cross and gather, they must follow the straightening of the supporting leg and shift softly upward and outward; only then is there lightness and steadiness. If the two palms are already crossed and motionless when the left leg straightens, a sluggish quality will appear. When enfolding, the wrists of the two palms must not bend limply, and the two arms must arrive at the same moment, forming the cross, in readiness to part the foot.

8. When the two hands grind and turn, the elbows must sink and the wrists be seated (the whole form requires "seating the wrist" in every movement); the wrist strength must not be weak, nor may the wrists collapse slackly, otherwise the internal jin will be prevented from reaching the fingers, and the use of ward-off, roll-back, press and push will be affected.

9. The right hand probing out is to press down the opponent's left elbow (taking the right part-the-foot as the example). The right hand wards from the right downward and the left hand covertly applies the gathering jin downward; this must be coordinated with the turning of the waist and hips and with sinking jin, and must not be slack.

10. When parting the foot the body must be stable, and must not stoop, lean back, tilt or lean sideways; there must be "empty the collar and lift the crown" and "sink the breath to the elixir field" — only then is it easy for the body to keep its balance.

11. In the settled posture of the right part-the-foot, the left leg (the supporting foot) must not be straightened, and must not stand utterly dead; otherwise it can neither regulate nor support the steadiness of the body's centre of gravity, nor obtain the opportunity and the position.

12. In going from the right part-the-foot to the left part-the-foot, first make the left leg bend and squat so that the centre of gravity descends; in the course of sitting back on the leg the right leg first comes down and then steps to the oblique direction (towards the south-east). At that moment neither the hands nor the feet may pause: one must "let the foot follow the hand's movement, turning as if divinely."

图 179
Part the Foot to Left and Right: the left palm, with the elbow bent near the chest, wiping from the inside to the right, and the right palm wiping from the right front to the left, the palms turning over
图 180
Part the Foot to Left and Right: the right foot stepping forward into a right bow stance, the right palm wiping and turning inward under the lower side of the left arm
图 181A
Part the Foot to Left and Right: the left palm wiping a flat circle forward over the upper side of the right arm and probing out to the left front, standing the palm
Book page 378

IV. Requirements

IV. Requirements

1. The direction of the left and right parts-the-foot must be correct: the right part-the-foot towards the south-east, the left part-the-foot towards the north-east.

2. In the right part-the-foot the directions of the right foot and the right hand must agree and must arrive at the same time; the left part-the-foot has the same requirement as the right.

3. The grinding and turning of the hands must be clear and must not be vague, and the intent of the movement must be strong.

4. Going from High Pat on Horse into the right part-the-foot, one should first lower the centre of gravity, bend the right leg and set it solid, and only then step the left leg to the left oblique angle (north-east). At the end of the right part-the-foot, coming to the left part-the-foot, the stepping must be light and nimble, and so one must first bend the left leg and lower the body's centre of gravity, and only after the left leg is set solid step the right leg to the right oblique angle (south-east), so as not to produce heaviness and sluggishness.

5. There must be "when one part moves, no part is unmoving". In the right part-the-foot, at the same moment that the right leg bends and squats and the centre of gravity descends, the right hand grinds and turns from the front to the right and inward and the left hand grinds and turns from the left outward, and the left foot lifts and becomes empty — all must move together; the hands must not move while the foot is still, nor the foot move while the hands are still.

6. In going from the right part-the-foot to the left part-the-foot there must be no pause: one must "let posture follow posture, movement thread through movement", "when the jin breaks the intent does not break", and the internal jin keeps on circulating.

7. Whichever foot parts, the gaze should be fixed in that direction.

V. Common Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Fault: the direction of the movement is not correct. The principal cause lies in unfamiliarity with the application. The opponent meets my right wrist, probing out, with his left hand from the front; I ward the opponent's left arm back to the left, and at the same time step my left foot half a step forward and to the left — and at that moment the opponent is to the right front of me, so that the direction of my parted foot becomes the south-east oblique, and not some other direction. Correction: the direction of the toes of the supporting foot must be reasonable and natural, pointing to the north-east; then, on the basis of turning the waist and hips, the right part-the-foot can proceed smoothly to the south-east.

图 181B
Part the Foot to Left and Right: the right palm held crosswise in front of the left chest, the left palm probing out to the left front, standing the palm
图 182
Part the Foot to Left and Right: the right hand crossed inside, the two palms enfolding, in readiness to part the foot
图 183
Part the Foot to Left and Right: the left foot parting out to the left oblique front, the two palms separating to the left, the fingertips upward

2. Fault: the parted foot is too high or too low. The principal cause is a lack of understanding of the application. I ward the opponent's left arm and at the same time my left hand gathers downward under the opponent's left wrist, so that the parts of him left open to my attack are only the middle and lower — and so a straight, level kick at the opponent's left flank is the more appropriate. Correction: since it is the flank that is being kicked, being higher than the waist or lower than the knee are both unreasonable. Of course the elderly and weak, and those who are dizzy and unsteady on their feet, may lower the requirement — lifting the foot only a little will do.

3. Fault: the gaze is fixed in one direction only and does not follow the movement. The principal cause lies in an insufficient grasp of the method of the eyes. Correction: the gaze must follow the movement of the principal hand and look level ahead, so that in practising the form the eyes arrive, the body arrives, the hands arrive and the step arrives, all together, "spirit and form united as one". Wherever the intent wants to go, the gaze must go with it; the eyes must follow the turning of the principal hand and look ahead, while of course also attending to above and below and to both sides. The neck must turn with the gaze; in this way "the mechanism lies in the eyes, and the enemy's disposition is known at once", and in martial terms one can see through the opponent's movement. The turning of the gaze, and its extension and far-seeing, are also good for restoring and strengthening the eyesight; therefore in a single part-the-foot the gaze must turn to four directions, and accumulated day after day in repeated training this is most beneficial to the health of the eyes.

4. Fault: when the two hands grind and turn they are either stiff or collapsed. The principal cause is that the intent of the pairs is unclear. The hand methods of Taijiquan abhor stiffness and sluggishness, and require firmness and softness to assist each other. Correction: in moving, lead the elbow with the hand and the shoulder with the elbow; the arm must be nimble, round and turning, the shoulder relaxed and sunk. To prevent the wrist from collapsing slackly one must attend to "seating the wrist". If the wrist is slack and powerless the hand will necessarily have no ward-off jin; therefore when grinding and turning, the front hand must carry jin through wrist and elbow, and the elbow too must circle. This keeps the ward-off jin from being lost, and one achieves neither stiffness nor collapse.

5. Fault: when parting the foot, the waist twists, producing a slanting and stooping or leaning of the upper body. The principal cause is an insufficient recognition that the waist is the key to the turning of the upper and lower body. Correction: the Treatise on Boxing says, "the waist is the great banner" — likening the waist to the great standard of the central army, which stands upright. Therefore when performing the right part-the-foot, as the left foot steps up and one faces the north-east, the waist and hips must turn to the north-east, so that shoulder and hip are joined; and when parting the foot to the south-east the waist and hips turn with the movement — and then there will be no twisting of the waist and no slanting of the upper body.

图 184
Part the Foot to Left and Right: the settled posture of the left foot parted out, the instep level at hip height, the two palms slanting outward with the fingertips up

6. Fault: when parting the foot the leg kicks out straight. The principal cause is an insufficient understanding of the application. Correction: to kick the leg one must first lift the leg (the knee), first concentrating the force at the knee joint, and then let the motive force travel joint by penetrating through to reach the tip of the foot, so as to strengthen the issuing of power.

7. Fault: when parting the foot the two hands separate to left and right too low or too high. The principal cause is an insufficient understanding of the application. Correction: as the foot parts, the two palms stand on edge and separate in arcs to left and right level with the shoulders — this is chiefly to take advantage of the momentum of the parted foot, and is not a press-and-strike attack. The arms must be arc-shaped, the palms higher than the shoulders, and the shoulders must not be lifted, so that one's own settling power is sufficient and the opponent cannot hold himself up.

Book page 379

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Mnemonics (taking the right part-the-foot as the example): (1) The hands — the right hand from outside inward, the left hand from inside outward; the two hands open and then close; the right hand presses obliquely forward; the arcs issue level with the shoulders. (2) The feet — the right leg squats and the left leg is empty; the left foot goes out obliquely forward; the heel lands first; the weight shifts to the left; the right foot rises slowly; remember the direction firmly.

2. Difficult points (taking the right part-the-foot as the example): (1) The grinding and turning of the two hands is unclear — one may use the method of breaking it down: with the feet and the direction unchanged, practise the right hand alone, circling from outside to the right and inward, then change to the left hand going left, outward and to the right, then practise the two hands together, and finally issue the right palm to the south-east after the grinding and turning. Once that is basically proficient, then add the foot movements and the change of direction. (2) The facing is unclear — stepping the left foot out one faces north-east, and issuing the right palm one faces south-east; practise repeatedly, first mastering the two hands' grinding and turning and the changing of the two directions, which is the difficult point and must be made clear. Then, having learned it, turning left to brush-the-knee-and-twist-the-step one faces north-east, and when parting the foot one faces south-east — and in this way the turning and changing of directions is easily made clear.

3. Joining: in going from High Pat on Horse into the right part-the-foot, one must first squat the right leg and sink the body; and in going from the completed right part-the-foot into the left part-the-foot, one must likewise first squat the left leg and "send" the right leg down, stepping out to the south-east oblique, while coordinating the hand movements. If the joining is poor, the quality is certain to be low; therefore in teaching one must specially bring out the practice of the joinings, and through repeated practice achieve continuity, roundness and liveliness.

4. The direction of the placed foot must be practised repeatedly and pointed out clearly. In the right part-the-foot, the left foot steps out to the left oblique, that is to the north-east; in the left part-the-foot, the right foot steps out to the right oblique, that is to the south-east. Going beyond or falling short will make the part-the-foot awkward or the stance unsteady.

VII. Technical Analysis

1. This movement is comparatively complex: it includes the two hands each moving in different directions, and at the same time the movement of the feet, the rising and falling of the centre of gravity, the repeated changing of direction, and support on one leg — all of these changing at the same moment. It is therefore rather hard to learn; but its very difficulty tends rather to arouse the practitioner's keen interest.

2. When parting the foot the movement of the hands is not placed at random: beyond taking advantage of the momentum of the parted foot, it also serves to confuse the opponent's line of sight and to scatter his attention. Because the right hand and the right foot strike out at the same moment and in the same direction, the opponent's gaze first meets the hand nearer his face, and so the hand's movement bemuses his attack and defence, which favours the true attack of my foot below — and this embodies the subtle use of now appearing, now hiding, and of the interchange of empty and full.

3. Once this movement is basically learned, the level of skill depends chiefly on whether the support on one leg is steady; technically one must attend to two things: (1) The supporting leg must be set down solidly and stand steady, bent and not straight, so that the lower body is stable. (2) The parting leg must not be lifted too fast — if fast, the body is easily pulled along. One should first lift the knee, and then at the same slow speed continue to part the lower leg, so as to avoid losing balance.

4. The speed at which the two hands separate must agree with the parting of the leg, and the movements must be coordinated.

5. The body must be "centred, upright, at ease and comfortable"; one must not wrongly resort to leaning back and the like to keep the body's balance.

Beyond all the above, the most crucial thing is to persevere in practising over months and years, to strengthen the power of the legs and of the whole body's muscles, and to raise one's skill unceasingly, so that the support on one leg becomes steady.

# Thirty-second Posture: Turn the Body and Kick with the Heel (Zhuan Shen Deng Jiao)

I. Application

Continuing from the left part-the-foot. If the opponent strikes with his right hand from behind me, I at once turn my body to the left, hollow the chest, raise the back and relax the waist, and above all make a good "empty the collar and lift the crown"; the left leg hangs raised, and as the waist turns the toes, of themselves hang down of itself. After the turn, the right foot is set firm, and the left foot at once kicks with the heel at the opponent's abdomen, the toes drawn up. As the two hands turn with the waist they close from outside inward, and as the left foot kicks out the two palms stand on edge to left and right and separate level with the shoulders; the gaze looks away in the direction of the left fingertips, and with the root power established the opponent will certainly fall back before the leg.

II. The Course of the Movement

1. The left foot comes down, the left knee staying raised, and with the right heel as the axis the body at once turns to the left rear through about 180°; as it turns the two palms close inward and gather and cross in front of the chest (the left palm outside), and the eyes follow the turning of the body, looking level ahead (see the first figure in the left-hand column of this page).

2. The left leg kicks slowly out to the left (west) with the heel, the toes pointing up; at the same time the two palms separate to left and right. The right leg gradually straightens up as the left foot kicks out, but the right knee stays slightly bent. The gaze attends to the left palm as it separates, and looks level ahead past the left palm (see the second figure in the left-hand column of this page).

III. Essential Points

1. When turning, the body must always maintain "above and below essentially one line", and the body's centre of gravity must not depart from the point of support.

2. When turning to the left the whole body's movements must be coordinated: the gaze looks to the left, the right arm swings left, the left arm withdraws and swings left, the left leg withdraws and swings left, and the head turns together with the turning of the waist and hips. The waist is the key to the turning of the upper and lower body, but the cooperation of other aspects must not be slighted.

3. When turning, the right leg sinks slightly downward so that the centre of gravity descends and the lower limbs are made stable. When kicking, the right leg straightens up again, but still does not straighten fully.

4. When kicking the body must be steady, and must not stoop, lean back, tilt or bend; the leg must kick out slowly, taking the heel as the point of application, without sudden change, and must not use rapid movements.

IV. Requirements

1. When turning, the upper body must not stoop forward or lean back, nor slant to left or right.

2. When turning, the left foot must not touch the ground.

3. After the turn the direction must be correct.

4. After the turn one must not kick the foot only after the movement has paused.

5. The movement must be even, and must not be sometimes fast and sometimes slow.

图 185
Turn the Body and Kick with the Heel: turning the body through about 180° to the left rear with the right heel as the axis, the two palms gathering inward and crossing in front of the chest
图 186
Turn the Body and Kick with the Heel: the left leg kicking out to the left with the heel, the toes pointing up, the two palms separating to left and right level with the shoulders

6. When the two hands cross they must be full and not collapsed, and the elbows must not be lifted so as to expose the ribs.

7. In the settled posture there must be the three joins (the hand joined with the foot, the elbow with the knee, the shoulder with the hip).

Book page 380

V. Common Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

V. Common Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Fault: on turning the body one stands unsteadily, so that the body slants or even the left foot touches the ground. The principal cause lies in not having grasped the correct position of the body's centre of gravity, and in poor control of the force of the turn. Correction: the waist and hips and the four limbs cooperate to produce a force turning to the left, and the turn must be made just right; besides applying the force properly there must also be a braking action. Therefore after the turn the right leg sinks, the left leg draws slightly inward, and the setting down of the right sole and, most fundamentally, the control of the waist and hips' turning, give one not only the ideal angle of turn (the direction needed) but also a light and nimble turn.

2. Fault: the direction of the turn is incorrect. The principal cause is paying insufficient attention to the application. When the opponent strikes with his right hand from behind me, my direction of attack and defence should be behind the position of "Part the Foot to Left and Right" (west) for it to accord with the requirement. Correction: after the left part-the-foot the movement is 45° + 90°, about 135° in all — that is, from the north-east turning to the west (the direction of the heel kick).

3. Fault: the left leg swings with the leg straight. The principal cause is wanting to use the force of the swung leg to turn the body, which loses the application's meaning as a heel kick, and in any case makes the direction of the turn hard to control. Correction: one must (This page carries one unnumbered push-hands photograph at the foot; it has no figure number and no caption.)

stand with the left leg raised and turning.

4. Fault: when kicking the leg the position of the two hands is poor. The principal cause is that the beginner concentrates too much on turning and on keeping balance. Correction: the arms separate at shoulder level — the left hand forward (west), the right hand oblique (north-east). If the two hands separate to 180° they scatter, which inevitably produces a thrust-out chest, and moreover the front of the chest is then too open and easily attacked.

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. A correct turning action is the key to this movement, and so it must be practised and savoured repeatedly. On the basis of practising each detail broken down, then practise the whole repeatedly.

2. The teacher should explain the turning as the key point and demonstrate it.

3. Two directions must be made clear: first, when the two hands cross the body faces the north-west; second, the kick goes to the west.

VII. Technical Analysis

The distinguishing feature of this movement is the turn, and the technical key point and difficulty is likewise the turn. The turn is carried out while supported on one foot, and therefore the key lies in the centre of gravity. As soon as the human body makes a movement the centre of gravity changes; the direction in which the centre of gravity moves is always the same as the direction in which the body moves, and the greater the weight and distance moved (as with the left leg in this movement), the greater the distance the centre of gravity travels. After the body has turned in the left heel kick, the right foot supports alone and the left leg hangs raised on the left side, so that the centre of gravity necessarily shifts left; and the beginner very easily becomes unsteady and sets the left foot down, or leans the upper body right to balance — which does not accord with what the boxing treatise says: "the hundred meeting-point, the central pole, one breath threading through." In sum, the technical key of the left heel kick is the turning, and to turn well is to use well the turning of the waist and hips and the appropriate coordinated movement of hands and legs.

II. The Course of the Movement

# Thirty-fourth Posture: Step Forward and Plant the Fist (Jin Bu Zai Chui)

Book page 381

I. Application

I. Application

Joining from the preceding posture. If the opponent again kicks in with his left leg, I use my left hand to brush away from the left along the line of his leg; he is then certain to lunge to the left, and I at once take a step forward with my left foot in pursuit, bending the left knee and settling solidly, and my right hand immediately closes into a fist and strikes down at his waist or his shin — either will do. This is called "planting the fist". At that moment the right leg is straightened, the waist and hips sink down into a flat curved form, the chest is contained, the gaze is forward, and one must above all take care to guard one's own central ground.

II. The Course of the Movement

1. The body turns gradually to the right, the right toe turns out and settles flat, the centre of gravity gradually shifts onto the right leg, and the left leg is lifted forward; at the same time the right palm turns downward, parallel with the ground, moves to the side of the body, turns over to the right and rear, closes into a fist, and comes to the side of the right waist; the left palm, as the body turns, goes from the front to the right, arcs down and brushes across the front of the right chest, the gaze attending to the left palm's downward brush (see the first two figures on this page).

2. The body continues to turn slightly right, the left leg takes a step forward, the heel landing first, and as the centre of gravity gradually shifts forward the whole sole of the left foot settles flat; as the left leg bends and the right leg extends into the left bow stance, the body gradually turns left, the waist and hips sink, and as the body turns the left palm continues to arc downward, brushing past the front of the left knee up to the side of the left knee; the right fist at the same time strikes down and forward, slightly below knee height, the gaze forward, the eyes attending to the right fist as it strikes out (see the figures further on this page).

III. Key Points

1. The brushing of the knee should be done at the moment the left heel has already landed and the weight is shifting forward and the left knee bending; it should not be done before the left foot has landed, nor after the left bow stance is already made. The bow must arrive, the brush must arrive, the fist must arrive — all three must arrive together.

图 194
the body turning right, the right palm turning over and closing into a fist at the right waist, the left palm sweeping down across the front of the right chest.
图 195A
the left foot stepping forward with the heel landing first, the weight beginning to shift forward, both arms still in transition.

2. Before the right fist strikes forward and down, take care that the body stays upright; as the right fist strikes down the upper body inclines forward with the waist folding, and the waist and hips sink — but when the waist folds, the head and neck and the waist must still be kept in one straight line (the cervical, thoracic and lumbar vertebrae essentially forming one straight line). Do not drop the head or hump the waist; maintain "the hundred meeting-point, the central pole, one breath threading through".

3. The eyes look forward past the right fist; do not raise the head, and do not lower it either.

4. The two elbows should be slightly bent, never straightened; the left palm should have the wrist seated.

IV. Requirements

1. The left leg is lifted and steps forward; the movement must be even, not now fast and now slow.

2. From the moment the body begins to turn right, both left and right hands must move together; take special care that the left hand does not pause.

3. The body should not turn right too far (it should not face north).

4. Once the whole set of movements is fairly proficient, the amount of exercise should be gradually increased. One way is to lower the height of the hip-joint, bringing the knee nearly level with the hip, so that the muscular load on the waist and legs is increased.

The centre of gravity should be kept at one level, the body neither rising nor falling abruptly, and one should not cut corners by borrowing force. When the movement changes, the hip-joint draws in and lowers, and the body stays centred and upright; in this way the leg strength can be increased, and as the amount of exercise rises the constitution is further strengthened. Naturally, a practitioner whose health does not for the time being permit it must not drop too low all at once, lest he become over-tired.

5. The fist should not be gripped too tightly, nor yet left wholly slack so that it is an empty fist.

6. Do not drop the head or hump the waist.

图 195B
the left bow stance formed, the right fist planted down and forward, the left palm at the side of the left knee.
图 196
the left bow stance, seen in profile, the right fist striking down slightly below knee height.
图 197A
the left bow stance from the front, the right arm descending with the fist, the left hand pressing at the knee.
Book page 382

V. Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

V. Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Fault: the fist comes out too high, striking down from in front of the chest and beside the shoulder. The principal cause is that one has traced an empty circle. Correction: the fist should come out from the side of the waist and strike forward and down.

2. Fault: the eyes look downward. The principal cause is that one attaches too little importance to the application, mistakenly supposing that the eye should see the point the fist strikes. Correction: the gaze should attend to the right palm, but the main thing is that the eye must observe the opponent's changes — and so it should not look down.

3. Fault: the right hand closes into a fist well before it has reached the waist. The cause is a failure to understand the application. Correction: as the boxing saying has it, "Going out the hand is open; meeting a man it becomes a fist." The right hand should therefore close into a fist only just as it arrives at position.

4. Fault: the upper body bends forward and the head drops. The principal cause is neglecting the requirement of "above and below essentially one line". Correction: the body method should be centred and true; though the bend of the waist is large, one must still keep "the hundred meeting-point, the central pole, one breath threading through" — avoid bending the waist and rounding the back.

VI. Technical Analysis

Throughout the whole of the Yang-style set there are few movements in which the upper body bends forward; Step Forward and Plant the Fist is one of them. Its distinguishing feature is the outward inclination of the upper body. How is one to understand the operation of "the tailbone centred and true" in this movement? It is a matter of understanding the difference between being centred and true without deviation, and the deviation of the centred and true. In practising the form there must be extension and contraction; sometimes the bend of the waist is very great, but so long as the principle of "the hundred meeting-point, the central pole, one breath threading through" is still maintained, it is still permitted. This is what is called "the deviation of the centred and true" — the inner strength is still centred, true and undeviating. And so one must not bend the waist and round the back, must not drop the head and stoop.

# Thirty-fifth Posture: Turn the Body Over and Thrust Out the Fist (Fan Shen Pie Shen Chui)

I. Application

Joining from the preceding posture. If an opponent again strikes from behind with his fist, I turn my body over from the right towards the rear, settle solidly on the left foot, raise the right leg forward and set it down half a step, and at the same time raise the right fist and thrust it out to the rear and to the front, the back of the fist sinking downward — either taking control of the opponent's elbow, or secretly using the plucking energy. Either will do.

At the same time, the left hand follows the right fist and strikes out with the fist at the opponent's face to assist the thrusting momentum of the right fist; the body must advance with the movement — in this way one gains the advantage.

II. The Course of the Movement

1. The body straightens and turns right, and at the same time the left toe turns in and settles flat; as the body turns the right fist is raised, the elbow bent and the forearm brought horizontally across to the front of the left ribs, the centre of the fist facing down; the left palm arcs up from the left to a point above and in front of the left temple, the face towards the north. The eyes follow the turning of the body and shift in level gaze, the gaze attending to the movement of the two hands (see the first figure on this page).

2. The subsequent movements are the same as the twenty-fourth posture, "Thrust Out the Fist", only the direction of the form's route is reversed (this movement goes towards the east) (see the later figures on this page).
