# Thirty-seventh Posture: Right Heel Kick (You Deng Jiao)

Book page 383

I. Application

I. Application

Joining from the preceding posture. If the opponent uses his left hand to push my right arm away to the left, I at once follow the momentum and coil my right wrist under his wrist, and use my right hand to ward him off from right to left; at the same time the left toe turns out and settles flat, the body also turns slightly left, and I kick out straight ahead (to the east) with my right foot; the body turns from the left back to facing the front, the two hands separate in proportion to the foot, and the waist and hips sink.

Another application: when the opponent's left palm has been stuck by me and he strikes straight in with his right hand, I quickly ward it off to the left with my left hand and then kick out with my right foot.

II. The Course of the Movement

1. The body gradually turns left, the left toe turns out and settles flat, the left knee bends slightly and the left leg settles solid, the centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg, and the right leg is lifted forward. At the same time the left palm, as the body turns, moves to the left, forward and up. As it moves, the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm turns inward; the right palm changes and, from the right front, goes downward and scoops in an arc to the left, and as it scoops the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm turns inward and it clasps with the left palm, the two crossed before the chest with the right palm outside. The eyes look level to the front toward the right, the gaze attending to the clasping of the two palms (see the first two figures on this page).

2. The right foot continues to be lifted and is slowly kicked out straight ahead with the heel (to the east), the toe pointing up; as the right foot kicks out the left leg gradually straightens, the knee still slightly bent, and at the same time the two palms separate to left and right. The gaze attends to the right palm as it separates, and looks level to the right past the right palm (see the third figure on this page).

III. Key Points

1. The right heel kick should take the heel as its point of application.

2. In the heel kick the body must be stable — no leaning forward, no leaning back, no tilting. The whole body must be relaxed, the centre of gravity steady, the movements harmonious and coordinated, the chest broad and comfortable, the abdomen full, the centre of gravity lowered, so that the lower limbs are firm and the upper limbs agile, and the body is kept essentially in one line from top to bottom.

IV. Requirements

1. The turning of the waist to the left, the turning out of the left foot, the movement of the two hands and the lifting forward of the right leg must all be carried out at the same time. Because when I ward off the opponent's left hand to the left, the support of the waist's strength is necessary if the power is to reach every part of the limbs.

图 208
the left leg settled, the right leg lifted, the two palms crossing and clasping before the chest, the right palm outside.
图 209
the two palms clasped and crossed at the chest, the right knee raised, the gaze forward.
图 210
the right foot thrust out with the heel, the sole leading, the two palms separated to left and right at shoulder height.

2. When the right foot kicks out, the left leg that supports the whole body's weight must not be straightened completely, and the two separated arms must not be straightened completely either. "Strength is stored in the bent." And so the joints of the four limbs are required to be bent, not straight.

3. The direction of the kick must be exact: it must kick towards the right side (the east), because the opponent is at my right front.

V. Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Fault: the direction of the kick is inexact — it goes either too far left or too far right. The principal cause is that the left foot is withdrawn too far left, or not far enough. Correction: the left foot should be withdrawn to the left by about 45°; in the early stages of practice this must be checked and corrected repeatedly.

2. Fault: the separation of the two hands is out of proportion to the foot, with various errors of height, lowness, width, narrowness and speed. The principal cause is an insufficient understanding of the application in which the separation of the two hands is matched to the foot. Correction: the fingers should be raised to about eyebrow height, the right hand in the same direction as the right foot, the left hand on the left rear oblique — the foot must arrive and the hand must arrive.

3. Fault: when the two hands cross and clasp they are too close to the chest, which is called "collapsed", and in some cases the two hands are slack and without strength. The principal cause is insufficient attention to the hand method. Correction: the wrists should be seated and the palms comfortable, the two arms full — in this way breathing is smooth, and after long practice one can lead the hands with the body and lead the body with the hands, turning in circles along the momentum, which benefits both health and the martial application.

4. Fault: the direction of the body's turning is wrong — when the left foot turns out to the left, the upper body does not turn and still faces forward (east). The principal cause is a failure to understand the application. I use my right wrist, following the momentum, to ward the opponent's left wrist away to the left; if the waist's strength is used correctly, the whole body's strength can be concentrated on one point, whereas if the hand and waist are disconnected and one wards off with the strength of the hand alone, that does not meet the martial requirement. From the point of view of health, if the waist and hips are stiff and unmoving one cannot exercise the muscles of the waist and back, and there is a lack of the internal massaging effect on the internal organs. Hence the boxing treatise stresses, "At every moment keep your mind on the waist." Correction: the waist is the key to the turning of the upper and lower body; when warding off to the left the waist must turn left at the same time.

(There is also a push-hands photograph at the foot of this page; it is unnumbered and carries no caption.)

…concentrated on one point. If the hand and waist are disconnected and one wards off with the strength of the hand alone, that does not meet the martial requirement. From the point of view of health, if the waist and hips are stiff and unmoving one cannot exercise the muscles of the waist and back, and there is a lack of the internal massaging effect on the internal organs. Hence the boxing treatise stresses, "At every moment keep your mind on the waist." Correction: the waist is the key to the turning of the upper and lower body; when warding off to the left the waist must turn left at the same time.

Book page 384

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. The teacher must observe the movements of every part of the body from the front and from the side.

2. The emphasis must be placed on the stability of the heel kick; this must be practised over and over.

3. Paired practice following the application: A — performs Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch; B — uses his left hand from the front to push A's right arm to the left; A — follows the momentum and coils his right wrist under B's wrist, uses his right hand to ward B's left wrist away to the left, kicks out straight ahead with the right foot, and the two hands separate. The two then exchange places and practise again.

4. Progressive method: (1) The left hand shifts level to the left, the right hand arcs slightly downward and to the left, and the two hands clasp (cross) before the chest, the palms facing inward. (2) The same again, adding the turning of the left foot to the left, the lifting of the right leg, the face toward the north-east. (3) The same again, adding the kicking out of the right leg straight ahead (to the east) and the separation of the two hands.

VII. Technical Analysis

1. The distinguishing feature of this movement is that one foot stands alone while the other is lifted and kicks out; the difficulty lies in how to stand firm. And so the standing foot must have the knee joint bent and not straightened, the sole flat and firmly on the ground, its strength as though wound into the earth, so that the strength rises from the heel and the intention turns upward, while the spine is relaxed, sunk and upright, the sacrum stable and strong, the breath sunk into the lower abdomen, the crotch strength sinking down, and the hundred meeting-point on the crown of the head always lightly leading upward. This is "the empty leading of the crown, the breath sunk into the cinnabar field", the practice of lifting the crotch and threading to the crown, and it has the effect of drawing and lengthening from above and below. The lower frame must be practised so as to keep steady amid change, firm as the root of a great tree that cannot be shaken. To this end one must constantly readjust the centre of gravity in much practice, and so gradually master the correct position of the centre of gravity and attain stability standing on one foot.

2. The right heel kick transforms and attacks at once; and so in one's awareness one must not slur over the movement of the hands, but must have a clear purpose in their movement, so that the movement of the hands will not be scattered and strengthless.

3. In kicking the leg one generally tends to use force and kick out fast. According to the requirement of "the ten essentials of Taijiquan", the whole set of form movements should use intention and not force. And so in the right heel kick the leg should first be lifted with the force concentrated at the knee joint, the ligaments of the hip drawn open, and the leg kicked out gently and slowly. In practising Taijiquan the whole body must be loosened, not permitting the slightest clumsy force to lodge between the sinews, bones and blood vessels and so bind oneself; only then can one be light, nimble, changing, round and free. If instead of using force one uses intention, then wherever the intention goes the breath arrives; thus the blood and breath flow and pour in daily, circulating through the whole body without ever stagnating. Practised long and long, one obtains true inner strength.

# Thirty-eighth Posture: Left Beat the Tiger (Zuo Da Hu Shi)

I. Application

Joining from the preceding posture. If an opponent strikes from my left front with his left hand, I at once set my right foot down level with the left, and both hands turn to the left side with the body; the left foot steps out obliquely to the left, the knee bends and settles solid, the right foot becomes empty, forming the left bow stance, the face towards the side square. The two hands at the same time swing as fists, and as they descend they close to the left; I use my right palm to grip the opponent's left wrist and pluck it down to the left, bringing it opposite the region of the heart, while my left fist turns over upward from the outside to the left, comes to the side of the left corner of the forehead, the centre of the fist facing outward, and strikes swiftly at the opponent's head — or I may strike his back with the right fist. This posture advances by retreating, suddenly opening and closing the embrace with a fierce intent; hence it is called Beat the Tiger.

II. The Course of the Movement

1. The left leg gradually squats and the right foot descends. At the same time the left palm, from the left, passes across the front of the forehead and arcs level to the right, and as it moves the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm gradually turns inward; the right palm at the same time shifts slightly downward, and as it moves the arm rotates inward so that the centre of the palm gradually turns down. The gaze attends to the right palm (see the first figure on this page).

2. The left leg continues to squat, and the right foot comes down beside the left foot, the distance between the feet slightly narrower than the shoulders; the toe touches the ground first and the centre of gravity gradually shifts onto the right leg, the whole sole of the right foot settles flat, and the left foot is then lifted. As the centre of gravity shifts onto the right leg the two palms continue to move to the lower right, the left palm passing the right…

图 211
the left leg sinking, the right foot descending, the left palm arcing to the right across the front of the forehead, the right palm turning gradually face-down.
图 212
the right foot set down beside the left, the weight shifting onto the right leg, both palms continuing to move to the lower right.

…beside the upper arm, and as it moves the left arm continues to rotate outward so that the centre of the palm turns up; the two hands are slightly lower than the shoulders, the eyes look level to the front, the gaze attending to the two palms (see the second figure on this page).

3. The right leg continues to squat, the body turns left (to the north-by-west), and the left foot steps out obliquely to the left rear, the heel touching the ground first; as the centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg the whole sole settles flat, the left leg bends and the right leg extends, forming the left bow stance. As the centre of gravity moves and the body turns, the left palm, from the right chest and in front of the abdomen, passes in an arc up past the front of the left knee, tracing a curve from the lower right upward (the reverse brush of the knee), and stops above and in front of the left temple (closing into a fist just as it arrives). As the left fist arcs up from the left, the left arm turns with the body and the right arm bends slightly; the right palm moves level from the right, passes across the front of the chest to the left, and the right arm is bent at the elbow and laid horizontally in front of the upper abdomen; as it moves the right arm gradually rotates slightly outward so that the centre of the palm gradually turns obliquely down; as the right palm reaches the front of the chest it changes from palm to fist, the eye of the fist facing obliquely left, the centre of the fist facing obliquely down, so that the eyes of the left and right fists are essentially opposed above and below. At the same time the upper body turns slightly right; the gaze first attends to the left hand, and when the left fist is about to arrive above and in front of the left temple it looks level to the front (see the remaining figures on this page and on the next).

Book page 385

III. Key Points

III. Key Points

1. When the right foot comes down after the right heel kick, the left leg must "send" it — that is, the left leg slowly bends its knee and squats, so as to control the right leg's landing gently and slowly; only thus does one meet the requirement of lightness and steadiness. At the same time, the lowering of the centre of gravity accords with the application in which the right hand plucks the opponent's left fist down to the left side.

2. When the left foot steps to the left rear the upper body must be upright, and the body method must be "centred, true and undeviating". In practising the form, whether advancing, retreating, turning left or turning right, and whatever the transformations of the limbs' movement, from the crown of the head through the trunk down to the perineum there must always be one straight line.

3. In stepping the left leg, pay attention to the exchange of full and empty between the two legs: the right leg must be settled solid before the left leg is slowly stepped out, so that the movement is steady, extended, centred and true, with no unsteadiness anywhere.

图 213A
the left leg stepping out obliquely to the left rear, the left palm arcing up from the lower right to above the left temple.
图 213B
the left bow stance forming, the left fist at the left temple, the right arm bent across the upper abdomen.
图 214A
the left Beat the Tiger posture formed, seen from the front, both fists opposed above and below.

4. The movement of the two hands must follow arcs; there must be no angular corners. The arcs of Taijiquan's movements are the outward form that is necessarily present when the inner strength spirals and revolves; they are the technique of "sticking, connecting, adhering and following" and of "drawing in and dropping into emptiness", and this …accords with the application in which the two hands swing as fists, closing as they descend to the left and plucking down to the left side.

5. In the settled pose of Beat the Tiger the two arms should be full in their arcs; in the left Beat the Tiger, for instance, the right fist should be held somewhat away from the body.

IV. Requirements

1. The two palms close into fists only as they arrive at position.

2. The left foot in the left Beat the Tiger and the right foot in the right Beat the Tiger land on two oblique angles — the former to the north-west, the latter to the south-east. The direction must be correct.

3. The knee must arrive and the fist must arrive; it is not acceptable for the knee to have arrived in the bow while the hand is still tracing its arc. Above and below must keep each other company.

4. The level gaze shifts from the south-east to the north-west (in the right Beat the Tiger, from the north-west to the south-east).

V. Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Fault: in joining from the right heel kick, the right foot comes down and treads, but the left leg does not sink. The principal cause is a shallow apprehension of the application. Correction: as the right leg comes down the left leg should bend its knee and squat, the right leg brushing the ground, and the left leg steps out to the left rear — only thus does one meet the requirement of advancing by retreating. Moreover, lifting the right leg while bending the left puts a considerable load on the muscles of the left leg; if the right leg comes down and the left leg does not sink, the training effect is very much less.

2. Fault: the hands are not led by the waist — the hands move while the waist does not. The principal cause is a shallow understanding of how the inner strength is driven through…

图 214B
the left Beat the Tiger posture from the front-left, the left fist at the temple, the right fist in front of the upper abdomen.
图 215A
the left Beat the Tiger seen from behind, the left arm raised, the right fist at the abdomen, the weight on the left leg.
图 215B
the left Beat the Tiger in profile, the left bow stance, the left fist above the temple, the right fist guarding the abdomen.

…to the tips of the four limbs, and that the waist strength, used well, can augment the issuing of power. Correction: one must understand that the key to the turning of the upper and lower limbs is in the waist; the waist should lead the hands.

3. Fault: in the settled pose the direction of the two fists' eye is wrong, and their high and low positions are wrong. The principal cause is an insufficient understanding of the requirement for closing the fist. Correction: at the point where the fist comes out and lands, the fist and the forearm should form a straight line, so that the wrist is not easily injured when it meets resistance. And so in the left Beat the Tiger the right fist is below and slightly oblique, its eye facing obliquely inward; the left fist's eye faces obliquely right, its centre facing obliquely outward. The left fist, at the front of the left forehead, should be higher than the head; the right fist, below, should be in front of the upper abdomen.

4. Fault: the direction of the foot's movement is wrong. The principal cause is an insufficient understanding of the application. Correction: the direction in which the toe lands bears on whether the hip-joint is tight or open, and thus affects the body method. In joining from the right heel kick into the left Beat the Tiger, as the left leg sends the right leg down, the right toe is oblique (towards north-by-east), and when the left foot is lifted and steps to the left and right its toe faces obliquely north-west.

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. The teacher should observe the practitioner's movements from every direction — for instance from the front, to see the height and spacing of the two fists, and from an oblique angle, to see the direction of the stepping.

2. Help the practitioner quickly settle the direction of the foot and the facing of the body. One may make no demands on the two hands at first, practising the direction of the stepping repeatedly, and only then practise the stepping with the hands and feet coordinated. In the settled pose of the left Beat the Tiger the left foot is at an oblique angle towards the north-west, the body faces north-by-west, and the right foot is oblique.

(There is also a push-hands photograph at the foot of this page; it is unnumbered and carries no caption.)

…while the right foot is oblique towards the south-east and the body faces south-by-east.

3. Practise repeatedly the movement in which the left leg "sends" the right leg down, to deepen the apprehension of full and empty and to strengthen the legs.

4. Paired practice following the application: A — settles into the right heel kick. B — strikes at A with his left hand from A's left front. A — brings the right leg down and squats the left leg, changes the standing foot, steps the left foot to the left rear, uses the right leg to grip B's left wrist and plucks it down to the left side, and the left palm turns over upward from the outside, becomes a fist and strikes B's head. Apprehend the application of the two hands' movements, then exchange places and practise.

5. Progressive method: (1) The left leg squats and "sends" the right leg down. (2) The same, plus stepping the left leg. (3) The same, plus the movement of the two arms. (4) The settled pose (left Beat the Tiger). (5) The left toe turns in, the right leg is lifted, the two fists change to palms. (6) The same, plus stepping the right foot. (7) The same, plus the movement of the two arms. (8) The settled pose (right Beat the Tiger).

6. Guidance: for instance, why one must step to left and right — so that the learner understands the application of advancing by retreating.

# Thirty-ninth Posture: Right Beat the Tiger (You Da Hu Shi)

Book page 386

I. Application

I. Application

Joining from the preceding posture: if an opponent strikes from my rear right with his right hand, I at once lift my right foot and turn the waist to the right front, step the right foot out to the right side, bend the knee and settle solid, the left leg becomes empty forming the right bow stance, and the two hands at the same time turn in a circle to the right and then close into fists, forming the right Beat the Tiger. The application is the same as the left Beat the Tiger.

II. The Course of the Movement

1. The left toe turns in and the left leg settles solid, the right foot is gradually lifted with the heel leaving the ground first, and the body gradually turns right. At the same time the two fists change to palms, the left palm sinking slightly with its centre facing down; the right arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm turns face-up and moves to the front of the left upper arm. The gaze first attends to the left palm, then follows the turning of the body in a level shift (see the first figure on this page).

2. After the right foot is lifted, the body continues to turn right, then steps forward (to the south-east), the heel touching the ground first, and as the centre of gravity gradually shifts…

图 216A
the left toe turned in, the right foot lifted, the two fists changing to palms, the right palm turning face-up before the left upper arm.
图 216B
the right foot stepping forward to the south-east, the weight shifting, both palms in transition.

…onto the right leg until the whole sole settles flat, the right leg bends and the left leg extends, forming the right bow stance. As the body turns and the centre of gravity shifts forward, the right palm, from in front of the left upper arm, goes down past the top of the right knee (the reverse brush of the knee) and arcs up to the right; as it moves the right arm rotates inward so that the centre of the palm gradually turns outward, and it stops above and in front of the right temple (changing to a fist). The eye of the fist faces obliquely left, the centre of the fist obliquely outward; the left palm at the same time moves level as the body turns (lower than the shoulder), the elbow bent and the forearm laid across in front of the upper abdomen, the centre of the palm facing obliquely down, the eye of the fist facing obliquely inward. The eyes look level to the front (see the first two figures on this page).

III. Key Points

1. The turning in of the left foot, the changing of the two fists to palms and the turning of the waist with the lifting of the right leg must all begin together; when one thing moves, nothing is unmoved.

2. The left foot must be turned in sufficiently.

# Fortieth Posture: Turn the Body Back and Right Heel Kick (Hui Shen You Deng Jiao)

I. Application

The same as the thirty-seventh posture, the right heel kick, save that the direction of the joining is slightly different.

II. The Course of the Movement

1. Pivoting on the ball of the left foot, the heel grinds inward and settles flat, the body gradually turns left, and the centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg. At the same time the two fists change to palms and shift level to the left as the body turns; the right palm arcs down and to the right, and the eyes follow the turning of the body in a level shift (see the last figure on this page).

图 217A
the right foot stepping out to the south-east, the right palm sinking and beginning its arc up past the right knee.
图 217B

2. The centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg, the body continues to turn left, and the right foot is drawn back. At the same time the left palm reaches slightly upward to the left front, and the right palm goes down, passes in front of the abdomen to the left, and clasps and crosses with the left palm before the chest (facing north), the left palm inside and the right palm outside, the centres of both palms facing inward. The gaze attends briefly to the left palm as it reaches up, then turns to look level to the front, as in the first figure on this page (the same as an earlier figure).

3. The same as the right heel kick, as in the second figure on this page (the same as another earlier figure).

Book page 387

III. Key Points

III. Key Points

1. The left heel grinds inward, so that the left toe points north-by-slightly-east; only then does it not interfere with the kick.

2. The movement of the two arms must be led by the turning of the waist. The boxing treatise says, "The master is in the waist"; and so the turning of the waist should gradually lead the turning of the four limbs.

IV. Requirements

1. When the centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg the body method must be centred and true; the upper body must not lean forward or backward.

2. The direction of the movement must be exact: when the two palms clasp and cross, the body must turn to face north, and only at the kick does it turn to the east.

The rest is the same as the right heel kick.

# Forty-first Posture: Twin Peaks Pierce the Ears (Shuang Feng Guan Er)

I. Application

Joining from the preceding posture. If an opponent strikes with both hands from the right side, I at once move my left toe slightly to the right and stand firm. The right foot at the same time swings round to the right side, the knee is lifted, the toe hanging down. The body at the same time turns to the right cardinal oblique angle (towards the south-east). I quickly bring the backs of both hands from above downward, separate the opponent's two wrists to left and right and pin them, and at once close both hands into fists and drive them from below upward at the opponent's two ears with the tiger's mouths facing each other. The right foot at the same time descends forward and becomes solid; and it is best if the body carries a slight intention of attacking.

II. The Course of the Movement

1. The right foot comes down, the right knee is lifted, the toe hangs down relaxed, and pivoting on the ball of the left foot the body turns right through 45° (towards the south-east). At the same time the two palms, as the body turns, arc from left to right and move before the chest, and as they move the elbows bend and the two arms rotate outward so that the centres of the palms face obliquely inward and up, the two elbows hanging down, the two arms forming arcs, and the two palms a shoulder's width apart. The eyes look level as the body turns, the gaze attending to the two palms' downward movement (see the first figure on this page).

2. The left leg gradually squats, the right leg steps forward one pace (to the south-east), the heel touching the ground first, and as the centre of gravity gradually shifts onto the right leg the whole sole settles flat; the right leg bends and the left leg extends, forming the right bow stance. At the same time the two palms go from the front downward, separate past the two sides of the right knee to left and right, and then converge upward from below; as they move the two arms rotate inward, and on reaching the upper front the two palms close into fists, the arms forming pincers, the two fists slightly higher than the head, their two tiger's mouths facing obliquely down at each other. The eyes look level to the front, the gaze attending to the two fists (see the remaining figures on this page and on the next).

III. Key Points

1. When the body turns it must be centred and true; it must not lean forward or backward.

2. After the turn the left leg squats and the right leg has a slight intention of lifting upward; this makes it easier to draw in the hips. The loosening of the shoulders, the sinking of the elbows, the lifting of the leg and the drawing in of the hips must all be done together.

3. In stepping the right foot forward, the left leg must first be settled solid and the root of the right hip drawn in; then the left leg gradually squats and the two hands reach downward at the same time as the knee extends, and the right leg steps forward under control, the upper body still kept upright, and the speed of the step must be even.

图 222
the right foot lowered and the right knee raised, the toe hanging relaxed, both palms arcing from left to right before the chest, the elbows down.
图 223
the right foot stepping forward to the south-east, the two palms separating past the sides of the right knee.
图 224
the right bow stance forming, the two palms converging upward, about to close into fists.

4. The two palms should close into the two fists only when the elbows are hanging and the palms have turned from below upward. The driving through of the two fists with the tiger's mouths facing each other must be coordinated with the right bow stance; the width between the two fists should be about one tiger's mouth (about 20 cm).

5. Sink the hips, sink the breath, loosen the shoulders; when the two palms have come down level with the knee, the two elbows sink to lead the two palms' descent — the two palms must not descend by themselves. Use the strength of the whole body, so that the backs of the palms descend steadily, calmly and cleanly.

IV. Requirements

1. The turning of the body to the right must be steady.

2. After the body has turned right the left leg must be settled solid, and the stepping out of the right leg must be light and nimble — it must not come down in a rush.

3. The fists should not be gripped too tightly, nor yet be wholly slack and strengthless; they should be such that they cannot be forced open, and cannot be broken up when struck.

4. The whole movement must be continuous and without pauses. The requirement is that after the body has turned towards the south-east the left foot immediately squats and the two palms are drawn back and moved down — and one must not let the other movements pause in order to keep the centre of gravity steady. In martial terms, immediately after the turn one must separate the opponent's two wrists, struck in from the right side, to left and right; and if the movement pauses at that moment, one will be struck on the body by the opponent's fist.

5. When the two fists drive through with the tiger's mouths facing each other, the arms must not be straightened; they must still keep their arcs, and the body must not lean forward and reach out.

V. Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Fault: the direction of the right turn is not exact (it is not towards the south-east). One principal cause is poor control, making the angle of the turn too small or too large. The second is a shallow understanding of the application. The opponent strikes from the right side, and so after the turn one should face the right-hand side (the south-east). Correction: the turn should be practised repeatedly, checking after each turn whether the direction is right, with particular attention to the angle through which the left foot grinds; after much practice one gradually achieves controlled rotation.

2. Fault: after the turn the left knee does not bend and the body does not sink. The principal cause is a failure to understand the application. If one tries with the backs of the two hands alone to separate and pin the opponent's two wrists to left and right, one's strength is necessarily limited; but if the sinking strength of the body and the two elbows is added to the two hands, then the strength…

图 225A
the two fists driven up at the ears, the tiger's mouths facing each other, seen from the front.
图 225B
the completed Twin Peaks posture, the two fists at head height, arms pincer-shaped, seen from the front.

…is greater. Correction: after the turn the left leg must squat and the two elbows sink to lead the two palms' descent.

3. Fault: the stepping of the right leg forward is sluggish and heavy. The principal cause is that the root of the left hip has not been drawn in and the left leg has not been settled solid. Correction: "Movement originates in the waist and spine, and strength runs through to the four tips" — and so the waist's hollow governs the two legs. If stepping is to be light and nimble, the left and right waist hollows must alternately draw and exchange in order to distinguish full from empty; when full and empty are clear, the left leg seems able to coil its root into the ground. In this way the right leg's stepping forward becomes light and nimble.

Book page 388

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. The emphasis of the teaching should be placed on the rotation supported on one foot, feeling out the coordination of the turning of the waist and hips, the lifting of the knee and the grinding turn of the left foot, so that the rotation is steady.

2. Teaching mnemonic: turn, sink, extend, strike.

3. The difficulty of this method lies in the bending and sinking of the left leg; this requires leg strength and must be practised long. While strengthening the legs one also masters the technique, and thereby strengthens the constitution as well. In practice the teacher must remind the practitioner that the upper body must be straight and the central axis must not bend.

4. Paired practice following the application: A — performs the right heel kick; B — strikes at A with both hands from A's right side; A — turns the body right, the right leg swings round, the two hands go from above downward, separate and pin B's two wrists to left and right, and immediately drives the two fists hooking at B's two ears. The two then exchange.

5. Progressive method: (1) First practise the turn alone, requiring the correct direction, the lifting of the leg and the moving of the two hands before the body. (2) The same, plus the squatting of the left leg, the right leg stepping forward with the heel coming down, and the two hands separating to left and right at the level of the knee. (3) The same, plus the shifting forward of the centre of gravity and the two hands hooking upward at the front.

6. Of the beginner one should require only that the movements be correct. Of the long-term practitioner one should require lightness and nimbleness. The boxing treatise says, "With a single movement, the whole body should be light and nimble", and "In every posture, move lightly, stop silently, and drive it only with intent and meaning." Only by using little strength and practising "lightly" can the movements become more and more nimble, and gradually attain to the highly sensitised "spirit" that is "unable to bear even a feather added".

VII. Technical Analysis

1. This movement is a turn performed supported on one foot, pivoting on the ball of the left foot. Because the angle of the turn is not great, and both the two arms and the right leg can play a part in driving and checking it, it can generally be accomplished fairly well.

2. The squatting of the left leg and the stepping forward of the right leg are not easy to do well. Because in squatting supported on one leg the load on the quadriceps and so on is considerable; yet the two hands merely come down and separate, with little effect on the steadiness of the centre of gravity. But to step the right leg out lightly and nimbly requires the loosening of the right hip, and this is not easy to do well. Long practice can open the root of the hip, and then the turning of the waist and legs becomes nimble and the stepping light and broad.

# Forty-second Posture: Left Heel Kick (Zuo Deng Jiao)

I. Application

Joining from the preceding posture. If an opponent strikes at my left flank, I quickly use my left hand to stick to his right arm and ward it off from the inside outward. The right foot shifts slightly to the right in place, and the left foot at the same time is lifted forward and kicks at the opponent's abdomen. The rest is the same as the thirty-second posture, Turn the Body and Heel Kick.

II. The Course of the Movement

1. The body turns slightly right, the right toe turns out and settles flat, the centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely onto the right leg, and the left foot is lifted forward. At the same time the two fists change to palms and separate in arcs to left and right, then go down, pass in front of the abdomen, and clasp and cross before the chest, the left palm outside; as they move the two arms rotate outward so that the centres of the palms gradually turn inward. The gaze first attends to the two palms as they trace their arcs, and when the two arms are about to cross it turns to look level to the left (see the first two figures on this page).

2. The left foot is slowly kicked out to the left (the east) with the heel. At the same time the two palms separate to left and right, and the right leg gradually straightens as the left kicks out, though the knee remains slightly bent. The gaze attends to the left palm as it separates, and looks level to the front past the left palm (see the third figure on this page).

3. The rest is the same as the right heel kick, only the direction is reversed.

图 227

# Forty-third Posture: Turn the Body and Right Heel Kick (Zhuan Shen You Deng Jiao)

Book page 389

I. Application

I. Application

Joining from the preceding posture. If an opponent strikes from the left behind, I pivot on the ball of my right foot and turn my body to the right and rear, and as the body turns the left foot is drawn back and suspended to the right, then comes down and settles solid with the toe pointing forward (north). At this moment the ball of the right foot is the pivot of the whole body's turn. The two hands close and are gathered before the body; I quickly use my right wrist to stick to the opponent's elbow and wrist, and from above downward cut it out to the left side. At the same time the right foot is lifted and kicks at the opponent's ribs and abdomen, and the left and right hands separate to left and right accordingly.

II. The Course of the Movement

1. The right heel leaves the ground, and pivoting on the ball of the right foot the body turns rapidly to the right and rear. At the same time the left foot, as the body turns, swings from left through front to right rear, and after the turn comes down beside the inner side of the right ankle, the toe touching the ground first; as the centre of gravity gradually shifts the whole sole settles flat, and immediately the left leg squats slightly and the right foot is lifted. At the same time the two palms, as the body turns, arc from left and right and clasp and cross before the chest, the right palm outside, the centres of both palms facing inward, the face towards the north. The eyes follow the turning of the body in a level shift, the gaze attending to the clasping of the two palms (see the figures on this page and on the next).

2. The rest is the same as the right heel kick.

III. Key Points

1. The turn must be just right: too much or too little and the direction will be wrong. And so it must be controlled. Therefore the left foot and the crossing of the two arms must cooperate with the waist in doing the turning well.

2. In the instant of steadiness after the turn, the right leg squats and "sends" the left leg down to settle solid; then the right heel kick is made.

3. In turning, the direction is fixed by the right heel landing correctly.

4. The clasping and crossing of the two hands must begin at the same time as the turning of the body, and be completed at the same time.

5. The rest is the same as the right heel kick.

IV. Requirements

1. The rotation of the waist must be relaxed, sunk and upright — not swaying. To use the leg to swing is to be loose and disconnected.

图 229
the body turning to the right rear, the left foot swinging round, the two palms beginning to close before the chest.
图 230A
the left foot coming down beside the right ankle, the toe touching first, both palms crossed before the chest.
图 230B
the two palms clasped and crossed before the chest, the body facing north, the right foot about to be lifted.

2. After the turn the angle must be correct and the body must face north. The kick goes due east.

3. The rotation must be light, nimble and natural, and the movements neither hurried nor slow.

V. Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Fault: swaying after the turn, or an unsteady stance. The principal cause is a failure to attend to relaxation and the use of stiff force instead. In turning, some do not relax the waist and hips, some swing the left leg through too great an arc, and some have poor control of the suspended turning of the left leg. Correction: the tailbone must be centred and true, the waist and hips relaxed, and there must be control over the landing position of the right heel and over the left knee.

2. Fault: the left foot comes down too fast, destroying the evenness and roundness. The principal cause is poor management of the centre of gravity — in order to keep balance and avoid falling, the left leg is landed too early. Correction: after the turn the right heel should land slowly; then the left leg is suspended and lifted, the right leg squats slightly, and only then does the left leg gradually come to the ground.

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. For the elderly and the weak the requirement for the rotation may be lowered and the left leg held lower.

2. The difficulty of this movement lies in the rotation, and so the emphasis of practice should be placed on the rotation. No demands are made on the two hands; building on the preceding movement, the left knee is lifted in turning, remains lifted after the turn, the right leg sinks, and only then does the left foot slowly come to the ground.

3. Mnemonic: release — the left leg is let down and suspended; land — the left leg descends and settles; turn — the waist and hips turn the body round; rise — the left leg rises slightly; sink — the left leg squats; kick — the right leg kicks out; close — the two hands cross before the chest.

VII. Technical Analysis

In Turn the Body and Heel Kick the body rotates through nearly 360°; the preceding left heel kick goes to the east, and in Turn the Body and Heel Kick the body turns and then the right foot goes to the east. In both cases the direction of the kick is east — only the direction of the turn and the leg are changed. The key lies in the rotation to the right and rear. The requirement for the rotation is first that it be steady, and second that it be exact (that is, the direction after the turn must be exact). And so the technique of Turn the Body and Heel Kick must first be analysed in terms of the rotation. All things…

图 231A
the right heel landing slowly after the turn, the left knee still raised, the two palms crossed at the chest.
图 231B
the left foot suspended and lifted, the right leg squatting slightly, the body steadied before the kick.
图 232
the right heel kick delivered towards the east, the sole leading, the two palms separated.

…can only move in a circle when acted upon by centripetal force; and so the swinging of the arms and legs must not go straight to and fro. The driving force of the rotation must come from the waist and hips. When the rotation is done well, the subsequent bending of the right leg to "send" the left leg down, and then the right heel kick, are not hard to do.

# Forty-fourth Posture: Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch (Jin Bu Ban Lan Chui)

I. Application

The same as the twelfth posture, Step Forward, Deflect, Parry and Punch.

II. The Course of the Movement

The left leg gradually squats, the right leg descends and the knee is lifted, and the waist turns slightly right; at the same time the right palm closes into a fist and arcs from the right downward and to the left across the front of the abdomen, the centre of the fist facing down; the left palm sinks slightly as the left leg squats, then arcs slightly upward from the left (the fingers no higher than the shoulder), and as it traces its arc the centre of the palm faces obliquely down-right. # Forty-ninth Posture: Part the Wild Horse's Mane to Left and Right (Zuo You Ye Ma Fen Zong)

Book page 392

I. Application

I. Application

Joining from the preceding posture: if an opponent uses a press from the right side to press my right arm, I at once turn my body to the right and move my left foot also to the right, drawing the right heel back to form the empty step. Then I use my right hand to stick to the opponent's left wrist and relax slightly to the left, and use my left hand to ward off his right wrist. At the same time I quickly bring the right foot up, bend the knee and settle solid, straighten the left leg, and at once use my right forearm to separate into the opponent's armpit; his root strength can then be plucked up by me, and his body will lean back. At this moment the left hand should also separate slightly to the rear, using sinking strength to assist the right hand's force (to assist the momentum of the right hand).

Another application is this: if an opponent strikes at my right chest with his right fist, I use the left Part the Wild Horse's Mane to ward his hand out with my left hand, and then strike out with a press.

II. The Course of the Movement
(A) Right Part the Wild Horse's Mane

1. The body turns slightly right, the left toe turns in and settles flat, the centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg, the left leg settles solid, and the right foot is lifted and drawn back (facing west). At the same time the left palm, the elbow bent, arcs to the front of the left chest, the palm facing obliquely down; the right hanging hand changes to a palm and scoops from the right downward and to the left in an arc to the front of the abdomen, and as it scoops the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm turns obliquely up and joins with the left hand, both arms forming arcs. The gaze attends to the left palm (see the first figure on this page).

2. The body continues to turn right, facing west, and the right foot slowly steps forward, the heel touching first; as the centre of gravity gradually shifts onto the right leg and the whole sole of the right foot settles flat, the right leg bends and the left leg extends, forming the right bow stance. At the same time the right palm, its centre facing obliquely up, arcs out with the radial side of the forearm to the upper right front as the body turns, the fingers at eyebrow height; the left palm plucks down in an arc to the side of the left hip. The gaze attends to the right palm as it separates, and reaches the right front slightly before the right palm does, the face towards the south-west (see the second figure on this page).

(B) Left Part the Wild Horse's Mane

1. The body turns slightly right (facing north-west), the right toe turns out and treads flat, the centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely onto the right leg, the right leg settles solid, and the left leg is lifted forward. At the same time the right palm, as the body turns, arcs with the elbow bent to the front of the right chest…

图 263
the left toe turned in and settled, the right foot drawn back, the left palm at the left chest, the right palm scooping to the front of the abdomen.
图 264
the right foot stepping forward, the right palm arcing out to the upper right, the left palm plucking down to the left hip.
图 265
the right bow stance formed, seen in profile, the right forearm separating outward, the left hand at the left hip.

…and as it moves the arm rotates inward so that the centre of the palm gradually turns down; the left palm scoops in an arc to the right to the front of the abdomen, and as it scoops the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm turns obliquely up and joins with the right palm, both arms forming arcs. The eyes follow the turning of the body in a level shift, the gaze attending to the right palm (see the first two figures on this page).

2. The body continues to turn gradually left (facing west), the left foot steps forward, the heel touching first; as the centre of gravity gradually shifts onto the left leg and the whole sole settles flat, the left leg bends and the right leg extends, forming the left bow stance. At the same time the left palm, its centre facing obliquely up, arcs out with the thumb side of the hand to the upper left front as the body turns, the fingers at eyebrow height; the right palm plucks down in an arc to the side of the right hip. The gaze attends to the left palm as it separates, and reaches the left front slightly before the left palm does, the face towards the south-west (see the remaining figures on this page).

3. Thereafter the left and right Part the Wild Horse's Mane are identical in movement, only the direction changing again and again (once to the left, once to the right), as in the further figures on this page and on the next (the same as earlier figures).

III. Key Points

1. Whether the right or the left hand separates, the power is issued from the waist. The Boxing Treatise stresses, "At every moment keep your mind on the waist", and "The nine joints above and below — the strength issues from the waist at every joint." When the waist's strength is used correctly it can concentrate the whole body's strength on one point; and one must thread from shoulder to elbow to hand, joint by joint, issuing outward. The separation of the hand and the turning of the waist and the bow stance must also be coordinated. The strength must go from the foot to the leg, to the waist, and take form in the fingers: its root is in the foot, its master in the waist. When I separate into the opponent's armpit I must pluck up his root strength; if I use only the strength of the hand, that is far from enough.

2. The bow stance of Part the Wild Horse's Mane is a little wider than the ordinary bow stance, but not as much as a 45° oblique angle. If the lateral distance of the bowed-out foot is small the stance is unsteady and one cannot give strength to the separating hand.

3. The toe of the bowed-out leg must be in the same direction as the knee.

4. Whether closing or splitting, the shoulders must sink and the elbows hang.

5. The route of the separating hand is first forward, then outward (the right hand to the right, the left hand to the left).

6. When the left and right Part the Wild Horse's Mane is repeated many times (three, five or more), although the movements alternate left and right they must be continuous; and so each posture must carry on from the last, with no dividing pause.

图 266
the body turned right, the right palm arcing to the front of the right chest, the left palm converging upward from the abdomen.
图 267
the left foot stepping forward, the left palm arcing out to the upper left, the right palm plucking down to the right hip.
图 268
the left bow stance formed, seen in profile, the left forearm separating outward at eyebrow height.
IV. Requirements

1. Empty and full must be clear. The body, the hands and the steps are all to be distinct, and the internal and external conversions of empty and full must also agree. That is why internal and external, above and below, left and right, front and rear are all to be clearly distinguished as empty or full. The sinking of the lower limb is the key to the body's steadiness; therefore the first thing to attend to is the clear distinction of empty and full in the two legs. The more finely the empty and full of the two legs is distinguished, the more the feeling of the movement improves step by step. Beginners must make the full foot grind and a single foot be solid, and only then may the other foot be slowly lifted and slowly sent out; before the heel has landed, the centre of gravity may not change.

2. In left and right Part the Wild Horse's Mane there must be no pause between one posture and the next. It is to be threaded through, one posture succeeding another, connected and lively. But one must also avoid the fault of the hands and feet not having arrived in place — that is, of the movement not being complete — before going on to the next movement.

3. In advancing, the two feet are not to be in one line; the toe of the front foot is to face square to the front.

4. Opening out and drawing together must be combined.

V. Likely Errors, Their Causes, and Their Correction

1. Error: the two hands make a large circle, so the direction is not correct and the direction at the settled posture is unclear. The main cause is a poor grasp of the method of use. Take the right Part the Wild Horse's Mane as the example: the opponent attacks me from my right side, I step forward with the right foot and separate the right hand downward into his armpit. If my right hand describes a large circle, then when the hand arrives it is not under the opponent's armpit but in front of his head, and the possibility of "separating" is lost. Correction: it must first go forward and then outward, the fingers no higher than the eyebrows — only then can it separate into his armpit and pluck up his root strength.

2. Error: the turn of the body is too great, giving a loose and scattered appearance. Take the left Part the Wild Horse's Mane as the example: if the right foot is wrongly opened out to as much as 90°, so that the right toe points north, then when stepping up on the left one feels a pull in the right leg and a great awkwardness, and it also interferes with the left foot's stepping forward correctly. The main cause is an insufficient understanding of the method of use. Correction: the right foot should be opened out to about 45°.

3. Error: the two hands do not follow an arc but go straight out and straight back. The main cause is an inadequate understanding of Tai Chi's characteristic — circular motion…

…deeply. Tai Chi has a movement, and that is a circle; "a marvellous hand is one Tai Chi". It contains the two forces of yin and yang revolving and transforming. Correction: one must "have the straight within the curved" — every place a curve, every place a straight line, the unification of the curved and the straight; one must be able at any moment to transform the arc into a straight line and so strike.

4. Error: in the movement the stepping foot lands with a heavy sound, and empty and full are unclear. The main cause is that the supporting leg has not sat solid. Correction: besides the empty-full conversion of the stepping method, the waist and hips must also be brought into coordinated conversion, so that the stepping is light and nimble.

Book page 393

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

1. The mnemonic (taking the right Part the Wild Horse's Mane as the example): the right hand plucks and the left hand wards; ward, brush and strike; the left is solid and the right is empty, stepping slowly; the right hand plucks down and separates forward into the armpit; you receive my root strength and I myself pluck it up.

2. The learner must keep raising the standard of bow-stance advancing. Besides the empty-full distinction of the step already learned, one should also practise "even movement" and "unbroken continuity".

3. Use discussion to correct details, for example: ① How does the body turn — is there a turn when closing? ② Why must the arm first go forward and then outward?

VII. Technical Analysis
图 271
the push-hands application of the right Part the Wild Horse's Mane, outdoors: the attacker drives in with the right forearm, the defender separates it outward.

When using it one must step up with the right foot in good time, the right knee sat solid, the left leg extended, and separate the right forearm downward into the opponent's armpit. Why "in good time"? The important meaning here is that the victory lies in seizing the initiative of advancing; if one does not step up in good time, then either the opponent steps up towards me, or one fails to follow up the advantage. If one does not act promptly one loses the opportunity. But in practising the form one must still step forward slowly.

Posture Fifty — Grasping the Bird's Tail
I. Method of Use

Same as Posture Three, Grasping the Bird's Tail.

II. Course of the Movement

The body turns slightly right, the centre of gravity gradually shifting entirely onto the right leg, the left leg lifted from the ground. At the same time the right elbow draws back, and as it draws back the right arm rotates inward so that the centre of the palm turns down, arcing to the front of the chest, the right elbow slightly lower than the wrist; the left palm likewise arcs to the front of the abdomen, and as it moves the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm turns up. The two palms join, the left foot steps to the left side, the heel touching first, the foot turned out obliquely, the toes pointing south-west, the left leg bent and the right leg extended forming the left bow stance (the left foot slightly behind and to the right of the right foot). As the left foot steps to the left, the body turns slightly left; as soon as the left heel has touched the ground the body immediately turns gradually right; at the same time the left elbow sinks, the left arm arcs out to the upper left, the left palm at shoulder height, the wrist slightly bent, the centre of the palm facing obliquely up…

Posture Fifty-Two — the Jade Girl Works the Shuttle
I. Method of Use

#### (A) The Left Shuttle Following the Single Whip posture. Should the opponent, from my right rear, strike down with his right hand from above, I immediately turn my body to the right as I turn my left foot in, and the right foot is thereupon lifted back and set down in front of the left foot, the toes turned to sit apart to the right. The left hand draws back and closes beneath the right hand, and following this guards around the right upper arm, threading through at the right elbow; that is, I ward (peng) it up and out to the left front corner, lifting the opponent's wrist, while the left foot simultaneously advances, the knee bent and sat solid, the right leg extended…

The right hand thereupon becomes a palm, and in haste threads out from beneath the left elbow, striking at the opponent's chest and ribs; thus the opponent has no one who does not fall. In this posture the left and right hands thread through one another, now hidden now appearing, elusive and unfixed, taking advantage of his emptiness to strike — and so it is called the Jade Girl Works the Shuttle, using this to liken this movement's nimbleness and agility (see the first six figures on this page).

#### (B) The Right Shuttle Following the previous posture. Should the opponent strike from behind my right side with the head of his right fist, I immediately turn my left foot in, and at the same time the right foot steps one pace out to the right rear, the knee bent and sat solid, the body following this turning to the right, the left foot becoming empty; in haste I use my right forearm to stick to the outside of the opponent's right arm and lift it up to the right rear…

Following this the left hand is pressed down towards the opponent's right ribs; the rest is as in the previous posture (see the first figures on this page).

#### (C) The Left Shuttle Following the previous posture. Should the opponent strike from my left side with his left hand, I immediately sit apart with my right toes turned to the right, and the left foot is lifted and steps out to the left corner to sit solid, the hand technique being the same as the previous Left Shuttle (see the figures at the foot of this page and on the next).

#### (D) The Right Shuttle This posture is the same as the previous Right Shuttle (see the figures on the next page). One must note that the correct directions of the Jade Girl Works the Shuttle are at the four corners; this point must on no account be mistaken.

II. Course of the Movement

#### (A) The Left Shuttle 1. The upper body turns slightly right, the left toes are turned in and sat solid; at the same time the right hand hangs and becomes a palm, arcing downward from the right front to the left, the left palm also gradually arcing downward and moving across, the gaze shifting level and attending to the direction of both hands.

2. The body continues to turn gradually right, the centre of gravity shifting entirely onto the left leg, the right foot lifted; at the same time the right palm, following the body's turning, arcs upward from below through the front of the left chest to the right, the left hand continuing to arc downward and lick across. The gaze attends to the right palm as it wards up to the right.

3. The body continues to turn right, the right foot stepping out to the right front (north-west), the heel touching first, the centre of gravity gradually shifting entirely onto the right leg and the whole sole settling flat; the left foot then lifted forward, the left palm passing through the abdomen and arcing to the lower side of the right forearm, the centre of the left palm facing down, the backs of the two hands obliquely opposing; the right palm also continues to ward right as the body turns, that is, the right elbow sinks, naturally carrying the right palm to shift downward and return.

4. The left foot steps out one pace to the left front diagonal (south-west), the heel touching first, the waist turning slightly left; at the same time the left forearm wards up and forward from the lower side of the right forearm; the right palm (with a sinking elbow) threads back through the upper side of the left forearm, and as it threads the arm rotates inward so that the centre of the palm turns obliquely to the lower front. The eyes look level to the left front, the gaze attending to the left forearm as it wards forward.

5. The body gradually turns left, the centre of gravity gradually shifting onto the left leg, the left foot settling flat, the left leg bent and the right leg extended forming the left bow stance; at the same time the left forearm moves up and round to the front, and as it moves the arm rotates inward so that the centre of the palm turns obliquely…

At the same time, the right palm, following the body's turning, bends the elbow and crosses the forearm (the arm forming an arc) shifting to the front of the chest, and as it shifts the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm gradually turns to face inward; the left arm rotates outward, and as it sinks and the left elbow drops the left palm is naturally carried to move down, the hand sinking with the back at the outer side and the palm facing inward, the two warding arms gradually forming a shape close to a crossed ten. 2. 3. The waist continues to turn right, the right foot steps out to the right front diagonal (south-east), the heel touching first; at the same time, the right forearm wards up and forward from the lower side of the left forearm; the left palm sinks the elbow, threads back through the upper side of the right forearm, and as it threads the arm rotates inward so that the centre of the palm turns gradually to face the lower front. The eyes look level to the front, the gaze attending to the right forearm as it wards forward.

4. The centre of gravity gradually shifts onto the right leg, the right foot settling flat, the body gradually turning right, the right leg bent and the left leg extended forming the right bow stance. At the same time, the right forearm turns upward across the front, and as it turns the arm rotates inward so that the centre of the palm turns to face the upper front, the right palm stopping above in front of the forehead; the left palm simultaneously threads forward, the eyes looking level to the front, the gaze attending to the left palm as it pushes forward (see the first three figures on this page).

#### (C) The Left Shuttle 1. The waist turns slightly left, the whole centre of gravity gradually shifting onto the right leg, the left leg lifted forward; at the same time, the left arm, following the body's turning, bends the elbow and crosses the forearm (the arm forming an arc) shifting to the front of the chest, and as it shifts the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm gradually turns to face inward; the right arm rotates outward, and the sinking right elbow naturally carries the right palm to shift down, the palm facing inward, the left hand outside and the right hand within, gradually forming two warding arcs close to a crossed ten. The gaze attends to the right palm as it shifts down, then immediately turns to the left arm in front (see the seventh figure on this page).

2. 2 and 3. The movement is the same as steps 4 and 5 of the previous Left Shuttle.

III. Key Points

1. The Jade Girl Works the Shuttle has in all four threadings-through, the directions being towards the four diagonal corners (south-west, south-east, north-east, north-west).

2. In the four threadings the two hands each pass once through a shape resembling a crossed ten; the first has the left hand outside, the second the right hand outside, the third the left hand outside, the fourth the right hand outside.

3. At each turn of the body or step up, one must not rise up, so that the centre of gravity has no great fluctuation. In turning the body while stepping, because of the changes of direction and angle and the lack of coordination between the upper and lower, left and right, the beginner cannot avoid instability, swaying and rising and falling, which then affects the movement. Therefore one must first take care over the empty-full conversion of the stepping method, and make each step follow the body's turning.

4. In the movement the body must be kept upright, the chest contained and the back rounded; do not lower the head or bend the waist.

5. When warding up with one hand, guard against the shoulders rising or the elbows protruding; the pushing arm should not be straightened, but slightly bent — bent and not straight is what preserves the stored force.

6. When changing into the bow stance, one palm pushes forward, and the toes, knees, body, face and gaze must all be in the same direction as the push, all facing the diagonal corner.

IV. Requirements

1. The connecting movement from Single Whip to the Jade Girl Works the Shuttle is the easiest to overlook and the easiest to confuse; it requires a clear understanding. In my Single Whip posture I face east; now the opponent strikes down from above at my right rear. Therefore the transition for the first threading is: the upper body turns right, the right foot lifted back, set down in front of the left foot, the left foot stepping out at the south-west diagonal, performing the first threading (towards the south-west). This accords with the requirement of the method of use, and it also divides the transition movement clearly.

2. The upper and lower, left and right must mutually draw one another…

…turning over, one hand at the same time threads out to the front, one foot advances with the knee sat solid, one leg extended. In this way, between the two hands and between the two feet, the upper and lower, left and right mutually respond and have the sense of drawing and binding one another, so that the movement is expansive without being loose, the spirit gathered, and in the opening out the stored force is not lost. There must be no upper with no lower, no lower with no upper.

3. In the transition the right foot must turn over to the right with the body and be drawn back; otherwise one will not gain the advantage.

4. The movement must be centred, upright and comfortable. The body must be centred and not leaning; wherever the movement goes, the spine must point directly there — especially in going from the first threading to the second, and the third to the fourth, when the change of the body's direction reaches (180° + 90°) = 270°. If the turning-in of the foot is insufficient, the stance is unsteady, the upper body will then lean forward or backward or twist awkwardly, and this does not meet the requirement of being centred, upright and comfortable.

5. The turning of the two hands must not leave the centre line; they may not "scatter" — that is, the two hands may not leave the body.

6. When the two hands cross in a ten, the two hands must follow as the body turns (following the turn and closing).

7. The movement must be continuous and even.

Book page 396

V. Likely Errors, Their Causes, and Their Correction

V. Likely Errors, Their Causes, and Their Correction

1. Error: the direction is not correct. The main cause is a lack of understanding of the method of use, and insufficient turning-in of the foot. The first and second threadings have the opponent at my right rear, the third has him at the left, the fourth at the right rear — all are at diagonal (side) angles. Therefore the threading directions must all be diagonal. Correction: the key lies in the turning-in of the foot; the turning-in must be sufficient, and to turn the foot in well one must turn the waist and hips well.

2. Error: the buttocks protrude. The main causes are, first, using the shifting back of the buttocks to carry the turning of the body instead of turning the waist and hips to bring the body round; and second, in order to keep the balance easily, the buttocks are pushed back and the upper body leans forward. Correction: first one must tuck in the tailbone, then attend to sufficient turning-in of the foot.

3. Error: the movement pauses. The main cause is that the beginner, because he performs the movement while thinking, is always wanting to think of the hands and think of the feet, and so makes a slip and a pause; and further, the supporting foot is unsteady. If the movement is interrupted, then the old strength is spent and the new strength has not yet been born, and at this moment…

…is the easiest for people to catch. Therefore the movement must not pause; it must be continuous and unbroken, revolving endlessly, as the Treatise says: "Like the great river and the sea, flowing on without cease." Correction: one form joined to the next, continuous and lively, rise, receive, turn and close threaded through; one breath, and the strength gradually enough, the spirit gathered — and the opportunity of the lower posture is born of itself. Therefore there must be no place of pause.

4. Error: the movement is awkward, especially when one hand wards up and the other threads forward. The main cause lies in the lower limbs not being smooth. Correction: after stepping out at the diagonal, one should in turning follow round to the rear foot, so that the body follows the foot and the foot follows the body.

5. Error: the transition from Single Whip to the threading is unclear, so that one often feels that the hands and feet have nowhere to be placed. The main cause is an incomplete understanding of the method of use. The transition and connecting movements are chiefly to prepare the conditions for the main movement. In my position of Single Whip the opponent strikes down from above at my right rear; if in turning the body I take the right leg as full, this must produce a passive situation, and it will be difficult to turn and difficult to advance. I must draw back the right leg…

At the foot of this page is a push-hands photograph, outdoors, in which the upper hand lifts the opponent's arm from below; it carries no number and no caption.

…falling in front of the left foot, and the left foot then advances at the diagonal — and the lower limbs are lively. "The hand follows the foot, the foot follows the hand", the upper and lower drawing one another. Because the left hand circles a small circle, driven by the waist's turning right and left; the right hand's falling is to prepare for threading out from beneath the left elbow, and therefore at this moment the two hands' movements are only preparatory. Correction: the left foot turns in and the body turns slightly right, and this brings the right hand to move right; the right hand falls and the right foot is drawn back, the left hand also being brought to move left, forming a small circle. The foot is set down, the right hand moves up, the left hand moves down, the body turns right, and the left leg is lifted as preparation for the threading.

6. Error: the threading hand is pulled back without sinking the elbow. The main cause is an unclear grasp of the method of use. Closing is issuing; without closing there is nothing to issue. Correction: after closing (crossing), one must sink the elbow and draw back, and only then thread out. And the threading hand must not cross out sideways away from the elbow of the warding arm.

Book page 397

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

1. First make clear the directions and distinguish the four diagonal corners of the four threadings. Correct them one by one; the teacher may stand at the diagonal corner to guide the direction.

2. The transition at the beginning is the easiest for the beginner to muddle; therefore the teacher must divide this part of the movement clearly — that is, take steps 1–3 of the first Left Shuttle as the transition movement.

3. The graded method: learn the transition first, then consolidate one by one on this basis until all four threadings are learned.

4. Paired practice in accordance with the method of use: A — settled in the Single Whip posture, facing east. B — stands at A's right rear (south-west) and strikes down from above with his right hand. A — turns in the left foot, turns the body over, the right foot drawn back and set down, the left foot stepping out at the south-west diagonal, the left hand warding up, the right hand threading out to strike at B's chest and ribs. C — stands at A's right rear (south-east) and continues the practice as above; if there are only two people, B may move about to take the part.

5. After the movement is basically proficient, the practitioner should, with care, experience that the intention arrives, the eye arrives, the body arrives, the hand arrives and the step arrives, and that speaking of one brings all together; and should strive to achieve the union of spirit and form.

VII. Technical Analysis
图 308
the opening of the Grasping the Bird's Tail posture: the right elbow sinking, both palms closing before the chest, the left foot lifted.

1. The Jade Girl Works the Shuttle changes direction without cease, and its continuous single-leg supporting steps are of great benefit to the growth of the legs' strength; and the repeated revolutions and changes of direction give the body's position-sense receptors a good training.

2. Every posture has its rise, receive, turn and close. Issuing is the rise, receiving is the receive, changing is the turn, and forming the posture is the close. In the Jade Girl Works the Shuttle, the four threadings make up one overall posture, and each threading must be threaded through, every place fitting together, the fitting together bringing together the whole spirit; the four limbs' upper and lower, left and right, front and rear must all unite naturally. Therefore between the movements there must be no place of pause; there must be "one breath threaded through".

3. The long-time practitioner of Tai Chi must attend to the union of internal and external. The traditional method of practice is "first the intention stirs, then the internal moves, then the form appears"; that is, the internal moves and the external form follows, the external form closes with the internal movement, from internal to external and from external drawing the internal, until at last internal and external become one (the internal and external join). Therefore the long-time practitioner should not stop at speaking only of external movement; the breath and blood must be harmonised and the channels and vessels made free. One must achieve "the mind calm and the intention present", "the body upright and relaxed". Therefore, when practising the Jade Girl Works the Shuttle, one must first settle in the mind the opponent's attack, position and movement; and then deepen the method: as the movement opens and closes, cause the internal organs to make slight upward and downward, left and right, and variously sized peristaltic movements and massaging, so that the breath and blood flow lively and smooth along the channels and blood vessels. Practising in this way is better than practising the external form alone.

Book page 398

The two palms join, both arms forming arcs. The gaze attends to the right arm, see the figure at the foot of this page (the same as the first figure of the third posture).
