Posture Fifty-Seven — The Lower Posture
I. Method of Use

1. Following the previous posture. Should the opponent use his right hand to push my left hand outward or grip it with force, I immediately sit apart with the right leg turned slightly to the right and sit back down; at the same time the left hand is drawn back to the front of the chest in a lively circling movement, to await the opportunity to attack again.

2. Following the previous posture. Should the opponent strike with his left hand, I hastily grip his wrist with my left hand and pluck it down to the left, the right leg and the waist and hips sitting down at the same time, to borrow his strength and to store my own strength.

II. Course of the Movement

1. The waist turns slightly right, the right toes opened out and sat solid, the centre of gravity gradually shifting onto the right leg; the right leg slowly bends, the centre of gravity shifting back, the left leg slowly extending (keeping a bend in the knee). At the same time, the left hand is drawn back inward and curled, the fingers pointing forward (see the first figure on this page).

2. The right leg continues to squat down forming the left resting stance; at the same time, the left palm follows the centre of gravity back and down, bending the elbow and arcing down past the side of the chest, the left hand threading forward from the inner side of the left leg, the right leg at the same time rising slightly. The gaze attends to the left hand (see the second figure on this page).

III. Key Points

1. When the left palm arcs inward and down, it must follow the shifting back of the body's centre of gravity, loosening the waist and hips and sinking the shoulders and dropping the elbows; only thus can it be threaded joint by joint, carrying the left palm to draw in and move down.

2. The left palm's movement from drawing in and down to threading forward must be lively, the fingers pointing forward (east), the centre of the palm facing south, the wrist sat.

3. Guard against the body leaning forward, the head lowered, or the buttocks protruding; the upper body should be kept upright — but note that one must not stick out the chest.

4. The gaze follows the left palm; but when the left palm threads from below forward, one may not lower the head — the eyes must look level.

IV. Requirements

1. The squatting down of the right leg must be slow.

2. The upper body must be straight and not bent. The Boxing Treatise says: "The hundred meetings, the central pole, one breath threaded through." Any place where the body leans forward, leans back, or is crooked does not meet the requirement.

图 349
the right leg squatting, the waist turned right, the left palm at the left side, the right palm raised at the right.
图 350
the left resting stance formed, the left palm threading forward from the inner side of the left leg, the right palm at the right.

3. When squatting down, the left arm's drawing back must be greater than 90° and not too bent; and the drawing back of the hand must be carried by the waist.

Book page 401

V. Likely Errors, Their Causes, and Their Correction

V. Likely Errors, Their Causes, and Their Correction

1. Error: the two feet stand in one line and the person is unsteady. The main cause lies in the previous posture, Single Whip: the left foot was not shifted back far enough to the left and the lateral distance is too small. Correction: attend to the correct position of the two feet in the preceding Single Whip.

2. Error: the left arm is too straight or too bent. The main cause is a failure to sink the elbow, or making the palm's circle too large. Correction: the arm must be relaxed, lively, round and alive, and must be firm yet soft and springy; the rising, falling, extending and contracting must all follow arcs. The arm must avoid both stiffness, forming a straight arm, and looseness and slackness, with great rises and falls; generally the bend of the arm should be no more than about 100°.

3. Error: the upper body leans forward. The main cause is an inadequate understanding of the method of use. Because, whether in the plucking down or in drawing my left hand back to the front of the chest with a lively circle, what is used is the sitting down of the right leg and the waist and hips, borrowing his strength; and if the upper body leans forward, not only can one use only the strength of the arm, which is unfavourable for the plucking down and the freeing of the grip, but it also affects the gaze, which cannot observe the opponent well. Correction: the waist and hips must be relaxed, sunk and straight; only when the central pole is not bent can it support the eight directions.

4. Error: the resting stance is incorrect — some have the hip lower than the knee and it looks as though the posture is very low, but in fact the muscles of the front of the upper leg are in a relaxed state, and with the calf lifting the thigh it is an effort-saving movement, forming an over-softness and lifelessness. The main cause is an inadequate understanding of the requirements of the resting stance. Correction: the resting stance requires the supporting leg (the right leg) to have the hip higher than or level with the knee, the front of the foot lightly on the ground, the body straight, and the weight mostly on the right leg.

5. Error: when squatting down the buttocks protrude. The main cause is failing to "tuck in the buttocks" (also called retracting the buttocks); protruding buttocks easily cause the body to twist. Correction: the waist and hips must be relaxed, sunk, straight and vertical, and the buttocks must naturally be drawn in.

6. Error: raising the shoulders, causing the right arm to be stiff and the left arm not round and lively. The main cause is that the beginner often uses the muscles around the shoulder to make the arm's movement, and some think only of relaxation and not of…

…of "sinking". Hence some raise the shoulders and some are loose without sinking. Correction: the shoulders must be loosened before the shoulder muscles and ligaments can be stretched, and thus the arm's extending, contracting, wrapping and winding can follow the mind's wish.

7. Error: after the centre of gravity has shifted back and the resting stance formed, the movement pausing. The main cause is an insufficient grasp of continuity and liveliness. Correction: in the movement there must be no hollow and no protrusion, no defect, no sharp corners; one must understand that when the old strength is spent and the new strength has not yet been born, this is precisely the moment when one is most easily taken advantage of. For this reason Tai Chi requires continuity and liveliness, unbroken, revolving endlessly, with no pause.

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

1. The emphasis of teaching is to be placed on the centre of gravity shifting onto the right leg, and sitting down with a straight body without sticking out the chest.

2. Use the method of comparison: A — performs the Single Whip posture. B — grips A's left hand with his right hand. A — ① first uses his left hand to break free downward (the mind not moving). ② then uses the shifting of the centre of gravity onto the right leg to sit the body straight down. The two compare and experience which method is more powerful, and which more easily plucks the opponent or frees the grip; naturally the shifting of the centre of gravity and sitting the body straight down is the more powerful.

3. The teacher observes the practitioner's movement from different angles: for example, whether the upper body is turned towards the east when seen from the front, whether the line of the hand's movement and whether the upper body is upright are correct when seen from the side; and corrects them one by one.

4. If the practitioner is weak or elderly, he may squat down less and make the frame higher.

VII. Technical Analysis

The Lower Posture is the movement of changing from the left bow stance into the resting stance; it requires the centre of gravity to shift back and the right leg to sit down with the body straight. Its key lies in the sitting down, and whether the sitting down is good or not determines whether the whole movement is correct. If when sitting down the heel of the hip is lower than the knee, then a "shallow pit" is formed, making the foundation of the leg hollow and unsteady, and the empty-full conversion of the two legs becomes instead un-lively (making the rising movement un-lively); if the heel of the hip is higher than the knee, then the amount of exercise is very small, and the effect of training the body is not well obtained. When practising the Lower Posture, first shift the centre of gravity slowly back; at the same time turn the right toes out about 45°; at this moment the left and right toes form an outward-turned shape of the character eight. In the process of the centre of gravity shifting back…

图 351
the left resting stance, the left palm threaded forward at the left, the right palm raised at the right rear.
图 352
the left bow stance, the left palm pushing forward, the right hand plucking down.
图 353
the solitary left stance, the left palm raised before the face, the right hand at the side of the right knee.

…in the process of the centre of gravity shifting back, one must "lift the top of the head", the centre of gravity gradually shifting onto the right leg, slowly bending the knee and loosening the hips; this is what is meant by the waist being relaxed, sunk, straight and vertical, and not a collapse forming the "lower posture".

Posture Fifty-Eight — The Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg

Posture Fifty-Eight — The Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg
I. Method of Use

#### (A) The Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg, Left Style Following the previous posture. Should the opponent lift upward with returning force, I take advantage of the situation to raise the body and lean forward, the right leg at the same time lifting and rising, striking the opponent's abdomen with the tip of the foot. The right hand follows and advances, bending the elbow, the tip of the index finger pointing upward, to close off the opponent's left hand; at this moment the left foot changes to empty and stands firm. The right hand may then follow and at any time control the opponent's left hand, and may also control the opponent's right hand — one need not be rigid about it.

Another method of use: after the right foot has been lifted and then immediately set down, the left foot steps forward, the two hands dividing the opponent's two hands, that is, using the two palms to press forward.

#### (B) The Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg, Right Style From the left style. Should the opponent strike with his right fist, my right hand sinks down, and I quickly raise the left hand to support the opponent's elbow, lifting the left knee; the rest is the same as the right style.

II. Course of the Movement

#### (A) The Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg, Left Style 1. The body gradually turns left, the left toes opened out, the centre of gravity gradually shifting onto the left leg; the left leg bending the knee and bowing forward, the right leg extended, the upper body gradually rising; at the same time, as the centre of gravity shifts forward, the left palm threads forward and upward, the right hand slightly sinking (still a hanging hand). The gaze attends to the left palm (see the first and second figures on this page).

2. The body continues to turn left, the centre of gravity continuing to shift forward onto the left leg; the right leg lifted forward from the rear, the sole of the foot lifted, the left leg gradually standing up. At the same time, the left palm arcs down to the side of the left knee (the centre of the palm facing down); the right hanging hand becomes a palm and follows down from the rear; as the right leg lifts forward and raises the knee, the right hand passes the right side of the leg and, above the front of the right leg, wards upward with the right forearm in an arc, bending the elbow and placing it above the front of the right knee, the fingertip pointing upward, level with the eyebrows, the centre of the palm facing left, forming the left solitary stance. The gaze first attends to the left palm as it shifts before, and when the left palm reaches the left knee, then looks toward the right palm as it wards up…

图 354
the right solitary stance forming, the right palm at the side of the right knee, the left knee lifted.
图 355
the right solitary stance settled, the left palm raised before the face, the right palm below at the side of the right knee.

…and slightly arriving before the right palm; then, looking level forward past the right palm (see the first figure on this page).

#### (B) The Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg, Right Style 1. The body gradually turns right, the left leg gradually bending the knee and squatting down, "sending" the right foot down to fall behind and to the right of the left foot, the toes touching the ground first; as the centre of gravity gradually shifts onto the right leg and the whole sole settles flat, the right knee bends and the left leg becomes empty and lifted. At the same time, the right palm follows the right leg and arcs down to fall above the front of the knee, the centre of the palm facing obliquely down; the left palm first follows the bending of the left knee and the squatting down and sinks, then rises and lifts forward and upward following the lifting of the left knee. The gaze attends to the right palm as it falls, and then turns to the left palm as it lifts (see the second figure on this page).

2. The body continues to turn right, the right leg continuing to gradually stand up, the left knee continuing to lift. At the same time, the right palm arcs down and falls to the side of the hip, the centre of the palm facing down, the left palm from below going forward and upward; as the left leg lifts the knee forward, the left hand passes the side of the left leg and, above the front of the left leg, wards upward in an arc, bending the elbow and placing it before the face, the elbow placed above the front of the left knee, the fingertip pointing upward, level with the eyebrows, the centre of the palm facing right. The gaze first attends to the right palm as it falls, and then immediately turns to the left palm as it wards up, arriving slightly before the left palm does, and looks level forward past the left palm (see the second figure on this page).

III. Key Points

1. In taking up the solitary stance from the Lower Posture after the left leg rests on the ground, first the left toes are opened out, then the centre of gravity slowly shifts forward: the left knee bows forward forming the left bow stance; then the right leg rises slightly, pushing the knee forward, and only then does one stand up — and this must not be done with the two legs straight.

2. In standing up, the left leg must first bend the knee and sit solid (taking the left solitary stance as the example), so that the lower frame is steady; then the right leg, led by the right knee, gradually lifts forward and upward, and at the same time the left leg gradually stands up. Guard against using the leaning forward of the upper body to make standing up easier; the upper body is still required to remain upright.

3. In the left solitary stance, when the right leg lifts the knee forward from the rear, the right hand must be placed to the side of the upper part of the right thigh and ward up together.

4. In going from the left solitary stance to the right solitary stance, attend to the fact that when the right foot falls, the left foot must at the same time squat down and "send" it down; it must not be that only the right leg falls while the left leg is still standing straight. When the left leg lifts the knee, the right leg must also gradually stand up accordingly.

5. When standing on one leg, you must "sink the shoulders and let the elbows hang", "sit the wrists", and "empty the collar and lift the crown"; the elbow must join with the knee, and the direction faced must be consistent. The leg that supports the body's weight should not be stiffened by force.

6. Every use of the word "lift" (tuo) in the explanations of the left and right standing-on-one-leg postures derives from the martial application of the movement. In practice, however, do not turn the palm upward merely because of the word "lift" — the fingers should point upward.

IV. Requirements

1. Rising from the crouching stance must be round, alive and nimble; there must be no pause or interruption, and the body must not sway.

2. In the settled standing-on-one-leg posture the centre of gravity must be stable; there must be no wavering.

3. The shoulders must join with the hips, and the elbows with the knees.

4. When rising, the rear foot must not be dragged forward along the ground, nor may it stamp hard against the ground.

5. The withdrawing of the foot must not change abruptly; it must accord with the body's movement and be drawn back slowly.

6. When the left and right standing-on-one-leg postures join, the one hand rising and the other descending must neither of them pause.

V. Common errors, their causes, and how to correct them

图 356
The settled left standing-on-one-leg posture: the right palm lifts above and in front of the right brow, the left palm presses down beside the left hip, the left knee is lifted high, and the right leg supports the body alone.

1. Error: you cannot crouch down, or having crouched you cannot rise. The main cause is weakness in the legs, so you must train diligently. Another cause is that the centre of gravity has not shifted forward sufficiently, which makes rising difficult. Correction: send the hips forward, shift the centre of gravity forward, settle the left leg firmly, then draw the right leg forward slowly — rising will then come easily.

2. Error: you stand unsteadily and the body sways. The main cause is likewise weakness in the muscles of the legs, waist and hips, so again you must train diligently. Another cause is that upper and lower do not coordinate, and the centre of gravity is not controlled. Correction: besides persisting in training, the upper and lower must follow one another.

3. Error: the elbow and the knee come apart — the knee lifts forward and up, but the lifting hand bends the elbow too much, bringing the elbow close to the chest. The main cause is insufficient understanding of the application: when the hand comes too close to the chest it loses its function of closing off the opponent's left hand or of propping up the opponent's elbow. Correction: move the elbow above the knee.

4. Error: the supporting leg stands straight and rigid. The main cause is insufficient understanding of the application. Correction: the two feet must be divided into empty and full — "the empty is not entirely without strength, the full is not entirely braced dead". If the supporting leg is braced dead and you yourself sway unsteadily, how can you kick forward with the raised toes, and how can you both attack and withdraw in defence? Therefore the supporting leg must be slightly bent.

VI. Teaching and practice methods

1. The emphasis should be placed on rising from the crouching stance. Practise repeatedly: train the rising from the crouching stance more to build leg strength, and pay attention to shifting the centre of gravity forward in order to improve technique. Therefore, in repeated practice the emphasis should be on improving the rising from the crouching stance.

2. In teaching, great importance must be attached to keeping the central axis unbent and the waist upright. On this basis, rise slowly from the crouching stance and hold to the requirement of "straightness".

3. In the joining of the left and right standing-on-one-leg postures, the "sending" must be practised well. As the supporting leg crouches, the teacher must remind the student not to let the descending leg touch the ground in haste.

VII. Technical analysis

1. There are two keys to the standing-on-one-leg posture: first, rising from the crouching stance; second, being able to stabilise the centre of gravity while the body is supported on one leg. This is "standing like a balance, moving like a wheel".

…like a wheel".

2. The application of the standing-on-one-leg posture is to lift the knee and kick at the opponent's abdomen with the toes, while the lifting hand closes off the opponent's hand. In practising the form the foot is not actually kicked out, but the intention should nonetheless be present. The uses of the knee and the foot are endlessly varied: sometimes in combat the foot is not used and the knee is used instead. The boxing treatises say, "when the foot comes, lift the knee" and "when close, add the knee" — this is the use of the knee. Therefore the lifted knee of the standing-on-one-leg posture has many and varied applications.

Posture Sixty-Six — Turn the Body and the White Snake Puts Out Its Tongue

I. Application

Turning the body and having the white snake put out its tongue is essentially the same as Parry and Punch, except that the fist is changed for the use of the palm, and the added point is that the palm must carry more sinking strength.

图 387A
The opening of Spread the Back Like a Fan: the right palm rotates outward and lifts above and in front of the right brow, the left palm extends forward as an upright palm, and the body sits back.
图 387B
Spread the Back Like a Fan in transition: the weight shifts forward, the right palm props upward in front of the right brow, and the left palm accordingly pushes forward.
图 388A
The settled Spread the Back Like a Fan posture: the left leg is bent forward in the bow stance, the left palm pushes forward at shoulder level, the right palm props up above and in front of the right brow, and the eyes look toward the left palm.
图 388B
The settled Spread the Back Like a Fan posture from the front: the left bow stance, the left palm pushing forward and the right palm propping up, the two arms spread apart one above the other, and the eyes looking straight ahead.

II. Sequence of movement

1. The body slowly turns right (toward the south); at the same time the left toes turn inward, the left leg settles firm, and the right foot becomes empty. As the trunk turns, the right palm is lowered in an arc and closes into a fist, which is placed for the moment in front of the left ribs, the elbow bent and the forearm horizontal, the centre of the fist facing down. The left palm is drawn back and raised in an arc to above and in front of the left brow. The gaze attends briefly to the right hand as it arcs, then looks level ahead. See the first figure on this page (the same as the hundred-and-twentieth figure).

2. The body continues to turn right (toward the west). The whole of the weight shifts onto the left leg, the right foot is lifted, and the left palm, following the turn, arcs down from the right and, passing along the outside of the right forearm, comes to rest outside the right elbow, while the right fist circles upward (a little higher than the left elbow). Follow the turn and look level ahead, attending also to the movement of the two hands. See the second figure on this page (the same as the hundred-and-twenty-first figure).

3. The right foot is set down forward (a little to the right), the heel touching first, and the body continues to turn right. At the same time the right fist continues forward with the turn and, at the farthest point, changes into a palm using sinking strength. The eyes look level ahead, attending also to the right fist (see the third figure on this page).

4. The body continues to turn right, and the right palm continues to pluck downward to the front of the waist, the centre of the palm facing up. The left palm arcs back to the front of the chest and pushes forward from above the inner side of the right forearm. At the same time the weight gradually shifts onto the right leg, the right leg bending and the left leg pressing out to form the right bow stance. The eyes look level ahead, and must attend also to the left palm as it pushes forward (see the fourth figure on this page).

Apart from the fact that the right fist becomes a palm which plucks forward and down with sinking strength, all the remaining sections of this posture are the same as Posture Twenty-Four, Parry and Punch.

Posture Seventy-Two — High Pat on the Horse with Threading Palm

Posture Seventy-Two — High Pat on the Horse with Threading Palm

I. Application

The application of the first part is the same as High Pat on the Horse. In the second part, while my extended right hand is being held by the opponent's left hand, I immediately draw the right hand back with the centre of the palm facing down, and the left hand, raised slightly, threads through with the palm and thrusts at the opponent's throat, while the right hand remains hidden below the left elbow, ready to meet any change.

II. Sequence of movement

(a) The movement of High Pat on the Horse is the same as Posture Thirty, High Pat on the Horse. See the second to the fourth figures on this page (the same as the hundred-and-seventieth to the hundred-and-seventy-second figures).

(b) Threading Palm, Left

1. The right leg gradually crouches, and the left leg is lifted and drawn back. At the same time the right arm gradually bends at the elbow and lies across, the arm curved, and is drawn in with a downward-left arc; as it is drawn in the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm turns to face upward; the left palm gradually turns palm-upward and threads up above the right palm. The eyes look level ahead (see the fifth figure on this page).

2. The left foot steps forward one pace, the heel touching first; as the weight gradually shifts onto the left leg the whole of the sole presses down firmly, the left leg bends and the right leg presses out to form the left bow stance. At the same time the left hand continues to thread forward and upward; as the left forearm passes above the right palm, the right arm immediately rotates inward so that the centre of the palm turns to face down, and the right palm comes to rest below the upper left arm, while the left palm threads out above the right palm, its centre still facing up, at the height of the chin. The gaze attends to the right palm as it is drawn in, and then to the left palm as it threads forward (see the sixth figure on this page).

III. Key points

1. When the left leg steps forward the right leg must crouch, so that the left leg takes a somewhat larger step. This both achieves the martial effect and increases the amount of exercise.

2. As the left palm threads through and the bow stance is about to form, the body turns slightly right in coordination.

3. When stepping, the upper body must be centred and upright, not leaning forward. The body method of taijiquan must be nimble, relaxed and calm, but it is not permitted to drop the head forward or to bend the trunk forward.

4. The step must be set down nimbly; strive to "step as a cat walks". Therefore, as the left leg steps forward, the right leg must "sink" and "send" the left leg forward; otherwise the step will easily become tense.

图 437
The opening of High Pat on the Horse with Threading Palm: the two hands spread apart front and back, the right hand extends forward and the left hand is drawn in beside the left waist, and the weight sits back.
图 438
The High Pat on the Horse movement: the right hand extends forward to the front of the chest, the left hand is drawn in beside the left waist, and the body is centred and upright.
图 439
The settled High Pat on the Horse: the right palm reaches forward at shoulder level, the left palm is drawn in beside the left waist, and the left leg is forward in the empty stance.

…forward; otherwise the step will easily become tense.

5. When the left palm threads out, the right arm must be curved and a space must be kept at the right armpit; it must not be clamped shut. Otherwise, on the one hand the posture will look awkward and fail to meet the requirement of roundness everywhere; on the other hand, the right hand under the armpit is there to meet changes, and if it is clamped shut it will lose its roundness and liveliness and its usefulness in meeting change will be reduced.

IV. Requirements

1. Although the lower limbs are changing step, "the hundred meetings and the central pole, one breath running through" must still be achieved; do not lean forward or backward.

2. The movements must be continuous without pause. When High Pat on the Horse has reached its position, immediately perform the threading palm; the two movements must not be separated but must be "unbroken as a thread".

V. Common errors, their causes, and how to correct them

1. Error: the threading arm is fully straightened. Straightening tenses the muscles, which makes the force excessive and the movement sluggish. The main cause is generally that the hand is thrust out with too much force, or that one subjectively wants the hand to reach farther, supposing that a thrust must strike home. The Boxing Treatises say that the principle is originally "give up yourself and follow others", but many mistakenly "give up the near and seek the far". The so-called difference of a hair's breadth leads to an error of a thousand miles. Therefore over-extending is harmful. Correction: leave a margin when the hand goes out, and keep the arm slightly curved when threading the palm.

2. Error: when the left foot steps, the right leg does not crouch, or crouches very little, and only the body's centre of gravity moves forward so that the left leg steps forward. The main cause is that the application is not deeply understood. Because the right hand I have extended is being held and gripped, a crouch gives the withdrawing right arm a sinking strength which can draw the opponent along, and I then thread the left palm straight through to the opponent's throat. Moreover, in form practice High Pat on the Horse is one of the few movements that bring the body to standing. For this reason, when threading the palm one should return to practising the form in the half-crouched state, so as to train and strengthen the legs. Correction: from the very start of the threading palm the right leg must crouch.

3. Error: upper and lower are disconnected, so that when threading the palm either the hand arrives first or the foot arrives first. The main cause is that the application is not deeply understood. For the issuing of strength there must be a root: the strength starts from the heel, is governed by the waist, is issued from the legs, and takes form in the fingers. If hand and foot are disconnected, from where will the strength start, and how will it reach? Correction: the thrust of the hand necessarily requires the supporting coordination of waist and legs; in practice strive to have the hand arrive when the foot arrives, and take particular care that the bowing leg does not move too fast.

图 440
The threading palm in transition: the right arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm turns to face upward, and the left palm turns palm-upward and threads up above the right palm.
图 441
The left foot steps forward, the left palm continues to thread forward, and the right palm comes to rest below the upper left arm.
图 442A
The settled threading palm: the left bow stance, the left palm threaded forward at the height of the chin, and the right palm resting below the upper left arm, the eyes looking straight ahead.

…coordination of waist and legs; in practice strive to have the hand arrive when the foot arrives, and take particular care that the bowing leg does not move too fast.

4. Error: threading and striking are not clearly distinguished, so that the left hand first goes up and then down. The main cause is a failure to understand the application. The threading palm thrusts at the opponent's throat; striking downward can only hit the chest. Correction: the palm must thread up along a downward-slanting line; it must not arc downward to strike.

VI. Teaching and practice methods

1. Mnemonic: at High Pat on the Horse the hand is held; bend the right leg and draw the right palm back; step the left leg nimbly forward; the left threading palm goes straight to the throat.

2. Constantly sharpen the distinction of empty and full. In the first half, when the Single Whip joins High Pat on the Horse, as the left foot is drawn back the right leg must be settled firm and the left leg lifted lightly; take care that the centre of gravity moves back, that the upper body does not lean forward, and that the left foot is not drawn back scraping the ground. When threading the palm, take care to settle the right leg firm so that the left leg steps forward nimbly. In teaching, observe and correct repeatedly so that the weight moves onto the supporting point and empty and full are clearly distinguished.

3. The learner should frequently and repeatedly practise the half-crouch position of the right leg, and the stepping forward and drawing back of the left leg, and may also alternate the legs, in order to feel empty and full and strengthen the legs.

4. Paired practice using the application: A — assumes the settled High Pat on the Horse; B — holds A's right hand with the left hand; A — crouches the right leg, draws the right hand back, steps the left leg forward and threads out the left palm; B — retreats slightly. In practice the teacher should explain the meaning and requirements of each detail of the movement, so that the learning becomes vivid.

5. So that beginners may simplify the movements while learning, they may learn with the hand still and the foot moving, or with the foot still and the hand moving, so that it is easier to watch and to imitate; but having once made clear the separate parts of hand and foot, they must immediately practise the hand and foot moving together. In this way they learn quickly and yet do not fall into disconnection and ruin of the movements.

VII. Technical analysis

In High Pat on the Horse with Threading Palm, attention must be paid to nimbleness; if the body is sluggish one cannot advance or retreat at ease. Therefore the body must be nimble: no sooner has the opponent's force touched my skin than my intention has already entered his very bones.

图 442B
The settled threading palm from another angle: the left bow stance, the left palm threaded forward and the right palm resting below the upper left arm, the body centred and upright, the eyes looking straight ahead.

Posture Seventy-Three — the Cross-Shaped Leg

Posture Seventy-Three — the Cross-Shaped Leg

I. Application

Continuing from the previous posture. If an opponent strikes across at me with his right hand from behind on my right, I quickly turn my body toward the right rear as I roll and turn, and at the same time the left arm turns up and bends back; as it embraces the right arm one above the other, I quickly separate the two hands forward and back to bar the opponent's hand. At the same time I quickly lift the right leg and thrust the heel at the opponent's right ribs; the opponent will then certainly fall back with the kick.

Note: In Master Yang Chengfu's book The Complete Book of Taijiquan: Substance and Application, Part One (1933 edition), only one plate of the settled Cross-Shaped Leg posture is given here; no sequence plates are listed, and the original way of practising it was the single swing-lotus leg. The method in this book is the form as finally revised and settled by Yang Chengfu, which has long been in wide circulation, and it is therefore taken as the final settled form of the present time. So that readers may understand something of the original way of practising it, it is described as follows:

After the left threading palm, the left toes turn inward and press down firmly, the body gradually turns right, and the weight gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg. At the same time the left palm, with the elbow bent, moves in an arc to the right past the face with the turn of the body, while the right palm remains below the upper left arm. The body continues to turn right, and the right foot is lifted and swings outward in an arc from left to upper right, the knee naturally slightly bent, the foot no higher than the shoulder, the instep turned somewhat to face right. At the same time the left palm strikes from above rightward and then leftward to meet the right foot.

Another method (a counter):

1. To counter the Cross-Shaped Leg, one may first brush the knee and then attack by other means.

2. To counter the Cross-Shaped Leg, one may also ward upward with the left hand, step the right foot forward, and use the right planting punch to counter it.

II. Sequence of movement

1. The body gradually turns right, the left toes turn inward and press down firmly, the weight gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg, and the right foot is lifted (the heel leaving the ground first). At the same time the left arm bends at the elbow and moves right, the centre of the palm facing inward, and the right palm, passing along the outside of the left arm, joins with the turn of the body to the right; as it joins, the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm turns to face inward, so that the two palms cross in front of the chest. The eyes follow the turn of the body and look level to the right, and the gaze must attend to the two palms embracing (see the first and second figures on this page).

2. The two palms separate to left and right. At the same time the right foot slowly…

图 443
The opening of the Cross-Shaped Leg: the body turns right, the two palms cross in front of the chest, and the right foot is lifted with the heel leaving the ground first.
图 444
The Cross-Shaped Leg in transition: the two palms separate to left and right, and the right foot is lifted and swings outward in an arc from left to upper right.
图 445A
The Cross-Shaped Leg thrust out: the right leg thrusts out to the right front with the heel, the two palms spread to left and right, the body is centred and upright, and the eyes look to the right.

…slowly outward to the right, the toes pointing up; as the right leg thrusts out the left leg gradually straightens, though at the settled posture the knee is still slightly bent. The gaze attends to the right palm as it separates out, and looking level to the right past the right palm (see the first figure on this page, and compare the rear view in figure 210).

III. Key points

1. The waist and hips turn right and the left heel closes in, but the upper body must not lean forward or backward. The coccyx must be held centred, the central axis must not bend, and the turning must not sway, so that the inner strength can reach the nimble, lively use that supports all eight directions.

2. The left hand, following the right turn of waist and hips, moves from left to right in coordination, while the right hand arcs upward from below; the two hands cross and embrace in front of the chest, and must be full, neither loose and scattered nor shrunk.

3. To thrust out the right leg one must first lift the leg and concentrate the strength at the knee joint, stretching the ligaments of the hips (the lifted knee should generally be no lower than hip level); thus the leg can thrust to the ribs and meet the requirement of the application.

4. After the thrust, when the body is supported on the single leg, the body must be upright, with the upper and lower essentially in one line. Chen Xin says, "When the body method is correct the body's pillar is upright, leaning nowhere, containing emptiness and spirit within." Therefore at that moment, from the crown of the head to the perineum, there must always be a vertical line; leaning forward or backward, tilting left or right, all fail the requirement of the body method. This requires the whole body to relax so that the movement and the shifting of waist and legs become harmonious and coordinated.

IV. Requirements

1. The direction must be true. From High Pat on the Horse with Threading Palm facing east, turn the waist and hips and thrust out with the right leg. The direction of the thrust is due west, and the face is also toward the west.

2. The stance must be steady; when thrusting the leg one must not pull the body about and set it askew.

3. The foot must arrive and the hand must arrive.

4. Empty and full must be clear. From the moment the left toes turn inward, the weight shifts onto the left leg, so that the right leg may lift its knee nimbly.

V. Common errors, their causes, and how to correct them

1. Error: when the left foot turns inward, the weight shifts to the right. The main cause is that the application is not deeply understood. The opponent strikes across at me from behind my right; if I shift my weight right as I turn, my body leans right, and I thus deliver myself to be struck. At the same time this hinders a rapid turning of the body, and so increases…

图 445B
The settled single-leg support in profile: after the right leg thrusts out the body is supported on one leg, upper and lower in one line, the two palms spread to left and right, and the waist and hips turned right.

…increases the difficulty of observing the opponent's movements, which is unfavourable for meeting the attack quickly. Moreover, with the weight shifted right the two feet are double-weighted, which is unfavourable for both attack and defence, and because the load on the legs is reduced the benefit of the training is also reduced. Correction: the left foot turns inward, the weight remains on the left foot, the waist and hips turn, and the upper body turns toward the south-west; this then creates favourable conditions for the kick that follows.

2. Error: the two hands cross in front of the chest too tightly and too flat. The main causes are, first, that one attends only to the arcing movement of the left hand and neglects the movement of the right hand, and second, that the application is not sufficiently understood. Tightness and flatness both narrow the protective range of the two hands, making one easy to attack. Correction: attend to fullness, and the right hand must go outward and upward.

3. Error: the direction of the kick is not true. The main cause is generally that the left foot does not turn in enough, so that the direction of the kick leans toward the south-west; secondarily, a failure to understand the application. The opponent attacks from behind my right, so the main direction of my kick should be to the rear, that is, due west. Correction: the key is that the left foot must turn inward by more than 90 degrees; then the right foot's thrust will not only find the true direction easily but will not be awkward.

4. Error: the movement is uneven, sometimes fast and sometimes slow. The main cause is insufficient strength in the legs: the foot turns in quickly, the knee lifts slowly, the kick goes out quickly. Taijiquan is one of the internal martial arts, and it requires "from within to without" and "drawing the within out by the without" in order to raise the benefit of the training; under the guidance of intent it requires that the movements be light and unhurried, neither slow nor hurried. Therefore one must "let the form follow the movement of intent", striving to make inner and outer join, intent and breath link, and to leave no place of interruption or of fast and slow. Correction: the foot must turn in with the turning of the waist, the left foot settling firm, then lift the leg lightly and slowly, and as the left leg gradually rises slowly thrust out the right foot.

VI. Teaching and practice methods

1. The teacher observes the degree of the left foot's inward turn from the south, and the direction of the kick from the west.

2. The emphasis in teaching should be placed on the kicking leg: practise much and repeatedly supporting on the left foot alone and lifting the right leg to kick, in order to strengthen the legs and attain the requirements of steadiness and nimbleness.

VII. Technical analysis

1. In the Cross-Shaped Leg, what defends is the hand and what attacks is the leg; the hand merely bars, and the application lies chiefly in the leg.

2. If the kicking leg is not practised well it is easy to hold the breath. The breathing of Yang-style taijiquan is required to be entirely natural: one should adopt the natural method of breathing — long, even, fine, slow, neither hurried nor sluggish.

Book page 411

Posture Seventy-Four — Step Forward and Point at the Groin with the Fist

Posture Seventy-Four — Step Forward and Point at the Groin with the Fist

I. Application

Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent withdraws his hand, I immediately set the right foot down while the left foot advances and the knee bends and settles firm. At this moment, if the opponent again kicks up from below with his right foot, I quickly use my left hand to deflect the opponent's right foot outward past my left knee, and the right hand immediately closes into a fist and strikes (points) at the opponent's groin, the body leaning very slightly forward.

II. Sequence of movement

1. The left leg gradually crouches, the right foot is set down and held suspended, and the body gradually turns right. At the same time the right palm arcs from the right downward, passes in front of the upper abdomen and circles to the left; as it circles the arm rotates inward so that the centre of the palm turns downward; the left palm, too, sinks as the left leg crouches and the body turns right, and arcs forward and upward to the right (see the first figure on this page).

2. The body continues to turn right, and the right foot steps forward and to the right (west by north), the heel touching first; then the right toes swing outward 45 degrees, and as the weight gradually shifts onto the right leg the whole foot presses down firmly. With the turn of the body the right palm moves from the left upward and past the chest to the right; as it moves the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm gradually turns downward. The left palm arcs across to the front of the left chest (see the second figure on this page).

3. The weight gradually shifts entirely onto the right leg, and the left foot steps forward from the inner side of the right ankle, the heel touching first, while the body continues to turn slightly right. At the same time the right palm, following the turn, continues right, back and forward in an arc and is drawn in beside the right waist and closed into a fist, while the left palm brushes downward in an arc from front to right and then left. The eyes look level ahead, and the gaze must attend to the left palm (see the third and fourth figures on this page).

4. The body continues to turn gradually left, and the weight gradually shifts onto the left leg until the whole foot presses down firmly, the left leg bending and the right leg pressing out to form the left bow stance. At the same time the left palm brushes in an arc to the front of the left knee and comes to the side of the left knee, while the right fist is driven forward and down at the height of the abdomen, the body folding slightly at the waist. The eyes look level ahead, and the gaze must attend…

图 446
The opening of Step Forward and Point at the Groin with the Fist: the body turns right, the right palm arcs from the right downward, passes in front of the upper abdomen and circles left, and the left palm accordingly arcs forward.
图 447
The right foot steps forward and to the right; the right palm passes the chest and moves right with its centre turning downward, and the left palm arcs across to the front of the left chest.
图 448
The left foot steps forward from the inner side of the right ankle; the right palm arcs and is drawn in beside the right waist and closed into a fist, and the left palm brushes downward in an arc.

…and the left palm's brushing to the left and the right fist's striking out (see the fifth figure on this page).

III. Key points

1. As the right foot descends there must be a downward "sending" by the left leg (bending the left leg), and attention must be paid to keeping the upper body upright.

2. As the left foot advances, when the waist and hips turn left the left hand's brushing of the knee and the right fist's forward strike must be performed at the same time, with upper and lower, left and right mutually drawing and linking one another, so that the movement is not scattered. If the turn of the body is too great, it will overshoot.

3. The right fist's forward strike must be coordinated with the left leg's bending, the right leg's pressing out and the body's slight forward lean, so that body arrives, hand arrives and step arrives.

IV. Requirements

1. Empty and full must be clear: as the right foot descends the left leg must sink and settle firm.

2. The line of the fist's travel must be correct: it should be slightly curved, driven from the waist forward and slightly downward.

3. While brushing, the weight is on the right leg.

V. Common errors, their causes, and how to correct them

1. Error: the fist is closed too early. The main cause is that the application is not sufficiently understood. Correction: the strike follows immediately upon the brushing movement, so the fist should be closed at the moment when the left hand has finished brushing and the right hand has arced to the region of the waist; before that the fist should not be closed.

2. Error: the upper body does not lean slightly forward but instead drops the head and bends forward at the waist. The main cause is inattention to keeping the coccyx centred; this is a defect of the body method. Correction: although the body leans slightly forward, "the hundred meetings and the central pole, one breath running through" is required, forming a straight line from the crown of the head to the perineum.

3. Error: the two hands' movement pauses, especially as the right foot descends. The main cause is that the left leg has not sunk and settled firm; in order to keep the body balanced the hand movement is therefore stopped, causing upper and lower to be disconnected. Correction: settle the left leg firm, and let the two hands move in an arc with the turning of the waist.

VI. Teaching and practice methods

1. In this movement the linking movement must first be done well: repeatedly coach the sinking and slight bending of the left leg as the right leg descends, to lay a good foundation for the movements that follow.

2. Explain clearly that the upper body stays upright, and that as the right fist…

图 449A
Step Forward and Point at the Groin with the Fist in transition: the right palm arcs right, back and forward and is drawn in beside the right waist and closed into a fist, while the left palm brushes downward in an arc from front to right and then left.
图 449B
The left palm brushes to the side of the left knee, and the right fist is driven forward and down from beside the waist, the body folding slightly at the waist.
图 450
The settled Point at the Groin: the left bow stance, the left palm brushed to the side of the left knee, and the right fist driven forward and down at the height of the abdomen, the eyes looking straight ahead.

Striking forward, when the body turns into a slight forward lean, the head must not drop and the waist must not be curved — let the practitioner understand that a curved waist blocks the flow of qi and blood; explain and demonstrate this repeatedly.

3. The teacher must constantly correct the lateral distance of the stepping and the direction the foot points during practice, so that the hip-root and the limbs relate well to one another and the stance is consequently solid.

VII. Technical Analysis

Advance Step and Strike Toward the Crotch has two movements: first, the parry of the left hand; second, the forward strike of the right hand — and two steps must be taken. This requires the movements to be continuous, upper and lower following one another. One must in particular train well the "calm mind and applied intent": before moving, dismiss all distracting thoughts, as if the ears heard nothing and the eyes saw nothing, so as to be in a state free of thought and worry. Once moving, concentrate the whole spirit on using intent to guide the performance of every movement. Therefore, in practising the form, mind comes first and body second, and one should use intent and not force, so that inner and outer become one.

Book page 412

Posture Seventy-Five — Step Up and Grasp the Bird's Tail

Posture Seventy-Five — Step Up and Grasp the Bird's Tail

I. Application

Same as Posture Three, Grasp the Bird's Tail: see the first figure on this page (the same as figure 131), and the next three figures (the same as figures 8 to 17); the sequence continues on the next page.

II. Course of Movement

图 451

图 453

图 454

The body straightens and turns left, the left toe swings outward 45° and presses down firmly; the weight Gradually shift the whole weight onto the left leg and lift the right leg forward. At the same time, the left palm bends at the elbow and moves in an arc from the left upward to before the left chest, palm facing to the right; the right fist becomes a palm and scoops in an arc from the front toward the left to below the left forearm, and as it scoops, the arm turns outward so that the palm turns to face obliquely up-left and joins the left palm, both arms forming an arc. The eyes glance at the right palm, then turn to the left palm and look level to the front — see the first figure on the previous page (the same as figure 131).

All the other sections are the same as Posture Three, Grasp the Bird's Tail.
