Facing to the right, the left hand bends at the elbow in front as an upward-facing palm with the fingertips pointing east, and the right upright palm is placed above and to the right of the left wrist; the right leg bends at the knee and sits down, and the left foot rests on its toes in an empty stance; the body faces due east and the eyes look due east (the book numbers this 圖 56).

#### Thirtieth Posture: Zuo You Fen Jiao (左右分脚, "Part the Feet, Left and Right") (Figures 57–60)

Movement one: From the preceding posture (Figure 56) the right hand extends forward, and when hand and arm have straightened as a palm facing downward, it continues to move level to the right; when the fingertips point south-east the arm drops and, bending at the elbow, sweeps upward and turns into a palm facing upward, placed beneath the left wrist with the fingertips pointing north-east. The left hand, following the direction in which the right hand turns, describes half a circle in front of the chest, turning from an upward-facing palm into a downward-facing palm, and is placed on top of the right wrist (as the line in the drawing shows), the fingertips pointing south-east; the two inner wrists rest against each other in a crossed shape. At the same time the left foot steps out most of a pace and becomes a bow stance, and the body twists to the left with the movement; while the body twists, the two hands clench into fists and are raised and placed in front of the left forehead with the two inner wrists resting against each other in a crossed shape, both as upright fists, the left fist inside and the right fist outside, the eyes looking east, as in Figure 57. … the two hands clench into fists and are raised and placed in front of the left forehead with the two inner wrists resting against each other in a crossed shape, both as upright fists, the left fist inside and the right fist outside, the eyes looking east, as in Figure 57.

图 76
Facing to the left, the body twisting to the left, the two hands clench into fists and are raised and crossed in front of the left forehead, the left fist inside and the right fist outside, both as upright fists; the two legs bend at the knees in a bow stance and the body angles south-east (the book numbers this 圖 57).

Movement two: From the preceding posture (Figure 57), while the two fists are raised, the right leg is lifted with the movement and at once kicks out toward the south-east, to the height of the hip with the instep level with the leg, and the left leg straightens. At the same time the two fists separate and become palms: the right hand falls toward the south-east and the left hand falls to the left, both as side palms, the two arms straight and level with the shoulders, the body facing due east and the eyes looking south-east, as in Figure 58. (In the drawing the left buttock has to be shown, so the direction is slightly off.)

图 77

Movement three: From the preceding posture (Figure 58), after the kick the foot falls forward at once into a bow stance with the toes pointing east; at the same time the two hands are drawn back and, in front of the right chest, take the form of a left upright palm and a right upward-facing palm (that is, the form of Right High Pat on Horse); the body and the line of sight both face due east, as in Figure 59.

Movement four: From the preceding posture (Figure 59) the two hands circle toward the left, turning into a left palm facing upward (below) and a right palm facing downward (above) in the crossed shape with the two wrists resting against each other; the hands then clench into fists and are raised and placed in front of the right forehead with the two inner wrists resting against each other in a crossed shape, both as upright fists, the left fist outside and the right fist inside. At the same time the body twists to the right and the eyes look due east; the shape is similar to Figure 57, but Figure 57 is the left-twisting form whereas this is the right-twisting form, and the hands and feet must all be transposed left for right. Refer to the explanation under "movement one"; the drawing is omitted. … the hands and feet must be transposed left for right; refer to the explanation under "movement one"; the drawing is omitted.

图 78
Facing to the right, the left palm faces upward below and the right palm faces downward above in the crossed shape with the two wrists resting against each other, the fingertips pointing south-east; the right leg is bent at the knee below and the left leg is straight behind; the body faces due east and the eyes look straight ahead (the book numbers this 圖 59).
图 79
Facing to the left, the left leg is lifted and kicks out toward the north-east with the instep level with the leg; the two fists separate and fall, becoming side palms, the left hand falling toward the north-east and the right hand to the right, the two arms level with the shoulders; the right leg is straight and standing, the body faces due east, and the eyes look north-east (the book numbers this 圖 60).

Movement five: From the preceding posture (the right-twisting form, the opposite of Figure 57), while the two fists are raised, the left leg is lifted with the movement and at once kicks out toward the north-east (the right leg changing from bent to nearly straight). At the same time the two fists separate and fall: the left hand falls toward the north-east and the right hand to the right, both as side palms, the two arms straight and level with the shoulders, the body facing due east and the eyes looking north-east, as in Figure 60 (Figure 58 is the right foot-parting, Figure 60 the left foot-parting).

This posture is a movement in which the left and right feet kick in succession; the right High Pat on Horse in the middle may, once the form is practised until familiar, be simplified: that is, after Figure 58 has fallen into the bow stance, the fists may be clenched and crossed directly and raised above the right forehead, and the movement of Figure 60 performed from there. In this way the successive left and right foot-partings can be made more compact. Originally, after High Pat on Horse there was only the name "Part the Feet, Left and Right", and this procedure is the basis of that usage.

#### Thirty-first Posture: Zhuan Shen Deng Jiao (转身蹬脚, "Turn the Body, Heel Kick") (Figures 61–62)

Movement one: From the preceding posture (Figure 60) the two hands are drawn back with the elbows bent, clench into fists, and are raised and placed in front of the right forehead, the left fist outside and the right fist inside, both as upright fists. At the same time the left knee bends into a lifted-leg form, the lower leg hanging down with the toes pointing down; the right toes then turn toward the north-west and the body also turns toward the north-west, the eyes looking due west, as in Figure 61. Movement two: From the preceding posture (Figure 61) the left foot is at once pressed out toward due west as a heel kick, the toes curving slightly inward; the movement of the two hands is the same as in Figure 60 but in the opposite direction, and the eyes look due west, as in Figure 62.

In all the forms above, before the foot kicks or presses out, there is a movement in which the fists are clenched and raised. Remember: whenever the left foot kicks (or presses out), the left fist is always outside and the right fist inside; whenever the right foot kicks, the right fist is always outside and the left fist inside. There are further kicking movements later, and the same rule still applies.

图 80
Facing to the left, the two hands clench into fists and are raised and crossed in front of the right forehead, the left fist inside and the right fist outside, both as upright fists; the left leg is lifted with the lower leg hanging down and the toes pointing down; the body and the line of sight face due west (the book numbers this 圖 61).
图 81
Facing to the left, the left foot presses out due west as a heel kick with the toes curving inward; the two hands separate and fall, becoming side palms, the left arm extending level toward due west and the right arm level toward due east, both level with the shoulders; the right leg is straight and standing, and the body and the line of sight face due west (the book numbers this 圖 62).

#### Thirty-second Posture: Jin Bu Zai Chui (进步栽捶, "Step Forward, Plant the Fist") (Figures 63–65)

Movement one: From the preceding posture (Figure 62), after the left foot has pressed out it at once falls one pace to the front-left of the right foot, the leg bending into a bow stance while the right leg straightens. At the same time the left hand falls, brushes past the left knee and is placed beside the left leg with the left arm vertical and the palm facing down; the right hand is first drawn back to the side of the right cheek and then pushed forward, changing from a side palm to a true palm. The body and the line of sight both face due west, as in Figure 63. This movement is the same as that of Figure 14 but in the opposite direction; refer to the relevant explanation under Figure 14.

Movement two: From the preceding posture (Figure 63) the right foot advances and falls one pace to the front-right of the left foot, the leg bending into a bow stance while the left leg straightens. At the same time the right hand brushes past the right knee and is placed beside the right leg, and the left hand is first raised to the side of the left cheek and then pushed forward; the movement is in each respect similar to that of the preceding posture, … but the hands and feet must be transposed left for right while the direction remains unchanged, as in Figure 64 (refer also to the explanation under Figure 18, which is in the opposite direction).

图 82
Facing to the right, the left hand, after brushing past the left knee, hangs beside the left leg with the palm facing down, and the right hand is first drawn back to the side of the right cheek and then pushed forward as a true palm; the left leg bends at the knee in front in a bow stance and the right leg is straight behind; the body and the line of sight face due west (the book numbers this 圖 63).

Movement three: From the preceding posture (Figure 64) the left foot advances one pace, returning to the bow stance of Figure 63. At the same time the left hand, after brushing past the left knee, turns along an arc from the left side upward and is placed beside the right elbow as a slanting upright palm; the right hand clenches into a fist and is raised to the side of the right cheek, then at once strikes downward and forward as an inverted fist, and must complete the movement at the same moment as the left upright palm. The body leans slightly forward and the eyes look in front of the right fist, as in Figure 65.

图 83
Facing to the right, the left hand, after brushing past the left knee, turns along an arc and is placed beside the right elbow as a slanting upright palm, and the right hand clenches into a fist as an inverted fist and strikes downward and forward; the left leg bends at the knee in front in a bow stance and the right leg is straight behind; the body leans slightly forward and the eyes look in front of the right fist (the book numbers this 圖 64).

The two movements above are diagrammed separately after the pattern of Brush Knee and Twist Step for the convenience of beginners; once the form is practised until familiar they should be performed as a continuous step-up with knee-brushing, omitting the forward-pushing movement of the left and right hands.

#### Thirty-sixth Posture: Tui Bu Da Hu (退步打虎, "Step Back, Strike the Tiger") (Figures 69–73)

Movement one: From the preceding posture (Figure 68), taking the remaining momentum of the body's lean toward the left-rear, the right leg falls toward the north-west and straightens, the left leg bending into a bow stance, while the right arm remains extended toward the south-east unchanged. The left hand is raised and, following a parabolic line, falls toward the south-east and is placed below and to the left of the right elbow, both hands as upright palms; the body and the line of sight both face south-east, as in Figure 69. This movement was originally performed with a jumping action — that is, when the right leg fell, the left foot kicked up; later, without the jump, it was changed to a crossed-step form in which the right leg kneels behind the left leg, as in the reference drawing to Figure 69. Nowadays the crossed step too has long been out of use.

Movement two: From the preceding posture (Figure 69) the two hands are unchanged; the left foot steps back one pace and the right leg bends into a bow stance. The direction is still south-east, as in Figure 70.

Movement three: From the preceding posture (Figure 70) the right hand is drawn back from above downward along an arc in front of the chest and clenches into an upright fist with the back of the fist facing outward; the left hand is raised from below upward along an arc on the left side to above the left forehead and clenches into a reversed fist with the tiger's mouth pointing down; the tiger's mouths of the two fists face each other above and below. At the same time, … the left leg bends, the right foot is drawn back half a pace and becomes an empty stance resting on the toes, and the body turns toward due east with the eyes looking straight ahead, as in Figure 71. In this movement there are two ways of doing it, one lifting the leg and one not; lifting the leg is very difficult, because this posture calls for successive backward steps and the leg must be lifted before one has steadied, which beginners all find hard. An empty stance is therefore used here, so that the body can stand steady. To practise the version with the leg lifted, refer to the front view of Figure 71.

#### Thirty-seventh Posture: Er Qi Jiao (二起脚, "Second Kick") (Figure 72)

This posture has two ways of kicking. One is exactly the same as the kick of Figure 58; the other is From the preceding posture (Figure 71) the right leg is first lifted toward the front and then kicks out to the right in a horizontal sweeping manner. At the same time the two hands divide level to left and right, both turning into palms facing downward, the right fingertips pointing south-east and the left fingertips north-east; the body faces due east and the eyes look south-east, as in Figure 72.

#### Thirty-eighth Posture: Shuang Feng Guan Er (双峰贯耳, "Twin Peaks Pierce the Ears") (Figures 73–74)

Movement one: From the preceding posture (Figure 72) the right foot falls forward with the movement into a bow stance. At the same time the two hands turn into palms facing upward and come together before the chest, then press down before the abdomen and turn into palms facing downward with the fingertips meeting; the two arms bend slightly in an encircling shape. The body and the line of sight both face due east, as in Figure 73. (In this drawing, for convenience of photography, the direction is angled slightly toward the south-east.)

图 94
Facing to the right, the two hands turn into upward-facing palms and come together before the chest, then press down before the abdomen as downward-facing palms with the fingertips meeting, the two arms slightly bent in an encircling shape; the right leg bends at the knee in a bow stance and the left leg is straight; the body and the line of sight face due east (the book numbers this 圖 73).

Movement two: From the preceding posture (Figure 73) the stance is unchanged; the two hands divide to left and right and turn upward, clenching into fists with the movement and being placed separately in front of the two temples as upright fists with the tiger's mouths facing each other, the two arms slightly bent and still in an encircling shape. The direction is still due east, as in Figure 74. (The two fists in that drawing show the pose of the two hands when they have risen from below but have not yet reached the front of the temples, and so are lower than the two fists in the front view. In the front view, because the camera angle was unsuitable, the two fists are also rather too high; when practising, they should be placed somewhat lower.)

图 95
Facing to the right, the two hands clench into fists and are placed separately in front of the two temples in an encircling shape with the tiger's mouths facing each other; the left leg bends at the knee in a bow stance and the right leg is straight; the body and the line of sight face due east (the book numbers this 圖 74).
图 96
Facing the front, the two hands clench into fists and are placed separately in front of the two temples in an encircling shape with the tiger's mouths facing each other, both as upright fists; the two legs bend at the knees in a bow stance, the body faces due east, and the eyes look straight ahead (the book numbers this 圖 74 正面圖, "front view of Figure 74").

#### Thirty-ninth Posture: Fan Shen Er Qi Jiao (翻身二起脚, "Turn the Body Over, Second Kick") (Figures 75–78)

Movement one: From the preceding posture (Figure 74) the left leg kneels and the right leg forms a bow; the body turns to the right and the two legs become a crossed step. The two upright fists also cross with the movement and are placed in front of the right cheek, the left fist outside and the right … fist inside; the two inner wrists cross, the left fist with its centre facing inward and the right fist with its centre facing outward. The body angles south-east and the eyes look due east, as in Figure 75.

图 97
Facing to the right, the two upright fists are crossed and placed in front of the right cheek, the left fist outside and the right fist inside, the left fist with its centre facing inward and the right fist with its centre facing outward; the two legs bend at the knees in a crossed step, the body angles south-east, and the eyes look due east (the book numbers this 圖 75).

Movement two: From the preceding posture (Figure 75) the right leg straightens and the body rises; the left foot kicks out toward the east with the movement (a heel kick may also be used). The two fists divide to left and right: the left hand falls along a parabolic line and extends level toward due east, and the right hand falls along a parabolic line and extends level toward the south, both as side palms. The movement is similar to that of Figure 60; the facing is unchanged and the eyes look east (slightly toward north), as in Figure 76.

图 98
Facing the front, the left leg is lifted and kicks out toward the east with the instep level with the leg; the two fists divide and become side palms, the left hand extending toward due east and the right hand toward the south, the two arms level with the shoulders; the right leg is straight and standing, the body faces due east, and the eyes look east, slightly toward north (the book numbers this 圖 76).

Movement three: From the preceding posture (Figure 76) the left foot does not come to the ground; the right toes turn to the right toward due west and the body turns in the same direction. The two palms clench into fists with the movement, are drawn back before the chest in a crossed form and placed in front of the right cheek, both as upright fists (the left fist inside and the right fist outside). The eyes look south-west, as in Figure 77.

图 99
Facing to the left, the two hands clench into fists, cross and are drawn back in front of the right cheek, the left fist inside and the right fist outside, both as upright fists; the right leg bends at the knee and is lifted with the toes pointing down, the left leg is straight and standing, and the eyes look south-west (the book numbers this 圖 77).

Movement four: From the preceding posture (Figure 77) the left foot steps forward and lands as a bow stance; the toes then turn toward the north-east and the pose becomes a sitting-leg form, and the right foot takes the movement The toes turn to point due east and the foot is drawn back by more than half a step to become a empty stance resting on the toes; the two fists are unchanged, but in turning the body they are carried with the movement to a position in front of the left cheek. The body angles north-east and the eyes look due east, as in Figure 78. A front view is also appended for reference.

图 100
Standing sideways, the two hands are clenched into fists and crossed in front of the cheek, the body angling north-east and the two legs bent at the knees; one hand is raised above guarding the face and the other is below, and the eyes look due east (the book numbers this 圖 78).
图 101
Front view: the two hands are clenched into fists, crossed and raised in guard before the face, one leg bent at the knee and lifted with the toes pointing down, the other leg bent at the knee taking the weight, and the eyes look due east (the book labels it 圖 78 正面圖).

Movement five: From the preceding posture (Figure 78) the right foot kicks out toward the east (because this is a turning form a heel kick may also be used, but the right foot has already come to the ground, so this differs from the lifted-leg kick of the preceding thirty-first form, the turning heel kick; a toe kick is therefore smoother. In "movement two" above, the left foot kicks because the pose is a squatting form, in which a heel kick is convenient). The two fists change to side palms, exactly as in the movement of Figure 58, the direction likewise being due east; the illustration is omitted.

Although this form is divided into five movements in the illustration, in continuous performance there are in fact only two consecutive movements — turning the body to kick the left foot and turning over the body to kick the right foot — with the right-foot kick as the principal one; it is therefore called 翻身二起脚 (Fan Shen Er Qi Jiao, "turn-the-body double lift kick"). Further, this form from the eastward direction of the preceding form, after the left and right kicks, turns back to the original direction; beginners easily mistake the direction, so take care.

#### 第四十式　撇身捶（图略）— Pie Shen Chui, "Deflecting Body Fist" (illustration omitted)

This form is a repeated form. From the preceding posture (as in Figure 58), when the right foot comes to the ground, perform the movements of Figures 45 and 46, but the direction is exactly opposite — it is toward the east, not toward the west; the illustration is omitted. Some practitioners substitute 高探马 (Gao Tan Ma, "High Pat on Horse") for this form, but it is not as good as 撇身捶, which is … is smoother, and so it is left unchanged.

#### 第四十一式　上步搬拦捶（图略）— Shang Bu Ban Lan Chui, "Step Up, Parry, Intercept and Punch" (illustration omitted)

This form is also a repeated form. From the preceding posture (as in Figure 46, but with the direction reversed) the left palm and right fist extend forward together, the left foot steps up with the movement and becomes a bow stance (as in Figure 22). The left palm is then drawn back slightly and the right fist is drawn back to the side of the right ribs and becomes an upright fist; the right leg sits with the movement and the left leg becomes an empty stance (as in Figure 23). The movement of Figure 24 follows. This form steps up rather than unloads the step, so it differs from the twenty-fourth form, and its direction is also reversed; it matches the direction of the ninth form — take care. For the remaining movements refer to the relevant explanations of Figures 47–49 or Figures 22–24; the illustration is omitted.

#### 第四十二式　如封似闭（图略）— Ru Feng Si Bi, "As if Sealing, as if Closing" (illustration omitted)

This form is also a repeated form. From the preceding posture (as in Figure 24) perform the movements of Figures 25, 26 and 27; the illustration is omitted.

#### 第四十三式　十字手（图略）— Shi Zi Shou, "Cross Hands" (illustration omitted)

#### 第四十四式　抱虎归山（图略）— Bao Hu Gui Shan, "Embrace the Tiger, Return to the Mountain" (illustration omitted)

#### 第四十五式　揽雀尾（图略）— Lan Que Wei, "Grasp the Sparrow's Tail" (illustration omitted)

#### 第四十六式　斜单鞭（图略）— Xie Dan Bian, "Diagonal Single Whip" (illustration omitted)

All four forms above are repeated forms. From the preceding posture (as in Figure 27) perform the eleventh form through to the fourteenth form; the movements and directions are exactly the same, and the illustration is omitted.

#### 第四十七式　野马分鬃（图79—图84）— Ye Ma Fen Zong, "Part the Wild Horse's Mane" (Figures 79–84)

Movement one: From the preceding posture (as in Figure 33, but not following the original path) the left toes turn toward the west and the right foot is drawn back half a step to become an empty stance; at the same time the two hands 掤 (peng, "ward off") toward the chest and become upright palms (as in Figure 79). The left elbow then bends so that the left palm comes near the right shoulder, and the right palm falls with the movement, becoming a hanging palm with the arm straight and angling to the left of the body; the body also turns slightly to the left (the feet do not move), and the eyes look toward the north-west, as in Figure 80. A front view is also appended for reference.

Movement two: From the preceding posture (Figure 80) the right foot advances half a step and becomes a bow stance; at the same time The two hands divide upward and downward: the right palm extends from below upward toward the north-west and becomes a palm facing up, while the left palm falls from the right shoulder and presses out toward the south-east, becoming a palm facing down. As the two hands divide upward and downward the palm centres must pass facing one another. When the right hand stretches up toward the north-west the right shoulder turns with it toward the north-west; the body and the line of sight both angle toward the south-west, as in Figure 81.

图 102
Facing to the left, the left hand as an upright palm and the right hand as a side palm form a press before the chest; one leg is bent at the knee in front and the other is straight behind, the body faces left, and the eyes look forward and downward (the book numbers this 圖 79).
图 103
Facing forward-right, the two hands form a press before the face; the right leg is bent at the knee and lifted with the toes touching the ground, the left leg is bent at the knee taking the weight, the body angles to the right, and the eyes look forward (the book numbers this 圖 80).
图 104
Front view: the two hands divide one above the other, one raised and one pressing down; the two legs stand bent at the knees, one before the other, and the eyes look forward (the book labels it 圖 80 正面圖).
图 105
Facing forward-left, the right hand as a palm facing up extends up toward the north-west and the left hand as a palm facing down presses down toward the south-east; the two arms divide diagonally above and below, the two legs stand bent at the knees, one before the other, and the body and line of sight angle toward the south-west (the book numbers this 圖 81).

Movement three: From the preceding posture (Figure 81) the footwork is unchanged and the body comes back from sideways to square. At the same time the two hands copy the movement of Figure 80: the right hand 掤 (peng, "wards off") back to the left shoulder and becomes an upright palm, and the left hand falls to the right and becomes a hanging palm; the body turns slightly to the right (the feet do not move), and the eyes look toward the south-west, as in Figure 82. Movement four: From the preceding posture (Figure 82) the left foot steps forward one step and becomes a bow stance; at the same time the two hands divide upward and downward: the left palm extends from below upward toward the south-west and becomes a palm facing up, and the right palm falls from the right shoulder and presses out toward the north-east, becoming a palm facing down. As they divide upward and downward the palm centres pass facing one another; the left shoulder turns with the extending left hand to the south-west, and the body and line of sight both angle toward the north-west, as in Figure 83.

图 106
Facing to the right, the two hands divide above and below on the left side, the right hand as a palm facing up and the left hand as a palm facing down; the two legs stand bent at the knees, one before the other, the body angles to the left, and the eyes look forward (the book numbers this 圖 82).
图 107
Facing to the left, the left hand as a palm facing up extends upward and the right hand as a side palm presses out downward; the two arms divide diagonally above and below, and the two legs, bent at the knees one before the other, form a large bow stance; the body and line of sight angle toward the north-west (the book numbers this 圖 83).

Movement five: From the preceding posture (Figure 83) the footwork is unchanged and the body comes back from sideways to square; the left hand 掤 (peng, "wards off") back to the right shoulder and the right hand falls to the left, the same as the movement of Figure 80 (but the footwork differs), as in Figure 84.

图 108
Facing to the right, the right hand as an upright palm lies across before the chest and the left hand as a hanging palm falls at the side of the body; the two legs stand bent at the knees, one before the other (the book numbers this 圖 84).
图 109
Facing to the left, the left hand as an upright palm wards off before the chest and the right hand as a hanging palm points downward; the two legs stand bent at the knees and apart, one before the other (the book numbers this 圖 85).

Movement six: From the preceding posture (Figure 84) the right foot steps forward one step and becomes a bow stance, and the two hands divide upward and downward, exactly as in the movement of Figure 81; the illustration is omitted.

Movement seven: From the preceding posture (as in Figure 81) the right foot is drawn back half a step and becomes an empty stance, and both hands 掤 (peng, "ward off") back before the chest and become upright palms, as in Figure 3. The movements of Figures 80 and 81 are then repeated once, up to the pose of Figure 85; refer to the explanations of movements one and two. The illustration is omitted.

#### 第四十八式　玉女穿梭（图86—图91）— Yu Nu Chuan Suo, "the Jade Lady Works the Shuttles" (Figures 86–91)

Movement one: From the preceding posture (Figure 85) the left foot is moved to half a step in front of the right and becomes an empty stance; at the same time the left hand scoops upward, the arm bending to form a ring-shaped embrace, and becomes a palm facing up placed before the left chest at shoulder height. The right hand falls from the upper right along a parabolic line onto the left forearm and turns over into a palm facing down. The body faces due west and the eyes look toward the south-west, as in Figure 86.

图 110
Facing to the left, the left hand as a palm facing up is bent at the arm and embraced in a ring before the left chest at shoulder height, and the right hand as a palm facing down rests upon the left forearm; the two legs stand bent at the knees, one before the other, the body faces due west, and the eyes look south-west (the book numbers this 圖 86).
图 111
Facing to the left, the two hands with arms bent are embraced before the chest with the palm centres facing one another, the left arm outside; the two legs stand bent at the knees one before the other, the right leg straight behind, and the body faces south-west (the book numbers this 圖 87).

Movement two: From the preceding posture (Figure 86) the left foot at once plants half a step out and becomes a bow stance, and the two hands, keeping their original form, send out toward the south-west with the movement, rotating the left arm outward as they go. When the left palm centre has turned to face downward, the right leg sits with the movement and the left foot returns to an empty stance. The left arm continues to rotate upward until the left palm centre turns toward the south-west and is about to become a reversed palm; the right hand then pushes out with the movement toward the south (slightly toward the west) and becomes an upright palm. The left foot returns once more to a bow stance and the body turns toward the south-west (the feet do not move), and the eyes look in that same direction, as in Figure 87.

Movement three: From the preceding posture (Figure 87) the right hand turns from an upright palm to a palm facing up, and the left hand is at once drawn back and rests upon the right forearm, becoming a palm facing down. At the same time the left toes, which point west, are turned to the right to point due east; the body turns back with it, and the right foot is moved to half a step in front of the left and becomes an empty stance. The body faces due east and the eyes look toward the south-east, as in Figure 88.

图 112
Facing to the right, the right hand as a palm facing up is bent at the arm and lies across before the chest, and the left hand as a palm facing down rests upon the right forearm; the two legs stand bent at the knees, one before the other, the body faces due east, and the eyes look south-east (the book numbers this 圖 88).

Movement four: From the preceding posture (Figure 88) the right foot plants out and becomes a bow stance, and the two hands send out toward the south-east; at the same time the right arm rotates. When the right palm centre has turned to face downward, the left leg sits with the movement and the right foot becomes an empty stance. The right arm continues to roll until the right palm centre turns toward the south-east and is about to become a reversed palm; the left hand then pushes out with the movement toward the south (slightly toward the east) and becomes an upright palm. The right foot returns to a bow stance and the body turns toward the south-east (the feet do not move), the eyes looking in the same direction, as in Figure 89. (Note: Figures 86 and 87 are the first left form of 玉女穿梭 (Yu Nu Chuan Suo, "the Jade Lady Works the Shuttles"), and Figures 88 and 89 are the first right form after turning the body. The two forms have the same movements, but the direction of the body and the left-right sides of the hands and feet are all reversed.)

图 113
Facing the front, the two hands with arms bent are embraced before the chest, one hand raised and the other lying across at the side of the chest; the two legs, bent at the knees one before the other, form a large bow stance, and the body faces south-east (the book numbers this 圖 89).

Movement five: From the preceding posture (Figure 89) the right hand falls to the left and becomes a hanging palm, and the left hand is raised to before the right shoulder and becomes an upright palm; at the same time the right foot is drawn back half a step and becomes an empty stance, the form … and the movement is the same as Figure 80 but with the direction reversed (it should be toward the east). The movement of Figure 81 then follows (its direction reversed from Figure 81). The above completes the form of 野马分鬃 (Ye Ma Fen Zong, "Part the Wild Horse's Mane"). From this pose the left foot steps forward one step and the movements of Figures 86 and 87 are performed; the body and the line of sight both face north-east, as in Figure 90 (this is the second left form after turning the body).

图 114
Facing to the left, the two hands with arms bent are embraced before the chest with the palm centres facing one another, the left arm outside; the two legs stand bent at the knees, one before the other, the left leg in front, and the body faces north-east (the book numbers this 圖 90).

Movement six: From the preceding posture (Figure 90) perform the movements of Figures 88 and 89; the body and the line of sight both face north-west (for the hand movements refer to the explanations of Figures 88 and 89, but the direction is reversed), as in Figure 91 (this is the second right form after turning back to the original direction).

图 115
Facing the front, the two hands with arms bent are embraced before the chest, one hand raised and the other lying across at the side of the chest; the two legs, bent at the knees one before the other, form a large bow stance, and the body faces north-west (the book numbers this 圖 91).

This form is also a repeated form. From the preceding posture (as in Figure 54) perform the movement of Figure 8, arriving at the pose of Figure 92; the illustration is omitted.

Facing the front, the two hands divide to left and right, one as an upright palm extending diagonally upward and the other as a hanging palm below; the two legs, bent at the knees one before the other, form a bow stance, and the body faces due east (the book numbers this 圖 92).

#### 第五十三式　下势（图93）— Xia Shi, "Sinking Posture" (Figure 93)

Movement one: From the preceding posture (Figure 92) the toes of both feet turn toward the east and the right leg straightens with the movement, making the left leg a bow stance. At the same time the left elbow bends, the palm centre turns toward the south and the hand remains an upright palm; the right hand releases its grasp, follows a parabolic line from behind to the front and comes to rest beneath the left wrist, becoming an upright palm with the palm centre facing north. The body and the line of sight both face due east, and the form is the same as Figure 22.

Movement two: From the preceding posture (as in Figure 22) the right foot retreats a little over half a step toward the north-west and the toes turn toward the south (slightly toward the west); the body squats down with the movement, the weight shifting to the side of the right leg, while the left leg straightens and its toes turn toward the south-east, the whole sole resting on the ground. As the body squats the two hands sink; the left arm straightens, the fingertips approaching the left foot, and becomes a side palm, while the right hand is drawn back before the chest, the fingertips approaching the left elbow, also becoming a side palm. The body faces south (slightly toward the east); do not bend at the waist or lower the head. The eyes look at the ground in front of the left foot, as in Figure 93.

图 117
Side view: the body squats low, the left leg straight and extended to the right with the whole sole on the ground, and the right leg bent at the knee taking the weight; the left arm straightens downward with the fingertips approaching the left foot, and the right arm is bent at the elbow and drawn back before the chest, both palms as side palms, the eyes looking at the ground in front of the left foot (the book numbers this 圖 93).

#### 第五十四式　金鸡独立（图94—图96）— Jin Ji Du Li, "Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg" (Figures 94–96)

Movement one: From the preceding posture (Figure 93) the body rises straight forward and the right leg straightens with the movement while the left leg bends and becomes a bow stance; the toes of both feet turn toward due east. The two hands rise together as the body straightens, the right hand extending in front of the left, both still as side palms with the palm centres facing … to left and right respectively. The body faces east and the eyes look in front of the right hand, as in Figure 94.

图 118
Facing to the left, the two hands form a press before the body and scoop upward; the two legs are bent at the knees one before the other, the front leg bent and the rear leg straight, the body faces due east, and the eyes look in front of the right hand (the book numbers this 圖 94).

Movement two: From the preceding posture (Figure 94) the right hand continues to rise, turns over into a reversed palm (thumb below) and is placed above and in front of the forehead with the fingertips pointing north; the left hand turns into a palm facing down and then presses downward with the fingertips pointing south and slightly tilted up. As the right hand rises, the right leg is lifted with it, the knee higher than the hip, the right foot before the left knee with the toes tilted up; the left leg is straight with a slight bend. The body and the line of sight both face due east, as in Figure 95 (in the front view appended the two hands are closer together, a more contained posture). This is the right form.

图 119
Side view: one hand is raised as a reversed palm above and in front of the forehead, the other presses down as a palm facing down; the right leg is bent at the knee and lifted with the knee higher than the hip and the toes tilted up, the left leg is straight with a slight bend, and the body faces due east (the book numbers this 圖 95).
图 120
Front view: one hand is raised as a reversed palm guarding above and in front of the forehead and the other, with the arm bent, presses down, the two hands being fairly close together; the right leg is bent at the knee and lifted with the toes tilted up, the left leg is standing, and the eyes look forward (the book labels it 圖 95 正面圖).

Movement three: From the preceding posture (Figure 95) the right foot falls forward and becomes a bow stance, and the right hand falls with it and turns into a palm facing down. Once the right foot is firmly planted the left leg is at once lifted, and at the same time the left hand passes upward from below through the right wrist and rises, turning over into a reversed palm (thumb below) placed in front of the left forehead. The direction is unchanged, as in Figure 96 (with front view appended). This is the left form.

The above performs "Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg" the same on left and right. If it is performed differently on left and right, … "Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg", refer to the posture of Figure 95 and, at the point where both hands are palms facing up with the left hand above and the right below (that is, before the left hand has turned into a reversed palm and the right hand into a palm facing down), change directly into the following "Retreat, Repulse the Monkey".

图 121
Side view: one hand is raised as a reversed palm guarding above and in front of the forehead and the other presses down as a palm facing down; the right leg is bent at the knee and lifted with the toes tilted up, the left leg is standing, and the body faces due east (the book numbers this 圖 96).
图 122
Front view: one hand is raised as a reversed palm placed above and in front of the forehead and the other, with the arm bent, presses down; the right leg is bent at the knee and lifted, the left leg is standing, and the eyes look forward (the book labels it 圖 96 正面圖).

#### 第五十五式　倒撵猴（图略）— Dao Nian Hou, "Retreat, Repulse the Monkey" (illustration omitted)

The left hand, originally an upright palm, is drawn back with the movement and turns into a palm facing up; it then draws slowly back before the chest beneath the right palm and, passing over the top of the right palm, extends forward, turning into an upright palm. #### 第七十式　搂膝指裆捶（图101—图102）— Lou Xi Zhi Dang Chui, "Brush the Knee, Point at the Groin, Punch" (Figures 101–102)

Movement one: From the preceding posture (Figure 100), after the right foot is slapped, the right foot lands with the movement in front and to the right of the left foot and becomes a bow stance; at the same time the right hand falls from beneath the left armpit toward the front and, before the right foot has landed, brushes past the right knee. On the other side, after slapping the foot, the left hand bends at the elbow and moves to the side of the left cheek as a side palm (fingertips forward, palm centre inward) and then at once extends forward, completing the posture of 搂膝拗步 (Lou Xi Ao Bu, "Brush the Knee and Twist Step"), as in Figure 101.

Movement two: From the preceding posture (Figure 101) the left foot at once steps up and lands in front and to the left of the right foot half a step to the side; first form an empty stance (either the heel or the ball of the foot may rest on the ground), with the right leg bearing the weight of the body. At the same time the left hand falls to the right of the left knee and brushes past the left knee, while the right hand bends at the elbow and draws up, closing into a fist with the movement (the tiger's mouth facing upward) and is placed beside the right ribs. When the three movements above are completed at the same instant, the left foot at once steps out half a step; the moment the heel touches the ground the knee bends, the palm falls, and the foot settles into a bow stance; at the same time the right fist extends with the movement forward and downward (the tiger's mouth still facing upward). Meanwhile the left hand, having brushed past the knee, has already returned in an arc to the front of the left knee and there takes the opportunity to place itself beside the crook of the right elbow. The movements of the left hand, the left foot, and the right fist must all reach their fixed points at the same moment, as in Figure 102.
