A Short Account of Wu-Style Taijiquan

A Short Account of Wu-Style Taijiquan
图 1
Half-length portrait of Hǎo Wéizhēn (1849–1920), wearing a skullcap, bearded,
in a dark front-buttoned jacket.

Wǔ Héqīng (武河清) of Yongnian in Hebei, courtesy name Yǔxiāng (禹襄, 1812–1880), came from a minor official-landlord family, and he and his two brothers practised martial arts at home. When Yáng Lùchán (楊露禪, 1799–1872) returned to his native village from Chenjiagou, the Yǔxiāng brothers admired his art and studied the old-frame Chen family taijiquan with him, grasping its essentials. In 1852 Yǔxiāng's elder brother Chéngqīng (澄清, 1800–1884) passed the metropolitan civil-service examination and took office as magistrate of Wuyang county in Henan. Yǔxiāng travelled to his brother's post and, taking the route through Wen county, stopped at Chenjiagou intending to seek further instruction from Lùchán's teacher Chén Chángxīng (陳長興, 1771–1853). It happened that Chángxīng was already old and ill — he was then 82 and died the following year — and at the time Chén Qīngpíng (陳青萍) was teaching the new-frame Chen taijiquan at Zhaobao town; Yǔxiāng therefore studied the new frame with Qīngpíng for over a month, and came to know its theory and method thoroughly. At a salt shop in Wuyang, Chéngqīng obtained Wáng Zōngyuè's (王宗岳, a man of the Qianlong reign) Taijiquan Manual. Yǔxiāng studied the manual and gained further insight; drawing on his own experience of practising, he expounded the sense of Wang's old text, writing ten annotations to the Thirteen Postures Practice Song, under the title Essential Words on Pushing Words; he further expanded this into the Thirteen Postures Practice Heart-Explanation in four sections, and distilled the essentials of training into the Ten Requirements of Body Method. All his writings rest on his own experience, and are therefore concise and to the point, without a single ornamental phrase.

Yǔxiāng's nephew Lǐ Jīnglún (李經綸), courtesy name Yìshē (亦畬, 1832–1892), began studying with Yǔxiāng in 1853. In his own study of taijiquan Yìshē imitated Yǔxiāng's method of practical testing — summoning village braves to test his own skill — and revised his notes again and again. Yìshē's grandson Huáiyīn (槐蔭) wrote in the 1935 Li Lianrang-hall edition Preface to the Taijiquan Manual: "This manual was written by my grandfather in his later years, and was completed only after many revisions. Whenever he found a posture ingenious or a key point of a technique, he would write it on a slip of paper and paste it at his seat, testing and pondering it. After some days, if he felt something was not right and ought to be changed, he would tear it down and substitute another slip. This pasting and tearing went back and forth until it was perfect and only then stopped; in time the book was complete." Lǐ Yìshē's taijiquan essays comprise the Five-Character Formula; the Secret Formula of Release, with its four seven-character lines on bracing, drawing, reaching and releasing; and Essential Words for Practice in Walking the Frame and Pushing Hands, which sets out that walking the frame is pushing hands and pushing hands is walking the frame, and that form practice and pushing hands complete each other. In the spread of taijiquan in modern times, the greater part of the credit for ceaseless innovation in teaching materials and methods goes to three generations of the Yang family; but in the study and summation of the art's theory, the first place goes to Wu and Li. Compared with the abstract generality of Wang Zongyue's Taijiquan Treatise, theirs is far more concrete and practical — they inherit and they develop, and so were able to form a school of their own.

The Wu Yuxiang form differs both from the old and new Chen frames and from the Yang large and small frames; it studies them and transforms them, forming a school of its own. Its characteristics are: a compact posture; unhurried movement; a footwork method that strictly distinguishes substantial from insubstantial; and a chest and abdomen that, in advancing, retreating and rotating rotating, always keep upright and centred. The outer form is governed entirely by the inner conversion of substantial and insubstantial and by a "hidden turning of inner qi"; each hand governs half the body, without overstepping, and the hand does not extend past the toe. There were originally leaping movements as well, but by the fourth transmission, with Hǎo Yuèrú (郝月如, 1877–1935), these were changed to no jumping and no leaping; the double lotus-swing was likewise changed so that the foot is not slapped — reforms made to suit the needs of the old and the physically weak.

In Wu-style pushing hands the footwork is of one kind only: three and a half steps forward and three and a half steps back.

Yǔxiāng taught and read for his own pleasure, and Yìshē practised medicine for a living; both held themselves to be scholars, and accepted very few pupils in their home district. Among those Li transmitted it to, the most refined in skill was his fellow-townsman Hǎo Hé (郝和), courtesy name Wéizhēn (為真, 1849–1920). When Wu-style taijiquan first came to Beijing in the early Republic, some called it the Li frame; and when Wéizhēn's son Yuèrú and his grandson Shàorú went together to Nanjing and Shanghai in 1928 to teach, some called it the Hao frame. Yuèrú left behind several writings on taijiquan. Among the later generations of Wu and Li, few devoted themselves to taijiquan, and so Wu-style was passed on and practised by the Hao family. Shàorú had not taught for many years, until the Shanghai Municipal Gymnasium, in order to recover the tradition, opened a Wu-style taijiquan class in 1961 and invited Hǎo Shàorú to teach, so that it might be spread more widely. Wu-style taijiquan had never before appeared in illustrated form; the posture plates in this book were photographed from Hǎo Shàorú, who also wrote the movement explanations.

(Gù Liúxīn)

Book page 572

Foreword

Foreword

I grew up in a family with a passion for taijiquan. Our native place is Yongnian county in Hebei. My grandfather's name was Hé, his courtesy name Wéizhēn. My father's name was Wénguì, his courtesy name Yuèrú. My grandfather learned taijiquan from our neighbour Mr Lǐ Yìshē (see note 1). Mr Li had been taught it by his maternal uncle, Mr Wǔ Yǔxiāng (see note 2). My grandfather studied with Mr Li for a long time, never interrupting for decades, right up to the time of Mr Li's death. Thus my grandfather came to possess deeply the subtleties of the Wu–Li school of taijiquan. While my grandfather was practising with Mr Li, my father was often at his side, because he was a pupil in Mr Li's traditional school. Through long observation and pondering, my father could already grasp the theory and practice of taijiquan before he came of age. From childhood I too, because of my surroundings, came early into contact with taijiquan. Afterwards, under my father's instruction, my love for it grew day by day, and by the age of fifteen I had formed the habit of practising every day.

Since Liberation, under the leadership and care of the Party, taijiquan has become a vigorous mass sport and one of the means of health care for the broad masses of the people. This has made me feel deeply that I ought to make public to the whole country the important taijiquan documents preserved in my family and the experience of three generations of my family in teaching taijiquan, and to take an active part in taijiquan research — so as to contribute my small strength to raising and developing this exceedingly precious part of our national cultural heritage. It was from this motive that I wrote this book in my spare time. In the course of writing it, Comrade Gù Liúxīn, director of the Shanghai Municipal Gymnasium, gave me powerful support: he not only read through the whole manuscript himself, but also selected a number of old martial manuals to append at the end of the book, and wrote the short account of Wu-style taijiquan. Comrade Zhōu Yuánlóng drew the diagrams on my behalf, and gave great assistance in the polishing of the text and in the arrangement. In addition, no few friends who love taijiquan took a great part in the work of compilation. Here I express my heartfelt thanks.

Because my own level is limited, shortcomings can hardly be avoided; I hope readers will not begrudge their corrections and criticism.

Hǎo Shàorú

Shanghai, on the eve of National Day, 1961

(Note 1) Lǐ Jīnglún, courtesy name Yìshē, a native of Yongnian county, a Qing provincial graduate, born in the ninth month of the twelfth year of the Daoguang reign and died in the eleventh month of the eighteenth year of the Guangxu reign (1832–1892).

(Note 2) Wǔ Héqīng, courtesy name Yǔxiāng, a native of Yongnian county, a Qing county scholar, born in the second month of the seventeenth year of the Jiaqing reign and died in the eleventh month of the sixth year of the Guangxu reign (1812–1880).

Book page 574

Chapter One — The Essentials of Taijiquan

Chapter One — The Essentials of Taijiquan
Key Points of Wu-Style Taijiquan

by Hǎo Yuèrú

(1) The body methods of taijiquan are chiefly these thirteen: enclosing the chest, drawing up the back, wrapping the hips, guarding the ribs, lifting the crown, suspending the crotch, loosening the shoulders, sinking the elbows, soaring and shifting, flashing and battling, the tailbone held central and upright, qi sunk to the elixir field, and a clear distinction of substantial and insubstantial.

1. What is above the heart is the chest. The chest must not be puffed out; it must relax downward, with the two shoulders drawing slightly forward and together. This is called enclosing the chest (涵胸). Only when the chest can enclose can one move qi by the mind.

2. At the spine between the two shoulders there should be a sense of swelling up; the two shoulders must be lively. One must not bow the head. This is called drawing up the back (拔背).

3. The two knees exert force, with an intent of turning inward, so that the two legs are as one leg, and yet can divide substantial from insubstantial. This is called wrapping the hips (裹胯).

4. The two flanks draw in slightly, taking the posture of gathering below and closing in front, with a feeling of looseness and ease within. This is called guarding the ribs (護肫).

5. Head and neck are straight and correct, neither low nor raised; the spirit threads through to the crown, lifting up the whole body. This is called lifting the crown (提頂).

6. The two thighs exert force, the buttocks push forward, and the lower abdomen has a sense of turning upward. This is called suspending the crotch (吊襠).

7. By intent, loosen the two shoulders and let the qi sink down, adding the single word "stillness" within the intent. This is called loosening the shoulders (鬆肩).

8. Carry qi by intent so that it moves through the two elbows; the wrists must be able to stay lively, and the tips of the elbows should always have a sense of hanging downward. This is called sinking the elbows (沉肘).

9. To have the intent to move but not yet to have moved — that is, the posture of preparation to move — is called soaring and shifting (騰挪).

10. Body, hands, waist and legs follow one another in accord, completing in a single breath and issuing outward, the jin like a loosed arrow, swift as thunder, invincible wherever it goes. This is called flashing and battling (閃戰).

11. The two thighs are powerful, the buttocks draw forward, and the root of the spine lifts the elixir field (the lower abdomen) forward. This is called the tailbone held central and upright (尾閭正中).

12. If one can achieve the tailbone held central and upright, enclosing the chest, guarding the ribs, loosening the shoulders and suspending the crotch, then one can send qi by intent to reach the abdomen without letting it float upward. This is called qi sunk to the elixir field (氣沉丹田).

13. The substantial and insubstantial of the two legs must be clearly distinguished. The insubstantial is not entirely without force: the point where the foot is placed and made substantial must have the posture of soaring and shifting. Soaring and shifting means that foot and chest have the sense of drawing and binding to each other; otherwise one becomes sunk to one side. The substantial is not entirely dead-weighted: the spirit threads through the substantial thigh, which props up the whole body, and there must be a sense of lifting upward. If substantial and insubstantial are not distinguished, one falls into double weighting (雙重).

(2) Hand, eye, body, step, essence, qi, spirit

The method of the hand requires that the momentum of the posture soar and shift, that there be a posture of preparation to move, and no sense of looseness or sprawl. The two shoulders must also be loosened, without the least force in them. Hand positions are in themselves not fixed: whether raised or lowered, extended or bent back, there must always be a corresponding intent — when the intent moves, the hand arrives. This is what is meant by "the hand responds as the mind directs". The posture of soaring and shifting is precisely "having intent", "carrying qi", and "concentrating the spirit". Carry qi by intent: in time one becomes refined; refined and more refined, one becomes spiritual; spiritual and more spiritual, one becomes numinous. Whoever grasps this principle will possess the wonder of spiritual clarity.

The spirit gathers in the eyes; the eye is the sprout of the heart-mind. Intent is born in the heart: wherever my intent wishes to go, there the gaze shoots straight, and the whole body also faces straight there. When the eye turns, the whole body turns. Regard stillness as movement and movement as stillness — always it must come from the gathering of the spirit.

In the body method, first seek "the tailbone held central and upright". Central and upright means "the root of the spine pointing forward". One must also guard the ribs: if the ribs are not guarded, the tail cannot stand firm, and the whole body has no governing principle. Wherever my intent wishes to go, there the "root of the spine" faces straight. The turning takes place in the two eye-of-the-waist points: turning left, the left waist-eye draws slightly upward and the right waist-eye lifts up the left; turning right, the right waist-eye draws slightly upward and the left waist-eye lifts up the right — and then the tailbone is naturally central and upright. In sum, each item of the body method must be matched one by one; joined together they are a single body method. If one place does not accord, the whole body goes awry — and so the body method may never be wrong. Though there be a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, one can never step outside this body method.

As for the footwork distinction of substantial and insubstantial: the insubstantial is not entirely without force — within it there must be soaring and shifting; the substantial is not entirely dead-weighted — the spirit must be concentrated through it. Soaring and shifting is called the insubstantial, and within the insubstantial there is the substantial; the spirit is called the substantial, and within the substantial there is the insubstantial. Insubstantial within substantial and substantial within insubstantial, substantial within insubstantial and insubstantial within substantial — this is the meaning.

(3) Rise, carry, open, close

In walking the taijiquan frame, each posture is divided into four movements. The first movement is rise (起) — as in the first movement of "left lazy tucking the robe". The second is carry (承) — as in the second movement of that posture. The third is open (開), which is also issuing — as in the third movement. The fourth is close (合), which is also gathering; gathering means storing — as in the fourth movement. But it is not rigid: there is opening within closing and closing upon closing. This is what is meant by neither losing nor resisting, every point exactly matching.

(4) Folding and conversion

Taijiquan has the art of folding and the method of conversion. Folding is mutual correspondence: where there is up there is down; where there is forward there is back; where there is left there is right. If the intent is to go up, then lodge a downward intent within it; if the intent is to go down, then lodge an upward intent within it. Forward and back, left and right, are all like this. This is what is called folding. Conversion means the step changes with the body; the source of the commanding intent lies between the waist-eyes. Converting to the left, the left waist-eye draws slightly upward and the right waist-eye lifts up the left; converting to the right, the right waist-eye draws slightly upward and the left waist-eye lifts up the right. This is what is meant by "the source of the commanding intent lies in the waist crevice".

(5) Yielding self to follow others

Taijiquan has the art of yielding self to follow others: wherever one is touched, there one is lively. If touched at the hand, the wrist is lively; if touched at the elbow, the elbow can be lively; if touched at the chest, the chest can be lively — and everywhere on the body likewise. Again, touched at the hand, the intent is at the elbow; touched at the elbow, the intent is at the shoulder; touched at the shoulder, the intent is at the chest; touched at the chest, the intent is at the waist; touched at the waist, the intent is at the thigh. Extend this: adhere, connect, stick and follow; neither lose nor resist; draw in and make empty; borrow force to send the other out — all are this same meaning.

Book page 576

Walking the Frame and Pushing Hands in Taijiquan

Walking the Frame and Pushing Hands in Taijiquan

by Hǎo Yuèrú

Taijiquan lies not in the form but in the momentum; not in the outer but in the inner. In daily practice of walking the frame, one must study and ponder the way of emptiness, looseness, roundness and liveliness; the spirit and qi must drum and surge; the whole body is like a balloon; the momentum values soaring and shifting; the body is as if suspended in the air. The two hands, whether high or low, bent or extended, one forward one back, one left one right, can all be lively and free. The two legs, whether advancing or retreating, turning left or right, changing substantial and insubstantial, all follow the wish of the intent. With time and deep practice, one reaches the state of not knowing that the hands dance and the feet stamp. When one understands the principle, practises the body method until familiar, is good at using intent and skilful at carrying qi, then at this stage every single movement accords with measure — there is no such thing as wrong.

The student of taijiquan must first seek the tailbone held central and upright. Central and upright means the root of the spine facing between the eyes. Stepping to the left, the left hip draws slightly upward to the left and the right hip lifts up the left; stepping to the right, the right hip draws slightly upward to the right and the left hip lifts up the right — and then the tailbone is naturally central and upright. Being central and upright, one can prop up in all eight directions; propping up in all eight directions, one can rotate freely, and there is nothing to be gained. Next, the footwork's substantial and insubstantial must be clearly distinguished. The insubstantial is not entirely without force — within it there must be soaring and shifting, that is, the posture of preparation to move. The substantial is not entirely dead-weighted — within it the spirit must be concentrated through, that is, the sense of lifting upward. Bear firmly in mind that when the two feet are in front-bow and rear-press, they must not be entirely dead-weighted: one must be insubstantial and one substantial, otherwise one falls into the fault of double weighting. The two shoulders must be loosened, without the least force: with force one cannot yield self to follow others and draw in to make empty. Sinking the elbows means the tips of the elbows always have a downward-sinking intent. The forearms and the two thighs must have within them the posture of soaring and shifting; without soaring and shifting they are not lively, and without liveliness there is no delight of roundness and life. One must also guard the ribs: if the ribs are not guarded, the tail cannot stand firm, and the whole body has no governing principle. One must also nourish qi: qi is nourished straight and without harm — that is, sinking into the elixir field and cultivating it without injury. One must also store jin: jin is stored by bending, with surplus, and must be gathered and concealed within the spine. Inhaling is closing and storing; exhaling is opening and issuing. For in inhaling one can naturally lift up — and can lift another up too; in exhaling one can naturally sink down — and can send another out. This is carrying qi by intent, not compelling qi by force, and it is the way of breathing in taijiquan. (The "breathing" spoken of here refers specifically to the taijiquan "open, close, store, issue" and differs from our ordinary breathing; readers should not mistake it.)

The art of taijiquan is exceedingly subtle and ingenious; it does not rely on great strength or quick hands. Great strength and quick hands are bestowed by nature at birth — what need is there to learn them? Therefore one who wishes to learn this art should first seek it through enclosing the chest, drawing up the back, wrapping the hips, guarding the ribs, lifting the crown, suspending the crotch, loosening the shoulders, sinking the elbows and clearly distinguishing substantial and insubstantial. When these are right, then seek to gather qi: qi is gathered in the spine and pours into the waist. Then seek soaring and shifting. Soaring and shifting is essence, qi and spirit. Essence, qi and spirit are concentrated through the two feet, the two legs, the two hands and the front sections of the two forearms. Wherever the other touches me, there I direct my attention; on the whole body there is not one inch without essence, qi and spirit, not one inch that is not taiji. Only then seek the method of advancing, retreating and rotating. The pivot of rotation lies in the waist crevice. When one can rotate freely without the least disorder, then seek the art of movement and stillness: stillness is nothingness, and from nothingness is born being — that is, intent. Intent has no fixed direction; it must prop up in all eight directions. In solo practice, each posture divides into four words — rise, carry, open, close. After each word, ask: can I prop up in all eight directions? If I cannot prop up in all eight directions, then ponder it at once. If two people In pushing hands my intent must come first. Though the other's hand be quick, it is no match for my intent coming first; though the other's strength be great, it is no match for my qi gathered in. If he strikes with immense force, I meet it with intent, touching only the skin or hair without letting it land, borrowing his force and taking advantage of his momentum — whichever of the eight directions is favourable, there I strike. Bear firmly in mind: do not use force, do not prize breath-force, do not resist, do not lose. One must follow the other and yet still be led by oneself; only having gained the moment and the momentum can one act effectively at will. Movement likewise is intent: the step moves but the body method is not disordered; the hand moves but the momentum is not scattered. In solo practice, at every movement ask: can I convert in all eight directions out of the movement? If I cannot convert in all eight directions, then ponder it at once. In two-person pushing hands, if I wish to go to him, first arrange the whole body well, keep the intent still ahead, fix upon his key point, and go straight at it. The moment my intent touches his skin or hair, if it can respond, one exhale and out he goes. If his force comes resisting and I do not let his force be issued, my intent still borrows his force — neither losing nor resisting — and strikes along his force. This is the marvel of borrowing force to strike, of four ounces deflecting a thousand catties. All of this is carrying qi by intent, not compelling qi by force. When one can strike by intent, in time even intent is not used, and the body method has nothing that does not accord. At this stage one has reached the realm of round harmony and subtle excellence. Say it is, and it is; say it is not, and it is not — every single movement follows the heart's desire. Truly one no longer knows that the hands dance and the feet stamp.

The student of taijiquan must comprehend the principle of taiji. To know the principle of taiji, one must first raise the whole spirit in practice, outwardly showing ease and composure, inwardly consolidating the spirit, with the momentum soaring and shifting and the abdomen drumming and surging. Taiji is the whole body, and the whole body is taiji. Like a balloon: advancing it does not bulge, retreating it does not cave, turning left it is not deficient, turning right it does not collapse — myriad changes, with no interruption whatsoever, completed in a single breath, without outer or inner, form and spirit both forgotten. Only then can one advance into the subtle and refined.

In pushing hands, my intent must be first. Wherever his force touches me, there my intent is employed. The moment his force touches my skin or hair, my intent has already entered his bones. I meet his force with my intent, not with my force colliding against his; exactly neither after nor before, my intent joins with his force. If the left is heavy, then the left is made empty; if the right is heavy, then the right is made void. Raise it and it grows higher; lower it and it grows deeper; advance it and it grows longer; retreat and it grows more pressing. Not a feather can be added, not a fly or insect can alight. Others do not know me, I alone know others. This is what is meant by adhering, connecting, sticking and following; neither losing nor resisting. The student of taijiquan must comprehend the meaning of yin and yang completing each other. In movement they divide; in stillness they join. Dividing is opening wide; joining is contracting small — and in both, the two qi of yin and yang open and close, convert, and answer each other, never parting from start to finish. Opening is largeness, not colliding; contracting is smallness, not dodging. In one movement there is no part that does not move; in one stillness there is no part that is not still. Movement is the turning of qi; stillness is the posture of preparation to move — this is what is meant by regarding stillness as movement and movement as stillness. Qi is like a cartwheel, the waist like the axle. It is not a matter of the two hands flailing and the body shifting about at random. The crux lies entirely in storing jin: storing jin is like drawing a bow, issuing jin like loosing an arrow. Without storing jin there is no force to loose the arrow. In issuing jin, upper and lower must follow one another; jin rises from the heel of the foot, pours into the waist, and takes form at the fingers. From foot to leg to waist, it must always be one whole qi. The waist is like the grip of the bow, the feet and hands like its tips; within there must be elasticity, and only then is there force to loose the arrow. Arrange oneself well: the moment he touches my skin or hair, my intent fixes upon his jin. To touch skin or hair is neither to lose nor to resist; to meet it with intent is the posture of following along. Being able to follow along, one can borrow force; being able to borrow force, one can strike — this is what is meant by borrowing force to strike, four ounces deflecting a thousand catties. At this stage the hand has measure: it can weigh the size of his jin, can gauge the length of his advance, without the least error. Advancing and retreating, looking left and right, everywhere exactly matching — this is what is meant by "know yourself and know the other, and in a hundred battles you will win a hundred". In daily walking of the frame and pushing hands, one must proceed from this: walking the frame is pushing hands, and pushing hands is walking the frame — the same principle throughout. In walking the frame, each posture must divide into four words: rise, carry, open, close. After each word ask: is it right? If slightly not right, change it at once. A hair's difference loses a thousand li. One who can grasp this meaning will find that walking, standing, sitting and lying are all taiji; the student must not fail to examine this minutely.

In daily practice of walking the frame, one must by intent sink the qi down and deliver it to the elixir field (by intent, not by force; not by straining qi, not by using breath), keeping and nourishing it, not letting it float up, with the abdomen loose and still and the momentum soaring. Practising according to the method, in time one can naturally gather qi into the bone (the spine). Then, by intent, turn the qi of the spine upward from the tailbone through the elixir field. Reaching this stage, one can carry qi by intent throughout the whole body. Wherever he touches me, there my intent arrives, and the qi likewise comes out after it, as echo answers sound, swift as lightning. There is no place on the whole body where it is not so. This is what is meant by "carrying qi as through nine winding pearls, reaching the smallest place; issuing jin like steel refined a hundred times, nothing so hard it cannot break" — and likewise "where intent arrives, qi arrives". Moreover the qi of the elixir field must be nourished straight and without harm, and only then can it be like the water of the long river and the great sea, inexhaustible in use, unfailing in supply. When the practice is mature and one has refined the whole body into a single family, just like a balloon — left heavy then left empty, right heavy then right void — things come and one responds, and nothing fails to match. All of this is "carrying qi by intent", not "compelling qi by force", "within and not without" — that is, "he who prizes breath-force has no force; he who nourishes qi is purely firm".

Note: "Pushing hands" in this text means taijiquan pushing hands. The text was slightly abridged and revised when published here.

Book page 580

Some Reflections on Teaching and Practice

Some Reflections on Teaching and Practice

Hǎo Shàorú

Drawing on more than thirty years of practising and teaching, I hold that whether teaching or practising, one must first of all fix one's eyes on the body method — the eight body methods of Wǔ Yǔxiāng — and must proceed from the inner outward.

The body method is one of the principal contents of taijiquan theory. In both teaching and practice, the body method is at once the most basic and, from first to last, the most important. Therefore the body method must be required strictly.

In practising taijiquan, to say nothing of reaching refined skill, even basic skill cannot be attained in a single step. Therefore in teaching or practising, one must broadly divide the work into two stages.

The first stage is the practice of the outer form: that is, learning the frame, with attention to the body method. But the eight body methods cannot all be grasped at once. One must first choose one or two as the emphasis emphasis, and after these are mastered, gradually add more. The coordination of the upper and lower limbs with the body method is also extremely important, because poor coordination will directly affect the body method. Coordination of the upper limbs is comparatively easy to master; but the lower limbs, since they must both support the body's stability and attend to distinguishing substantial from insubstantial, are more difficult for beginners. Only when these eight body methods are mastered can the muscles and bones of the whole body be lively and harmonious, with movements unified, and only then can one reach the stage of following the heart's desire.

The second stage is the practice of the inner form, also called inner jin. One must first take the practice of intent as one's guide, and gradually refine intent, qi and frame into one. From outer form to inner form, from coarse qi to refined qi. Then there is no outer and no inner, no coarse and no refined, all in a great oblivion. Only when practice reaches this stage can one climb the high peak of taijiquan art along a road of ceaseless advance. As for those who taste but briefly and stop, or who set up novelties out of thin air, they are not worth taking as models.

Book page 581

Explanation of the Sequence Diagrams

Explanation of the Sequence Diagrams

All the movements of Wu-style taijiquan are arranged according to the sequence of rise, carry, open, close. Four movements make up one sequence of rise, carry, open, close. For example, the four movements of the second posture, "left lazy tucking the robe", are the four diagrams in the sequence diagrams: Figure 1 is "rise", Figure 2 is "carry", Figure 3 is "open", Figure 4 is "close" — joined into one sequence. The entire set is arranged as sequences joined one to the next. Between one sequence and the next, though there appears to be a pause, one must keep the jin broken but the intent unbroken, and internally the sequences must still join in an unbroken thread — and so in practice one must not break off because of the sequence divisions.

A sequence is mostly formed from a single posture, as with the "left lazy tucking the robe" cited above, which has four movements and makes one sequence. But there are also cases where two, or even four or five postures combine into one sequence — for example the fourth posture, "single whip", and the fifth, "raise the hand", whose two postures are joined together as four movements into one sequence.

Some notes on the illustrations

Some notes on the illustrations

1. The photographs in these illustrations are traced from the author's own posture photographs.

2. So that the reader can check the direction of a posture against the pictures, the direction of the preparatory posture (Figure 1) is assumed as follows: facing the reader equals south, the back equals north, the reader's right-hand side equals east, the reader's left-hand side equals west. Once the reader becomes skilled in practice, any direction may be chosen according to the shape of the ground, and the preparatory posture need not always begin facing south.

3. Every solid or broken line in the pictures indicates the direction of travel of a hand or a foot. Every arrow in the pictures indicates the direction in which the movement passes from that picture into the next. Where a movement is simple enough to be made clear in words, its direction of travel is not shown in the picture; refer to the text and to the following picture.

4. An arrow drawn with a solid line indicates the direction of travel of the right hand or the right foot; one drawn with An arrow drawn with a broken line indicates the direction of travel of the left hand or the left foot.

5. Because the movement of the feet in taijiquan is very fine, shading is drawn beside the foot in order to indicate the angle of the foot to the ground, so that they may be told apart:

Illustrated explanation of the Wu-style taijiquan form

Illustrated explanation of the Wu-style taijiquan form
First posture — Preparatory posture (Figure 1)

The two feet stand together (about one fist apart), the two knees slightly bent, not stiff; the two arms hang naturally; the eyes look straight ahead. (Figure 1)

The requirement, when the two feet stand together and one has taken up the stance, is that the body be natural and calm; that the whole spirit be raised and distracting thoughts excluded; that the intent contain a lifting energy (ding jin), so that the head is upright and straight, the chin slightly drawn in; that the two shoulders be relaxed; that the abdomen be loosened, with the breath sunk to the dantian; that the chest be contained, the back pulled up, the crotch wrapped, and the ribs protected.

图 1
Line drawing (upper left of the page): a man standing facing the viewer, the two feet together, the two arms hanging naturally, the eyes looking level ahead. This is the posture photograph for the Preparatory posture, the first posture. Labelled at its side "Figure 1".
Second posture — Left grasp and tie the garment (Figures 2–5)

Movement one: the two legs bend at the knees and sink slightly; the body weight gradually moves onto the right leg, and the right leg becomes full (solid); the left heel lifts, the toe touches the ground, and the left leg becomes empty. At the same time the two arms bend slightly and the two hands move forward, resting at the sides of the hips, the backs of the hands upward, the fingers pointing forward, slightly flexed and separated. (Figure 2)

Throughout the form of Wu-style taijiquan, the two arms and two legs of every movement and posture may never be straightened, but must keep a certain bend; and when the body turns, the heel of the full leg must serve as the axis. Moreover, in every movement the head, trunk, chest, back and the other parts must accord with the requirements of the preparatory posture; this will not be repeated below.

Movement two: the body turns slightly to the left, and the left foot accordingly lifts and steps out toward the left diagonal (a 45-degree diagonal; the diagonals referred to from here on are all 45 degrees), the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the left leg slightly bent (the two legs are still empty-left and full-right). At the same time the two hands lift toward the chest, the fingers pointing up to form upright palms, the left hand outside, level with the mouth; the right hand inside, level with the heart, both palms turned slightly forward (the two elbows must sink); facing the southeast diagonal. (Figure 3)

图 2
Line drawing (middle of the right-hand side of the page): the man with knees slightly bent and sunk, the weight over the right leg, the two hands moved to the sides of the hips, the backs of the hands upward and the fingers pointing forward. Labelled at its side "Figure 2".

Movement three: the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, the left sole settles flat, the body weight moves onto the left leg, the right leg bends slightly, and the two legs become full-left and empty-right. At the same time the two hands push slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward; the shoulders must be relaxed and the elbows sunk), the palms still turned slightly forward, the left hand level with the eyes, the right hand level with the chest. (Figure 4)

Movement four: the two hands fall at the same time; when the two hands come level with the hips (with the two hands down they may not let the elbows stand out behind the back) they part to left and right, arc upward, and the upright palms come together before the chest with the intent of holding a ball, the two hands level with the mouth, the palms turned slightly forward. At the same time as the two hands part left and right, the right foot follows forward to beside the left heel, touching the ground with the toe. (Figure 5)

The requirement is to relax the shoulders and sink the elbows; there should be a lively roundness between the hands and the chest. The two legs are still full-left and empty-right.

图 3
Line drawing (lower left of the page): the man with the two hands raised before the chest as upright palms, the left hand outside and level with the mouth, the right hand inside and level with the heart; the left heel lifted with the toe touching the ground, and the body turned slightly left. Labelled at its side "Figure 3".
图 4
Line drawing (lower middle of the page): the man with the left leg bowed forward, the two hands pushing slowly forward, the left hand level with the eyes and the right hand level with the chest; an arrow in the picture marks the direction in which the two hands push. Labelled at its side "Figure 4".
图 5
Line drawing (lower right of the page): the man with the two hands parted left and right before the chest and arcing upward into joined upright palms, the right foot having followed to beside the left heel with the toe touching the ground. Labelled at its side "Figure 5".
Third posture — Right grasp and tie the garment (Figures 6–9)

Movement one: with the left heel as the axis (the right toe still touching the ground), the body turns slightly to the right, facing due south, the two legs still full-left and empty-right. (Figure 6)

Movement two: the waist revolves slightly to the right, and the right foot accordingly steps out toward the right diagonal, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the right leg slightly bent (the two legs still full-left and empty-right). At the same time the left hand moves from above downward and the right hand from below upward, drawing a small circle, still as upright palms (fingers pointing up): the right hand outside, level with the mouth; the left hand inside, level with the heart; both palms turned slightly forward (the two elbows must sink); facing the southwest diagonal. (Figure 7)

图 6
Line drawing (upper left of the page): the man with the two hands raised before the chest as upright palms, the right hand outside and level with the mouth, the left hand inside and level with the heart; the body turned slightly right, the two legs full-left and empty-right, the right toe touching the ground. Labelled at its side "Figure 6".
图 7

Labelled at its side "Figure 7".
图 8
Line drawing (upper right of the page): the man with the right leg bowed forward and the two hands pushing slowly forward; arrows and arcs in the picture mark the direction of the hands' circling and pushing. Labelled at its side "Figure 8".
图 9
Line drawing (middle left of the page): the man with the two hands pushed forward as facing upright palms, the right leg bowed forward, the weight on the right leg. Labelled at its side "Figure 9".
图 10
Line drawing (middle right of the page): the man with the two hands joined before the chest as upright palms, the two legs full-right and empty-left, the right toe touching the ground. Labelled at its side "Figure 10".

Movements three and four are the same as movements three and four of the second posture, "Left grasp and tie the garment", only that left and right are reversed and the direction is different. The direction of this posture is toward the southwest diagonal. (Figures 8– 9)

Fourth posture — Single whip (Figures 10–12)
Fifth posture — Raise the hand and lift the posture (Figure 13)

The two postures are joined into one section-sequence (as to what a section-sequence is, see the explanation of the section-sequence diagrams). Movements one, two and three are "Single whip"; movement four is "Raise the hand and lift the posture".

Movement one: with the right heel as the axis (the left toe still touching the ground), the body turns 90 degrees to the left, facing the southeast diagonal, still with the right leg full and the left leg empty. (Figure 10) Movement two: the left foot steps out, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the two legs still empty-left and full-right. (Figure 11)

Movement three: the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, the left sole settles flat, the right leg bends slightly, and the two legs become full-left and empty-right. At the same time the two hands part to left and right, the fingers pointing up, the palms turned outward, still as upright palms: the left hand level with the eyes, the right hand level with the mouth (the two elbows must sink); facing the diagonal east, slightly toward south. (Figure 12)

Movement four: the right leg draws in toward the left, with the right toe touching beside the left foot (the two legs still full-left and empty-right). At the same time the body turns slightly to the right, facing due south. The two hands follow the movement: the right hand arcs downward and to the left, scooping up from below and coming to rest before the abdomen, the fingers pointing forward; the left hand rises, the palm turned up, with the intent of lifting upward, level with the eyebrows (the shoulders must relax and the elbows sink). (Figure 13)

图 11
Line drawing (lower left of the page): the man with the left foot stepped forward, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the two hands as facing upright palms before the chest; a horizontal arrow to the left in the picture marks the direction of the movement. Labelled at its side "Figure 11".
图 12
Line drawing (lower middle of the page): the man with the right leg pressed straight and the left leg bowed forward, the two hands parted left and right as upright palms with the palms turned outward, the right heel lifted. Labelled at its side "Figure 12".
图 13
Line drawing (lower right of the page): the man with the two hands drawn in before the body, the right hand before the abdomen with the fingers pointing forward, and the left hand raised with the palm up, level with the eyebrows. Labelled at its side "Figure 13".
Sixth posture — The white goose spreads its wings (Figures 14–17)

Movement one: the right toe still touching the ground, with the left heel as the axis, the body turns slightly to the right, facing the southwest diagonal, the two legs still full-left and empty-right. (Figure 14)

图 14
Line drawing (upper left of the page): the man with the two hands as facing upright palms before the chest, the left hand raised and the right hand before the abdomen, the body turned slightly right, the right toe touching the ground. Labelled at its side "Figure 14".

Movement two: the right foot steps forward, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the right leg slightly bent (the two legs still full-left and empty-right). At the same time the right hand lifts from the outside, the palm held crosswise and raised to above the forehead, the palm turned forward; the left hand comes down from the inside, passing before the face as an upright palm, and comes level with the heart (the shoulders must relax and the elbows sink). (Figure 15)

Movement three: the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right sole settles flat, and the two legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the left hand pushes slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the left hand level with the chest and the palm turned slightly forward (the right hand must have the intent of turning upward; the shoulders must relax and the elbows sink). (Figure 16)

Movement four: the right hand extends slightly forward and the elbow hangs down; the two hands fall at the same time; when the two hands come level with the hips (as the two hands fall, the elbows may not stand out behind the back) they part to left and right, arc upward, and the upright palms come together before the chest with the intent of holding a ball, the two hands level with the mouth and the palms turned slightly forward. At the same time as the two hands part left and right, the left foot follows forward to beside the right heel, touching the ground with the toe; facing the right-front diagonal. (Figure 17)

图 15
Line drawing (lower left of the page): the man with the right foot stepped forward and the toe tilted up, the right hand held crosswise above the forehead with the palm forward, the left hand come down past the face to the height of the heart. Labelled at its side "Figure 15".
图 16
Line drawing (lower middle of the page): the man with the right leg bowed forward and the left hand pushing slowly forward level with the chest, the right hand above the forehead. Labelled at its side "Figure 16".
图 17
Line drawing (lower right of the page): the man with the two hands parted left and right before the chest, arcing upward and coming together as upright palms, the left foot having followed to beside the right heel with the toe touching the ground. Labelled at its side "Figure 17".

The requirement is that there be a lively roundness between the hands and the chest; the two legs are still full-right and empty-left.

In practising taijiquan, every movement requires relaxed shoulders and sunk elbows throughout; the reader is asked to bear this firmly in mind, and it will not be repeated below.

Seventh posture — Brush the knee and twist the step (Figures 18–21)

Movement one: the left toe shifts slightly and touches the ground behind to the left; with the right heel as the axis, the body turns 135 degrees to the left, facing due east, the two legs still full-right and empty-left. (Figure 18)

图 18
Line drawing (upper right of the page): the man revolving 135 degrees to the left on the right heel, facing due east, the two hands as upright palms before the chest, the right leg full and the left leg empty. Labelled at its side "Figure 18".

Movement two: the body turns slightly to the left, facing the northeast diagonal. The hands and feet follow the movement: the left foot steps out toward the left diagonal, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the left leg slightly bent, the two legs still full-right and empty-left; the left hand falls to before the abdomen; the right hand rises beside the right cheek, level with the ear, the fingers pointing up and the palm turned forward; facing the northeast diagonal. (Figure 19)

Movement three: the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, the left sole settles flat, the right leg bends slightly, and the two legs become full-left and empty-right. At the same time the left hand brushes downward past the left knee and comes to rest beside the left leg, the fingers pointing forward; the right hand pushes slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the fingers still pointing up, level with the eyes; the face still toward the northeast diagonal. (Figure 20)

图 19
Line drawing (middle left of the page): the man with the left foot stepped out toward the left diagonal, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the left hand fallen to before the abdomen, the right hand raised beside the right cheek, level with the ear, the fingers pointing up and the palm turned forward. Labelled at its side "Figure 19".

Movement four: the right hand falls past the side of the left leg (fingers pointing forward); when it comes level with the left hand, the two hands part to left and right and arc upward, and the upright palms come together before the chest with the intent of holding a ball, the two hands level with the mouth, the palms turned slightly forward; at the same as the two hands part left and right, the right foot in front follows to beside the left heel, touching the ground with the toe, and the two legs are still full-left and empty-right. (Figure 21)

图 20
Line drawing (middle left of the page): the man with the right heel pressing and the left leg bowed forward, the left hand brushed downward past the left knee and set beside the left leg, the right hand pushing slowly forward and level with the eyes; an arc-shaped arrow in the picture marks the direction of the right hand's push and fall. Labelled at its side "Figure 20".
图 21
Line drawing (middle of the page): the man with the two hands joined before the chest as upright palms, the two legs full-left and empty-right, the right foot having followed to beside the left heel with the toe touching the ground. Labelled at its side "Figure 21".
图 22
Line drawing (middle right of the page): the man with the two hands as upright palms before the chest, the right arm bent and held level in front, the left hand fallen to before the abdomen, the right foot in front. Labelled at its side "Figure 22".
Eighth posture — The hand plays the lute (Figure 22)
Ninth posture — Brush the knee and twist the step (Figures 23–26)

The two postures are joined into one section-sequence: movement one is "The hand plays the lute"; movements two, three and four are "Brush the knee and twist the step".

Movement one: the right foot steps back and settles, the toe pointed due east; the left foot draws in before the right and touches the ground with the toe, and the legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the two hands draw in and close with the body, still as upright palms: the left hand still level with the mouth, the right hand fallen to before the abdomen, both palms turned slightly forward; facing the northeast diagonal. (Figure 22)

The requirement is that there be a lively roundness between the hands and the chest.

Movement two: the left foot steps forward, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground. The two hands follow the movement: the left hand falls to before the abdomen, and the right hand rises beside the right cheek (as in the posture of Figure 19). Then the right heel presses, the right leg bends slightly, and the left sole settles flat accordingly, so that the left leg in front becomes the full left leg and the right leg becomes empty. At the same time the left hand brushes downward past the left knee and is set beside the left leg, the fingers pointing forward; the right hand pushes slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the fingers still pointing up, level with the eyes; facing the northeast diagonal. (Figure 23) (with the twisted step)

Then the right foot strides past the left and settles flat and firm outside the left foot, and the two legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the left hand rises level with the mouth and the right hand falls to rest before the chest, the fingers of both hands pointing up and the palms turned slightly forward; the face still toward the northeast diagonal. (Figure 24)

Movement three is the same as the explanation of Figure 23 within movement two of this posture, up to "with the twisted step". (Figure 25)

Movement four is the same as the explanation of movement four, Figure 21, of the seventh posture, "Brush the knee and twist the step". (Figure 26)

图 23
Line drawing (upper right of the page): the man with the right leg bowed forward and the left sole settled flat, the left hand brushed past the left knee and set beside the left leg with the fingers pointing forward, the right hand pushing slowly forward and level with the eyes. Labelled at its side "Figure 23".
图 24
Line drawing (lower left of the page): the man with the right foot striding past the left and settling flat and firm outside the left foot, the two legs full-right and empty-left, the left hand raised level with the mouth, the right hand fallen to rest before the chest, the fingers of both hands pointing up. Labelled at its side "Figure 24".
图 25
Line drawing (lower middle of the page): the man with the two hands as upright palms before the chest, the two legs full-right and empty-left; an arc-shaped arrow in the picture marks the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 25".
图 26
Line drawing (lower right of the page): the man with the two hands joined before the chest as upright palms, the two legs full-right and empty-left, the left foot having followed to beside the right heel with the toe touching the ground. Labelled at its side "Figure 26".
Tenth posture — The hand plays the lute (Figure 27)
Eleventh posture — Step up, deflect and intercept, punch (Figures 28–30)

The two postures are joined into one section-sequence: movement one is "The hand plays the lute"; movements two, three and four are "Step up, deflect and intercept, punch". Movement one is the same as the explanation of movement one of the eighth posture, "The hand plays the lute". (Figure 27)

Movement two: (step up to the left) the left foot still steps out toward the left-front diagonal, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground. The two hands follow the movement: the right hand is raised high above the head to the upper right, the palm turned left, the fingers slightly spread and pointing forward; the left hand falls to before the abdomen, the fingers pointing up and the palm turned right. Immediately the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, the left sole settles flat, and the right leg bends slightly, so that the left leg becomes full and the right leg empty. At the same time the two hands extend forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward); the face still toward the northeast diagonal. (Figure 28)

Movement three: (step up to the right) with the left heel as the axis, the body turns right; the right foot accordingly lifts, passes beside the left foot, and steps out toward the right-front diagonal, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground. At the same time the two hands follow the movement: the left hand is raised high above the head to the upper left, the palm turned right, the fingers slightly spread and pointing up; the right hand comes down past the face and falls straight to before the abdomen, the fingers pointing up and the palm turned left. Immediately the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right sole settles flat, and the left leg bends slightly, so that the two legs become empty-left and full-right. At the same time the two hands extend forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward); facing the southeast diagonal. (Figure 29)

图 27
Line drawing (lower left of the page): the man with the two hands as upright palms before the chest, the right arm bent and held level in front, the left hand fallen to before the abdomen; a downward arrow in the picture marks the direction. Labelled at its side "Figure 27".
图 28
Line drawing (lower middle of the page): the man with the right hand raised high above the head to the upper right, the palm turned left and the fingers pointing forward, the left hand fallen to before the abdomen with the fingers pointing up, the left leg bowed forward and the two hands extending forward. Labelled at its side "Figure 28".
图 29
Line drawing (lower right of the page): the man with the left hand raised high above the head to the upper left, the palm turned right, the right hand fallen to before the abdomen with the fingers pointing up, the right leg bowed forward; an arc-shaped arrow and a horizontal arrow to the right in the picture mark the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 29".

Movement four: (deflect, intercept, punch) the left hand comes down past the face, arcs to the left, scoops up from below, and again rises and falls forward to before the abdomen, the fingers pointing up. The left foot accordingly lifts, passes beside the right foot, and steps out due east, touching the ground first with the heel; the right hand falls to beside the right hip and closes into a fist. Immediately the left sole settles flat, the left leg bows forward, the right foot follows forward and touches with the toe beside the left heel, so that the left leg becomes full and the right leg empty. At the same time the right fist drives slowly forward along the back of the left hand (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the eye of the fist turned up, level with the heart; facing due east. (Figure 30)

图 30
Line drawing (upper right of the page): the man with the left leg bowed forward and the left sole settled flat, the right fist driving forward along the back of the left hand with the eye of the fist turned up and level with the heart, and the right foot having followed to beside the left heel with the toe touching the ground. Labelled at its side "Figure 30".
Twelfth posture — As if sealing, as if closing (Figures 31–34)

Movement one: the left leg does not move; the right foot and right fist shift back at the same time; the right foot withdraws behind the left, the toe pointed toward the right-front diagonal, the right leg slightly bent, the two legs still full-left and empty-right; the right fist is set beside the right hip, the eye of the fist still turned up. At the same time the left hand rises as an upright palm to before the chest, the palm turned right; facing due east. (Figure 31)

图 31
Line drawing (middle left of the page): the man with the left hand raised as an upright palm to before the chest with the palm turned right, the right fist set beside the right hip with the eye of the fist turned up, and the right foot withdrawn behind the left with the toe pointed toward the right-front diagonal. Labelled at its side "Figure 31".

Movement two: the body shifts back, the right leg becomes full, and the left leg draws back with the toe touching before the right foot, so that the left leg becomes empty. At the same time the right fist opens into a palm, rises and joins the left hand, and the two become upright palms drawn in before the chest, both palms turned forward. (Figure 32)

Movement three: the left leg steps forward, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the left leg slightly bent; the legs are still full-right and empty-left. (Figure 33)

图 32
Line drawing (upper left of the page): the man with the two hands drawn in before the chest as upright palms with both palms turned forward, the body shifted back, the right leg full and the left leg empty, the left toe touching before the right foot. Labelled at its side "Figure 32".
图 33
Line drawing (upper middle of the page): the man with the left leg stepped forward and the toe tilted up with the heel touching the ground, the two hands as upright palms before the chest; a horizontal arrow to the right in the picture marks the direction. Labelled at its side "Figure 33".
图 34
Line drawing (upper right of the page): the man with the two hands pushed slowly forward in parallel, level with the chest, the right leg full and the left leg empty, the left toe touching beside the right foot. Labelled at its side "Figure 34".

Movement four: the two hands push slowly forward in parallel, level with the chest (the upper body may not lean forward or backward). At the same time the left leg bows forward and the left sole settles flat, so that the left leg becomes full; the right foot follows forward and touches with the toe beside the left foot, so that the right leg becomes empty (the left heel should have the intent of pressing out); facing due east. (Figure 34)

Thirteenth posture — Embrace the tiger and push the mountain (Figures 35–38)

Movement one: the right foot moves behind and past the left heel to touch the ground on the left side behind the left foot; with the left heel as the axis, the body turns 180 degrees to the right-rear, facing due west, the two legs still full-left and empty-right. (Figure 35)

图 35
Line drawing (left of the page): the man with the right foot moved behind and past the left heel to touch the ground on the left side behind the left foot, the body turned 180 degrees to the right-rear and facing due west, the two hands before the chest. Labelled at its side "Figure 35".

Movement two: the body turns slightly to the right; the hands and feet follow the movement; the right foot steps out toward the right-front diagonal, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the right leg slightly bent, the two legs still full-left and empty-right; the right hand falls to before the abdomen; the left hand rises beside the left cheek, level with the ear, the fingers pointing up and the palm turned forward; facing the northwest diagonal. (Figure 36)

图 36
Line drawing (upper left of the page): the man with the right foot stepped out toward the right-front diagonal, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the right hand fallen to before the abdomen, the left hand raised beside the left cheek, level with the ear, the fingers pointing up and the palm turned forward; a leftward arrow in the picture marks the direction. Labelled at its side "Figure 36".
图 37
Line drawing (upper middle of the page): the man with the right leg bowed forward and the right sole settled flat, the right hand circling downward and outward to the left before the abdomen with the palm toward the chest in the manner of embracing a tiger, and the left hand pushing slowly forward as an upright palm level with the eyes; an arc-shaped arrow in the picture marks the right hand's circling. Labelled at its side "Figure 37".
图 38
Line drawing (upper right of the page): the man with the two hands joined before the chest as upright palms with the intent of holding a ball, the left foot having followed to beside the right heel with the toe touching the ground, the two legs full-right and empty-left. Labelled at its side "Figure 38".

Movement three: the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right sole settles flat, and the legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the right hand circles downward and outward to the left before the abdomen and closes into a fist at the right of the abdomen, the palm toward the chest, the right arm in the manner of embracing a tiger; the left hand pushes slowly forward as an upright palm (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the left hand level with the eyes; facing the northwest diagonal. (Figure 37)

Movement four: the right fist, its centre turned down, moves downward and opens into a palm past the side of the right leg; the left hand accordingly falls with its palm turned down; when the two hands have descended to the same level, the two hands part to left and right at the same time and arc upward, and the upright palms come together before the chest with the intent of holding a ball, the two hands level with the mouth, the two palms turned slightly forward. At the same time as the two hands part left and right, the left foot follows forward to beside the right heel, touching the ground with the toe, and the two legs are still full-right and empty-left. (Figure 38)

The requirement is that there be a lively roundness between the hands and the chest and arms.

Fourteenth posture — The hand plays the lute (Figures 39–40)
Fifteenth posture — Right lazy tie the garment (Figures 41–42)

The two postures are joined into one section-sequence: movements one and two are "The hand plays the lute"; movements three and four are "Right lazy tie the garment". Movement one: the left foot steps back and settles, the toe pointed toward the southwest diagonal; the right foot draws in before the left and touches the ground with the toe, and the two legs become full-left and empty-right. The two hands turn left with the body, and the upright palms are drawn in before the chest: the right hand still level with the mouth, the left hand fallen to before the abdomen, both palms turned slightly forward; facing due west. (Figure 39)

图 39
Line drawing (upper left of the page): the man with the two hands drawn in before the chest as upright palms, the right hand level with the mouth and the left hand fallen to before the abdomen, the right foot drawn in before the left and touching the ground with the toe, the two legs full-left and empty-right. Labelled at its side "Figure 39".

The requirement is that there be a lively roundness between the hands and the chest and arms.

Movement two: the right foot steps forward, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the right leg slightly bent, the two legs still full-left and empty-right. (Figure 40)

Movements three and four are the same as movements three and four of the third posture, "Right grasp and tie the garment", except that the direction differs slightly: this posture faces due west. (Figures 41–42)

图 40
Line drawing (lower left of the page): the man with the right foot stepped forward, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the two hands as upright palms before the chest; a horizontal arrow to the left in the picture marks the direction. Labelled at its side "Figure 40".

Line drawing (lower middle of the page): the man with the right leg bowed forward and the two hands pushing slowly forward; an arc-shaped arrow and a downward arrow in the picture mark the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 41".
图 42
Line drawing (lower right of the page): the man with the two hands joined before the chest as upright palms with the intent of holding a ball, the left foot having followed to beside the right heel with the toe touching the ground. Labelled at its side "Figure 42".
Sixteenth posture — Single whip (Figures 43–45)
Seventeenth posture — Raise the hand and lift the posture (Figure 46)

The two postures are joined into one section-sequence: movements one, two and three are "Single whip"; movement four is "Raise the hand and lift the posture".

Movement one: the left foot lifts and moves to touch the ground on the left side behind the right foot; with the right heel as the axis, the body turns 135 degrees to the left-rear, facing a diagonal slightly east of south, the two legs still full-right and empty-left. (Figure 43)

图 43
Line drawing (upper right of the page): the man revolving 135 degrees to the left-rear on the right heel and facing a diagonal slightly east of south, the two hands joined before the chest as upright palms, the left foot moved to touch the ground on the left side behind the right foot, the two legs full-right and empty-left. Labelled at its side "Figure 43".

Movements two and three are the same as movements two and three of the fourth posture, "Single whip". (Figures 44–45)

Movement four is the same as the movement of the fifth posture, "Raise the hand and lift the posture" — that is, the same as movement four of the joined fourth and fifth postures. (Figure 45)

图 44
Line drawing (lower left of the page): the man with the two hands as upright palms before the chest with the fingers pointing up, and the right arm bent and held level in front; a horizontal arrow to the right in the picture marks the direction. Labelled at its side "Figure 44".
图 45
Line drawing (lower middle of the page): the man with the right arm bent and held crosswise before the forehead and the left hand as an upright palm before the chest, the right leg bowed forward; an arc-shaped arrow in the picture marks the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 45".
图 46
Line drawing (lower right of the page): the man with the left hand raised above the forehead with the palm up, the right hand before the chest, and a downward arrow below the right hand marking the direction. Labelled at its side "Figure 46".
Eighteenth posture — Watch the punch from beneath the elbow (Figures 47–50)

Movement one: the right foot steps forward, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground; the left leg is still full and the right leg empty. At the same time the right hand rises to before the chest, the fingers pointing up and the palm turned slightly forward. (Figure 47)

Movement two: the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right sole settles flat, and the left leg bends slightly, so that the right leg becomes full and the left leg empty. At the same time the right hand pushes slowly out from before the chest (the upper body may not lean forward or backward); facing due south. (Figure 48)

Movement three: the left leg does not move; the right toe turns 90 degrees to the left and the waist revolves slightly to the left, toward due east, the two legs still full-right and empty-left. (Figure 49)

Movement four: the two hands close into fists and the body turns left toward due east. At the same time the right fist circles beneath the left elbow with the eye of the fist turned inward; the left forearm straightens upright accordingly, the fist level with the crown of the head and the eye of the fist turned left (the two arms forming a right angle). At the same time as the body turns left, the left foot draws close beside the right heel, the heel lifted and the toe touching the ground, the two legs still full-right and empty-left. (Figure 50)

图 47
Line drawing (middle left of the page): the man with the right foot stepped forward, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the right hand raised to before the chest with the fingers pointing up and the palm turned slightly forward, and the left fist at the waist. Labelled at its side "Figure 47".

Line drawing (middle, slightly left, of the page): the man with the right leg bowed forward and the right hand pushing slowly out from before the chest, the left fist at the waist. Labelled at its side "Figure 48".

Labelled at its side "Figure 50".
Nineteenth posture — Left push back the monkey (Figures 51–54)

Movement one: the two fists open into upright palms, the fingers pointing up and the palms turned outward, parted left and right, level with the shoulders. The left foot shifts slightly back and touches the ground; with the right heel as the axis, the body turns 90 degrees to the left and the right leg sits full, the two legs still full-right and empty-left; facing due north. At the same time the two hands come together facing each other before the chest with the intent of holding a ball, level with the mouth. (Figure 51)

The requirement is that there be a lively roundness between the hands and the chest and arms. Movements two, three and four are the same as movements two, three and four of the seventh posture, "Brush the knee and twist the step", except that the direction and angle differ: this posture is toward due west. (Figures 52–54)

图 51
Line drawing (upper left of the page): the man with his back to the reader, the two fists opened into upright palms with the palms turned outward and parted left and right level with the shoulders, the left foot shifted slightly back and touching the ground, and the body turned 90 degrees left to face due north. Labelled at its side "Figure 51".
图 52
Line drawing (upper middle, slightly left, of the page): the man with his back to the reader, the left foot stepped forward with the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the left hand fallen to before the abdomen, and the right hand raised beside the right cheek. Labelled at its side "Figure 52".
图 53
Line drawing (upper middle, slightly right, of the page): the man with his back to the reader, the right leg bowed forward, the left hand brushed past the left knee and set beside the left leg, and the right hand pushing slowly forward level with the eyes; an arc-shaped arrow in the picture marks the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 53".
图 54
Line drawing (upper right of the page): the man with his back to the reader, the two hands joined before the chest as upright palms, and the right foot having followed to beside the left heel with the toe touching the ground. Labelled at its side "Figure 54".
Twentieth posture — Right push back the monkey (Figures 55–58)

Movement one: the right foot lifts and moves behind the left foot to touch the ground with the toe on the left side of the left heel; with the left heel as the axis, the body turns 225 degrees to the right-rear, facing due south, the two legs still full-left and empty-right. (Figure 55)

图 55
Line drawing (middle right of the page): the man revolving 225 degrees to the right-rear on the left heel and facing due south, the two hands as upright palms before the chest, the right foot moved behind the left foot to touch the ground with the toe on the left side of the left heel, the two legs full-left and empty-right. Labelled at its side "Figure 55".

Movement two: the body turns slightly to the right; the hands and feet follow the movement; the right foot steps out toward the right-front diagonal, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the right leg slightly bent, the two legs still full-left and empty-right; the right hand falls to before the abdomen; the left hand rises beside the left cheek, level with the ear, the fingers pointing up and the palm turned outward; facing the southwest diagonal. (Figure 56)

Movement three: the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right sole settles flat, the left leg bends slightly, and the legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the right hand brushes downward past the right knee and is set beside the right leg, the fingers pointing forward; the left hand pushes slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the fingers still pointing up, level with the eyes. (Figure 57)

Movement four: the left hand falls past the side of the right leg (the fingers pointing forward); when it comes level with the right hand, the two hands part left and right and arc upward, and the upright palms come together before the chest with the intent of holding a ball, the two hands level with the mouth, the palms turned slightly forward. At the same time as the two hands part left and right, the left foot follows forward to beside the right heel, touching the ground with the toe, and the two legs are still full-right and empty-left. (Figure 58)

Twenty-first posture — Left push back the monkey (Figures 59–62)

Movement one: the left foot lifts and moves behind the right foot to the right side of the right heel, touching the ground with the toe; with the right heel as the axis, the body turns 225 degrees to the left-rear, facing due north, the two legs still full-right and empty-left. (Figure 59)

Movements two, three and four are the same as movements two, three and four of the seventh posture, "Brush the knee and twist the step", except that the direction and angle differ: this posture is toward the northwest. (Figures 60–62)

Twenty-fourth posture — The white goose spreads its wings (Figures 68–70)

The two postures are joined into one section-sequence: movement one is "The hand plays the lute"; movements two, three and four are "The white goose spreads its wings".

Labelled at its side "Figure 66".

Movement one: the left foot steps back and settles, the toe pointed due south; the right foot draws in before the left and touches the ground with the toe, so that the left leg becomes full and the right leg empty. At the same time the two hands draw back with the body as upright palms: the right hand is drawn in before the chest, level with the mouth, and the left hand falls to before the abdomen, both palms turned slightly forward; facing the southwest diagonal. (Figure 67)

The requirement is that there be a lively roundness between the hands and the chest and arms.

Movement two: the right foot steps forward, the toe tilted up and the heel touching the ground, the right leg slightly bent, the two legs still full-left and empty-right. At the same time the right hand is raised above the forehead, the palm held crosswise and turned forward; the left hand moves to before the heart, the fingers pointing up. (Figure 68)

Movements three and four are the same as movements three and four of the sixth posture, "The white goose spreads its wings". (Figures 69–70)

Movements one, two, three and four are the same as the four movements of the seventh posture, "Brush the knee and twist the step". (Figures 71–74)
