Labelled at its side "Figure 76".

Movement one: the right foot steps back and settles, the toe pointed toward the southeast diagonal; the left foot draws in before the right and touches the ground with the toe, and the two legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the two hands turn right with the body and draw in before the chest as upright palms: the left hand still level with the mouth, the right hand fallen to before the abdomen, both palms turned slightly forward; facing due east. (Figure 75)

The requirement is that there be a lively roundness between the hands and the chest and arms.

Movement two: the right hand turns upward and circles up to the right; when it reaches before the face the palm is turned down; at the same time the left hand (its palm turned down) arcs from before the chest down and to the left to beside the left leg; then the two hands press straight down. The upper body bends forward and, following the momentum, sinks slightly. The fingers of the left hand point forward and are set to the left of the left shin; the fingers of the right hand point left and are set before the two legs. (Figure 76)

The requirement is that when the body bends forward the head still be upright and pointed forward, the two arms slightly bent, and the two legs still full-right and empty-left.

Movement three: the upper body straightens up; the two arms rise accordingly. The right hand is above the crown of the head, the palm turned slightly forward, the fingers pointing left; the left hand is held as an upright palm before the chest, the fingers pointing up, the palm turned slightly forward. At the same time the left foot steps forward, the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, the left sole settles flat, the left toe points due east, the right leg bends slightly, and the two legs become full-left and empty-right; the left hand pushes slowly forward accordingly (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the hand level with the chest. (Figure 77)

Movement four: with the left heel as the axis, the left toe turns 135 degrees to the right and settles, the body bows to the right-rear, and the right toe tilts up accordingly. At the same time the left hand rises above the crown of the head, the heart turned slightly forward and the fingers pointing right; the right hand falls accordingly and becomes an upright palm set before the chest, the fingers pointing up and the palm turned slightly forward; the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right sole settles flat, the left leg bends slightly, and the two legs become full-right and empty-left. The right hand then pushes slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), level with the chest; facing due west. (Figure 78)

Thirtieth posture — Three Yong-shan peaks (Figures 79–82)

Movement one: the right foot steps back one long pace and settles, the toe pointed toward the right-front diagonal; the left leg draws back, touching with the toe before the right foot, and the two legs still become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the two hands are drawn in before the chest as upright palms, the left high and the right low, the left hand level with the mouth, both palms turned slightly forward; facing due west. (Figure 79)

Movement two: the left foot steps forward, touching first with the heel; then the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, the left sole settles flat, the right leg bends slightly, so that the left leg becomes full and the right leg empty. At the same time the two hands push slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), both palms still turned slightly forward, the left hand level with the eyes and the right hand level with the chest. (Figure 80)

Movement three: the left toe turns slightly outward, and the left leg sits full; the right foot steps forward one long pace, touching first with the heel; then the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, and the right sole settles flat, the right toe pointing straight ahead, the right leg bends slightly, and the legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the right hand arcs upward, level with the eyebrows; the left hand arcs downward, level with the heart; and as the right leg bows forward the two hands push slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), both palms still turned slightly forward, the right hand level with the eyes and the left hand level with the chest. (Figure 81)

Movement four is the same as movement four of the third posture, "Right grasp and tie the garment", except that the direction and angle differ: this posture faces due west. (Figure 82)

Thirty-second posture — Lower the posture (Figure 86)

The two postures are joined into one section-sequence: movements one, two and three are "Single whip"; movement four is "Lower the posture".

Movement one is the same as movement one of the sixteenth posture, "Single whip". (Figure 83)

Movements two and three are the same as movements two and three of the fourth posture, "Single whip". (Figures 84–85)

At the same time the left hand falls to before the abdomen, the left arm slightly bent, the fingers pointing forward; the right hand rises level with the crown of the head, the palm turned up; facing due east, with the upper body leaning slightly toward south. (Figure 86)

Movement one: the left foot steps forward, the toe pointing toward the left corner, touching the ground with the heel; the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, the left sole settles flat, and the two legs become full-left and empty-right. Movement two: with the left heel as the axis, the body turns right and the left toe accordingly turns inward 90 degrees, sitting the left leg full. (Figure 88)

Movement three: the right toe turns inward about 90 degrees and settles, sitting the right leg full, and at the same time the body turns left; the left foot steps out to the left, touching first with the heel; then the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, the left sole settles flat with the toe pointing toward the left corner, and the two legs still become full-left and empty-right. At the same time the left hand moves upward past the abdomen and the right hand arcs from the right downward; the left hand is raised to before the forehead, level with the head, the palm turned slightly forward, and the right hand falls and scoops up to the left to before the abdomen, the palm turned slightly down, the two hands facing each other above and below; facing the southeast diagonal. (Figure 89)

Movement four is the same as movement two of this posture. (Figure 90)

Thirty-fourth posture — Single whip (Figure 91)
Thirty-fifth posture — Raise the hand and lift the posture (Figures 92–93)
Thirty-sixth posture — High pat the horse (Figure 94)

Three postures are joined into one section-sequence: movement one is "Single whip"; movements two and three are "Raise the hand and lift the posture"; movement four is "High pat the horse".

Movement one: the right toe turns inward about 90 degrees and settles; the right leg sits full, and at the same time the body turns left; the left foot steps out to the left, touching first with the heel; then the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, the left sole settles flat with the toe pointing toward the left corner, and the two legs still become full-left and empty-right. At the same time the left hand rises and the right hand falls, both becoming upright palms; when the two hands come level with the mouth they part to left and right, the left hand level with the eyes and the right hand level with the mouth; facing a diagonal slightly east of south. (Figure 91)

Movement two: the right foot lifts, passes along the inner side of the left foot, and steps forward, touching first with the heel; then the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right sole settles flat with the toe pointing ahead, the left leg bends slightly, and the legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the body turns slightly right. The two hands follow the movement: the right hand moves from the right downward and scoops to the left to before the abdomen, the fingers pointing forward; the left hand rises, the palm turned up, with the intent of lifting upward, level with the crown. As the right leg bows forward, the right hand pushes slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the right hand level with the chest; facing due south. (Figure 92)

Labelled at its side "Figure 91".

Movement three: the right toe turns inward about 45 degrees, pointing toward the southeast diagonal, and at the same time the waist revolves slightly left, sitting the right leg full; the two legs are still full-right and empty-left. (Figure 93)

图 92
Line drawing (lower left of the page): the man with the left hand raised level with the crown and the palm turned up, and the right hand scooping to the left before the abdomen; an arc-shaped arrow in the picture marks the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 92".

Labelled at its side "Figure 93".

Line drawing (lower right of the page): the man with the two hands as upright palms before the chest; arcs and arrows in the picture mark the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 94".

Movement four: the left hand arcs from the front downward and inward to before the abdomen, the palm turned up and the fingers pointing right; the right hand accordingly draws in near the right hip, then rubs and presses toward the chest, the palm turned down, level with the chest, facing the left hand above and below (both arms forming a half-circle). At the same time the body continues to turn left, facing due east. At the same time the left foot shifts close beside the right, touching the ground with the toe, and the two legs are still full-right and empty-left. (Figure 94)

Thirty-seventh posture — Left subdue the tiger (Figures 95–96)
Thirty-eighth posture — Right kick (Figures 97–98)

The two postures are joined into one section-sequence: movements one and two are "Left subdue the tiger"; movements three and four are "Right kick".

图 95
Line drawing (right of the page): the man with the left hand raised above the crown of the head in a fist and the right fist resting before the abdomen, the left foot stepped out toward the left-front diagonal touching first with the heel, the left leg bowed forward. Labelled at its side "Figure 95".
图 96
Line drawing (lower left of the page): the man with the body turned slightly left, the two hands closed into fists with the eyes of the fists facing each other above and below, the left leg bowed forward and the right leg behind; a rightward arrow in the picture marks the direction. Labelled at its side "Figure 96".
图 97
Line drawing (lower middle of the page): the man with the right foot lifted and kicking forward, the two hands before the chest; a leftward arrow in the picture marks the direction. Labelled at its side "Figure 97".
图 98
Line drawing (lower right of the page): the man with the two hands before the chest and the two fists facing each other above and below, the right foot lifted; a circular arc in the picture marks the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 98".

Movement one: the body turns slightly to the left; the left foot steps out toward the left-front diagonal, touching first with the heel; the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, the left sole settles flat, so that the left leg becomes full and the right leg empty. As the left leg bows forward the two hands follow the movement: the left hand rises along the left leg and forward and up past the face, above the crown of the head; the right hand drops from before the chest outward and downward and the forearm rotates outward, coming to rest before the abdomen; the two hands close into fists at the same time, the eyes of the fists facing each other above and below, and as the fists close the body turns to the right. (Figure 95) Movement two: the whole weight shifts onto the left leg; the right foot lifts and touches forward with the toe beside the left foot. (Figure 96)

Movement three: the right leg lifts and the right toe kicks out to the right, level with the knee. At the same time the right fist rises and the left fist falls; when the two fists come level with the eyebrows both become upright palms and part to left and right, the right high and the left slightly lower, the right hand level with the eyebrows, the right arm in line with the right leg; the left leg bends slightly. (Figure 97)

Movement four: the left and right hands come together before the chest. At the same time the right leg does not move; the right shin hangs down, the toe pointing down, the heel near the left knee; facing the right-front diagonal. (Figure 98)

Line drawing (middle left of the page): the man with the left hand raised above the forehead and the right hand before the chest, the right leg lifted with the toe pointing down and the heel near the left knee. Labelled at its side "Figure 99".
Thirty-ninth posture — Right subdue the tiger (Figures 99–100)
Fortieth posture — Left kick (Figures 101–102)
图 100
Line drawing (lower left of the page): the man with the left hand raised above the forehead and the right fist at the abdomen, the right toe touching beside the left foot; a leftward arc-shaped arrow in the picture marks the direction. Labelled at its side "Figure 100".

Line drawing (lower middle of the page): the man with the left leg slightly bent and the right leg lifted and kicking out to the left level with the knee, the two hands as upright palms before the chest parting left and right; a downward arc-shaped arrow in the picture marks the direction. Labelled at its side "Figure 101".

Line drawing (lower right of the page): the man with the right leg lifted, the toe pointing down and the heel near the left knee, the two hands joined before the chest; an arc-shaped arrow in the picture marks the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 102".

The two postures are joined into one section-sequence: movement one, movement two is "Right subdue the tiger"; movements three and four are "Left kick".

Movements one, two, three and four are the same as the explanation of the four movements of the thirty-seventh posture, "Left subdue the tiger", joined with the thirty-eighth posture, "Right kick", except that left and right are reversed and the direction differs slightly: this posture's heel-push is toward the northeast diagonal. (Figures 99–102)

Forty-first posture — Turn the body and push with the heel (Figures 103–104)
Forty-second posture — Single whip (Figure 105)
Forty-third posture — Tread the step and strike a blow (Figure 106)

Three postures are joined into one section-sequence: movements one and two are "Turn the body and push with the heel"; movement three is "Single whip"; movement four is "Tread the step and strike a blow".

Movement one: with the right heel as the axis, the body turns 180 degrees to the left-rear; facing due west. (Figure 103)

图 103
Line drawing (middle right of the page): the man revolving 180 degrees to the left-rear on the right heel and facing due west, the two hands before the chest, the left foot lifted; a horizontal arrow to the left in the picture marks the direction. Labelled at its side "Figure 103".

Movement two: the left toe tilts up and pushes forward with the heel, level with the knee, the right leg slightly bent. At the same time the two hands part left and right as upright palms, the left high and the right slightly lower, the left hand level with the shoulder, the left arm in line with the left leg; facing due west; the weight is still on the right leg, which bends slightly. (Figure 104)

Movement three: the left leg falls straight down, touching first with the heel, and at the same time the two hands come together before the chest. Then the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, and the left sole settles flat and becomes full; as the left leg bows forward, the two hands part to left and right following the leg, forming the single-whip posture. (Figure 105)

Movement four: the left hand falls past the left hip, arcs up to the left and forward and down, and is still drawn back to beside the hip (without pausing), the palm turned down. At the same time the right hand rises past the right ear, arcs forward and down and back, and is still drawn back beside the right ear (without pausing) and closes into a fist, the eye of the fist turned left. As the two hands circle, the right foot steps up, the sole settling flat beside the left foot; then the left foot steps forward and settles, the toe pointing west; the right foot follows forward and touches with the toe behind the left foot, so that the left leg becomes full and the right leg empty; the upper body bends forward and, following the momentum, sinks slightly. At the same time as the body bends forward and sinks, the right fist drives down and forward past the chest from beside the ear, the centre of the fist turned inward, set before the two legs; at the same time the left palm presses down from beside the hip, the fingers pointing forward, set to the left of the shin. (Figure 106)

The requirement: when the body bends forward and sinks, the head must still be upright and the eyes look forward. The two arms must be slightly bent.

图 104

Forty-fourth posture — Turn the body over, second rise (Figures 107–108)
Forty-fifth posture — Drape the body (Figures 109–110)

The two postures are joined into one section-sequence: movements one and two are "Turn the body over, second rise"; movements three and four are "Drape the body".

Line drawing (upper middle of the page): the man with the left leg bowed forward and the left sole settled flat, the left hand level with the mouth and the right hand level with the chest, the two hands pushing slowly forward; an arc-shaped arrow in the picture marks the direction of the hands. 图 108乙
Line drawing (upper right of the page): the man with the right leg lifted and the right toe kicking forward level with the knee, the two hands parted left and right with the right high and the left slightly lower, the right hand level with the shoulder; an arc-shaped arrow in the picture marks the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 108 乙".

Movement one: with the left heel as the axis, the body flips over to the right-rear, and the left toe accordingly turns 135 degrees to the right, sitting the left leg full. At the same time the right fist rises with the turn of the body, passes before the face, and falls to the right-rear, becoming an upright palm before the chest; the left hand likewise rises as an upright palm to before the chest, the two hands right high and left low. The right leg turns with the body toward due east, and the right foot steps forward, touching first with the heel (as in the right lazy-tie-the-garment posture). The left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right sole settles flat, the left leg bends slightly, and the legs become full-right and empty-left; the two hands push slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward); facing due east. (Figure 107)

Movement two: the right toe turns slightly outward and settles; the left foot steps forward one long pace, touching first with the heel; then the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, and the left sole settles flat and becomes full. At the same time the two hands, before the chest, circle with the left hand moving up and the right hand moving down; when the left hand comes level with the mouth and the right hand level with the chest, they push slowly forward as the left leg bows forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward). (Figure 108 甲) Then the left toe turns slightly outward and settles, the whole weight shifts onto the left leg, the right leg lifts and the right toe kicks forward, level with the knee, the left leg bending slightly; at the same time the two hands part left and right, the right high and the left slightly lower, the right hand level with the shoulder, the right arm in line with the right leg, and the right hand having the intent of slapping the top of the right foot; facing due east. (Figure 108 乙) Movement three: the right leg falls; the right foot passes behind the left heel and settles flat on the left side behind the left heel, the two legs full-right and empty-left. At the same time the two hands draw in before the chest, the right hand level with the mouth and the left hand level with the chest. (Figure 109 甲) Then the left foot steps back one pace, the toe pointing toward the left-front diagonal, the left leg slightly bent, still empty-left and full-right; at the same time the two hands shift back with the retreating step. The weight shifts back, sitting the left leg full, and the right toe tilts up, so that the legs become full-left and empty-right; at the same time the two hands move from the front downward, drawing back in an arc before the chest. Then the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right sole settles flat, and the legs still become full-right and empty-left; at the same time the two hands push slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the right hand level with the eyes and the left hand level with the chest; facing due east. (Figure 109 乙)

Labelled at its side "Figure 109 甲".
图 109乙
Line drawing (lower middle of the page): the man with the right leg bowed forward and the right sole settled flat, the two hands pushing slowly forward with the right hand level with the eyes and the left hand level with the chest; an arc-shaped arrow in the picture marks the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 109 乙".

Labelled at its side "Figure 110".

Movement four: the right leg draws back and touches with the toe before the left foot, and the body shifts back, so that the left leg becomes full and the right leg empty; the two hands shift back with the body and close into fists, the left fist set before the abdomen and the right fist level with the chest, the centres of the fists facing each other above and below and both arms forming a half-circle; facing due east. (Figure 110)

Labelled at its side "Figure 111".

Labelled at its side "Figure 112".
Forty-eighth posture — Step up, deflect and intercept, punch (Figure 115)

Three postures are joined into one section-sequence: movements one and two are "Step back and kick"; movement three is "Turn the body and push with the heel"; movement four is "Step up, deflect and intercept, punch".

Movement one: the right foot withdraws behind the left and settles, the toe pointed toward the right-front diagonal; the weight shifts back, the left leg draws in with the toe touching before the right foot, so that the right leg becomes full and the left leg empty. At the same time the two fists shift back with the body: the left circles up and the right circles down, the left fist level with the chest and the right fist set before the abdomen, the centres of the fists facing each other above and below and both arms forming a half-circle; facing due east. (Figure 111)

Movement two: the whole weight shifts onto the right leg, which bends slightly; the left leg lifts and the left toe kicks forward, level with the knee. At the same time the two fists open into upright palms parted left and right, the left high and the right slightly lower, the left hand level with the shoulder, the left arm in line with the left leg; facing due east. (Figure 112)

Movement three: the left leg does not move; the shin hangs down, the toe pointing down; with the right heel as the axis, the body and the right toe turn about 270 degrees to the right-rear, and then the left foot settles flat to the north (slightly toward east), the right leg bending slightly and becoming empty. Before the turn, the two hands draw in as upright palms to before the chest above the left leg as the body revolves; when the left foot lands, the left and right palms turn down, the two hands with the intent of pressing down, the fingers pointing forward, the two arms slightly bent; facing the northeast diagonal. (Figure 113) Then the whole weight shifts onto the left leg, and the two hands and the right leg lift together; the right toe tilts up and pushes forward with the heel, level with the knee, the two legs bending slightly. At the same time the two hands part left and right as upright palms, the right high and the left slightly lower, the right hand level with the shoulder, the right arm in line with the right leg; facing due east. (Figure 114)

Labelled at its side "Figure 113".

Labelled at its side "Figure 114".

Labelled at its side "Figure 116".

Movement four: the right leg falls forward and the right foot settles beside the left heel; the left foot steps forward and up, and the left leg then bows forward and becomes full; the right foot follows forward, touching with the toe beside the left heel, and the legs still become full-left and empty-right. As the right foot steps up, the left hand arcs up and forward and falls to before the chest, and the right hand falls beside the right hip and closes into a fist. As the right foot follows, the right fist drives slowly forward along the back of the left hand (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the eye of the fist turned up, level with the heart; facing due east. (Figure 115)

Fifty-fifth posture — The wild horse parts its mane (Figures 132–135)

Movement one: the left foot steps up toward the southwest diagonal. At the same time the left hand arcs from before the abdomen up and to the right, rising to before the forehead level with the crown, the palm turned outward; the right hand arcs down and scoops up to the left to before the abdomen, the fingers pointing up. As the two hands arc, the right foot follows forward and touches with the toe beside the left heel, so that the legs become full-left and empty-right; facing the southwest diagonal. (Figure 132)

Movement two: the right foot steps up toward the northwest diagonal and the body turns right. At the same time the right hand arcs from before the abdomen up and to the left, rising to before the forehead level with the crown, the palm turned outward; the left hand arcs down and scoops up to the right to before the abdomen, the fingers pointing up. As the two hands arc, the left foot follows forward and touches with the toe beside the right heel, so that the legs become full-right and empty-left; facing the northwest diagonal. (Figure 133)

Movement three: the same as the explanation of movement one of this posture, except that after the left foot steps up the body turns slightly to the left. (Figure 134)

Movement four: the right foot steps up toward due west. At the same time the left hand arcs downward and the right hand rises from before the abdomen, the two hands becoming upright palms as in the right lazy-tie-the-garment posture. Then the two hands push slowly forward, the left hand inside and level with the chest, the right hand outside and level with the eyes; the left foot accordingly follows forward and touches with the toe behind the right heel, so that the legs become full-right and empty-left; facing due west. (Figure 135)

Fifty-sixth posture — Single whip (Figures 135–139)

Movement one: the left toe shifts back to the left and touches the ground; with the right heel as the axis, the body and the right toe turn 135 degrees to the left, facing the southeast diagonal, still with the right leg full and the left leg empty. At the same time the left hand circles down, to the left and up, and joins the right hand before the chest, the two hands still as upright palms, level with the mouth. (Figure 136)

Movements two and three are the same as movements two and three of the fourth posture, "Single whip". (Figures 137–138)

Fifty-seventh posture — The jade maiden works the shuttle (Figures 140–143)

Movement one: the right leg bows forward and the weight shifts onto the right leg; the left foot then steps up toward the southwest diagonal and the right foot immediately follows forward, touching with the toe beside the left heel, so that the left leg becomes full and the right leg empty. At the same time the left hand falls, circles forward and up, and is lifted past the face to above the forehead, the fingers pointing right; the right hand rises slightly and, as the body shifts forward and the right foot follows, pushes slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward); facing the southwest diagonal. (Figure 140)

Movement two: the right foot lifts, passes behind the left foot to the left side of the left heel, and touches the ground with the toe; with the left heel as the axis, the body and the left toe bend back to the right at the same time; then the right foot steps up and settles toward the southeast diagonal, the left foot follows forward and touches with the toe beside the right heel, so that the right leg becomes full and the left leg empty. At the same time as the body turns and the foot steps up, the left hand arcs down and the right hand arcs up; the right hand is lifted past the face and set above the forehead, the fingers pointing left; the left hand falls to before the chest. As the body shifts forward and the left foot follows, the two hands push the mountain forward slowly (the upper body may not lean forward or backward); facing the southeast diagonal. (Figure 141)

Movement three: the left foot steps up and settles toward the northeast diagonal, the right foot follows forward and touches with the toe beside the left heel, so that the legs become full-left and empty-right. At the same time the left hand arcs up, is lifted past the face, and is set above the forehead with the fingers pointing right; the right hand falls to before the chest. As the body shifts forward and the right foot follows, the two hands push slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward); facing the northeast diagonal. (Figure 142)

Movement one: the left foot falls and touches with the toe behind the right heel; the two hands become upright palms parted left and right, level with the shoulders; with the right heel as the axis, the body and the right toe turn 90 degrees to the left, sitting the right leg full; as the body turns the two hands come to face each other and join before the chest with the intent of holding a ball, level with the mouth. (Figure 160)

The requirement is relaxed shoulders and sunk elbows, with a lively roundness between the hands and the chest and arms, and the two legs must be empty-left and full-right.

图 205
Line drawing (middle left of the page): the man revolving to the right-rear on the left heel with the left toe turned 135 degrees to the right and settled, the right toe tilted up and the right leg lifted and arcing forward as the body turns, and the two hands parted left and right as upright palms with the fingers pointing up, level with the shoulders; a circular arc in the picture marks the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 205".

Movement one: the left foot steps out due east, touching first with the heel; the right heel presses, the left leg bows forward, the left sole settles flat, the right leg bends slightly, and the two legs become full-left and empty-right. The left hand passes in front of the right hand (its palm turning down), rises and is lifted past the face (the palm turning up as it lifts), and is set above the forehead, the fingers pointing right; the right elbow hangs down, and the right hand becomes an upright palm and pushes slowly forward as the left leg bows forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the right hand level with the chest; facing due east. (Figure 204)

Movement two: with the left heel as the axis, the body turns to the right-rear and the left toe turns 135 degrees to the right and settles, the whole weight shifting onto the left leg; the right toe tilts up and the right leg lifts, arcing forward from the left as the body turns, the sole facing forward and level with the knee, the two legs bending slightly. At the same time as the turn, the left hand drops from the front to the outside of the right hand and crosses it before the chest, forming the shape of a cross. As the right leg lifts and arcs, the two hands part left and right as upright palms with the fingers pointing up, level with the shoulders; facing due west. (Figure 205)

Movement three: the right sole settles flat beside the left foot; the left foot steps forward and up, the toe pointing toward the left-front diagonal, the left leg bows forward, and the right foot then follows forward, touching with the toe beside the left foot, the two legs still becoming full-left and empty-right. As the left foot steps up, the left hand brushes down past the chest and the left knee and is set beside the left leg with the fingers pointing forward; the right hand at the same time falls beside the right hip and closes into a fist, the centre of the fist turned down, and as the right foot follows it drives slowly forward and down, the right fist level with the chest and the two arms slightly bent; the body at the same time leans slightly forward; facing due west. (Figure 206)

Movement four: the right foot steps forward and up. At the same time the right fist opens; the two hands straighten with the upper body into upright palms and rise to before the chest, the right hand high and the left low, and push slowly forward (the upper body may not lean forward or backward), the palms turned slightly forward, the right hand level with the eyes and the left hand level with the chest. As the two hands push forward the left foot follows forward, touching with the toe behind the right heel, and the two legs become full-right and empty-left; the face still toward due west. (Figure 207)

Five postures are joined into one section-sequence: movement one is "Step up to seven stars"; movement two is "Step back and bestride the tiger"; movement three is "Turn the foot and swing the lotus" and "Bend the bow and shoot the tiger"; movement four is "Double embracing punch".

Movement one: the left foot steps forward, the toe pointing straight ahead, sitting the left leg full; the body turns slightly right; the right foot follows forward and touches with the toe beside the left heel, so that the two legs become full-left and empty-right. At the same time the right hand moves down to the right past the hip and scoops forward, and together with the left hand rises to before the chest; the two hands cross, level with the mouth, the fingers pointing up, the right hand outside, the backs of the hands facing each other; the face toward due east. (Figure 212)

Movement two: the right foot steps back and settles, the toe pointed toward the right-front diagonal; the left foot draws back and touches with the toe before the right foot, so that the two legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the two hands follow the movement: the right hand parts to the upper right and the left hand to the lower left; the right hand is held as an upright palm circling before the right of the head, level with the crown, and the left hand, its palm turned down and the fingers pointing forward, is set before the left hip, the two arms bent; facing due east. (Figure 213)

图 213
Line drawing (middle right of the page): the man with the right hand held as an upright palm circling before the right of the head, level with the crown, and the left hand, its palm turned down and the fingers pointing forward, set before the left hip, the left toe touching before the right foot, the two legs full-right and empty-left; a circular arc in the picture marks the direction of the hands. Labelled at its side "Figure 213".

Movement three: (turn the foot and swing the lotus) the left foot lifts (level with the knee, the toe pointing down) and swings out to the right; following the momentum, with the right sole as the axis, the body turns to the right-rear, and the left foot falls at the northeast diagonal and settles; the right foot then lifts, passes before the left leg, rises and swings crosswise to the right. The two hands remain as they were during the turn; when the right foot swings up, the left hand rises to the upper right corner level with the right hand, and then the two hands (left first, then right) come down from above to meet and slap the top of the right foot as it swings out (Figure 214 shows the posture of turning the foot and swinging the lotus just before the foot is slapped). (Bend the bow and shoot the tiger) Then the right foot falls toward the southeast diagonal, touching first with the heel; then the left heel presses, the right leg bows forward, the right foot settles flat, and the two legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the two hands arc upward, forward and down, draw back past the right knee, and rise past the lower abdomen to before the chest, closing into fists; the weight shifts back, and as the right leg bows forward again the left fist parts to the upper-left diagonal and the right fist to the lower-right diagonal, forming the shape of drawing a bow, the left fist with its centre turned forward and level with the mouth, the right fist with its centre turned down and set before the right hip; facing the northeast diagonal. (Figure 215)

Movement four: the left leg lifts and steps forward one long pace, touching first with the heel; then the right leg becomes full and the right foot follows forward, touching with the toe behind the left heel, so that the two legs become empty-right and full-left. As the left foot steps up the two fists fall respectively beside the left and right hips; as the right foot follows, the two fists lift slightly and then drive slowly forward and down, the eyes of the fists facing each other, level with the abdomen, the two arms slightly bent; facing due east. (Figure 216)

Ninety-fifth posture — The hand plays the lute (Figure 217)

Movement: the right foot lifts and moves behind the left foot, settling with the toe pointing due south; the left foot draws back and touches with the left toe before the right foot, so that the two legs become full-right and empty-left. At the same time the body turns right, and the two fists lift and become upright palms, each circling once before the chest, forming the hand-plays-the-lute posture, the left hand level with the mouth and the right hand fallen to before the abdomen; facing a diagonal south of east. (Figure 217)

# Illustrated explanation of Wu-style taijiquan push-hands Taijiquan push-hands was originally called "hitting hands". Of what Wu Yuxiang and Li Yishe handed down, there is only the one kind — moving-step push-hands. Why adopt only moving-step push-hands and not fixed-step? The reason is that moving-step push-hands can be applied with agility and has no defect of stiffness; it trains both the stepping method and the body method, and at the same time allows practice of "stick, connect, adhere, follow". Moreover, in the course of the movement one is constantly able to keep a centred and stable posture, and can still issue energy while in motion. Once practised to familiarity, one can reach what the ancients called "walking, stopping, sitting, lying" — all of them states of practising the form.

图 220
Line drawing (lower left of the page): two men in contact pushing each other, the man on the right with his left hand pressing on the other's right arm, both men's steps one before the other. Labelled at its side "Figure 220".
图 221
Line drawing (lower middle of the page): two men in contact pushing each other, the man on the right stepping forward, both men's steps crossed. Labelled at its side "Figure 221".
图 222
Line drawing (lower right of the page): two men in contact pushing each other, the man on the right with his right hand extended forward and his left hand pressing on the other's arm. Labelled at its side "Figure 222".

The stepping method of Wu-style push-hands is three and a half steps forward, three and a half steps back. On the first and second steps forward, the advancing foot is placed on the outside of the opponent's front foot; on the third step forward, one foot is placed between the opponent's steps; on the fourth step the rear foot moves up beside the front foot with the toe touching the ground lightly, which is called a half-step. Whether placed on the outside of the opponent or between his steps, one should keep slightly close to the opponent's front foot. On one straight line I advance and he retreats, and he advances and I retreat. Above, the four hands of "ward-off, roll-back, press, push" are applied, the same as in the other kinds of push-hands, so they will not be drawn and explained again; only a few of the postures in which energy is issued are set out below for reference. # Appendix — Classical treatises on the art

Book page 647

Treatise on taijiquan

Treatise on taijiquan

Wang Zongyue of Shanyou

Taiji is born of wuji and is the mother of yin and yang. In movement it divides; in stillness it joins. Neither excess nor deficiency: follow the bend and yield to the extension. When the other is hard and I am soft, this is called "walking away"; when I am yielding and the other is against his own advantage, this is called "sticking". If the movement is urgent, respond urgently; if the movement is slow, follow slowly. Though the transformations are myriad, the principle is one throughout. From familiarity with the postures one gradually awakens to understanding energy (dong jin); from understanding energy one ascends step by step to the divine illumination. Yet without long application one cannot break through to sudden comprehension. Empty the collar and lift the crown of the head; sink the breath to the dantian. Neither lean nor incline; now hidden, now revealed. If the left is heavy, the left becomes empty; if the right is heavy, the right vanishes. Look up and it grows higher; look down and it grows deeper. Advance and it grows longer; retreat and it grows more pressing. Not even a feather can be added, nor an insect alight. The other does not know me; I alone know the other. That the hero meets no enemy wherever he turns comes about from this alone. There are very many side doors to this art; though the postures differ, they amount to no more than the strong cheating the weak and the slow giving way to the quick. Strength beating weakness and a slow hand yielding to a quick hand are all natural endowments of the inborn body, not something that comes from learning. Consider the saying "four ounces deflect a thousand catties" — plainly it is not victory by strength. Observe the form of the aged defeating a crowd — of what use is speed? Stand like a balance beam; move like a wheel. Lean to one side and you follow; be double-weighted and you stagnate. One constantly sees men of several years' pure practice unable to transform, and it is invariably because they let themselves be controlled by the other — they have not awakened to the fault of double-weighting. To avoid this fault one must know yin and yang. Sticking is walking away, and walking away is sticking; yin does not leave yang, nor yang leave yin. Only when yin and yang aid each other is there understanding of energy. After understanding energy, the more one practises the finer it becomes; silently recognizing and pondering, one gradually arrives at doing as the heart desires. The root of it is to give up the self and follow the other; many mistake this and give up the near to seek the far. As the saying goes, "a difference of a hair's breadth is an error of a thousand li" — the student cannot but examine this carefully. This is the treatise.

The thirteen postures (also called the long form, also called the thirteen postures)

Wang Zongyue of Shanyou

The long form: it is like the great Yangtze and the great sea, rolling on without cease.

The thirteen postures: ward-off, roll-back, press, push, pluck, split, elbow, shoulder, advance, retreat, look left, gaze right, and central equilibrium. Ward-off, roll-back, press and push are the four cardinal directions, kan, li, zhen and dui. Pluck, split, elbow and shoulder are the four diagonal corners, qian, kun, gen and xun. These are the eight trigrams. Advancing, retreating, looking left, gazing right and central equilibrium are metal, wood, water, fire and earth. These are the five elements. Taken together, they are called the thirteen postures.

Song of practising the thirteen postures (author unknown)

Do not slight the thirteen postures in all; Their life and intent have their source in the waist's gap. In changing fullness and emptiness, take care; Let breath go through the body, not dulled in the least. Touched in stillness, moving yet still as before; To change with the enemy is the wonder. In every posture keep the mind weighing intent; What is gained comes without felt expenditure of effort. Moment by moment keep the mind at the waist; Within the belly, loose and still, the breath rises. The tailbone centred, spirit threading the crown; The whole body light and nimble, each part suspended. Attend closely and seek it out in yourself; Bend and extend, open and close, follow what is free. Crossing the threshold needs guiding by word of mouth; Ceaseless application, and the method settles of itself. If you ask what the standard of body and use is: Intent and breath are the lord, bone and flesh the minister. Push the question of intent to its end — where does it lie? Long life, lengthened years, an unwithering spring. Sing, O sing — a hundred and forty lines; Every word is true, its meaning beyond doubt.

If one does not seek it out along this path, one wastes one's labour and will only lament too late!

Song of pushing hands　Revised by Wang Zongyue

Song of pushing hands　Revised by Wang Zongyue

Ward-off, roll-back, press and push — take them seriously; When upper and lower follow one another, the opponent finds no way in. Let him come at me with all his giant strength — A pull of four ounces deflects a thousand catties. Sink the chest, raise the back, wrap the crotch, protect the ribs, lift the crown, suspend the crotch, soar and shift, flash and battle.

Essential words on pushing hands　Wu Yuxiang

Explanation: Use the mind to move the breath; one must be sunk and steady, and only then can it gather and enter the bones — this is what is meant by "the source of the command of intent lies in the gap of the waist." The intent and breath must be exchanged with agility, and only then is there the delight of roundness and liveliness — this is what is meant by "in changing and turning, fullness and emptiness must be heeded." Stand with the body centred and upright, at ease and comfortable, bracing in all eight directions; move the breath like a nine-bend pearl, so that no subtlety is unreached — this is what is meant by "the breath goes through the whole body without the least dullness."

In issuing power one must be sunk, steady, loose and still, concentrating on a single direction — this is what is meant by "touched in stillness, moving yet still as before." In going and returning there must be folding; in advancing and retreating there must be turning — this is what is meant by "to change with the enemy is the wonder." Seek the straight within the curved, store and then issue — this is what is meant by "in every posture keep the mind weighing intent; moment by moment keep the mind at the waist." If the spirit can be raised, then there is no fear of slowness and heaviness — this is what is meant by "within the belly, loose and still, the breath rises." With an insubstantial crown lifting the power, the breath sunk to the elixir field, neither leaning nor inclining — this is what is meant by "the tailbone centred, spirit threading the crown; the whole body light and nimble, the crown suspended." Move the body with the breath, and one must be smooth and compliant, and only then can one be agile and follow the mind — this is what is meant by "bend and extend, open and close, follow what is free." The mind is the command, the breath the banner, the spirit the commander-in-chief, the body the servant — this is what is meant by "intent and breath are the lord, bone and flesh the minister." Explanation: Though the body moves, the mind values stillness; the breath must gather, the spirit should be at ease. The mind is the command, the breath the banner, the spirit the commander-in-chief, the body the servant; moment by moment keep the mind on it, and only then is anything attained. First in the mind, afterwards in the body. When it is in the body, one no longer knows that the hands dance and the feet stamp. This is what is meant by "completing it in one breath," "giving up the self and following others," "drawing him in to fall into emptiness," "four ounces deflecting a thousand catties." Know that when one thing moves, nothing is unmoved; when one thing is still, nothing is unstilled. Regard movement as stillness, regard stillness as movement; inwardly solidify the spirit, outwardly show ease and comfort. One must follow others, not proceed from oneself; following others one lives, proceeding from oneself one stagnates. He who prizes breath has no power; he who nourishes breath is purely firm. When the other does not move, I do not move; when the other moves slightly, I move first. Leaning on others with oneself, one must know oneself, and only then can one turn and follow and follow and meet; sticking to others with oneself, one must know others, and only then can one be neither behind nor before. If the spirit can be raised, there is no fear of slowness and heaviness; if sticking and leaning can follow with agility, only then is the wonder of falling into emptiness seen. In going and returning, yin and yang must be distinguished; in advancing and retreating, there must be turning and closing. The opportunity is issued from oneself; the force is borrowed from others. In issuing power, upper and lower must follow one another, and then one goes forward invincible; in standing, the body must be centred and upright, not inclining, and then it can brace in all eight directions. Still as a mountain, moving as a river. Step as if on the brink of an abyss, move power as if drawing silk, store power as if drawing a bow, issue power as if loosing an arrow. Move the breath like a nine-bend pearl, so that no subtlety is unreached; move power like steel tempered a hundred times, and what hardness will it not shatter. In form like a falcon seizing a hare, in spirit like a cat catching a mouse. Seek the straight within the curved, store and then issue. Gathering is issuing, continuous without break. Utterly soft, and only then can one be utterly firm; able to stick and lean, and only then can one be agile. Nourish the breath by what is straight and it does no harm; store the power by what is curved and it has surplus. Gradually one comes to respond to things as they come — this too is "knowing to stop, and so attaining."

Again it is said:

First in the mind, afterwards in the body; belly loose, breath gathered into the bones, spirit at ease, body still, moment by moment keeping the mind. Remember always: when one thing moves, nothing is unmoved; when one thing is still, nothing is unstilled. Regard stillness as movement, regard movement as stillness. In moving, pulling to and fro, the breath clings to the back, gathered into the spine — be still. Inwardly solidify the spirit, outwardly show ease and comfort. Step as a cat walks, move power as if drawing silk. The whole body's intent lies in storing spirit, not in breath; if in breath, then it stagnates. He who has breath has no power; he who has no breath is purely firm. The breath is like a cartwheel, the waist like the axle.

Again it is said:

When the other does not move, I do not move; when the other moves slightly, I move first. As if loose yet not loose, about to unfold yet not — unfold. The power breaks but the intent does not break.

Again it is said:

In every movement, the hand alone first applies force, and then immediately loosens. One must still thread it through, and this is nothing other than beginning, sustaining, turning and closing. First the intent moves, then the power moves; the transition must be strung on a single thread. The breath should be stirred and agitated, the spirit should be gathered inward. Do not allow any place of defect, do not allow any place of concavity or convexity, do not allow any place of break or interruption. Its root is in the feet, it issues from the legs, it is governed by the waist, it takes form in the fingers. From feet to legs to waist, it must always be one complete breath. Advancing and retreating, only then does one gain the opportunity and the position; where one does not gain opportunity and position, the body becomes scattered, and one must come to lean and tilt — the fault must be sought in the waist and legs, and it is so above and below, before and behind, left and right. All of this is intent, not outward form: where there is above there is below, where there is front there is back, where there is left there is right. If the intent wishes to go up, then lodge the intent below; if a thing is about to be lifted, and you add a breaking force to it, then its root breaks of itself, and it is destroyed swiftly, beyond doubt. Fullness and emptiness should be clearly distinguished: each place has its own fullness and emptiness, and every place is always this one fullness and emptiness; the whole body is threaded joint by joint — do not let there be the least interruption.

Releasing in pushing hands

Five-word formula　Li Yiyu
One: the mind is still

If the mind is not still, then it is not focused; as soon as one raises a hand, front, back, left and right have no fixed direction at all — hence the mind must be still. At first the movements cannot come from oneself; one must calm the mind and personally recognise it, following what the other does, yielding and extending with him, neither losing nor resisting, not extending and contracting on one's own. If he has force, I too have force, and my force is first; if he has no force, I — also have no force, and my intent is still first. One must keep the mind on it moment by moment: wherever one is touched, the mind must be applied there; one must seek the news within "neither losing nor resisting." Working on in this way, in a year or half a year one can apply it in the body. This is entirely intent, not the use of force; in time, others are controlled by me, and I am not controlled by others.

Two: the body is agile

If the body is stagnant, then one cannot advance and retreat freely; hence the body must be agile. In raising a hand one must not have a stupid look. When the other's force has just touched my skin and hair, my intent has already entered his bones; both hands brace, and one breath runs through. When the left is heavy, the left empties and the right has already gone; when the right is heavy, the right empties and the left has already gone. The breath is like a cartwheel: the whole body must follow along. Where it does not follow, the body becomes scattered and cannot get force — the fault must be sought in the waist and legs. First use the mind to command the body, following others and not oneself. Afterwards the body can follow the mind, and even proceeding from oneself is still following others. Proceeding from oneself one stagnates; following others one lives. If one can follow others, then in the hands there is measure. Weigh the size of his force, and there is no error of a fraction; gauge the length of his advance, and there is no difference of a hair. Advancing and retreating, everywhere exactly fitting — the longer the work, the finer the skill.

Three: the breath gathers

If the breath's momentum is scattered and loose, then there is no containment, and the body easily scatters; one must cause the breath to gather into the spine. The breathing is numinous and unobstructed, and the whole body has no gap. Inhaling is closing and storing; exhaling is opening and issuing. For inhaling naturally lifts one up, and can also lift the other up; exhaling naturally sinks one down, and can also send the other out. This is moving the breath by intent, not driving the breath by force.

Four: the power is whole

The power of the whole body is trained into one family, distinguishing clearly fullness and emptiness. In issuing power there must be a root: the power rises from the heel, is governed at the waist, takes form in the fingers, and issues from the spine and back. One must also raise up the whole of one's spirit: at the moment when the other's power is about to issue but has not yet issued, my power has already joined his power — exactly neither behind nor before, like skin catching fire, like a spring gushing out. Advancing and retreating, there is not the least scattering; seek the straight within the curved, store and then issue, and only then can one succeed at once with the hand. This is what is meant by "borrowing force to strike the man, four ounces deflecting a thousand catties."

Five: the spirit gathers

When the above four are all present, they all return to the gathering of the spirit. When the spirit gathers, then one breath forges and casts, refining the breath and returning it to the spirit, and the breath's momentum soars and shifts. The spirit is poured in; opening and closing have order; fullness and emptiness are clear. When the left is empty, the right is full; when the right is empty, the left is full. Emptiness is not being utterly without force — the breath's momentum must have soaring and shifting; fullness is not being utterly locked up — the spirit must be valued and poured in. The crux lies entirely in the transforming within the chest and waist, not outside. Force is borrowed from others; breath issues from the spine. How can breath issue from the spine? The breath sinks downward, gathering from both shoulders into the spine and pouring into the waist — this is the breath going from above to below, and it is called closing. From the waist it takes form in the spine, spreads to both arms, and is applied in the fingers — this is the breath going from below to above, and it is called opening. Closing is gathering; opening is issuing. If one can understand opening and closing, then one knows yin and yang. Arriving at this stage, one day's work is one day's refinement of skill, until gradually one follows what the mind desires, and nothing fails to accord with one's intent.

Book page 652

Secret formula for releasing　Li Yiyu

Secret formula for releasing　Li Yiyu

Lift, draw, loosen, release

Lift up his body, borrowing his force. Within it is the word "numinous." Draw him to the front of the body, and the power only then stores. Within it is the word "gather." Loosen my power and do not let it bend. Within it is the word "still." In releasing, the waist and feet must recognise the exact point. Within it is the word "whole."

Essential words on practising the form and pushing hands　Li Yiyu

The men of old said: "One can draw in and let fall into emptiness, and can deflect a thousand catties with four ounces; one cannot draw in and let fall into emptiness, and cannot deflect a thousand catties with four ounces." The words are very comprehensive, and the beginner has no way to grasp them. I add a few phrases to explain them, so that those who have the will in this art may find the way in, and so advance daily with achievement. If one wishes to draw in and let fall into emptiness, and to deflect a thousand catties with four ounces, one must first know oneself and know others. If one wishes to know oneself and know others, one must first give up up the self and follow others. If one wishes to give up the self and follow others, one must first gain the opportunity and the position. If one wishes to gain opportunity and position, one must first make the whole body one family. If one wishes to make the whole body one family, one must first have no defect in the whole body. If one wishes to have no defect in the whole body, one must first have the spirit and breath stirred and agitated. If one wishes the spirit and breath stirred and agitated, one must first raise up the spirit, so that the spirit cannot scatter outward. If one wishes the spirit not to scatter outward, one must first have the spirit and breath gather and enter the bones. If one wishes the spirit and breath to gather and enter the bones, one must first have strength in the front section of both thighs. Both shoulders loosen, the breath sinks downward, the power rises from the heel, changes in the legs, is contained in the chest, moves in both shoulders, and is governed in the waist. Above, the two arms are linked; below, the two legs follow. The power is exchanged from within: gathering is closing, releasing is opening. When still, all is still; stillness is closing, and within closing is lodged opening. When moving, all moves; movement is opening, and within opening is lodged closing. Touched, one then turns and revolves freely, and nowhere fails to get force. Only then can one draw in and let fall into emptiness, and deflect a thousand catties with four ounces. In ordinary practice of the form, this is the work of knowing oneself: at each movement, first ask whether one's whole body accords with these several items; if it accords but slightly not, then change at once — hence in practising the form one should be slow and not fast. Pushing hands is the work of knowing others; movement and stillness are indeed knowing others, but it is still asking oneself. If one has arranged oneself well, then when another touches me, I do not move him a hair's breadth, but take advantage of his momentum to enter, join and fix his power, and he falls out of himself. If one has a place where one cannot get force, then it is double-weighting not yet transformed, and one must seek it in the opening and closing of yin and yang. This is what is meant by "know yourself and know others, and in a hundred battles you will win a hundred victories."

Note: The above classical treatises on boxing are selected and transcribed from the definitive edition of the Taijiquan Manual that Li Yiyu copied out and presented to Hao Weizhen in 1881; the text has not been altered by later hands.

Book page 653

Four-word secret formula　(author to be verified)

Four-word secret formula　(author to be verified)

Fu (spread): Fu means moving the breath in one's own body and spreading it over the other's power, so that he cannot move.

Gai (cover): Gai means using the breath to cover the place from which the other comes.

Dui (match): Dui means using the breath to match the place from which the other comes, fixing the aim and then going out.

Tun (swallow): Tun means using the breath to swallow him wholly and enter into transformation.

These four words are without form and without sound; only after understanding power, when one has refined to the most exquisite stage, can one know them — completely it is spoken of in terms of breath. If one can nourish one's breath by what is straight and without harm, only then can one apply it to the four limbs, and the four limbs will speak without words.

Textual note: Li Fuyin, grandson of Li Yiyu, compiled the Lianrang Hall edition of the Taijiquan Manual in 1935 and took the "Four-word secret formula" to be a work of Wu Yuxiang, basing this on the Brief Account of My Late Grandfather, the Honourable Lianquan, written by Wu Laixu, grandson of Wu Yuxiang. Laixu said of his grandfather that "receiving the art, his insights came entirely from the four-word formula," and so Fuyin took the "Four-word secret formula" to be Wu Yuxiang's work. Considering that this formula's boxing theory is lofty and subtle, with a level above Li Yiyu's "Secret formula for releasing"; that Li Yiyu's Taijiquan Manual, written out for Hao He in 1881, fully records Wu Yuxiang's boxing treatises; that Wu Yuxiang died in 1880; and that Wu and Li stood as teacher and student and lived in the same village — if this formula were Wu Yuxiang's work, there is no way it would not have been included. Hence this formula is probably not Wu Yuxiang's work, and may have been composed by a disciple of Wu or of Li. Li Yiyu died in 1892, so it is also possible that he wrote this formula. It is singled out here for further examination.

(Appendix note by Gu Liuxin)

Preface

Preface

Guided by the Party's policy of "letting a hundred flowers bloom, a hundred schools of thought contend," the editor drew on the posthumous work of her late father, Mr. Sun Lutang — The Study of Taijiquan (《太极拳学》) — and on the way he practiced in his later years, and compiled Sun-Style Taijiquan (《孙式太极拳》), published in 1957. To meet the needs of the broad masses in their physical training, the editor has now revised the 1957 edition. The movement descriptions have been amended and expanded, the movement photographs have been retaken, and the applications of certain principal movements have been added, while the original structure has been retained in the main. Although the editor received instruction from her late father in person from early childhood, she is conscious that her own skill falls short of depth and purity; still, for the convenience of those who love Sun-style Taijiquan and wish to practise it, she has done her best.

Confined as it is by the editor's level, the book will inevitably contain errors; readers are earnestly asked to point them out.

— The Editor

Brief Introduction to Sun-Style Taijiquan

Brief Introduction to Sun-Style Taijiquan

The founder of Sun-style taiji (太极, tàijí) quan was Sun Fuquan (孙福全, Sūn Fúquán), courtesy name Lutang (禄堂, Lùtáng), late sobriquet Hanzhai (涵斋, Hánzhāi), a native of Wanxian in Hebei. From childhood he was passionately fond of martial arts. He studied Xingyi Quan (形意拳, Xíngyì Quán) under Li Kuiyuan (李魁垣, Lǐ Kuíyuán), and then studied under Li's own teacher Guo Yunshen (郭云深, Guō Yúnshēn), from whom he received the true transmission. He also studied Baguazhang (八卦拳, Bāguàzhāng) under Cheng Tinghua (程廷华, Chéng Tínghuá). After several years of study and polishing his skill ran deep. He later studied taijiquan under Hao Weizhen (郝为真, Hǎo Wéizhēn). Sun Lutang (孙禄堂, Sūn Lùtáng) devoted his whole life to the study of martial arts; he was proficient in Xingyi, Baguazhang and taijiquan, and gathering the essential meaning of the three schools into one, he created Sun-style taijiquan.

The characteristics of Sun-style taijiquan are: advance and retreat follow one another; when stepping forward one must follow, when stepping back one must withdraw. The movements are extended, rounded and lively, nimble and natural. In practice the two feet are clearly distinguished as empty and full (虚实, xūshí). The whole set, once begun, is like drifting clouds and flowing water, continuous and unbroken. At every turn of the body "opening" and "closing" (开合, kāihé) join, and so it is also called kaihe huobu taijiquan (开合活步太极拳, kāihé huóbù tàijíquán). It is suitable for people of any age and any constitution to practise.

Book page 658

General Explanation of Taijiquan

General Explanation of Taijiquan

Taijiquan is one of the martial arts peculiar to our country. It is an exercise of "cultivating both within and without" (inwardly it governs calming the mind and nurturing the nature, outwardly it governs training the body); it takes suppleness and curvature as its substance and firmness and straightness as its function. Without suppleness and curvature one cannot neutralize; without firmness and straightness one cannot apply. In substance and function it is the fighting method of "using softness to overcome hardness, drawing aside four ounces to deflect a thousand catties." In practising this quan one should sink the qi to the dantian (丹田, dāntián), neither lean nor incline, so that inner and outer join; one must on no account use clumsy strength. One should move the strength by the intent (意, yì) — where the intent arrives, the strength arrives.

As to the method of practising taijiquan, my late father often said: Mr. Hao Weizhen spoke of three levels of mental state in practising taijiquan. At the first stage of practice it is as though the body were in water, both feet treading the ground, and the movements meet the resistance of the water. At the second level it is as though the body were in water with both feet floating up, like a swimmer drifting in the water, able to move freely. At the third level the body is light and nimble, the two feet as if walking on the surface of the water — treading on the brink of the abyss, on thin ice — with the spirit and qi gathered inward, not daring to let there be the slightest scattering or disorder. Then the quan is accomplished.

The postures and movements of taijiquan all have definite essential points, and each has its own meaning. The essentials are introduced in summary below:

Head: The head should push up, but one must not use strength. The chin is naturally drawn in, the top of the head upright, the spirit concentrated. The whole body is relaxed and open; in lifting, pressing, extending and contracting one always uses intent and does not use clumsy strength, and the mind is naturally empty and numinous. This is what is called "empty and numinous, suspending the head-top" (虚灵顶劲, xūlíng dǐngjìn).

Mouth: The mouth should be loosely closed, the tongue touching the upper palate, breathing through the nose.

Chest: The chest should be contained and must not be thrust out. When the chest is contained the qi sinks to the dantian. When the chest is thrust out the qi surges into the chest region, the upper is heavy and the lower light, and the heels float — a thing taboo to the martial practitioner. When the chest is contained the qi clings to the back, and strength issues from the spine — this is true strength. The above is what is called "containing the chest and raising the back" (含胸拔背, hánxiōng bábèi).

Shoulders: Both shoulders must be relaxed and hanging down. One must especially avoid hunching the shoulders, otherwise the qi surges upward.

Book page 659

General Explanation of Taijiquan (continued)

General Explanation of Taijiquan (continued)

Elbows: The two elbows should hang loosely downward, the two arms naturally bent. This is the meaning of "seeking the straight within the curved, storing and then issuing."

Hands: The five fingers are spread, the wrist sunk (塌腕, tāwàn), the tiger's mouth slightly rounded, the palm slightly drawn in, as though grasping and holding a ball.

Waist: The waist must be sunk (塌, tā). For the waist is the pivot of the whole body's movements and the source of strength. A person's turning, advancing and retreating, and the changes of empty and full all depend on the waist strength running through them.

Legs: The two legs are bent, and one must clearly distinguish empty and full — that is, the body's centre of gravity is placed on one leg. If the centre of gravity moves onto the right leg, then the right leg is full and the left leg is empty. Conversely, the left leg is full and the right leg is empty. Distinguishing empty and full is the essential meaning of taijiquan; moving thus, the turning is light and nimble. Otherwise the stepping is heavy and sluggish, and one is easily led about by others.

Breathing: What is called "sinking the qi to the dantian" (three inches below the navel) means deep and long abdominal breathing. But one must on no account use strength to press the qi downward; one must simply let the breathing be entirely natural (呼吸, hūxī).

Intent and strength: One of the characteristics of taijiquan is that it uses intent and does not use strength. For taijiquan requires the use of living strength; the whole body must be relaxed and open, not allowing the least bit of clumsy strength to linger between sinews, bones, blood and vessels. It requires being extremely soft and yet extremely firm and hard, extremely heavy and yet extremely nimble. Where the intent arrives the strength arrives, applied with ease. If clumsy strength is used, then it is sluggish and not nimble. If the strength floats on the outside, it does not accord with the requirements of taijiquan. What is meant by using intent and not using strength, and how does living strength arise of itself? It is because where the intent goes the qi arrives; thus the qi and blood flow and pour, day by day infusing and circulating through the channels and network vessels of the whole body, never for a moment stagnating. With long practice true inner strength (内劲, nèijìn) is then produced.

Movement and stillness: The quiet sitting of qigong is seeking movement within stillness; boxing art is seeking stillness within movement. In practising the quan the mind must be still and the spirit concentrated; only then can the movements be rounded and lively.

The above has discussed the essentials of movement separately. But the student must certainly note that taijiquan is an exercise of the whole body, and what is trained lies in the spirit. The spirit is the commander, the body is the servant; if the spirit can be raised, then the movements are naturally light and nimble. Only when mind and intent are in harmony with the movements of the form can inner and outer join as one. In practice one must take care that above and below follow one another, and that all parts of the body are complete and unified. If there is one place where the movement is not whole, the spirit and qi will be scattered and disordered. Furthermore, in practising the quan one should move the strength by the intent, linked without interruption, "like the long Yangtze River, rolling on without cease." "In movement, like drawing silk" —

Book page 660

General Explanation of Taijiquan (continued)

General Explanation of Taijiquan (continued)

— such is the meaning.

To make it easy for the reader to remember, these essential points are now put into a mnemonic verse as follows:

Taijiquan is originally an inner-school boxing (内家拳, nèijiāquán);
do not use clumsy strength — intent comes first.
Empty and numinous, suspending the head-top (顶头, dǐngtóu), the spirit concentrated;
draw the chin back and it is then natural.
Containing the chest, one can naturally raise the back;
on no account form "hunchback shoulders."
In practice sink the shoulders and drop the elbows;
with shoulders hunched and elbows suspended it is not the quan.
Sinking the waist (塌腰, tāyāo) can raise the strength of the whole body;
if the waist is not sunk, nimbleness is difficult.
The two legs bent distinguish empty and full;
here lies the essential meaning of taiji.
Breathing (呼吸, hūxī) sinks down to the dantian point;
let it be purely natural, do not force it.
Above and below follow one another and become one body;
the movements, continuous and unbroken, are forever linked.
Seek stillness within movement, movement within stillness;
in practice the spirit and qi must be complete in every part.
Be sure to remember these points and not forget them;
with lasting practice the benefit will show of itself.
Book page 661
