Part One. Two: Explanation of the Movements
First Posture: Beginning Posture (起式, Qǐ Shì)
  • ① The body stands upright, both hands hang down, both shoulders relax; the tips of the two feet are separated by about 90°; the eyes look straight ahead, the mind is quiet, and one pauses briefly. (图 1)

The eyes look straight ahead, the mind is quiet, and one pauses briefly. (图 1)

图 1
practitioner standing upright facing front, arms hanging naturally at the sides, feet apart, weight evenly on both legs.
  • ② The tip of the right foot lifts, and pivoting on the heel the foot turns half a face-width to the left to form 45° with the left foot; at the same time the body turns slightly to the left and faces diagonally forward-left; the eyes look straight ahead. (图 2)
图 2
practitioner standing with the body turned slightly to the left, right toes raised and pivoting on the right heel, feet at roughly 45° to one another.

Key points (要点, yàodiǎn): the whole body relaxes, the waist sinks (塌腰, tāyāo), but it must not become rigid and stiff; the tongue rests against the upper palate, and the breathing is natural.

Second Posture: Lazy Tucking the Robe (懒扎衣, Lǎn Zhā Yī)
  • ① Both arms slowly rise forward and upward to the height of the shoulders, the two palms facing each other and drawn slightly inward, about 18 cm apart, the fingertips pointing forward, as if holding a ball; the two legs do not move; the eyes look at the space between the two hands. (图 3)
图 3
practitioner standing with both arms raised forward to about shoulder height, palms facing each other as if holding a ball, legs unchanged.
  • ② Both hands drop to the front of the abdomen, and at the same time both legs slowly bend and the left heel slowly rises in accompaniment. (图 4)
  • ③ The left foot steps forward, the heel touching the ground first; at the same time both hands slowly extend upward and forward, the two hands still as if holding a ball, the arms slightly bent; as the two hands extend, the right foot follows with a step forward to the inner side of the left ankle, about 10 cm apart, the toe touching the ground; the eyes look at the space between the two hands. (图 5、6)
  • ④ Both hands rotate horizontally to the right; when the turn has brought the practitioner to face directly forward, the right hand rotates outward with the palm facing up; the left hand rotates inward with the palm facing down and, supporting the right wrist, rotates to the right along with it; at the same time the right heel comes to the ground and the tip of the left foot lifts and rotates to the right, and the tip of the right foot thereupon swings outward by about 90°; the eyes look at the right hand. (图 7、8)
  • ⑤ The right hand draws a half-circle to the right and backward while the left hand follows the movement of the right hand; when the right hand has turned to the front of the right shoulder with the forearm upright and the palm turned diagonally upward, it then turns toward the front, the left hand supporting
图 4
the whole body sinks into a crouch, both hands come down in front of the abdomen, the left heel is lifted.
图 7
both hands rotate to the right in front of the chest, the right palm facing up, the left hand supporting the right wrist.
图 10
both hands push forward with the arms slightly bent, the right foot in front and the left foot behind.
图 5
the left foot has stepped forward, both hands extended forward as if holding a ball.
图 8
both hands rotate to the lower right, the right palm turned diagonally upward.
图 6
the right foot has followed up to the inner side of the left ankle, the toe touching the ground, both hands holding a ball in front of the chest.
图 9
the right hand having drawn a half-circle to the right and backward, the forearm is upright and the left hand supports the right wrist.

The right wrist pushes forward together with it, both arms slightly bent; at the same time the right foot steps forward, the heel touching the ground first and gradually settling; the left foot thereupon follows behind the right foot, about 10 cm apart, the toe touching the ground; the eyes look at the right hand, and one pauses briefly. (图 9、10)

Key points (要点, yàodiǎn): the movement must run through in a single continuous flow and must not be interrupted.

Application (用法, yòngfǎ): Lazy Tucking the Robe is composed of warding off, rolling back, pressing and pushing (掤捋挤按, péng lǚ jǐ àn). ① Ward-off (掤, péng): when the opponent strikes with the hand, one presses his wrist down with the front hand and draws it backward, The rear hand quickly seeks out his elbow. If the opponent's attacking hand comes high, then both hands lift his arm from below and drive it backward and downward, or one may also drive it level toward the side and rear.

图 11
practitioner standing, both hands held in front of the chest at about shoulder height, forearms curved, palms facing each other.
  • ② Press (挤, jǐ), that is, squeezing the opponent out. The intent is that the forearm grates against the opponent's arm like a file. If one can make his body lean to one side and lose its central equilibrium, and his arm is then wrapped by one's arm and pressed against his body so that he cannot raise it to fend or prop, then this is the best moment for pressing. In application, press is squeezed out diagonally forward and upward from in front of the chest. If applied skilfully, it can send the opponent up off the ground. If the press is to have power, the wrapping strength of both arms is the key: once the opponent is wrapped, one must rapidly advance the step and bring the body up, closely adhering to him.
图 12
practitioner standing, both hands held forward in front of the chest, palms facing each other, feet apart with the weight settled.
  • ③ Ward-off (掤, péng), that is, propping (not dead propping with brute resistance). When the opponent rushes at one with both hands, one sticks both arms upward to his hands, sits the waist back and withdraws the left step, turns the waist slightly to the right, pats to the right with the left hand and hangs to the right with the right hand; at this moment the opponent's force has already been neutralized, and one issues at the appropriate instant. The subtlety of the ward-off method lies in "sticking": neither letting go nor resisting, the two arms like springs, so that what the opponent touches seems both present and absent. Ward-off may be done with both hands or with one; if one wards off the opponent's two hands with a single hand, one gains the more advantageous position.
  • ④ Push (按, àn): if the opponent attacks toward one, one lightly presses down both of his arms with both hands and immediately pushes out forward. Push may be done with one hand or both, with opening energy or closing energy as the situation determines, but one must stick to the opponent's arms so that he cannot turn and move freely.
图 13
practitioner in a wider stance with the arms opened out to the sides at shoulder height, both palms turned outward.
Third Posture: Opening the Hands (开手, Kāi Shǒu)
图 14
both hands opened left and right in front of the chest until they face the two shoulders, fingertips pointing up, the practitioner standing with one foot before the other.
图 15
both hands brought together in front of the chest, about a face-width apart, both knees bent, the tip of the left foot touching the ground.
图 16
both hands raised level to the left and right, the arms in a level-raise position, the two palms facing outward, standing with the feet apart.

Following on from the previous posture, the left heel comes to the ground and the tip of the right foot lifts, [The left foot] buckles inward to the left by about 90°, and the body turns to the left along with it; at the same time, with the two palms facing each other and the fingertips pointing upward, [the hands] separate to left and right (as if holding a balloon whose air expands outward, opening until the tiger's mouths of the two hands face the two shoulders), the two hands about 10 cm apart, and one pauses slightly. (图 11)

Fourth Posture: Closing the Hands (合手, Hé Shǒu)

Following on from the previous posture, with the two palms facing each other the hands slowly close inward; when they have come to about a face-width apart, one pauses slightly; at the same time both legs bend, the right foot is on the ground, the left heel lifts with the toe touching the ground; the eyes look at the space between the two hands. (图 12)

Key points (要点, yàodiǎn): the whole body must relax; there must not be the slightest forced strength.

Application (用法, yòngfǎ): Opening and Closing the Hands — if the opponent suddenly embraces one's two arms from behind with both hands, one immediately props against his two arms with the elbows, quickly presses downward, and following the momentum turns the body to the left or turns the body to the right.

Fifth Posture: Single Whip (单鞭, Dān Biān)

Following on from the previous posture, the two hands rotate inward and, as if driving a long pole, slowly separate to left and right, the two arms reaching a level-raise position, the two palms facing outward, the palm upright, at the height of the eyes; at the same time the left foot steps sideways to the left, the leg slightly bent; the right leg slightly straightened; the eyes look at the right hand, and one pauses briefly. (图 13)

Key points (要点, yàodiǎn): the upper body must be straight, the two shoulders must be relaxed, the breathing must be natural, and one must not use clumsy strength to press qi (气) down into the dantian (丹田, dāntián).

Application (用法, yòngfǎ): ① Single Whip deals with opponents on both the left and right sides. Although the two hands separate at the same time, one must be empty and the other full (虚实, xūshí); which is full and which is empty depends on how near or far the opponent's attacking force is. If the left hand ...a solid strike. The centre of gravity must fall on the left leg, while one keeps watch to the right; at the same time the right foot may be raised to kick an opponent on the right.

图 17
practitioner standing upright with both feet together, both arms extended forward in front of the chest, elbows bent, hands at chest height.
  • ② If two opponents on either side stand very close, or have already caught and held both of one's arms, one immediately strikes with the elbow or leans in with the shoulder, and at the same time may kick with the foot on the other side.
图 18
practitioner standing with feet together, both arms extended forward at chest height, one hand slightly in front of the other.
Sixth Posture: Raising the Hand to Upper Posture (提手上式, Tí Shǒu Shàng Shì)

Following on from the previous posture, the body's centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg; the left hand then traces an arc in front of the face up to in front of the forehead, palm facing outward; the right hand traces an arc downward to in front of the abdomen, fingers pointing down, palm facing right; at the same time the sole of the right foot draws in close to the left leg, the tip of the foot touching the ground level with the tip of the left foot, both legs slightly bent; the eyes look forward. (图 14)

图 19
practitioner standing with feet together, both arms extended forward in front of the chest with palms turned outward.

要点 (yàodiǎn) Key points: the body must be kept steady and level, and the waist sunk (塌腰, tā yāo).

用法 (yòngfǎ) Application: if the opponent grips one's two wrists with both hands, one turns both arms outward in opposite directions, one upward and one downward, at the same time; this is certain to free them. If the opponent is very close, one may lift the knee of the empty leg and strike at his abdomen.

Seventh Posture: White Crane Spreads its Wings (白鹤亮翅, Bái Hè Liàng Chì)
  • ① Following on from the previous posture, the left hand moves down from in front of the forehead to in front of the left chest, the elbow held close against the ribs, palm facing outward; the right hand is lifted from in front of the abdomen up above the forehead, the back of the hand close against the forehead; at the same time the right foot steps forward and the heel touches the ground, the distance between the two feet being such as not to disturb the body's centre of gravity. (图 15)
  • ② The right hand moves downward past the right side of the face (almost touching but not touching) to in front of the right chest, the tip of the elbow hanging down, palm facing outward, at the same height as the left hand; both hands push forward together; at the same time the tip of the right foot slowly comes to the ground and the body's centre of gravity shifts forward onto the right

...leg; the left foot then follows up to the inside of the right foot, the tip of the foot touching the ground; the eyes look between the two hands. (图 16, 17)

要点 (yàodiǎn) Key points: sink the waist (塌腰, tā yāo); the two arms are slightly bent; pause briefly.

用法 (yòngfǎ) Application: ① I strike the opponent with my right hand. If he presses my right wrist downward with his left hand, I at once advance the step, withdraw the right hand and let it sink loosely downward, while the left hand sticks to his right wrist and plucks it downward; the right hand then rotates and strikes upward at his chest or head.

图 20
practitioner in a standing pose with the left leg forward and bent, the left hand lowered to the outside of the left hip, the right arm raised out to the right side at about shoulder height, palm turned upward; the gaze directed toward the right hand.
  • ② If the opponent attacks with both hands, I separate his hands, one upward and one downward, and at the same time swiftly advance the step and strike his chest with both hands.
Eighth Posture: Opening the Hands (开手, Kāi Shǒu)

The movement is the same as the Third Posture, "Opening the Hands". (图 18)

Ninth Posture: Closing the Hands (合手, Hé Shǒu)

The movement is the same as the Fourth Posture, "Closing the Hands". (图 19)

图 21
practitioner with the right leg stepped forward into a bow-like stance, the right arm extended forward, the left hand lowered; body facing forward.
Tenth Posture: Brush the Knee and Twist the Step (搂膝拗步, Lōu Xī Ào Bù) — left form
  • ① Following on from the previous posture, the left hand brushes to the right and downward to the outside of the left hip, the thumb about 10 cm from the hip; at the same time the left foot steps diagonally forward to the left, the right hand rotates outward, arcs upward and down to the right, and is raised to the height of the right shoulder, palm facing upward; the eyes look at the right hand. (图 20)
  • ② The right hand pushes out level toward the left front, the arm slightly bent, the wrist sunk, palm facing forward; at the same time the right foot follows up to the side of the inner ankle of the left foot, the tip of the foot touching the ground, and the centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg; the eyes look at the tip of the index finger of the right hand; pause briefly. (图 21)

要点 (yàodiǎn) Key points: the forward push of the right hand and the following step must be coordinated as one; the right elbow must be bent and the wrist sunk.

用法 (yòngfǎ) Application: if the opponent strikes at me with his right fist, I brush to the left with my left hand and strike his chest with my right hand.

图 22
practitioner in a low stance with the left leg forward and bent, the right arm extended forward at chest height and the left arm held low, palm turned upward.
Eleventh Posture: Hand Plays the Pipa (手挥琵琶, Shǒu Huī Pí Pá) — left form

Following on from the previous posture, the fingers of both hands are straightened, the tiger's mouths facing upward; the right foot steps back, the tip of the foot touching the ground first (the distance stepped back being such as not to disturb the body's centre of gravity), and the whole foot then settles slowly to the ground; at the same time the right hand pulls back and the left hand extends forward, both elbows hanging down; the left foot steps back to in front of the right foot, the tip of the foot touching the ground; the eyes look straight ahead. (图 22)

图 23
practitioner in a walking stance with the left leg forward, the left arm bent in front of the chest and the right arm extended forward at chest height, palm turned upward.

用法 (yòngfǎ) Application: if the opponent strikes with his right fist, one's right palm presses his wrist and the left hand presses his elbow, and following the momentum one seizes (攫) or breaks (撅) it.

Twelfth Posture: Advance the Step, Deflect, Bar and Punch (进步搬拦捶, Jìn Bù Bān Lán Chuí)
  • ① Following on from the previous posture, the left hand rotates inward and brushes downward and to the left to in front of the ribs, palm facing down; the right hand rotates outward and upward, extends forward past beneath the left hand, palm facing up; at the same time the left foot steps forward, the tip of the foot turned slightly outward. (图 23)
  • ② The right hand rotates inward and brushes back to in front of the right ribs, palm facing down, while the left hand rotates outward and extends forward, palm facing up; at the same time the right foot steps forward, the tip of the foot turned slightly outward as it comes to the ground. (图 24)
图 24
practitioner with the right leg stepped forward and bent, the right arm drawn back toward the right ribs and the left arm extended forward, palm turned upward.
  • ③ Without pausing from the movement above, the left foot steps forward one pace; at the same time the right hand rotates outward and inward and forms a fist, striking straight out over the left wrist, the fist level with the chest, the eye of the fist facing up; the left hand rotates inward and closes into a fist, drawn back, the centre of the fist facing down; the right foot follows up to the inside of the left ankle, the tip of the foot touching the ground; the eyes look at the middle joint of the index finger of the right hand. (图 25, 26)

用法 (yòngfǎ) Application: if the opponent strikes at one's chest with his left hand, one hooks his wrist with one's left hand (the tiger's mouth facing oneself), plucks and holds it, drawing it backward and to the right, and at the same time strikes at the opponent with the right hand.

图 25
practitioner with the left leg forward and the right foot following behind, the right fist thrust straight forward at chest height and the left fist drawn back at the waist.
Thirteenth Posture: As if Sealing, As if Closing (如封似闭, Rú Fēng Sì Bì)
图 26
practitioner with the right leg forward and the left foot following, the right fist thrust forward at chest height and the left fist at the waist.

Following on from the previous posture, the right fist draws back; the left fist extends slightly forward from beneath the right arm, and when the two fists come level it changes into a palm, both palms facing forward; as the right hand withdraws, the right foot steps back (the distance stepped back being such as not to disturb the body's centre of gravity); immediately the two hands and the left foot withdraw together, the left foot coming to in front of the right foot, the tip of the foot touching the ground, and the two hands coming in front of the chest; the eyes look forward. (图 27)

用法 (yòngfǎ) Application: I strike some part of the opponent with my right hand. If he pushes my wrist or elbow sideways with his left hand, I sit the waist back and my left hand cuts across his wrist from outside my right arm, leading it to the right along with his force, while at the same time my right hand presses his elbow, issuing according to the momentum.

图 27
practitioner standing with both hands drawn back in front of the chest, palms facing forward, feet together; the body upright.
Fourteenth Posture: Embrace the Tiger and Push the Mountain (抱虎推山, Bào Hǔ Tuī Shān)

Following on from the previous posture, the two hands push forward together, level with the chest, the two arms slightly bent; at the same time the left foot steps forward and the right foot follows, about 10 cm from the left foot; the eyes look between the two hands; pause briefly. (图 28)

图 28
practitioner in a forward stance with both arms extended forward at chest height, palms facing forward.

用法 (yòngfǎ) Application: if the opponent's hand is on the inside and one's hand on the outside, one wraps inward around his hand and issues; or if his hand is on the outside and one's hand on the inside, one props his hand out with opening energy (开劲) and issues. In all cases one must stick to the opponent's hand so that he cannot move freely, for otherwise, if one only knows how to lunge fiercely forward, one will certainly be taken advantage of by him. This posture is best used to strike at the opponent's trunk.

Fifteenth Posture: Opening the Hands (开手, Kāi Shǒu) — turning to the right

Following on from the previous posture, the tip of the left foot lifts and the foot turns in toward the right; the body then turns about 90° to the right and the right foot settles firmly to the ground; the two hands separate horizontally until the tiger's mouths of the two hands are the width of the shoulders apart, the five fingers spread; pause briefly. (图 29)

Sixteenth Posture: Closing the Hands (合手, Hé Shǒu)

The movement is the same as the Fourth Posture, "Closing the Hands". (图 30)

图 29
practitioner standing with feet together, both arms opened out from the body at chest height, palms turned forward.
图 32
practitioner in a side-facing stance with the right leg forward, the right arm extended forward and the left hand held low.
Seventeenth Posture: Brush the Knee and Twist the Step (搂膝拗步, Lōu Xī Ào Bù) — turning to the right

The movement is the same as the Tenth Posture, "Brush the Knee and Twist the Step", only the direction is reversed. (图 31, 32)

图 30
practitioner standing with feet together, both arms extended forward in front of the chest, palms facing inward toward each other.
Eighteenth Posture: Lazily Tucking the Robe (懒扎衣, Lǎn Zhā Yī)
  • ① Following on from the previous posture, the left hand rotates outward and inward, palm facing up, the right hand extends forward, palm facing down, the two hands forming the shape of holding a ball; at the same time the left foot steps back, coming to the ground at an angle of 45°; immediately the two hands trace an arc downward together to in front of the abdomen, and the right foot withdraws to in front of the left foot, the tip of the foot touching the ground. (图 33, 34)
图 33
practitioner in a forward stance with the left hand raised at chest height and the right hand lowered, the body turned slightly.
图 31
practitioner standing with the left leg forward and the arms held in front of the chest, the body turned to one side.
  • ② The right hand rotates inward, the left hand rotates outward and is lifted to in front of the chest, the left hand supporting the right hand...
图 34
practitioner in a stance with the right leg forward and the body turned, the left hand raised in front of the chest and the right hand extended forward and downward.

The hands push out forward together from above the wrist, the right palm facing upward and the left palm facing downward; at the same time the right foot steps forward, the left foot following up to the side of the right ankle with the toe touching the ground. (图 35)

图 35
practitioner in a forward stance, both hands held up in front of the chest, the left hand above and the right below, palms facing each other.
  • ③ The left foot then withdraws to the rear; at the same time both hands draw back level to a half-circle in front of the right shoulder, the palms facing outward; the body's weight sits back and the right toe lifts. (图 36)
图 36
practitioner with the left leg withdrawn behind, both hands drawn back at the right shoulder, palms turned outward.
  • ④ Both hands push out forward together from in front of the right shoulder, the arms slightly bent, while the right toe gradually comes to the ground and the left foot immediately follows to about 10 cm behind the right foot; the eyes look at the right hand. (图 37)
图 37
practitioner in a forward stance, both hands pushed out forward in front of the chest, the right foot forward and the left foot following behind.
Nineteenth Posture: Opening the Hands (开手, Kāi Shǒu)

The movement is the same as the Third Posture, "Opening the Hands". (图 38)

图 38
practitioner standing with feet together and body upright, both arms opened out to the sides at chest height, palms turned forward.
Twentieth Posture: Closing the Hands (合手, Hé Shǒu)
图 39
practitioner standing with feet together, both arms extended forward in front of the chest, palms facing inward toward each other.

practitioner in a wider stance with the arms opened out low to the sides, both palms turned outward.

The movement is the same as the Fourth Posture, "Closing the Hands". (图 39)

Twenty-First Posture: Single Whip (单鞭, Dān Biān)

The movement is the same as the Fifth Posture, "Single Whip". (图 40)

图 41
practitioner in a forward stance, the right arm extended forward at chest height and the left hand held at the chest.
图 44
practitioner seen from behind in a stance, one arm raised at shoulder height and the other held forward.
Twenty-Second Posture: Looking at the Fist Below the Elbow (肘下看捶, Zhǒu Xià Kàn Chuí)

Following on from the previous posture, the left hand turns downward with the thumb pointing up, and the right hand becomes a fist, the arm bending so that it passes down through the region in front of the abdomen and extends out below the left elbow with the eye of the fist facing upward; at the same time the right foot steps forward to behind the left foot, the toe touching the ground. The right foot then withdraws to the rear, and the left foot withdraws to in front of the right foot, the toe touching the ground; the two hands do not move; the eyes look forward. (图 41、42)

图 42
practitioner in a stance with the left arm held forward and the right fist brought under the left elbow.
图 45
practitioner with the body turned, both arms held in front of the chest, feet apart.

Application (用法): one strikes some part of the opponent with the left hand; the opponent uses ward-off (掤, péng). At this moment one relaxes the shoulders and drops the elbows, wrapping strength is turned inward through the arm, and at the same time one advances the step and strikes the opponent's chest with the right fist from below the left elbow.

图 43
practitioner standing upright, the left hand raised in front of the chest and the right fist held low at the left elbow.
图 46
practitioner standing with feet together, both hands held in front of the chest, one above the other.

The right fist strikes the opponent's chest from below the left elbow.

Twenty-Third Posture: Step Back and Repulse the Monkey, Left Form (倒撵猴, Dào Niǎn Hóu — 左式)
  • ① Following on from the previous posture, the left hand rotates inward and is drawn back to in front of the chest, then sweeps to the left in an arc to the outside of the left hip, the palm facing downward and the fingertips pointing forward, the thumb about 8 cm from the hip; the right hand rotates outward to the right and downward and is then raised up to shoulder height with the palm facing upward; at the same time the right toe lifts and hooks inward, the toe touching the ground; the left foot steps diagonally to the left with the heel coming to the ground; the eyes look at the right hand. (图 43)
图 47
practitioner standing with the left hand held low at the left hip and the right arm raised forward at shoulder height.
  • ② The right hand pushes out forward to the left, passing in front of the corner of the mouth, the arm slightly bent and the palm facing left; at the same time the right foot follows forward to behind the left foot at a distance of about 10 cm, the toe touching the ground. (图 44)

Key points (要点): the movements of the hands and feet must run through as a single continuous flow, without interruption.

Twenty-Fourth Posture: Step Back and Repulse the Monkey, Right Form (倒撵猴 — 右式)
  • ① Following on from the previous posture, the left toe lifts and the heel turns inward; the right hand sweeps diagonally to the right to the outside of the right hip (the thumb about 8 cm from the hip) with the palm facing downward; the left hand rotates outward and upward to the level of the left shoulder with the palm facing upward; the eyes look at the left hand. (图 45)
图 48
practitioner with the right hand held low at the right hip and the left arm raised forward at shoulder height.
  • ② The left hand then pushes out forward to the right, passing in front of the corner of the mouth; all other movements are the same as in the left form, only the direction is reversed. (图 46)

Key points (要点): practice the left and right forms in alternation; the number of repetitions is not fixed, but must be an even number.

Twenty-Fifth Posture: Hands Play the Lute, Right Form (手挥琵琶, Shǒu Huī Pí Pá — 右式)

practitioner standing with feet together, both arms curved in front of the chest at shoulder height, palms facing inward.

The movement is the same as the Eleventh Posture, "Hands Play the Lute", only the direction is reversed. (图 47)

The movement is the same as the Seventh Posture, "White Crane Spreads Its Wings". (图 48)

practitioner standing with feet together and body upright, both arms curved in front of the chest at shoulder height, palms facing inward.

Thirty-First Posture: Three Penetrations of the Back (三通背, Sān Tōng Bèi)
  • ① Following on from the previous posture, the right hand rotates outward (palm facing upward), sweeps in an arc downward and backward, and when it reaches the forehead rotates inward and presses straight down to the front of the left fibula, about 30 cm from the left toe; as the right hand sweeps backward, the left hand is drawn back to the outside of the left hip with the palm facing downward; while the right hand presses down, the left foot withdraws to in front of the right foot with the toe touching the ground, both legs slightly bent; the eyes look at the right hand. (图 55、56)
图 52
practitioner in a side-facing stance with the left leg forward and both arms extended forward at chest height.
  • ② The right arm is raised, the back of the hand resting against the forehead, the body straightening up with it, the weight inclined toward the right leg, and the left hand from the side of the hip—

—extends forward, level at chest height, the palm facing forward and the wrist sunk; at the same time the left foot steps forward, the distance between the two feet being such that the body's central equilibrium is not disturbed; the eyes look at the index finger of the left hand. (图 57)

图 53
practitioner in a forward stance, the left hand at the left knee and the right arm extended forward at chest height.
图 56
practitioner bending deeply forward with both arms reaching down toward the ground.
  • ③ The left toe lifts and hooks to the right through about 120°, while the body turns right and the right toe lifts and swings outward through about 120°; the left hand sweeps in an arc upward to the forehead; the right hand pushes out forward level at shoulder height, the palm facing forward with the wrist sunk; the eyes look at the right hand. (图 58)
图 54
practitioner in a stance with the body turned, one arm drawn low across the body and the other extended forward.
图 57
practitioner in a forward stance with the right arm raised in front of the forehead and the left arm extended forward and downward.
  • ④ The left hand extends forward from the forehead until it is level with the right hand, the two palms facing each other and the fingertips pointing forward; at the same time the right foot withdraws to directly behind the left foot and lands on a diagonal. (图 59)
图 55
practitioner in a stance with the left arm raised overhead and the body turned.
图 58
practitioner in a wide stance with the right arm extended forward at shoulder height and the left hand raised in front of the forehead.
  • ⑤ The two hands, held as loose fists, sweep downward in an arc to in front of the abdomen; at the same time the left foot withdraws to in front of the right foot, the toe touch-

...to the ground; the eyes look straight ahead. (Fig. 60)

  • ⑧ Both fists, kept close to the body, are raised to the front of the chest and then extended forward and upward, to the height of the eyebrows; at the same time the left foot steps forward and the ball of the foot lands with the toes turned outward, the weight of the body still on the right leg, with a brief pause. Immediately the fists travel in an arc downward to the front of the abdomen; the right foot steps straight forward past the left foot and the ball of the foot lands; the eyes look straight ahead. (Figs. 61, 62)
图 59
practitioner in a bow stance, left leg forward and right leg back, right arm extended forward at shoulder height with the left hand held near the chest.
图 60
practitioner standing with weight on the rear leg, torso turned, both hands held open in front of the chest at about shoulder height.
图 61
practitioner in a bow stance with both forearms raised in front of the chest and the left foot forward.

Key points (要点, yàodiǎn): above and below must move in coordination; when the left foot withdraws to a position in front of the right foot, the waist sinks downward.

Application (用法, yòngfǎ): ① If the opponent attacks with his left hand, one intercepts his wrist with one's left hand and presses his elbow with one's right hand, withdraws the step backward, and pulls him down.

  • ② If the opponent attacks one's head with his right hand, one then intercepts his wrist from below upward with one's right hand, supports his elbow with one's left hand, draws the left foot in and turns the waist to the right, and seizes and throws him off behind from above.
  • ③ If the opponent sinks his shoulder and draws in his arm, one then continues to turn the waist until facing backward, withdraws the right foot to behind the left foot, and, following the momentum of the opponent's withdrawing hand, pulls him downward and backward.
Thirty-Second Posture: Lazily Tucking the Robe (懒扎衣, Lǎn Zhā Yī)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, both hands open and lift upward (the right palm facing upward, the left palm facing downward) to the front of the right shoulder; at the same time the right foot steps forward, the left foot immediately follows to behind the right foot and the ball of the foot lands, with a brief pause, and then the step is withdrawn backward; both hands travel in a level arc backward to the front of the right shoulder, the palms facing outward; the weight of the body shifts back onto the left leg, the ball of the right foot lifts; the eyes look at the right hand. (Figs. 63, 64)
  • ② Both hands push forward together from in front of the right shoulder, the two

...the arms slightly bent, the left hand supporting the right wrist; at the same time the ball of the right foot gradually comes to the ground, and the left foot immediately follows to a position about 10 centimetres behind the right foot; the eyes look at the right hand. (Fig. 65)

Thirty-Sixth Posture: Cloud Hands (云手, Yún Shǒu)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, the left hand travels downward and in an arc to the right to below the right armpit, the palm slanted downward; at the same time the left foot moves
图 62
practitioner in a bow stance with both arms extended forward, the body leaning slightly forward.

practitioner in a bow stance with the arms curved in front of the chest, palms turned outward.

practitioner in a forward stance with the arms held level at shoulder height, the hands formed into fists.

...the right foot draws in close, the ball of the foot lands, the eyes look at the right hand, with a brief pause. (Fig. 69)

  • ② The left hand travels upward and in an arc to the left side of the body, the palm facing left and the fingertips pointing up; the right hand travels downward and in an arc to below the left armpit, the palm slanted downward; at the same time the left foot steps sideways to the left, the ball of the foot turned slightly outward, and the right foot draws in close to the left foot and lands at a distance of about 10 centimetres from it (both balls of the feet slanting slightly to the left); the eyes look at the left hand, with a brief pause. (Fig. 70)
  • ③ The right hand travels upward and in a downward arc, and the left hand travels downward and in an upward arc; the left foot steps sideways to the left and the right foot draws in close to the left foot. The cycle is repeated three times; see Figs. 69, 70.

Key points (要点, yàodiǎn): when the left and right hands travel upward in an arc, both palms face outward and rise no higher than the eyebrows; the body turns with the hands.

Application (用法, yòngfǎ): if the opponent strikes from the left or right, one immediately turns the waist and intercepts with the arm, and, following his momentum, seizes and throws him out.

Thirty-Seventh Posture: High Pat the Horse (高探马, Gāo Tàn Mǎ)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, while the two hands move from left to right in cloud-hands, the left hand travels in an arc downward to the front of the chest and is lifted slightly, the elbow kept close to the body and the tiger's mouth (虎口, hǔkǒu) facing upward; the right hand, having moved in an arc to the level of the face, drops and extends forward, the tiger's mouth facing upward, the height level with the chest, both arms slightly bent; at the same time the left foot withdraws backward and the right foot, following the right hand, lands forward in front of the left foot, the ball of the foot landing and forming a "T" shape with the left foot, both legs slightly bent; the eyes look at the right hand. (Fig. 71)

  • ① Following the preceding posture, the left hand rotates outward, the palm facing upward; the right hand rotates inward toward the body to the front of the chest, the palm facing downward; the two hands

...the palms about 10 centimetres apart, and the two hands about 6 centimetres from the chest; at the same time the ball of the right foot turns inward and the ball of the foot lands, facing the ball of the left foot; the eyes look at the right hand. (Fig. 72)

practitioner standing with the right hand pressed forward at chest height and the left hand lifted near the chest.

Left Kick (左起脚, Zuǒ Qǐ Jiǎo)

Following the preceding posture, the two hands separate as in the single-whip posture, and the left foot lifts to the left front diagonally until it touches the left hand, then immediately returns to its original position with the ball of the foot landing; at the same time the two hands perform the closing-the-hands movement, with a brief pause. (Figs. 77, 78)

Fortieth Posture: Turn the Body and Kick (转身蹬脚, Zhuǎn Shēn Dēng Jiǎo)

Following the preceding posture, the right foot and the body turn slightly to the left, and the left foot immediately kicks upward, the toes hooked back, thrusting out forward and to the left; the two hands separate so that hand and foot meet; the eyes look at the index finger of the left hand. (Fig. 79)

Forty-First Posture: Advancing Step and Strike with the Fist (践步打捶, Jiàn Bù Dǎ Chuí)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, the left foot lands forward with the ball of the foot turned outward; at the same time the left hand sweeps back in front of the left hip, the palm facing downward; the right hand extends downward and forward, the palm facing upward, with a brief pause. (Fig. 80)
  • ② The right foot steps forward past the left foot, the ball of the foot turned outward; at the same time the left hand extends forward, the palm facing upward; the right hand draws back to the front of the chest, the palm facing downward, with a brief pause. (Fig. 81)
  • ③ The left foot steps forward, the ball of the foot turned inward; at the same time the left hand rotates inward and changes into a fist, pulling down to the front of the left hip; the right hand rotates outward and changes into a fist, travels in an arc backward, upward and forward, and strikes out past the forehead toward the inside of the left ankle; the body follows downward, the left leg bending at the knee and the right leg slightly bowed; the eyes look at the right hand. (Figs. 82, 83)

Key points (要点, yàodiǎn): the movements must run through in one continuous flow; the waist must be kept sunken; the eyes follow the hands.

图 77
practitioner balancing on the right leg with the left leg raised to the side, both arms opened out to the sides.
图 78
practitioner with the left leg raised in front and both hands held together before the chest.
图 79
practitioner balancing on the right leg with the left leg extended forward at hip height, both arms opened out to the sides.

Application (用法, yòngfǎ): if the opponent crouches and strikes one's lower body, ...such as advancing the step and striking the crotch with the fist (进步指裆捶, jìn bù zhǐ dāng chuí), or grabs my left foot, then I immediately sweep it aside with my left hand and strike down from above with my right fist.

Forty-Second Posture: Turn the Body and Right Kick (翻身右起脚, Fān Shēn Yòu Qǐ Jiǎo)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, the left foot turns inward; at the same time the right fist travels upward past the forehead and then carves an arc forward, the centre of the fist facing upward, and the body turns 180° to the right along with it; the left fist is then withdrawn downward and backward to the front of the right hip; the right foot turns slightly outward. (Figs. 84, 85)
  • ② The left hand travels from the side of the left hip upward past the face and sweeps downward in front of the chest, stopping at the outer side; the right fist changes into a palm and extends upward and forward, the palm facing outward; at the same time the left foot steps forward, the toes turned slightly outward; the right foot lifts and kicks forward, the right hand slaps the top of the right foot, at the height of the chest; the eyes look at the right hand. (Figs. 86, 87)

Application (用法, yòngfǎ): if the opponent

...strikes at me from the right, then I immediately turn the body to the right and intercept the opponent's hand with my right hand, and at once kick at him with the left foot; at the same moment that the left foot lands I raise the right foot and kick, and this is why it is called the "two raises" (二起, èr qǐ).

Forty-Third Posture: Drape the Body and Subdue the Tiger (披身伏虎, Pī Shēn Fú Hǔ)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, the right foot withdraws a step to behind the left foot; at the same time the left hand extends forward, the two palms facing each other as though cradling a ball, and the waist sinks downward, with a brief pause. (Fig. 88)
  • ② The left foot withdraws one step backward; the two hands change into fists, draw back downward, and pass by the side of the left hip, carving an arc backward, upward and then downward to the front of the abdomen, with a brief pause; at the same time the tip of the right foot lifts and swings straight to the left; the left foot turns slightly inward. (Figs. 89, 90)

Key points (要点, yàodiǎn): the two hands are drawn back without stopping.

Application (用法, yòngfǎ): if the opponent grips both my wrists with both hands, ...I withdraw the step to the left, and turning the waist to the right swing both arms free. This posture is likewise a kind of throwing method. If the opponent grips both my wrists, or I grip both of his wrists, I withdraw the right foot backward and draw his two arms backward and downward; then hook the left foot inward, turn the body to the right, and swing both hands upward above the head, so that the opponent's two arms pass over my left shoulder and his body is carried on my back.

Forty-Fourth Posture: Left Kick (左起脚, Zuǒ Qǐ Jiǎo)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, the two fists change into palms and are lifted to the front of the chest as in the closing-the-hands movement; at the same time the right leg lifts slightly, the toes turned outward, and lands obliquely; the left knee bends slightly and comes close to the inner side of the right leg, the tip of the foot touching the ground; both legs are bent; the eyes look straight ahead, with a brief pause. (Fig. 91)
  • ② The two hands separate as in the single-whip posture; at the same time the left

Forty-Fifth Posture: Turn the Body and Right Heel Kick (转身右蹬脚, Zhuǎn Shēn Yòu Dēng Jiǎo)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, the left foot is drawn back and the knee raised, and the body turns 270° to the right; then the left foot descends to the outer side of the right foot; the right heel lifts and twists round until it faces the tip of the left foot; at the same time the two hands come together as in the closing-the-hands movement. (Figs. 93, 94)
  • ② The body then turns slightly to the right, the right foot turns slightly outward, and the two hands separate left and right as in the single-whip posture; at the same time the right foot thrusts out in a heel kick; the eyes look at the index finger of the right hand. (Fig. 95)

Application (用法, yòngfǎ): if the opponent strikes at my head with a hook punch (single peak pierces the ear, 单峰贯耳, dān fēng guàn ěr), I raise my hand to intercept it, and at the same time lift the foot and kick at the opponent's abdomen. Hand and foot must issue together before the opponent can be subdued.

Forty-Third Posture: Step Up, Parry, Intercept and Punch (上步搬拦捶, Shàng Bù Bān Lán Chuí)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, the right foot descends to the front of the left foot, the toes turned outward; at the same time the left hand extends downward and forward, the palm facing upward; the right hand sweeps back to the front of the right ribs, the palm facing downward. (Fig. 96)
  • ② The left foot steps up, the tip of the foot kept straight; at the same time the left hand rotates inward, the palm facing downward, and the two hands immediately change into fists; the right fist strikes out forward, the eye of the fist facing upward, and the left fist is drawn back beneath the right elbow, the centre of the fist facing downward; the right foot follows up to behind the left foot, the tip of the foot touching the ground; the eyes look at the right fist. (Figs. 97, 98)

Fifty-Sixth Posture: Parting the Wild Horse's Mane (野马分鬃, Yě Mǎ Fēn Zōng)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, the left foot draws in beside the right foot, the whole sole on the ground; at the same time the left hand sweeps downward in an arc to the front of the abdomen; the eyes look at the right hand. (Fig. 114)
  • ② The left hand goes upward past the chest and then sweeps in an arc to the left to the left side of the body; at the same time the left foot steps out to the left, the tip of the foot turned slightly outward; the eyes look at the left hand. (Fig. 115)
  • ③ The right hand sweeps downward in an arc to the front of the abdomen, then upward past the face and in an arc to the right to the right side of the body; at the same time the right foot draws in beside the left foot (the tip of the foot touching the ground, the two feet about 10 cm apart), and then steps out one pace to the right; at this point the single-whip posture is resumed, but the weight is biased toward the right leg. (Figs. 116, 117)
  • ④ The left foot steps forward in front of the right foot, the tip of the foot turned outward and set down diagonally, the two legs bent; at the same time the two hands go downward and cross in front (the palms turned slightly outward, the left hand above, the right hand below, the two arms slightly curved), and immediately separate to left and right, each drawing a circle to the front of the chest, the right palm facing upward, the left palm facing downward; the eyes look at the lower front. (Figs. 118, 119)
Fifty-Seventh Posture: Lazily Tucking in the Robe (懒扎衣, Lǎn Zhā Yī)
  • ① Following the preceding posture, the right foot steps forward; the left foot then follows up behind the right foot, the tip of the foot touching the ground, pausing briefly and then withdrawing; at the same time the weight of the body shifts to the left leg, the tip of the right foot raised; the left hand supports the right wrist and the two push forward together (the right palm facing upward, the left palm facing downward), then wind level to the right and to the rear to the front of the right shoulder, both palms facing outward. (Figs. 120, 121, 122)
  • ② The two hands push forward together; the left foot follows up to about 10 cm behind the right foot, the tip of the foot touching the ground; the eyes look at the index finger of the right hand. (Fig. 123)

Following the preceding posture, the left hand goes upward and to the right in an arc until the back of the hand presses against the forehead; the body turns to the right, and the raised tip of the left foot turns to the right along with it. At the same time the right foot swings outward, its tip turned slightly inward, and the right hand keeps its wrist sunk and does not move; the eyes look at the index finger of the right hand. Sixty-Second Posture: The Jade Maiden Works the Shuttle (玉女穿梭, Yù Nǚ Chuān Suō)

(Fig. 128)

Sixty-Eighth Posture: Cloud Hands Lower Posture (云手下式, Yún Shǒu Xià Shì)

Continuing from the previous posture, when the two hands have moved to the right side, the right palm turns over to face upward and pushes forward level, the wrist sinking; the left hand still moves upward in an arc to the front of the left hip; at the same time the right foot follows up behind the left foot. Then the left hand pushes forward from the back of the right hand, the wrist sinking, the palm facing obliquely forward; the right hand draws back to the side of the right hip, the palm facing downward; the left foot steps forward, both legs bent; the weight of the body shifts onto the right leg; the eyes look at the left hand. (Fig. 147, 148, 149)

Sixty-Ninth Posture: Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg (金鸡独立, Jīn Jī Dú Lì)
  • ① Continuing from the previous posture, the weight of the body shifts forward; the right hand is lifted forward and upward from the side of the right hip to beside the ear, the fingertips level with the ear; the left hand moves downward in an arc to the side of the left hip, the fingertips pointing down; at the same time the right leg, close against the left leg, is lifted upward to a right angle with the body, the tip of the foot tilted up, the heel pressing down; the left leg is slightly bent, the waist sunk (塌腰, tā yāo); the eyes look forward, with a slight pause. (Fig. 150, 151)
  • ② The right foot comes down forward, the leg still bent; at the same time the right hand moves downward in an arc to the side of the right hip, the fingertips pointing down; the left hand goes upward from the side of the left hip to beside the ear, the fingertips level with the ear; the left leg, close against the right leg, is lifted upward. (Fig. 152)

  • ① Following on from the previous posture, the heel of the right foot lifts, the body turns 360° to the right, and when it has turned to face southwest the left foot lands, the tips of the two feet facing each other; immediately the tip of the left foot turns up and twists to the right; the right foot is lifted and swung out to the right; the two hands trace an arc upward and to the right and, when they reach the right front, strike against the right knee (the left hand strikes first, the right hand after); the eyes look at the right leg. Ninety-Fourth Posture: Bending the Bow to Shoot the Tiger (弯弓射虎, Wān Gōng Shè Hǔ)

Following on from the previous posture, the two hands extend forward at the same time; in the course of extending, the two hands rotate inward, both palms facing down, level with the shoulders, the two arms slightly bent; the weight of the body shifts forward onto the right leg along with the movement; the eyes look between the two hands. (Fig. 201)

Application (用法): if the opponent strikes with the left hand, one advances the right foot toward the opponent's left side and at the same time intercepts the incoming hand with both hands, wraps it and presses it downward to drain its force, and then strikes at the opponent's chest. The key to this posture lies in the joining of the hands and the advance of the step being as one.

Ninety-Fifth Posture: Double Thrusting Punch (双撞捶, Shuāng Zhuàng Chuí)

Application (用法): suppose both hands press forward and the opponent presses down with both hands; one then follows the momentum and separates the hands downward, and, passing around the outside of the opponent's two arms, strikes up at the chest.
