Part Two (下编, Xià Biān)

Book page 703

1. The Push-Hands Method of Taijiquan (太极拳推手法, Tàijíquán Tuīshǒu Fǎ)

1. The Push-Hands Method of Taijiquan (太极拳推手法, Tàijíquán Tuīshǒu Fǎ)

Every martial art contains two parts, "substance" (体, tǐ) and "application" (用, yòng), and substance and application are mutually connected; Taijiquan is no exception. The various postures of the Taijiquan form are the substance, the art of knowing oneself (知己功, zhī jǐ gōng); although application is present within them, in solo practice it is not easy to experience the methods and the subtle excellences of application, and hence there is Taijiquan push-hands (推手, tuī shǒu) in order to put the art to use.

Taijiquan push-hands takes the practice of application as its main concern and seeks the gateway to effective use. Its methods of use comprise the eight methods (八法, bā fǎ): warding-off (掤, bīng), rolling-back (捋, lǚ), pressing (挤, jǐ), pushing (按, àn), plucking (采, cǎi), rending (挒, liè), elbowing (肘, zhǒu), and leaning (靠, kào); among the eight methods, the four hands (四手, sì shǒu) of warding-off, rolling-back, pressing and pushing are the foundation. In beginning push-hands one must first take the "four hands" as the basic method of practice, drilling them repeatedly and experiencing them with care, until one has trained to the point of adhering, joining, sticking and following (粘连黏随, zhān nián nián suí), neither losing contact nor resisting (不丢不顶, bù diū bù dǐng), with hands and feet nimble and measured, able to judge accurately the magnitude of the opponent's force (劲, jìn); only then can one attain the effects of "leading the opponent in to fall into emptiness" (引进落空, yǐn jìn luò kōng) and "moving a thousand catties with a pull of four ounces" (牵动四两拨千斤, qiān dòng sì liǎng bō qiān jīn). Plucking, rending, elbowing and leaning, and all the various hand techniques, emerge as transformations from within these. At this point one is able to make the whole body insubstantial and numinous, round and lively without obstruction, and infinitely variable — something that brush and ink cannot fully set forth.

The footwork of push-hands comprises static (fixed) step, moving (live) step, joined step, and following step, and so on. A beginner at push-hands should take the static step as the root; only after the static step is proficient does one practise the moving step. In the course of this, joined step and following step may both be used, giving four kinds: static step (joined, following) and moving step (joined, following).

1. The Static-Step Push-Hands Method (静步推手法, Jìng Bù Tuī Shǒu Fǎ)

（1）Starting Posture (起式, qǐ shì) (the woman is A, the man is B)

  • ① A and B stand facing each other, about two paces apart. (Fig. 一)
  • ② A and B each advance the left foot, the left hand in front with the palm facing backward, the right hand resting on the left forearm, the right wrist about 15 cm from the chest. (Fig. 二)

（2）A presses (挤, jǐ) and B rolls back (捋, lǚ)

A first presses his right hand toward B's face. B at once lightly catches A's right wrist with his right hand, while his left hand passes from beneath A's right arm up and over and lightly catches A's right elbow, and the two hands together thrust (擩, rǔ) diagonally to the right.

A then straightens the right arm and wraps the wrist inward until the palm faces inward; at the same time the left hand presses toward his own right forearm, the eyes looking at B. (Fig. 三)

（3）B rolls back and pushes (按, àn)

While A is using the press, B draws both hands back along with the body, neither losing contact nor resisting, with the tip of the front foot turned up; only after A has brought out his strength does B push.

B then pushes both hands toward A's left arm, the left hand pressing on the back of A's left hand, the right hand pressing A's left elbow. (Fig. 四, 五)

（4）A rolls back and B presses

When B's two hands come pushing in, A shrinks his body backward, and at the same time his left hand lightly catches B's right wrist, while his right hand turns upward from beneath B's left arm and also lightly catches B's left elbow, and the two hands together thrust diagonally to the left.

B then straightens the left arm and wraps the wrist inward until the palm faces inward, and at the same time the right hand presses toward his own left forearm, the eyes looking into A's eyes. (Fig. 六)

图 209
A and B stand facing each other, about two paces apart. (The book prints this as "Fig. 一".)
图 210
A and B each advance the left foot, left hand in front, the right hand resting on the left forearm. (The book prints this as "Fig. 二".)
图 211
A presses his right hand toward B's face; B's two hands catch A's right wrist and right elbow and thrust diagonally. (The book prints this as "Fig. 三".)

In the order given above, the pushing is carried on in a continuous cycle.

（5）The method of changing sides in push-hands

To change from the left-side form to the right-side form (that is, with A and B each having the right foot in front), when B uses the thrust, A (not using the press) leads B's right hand backward with his own right hand and winds his left hand over B's right elbow, and at the same time withdraws the left foot to behind the right foot, just as in the thrust of the left-side form; B then advances the right foot and uses the press. A thrusts and pushes again, B thrusts again, and the drill is repeated in a cycle. This is the method of changing sides for a beginner at push-hands. Once it is familiar, the change may be made at will.

2. The Live-Step Push-Hands Method (活步推手法, Huó Bù Tuī Shǒu Fǎ)

The hand technique is the same as in the static step, except that in stepping forward one advances the front foot first, and in stepping backward one withdraws the back foot first. Both the advance and the retreat are of three steps. The footwork must be coordinated and as one with the hand technique; the advance is the two forms of push and press, the retreat is the two forms of thrust and thrust, drilled in a cycle. These are the forms for a beginner's entry into the art; once familiar, one can of oneself respond to the moment and adapt, and is no longer bound by fixed methods.

3. Plucking, Rending, Elbowing, Leaning (采、挒、肘、靠, Cǎi, Liè, Zhǒu, Kào)

Warding-off, rolling-back, pressing and pushing are the four cardinal directions (四正, sì zhèng). Plucking, rending, elbowing and leaning are the four corners (四隅, sì yú). The four corners are also called the great roll-back (大捋, dà lǚ).

Plucking means to pluck and hold the opponent's hand, so that it is not easy for him to change.

Rending means to rend the opponent open with the palm, so that he loses his centre of gravity and the direction of his force is changed or broken off. But one must on no account grip the opponent's arm and drag at it with dead strength, for this loses the intent and one is then controlled by the other.

图 212
A and B each advance the left foot, the right hand resting on the left forearm, while B's two hands catch A's right arm. (The book prints this as "Fig. 四".)
图 213
A and B with the right foot in front, joining right hands, the left hand resting on the right forearm. (The book prints this as "Fig. 五".)
图 214
A and B with the right foot in front, the hands crossed, A pressing toward B with the right arm. (The book prints this as "Fig. 六".)

Elbowing (肘, zhǒu) means to drive the elbow against the opponent.

Leaning (靠, kào) means to press and lean against the opponent with the shoulder.

The footwork of the great roll-back is a wide and swift stride; only when the two legs have skill can one be nimble and changeable.

4. The Use of Force and the Listening to Force in Push-Hands (推手的用劲和听劲, Tuī Shǒu de Yòng Jìn hé Tīng Jìn)

In beginning push-hands one must not use clumsy strength, but must seek out the secret within the four words warding-off, rolling-back, pressing and pushing; these four words contain infinite transformations, and the student must experience them deeply.

For example: warding-off has the distinctions of straight warding-off and lateral warding-off, above and below. In rolling back one must stick to the opponent's hand, then immediately change direction and trace a circle, so that the opponent's force cannot issue forth, or if it issues forth is at once dissolved.

Warding-off is divided into upward, downward and level warding-off. In thrusting, one hand must press and hold the opponent's wrist and the other hand press the opponent's elbow, so that the opponent has no room to move and is thrust out along the line of his own force. Again, within the thrust there is also a warding-off force, which should not be used lightly.

Pressing has various methods: straight pressing, slanting pressing, and pressing with the addition of the elbow. If one presses with the arm along a curve, one can change the point of force at any moment and with any configuration, and force may be issued from any place.

Pushing includes lightness and nimbleness or heaviness and solidity, left solid and right empty or right solid and left empty, the two hands opening or closing; in sum, one must change according to the configuration.

When two people drill push-hands together, besides attending to experiencing the methods of using force, one must accomplish bending and extending in accord with the other, neither losing contact nor resisting, not using clumsy strength, calming the mind and listening to force. In time, one can lead the opponent in to fall into emptiness and move a thousand catties with a pull of four ounces.

As for "listening to force" (听劲, tīng jìn), one must on no account mistake it for two parties opposing each other with strength. One commonly sees, in push-hands, two people locking strength against each other, one asking whether the other has force yet, the other answering that he has or has not — this is a great error. "Listening to force" is to sense the magnitude and direction of the opponent's applied force and so change at once; one must on no account lock against it. In beginning practice, train the two arms first; with long practice the whole body can sense it. If one can listen to force, then when the opponent issues force one can dissolve it and make him fall into emptiness. If one cannot listen to force, one need not measure oneself against others; the student must certainly attend to this.

Book page 707

2. The Martial Application of Taijiquan (太极拳技击, Tàijíquán Jì Jī)

2. The Martial Application of Taijiquan (太极拳技击, Tàijíquán Jì Jī)

The martial application of Taijiquan is nothing other than the eight methods: warding-off, rolling-back, pressing, pushing, plucking, rending, elbowing and leaning. These eight methods are all contained within the Taijiquan form; push-hands is the practising of these eight methods for use. At present, whether one practises the form or practises push-hands, both are the familiarising of these eight methods, and so it is said that the eight methods are the application of Taijiquan. But to practise the form alone is to have substance without application, and its defect lies in having no change. To practise push-hands alone is to have application without substance, and its defect lies in having no root. If one practises only for the cultivation of body and mind, then practising the form is already sufficient; but if one wishes to obtain its application, one must practise both.

In terms of practising substance, Taijiquan is the art of knowing oneself (知己功夫, zhī jǐ gōng fu); only after long and thoroughly proficient practice can one make the whole body insubstantial and numinous, round and lively without obstruction, heavy and still as Mount Tai, light and nimble as a feather, with spirit (神, shén) and vital energy (气, qì) blended and fused, whereby one may of oneself dispel illness and prolong life. In terms of practising application, it is the art of knowing others (知人功夫, zhī rén gōng fu); only after long practice with pure skill can the hands and feet be nimble and alive, leading the opponent in to fall into emptiness and moving a thousand catties with a pull of four ounces. Hence only by practising both substance and application does one come to know oneself and know others; if one cannot know oneself and know others, one cannot measure oneself against others. One commonly sees those who claim to study only "martial application": using force for the sake of using force, they must apply clumsy strength, and so enter a wrong road. The student is asked to guard against this.

To become proficient in the martial application of Taijiquan, one should take the practice of the form as the main thing and seek skill from the waist and legs. For martial application first demands quick reaction; to react quickly one must have each single hand and each single posture thoroughly proficient, with waist and legs nimble and strong, before one can respond to the opponent with lightness, nimbleness, roundness and liveliness. Further, one must be able to "listen to force", for only thus can one stick to the opponent, respond to the moment and adapt, hear one and know a hundred, and change without limit.

In Part One the methods of use of some of the postures have been outlined, but the student must not memorise them by rote and rigidly. One should make the form proficient and practise push-hands diligently. In beginning the static-step push-hands, the work lies mainly in the waist; when the waist is extremely nimble, one has more than enough for dissolving the opponent's force. Once proficient, one practises the moving-step push-hands, where the work lies mainly in the legs; when the skill is pure, one advances, retreats and changes direction swiftly. Thereafter one goes through the four corners, and after that the free hand (散手, sàn shǒu). The two parties may then disregard the rules and attack and dissolve at will, each against the other.

In sum, the martial application of Taijiquan — that is, free hand — has no fixed rule or method, but changes at any time and in any configuration as the opportunity arises; this is the meaning of the saying that free hand has no fixed forms. A single posture in the art may be used in several ways, and several postures may be used as one, but one must always weigh the time and gauge the configuration before acting. Exactly as the classic says, "When the other does not move, "I do not move; if the opponent moves, I move first." This is what is meant by "the intent (意, yì) precedes the enemy." That is to say: however fierce and swift the opponent's action, one can dissolve it and turn it to one's own use. One must not wait for the opponent's technique to land upon one's own body; nor may one always use a single technique, for without change one is controlled by others. It is hoped that the student will draw inferences from one instance to three, know the applications without being bound by the applications, and diligently practise push-hands; then one may attain the mystery of Taijiquan as a fighting art. Appendix: Reference Materials I. Wang Zongyue: A Treatise on Taijiquan Taiji (太极, Tàijí) is born of Wuji (无极, Wújí); it is the mechanism of movement and stillness, the mother of yin and yang (阴阳, yīn yáng). When moved, they separate; when still, they unite. Neither excess nor deficiency — follow the bend and yield the extension. When the opponent is hard and I am soft, this is called "yielding" (走); when I am favourable and the opponent adverse, this is called "sticking" (黏). If he moves quickly, respond quickly; if he moves slowly, follow slowly. Though the transformations are countless, the principle is one throughout. From familiarity with the techniques one gradually awakens to "understanding energy" (懂劲, dǒng jìn); from understanding energy one ascends step by step to spiritual clarity (神明, shén míng). Yet without long effort one cannot suddenly penetrate it. With an insubstantial and numinous uplifting of the crown (虚灵顶劲, xū líng dǐng jìn), the qi (气) sinks to the elixir field (丹田, dāntián). Neither leaning nor inclining, now hidden, now appearing. Where the left is heavy, the left is made empty; where the right is heavy, the right is made obscure. Raise it and it becomes higher still; lower it and it becomes deeper still. Advance upon it and it grows longer; retreat from it and it grows more urgent. Not a feather may be added, not a fly may alight. Others do not know me; I alone know others. The hero who meets no match wherever he turns attains this through nothing else. There are many side doors to this art; though the postures differ, they come to no more than the strong bullying the weak and the slow yielding to the fast. Strength beating weakness, a slow hand yielding to a fast hand — all of these are inborn natural abilities, and have nothing to do with what is achieved by study. Consider the saying "four ounces deflect a thousand catties": it is plain that this is not a victory of force. Observe the form whereby the aged can hold off a crowd: what can speed do there? Stand like a balance, move like a wheel. Lean to one side and you follow; double-weight (双重, shuāng zhòng) and you stagnate. One often sees those whose pure effort of many years cannot transform — all are controlled by others and in the end cannot control others; this is simply that the fault of double-weighting has not been understood. To avoid this fault one must know yin and yang. Sticking is yielding, and yielding is sticking. Yin does not depart from yang, yang does not depart from yin; only when yin and yang aid each other is there understanding of energy. After understanding energy, the more one practises the finer one becomes; silently recognizing and pondering, one gradually arrives at "doing as the heart desires." The root is to "give up oneself and follow others" (舍己从人, shě jǐ cóng rén); most mistake it by giving up the near to seek the far. As it is said, "a hairsbreadth's difference, and the error is a thousand li" — the student must not fail to examine this with care.

Long Boxing (长拳, cháng quán) is like the great Yangtze and Yellow Rivers, flowing on without cease. The Thirteen Postures (十三势, shísān shì) are: warding-off (掤, bēng), roll-back (捋, lǚ), press (挤, jǐ), push (按, àn), pluck (采, cǎi), rend (挒, liè), elbow (肘, zhǒu), lean (靠, kào) — these are the eight trigrams; and advancing step, retreating step, leftward looking, rightward glancing and central equilibrium — these are the five phases. Taken together they make the Thirteen Postures. Warding-off, roll-back, press and push correspond to Kan, Li, Zhen and Dui — the four cardinal directions; pluck, rend, elbow and lean correspond to Qian, Gen, Xun and Kun — the four diagonal corners; advance, retreat, look, glance and settle correspond to metal, wood, water, fire and earth.

II. Wu Yuxiang: A Treatise on Taijiquan

Before heaven and earth existed, within the infinite void, there was one undifferentiated qi — this is Wuji, and Wuji gives rise to Taiji. Taiji is the root of heaven and earth, the origin of all things. In Taijiquan, as soon as there is the slightest movement, the whole body must be light and nimble, and above all threaded through. The qi should be stirred and agitated; the spirit (神, shén) should be gathered inward. Let there be no place of defect, no place of bulge or hollow, no place of break or interruption. The root is in the feet, issued through the legs, commanded by the waist (腰, yāo), and expressed in the fingers. From foot to leg to waist, there must always be one complete qi. Only then, advancing and retreating, can one seize the moment and the configuration. If there is any place where one fails to seize the moment and configuration, the body becomes scattered. The fault for this must be sought in the waist and legs. This holds above and below, before and behind, left and right. All of this lies in the intent (意), not outside but within. Where there is above there is below; where there is front there is back; where there is left there is right — if the intent is to rise, then a downward intent is lodged within it. It is like lifting up an object while adding to it the intent of filing it down. Then its root is severed of itself, and one may push it and hasten it without obstruction. Empty and full (虚实, xū shí) must be clearly distinguished. Each place has its own empty and full; every place is altogether this one empty and full. The whole body is threaded joint by joint, with not the slightest hair's-breadth of interruption permitted. (Original note: these were the bequeathed teachings of the venerated Master Zhang Sanfeng of Wudang Mountain, wishing that heroes under heaven might prolong their years and increase their longevity, and not merely make of it the least of the martial arts.)

III. An Explanation of the Heart of Practice in the Thirteen Postures Use the heart to move the qi (以心行气, yǐ xīn xíng qì); one must make it sink and settle, for only then can it be gathered and drawn into the bones. Use the qi to move the body; one must make it smooth and compliant, for only then can it be convenient and follow the heart. If the spirit of vitality can be raised, there is no fear of sluggishness and heaviness — this is what is called the suspended crown (顶头悬, dǐng tóu xuán). The intent and the qi must be changed with nimbleness, for only then is there the delight of roundness and liveliness — this is what is called the transformation of empty and full. In issuing energy (发劲, fā jìn) one must sink and settle, be relaxed and still, and concentrate upon one direction. In standing the body one must be centred, upright, at ease and comfortable, supporting the eight directions; in moving the qi, be like a pearl of nine turnings, with no minute place unreached; in moving, be like steel a hundred times refined, with no hardness it cannot break. In form, like a falcon striking a rabbit; in spirit, like a cat catching a mouse. Still, like a mountain; moving, like a river. Storing energy (蓄劲, is like drawing a bow; issuing energy is like loosing an arrow. Seek the straight within the curved; store and then issue. Force issues from the spine (脊, jǐ); the step changes with the body. Gathering is issuing, and issuing is gathering; broken and then reconnected, going and returning must have folding, advancing and retreating must have conversion. Utterly soft, and thereafter utterly hard; able to breathe, and thereafter able to be nimble. The qi is nourished by straightness and so does no harm; energy is stored by curving and so has surplus. The heart is the command, the qi the banner, the waist the great standard. First seek expansion, then seek compactness, and only then does one arrive at fine closeness.

It is also said: first in the heart, afterward in the body; the belly is relaxed and clean, the qi is gathered into the marrow of the bones. The spirit at ease, the body still — this must be in the heart at every moment. Remember firmly: when one thing moves, there is nothing that does not move; when one thing is still, there is nothing that is not still. In pulling and moving to and fro, the qi clings to the back and is gathered into the spinal bones. Inwardly consolidate the spirit; outwardly show ease and rest. Step like a cat walking; move energy like drawing silk. In the whole body the intent lies in the spirit, not in the qi; to be in the qi is to stagnate. Where there is qi it drags force along; where there is no qi it is purely hard — qi is like the wheel, the waist is like the axle.

IV. Verse of the Thirteen Postures

Do not lightly regard the thirteen general postures; The source of life and intent lies in the hollow of the waist. In changing and turning empty and full, take care; Let the qi pervade the body without the least stagnation. In stillness, touched, one moves, yet moving is still as before; Changing according to the opponent, one shows the marvellous. In every posture keep the heart, weigh and use intent; What is attained is won without noticing the effort spent. At every moment keep the heart upon the waist; Within the belly, relaxed and clean, the qi rises up. With the tailbone centred, the spirit runs through the crown; The whole body light and nimble, the crown suspended. Attend with care and seek it out in push-hands; Bending and extending, opening and closing, follow what is natural. To enter the gate and find the road, an oral transmission is needed; The exercise never ceases, and the method is self-cultivated. If you ask what standard governs substance and function: Intent and qi are the ruler, bone and flesh the minister. Consider what the use of intent finally comes to — Prolonging life and lengthening years, a spring that does not age. Sing it, sing it — a hundred and forty words; Every word is true and exact, the meaning leaves nothing out. If you do not seek it out in this direction, Your effort is wasted, and you will be left lamenting.

V. Verse of Push-Hands

Warding-off, roll-back, press and push must be taken in earnest; Above and below following one another, the opponent finds it hard to enter. Let him come at me with giant force; A pull of four ounces deflects a thousand catties. Draw him in to fall into emptiness, and issue as he closes; Stick, connect, continue, follow — neither losing contact nor butting.

VI. Li Yiyu: The Five-Word Formula

Stillness of Heart

If the heart is not still, it is not single-minded: as soon as one raises a hand, front and back, left and right, there is no fixed direction at all — hence the need for stillness of heart. At first one's movements cannot be governed by oneself; one must calm the heart and experience it in the body, moving as the other moves, following the bend and yielding the extension, neither losing contact nor butting, and not shortening or lengthening of oneself. If he has force, I also have force, and my force is first; if he has no force, I also have force, and my intent is still first. One must keep watch at every moment: wherever contact is made, the heart must be applied there, and one must seek the news within "neither losing contact nor butting." Working on from this, with days and months accumulated, one can then apply it in the body; this is entirely the use of intent, not the use of strength, and in time others are controlled by me, and I am not controlled by others.

Nimbleness of Body

If the body is sluggish, one cannot advance and retreat freely — hence the need for nimbleness of body. In raising a hand there must be no appearance of dullness; no sooner does his force begin to intrude upon my skin than my intent has already entered into his bones. The two hands prop each other up, one qi threaded through. When the left is heavy, the left is made empty, and the right has already gone; when the right is heavy, the right is made empty, and the left has already gone. The qi is like a wheel, and the whole body must follow along with it. Where there is any place that does not follow, the body becomes scattered and loses its power; the fault is to be sought in the waist and legs. First use the heart to command the body, following others and not oneself; afterward bring the body to follow the heart, so that although from oneself it still follows others. From oneself, one stagnates; following others, one lives. If one can follow others, the hands have measure. Measure the size of his energy, and not a fraction is mistaken; weigh the length of his coming, and not a hair's-breadth is off. Advancing and retreating, every place fits exactly. The longer the practice, the finer the skill.

Gathering of Qi

If the qi's force is scattered and diffuse, there is no containment; the body is easily disordered — one must make the qi gather into the spinal bones. Breathing becomes penetrating and numinous, with no gap anywhere in the body. The in-breath is closing (合, hé) and storing (蓄, xù); the out-breath is opening (开, kāi) and issuing (发, fā). For the in-breath can naturally lift up, and can also lift a person up; the out-breath can naturally sink down, and can also send a person out. This is to move the qi by intent, not to move the qi by strength.

Whole Energy The energy of the whole body is trained into a single family. Distinguish clearly between empty and full, and the issuing of energy must have a root. Energy rises from the heels, is governed at the waist, takes form in the fingers, and issues from the spine. Further, one must raise up the whole of one's spirit: at the moment when his energy is about to come out but has not yet issued, my energy has already joined his energy, exactly neither after nor before — like skin catching fire, like a spring gushing forth. Advancing and retreating, there is not the slightest scattering or disorder. Seek the straight within the curved; store and then issue — only thus does it take effect as the hand moves. This is called borrowing force to strike the man, four ounces deflecting a thousand catties.

Gathering of Spirit

When the preceding four are all complete, they return altogether to the gathering of spirit (神聚, shén jù). When the spirit is gathered, then the one qi is forged and smelted. Train the qi to return to the spirit, and the momentum of the qi shifts and manoeuvres. The spirit is poured in continuously; opening and closing have their proper order, and empty and full are clear. When the left is empty, the right is full; when the right is empty, the left is full. Empty is not being wholly without force — the momentum of the qi must be able to shift and manoeuvre. Full is not occupying everything to the death — the spirit must value continuous pouring in. The essential point lies entirely in the chest and the waist; the application is not on the outside. Force is borrowed from the other; qi issues from the spine. How can qi issue from the spine? The qi sinks downward, and from the two shoulders is gathered into the spinal bones and poured into the waist — this is the qi going from above to below, and is called closing (合, hé). From the waist it takes form in the spinal bones, spreads to the two arms, and is applied at the fingers — this is the qi going from below to above, and is called opening (开, kāi). Closing is gathering; opening is issuing. If one can understand opening and closing, one knows yin and yang. On reaching this stage, one day of practice brings one day of refinement in skill, until gradually one follows the heart's desire and nothing fails to accord with one's intent.

VII. Secret Formula of Release and Discharge

The Four Words: Lifting, Drawing, Loosening, Releasing

Lifting opens his energy and borrows his force — within it is the word ling (灵, numinous). Drawing him to the front of the body, his energy then begins to store — within it is the word lian (敛, gathering). Loosening my own energy, do not let it bend — within it is the word jing (静, stillness). At the release, the waist and feet must recognize the target — within it is the word zheng (整, wholeness).

VIII. Essential Words on Practising the Form and Practising the Hands The men of old said: if one can draw the other in to fall into emptiness, one can then four ounces deflect a thousand catties; if one cannot draw the other in to fall into emptiness, one cannot four ounces deflect a thousand catties. The saying is very summary; the beginner has no way to grasp it. I add several phrases to explain it, so that those who have the will for this art may have a point of entry, and so advance a little each day in achievement. If one wishes to draw [the other] in to fall into emptiness and four ounces deflect a thousand catties, one must first know oneself and know the other. If one wishes to know oneself and know the other, one must first give up oneself and follow the other. If one wishes to give up oneself and follow the other, one must first gain the opportunity and gain the position. If one wishes to gain the opportunity and gain the position, one must first make the whole body one family. If one wishes to make the whole body one family, one must first have no flaw anywhere in the whole body. If one wishes to have no flaw anywhere in the whole body, one must first have spirit and qi drumming and surging. If one wishes to have spirit and qi drumming and surging, one must first raise up the spirit. If one wishes to raise up the spirit, one must first keep the spirit from scattering outward. If one wishes to keep the spirit from scattering outward, one must first gather spirit and qi into the bones. If one wishes to gather spirit and qi into the bones, one must first have strength in the front section of the two legs. The two shoulders loosen and open, the qi sinks downward, energy rises from the heels, exchanges in the legs, is contained in the chest, moves in the two shoulders, and is governed in the waist; above it connects with the two arms, below it follows the two legs, and energy changes from within. Gathering is closing; issuing is opening. When still, all is still; stillness is closing, and within closing is lodged opening. When moving, all moves; movement is opening, and within opening is lodged closing. Touch it, and it revolves freely, with nothing that does not gain force — only then can one draw the other in to fall into emptiness and four ounces deflect a thousand catties. Practice of the form on ordinary days is the work of knowing oneself. At each movement one must first ask oneself whether the whole body accords with these several items. If it accords only slightly not, change it at once. This is why in practising the form one wants slowness, not speed. Push-hands is the work of knowing others; stillness and movement are indeed knowing others, yet it is still a question of asking oneself. If one has arranged oneself well, then when the other touches me, I do not move him the least bit, but enter along his tendency, join and fix his energy, and he falls out of himself. If one has a place where one does not gain force, that is double-weighting not yet transformed, and it must be sought in the opening and closing of yin and yang. This is what is called knowing oneself and knowing the other, and in a hundred battles a hundred victories.
